passages.topic: Urban environment — green roofs
passages.title: Gardens in the Sky

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the flat roofs of city buildings were regarded as wasted space. They were covered in tar or gravel, and the only people who ever went up there were maintenance workers checking for leaks. Today, in cities across Europe, Asia and North America, a growing number of these roofs are being turned into gardens. Specialists usually divide green roofs into two broad types. Extensive roofs have a thin layer of soil, often less than fifteen centimetres deep, planted with low, tough species such as mosses and small succulents that need almost no attention. Intensive roofs are closer to ordinary parks: they have much deeper soil, can support shrubs and even small trees, and are designed for people to walk and sit on.

The idea of planting on top of buildings is very old, but the modern green roof is a recent invention. Its development owes a great deal to research carried out in Germany in the 1960s and 1970s. Engineers there tested new waterproof membranes that could stop plant roots from damaging the building below, and they developed lightweight growing materials that held water without becoming too heavy. These technical advances turned what had been a risky experiment into a practical building method, and by the 1990s several German cities were offering grants to property owners who installed planted roofs.

One of the main attractions of a green roof is its effect on temperature. On a hot summer afternoon, a conventional dark roof can reach 70°C, and much of that heat passes into the rooms directly beneath it. A planted roof, by contrast, tends to stay close to the temperature of the surrounding air, because the plants shade the surface and lose moisture through their leaves. As a result, the top floor of the building needs less air conditioning. When many roofs in the same district are planted, the effect can also reduce the "urban heat island" – the tendency of cities to remain warmer than the surrounding countryside, particularly at night.

Green roofs also help cities manage rainwater. On an ordinary roof, rain runs straight into gutters and drains, and during a storm the drainage system can become overloaded, leading to flooding in the streets. Soil and plants absorb a large share of this water and release it slowly, some of it back into the air. Measurements from one city suggested that planted roofs could hold between half and nine-tenths of the rain from a light shower. In heavy, prolonged storms, however, the soil quickly becomes saturated, so the benefit is considerably smaller.

There are living benefits as well. Bees, butterflies and other insects visit flowering roofs, and some birds have begun to nest on them. People appear to benefit too. In office buildings with accessible roof gardens, managers report that staff use them for breaks and informal meetings, and surveys suggest that employees who can see planted areas from their desks describe themselves as feeling less tired during the working day.

Despite these advantages, green roofs are not suitable for every building. Wet soil is heavy, and before any roof is planted an engineer must check that the structure can carry the extra load. Older buildings may need to be reinforced, which can make a project expensive. Installation also costs more than laying a conventional roof. Supporters point out, though, that the extra layers protect the waterproof membrane from sunlight and sudden changes in temperature, which are the main causes of its decay. A membrane that might last around twenty years on an exposed roof may last twice as long under a covering of plants. Intensive roofs, however, bring an additional expense: like any garden, they must be watered, weeded and cared for.

A number of cities now require green roofs on large new buildings, and others offer lower taxes or faster planning approval to developers who include them. Yet success is not automatic. The most common reason for failure is poor planting: species chosen for their appearance rather than their suitability for local conditions. A roof in a dry climate planted with grass that needs regular rain will soon turn brown, whatever its design. Green roofs work best, in other words, when they are treated not as decoration but as small ecosystems suited to their surroundings.

lesson.title: Locating answers quickly
lesson.text: In an easy Multiple Choice set, most questions point you to one paragraph. Use names, numbers and distinctive terms in the question (for example Germany, 70°C, membrane) as signposts, then read the whole sentence around them. The answer usually paraphrases one sentence. Avoid choosing an option simply because it shares a word with the passage.
lesson.example: Passage: "Few visitors came in winter because the road was often closed." Question: Why were there few winter visitors? Correct idea: access was difficult. A tempting wrong option would be the weather was too cold, because it sounds logical but is not stated.

questions.text: For much of the twentieth century, city roofs were generally seen as

an area of little value.
a danger to maintenance workers.
a suitable location for gardens.

questions.explanation: "Wasted space" is paraphrased as "an area of little value". D describes the present day, not the twentieth century. Maintenance workers are mentioned, but the passage never says roofs were dangerous (C).

questions.text: According to paragraph A, intensive green roofs differ from extensive ones because they

options.text: need no maintenance at all.
are mainly used to grow food.
have deeper soil and can support bigger plants.
are found only on new buildings.

questions.evidence: Intensive roofs ... have much deeper soil, can support shrubs and even small trees
questions.explanation: "Shrubs and small trees" = "bigger plants". A describes extensive roofs. Growing food (B) and new buildings (D) are not what distinguishes the two types.

questions.text: What was the main contribution of German research in the 1960s and 1970s?

options.text: It introduced the idea of planting on buildings.
It developed materials that made green roofs practical.
It persuaded governments to pay for green roofs.
It proved that green roofs were popular with the public.

questions.evidence: tested new waterproof membranes ... developed lightweight growing materials ... turned what had been a risky experiment into a practical building method
questions.explanation: The research made green roofs practical. A is contradicted: "The idea ... is very old". C is a word-match trap, because the grants came later from cities, not from the research.

questions.text: What does the writer say about the temperature of a planted roof on a hot day?

options.text: It is usually cooler than the air around it.
It reaches around 70°C in the afternoon.
It remains similar to the air temperature.
It rises more slowly at night.

questions.evidence: A planted roof ... tends to stay close to the temperature of the surrounding air
questions.explanation: "Stay close to" = "remains similar to". The figure of 70°C refers to a conventional roof (B). A goes further than the passage.

questions.text: What point does the writer make about green roofs and rainwater?

options.text: They can prevent all flooding in city streets.
Their effectiveness depends on how heavy the rain is.
They collect rain that can later be used in buildings.
They remove the need for gutters and drains.

questions.evidence: planted roofs "could hold between half and nine-tenths of the rain from a light shower. In heavy, prolonged storms ... the benefit is considerably smaller"
questions.explanation: The benefit changes with the intensity of the rain. A and D use extreme wording the passage does not support. Storing rain for use in buildings (C) is not mentioned.

questions.text: Why may a green roof last longer than a conventional roof?

options.text: Its plants protect the waterproof layer from damaging conditions.
It is built using stronger structural materials.
It is checked more regularly by engineers.
Less rain reaches its surface.

questions.evidence: the extra layers protect the waterproof membrane from sunlight and sudden changes in temperature, which are the main causes of its decay
questions.explanation: "Sunlight and temperature changes" = "damaging conditions". Reinforcement (B) is mentioned only as a cost for older buildings.

questions.text: What is the writer's main purpose in paragraph G?

options.text: to argue that every new building should have a green roof
to compare the policies of different cities
to stress the importance of choosing suitable plants
to explain why green roofs are expensive

questions.evidence: The most common reason for failure is poor planting ... Green roofs work best ... when they are treated ... as small ecosystems suited to their surroundings
questions.explanation: The paragraph's central message concerns suitable planting. City policies are mentioned only briefly (B), and the writer never argues that every building needs a green roof (A).

passages.topic: History of transport — railways and standard time
passages.title: When Every Town Kept Its Own Time

paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, time was a local matter. Each town set its clocks by the sun, declaring noon to be the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky. Because the sun appears to move from east to west, towns only a short distance apart kept slightly different times: a town some 100 kilometres west of its neighbour might be several minutes behind it. For centuries this caused almost no difficulty. When the fastest way to travel was on horseback or by stagecoach, a journey between towns took many hours, and a difference of a few minutes went unnoticed.

The arrival of the railways changed this situation completely. Trains could cover in an hour a distance that had once taken a day, and they had to run to precise timetables. Early railway companies printed timetables listing the local time at every station, which left many passengers confused about when their train would actually depart. Some stations displayed two clocks, one showing local time and the other the time used by the railway. Missed connections were common. More seriously, on lines where trains travelling in opposite directions shared a single track, drivers working to different times could find themselves on the same section of line at the same moment, with a real risk of collision.

In Britain, railway companies responded by adopting a single time across their networks, based on the time kept at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, near London. The first company did so in 1840, and others soon followed. The change spread rapidly beyond the railways: by the mid-1850s the great majority of public clocks in Britain showed Greenwich time. Remarkably, the law did not catch up until 1880, when Greenwich time was finally made the official time for the whole of Great Britain. For a quarter of a century, therefore, the country had in practice a national time that did not legally exist.

In North America the problem was far greater, because of the enormous distances involved. By the early 1880s, railways in the United States were using dozens of different local times. In November 1883, the railway companies agreed to divide the continent into a small number of time zones, each one hour apart. The change was organised by the railways rather than by the government, and it was not universally welcomed. Some newspapers complained that the railways had no right to alter the time, and a number of cities refused to change their clocks for several years. National legislation making the zones official did not arrive until 1918.

Meanwhile, the question had become international. In 1884, representatives of more than twenty countries met in Washington to choose a single line of longitude – a "prime meridian" – from which distances and times around the world could be measured. They selected the meridian passing through Greenwich. However, the conference did not create a worldwide system of time zones. Each country decided for itself when, and whether, to adopt one, and the process took decades. Some countries chose to set their clocks half an hour, rather than a whole hour, away from their neighbours, and a few continue to do so today.

The introduction of standard time did more than make railway travel safer and simpler. It changed the way people related to time itself. Instead of following the sun, daily life increasingly followed the clock: factories, offices and schools began their work at fixed hours that were the same across whole regions. Today, when mobile phones adjust their clocks automatically as travellers cross from one zone to another, it is easy to forget that the idea of a shared time is a relatively recent invention, created not by scientists or governments but, in large part, by the practical needs of the railway.

lesson.title: Watch for "more seriously", "however" and "rather than"
lesson.text: Signal words show which idea the writer considers most important or which idea is being corrected. If a passage says "X caused confusion; more seriously, it caused Y", a question about the most serious problem wants Y, not X. Likewise, "A rather than B" means A is true and B is not. Distractors are often built from the idea that the signal word pushes aside.
lesson.example: Passage: "The festival was moved to spring, partly because of cost but mainly because of the risk of storms." Question: What was the main reason for the change? Answer: the weather risk. Cost is the distractor, because it was only a partial reason.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: Before the railway era, towns decided the time by

options.text: receiving signals from a national observatory.
observing the position of the sun.
following the timetables of stagecoach companies.
agreeing on a time with neighbouring towns.

questions.evidence: Each town set its clocks by the sun, declaring noon to be the moment when the sun stood highest
questions.explanation: "Set its clocks by the sun" = "observing the position of the sun". The observatory (A) only becomes relevant later, in Paragraph C.

questions.text: Why were differences in local time unimportant for many centuries?

options.text: Most towns were located very close to one another.
Few people owned clocks or watches.
Journeys were too slow for small differences to matter.
Towns deliberately kept the same time as their neighbours.

questions.evidence: a journey between towns took many hours, and a difference of a few minutes went unnoticed
questions.explanation: Slow travel meant small differences did not matter. D is the opposite of the passage, which says towns kept different times. B is never mentioned.

questions.text: According to paragraph B, what was the most serious consequence of using different local times on the railways?

options.text: Passengers missed their connections.
Stations needed to display two clocks.
Timetables were difficult to understand.
Trains might crash into each other.

questions.evidence: More seriously ... drivers working to different times could find themselves on the same section of line ... with a real risk of collision
questions.explanation: The signal "More seriously" marks the most serious consequence. A, B and C are real problems but are presented as less serious.

questions.text: What does the writer find surprising about the situation in Britain?

options.text: Greenwich time was used widely before it became the legal time.
Only one railway company adopted Greenwich time.
The law required railways to use Greenwich time from 1840.
Public clocks continued to show local time until 1880.

questions.evidence: by the mid-1850s the great majority of public clocks ... showed Greenwich time. Remarkably, the law did not catch up until 1880
questions.explanation: "Remarkably" shows what the writer finds surprising: the practice came before the law. B and D contradict the passage. C wrongly attaches the law to the year 1840.

questions.text: What does the writer say about the time zones introduced in North America in 1883?

options.text: They were created by the national government.
They were accepted immediately by every city.
They were set up by the railways and faced some opposition.
They were based on a system already used in Europe.

questions.evidence: organised by the railways rather than by the government, and it was not universally welcomed ... a number of cities refused
questions.explanation: Both parts of C are supported. A is contradicted by "rather than by the government", and B by "cities refused".

questions.text: What was the result of the 1884 conference in Washington?

options.text: A worldwide system of time zones was introduced.
A reference line for measuring time and distance was chosen.
All countries agreed to set their clocks one hour apart.
Greenwich time became the legal time in the United States.

questions.evidence: choose a single line of longitude ... from which distances and times ... could be measured. They selected the meridian passing through Greenwich
questions.explanation: A "prime meridian" is paraphrased as "a reference line". A is contradicted by "did not create a worldwide system of time zones". C is contradicted by the half-hour offsets.

questions.text: What is the main point of paragraph F?

options.text: Mobile phones have made time zones unnecessary.
Standard time changed the organisation of everyday life.
Scientists played the leading role in creating standard time.
Railway travel is now safer than any other form of transport.

questions.evidence: It changed the way people related to time ... factories, offices and schools began their work at fixed hours
questions.explanation: This is the paragraph's central idea. C is contradicted: "not by scientists or governments". Phones (A) appear only as a modern example, and the paragraph never says zones are unnecessary.

passages.topic: Psychology — contagious yawning
passages.title: Why Are Yawns Catching?

paragraphs.text: Almost everyone has noticed that yawning seems to spread. When one person in a meeting yawns, others often follow within a few minutes, and many people find that simply reading about yawning makes them want to yawn. Yawning itself is extremely common in nature: it has been observed in most animals with a backbone, from fish to birds and mammals, and even human babies yawn before they are born. The spread of yawning from one individual to another, however, is far less widespread, and explaining why it happens has become an intriguing puzzle for psychologists.

So-called "contagious yawning" – yawning in response to seeing or hearing another individual yawn – has been reliably recorded in humans and in chimpanzees. Some studies have reported it in dogs, which appear to yawn more often after watching their owners yawn, although the evidence for dogs is less consistent. In most other species that have been studied, individuals yawn regularly but do not seem to be influenced by the yawns of others.

In humans, contagious yawning appears to develop gradually during childhood. In a number of experiments, young children watched videos of people yawning while researchers recorded their reactions. Children under the age of about four rarely yawned in response, whereas older children did so much more often. This pattern interested researchers because the same period of childhood is when children become better at understanding what other people are thinking and feeling.

This observation led to one of the most popular explanations: that contagious yawning is connected with empathy, the ability to share and understand the feelings of others. Supporters of this view point to studies in which people were more likely to "catch" a yawn from a family member or close friend than from an acquaintance, and least likely to catch one from a stranger. If contagious yawning were a simple automatic reflex, they argue, the relationship between the two people should make no difference.

A different explanation focuses not on social bonds but on the brain's temperature. According to this theory, yawning draws in a large amount of air and increases blood flow in the head, which may help to cool the brain when it becomes slightly too warm. The theory makes a clear prediction: people should yawn less when the air around them is very hot, because hot air would have little cooling effect. Some field studies have found exactly this pattern, with people yawning more often in mild conditions than in hot summer weather. Supporters suggest that when one member of a group yawns, others may follow because they share the same conditions, and a group that stays alert may be better able to notice danger.

In recent years the empathy explanation has faced challenges. Several large studies have found only a weak connection between how often people catch yawns and how they score on tests of empathy. These studies found that age was a more reliable predictor: in general, older adults were less likely to yawn contagiously than younger adults. Other factors, such as how tired a person is and how closely they are paying attention to the person yawning, also seem to play a role.

Where does this leave the puzzle? It is possible that no single theory will explain every case, and that contagious yawning is influenced by a mixture of biological and social factors. What is clear is that a behaviour most people take for granted raises surprisingly deep questions about how human beings respond to one another – and about how much of that response takes place without our noticing.

lesson.title: Questions about theories and evidence
lesson.text:
Science passages often present a theory, the evidence for it, and then evidence against it. Keep three things separate: what a theory claims, what a study found, and what the writer concludes.

A distractor may state a theory's claim as if it had been proved, or state the writer's conclusion more strongly than the writer does. Watch hedging words such as may, suggests, appears and some.
lesson.example: Passage: "The results suggest that sleep may help memory, but the sample was small." Question: What does the writer say about the results? A good answer: they are promising but limited. A trap: they prove that sleep improves memory, because it turns "suggest" into "prove".

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of paragraph A?

options.text: to explain why humans yawn more than other animals
to introduce the question of why yawning spreads between individuals
to show that yawning begins before birth
to describe the physical process of yawning

questions.evidence: explaining why it happens has become an intriguing puzzle for psychologists
questions.explanation: The paragraph builds towards this question, which the rest of the passage then explores. C is only a supporting detail. A and D are not discussed.

questions.text: According to paragraph B, contagious yawning

options.text: is found in every species that yawns.
has been clearly shown in humans and chimpanzees.
is more common in dogs than in humans.
does not occur in any animal apart from humans.

questions.evidence: has been reliably recorded in humans and in chimpanzees
questions.explanation: "Reliably recorded" = "clearly shown". A and D are contradicted by the passage. The evidence for dogs is described as "less consistent", which does not support C.

questions.text: What did experiments with young children show?

options.text: Children under about four seldom yawned after watching others yawn.
Children yawned more often than adults.
Children only yawned when watching family members.
Children stopped yawning contagiously as they grew older.

questions.evidence: Children under the age of about four rarely yawned in response
questions.explanation: "Rarely" = "seldom". D reverses the pattern described. Family members (C) are mentioned in Paragraph D, not in these experiments.

questions.text: Why do supporters of the empathy theory refer to yawns caught from family members?

options.text: to show that yawning is an automatic reflex
to show that the relationship between people affects contagious yawning
to prove that strangers never cause others to yawn
to explain why children yawn less than adults

questions.evidence: people were more likely to 'catch' a yawn from a family member ... If contagious yawning were a simple automatic reflex ... the relationship between the two people should make no difference
questions.explanation: The example is used to show that the relationship matters. A is the view it argues against. C is too extreme, because strangers are "least likely", not "never".

questions.text: According to the temperature theory, people should

options.text: yawn more often in hot weather.
yawn less often when the air is very hot.
yawn only when they are in a group.
become warmer after yawning.

questions.evidence: people should yawn less when the air around them is very hot
questions.explanation: This is stated directly as the theory's prediction. A is the opposite. D contradicts the claimed cooling effect.

questions.text: What have recent large studies suggested?

options.text: Empathy is the main cause of contagious yawning.
Younger adults yawn contagiously less than older adults.
The link between empathy and contagious yawning may be weaker than believed.
Tiredness has no effect on contagious yawning.

questions.evidence: found only a weak connection between how often people catch yawns and how they score on tests of empathy
questions.explanation: "Only a weak connection" supports "weaker than believed". B reverses the age finding. D is contradicted by the mention of tiredness.

questions.text: Which statement best reflects the writer's conclusion?

options.text: The temperature theory has now been proved correct.
Contagious yawning is too simple to deserve further study.
Contagious yawning probably has more than one cause.
The empathy theory should be completely rejected.

questions.evidence: contagious yawning is influenced by a mixture of biological and social factors
questions.explanation: "A mixture of factors" = "more than one cause". The writer hedges ("It is possible"), so the strong claims in A and D are unsupported. B contradicts "surprisingly deep questions".

passages.topic: Agriculture — vertical farming
passages.title: Farming Upwards

paragraphs.text: Traditional farming spreads outwards across fields. Vertical farming grows upwards. In a vertical farm, crops are grown indoors on shelves stacked several layers high, often inside a converted warehouse or factory. Instead of sunlight they receive light from rows of LED lamps, and instead of soil their roots sit in trays of water enriched with nutrients, a method known as hydroponics. Temperature, humidity and even the colour of the light can be controlled by computer. Supporters describe these buildings as the future of food production; critics see them as an expensive solution to a problem that ordinary farms already solve quite well.

The idea is not entirely new. Glasshouses have allowed growers to control conditions for centuries, and hydroponic systems were being tested in the early twentieth century. What changed in the 2000s was the price and efficiency of LED lighting. Older lamps produced a great deal of heat, which meant they could not be placed close to the plants, and they used large amounts of electricity. LEDs are cooler and more efficient, allowing shelves to be stacked closely together. This single development made commercial vertical farming possible.

Its supporters point to several advantages. Because water in a hydroponic system is collected and reused rather than soaking into the ground, vertical farms typically use a small fraction of the water needed to grow the same crop outdoors; some operators claim savings of more than ninety per cent. The crops are protected from storms, droughts and frost, so harvests are predictable throughout the year. Pests find it hard to enter a sealed building, and many farms use no chemical pesticides at all. Finally, because they can be built inside or close to cities, vertical farms can deliver produce to shops within hours of harvest, reducing both transport costs and the time the food spends losing freshness.

However, the range of crops that can be grown profitably is narrow. Almost all vertical farms produce leafy vegetables, such as lettuce and spinach, together with herbs such as basil. These plants grow quickly, stay small and can be sold at relatively high prices. Staple crops such as wheat, rice and potatoes are a different matter. They take months to mature, need a great deal of space, and sell for low prices per kilogram. Calculations suggest that the electricity needed to light a field's worth of wheat indoors would make the resulting bread far too expensive for ordinary consumers.

Energy, in fact, is the industry's central challenge. Sunlight is free; electric light is not. Even with efficient LEDs, lighting and climate control account for a large share of a vertical farm's running costs, and when electricity prices rose sharply in several countries in the early 2020s, a number of well-known vertical farming companies closed or reduced their operations. Some newer farms are responding by building next to solar or wind power installations, or by using software to run their lights mainly at night, when electricity is cheaper.

There are also questions about whether the environmental benefits are as large as claimed. Saving water is valuable, but if the electricity for the lamps comes from burning fossil fuels, a lettuce grown indoors may be responsible for more greenhouse gas emissions than one grown in a field and transported a long distance. The overall environmental effect, therefore, depends heavily on where the farm's energy comes from.

For these reasons, most researchers now see vertical farming not as a replacement for conventional agriculture but as an addition to it. It is likely to be most useful where land or water is scarce, where the climate is too harsh for outdoor growing for much of the year, or where consumers are willing to pay for extremely fresh produce. Fields will continue to feed the world; vertical farms may simply help to fill some of the gaps.

lesson.title: Numbers and comparisons
lesson.text: When a question contains a number, a percentage or a comparison word (more, less, cheaper, faster), check exactly what is being compared with what. Distractors often use the correct figure but attach it to the wrong thing, or they reverse a comparison. Read the whole sentence containing the number, not just the number.
lesson.example: Passage: "The new engine uses 30% less fuel than the older model, although it costs more to build." Question: What advantage does the new engine have? Answer: lower fuel use. A likely trap: it is 30% cheaper, which uses the right number for the wrong thing.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the last sentence of paragraph A?

options.text: to show that vertical farms have already replaced traditional farms
to present contrasting opinions about vertical farming
to explain how vertical farms are controlled by computer
to suggest that critics do not understand the technology

questions.evidence: Supporters describe these buildings as the future ... critics see them as an expensive solution
questions.explanation: The sentence sets two opposing views side by side. Computer control (C) is mentioned in an earlier sentence. The writer does not judge the critics (D).

questions.text: According to paragraph B, commercial vertical farming became possible because

options.text: hydroponic systems were invented.
glasshouses became cheaper to build.
improved lamps allowed plants to be grown in close layers.
electricity became free for farmers.

questions.evidence: LEDs are cooler and more efficient, allowing shelves to be stacked closely together. This single development made commercial vertical farming possible
questions.explanation: "Stacked closely together" = "close layers". Hydroponics (A) and glasshouses (B) existed earlier and are not credited as the key change.

questions.text: How do vertical farms save water?

options.text: They grow plants that need very little water.
They reuse the water in their growing systems.
They collect rainwater from the roof.
They grow crops mainly during cooler seasons.

questions.evidence: water in a hydroponic system is collected and reused rather than soaking into the ground
questions.explanation: "Collected and reused" = "reuse". Rainwater (C) and seasonal growing (D) are not mentioned. The figure of ninety per cent describes the size of the saving, not how it is achieved.

questions.text: Which advantage of locating vertical farms near cities is mentioned?

options.text: Workers are easier to find.
Land is cheaper.
Food reaches shops quickly.
Electricity is less expensive.

questions.evidence: vertical farms can deliver produce to shops within hours of harvest
questions.explanation: "Within hours" = "quickly". Workers (A) and land prices (B) are not mentioned. Cheaper electricity (D) is linked to night-time use in Paragraph E, not to city locations.

questions.text: Why are staple crops such as wheat not grown in vertical farms?

options.text: They cannot be grown using hydroponics.
The cost of lighting them would be too high.
Consumers prefer wheat grown outdoors.
They are easily damaged by pests indoors.

questions.evidence: the electricity needed to light a field's worth of wheat indoors would make the resulting bread far too expensive
questions.explanation: The obstacle is the cost of lighting. A is not stated, since the passage never says hydroponics cannot grow wheat. C and D are not mentioned.

questions.text: What does the writer say about the environmental impact of vertical farming?

options.text: It is always lower than that of traditional farming.
It is mainly caused by transporting produce.
It depends largely on the source of electricity.
It has been proved to be greater than that of field farming.

questions.evidence: The overall environmental effect ... depends heavily on where the farm's energy comes from
questions.explanation: "Depends heavily" = "depends largely". A and D are too absolute: the passage says a lettuce may produce more emissions, which is not proof.

questions.text: Which statement best summarises the writer's conclusion?

options.text: Vertical farming will eventually replace traditional agriculture.
Vertical farming is likely to play a limited supporting role.
Vertical farming is only useful in very cold countries.
Vertical farming has failed because of high energy prices.

questions.evidence: not as a replacement for conventional agriculture but as an addition to it ... vertical farms may simply help to fill some of the gaps
questions.explanation: "An addition" and "fill some of the gaps" = "a limited supporting role". A is directly contradicted. C narrows one example (harsh climates) too far, and D overstates the business closures described in Paragraph E.

passages.questionTypeDetail: Multiple Choice (single answer A–D, plus one "Choose TWO letters" question)
passages.topic: Linguistics — children growing up with two languages
passages.title: Growing Up with Two Languages

paragraphs.text: More than half of the world's population is thought to use two or more languages in daily life, and many children grow up hearing more than one language from birth. Yet for much of the twentieth century, parents in many countries were advised to avoid raising children bilingually. Teachers and doctors warned that learning two languages at once would confuse young children, slow their development and harm their performance at school. Some families who spoke a minority language at home were even encouraged to abandon it.

These warnings were based largely on early studies that compared bilingual and monolingual children on vocabulary and intelligence tests. The bilingual children often scored lower. Later researchers pointed out serious problems with these studies. The tests were usually given only in the majority language, and the bilingual children in them often came from poorer families than the monolingual children they were compared with. When studies from the 1960s onwards took account of these factors, the supposed disadvantage largely disappeared.

One behaviour that particularly worried parents was "code-mixing": using words from both languages in the same sentence. A child might say "I want more leche", mixing English with the Spanish word for milk. For many years this was taken as a sign that the child could not tell the two languages apart. Researchers now interpret it quite differently. Young bilingual children mix words mainly when they do not yet know a word in the language they are speaking, and they tend to adjust their choice of language to the person they are talking to. Adult bilinguals mix languages too, often deliberately, and linguists regard this as a normal and skilful use of two languages rather than a sign of confusion.

It is true that, if each language is measured separately, bilingual children often know fewer words in each one than monolingual children of the same age. However, when the words they know in both languages are counted together, their total vocabulary is usually similar to, and sometimes larger than, that of monolingual children. The gap in each individual language also tends to narrow as children grow older and continue to use both languages.

Parents often ask which method of raising a bilingual child works best. A popular approach is "one parent, one language", in which each parent always speaks a different language to the child. Many families find this helpful, but research suggests that the particular method matters less than the amount and variety of exposure a child receives. A child who hears a language only occasionally, or only in one setting, is unlikely to become confident in it. Children are also sensitive to attitudes: if they sense that one of their languages is not valued, they may start refusing to speak it.

In recent decades, some researchers have gone further and claimed that bilingualism brings cognitive advantages. Because bilinguals constantly select one language while keeping the other inactive, it has been suggested that they become better at controlling their attention and switching between tasks. Several studies reported such benefits, but others, including some very large ones, have failed to find them. At present, the question remains a matter of lively debate.

What researchers do agree on is that growing up with two languages does not harm children's development. The old advice to abandon a home language is now regarded as mistaken, and many specialists believe that it may have cost families an important part of their cultural connections. For most children, learning two languages is simply a normal part of growing up in a multilingual world.

lesson.title: "Choose TWO letters" questions
lesson.text: In a Choose TWO question, treat each of the five options as a separate True/False check against the passage. Usually two options are clearly supported, and the other three are unsupported, contradicted, or attributed to the wrong time or group. Do not choose an option just because it sounds reasonable. Each correct option must be stated in the passage. The two letters can be written in either order.
lesson.example: Passage: "Volunteers repaired the fence and planted trees; they did not have time to paint the shed." Which TWO things did the volunteers do? A repaired the fence ✓ B painted the shed ✗ C planted trees ✓ D built a shed ✗ E cut the grass ✗ (not mentioned).

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: In the twentieth century, some families were advised to

options.text: teach their children a second language at school.
stop using a minority language at home.
speak two languages to children from birth.
have their children's intelligence tested.

questions.evidence: Some families who spoke a minority language at home were even encouraged to abandon it
questions.explanation: "Abandon" = "stop using". C is the opposite of the advice given at the time. Intelligence tests (D) appear in Paragraph B, but as a research method, not as advice to families.

questions.text: According to paragraph B, early studies of bilingual children were unreliable partly because

options.text: they included too few children.
the tests were in only one language.
the bilingual children were younger.
researchers did not publish their results.

questions.evidence: The tests were usually given only in the majority language
questions.explanation: "Only in the majority language" = "in only one language". The other problem mentioned is family income, not sample size (A) or the children's age (C).

questions.text: How do researchers now view code-mixing in young children?

options.text: as evidence that children confuse their languages
as a habit children should be discouraged from developing
as a normal strategy, often used when a word is not known
as something that happens only in adults

questions.evidence: Young bilingual children mix words mainly when they do not yet know a word ... linguists regard this as a normal and skilful use
questions.explanation: Option C combines both points. A is the old interpretation. D is contradicted, because the passage says adults mix languages "too".

questions.text: What does the writer say about bilingual children's vocabulary?

options.text: It is smaller overall than that of monolingual children.
It is larger in each language than that of monolingual children.
Its combined size is usually comparable to that of monolingual children.
It stops growing once children start school.

questions.evidence: when the words they know in both languages are counted together, their total vocabulary is usually similar to ... that of monolingual children
questions.explanation: "Counted together ... similar" = "combined size ... comparable". A contradicts this. B confuses combined vocabulary with vocabulary in each language, where bilingual children often know fewer words.

questions.text: According to paragraph E, what matters most in raising a bilingual child?

options.text: following the "one parent, one language" method
beginning before the child is one year old
how much varied contact the child has with each language
using both languages in every conversation

questions.evidence: the particular method matters less than the amount and variety of exposure a child receives
questions.explanation: "Amount and variety of exposure" = "how much varied contact". A is a word-match trap: the method is mentioned but is said to matter less. B and D are not mentioned.

groups.title: Choose TWO letters
groups.instruction: Choose TWO letters, A–E.

questions.text: Which TWO of the following statements about bilingualism are supported by the passage?

options.text: All studies have confirmed that bilinguals have better attention control.
Children may reject a language they feel is not valued.
Bilingual children always start speaking later than other children.
The advice to give up home languages is now seen as wrong.
Adult bilinguals never mix their languages.

questions.evidence:
if they sense that one of their languages is not valued, they may start refusing to speak it
The old advice to abandon a home language is now regarded as mistaken

evidenceItems.evidence: if they sense that one of their languages is not valued, they may start refusing to speak it
The old advice to abandon a home language is now regarded as mistaken

questions.explanation: A is contradicted by "others ... have failed to find them" in Paragraph F. C is never stated. E is contradicted by "Adult bilinguals mix languages too" in Paragraph C.

passages.topic: Museums — the collections visitors never see
passages.title: What Museums Keep Hidden

paragraphs.text: Visitors walking through the galleries of a large museum may feel they are seeing its treasures, but in most cases they are seeing only a small fraction of them. Surveys of major museums have found that many display less than ten per cent of the objects they own, and for some natural history museums, which may hold millions of insect, plant and rock specimens, the proportion is far smaller. The rest are kept in storerooms, often in a separate building some distance from the public galleries.

The most obvious reason is space. Collections grow steadily through donations, purchases and archaeological excavations, but gallery space grows slowly, if at all. A museum that attempted to display everything would produce galleries so crowded that visitors would struggle to notice anything. Curators, the specialists who look after collections, therefore select objects that tell a clear story and leave the rest in storage.

Space is not the only consideration. Many objects are damaged by light. Textiles, watercolours, photographs and documents on paper fade when exposed for long periods, and the damage cannot be reversed. Museums often limit such items to a few months on display before returning them to dark storage for several years to "rest". Other objects are simply too fragile to be moved or handled regularly, or require conditions of temperature and humidity that would be uncomfortable for visitors.

Storage, however, does not mean neglect. A modern museum store is a carefully controlled environment. Temperature and humidity are kept stable, because rapid changes cause materials such as wood and ivory to expand and shrink, eventually cracking. Objects are wrapped in special acid-free materials, stored in numbered boxes and drawers, and recorded in a catalogue so that they can be found quickly. Pests such as moths and beetles, which can destroy wool, feathers and wood, are monitored with traps and inspections.

The stored objects are also used, even if the public does not see them. Researchers from universities around the world visit museum stores to examine specimens; a single collection of preserved birds, for example, may allow scientists to measure how the size of a species has changed over a century. Objects are lent to other museums for temporary exhibitions, and many are used in teaching sessions, where students are allowed to handle items that would be kept behind glass in a gallery.

In recent years, museums have looked for ways to make hidden collections more visible. Some have built "open stores" – storage areas with glass walls through which visitors can see shelves of objects – or offer guided tours of their storerooms. Many more have started to photograph their collections and publish the images online, together with catalogue information. This digitisation is slow and costly: a large museum may need decades to record its entire collection, and it must pay for photography, staff time and computer systems. Nevertheless, it allows people who could never visit in person to explore collections from anywhere in the world.

It is tempting to regard museum storerooms as places where objects are forgotten. In reality, they are closer to libraries: organised, protected and constantly consulted. The galleries may show a museum's public face, but much of its most important work takes place out of sight.

lesson.title: Reason and cause questions
lesson.text: Questions beginning Why ...? or containing because, the reason, led to or as a result test cause and effect. In the passage, look for linking language such as because, since, as, so, therefore, this means that, due to. Make sure the option gives the cause of the specific effect in the question. A passage often lists several causes for different effects, and distractors borrow a real cause from the wrong effect.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The library closed early because of staff shortages; it also stopped lending DVDs, since few people borrowed them." Why did the library stop lending DVDs?
Answer: low demand. Trap: staff shortages, which is the cause of a different change.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: What does the writer say about natural history museums?

options.text: They display more of their collections than other museums.
They usually display a very small share of their specimens.
They keep their stores inside the main museum building.
They own fewer objects than art museums.

questions.evidence: for some natural history museums, which may hold millions of ... specimens, the proportion is far smaller
questions.explanation: The "far smaller" proportion refers to the share of the collection on display. A is the opposite. The passage says stores are often in a separate building, so C is wrong.

questions.text: According to paragraph B, curators choose only some objects for display because

options.text: most objects are too valuable to show.
visitors prefer small exhibitions.
too many objects would make galleries confusing.
donors ask for their gifts to be kept private.

questions.evidence: A museum that attempted to display everything would produce galleries so crowded that visitors would struggle to notice anything
questions.explanation: "So crowded ... struggle to notice anything" = "confusing". A, B and D are not given as reasons.

questions.text: Why are some textiles and paper documents displayed for only short periods?

options.text: They are frequently borrowed by other museums.
Exposure to light damages them permanently.
They are too heavy to remain on display.
Visitors lose interest in them quickly.

questions.evidence: Textiles, watercolours, photographs and documents on paper fade ... and the damage cannot be reversed
questions.explanation: "Cannot be reversed" = "permanently". Lending (A) is mentioned in Paragraph E, but not as a reason for short display periods.

questions.text: Why is it important to keep temperature and humidity stable in stores?

options.text: to make the stores comfortable for researchers
to prevent pests from entering
to stop some materials from cracking
to reduce the cost of heating

questions.evidence: rapid changes cause materials such as wood and ivory to expand and shrink, eventually cracking
questions.explanation: Pests (B) are dealt with separately, using traps and inspections. Comfort (A) and cost (D) are not mentioned in relation to stable conditions.

questions.text: The example of the preserved birds is used to show that stored objects

options.text: are more valuable than objects on display.
can be used for scientific research.
are frequently damaged by handling.
are often lent to other museums.

questions.evidence: Researchers ... visit museum stores to examine specimens; a single collection of preserved birds ... may allow scientists to measure how the size of a species has changed
questions.explanation: The birds illustrate research use. Lending (D) is a separate point in the same paragraph, so it is a distractor from the wrong sentence.

questions.text: What does the writer say about digitising collections?

options.text: It is quick and inexpensive.
It has replaced guided tours of stores.
It is expensive but widens access to collections.
It has already been completed by most large museums.

questions.evidence: This digitisation is slow and costly ... Nevertheless, it allows people who could never visit in person to explore collections
questions.explanation: "Costly" = "expensive", and "people who could never visit ... explore collections" = "widens access". A and D are contradicted by "slow" and "decades".

questions.text: In the final paragraph, the writer compares museum stores to libraries in order to

options.text: suggest that museums should lend objects to the public.
emphasise that stores are well managed and regularly used.
argue that museums need more storage space.
show that museums and libraries are losing visitors.

questions.evidence: they are closer to libraries: organised, protected and constantly consulted
questions.explanation: "Organised, protected" = "well managed", and "constantly consulted" = "regularly used". The other options are not supported by the paragraph.

passages.topic: Archaeology and science — dating the past with tree rings
passages.title: Reading the Rings

paragraphs.text: In many parts of the world, a tree adds one layer of new wood to its trunk every year. In spring, when growth is rapid, the new wood is pale and open; later in the season it becomes denser and darker. Together, the two bands form a single annual ring, and counting the rings on a stump reveals the tree's age. The rings, however, contain more information than a simple count. Their width varies from year to year according to growing conditions. In a dry region a year of good rainfall produces a wide ring, while a drought year produces a narrow one. It is this variation, rather than the rings themselves, that has made tree rings one of the most precise dating tools available to archaeologists.

The method, known as dendrochronology, was developed in the early twentieth century by Andrew Ellicott Douglass, an American astronomer. Douglass was not originally interested in archaeology at all. He hoped that tree rings might preserve a record of past climate, which in turn might reveal whether changes in the Sun's activity affected rainfall on Earth. While examining timber in the south-western United States, he noticed that trees from the same area shared the same sequence of wide and narrow rings, regardless of how old each tree was. A particular run of narrow rings – the mark of a series of dry years – appeared in tree after tree, like a barcode.

This observation made "cross-dating" possible. A researcher begins with a living tree, whose outermost ring is known to belong to the current year, and records its pattern of ring widths back to the centre. Older timber, perhaps from a house built a century ago, will show part of the same pattern in its outer rings, together with an older sequence that extends further back in time. By overlapping the patterns of progressively older pieces of wood – from buildings, archaeological sites and trees preserved in bogs – researchers can build a continuous chronology stretching back hundreds or even thousands of years. In parts of Europe, such chronologies now extend back more than ten thousand years.

The first great test of the method came from the ancient settlements of the American South-West. Archaeologists had collected wooden beams from ruined villages, but although these beams could be matched with one another, they could not at first be connected to the chronology built from living trees. For several years there remained a gap between the two sequences. In 1929 a single charred beam, recovered from a ruin in Arizona, contained rings that overlapped with both. Almost overnight, dozens of settlements that had previously been dated only by estimate could be assigned the precise years in which their timbers had been cut.

That precision is the method's great strength. Other scientific techniques usually provide a range of possible dates, sometimes spanning centuries. A timber with its outermost ring intact, by contrast, can be dated to a single year, and sometimes even to the season in which the tree was felled. Tree-ring chronologies have therefore become essential for checking other methods. Radiocarbon dating, which measures the decay of a form of carbon in once-living material, gives results that must be corrected because the amount of that carbon in the atmosphere has varied over time. Tree rings of known age provide the reference against which those corrections are made.

The method nevertheless has important limitations. It works only with species that form clear annual rings, which excludes many tropical trees growing in climates without a distinct season. A sample needs enough rings, often at least fifty, for its pattern to be matched with confidence. The outer layers of a beam are frequently trimmed away by carpenters or lost to decay, in which case researchers can give only the earliest possible felling date, not the actual one. Finally, the date of a piece of wood is not necessarily the date of the structure in which it is found. Timber was expensive and was often reused, so a beam cut in one century may have been built into a house in the next.

Archaeologists therefore treat a tree-ring date as a precise statement about a tree, not automatically about a building or an event. Interpreted with that caution, the rings offer something rare in the study of the past: a calendar written by nature itself, with one entry for every year.

lesson.title: Inference questions ("suggests", "implies", "can be inferred")
lesson.text: An inference question asks for something the passage does not say in one sentence but makes clearly true when you combine the information. A correct inference is a small, safe step from the text. It is never a guess, a general-knowledge fact, or an exaggeration. To test an option, ask: "If the passage is true, must this also be true?" If the answer is only "possibly", reject it. Strong distractors in inference questions are often reasonable-sounding ideas that the passage never supports, or that go one step too far.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The shop's winter sales fell every year until it began delivering to customers' homes; since then, winter has become its busiest season." What can be inferred?
Correct: delivery helped the shop overcome a seasonal problem. Too far: home delivery is the best strategy for all shops.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: According to paragraph A, what makes tree rings especially useful for dating?

options.text: Every tree produces the same number of rings.
The width of rings differs according to conditions each year.
Pale and dark bands can be counted separately.
Trees in dry regions grow more slowly.

questions.evidence: Their width varies from year to year according to growing conditions ... It is this variation, rather than the rings themselves, that has made tree rings one of the most precise dating tools
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly locates the usefulness in the variation. C describes how a single ring forms but is not the reason for its usefulness. D is related to the rainfall point but is not stated.

questions.text: What can be inferred about Douglass from paragraph B?

options.text: He was trained as an archaeologist before studying astronomy.
His discovery arose from research with a different aim.
He proved that the Sun controls rainfall on Earth.
He was the first person to count tree rings.

questions.evidence: Douglass was not originally interested in archaeology at all. He hoped that tree rings might preserve a record of past climate
questions.explanation: His dating method grew out of climate research, which is a different aim. A reverses his background: he was an astronomer. C goes too far, because he only "hoped" to find evidence. D is not stated.

questions.text: In paragraph B, the writer compares a sequence of rings to a barcode in order to show that

options.text: it can be read quickly by machines.
it is identical in every tree in the world.
it forms a recognisable pattern that can be matched.
it records only periods of drought.

questions.evidence: A particular run of narrow rings ... appeared in tree after tree, like a barcode
questions.explanation: The comparison stresses a distinctive, repeatable pattern that can be matched, which leads directly into cross-dating in Paragraph C. B is too extreme, because trees are said to share patterns "from the same area", not worldwide.

questions.text: Why was the beam found in 1929 so important?

options.text: It was the oldest piece of wood ever discovered.
It proved that the settlements had been destroyed by fire.
It linked the archaeological sequence to the chronology of living trees.
It showed that earlier estimates for the settlements had been accurate.

questions.evidence: they could not at first be connected to the chronology built from living trees ... a single charred beam ... contained rings that overlapped with both
questions.explanation: "Overlapped with both" = "linked". B is a trap based on the word "charred". D is contradicted, because the settlements had been dated "only by estimate" and could now be given precise years.

questions.text: What does the writer suggest about radiocarbon dating?

options.text: It has been replaced by tree-ring dating.
It depends partly on tree-ring evidence for accuracy.
It gives more precise dates than tree rings.
It cannot be used on wood.

questions.evidence: results that must be corrected ... Tree rings of known age provide the reference against which those corrections are made
questions.explanation: Radiocarbon dating relies on tree rings for correction. A goes beyond the passage. C reverses the comparison, since tree rings are the more precise method.

questions.text: If a beam has lost its outer layers, researchers can

options.text: date the building but not the tree.
give the actual year of felling only if it has fifty rings.
state the earliest year in which the tree could have been cut.
calculate the season in which it was cut.

questions.evidence: researchers can give only the earliest possible felling date, not the actual one
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase. B combines two separate limitations incorrectly. D applies only to timber "with its outermost ring intact" (Paragraph E).

questions.text: What is the main point of paragraph G?

options.text: Tree-ring dates should be applied to buildings with care.
Tree-ring dating is too unreliable for archaeology.
Buildings are usually older than the timber inside them.
Nature provides a complete record of historical events.

questions.evidence: Archaeologists therefore treat a tree-ring date as a precise statement about a tree, not automatically about a building ... Interpreted with that caution
questions.explanation: The paragraph urges caution when linking a tree's date to a structure. B contradicts the praise that follows. C reverses the point about reused timber, which may make wood older than the building.

passages.topic: Business and psychology — the open-plan office
passages.title: Walls Down, Voices Up

paragraphs.text: Few changes to working life have been as widespread, or as widely resented, as the open-plan office. In many countries, a large majority of office employees now work in shared spaces without walls, and the private office has become a privilege reserved for a small number of senior staff. Yet the open-plan office was not originally conceived as a way of saving money, which is how many employees now regard it. It began as an idealistic attempt to change how organisations communicate.

In the late 1950s, a team of German consultants proposed a design they called Bürolandschaft, or "office landscape". Instead of rows of identical desks or corridors of closed rooms, desks would be arranged in irregular groups according to how often people needed to work together, separated by plants and low screens. The designers believed that hierarchy was built into the architecture of traditional offices, and that removing walls would encourage information to flow freely between departments and levels of seniority.

A few years later, an American designer named Robert Propst developed a flexible system of movable panels and work surfaces, intended to give each employee a varied, adaptable workspace. His system was highly successful commercially, but not in the way he had intended. Companies discovered that the panels could be arranged into small, identical boxes, packing more employees into less space than ever before. The result was the cubicle, which became a symbol of dull office life. Propst himself later expressed deep regret about what his invention had become.

The modern open-plan office, which usually removes even the cubicle walls, has been promoted with arguments similar to those of the 1950s. Supporters claim that when colleagues can see one another, they talk more, share ideas more readily and solve problems faster. Companies also point out, less idealistically, that open offices are cheaper: they require less floor space per employee and are easier to reorganise when teams change.

The evidence for the first of these claims is weaker than its popularity suggests. In one widely discussed study, researchers equipped employees at two large companies with electronic badges that recorded when they spoke face to face with colleagues, and they also monitored the employees' email and messaging. The companies were in the process of moving from partly enclosed offices to fully open ones. Contrary to expectations, face-to-face interaction fell sharply after the move, while electronic messages increased. Employees, it seems, responded to their loss of privacy by withdrawing from visible conversations, often wearing headphones to signal that they did not wish to be disturbed.

Other research has focused on noise and interruption. Surveys consistently find that noise, particularly other people's conversations, is the most common complaint in open offices. Tasks that demand concentration, such as writing or detailed analysis, appear to suffer most, and some studies have linked open-plan environments with higher levels of reported stress and sick leave, although the causes of these patterns are difficult to separate from other features of the workplace.

Some organisations have responded with "activity-based working". Employees no longer have fixed desks; instead they move between different zones depending on the task – quiet rooms for concentrated work, open areas for discussion, small booths for telephone calls. When this arrangement works, it gives employees some control over their surroundings. When it is introduced mainly to reduce the number of desks, however, employees may spend part of every morning searching for a place to sit.

The history of the open office suggests that the real problem is not openness itself. The designers of the office landscape understood that different kinds of work require different conditions; what has usually been lost is not walls but choice. An office in which people can move away from noise when they need to concentrate, and come together when they need to collaborate, is likely to serve them better than either a corridor of closed doors or a single undivided hall.

lesson.title: Whose opinion is it?
lesson.text:
At Medium level, passages often contain several voices: designers, companies, researchers, critics and the writer. Questions may ask what one particular group believed or what the writer thinks. A common distractor states an opinion that really appears in the passage but belongs to someone else.

Before answering, identify the speaker in the question stem, then find that speaker in the passage. Useful clues: according to X, X argued, critics claim, it is often said (not necessarily the writer's view), and in my view, arguably, it seems clear, the real problem is (often the writer's view).
lesson.example:
Passage: "Many parents believe homework builds discipline. The evidence, however, suggests its value depends largely on the child's age." What is the writer's view?
Correct: the benefits of homework vary with age. Trap: homework builds discipline, which is the parents' belief.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: What point does the writer make in paragraph A?

options.text: Open-plan offices were first designed to reduce costs.
Employees' view of open-plan offices differs from their original purpose.
Private offices are becoming more common for senior staff.
Most employees prefer open-plan offices.

questions.evidence: the open-plan office was not originally conceived as a way of saving money, which is how many employees now regard it
questions.explanation: This sets employees' current view against the original purpose. A states the employees' view as if it were the historical fact. C reverses the trend. D is contradicted by "widely resented".

questions.text: The designers of the Bürolandschaft believed that

options.text: offices should contain more plants.
traditional office design reinforced differences in status.
employees should sit in straight rows.
departments should be kept separate.

questions.evidence: The designers believed that hierarchy was built into the architecture of traditional offices
questions.explanation: "Hierarchy built into the architecture" = "design reinforced differences in status". Plants (A) are only a design detail. C and D describe the arrangements the designers were rejecting.

questions.text: What does paragraph C suggest about Robert Propst's system?

options.text: It failed to sell in large numbers.
It was designed to create small identical workspaces.
It was used in a way that contradicted his intentions.
It removed the need for walls in offices.

questions.evidence: highly successful commercially, but not in the way he had intended ... Propst himself later expressed deep regret
questions.explanation: Companies used the system to create cubicles, which went against his aims. A is contradicted by "highly successful commercially". B describes how companies used the system, not what it was designed for.

questions.text: According to paragraph D, which reason for open offices do companies present as more practical than idealistic?

options.text: the sharing of ideas
faster problem-solving
lower costs
closer relationships between colleagues

questions.evidence: Companies also point out, less idealistically, that open offices are cheaper
questions.explanation: The signal "less idealistically" marks the practical argument. A, B and D are the idealistic claims made by supporters.

questions.text: What was unexpected about the results of the badge study?

options.text: Employees spoke to each other less in the open office.
Employees sent fewer electronic messages.
Employees refused to wear the badges.
Employees preferred their new open office.

questions.evidence: Contrary to expectations, face-to-face interaction fell sharply after the move
questions.explanation: "Contrary to expectations" identifies what was unexpected. B reverses the finding, since electronic messages increased. D is not stated and is unlikely given the headphone detail.

questions.text: What does the writer say about the link between open offices and stress?

options.text: It has been proved beyond doubt.
It has not been investigated.
It is hard to establish as a direct cause.
It affects only people doing analytical work.

questions.evidence: some studies have linked open-plan environments with higher levels of reported stress ... although the causes of these patterns are difficult to separate from other features of the workplace
questions.explanation: A link exists, but its cause is uncertain. A overstates the finding and B contradicts it. D confuses stress with the separate point that concentration tasks "suffer most".

questions.text: What is the writer's overall view?

options.text: Offices should return to private rooms for every employee.
Activity-based working is always successful.
Offices should offer employees a range of spaces to choose from.
The open-plan office was a mistake from the beginning.

questions.evidence: what has usually been lost is not walls but choice. An office in which people can move away from noise ... and come together ... is likely to serve them better
questions.explanation: The writer argues for choice between different spaces. A is rejected in "either a corridor of closed doors". B is contradicted by the conditions described in Paragraph G. D conflicts with the writer's respect for the original designers.

passages.topic: Engineering — the bridge that swayed
passages.title: The Bridge That Would Not Keep Still

paragraphs.text: In June 2000, a new footbridge opened across the River Thames in central London. Slim and elegant, it was the first new crossing over the river in the centre of the city for more than a century, and on its opening day an estimated 90,000 people walked across it. Within minutes of the crowds arriving, however, the bridge began to sway noticeably from side to side. Pedestrians grabbed the handrails; some stopped walking altogether. Two days later, the bridge was closed. It would not reopen for almost two years.

Newspapers quickly nicknamed it the "wobbly bridge", and many assumed that its designers had made an elementary mistake. The truth was more interesting. The bridge was structurally safe, and it had been designed to cope with the forces that engineers normally expected pedestrians to produce. What the designers had not anticipated was a particular interaction between the structure and the people walking on it – a phenomenon that, at the time, was barely described in engineering guidance.

When people walk, most of the force they apply to the ground is vertical, but a small part is sideways. Because we shift our weight from one foot to the other, each step pushes slightly left and then slightly right. On a solid surface these small sideways forces are random: different walkers step at different moments, and the pushes cancel one another out. On a flexible bridge, the situation can change. If the deck begins to move even slightly to one side, people instinctively adjust their walking to keep their balance, widening their stance and timing their steps to the movement beneath them. As more pedestrians do this, their sideways pushes start to occur in step with the sway, so that instead of cancelling out, they reinforce it. The bridge moves further; more walkers adapt; the movement grows again.

Engineers call this "synchronous lateral excitation". Crucially, it does not happen gradually as a crowd grows. Tests carried out on the bridge after its closure, in which increasing numbers of volunteers were asked to walk across, showed that the sway remained small until the number of walkers passed a particular level. Beyond that point, the movement increased suddenly and dramatically. This explained why the problem had not been noticed during construction, when only a few people used the bridge at a time.

The engineers also discovered that their bridge was not the first to behave in this way. Similar sideways movement had been reported on a number of crowded footbridges in other countries, and even on some road bridges during large public events. However, these incidents had generally been described only briefly, in reports that received little attention, and they had never been brought together into a general understanding of the problem. The London bridge, because it was so new and so publicly visible, forced the issue into the open.

Rather than stiffening the entire structure, which would have spoiled its slender design and required major reconstruction, the engineers chose to add dampers. These devices, fitted beneath the deck and around the supports, absorb the energy of movement in a similar way to the shock absorbers of a car. Once the bridge's motion was damped, even large crowds could no longer build up the sway, because the movement never grew large enough for walkers to begin adjusting their steps. The work cost several million pounds, and when the bridge reopened in 2002, test crowds crossed it without difficulty.

The episode had consequences well beyond one river crossing. Its investigation was published in detail, and design codes in several countries were revised to require engineers to consider sideways crowd effects on footbridges. In that sense, the embarrassment of the opening weekend produced a lasting benefit: a problem that had occurred quietly for decades was finally understood.

lesson.title: Explanations of processes
lesson.text:
Some passages explain how something happens through a chain of causes (A leads to B, which strengthens A...). Questions may test one link in the chain or the chain as a whole. Distractors often present the right elements in the wrong order, or they describe the trigger as if it were the whole explanation.

Before looking at the options, write the chain yourself in three or four short notes (for example: small sway → walkers adjust step → push in time → bigger sway). Then choose the option that matches your notes.
lesson.example: Passage: "As more cars joined the road, traffic slowed; slower traffic made drivers brake sharply, which slowed it further." Why did the traffic keep slowing? Correct: drivers' reactions made the slowdown worse. Trap: there were too many cars, which is only the starting point.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: What does the writer say about the response of newspapers?

options.text: It correctly identified the cause of the problem.
It reflected a mistaken assumption about the designers.
It persuaded the authorities to close the bridge.
It exaggerated the number of people on the bridge.

questions.evidence: many assumed that its designers had made an elementary mistake. The truth was more interesting
questions.explanation: The writer presents the newspapers' view as a mistaken assumption. A is the opposite. The closure is not linked to newspapers (C), and the figure of 90,000 is the writer's own estimate (D).

questions.text: According to paragraph B, the bridge was closed because

options.text: it was in danger of collapsing.
it had been built with poor materials.
of an unexpected effect of people walking on it.
it could not support vertical forces.

questions.evidence: What the designers had not anticipated was a particular interaction between the structure and the people walking on it
questions.explanation: "Not anticipated" = "unexpected". A and B are contradicted by "structurally safe". D is wrong, because the passage identifies sideways forces, not vertical ones, as the problem.

questions.text: Why do sideways forces from walkers normally cause no problem?

options.text: They are much smaller than the weight of a bridge.
They are produced at different times and cancel each other.
People walk more slowly on bridges.
Most bridges are designed to move with walkers.

questions.evidence: these small sideways forces are random: different walkers step at different moments, and the pushes cancel one another out
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase. A sounds logical but is not stated. D is contradicted: the passage does not say bridges are designed to move with walkers.

questions.text: Which sequence best describes the process explained in paragraph C?

options.text: Walkers push sideways in step → the bridge begins to move → walkers lose balance.
The bridge moves slightly → walkers adjust their steps → their pushes increase the movement.
Crowds become larger → the bridge becomes heavier → the deck bends downwards.
Walkers widen their stance → the bridge stops moving → walkers return to normal steps.

questions.evidence: If the deck begins to move even slightly ... people instinctively adjust their walking ... their sideways pushes start to occur in step with the sway, so that ... they reinforce it
