questions.explanation: B gives the correct order. A reverses cause and effect. C refers to vertical bending, which is not described. D contradicts the reinforcing cycle.

questions.text: What did the tests with volunteers reveal?

options.text: The sway increased steadily as each person joined.
The sway began suddenly once numbers exceeded a certain point.
The sway was caused by volunteers walking too quickly.
The sway could be prevented by asking people to stop walking.

questions.evidence: the sway remained small until the number of walkers passed a particular level. Beyond that point, the movement increased suddenly
questions.explanation: The movement began suddenly after a threshold was reached. A is directly contradicted by "does not happen gradually". C and D are not supported.

questions.text: What does paragraph E suggest about earlier cases of swaying bridges?

options.text: They had been caused by poor construction.
They had led to changes in design rules.
They had not been widely recognised as a general problem.
They had occurred only on footbridges.

questions.evidence: described only briefly, in reports that received little attention ... never been brought together into a general understanding of the problem
questions.explanation: The earlier cases were not recognised as a general problem. D is contradicted by the mention of road bridges. B confuses these earlier cases with the rule changes that followed the London bridge (Paragraph G).

questions.text: Why did the engineers choose dampers rather than stiffening the bridge?

options.text: Dampers would prevent all vertical movement.
Stiffening would have been cheaper but slower.
Dampers allowed the original design to be kept.
Stiffening had already failed in tests.

questions.evidence: Rather than stiffening the entire structure, which would have spoiled its slender design and required major reconstruction
questions.explanation: Dampers preserved the slender design. A wrongly introduces vertical movement. B and D are not stated: the passage never compares the cost of the two options.

passages.topic: Environment and wildlife — light pollution
passages.title: The Vanishing Dark

paragraphs.text: For almost all of history, night meant darkness. Even in towns, the only light after sunset came from fires, candles and, eventually, oil and gas lamps, which lit little more than the ground around them. Today, the situation has been reversed. Satellite images show continents outlined in light, and in many wealthy regions it is now difficult to find anywhere that is truly dark at night. Scientists use the term "light pollution" to describe artificial light that is excessive, badly directed or present where and when it is not needed.

The most familiar consequence is the loss of the night sky. On a clear night far from any town, several thousand stars are visible to the naked eye, together with the faint band of the Milky Way. In a large city, the glow of streetlights, buildings and advertising reflected by the atmosphere reduces this to a few dozen. Surveys suggest that a large proportion of people in industrialised countries now live where the Milky Way can no longer be seen. Astronomers were the first to complain; professional observatories have repeatedly been forced to move to ever more remote mountains.

It is now clear, however, that the effects extend far beyond astronomy. Many animals depend on natural patterns of light and darkness. Newly hatched sea turtles, for example, find their way from the nest to the sea by heading towards the brightest horizon, which on an undeveloped beach is the sky above the water. On beaches lined with hotels and roads, hatchlings may crawl inland instead, where many die from exhaustion or are killed by traffic. Migrating birds that travel at night are attracted and disoriented by brightly lit buildings, and large numbers are killed each year in collisions. Insects are drawn to streetlights, where they circle until they are exhausted or eaten, and some researchers believe this may be contributing to declines in insect populations in some regions.

Humans may be affected too. The body's internal clock, which regulates sleep and many other processes, is set largely by light, and it is particularly sensitive to light at the blue end of the spectrum. Exposure to bright artificial light in the evening can delay the release of hormones that prepare the body for sleep. Researchers are still investigating how far outdoor lighting, as opposed to screens and indoor lamps, contributes to such effects, but the direction of the evidence has led some health organisations to recommend limiting unnecessary light at night.

One recent development has had surprising consequences. Over the past two decades, many cities have replaced older streetlights with light-emitting diodes (LEDs). LEDs use far less electricity, last much longer and can be directed more precisely, so the switch was widely expected to reduce light pollution. In some places it did. Elsewhere, however, the cheaper running costs encouraged authorities and businesses to install more lights, or brighter ones, so that total energy savings were smaller than predicted and the amount of light emitted actually increased. Many early LED lamps also produced a cold, bluish light, the very part of the spectrum to which both humans and many animals are most sensitive.

Unlike most forms of pollution, light pollution can be reduced almost instantly, and often at low cost. Shielded fittings that direct light downwards, where it is needed, rather than sideways and up into the sky, reduce glare and wasted energy. Lights can be dimmed or switched off late at night when streets are empty, and lamps with warmer colours can replace harsh blue-white ones. Several towns have adopted such measures and have been formally recognised as "dark sky" places, attracting visitors who come specifically to see the stars.

The obstacle is less technical than psychological. Light is widely associated with safety and progress, and proposals to reduce it are often met with concern about crime or accidents. Yet the evidence that more light always produces greater safety is surprisingly mixed, and badly designed lighting can create glare that makes it harder, not easier, to see. The aim of reducing light pollution is not to return cities to darkness but to use light more intelligently – in the right places, at the right times and in the right amounts.

lesson.title: "Why does the writer mention ...?"
lesson.text:
Some questions ask about the function of a detail: an example, a statistic, a comparison or a case study. The answer is not what the detail says but why it is there. Look at the sentence just before the detail, which is often the general claim, and ask: What point does this example prove or illustrate?

A frequent distractor simply restates the content of the example itself. That option is true, but it does not answer the question about purpose.
lesson.example: Passage: "Small habits can have large effects. A person who saves just two dollars a day will have over seven hundred dollars after a year." Why does the writer mention two dollars a day? Correct: to illustrate that small habits add up. Trap: to recommend a specific saving amount.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: In paragraph A, the writer defines light pollution as artificial light that is

options.text: produced by old types of lamps.
stronger than natural light.
unnecessary or poorly controlled.
visible from satellites.

questions.evidence: artificial light that is excessive, badly directed or present where and when it is not needed
questions.explanation: "Badly directed" = "poorly controlled", and "not needed" = "unnecessary". D uses the satellite detail from the same paragraph, but that detail is not part of the definition.

questions.text: Why does the writer mention professional observatories in paragraph B?

options.text: to show that astronomers were among the earliest to be affected
to explain why mountains are dark at night
to argue that observatories should be built in cities
to suggest that astronomy is no longer possible

questions.evidence: Astronomers were the first to complain; professional observatories have repeatedly been forced to move
questions.explanation: The observatories illustrate how early astronomers were affected. D goes too far: observatories moved, but astronomy did not stop. B and C are not supported.

questions.text: Why does the writer describe the behaviour of newly hatched sea turtles?

options.text: to show that turtles are more affected than birds
to illustrate how artificial light can mislead animals that use natural light
to explain why hotels should not be built on beaches
to prove that most turtle hatchlings die on developed beaches

questions.evidence: Many animals depend on natural patterns of light ... hatchlings may crawl inland instead
questions.explanation: The turtles are an example of the general claim that animals relying on natural light are misled. D overstates "many die". Hotel policy (C) is not discussed. The paragraph does not compare turtles with birds (A).

questions.text: What does the writer say about the effect of outdoor lighting on human sleep?

options.text: It is the main cause of sleep problems.
It has no effect compared with screens.
Its exact contribution is not yet clear.
It has been proved by health organisations.

questions.evidence: Researchers are still investigating how far outdoor lighting, as opposed to screens and indoor lamps, contributes to such effects
questions.explanation: "Still investigating how far" = "exact contribution not yet clear". A and D overstate the evidence. B is not stated.

questions.text: What was unexpected about the introduction of LED streetlights?

options.text: They used more electricity than older lights.
They sometimes led to more light being produced overall.
They proved too expensive for many cities.
They could not be directed precisely.

questions.evidence: the switch was widely expected to reduce light pollution ... Elsewhere ... the amount of light emitted actually increased
questions.explanation: The result went against expectations. A is contradicted by "use far less electricity". D is contradicted by "can be directed more precisely".

questions.text: According to paragraph F, one advantage of tackling light pollution is that

options.text: the results can be achieved quickly.
it requires advanced new technology.
it has eliminated crime in dark sky towns.
it is supported by all local residents.

questions.evidence: Unlike most forms of pollution, light pollution can be reduced almost instantly, and often at low cost
questions.explanation: "Almost instantly" = "quickly". B contradicts the simple methods listed. C and D are not stated: dark sky towns attract visitors, but nothing is said about crime or universal support.

questions.text: What is the writer's main point in paragraph G?

options.text: Cities should switch off all their streetlights.
More lighting reliably improves public safety.
The chief challenge is changing attitudes towards light.
Glare is the most serious form of light pollution.

questions.evidence: The obstacle is less technical than psychological. Light is widely associated with safety and progress
questions.explanation: The key challenge is people's attitudes. A is contradicted by "not to return cities to darkness". B is contradicted by "surprisingly mixed". Glare (D) is only one supporting point.

passages.topic: Education and psychology — learning through testing
passages.title: Remembering by Recalling

paragraphs.text: Ask students how they prepare for an examination and most will describe some version of the same routine: reading their notes again, highlighting important sentences and reading them once more. The method feels productive. With each rereading the material seems more familiar, and familiarity creates a comfortable sense of understanding. A substantial body of research, however, suggests that rereading is among the least effective ways of learning, and that a very different activity – trying to recall information from memory – is considerably more powerful.

This finding, often called the "testing effect", is not new. Psychologists noticed as early as the beginning of the twentieth century that people who spent part of their study time reciting material from memory remembered it better than those who spent the whole time reading it. For decades, however, the idea attracted little attention in education, where tests were seen almost entirely as a way of measuring learning, not as a way of producing it.

Interest revived in the early 2000s following a series of carefully controlled experiments. In a typical design, students read a short scientific text and were then divided into groups. One group read the text several more times; another read it once more and then wrote down everything they could remember, without looking at the text. When the students were tested five minutes later, the group that had spent more time rereading performed slightly better. When they were tested a week later, the result was reversed: the students who had practised recall remembered substantially more, while those who had reread had forgotten much of what they had studied.

Perhaps the most striking finding concerned the students' own predictions. Asked how well they expected to remember the text in a week, the rereading group was more confident than the recall group. Rereading had made the text feel easy, and the students mistook this ease for durable learning. Recall, by contrast, felt effortful and uncertain, since students were constantly aware of what they could not remember, and so they underestimated its benefits. Researchers argue that this mismatch between how learning feels and how well it works explains why ineffective methods remain so popular.

Why should retrieval be so effective? One explanation is that each act of recall strengthens the pathways by which a memory can be found again, in the same way that a path through a field becomes clearer each time someone walks along it. Another is that retrieval shows learners exactly which parts of the material they have not yet mastered, allowing them to focus their efforts. The benefits appear to be greatest when practice is spread out over time rather than concentrated in a single session, and when learners check their answers afterwards, so that mistakes are corrected rather than reinforced.

None of this means that schools should simply give students more examinations. The tests used in the research were usually short, frequent and carried no consequences for students' grades – quizzes, flashcards, or simply closing the book and writing a summary from memory. High-stakes tests, which may produce anxiety and encourage last-minute cramming, are a different matter, and there is little evidence that increasing their number improves learning. Some researchers have therefore suggested replacing the word "testing" with "retrieval practice", to make clear that the goal is learning rather than assessment.

The broader lesson concerns what might be called "desirable difficulty". Methods that make learning feel smooth and easy often produce knowledge that fades quickly, whereas methods that demand effort – recalling, explaining, applying information in new situations – tend to produce knowledge that lasts. For students who are used to measuring progress by how comfortable they feel, this is an uncomfortable message. The sense of struggle during study, it seems, is frequently a sign not of failure but of learning taking place.

lesson.title: Timing and conditions
lesson.text:
Research passages often report that a result appears only under certain conditions: after a delay, in one group, or when a task is difficult. Medium-level distractors ignore these conditions and state the result as if it were always true.

When a stem mentions a time or condition (immediately, after a week, when students..., at first), locate that exact condition in the passage. Then check whether the option keeps the condition or quietly drops it.
lesson.example: Passage: "The fertiliser increased growth, but only in sandy soils." What did the study find? Correct: the fertiliser helped plants in certain soils. Trap: the fertiliser increased plant growth, which drops the condition.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: According to paragraph A, students like rereading because it

options.text: helps them finish their notes more quickly.
gives them a feeling that they understand the material.
has been recommended by researchers.
allows them to recall information without effort.

questions.evidence: familiarity creates a comfortable sense of understanding
questions.explanation: "A comfortable sense of understanding" = "a feeling that they understand". C is contradicted by the research. D describes recall, not rereading.

questions.text: What does the writer say about attitudes to tests in education before the 2000s?

options.text: Tests were considered mainly a means of assessment.
Tests were thought to be the best way of learning.
Teachers used recitation in most lessons.
Researchers were unaware of the testing effect.

questions.evidence: tests were seen almost entirely as a way of measuring learning, not as a way of producing it
questions.explanation: "Measuring learning" = "assessment". D is contradicted: psychologists had noticed the effect early in the twentieth century. B reverses the attitude.

questions.text: In the experiments described in paragraph C, the rereading group

options.text: performed better on both tests.
performed worse on both tests.
did slightly better at first but worse after a week.
forgot less than the recall group over a week.

questions.evidence: tested five minutes later, the group that had spent more time rereading performed slightly better ... a week later, the result was reversed
questions.explanation: This is the time condition. A and B each ignore one of the two tests. D contradicts "had forgotten much".

questions.text: What surprised researchers about the students' predictions?

options.text: The recall group expected to remember nothing.
The group that learned less was more confident.
Both groups predicted their results accurately.
The rereading group believed recall was more useful.

questions.evidence: the rereading group was more confident than the recall group
questions.explanation: The rereading group learned less (Paragraph C) but was more confident. A is too extreme. C is contradicted by the "mismatch" described.

questions.text: According to paragraph E, retrieval practice is most beneficial when

options.text: it is carried out in one long session.
learners avoid looking at the answers.
it is spaced over time and followed by checking.
it involves walking while studying.

questions.evidence: greatest when practice is spread out over time ... and when learners check their answers afterwards
questions.explanation: Both conditions are in C. A reverses the first condition and B reverses the second. D misreads the path analogy, which is only a comparison.

questions.text: Why have some researchers suggested using the term "retrieval practice"?

options.text: to show that the method is only for older students
to separate the method from anxious, high-stakes assessment
because the word "testing" is too informal
to encourage schools to hold more examinations

questions.evidence: High-stakes tests, which may produce anxiety ... Some researchers have therefore suggested replacing the word 'testing' with 'retrieval practice', to make clear that the goal is learning rather than assessment
questions.explanation: The new term separates the method from stressful assessment. D is contradicted by "None of this means that schools should simply give students more examinations".

questions.text: Which of the following best summarises the idea of "desirable difficulty"?

options.text: Difficult subjects are the most valuable to study.
Students should avoid methods that feel comfortable.
Effortful learning methods tend to produce longer-lasting knowledge.
Struggling during study shows that a student is failing.

questions.evidence: methods that demand effort ... tend to produce knowledge that lasts
questions.explanation: This is the core idea. A concerns difficult subjects, not methods. B is too absolute. D reverses the final sentence.

passages.topic: Economic history — the shipping container
passages.title: The Box That Changed the World

paragraphs.text: Until the middle of the twentieth century, loading a cargo ship was slow, expensive and physically exhausting work. Goods arrived at the docks in an enormous variety of forms – sacks of coffee, barrels of oil, crates of machinery, bundles of timber – and each item had to be lifted individually into the ship's hold and carefully arranged so that the load would not shift at sea. A large ship could spend a week or more in port being loaded or unloaded, and the cost of handling cargo at the docks was often greater than the cost of carrying it across the ocean. Theft was also common, since goods passed through many hands.

The solution now seems obvious: pack the goods into large standard metal boxes at the factory, move the boxes by truck or train to the port, and lift them directly onto the ship with a crane. Versions of this idea had been tried before, but they had never spread widely. The person most associated with making it work was Malcom McLean, the owner of a road haulage company in the United States. In 1956 he sent a converted oil tanker carrying fifty-eight metal containers from New Jersey to Texas. The cost of loading, according to his own calculations, was a small fraction of what traditional methods would have required.

McLean's real insight was that the box itself mattered less than the system around it. Ships had to be redesigned with frames to hold the containers securely; ports needed enormous cranes and large areas of flat land where boxes could be stacked; and trucks and railways needed equipment to carry them. Without all these elements, containers offered little advantage. This made the early years difficult, because investing in any one part of the system seemed risky until the others were in place.

A further obstacle was the lack of agreement on size. Different companies built containers of different dimensions, which meant that one company's boxes might not fit another company's ships or cranes. Only after lengthy negotiations during the 1960s were international standards agreed, based on boxes twenty and forty feet long with standard fittings at each corner. Standardisation allowed containers to move freely between shipping lines, ports and countries, and it is widely regarded as the moment when containerisation became a global system rather than a collection of separate experiments.

The effects on ports were dramatic. Many of the great harbours of the past, located in the centres of old cities, lacked the space for container terminals and could not accommodate the new, larger ships. Traffic shifted to new facilities built on open land, sometimes at a considerable distance from the traditional docks. In several cities, waterfront areas that had been busy for centuries became largely empty within two decades. For dock workers, the consequences were severe. Work that had once required gangs of dozens of men could now be done by a few crane operators, and in many ports the number of dockside jobs fell sharply. Unions resisted, and the introduction of containers was accompanied in several countries by long and bitter disputes.

For the wider economy, however, the container dramatically reduced the cost and time of moving goods. Because transport became cheap and predictable, it became practical for manufacturers to make different components in different countries and assemble them elsewhere. Economists have argued that the container contributed at least as much to the growth of international trade in the late twentieth century as the reduction of trade barriers negotiated between governments, although measuring its precise effect is difficult.

Today the container is so ordinary that it is rarely noticed. Most of the manufactured goods in any shop have spent part of their journey inside one. The story of its success is a reminder that technical inventions often matter less on their own than the systems, agreements and changes in organisation that allow them to be used.

lesson.title: When the question and the passage share no words
lesson.text:
As difficulty rises, question stems use almost none of the passage's vocabulary. For example, a stem may say "workers' reaction" where the passage says "dockers' unions ... strikes". You cannot find the answer by scanning for matching words. Instead:

1. Turn the stem into a simple idea ("How did the workers feel?").

2. Use the question order and paragraph topics to find the right section.

3. Look for synonyms, examples or descriptions of the idea, not the same words. The option that repeats passage wording most closely is often the trap.
lesson.example: Stem: "How did residents respond to the new airport?" Passage: "Petitions were signed by thousands living nearby, and weekly protests continued for a year." Answer idea: strong opposition. No words are shared, but the meaning matches.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: What does paragraph A suggest about the shipping industry before containers?

options.text: Crossing the ocean was the most expensive part of a journey.
Handling goods in port was a major cost.
Ships were too small to carry heavy cargo.
Theft rarely occurred at sea.

questions.evidence: the cost of handling cargo at the docks was often greater than the cost of carrying it across the ocean
questions.explanation: Handling in port was often the larger cost. A reverses the comparison. D contradicts "Theft was also common".

questions.text: What point does the writer make about McLean's 1956 voyage?

options.text: It was the first time goods had been carried in containers.
It was a failure that delayed the use of containers.
It showed that the new method could greatly cut costs.
It was organised by a government agency.

questions.evidence: The cost of loading ... was a small fraction of what traditional methods would have required
questions.explanation: "A small fraction" = "greatly cut costs". A is contradicted by "Versions of this idea had been tried before". McLean owned a private company, so D is wrong.

questions.text: According to paragraph C, why were the early years of containerisation difficult?

options.text: Ship owners did not believe containers were safe.
Each part of the system depended on the others being developed.
Containers were too expensive to manufacture.
Trucks were not allowed to enter ports.

questions.evidence: Without all these elements, containers offered little advantage ... investing in any one part of the system seemed risky until the others were in place
questions.explanation: This describes mutual dependence between parts of the system. A, C and D are not stated.

questions.text: What was the main significance of the international agreements of the 1960s?

options.text: They made containers interchangeable across the whole transport network.
They reduced the size of cargo ships.
They required all ports to build new terminals.
They ended conflicts with dock workers.

questions.evidence: Standardisation allowed containers to move freely between shipping lines, ports and countries
questions.explanation: "Move freely between" = "interchangeable". B, C and D are not effects of the agreements described.

questions.text: How did many traditional city-centre ports respond to containerisation?

options.text: They expanded rapidly to handle more ships.
They were unable to adapt and lost much of their activity.
They became the main container terminals.
They were redesigned for smaller ships.

questions.evidence: lacked the space ... Traffic shifted to new facilities ... waterfront areas ... became largely empty
questions.explanation: The old ports could not adapt and lost activity. A and C are the opposite. D is not mentioned.

questions.text: How did dock workers react to the introduction of containers?

options.text: They welcomed the easier working conditions.
They moved to jobs in manufacturing.
They opposed the change, sometimes for long periods.
They trained as crane operators in large numbers.

questions.evidence: Unions resisted ... accompanied in several countries by long and bitter disputes
questions.explanation: "Resisted" and "long ... disputes" = "opposed ... for long periods". The stem shares no words with the passage, so this answer depends on paraphrase. D is a trap built from "crane operators".

questions.text: What is the writer's main purpose in the final paragraph?

options.text: to predict the future of container shipping
to draw a general lesson about technology and organisation
to criticise the impact of containers on cities
to praise McLean as an inventor

questions.evidence: technical inventions often matter less on their own than the systems, agreements and changes in organisation that allow them to be used
questions.explanation: The paragraph ends on a general lesson. D is a trap, because the lesson actually downplays individual invention.

passages.topic: Linguistics and culture — whistled languages
passages.title: Speaking in Whistles

paragraphs.text: On a steep hillside, a farmer purses her lips and produces a series of piercing, rising and falling notes. Across the valley, more than a kilometre away, a neighbour stops work, listens, and whistles back. The two are not exchanging simple signals like those used to call a dog. They are having a conversation, using a whistled form of their ordinary spoken language. Such "whistled languages" have been documented in dozens of communities around the world, from the mountains of Turkey and the Pyrenees to parts of West Africa, Mexico and Papua New Guinea.

A whistled language is not an independent language with its own vocabulary and grammar. It is a way of transposing an existing spoken language into whistles. Because the mouth cannot whistle consonants and vowels in the ordinary way, speakers represent the most important features of speech – changes in pitch, the rhythm of syllables, and the way the sound is interrupted or shaped – using variations in a single whistled tone. Listeners fluent in both the spoken and whistled forms can reconstruct words and sentences from these clues, much as readers can understand a text in which many letters are missing.

The way this transposition works depends on the spoken language. In languages where pitch distinguishes one word from another, such as many languages of West Africa and East Asia, whistlers mainly reproduce the pitch patterns of the words. In languages like Spanish or Turkish, where pitch is less important, whistlers instead imitate the qualities of vowels and consonants, turning them into higher and lower notes and different kinds of transition between them. Whistled forms of the same language may therefore differ considerably between regions.

Whistled languages share a clear geographical pattern: they occur mainly in places with steep mountains or dense forest, where people live and work far apart and where travelling between them is slow. A whistle carries much further than a shout, since its energy is concentrated in a narrow range of frequencies and stands out clearly from natural background noise. In good conditions, whistled speech can be understood over several kilometres. For shepherds, farmers and hunters, it offered a way of exchanging detailed information – about lost animals, approaching weather or the arrival of visitors – without making a long and difficult journey.

In the second half of the twentieth century, most whistled languages declined rapidly. Roads reached previously isolated villages, many young people moved to towns, and, above all, the telephone and later the mobile phone made long-distance communication possible without whistling. Where the practice survived, it was often used only by older people. On the island of La Gomera in the Canary Islands, however, the local whistled form of Spanish, known as Silbo Gomero, has undergone a revival. Since the late 1990s it has been a compulsory subject in the island's schools, and it has received international recognition as part of the world's cultural heritage. Today many schoolchildren on the island can whistle, although relatively few use it in everyday life.

Whistled languages have also attracted the attention of brain scientists. In most people, the processing of spoken language takes place mainly in the left half of the brain, while the right half plays a larger role in processing music and melody. Researchers working with speakers of whistled Turkish found that, when listening to whistled speech, both halves of the brain were heavily involved. The finding suggests that the brain's division of labour for language may be more flexible than was once assumed, and that it depends partly on the physical form in which language reaches the ear.

For linguists, whistled languages offer a rare natural experiment in how much information speech really needs. The fact that fluent listeners can understand whole sentences from a single varying tone shows how much of ordinary speech is redundant, and how skilfully the human mind fills in missing details. For the communities that use them, however, they are something more personal: a sign of a distinctive way of life, shaped by the landscape in which it developed.

lesson.title: Options that are "true but incomplete"
lesson.text: At Medium level, two options can both look correct. Often one of them is true but covers only part of what the question asks, or only part of the evidence. Compare the two final candidates against the whole relevant sentence or paragraph. The correct option usually summarises the full point, while the distractor captures only one detail of it.
lesson.example: Passage: "The village was abandoned because the river dried up and the new road bypassed it." Why was the village abandoned? A the river dried up (true but incomplete). B it lost both its water supply and its transport connection (complete). If only one letter is allowed, choose B.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: The writer describes the two farmers in paragraph A in order to show that

options.text: whistles are mainly used to control animals.
whistled languages allow real conversations over long distances.
farmers in mountainous areas rarely meet each other.
whistled languages are found only in Europe.

questions.evidence: more than a kilometre away ... They are having a conversation, using a whistled form of their ordinary spoken language
questions.explanation: The scene shows real conversation over distance. A is rejected directly ("not ... simple signals like those used to call a dog"). D is contradicted by the list of countries.

questions.text: According to paragraph B, a whistled language is best described as

options.text: a separate language with its own grammar.
a system of simple signals.
a spoken language converted into whistled form.
a way of writing a language without letters.

questions.evidence: not an independent language ... It is a way of transposing an existing spoken language into whistles
questions.explanation: "Transposing" = "converting". A is denied directly. D misreads the "missing letters" comparison, which is only an analogy.

questions.text: What does paragraph C say about whistled forms of languages such as Spanish and Turkish?

options.text: They reproduce mainly the pitch of words.
They represent the sounds of vowels and consonants.
They are identical in every region.
They are easier to learn than other whistled languages.

questions.evidence: In languages like Spanish or Turkish ... whistlers instead imitate the qualities of vowels and consonants
questions.explanation: A describes languages where pitch distinguishes words. C is contradicted by "may therefore differ considerably between regions".

questions.text: Why are whistled languages found mainly in mountains and forests?

options.text: Whistling is easier in cool, damp air.
People there are separated by difficult terrain, and whistles travel far.
Other forms of communication are forbidden there.
Background noise is louder in those areas.

questions.evidence: where people live and work far apart and where travelling between them is slow. A whistle carries much further than a shout
questions.explanation: B combines both parts of the explanation. An option giving only one part would be incomplete. A and C are not stated. D reverses the point: whistles stand out from background noise.

questions.text: What does the writer say about Silbo Gomero today?

options.text: It is used by most islanders in daily conversation.
It has disappeared despite efforts to save it.
It is widely taught, though not widely used in ordinary life.
It is spoken only by older residents.

questions.evidence: a compulsory subject in the island's schools ... many schoolchildren ... can whistle, although relatively few use it in everyday life
questions.explanation: C captures both halves of the final sentence. A contradicts "relatively few". D describes where the practice survived elsewhere, not La Gomera.

questions.text: What did the research with speakers of whistled Turkish suggest?

options.text: Whistled speech is processed only in the right half of the brain.
The way the brain handles language may depend on its physical form.
Music and language are processed in the same way by everyone.
Whistlers have larger brains than other speakers.

questions.evidence: the brain's division of labour for language may be more flexible ... and that it depends partly on the physical form in which language reaches the ear
questions.explanation: This is a paraphrase of the finding. A contradicts "both halves". C and D are not stated.

questions.text: According to paragraph G, what do whistled languages reveal to linguists?

options.text: Ordinary speech contains more information than listeners need.
Human speech is extremely difficult to understand.
Whistled languages are older than spoken languages.
Listeners need every sound in order to understand a sentence.

questions.evidence: shows how much of ordinary speech is redundant
questions.explanation: "Redundant" = "more information than listeners need". D is the opposite. C is not mentioned.

passages.topic: Transport and urban policy — charging drivers to enter cities
passages.title: Paying to Drive

paragraphs.text: Traffic congestion is one of the most familiar problems of modern cities, and one of the most expensive. Drivers and passengers lose hours in slow-moving traffic, goods deliveries are delayed, and vehicle engines running at low speeds produce more pollution per kilometre than those travelling freely. For decades, the standard response was to build more roads. Yet in many cities new roads filled with traffic almost as soon as they opened, as people who had previously avoided driving at busy times began to do so. Transport economists concluded that congestion could not simply be built away.

An alternative idea had been proposed by economists as early as the 1920s. Road space in a busy city centre, they argued, is a scarce resource, yet drivers pay nothing extra to use it at the times when it is most in demand. Each additional car slows down all the others, but the driver does not bear that cost. If drivers were charged for entering congested areas at busy times, some would change their route, their timing or their means of transport, and the remaining traffic would flow more freely.

For many years the idea remained largely theoretical, because it was thought to be both technically difficult and politically impossible. The first city to apply it on a large scale was Singapore, which in 1975 required drivers to buy a special permit to enter the central business district during the morning rush hour. Traffic in the zone fell sharply. Later schemes, including one introduced in London in 2003, used cameras to record vehicle number plates automatically, making it possible to charge drivers without toll booths or permits.

Perhaps the most instructive case is that of Stockholm. When the Swedish capital proposed a congestion charge in the early 2000s, the plan was deeply unpopular: opinion polls suggested that a clear majority of residents opposed it, and local newspapers were largely hostile. The city decided to introduce the charge on a trial basis for seven months in 2006, followed by a referendum in which residents would decide whether to keep it.

During the trial, traffic crossing the charging zone fell by around a fifth – a larger reduction than many planners had predicted. Journey times became shorter and more reliable, and public transport, which had been expanded in preparation, carried more passengers. As residents experienced these changes, their attitudes shifted. By the time of the referendum, a majority of voters in the city supported keeping the charge, and it was made permanent in 2007. Support continued to grow in the years that followed, to the point where later surveys found that many residents struggled to remember why the scheme had once been so controversial.

Researchers who studied the Stockholm case identified several reasons for this change of opinion. The most important was that the benefits of reduced traffic were immediate and visible, whereas the fears that had dominated public debate – that shops would lose customers or that traffic would simply move to other roads – largely failed to materialise. The charge was also presented as part of a broader package that included better buses and trains, so that drivers who stopped using their cars had realistic alternatives.

Congestion charging is not a solution for every city. Critics argue that a fixed charge affects poorer drivers more heavily than wealthier ones, and that people who have no practical alternative to driving – because of their working hours or the absence of public transport – may simply pay more without changing their behaviour. Supporters respond that the revenue raised can be used to improve public transport, which is used disproportionately by people on lower incomes. How these arguments balance out depends heavily on how a particular scheme is designed and how its revenue is spent.

lesson.title: Questions about change over time
lesson.text: Passages about policies or developments often describe a before, a during and an after. Questions may ask how something changed, for example public opinion or traffic levels. Distractors frequently describe the correct situation at the wrong stage (what people thought before instead of after). Mark the time signals in the passage (initially, at first, during the trial, once, subsequently, by the end) and match each fact to its stage.
lesson.example: Passage: "At first, most residents opposed the new park; after it opened, surveys showed strong approval." How did opinion develop? Correct: it moved from opposition to support. Trap: most residents opposed the park, which is true, but only of the first stage.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: What did transport economists conclude about building new roads?

options.text: It was the most effective way of reducing congestion.
It tended to attract additional traffic.
It was too expensive for most cities.
It reduced pollution from vehicles.

questions.evidence: new roads filled with traffic almost as soon as they opened, as people who had previously avoided driving ... began to do so
questions.explanation: New roads attract new traffic. A is the belief that economists rejected. C and D are not stated.

questions.text: According to paragraph B, the economists' argument was based on the idea that

options.text: drivers should pay for road repairs.
each driver creates delays for others without paying for them.
cars should be banned from city centres.
public transport is always faster than driving.

questions.evidence: Each additional car slows down all the others, but the driver does not bear that cost
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase. A, C and D are not part of the argument.

questions.text: What was the main innovation of later schemes such as London's?

options.text: They charged drivers for the whole day.
They applied only to commercial vehicles.
They used cameras instead of permits or toll booths.
They were introduced without public consultation.

questions.evidence: used cameras to record vehicle number plates automatically, making it possible to charge drivers without toll booths or permits
questions.explanation: The cameras replaced permits and booths. A, B and D are not mentioned.

questions.text: How did public opinion in Stockholm change?

options.text: It moved from strong support to opposition.
It remained divided throughout the trial.
It moved from majority opposition to majority support.
It was never measured before the referendum.

questions.evidence: "a clear majority of residents opposed it" (Paragraph D) ... "By the time of the referendum, a majority of voters ... supported keeping the charge" (Paragraph E)
questions.explanation: This answer requires matching each fact to its stage. A reverses the direction. D is contradicted by the opinion polls mentioned in Paragraph D.

questions.text: What does the writer say about the fall in traffic during the trial?

options.text: It was smaller than expected.
It exceeded many planners' predictions.
It occurred only on public holidays.
It caused longer journey times.

questions.evidence: traffic ... fell by around a fifth – a larger reduction than many planners had predicted
questions.explanation: "Larger than predicted" = "exceeded predictions". A is the opposite. D contradicts "Journey times became shorter".

questions.text: According to researchers, a key reason for the change in Stockholm residents' views was that

options.text: the charge was reduced after the trial.
shops reported large increases in sales.
the problems people had feared mostly did not happen.
traffic moved to roads outside the zone.

questions.evidence: the fears that had dominated public debate ... largely failed to materialise
questions.explanation: "Failed to materialise" = "did not happen". D is one of the fears that did not happen. B goes beyond the passage, which says only that the feared loss of customers did not occur.

questions.text: What is the writer's position in paragraph G?

options.text: Congestion charging is always unfair to poorer people.
The fairness of a scheme depends on its design and use of revenue.
Critics of congestion charging have no valid arguments.
All cities should adopt congestion charging.

questions.evidence: How these arguments balance out depends heavily on how a particular scheme is designed and how its revenue is spent
questions.explanation: The writer takes a conditional position. A presents the critics' view as absolute. D is contradicted by "not a solution for every city".

passages.topic: Psychology and consumer behaviour — does more choice make us less likely to choose?
passages.title: The Trouble with Choice?

paragraphs.text: Few ideas in popular psychology have spread as widely as the claim that too much choice is bad for us. Its best-known source is an experiment conducted in an upmarket food shop at the end of the twentieth century. On some days, shoppers passing a tasting table were offered a selection of twenty-four varieties of jam; on others, only six. The larger display attracted more visitors, who stopped to look and taste. But when it came to buying, the result was reversed: around three per cent of those who visited the large display went on to purchase a jar, compared with roughly thirty per cent of those who saw the small one.

The finding was striking because it contradicted a principle that had seemed almost self-evident, both to economists and to businesses: that people are better off with more options, since additional choices can only increase the chance that someone finds exactly what they want. The jam study, together with related laboratory experiments involving chocolates and essay topics, suggested that beyond a certain point, extra options could discourage people from choosing at all, or leave those who did choose less satisfied with the result. The phenomenon became known as "choice overload", and it was soon cited in books, business advice and even government policy documents, where it was used to argue for simplifying everything from pension plans to product ranges.

Explanations for the effect focused on the mental cost of deciding. Comparing many alternatives takes time and effort; each option rejected represents a possible loss; and a large range raises expectations, so that any single choice is more likely to disappoint. People faced with such difficulties may postpone the decision, choose a default option, or walk away altogether.

As the idea grew in popularity, however, other researchers tried to reproduce the original results, and many could not. Some found that larger assortments made no difference to people's willingness to choose; a few found that more options actually increased purchases or satisfaction. When one research team gathered together the results of dozens of published and unpublished experiments and combined them statistically, the average size of the choice-overload effect was close to zero. For a time, it seemed possible that the effect had been little more than a statistical accident, amplified by the tendency of journals and the media to report surprising findings more readily than unsurprising ones.

That conclusion, though, may have been premature. An average close to zero does not necessarily mean that an effect never occurs; it can also arise when an effect is strong in some situations and absent or reversed in others. Later analyses therefore asked not whether choice overload exists but when. They identified several conditions under which large assortments were more likely to discourage decisions: when the options were difficult to compare, when people had no clear preferences in advance, when the choice was complex or important, and when decision-makers were under time pressure. When shoppers already knew what they wanted, or when the options were arranged in a way that made comparison easy, large assortments caused few problems.

This more complicated picture has practical consequences. Retailers who dramatically reduced their product ranges on the strength of the jam study did not always see the increase in sales they expected, and some lost customers who had valued variety. Conversely, organisations offering complex, unfamiliar choices – such as pension funds or health insurance plans – may indeed help people by limiting the number of options or by providing clear categories, comparison tools or a well-designed default.

The history of the jam study offers a lesson not only about choice but about how psychological findings travel. A single vivid experiment, easy to describe in a sentence, can come to stand for a much more uncertain and conditional reality. The problem is rarely that the original researchers were wrong; the original result may well have been genuine in the circumstances in which it was obtained. The difficulty lies in treating a finding from one setting as a general law of human behaviour.

lesson.title: Hard Multiple Choice — precise claims and the writer's qualified position
lesson.text:
At Hard level:

Every option may contain passage language. You must judge the strength and scope of each claim (some / most / all, may / does, in certain conditions / generally). The writer often takes a qualified position. They accept part of an argument and reject part of it. The correct option reflects that balance. Distractors state one side too strongly.

Evidence may be spread across paragraphs. A question about "the later research" may need information from two places.

Strategy: for each option, underline its claim word (e.g. proved, always, no effect, depends) and check whether the passage supports that exact strength.
lesson.example: Passage: "The drug helped some patients, but in larger trials the average benefit was close to zero, although certain groups still seemed to respond." Best summary: the drug's benefit appears limited to particular groups. Too strong: the drug does not work. Also too strong: the drug is effective.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: What does the writer suggest about the jam study's results in paragraph A?

options.text: The large display was less popular with shoppers than the small one.
The large display was more effective at attracting interest than at producing sales.
Shoppers who saw the small display tasted more jam.
The number of jams had no effect on shoppers' behaviour.

questions.evidence: The larger display attracted more visitors, who stopped to look and taste. But when it came to buying, the result was reversed
questions.explanation: The large display attracted more interest but produced fewer sales. A reverses the visitor finding. D contradicts the sales difference.

questions.text: Why was the jam study considered surprising?

options.text: It was carried out in a shop rather than a laboratory.
It challenged a widely accepted assumption about the value of options.
It showed that people prefer cheaper products.
It was the first experiment to study consumer behaviour.

questions.evidence: it contradicted a principle that had seemed almost self-evident ... that people are better off with more options
questions.explanation: "Seemed almost self-evident" = "widely accepted assumption". A is a detail of the setting, not the reason the result was surprising.

questions.text: What does the writer imply about the way choice overload was used in paragraph B?

options.text: It was applied in areas far beyond the original research.
It was rejected by governments as unscientific.
It was supported by evidence from pension plans.
It was only accepted by businesses.

questions.evidence: cited in books, business advice and even government policy documents ... simplifying everything from pension plans to product ranges
questions.explanation: The word "even" and the range from pensions to products show how far the idea spread beyond its original evidence. This is an inference, and it is supported by the writer's later warning in Paragraph G. C is a trap: pensions were a policy target, not a source of evidence.

questions.text: What did the combined analysis described in paragraph D find?

options.text: Choice overload occurs in most situations.
More options always increase satisfaction.
The average effect across studies was negligible.
The original jam study had been falsified.

questions.evidence: the average size of the choice-overload effect was close to zero
questions.explanation: "Close to zero" = "negligible". B turns "a few found" into "always". D is not supported, and Paragraph G says the result "may well have been genuine".

questions.text: Why does the writer think the conclusion in paragraph D "may have been premature"?

options.text: Later studies found the original experiment had been misreported.
An average result can hide an effect that varies across situations.
Unpublished studies were not included in the analysis.
The effect was later shown to be larger than originally claimed.

questions.evidence: An average close to zero does not necessarily mean that an effect never occurs; it can also arise when an effect is strong in some situations and absent or reversed in others
questions.explanation: This is the writer's stated reason. C is contradicted: the combined analysis included "published and unpublished experiments". D is not stated.

questions.text: According to paragraph E, large assortments are LEAST likely to cause difficulties when

options.text: the decision is important and complex.
people are short of time.
shoppers have clear preferences beforehand.
the options are hard to compare.

questions.evidence: When shoppers already knew what they wanted ... large assortments caused few problems
questions.explanation: "Already knew what they wanted" = "clear preferences beforehand". A, B and D are the conditions under which large assortments are more likely to cause problems. This question tests careful reading of the direction of each condition.

questions.text: Which of the following best reflects the writer's view in paragraph G?

options.text: The researchers behind the jam study made serious errors.
Psychological findings should never be reported in the media.
A result valid in one context may be wrongly treated as universal.
Choice overload has been shown to be a myth.

questions.evidence: The difficulty lies in treating a finding from one setting as a general law of human behaviour
questions.explanation: This matches C. A is denied: "The problem is rarely that the original researchers were wrong". D is too strong for the writer's conditional view. B is too extreme and is never stated.

passages.topic: Archaeology — why did humans begin to farm?
passages.title: The Puzzle of the First Farmers

paragraphs.text: For more than ninety per cent of the time that modern humans have existed, they lived by hunting animals and gathering wild plants. Then, beginning around eleven thousand years ago in the region of south-west Asia often called the Fertile Crescent, and somewhat later and independently in several other parts of the world, some groups began to cultivate crops and keep domestic animals. Farming eventually made possible permanent villages, cities, writing and states. It is tempting, therefore, to see its adoption as an obvious improvement that people embraced as soon as they understood how to plant seeds. Archaeological evidence suggests that the reality was far less straightforward.

One reason for doubt comes from human skeletons. Studies comparing the remains of late hunter-gatherers with those of early farmers in the same regions have repeatedly found that the farmers were, on average, somewhat shorter, and that their bones and teeth show more signs of poor nutrition, disease and heavy physical strain. A diet based on a small number of cereal crops was less varied than that of foragers; people living closely together in permanent settlements with their animals were more exposed to infections; and a single failed harvest could bring hunger. Farming produced more food per area of land, allowing populations to grow, but it did not obviously make individual lives easier or healthier.

If farming was not immediately attractive, why did people adopt it? Several explanations have been proposed. One emphasises population pressure: as numbers of hunter-gatherers rose, wild food in some areas may have become insufficient, forcing people to find ways of producing more from the same land. A second focuses on climate. At the end of the last Ice Age, the climate of south-west Asia became warmer and wetter, allowing wild cereals to spread; but this warm period was interrupted by a return to colder, drier conditions lasting more than a thousand years. According to this view, communities that had come to depend on abundant wild cereals began deliberately planting them when natural supplies declined.

A third explanation places social life, rather than hunger, at the centre. Communities that gathered periodically for feasts, ceremonies and exchanges between groups would have needed large quantities of food at particular times – and cereals, which can be stored, and grain for brewing, might have been especially valuable for such occasions. On this view, cultivation began as a way of supporting social and religious gatherings, and only later became the basis of everyday subsistence.

Evidence relevant to this debate emerged from excavations at a hilltop site in what is now south-eastern Turkey, which began in the 1990s. There, archaeologists uncovered large circular enclosures formed by massive carved stone pillars, some weighing many tonnes and decorated with images of wild animals. Dating showed that the earliest structures had been built around eleven and a half thousand years ago – before there is clear evidence of domesticated plants or animals in the region. The builders, in other words, appear to have been hunter-gatherers, yet they were able to organise the labour of large numbers of people over long periods. Remains of wild animals and plants found at the site suggest that substantial quantities of food were processed there.

The discovery has been interpreted in different ways. Some researchers see it as strong support for the social explanation: the need to feed people gathered for construction and ceremonies may have encouraged the intensive harvesting, and eventually the cultivation, of wild cereals, some of the earliest domesticated forms of which have been traced to the surrounding area. Others are more cautious, noting that a single site, however remarkable, cannot show what motivated communities across a large region, and that climate and population changes could have been operating at the same time. What the site does make difficult to maintain is the older assumption that complex social organisation and monumental building could only follow the development of farming.

Many archaeologists now doubt that any single cause will explain the origins of agriculture everywhere. Farming arose independently in several regions with different climates, crops and societies, and the process in each seems to have been gradual, lasting centuries or millennia, with long periods in which people combined cultivation with hunting and gathering. The question may be less "Why did people invent farming?" than "Why did people, over many generations and for a variety of reasons, come to depend on it?"

lesson.title: Competing theories and how the evidence bears on them
lesson.text:
Hard passages often compare several explanations and then introduce evidence that affects them differently. Questions may ask which theory a finding challenges or what a discovery implies for an explanation. Build a quick grid in your head or on paper:

Theory Main claim Evidence for Evidence against

Then answer from the grid. Distractors frequently attach evidence to the wrong theory, or treat "challenges" as "disproves".
lesson.example: Passage: "Theory X says the lake dried because of farming; Theory Y blames a drought. Sediment shows the lake shrank before farms were built." What does the sediment suggest? Correct: it weakens Theory X. Traps: it proves Theory Y (too strong) and it supports Theory X (wrong direction).

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: What is the writer's purpose in paragraph A?

options.text: to argue that farming was a mistake
to question the idea that farming was an obvious improvement
to explain how seeds were first planted
to show that farming began in only one region

questions.evidence: It is tempting ... to see its adoption as an obvious improvement ... Archaeological evidence suggests that the reality was far less straightforward
questions.explanation: The paragraph sets up an assumption in order to question it. A is too strong: the writer never calls farming a mistake. D is contradicted by "independently in several other parts of the world".

questions.text: What does the evidence from skeletons suggest about early farmers?

options.text: They lived longer than hunter-gatherers.
Their populations were smaller than those of hunter-gatherers.
Their health was generally no better, and often worse, than that of foragers.
They suffered from hunger every year.

questions.evidence: the farmers were, on average, somewhat shorter ... more signs of poor nutrition, disease ... it did not obviously make individual lives easier or healthier
questions.explanation: C matches the careful strength of the claim ("no better, and often worse"). B reverses the claim about population, since farming allowed "populations to grow". D exaggerates: a failed harvest "could" bring hunger, not every year.

questions.text: According to the climate explanation in paragraph C, people began planting cereals because

options.text: the warmer, wetter climate made farming easier.
wild cereal supplies fell after conditions became colder and drier.
populations had grown too large for the land.
wild animals had disappeared from the region.

questions.evidence: interrupted by a return to colder, drier conditions ... communities that had come to depend on abundant wild cereals began deliberately planting them when natural supplies declined
questions.explanation: The trigger is the decline in wild supplies. A is a trap: the warmer period explains why wild cereals spread, not why people began planting. C belongs to the first explanation.

questions.text: How does the social explanation differ from the other two explanations?

options.text: It argues that farming began in response to food shortages.
It suggests that farming developed first to meet the needs of gatherings.
It denies that cereals were important to early communities.
It claims that farming began at the end of the Ice Age.

questions.evidence: places social life, rather than hunger, at the centre ... cultivation began as a way of supporting social and religious gatherings
questions.explanation: The social theory focuses on gatherings rather than hunger. A describes the other explanations. C is contradicted, because cereals are central to this view.

questions.text: Why is the dating of the site in Turkey significant?

options.text: It shows the site was built by early farmers.
It proves that the climate explanation is wrong.
It indicates that the builders had not yet adopted farming.
It shows that domesticated animals were kept at the site.

questions.evidence: built ... before there is clear evidence of domesticated plants or animals in the region. The builders ... appear to have been hunter-gatherers
questions.explanation: The dates place the building before farming. A is the opposite. B is too strong: Paragraph F notes climate may have operated "at the same time". D is contradicted by the remains of wild animals.

questions.text: What does the writer consider the most secure conclusion that can be drawn from the site?

options.text: Feasting was the only cause of agriculture.
Large-scale building did not have to wait for the development of farming.
Climate change had no influence on early farming.
Farming began at this single site and spread outwards.

questions.evidence: What the site does make difficult to maintain is the older assumption that complex social organisation and monumental building could only follow the development of farming
questions.explanation: The writer separates contested interpretations from this firmer conclusion. A and D contradict the cautious view that "a single site ... cannot show what motivated communities across a large region". C is contradicted by the same paragraph.

questions.text: Which statement best reflects the view expressed in paragraph G?

options.text: The origins of farming can be explained by population growth alone.
Farming was adopted suddenly in most regions.
Agriculture probably developed gradually and for different reasons in different places.
People abandoned hunting as soon as they began farming.

questions.evidence: any single cause ... Farming arose independently in several regions ... the process in each seems to have been gradual
questions.explanation: C combines "gradual" with "different reasons". A reduces the explanation to one cause, which the writer rejects. B and D are contradicted by "gradual" and by the "long periods" in which people combined cultivation with hunting and gathering.

passages.topic: Geography and climate — glaciers and the problem of "peak water"
passages.title: Borrowed Water

paragraphs.text: Mountain glaciers are sometimes described as the "water towers" of the world. During cold months they store precipitation as ice, and during warm months they release it gradually as meltwater, feeding rivers that supply drinking water, farms and hydroelectric power stations far downstream. In several regions – parts of the Andes and Central Asia, for example – glacier melt makes up a substantial proportion of river flow during the hottest and driest part of the year, precisely when rainfall is lowest and demand for water is highest.

As the climate warms, most of the world's mountain glaciers are shrinking. It might seem to follow that the rivers they feed are already carrying less water. In many places, however, the opposite has been observed: summer river flows have increased. The explanation is that a retreating glacier is losing more ice each year than it gains from snowfall. The extra meltwater is not new water but water drawn from a store that accumulated over centuries. In effect, downstream users are receiving a temporary bonus, borrowed from the glacier's past.

This situation cannot last. As a glacier becomes smaller, the area of ice exposed to summer warmth also shrinks, so that even if temperatures continue to rise, the total volume of meltwater eventually starts to fall. Scientists call the moment of maximum meltwater "peak water". After this point, summer flows decline, and they continue to decline until the glacier has either disappeared or reached a new, much smaller balance with the climate. The river will then depend on rainfall and seasonal snowmelt alone, which in dry regions may provide little water in late summer.

Estimating when peak water will occur is difficult, and the answer varies greatly between regions. It depends on the size of the glaciers, their altitude, how quickly the local climate is warming, and how much of a river's flow comes from ice rather than rain. Studies of some small, low-altitude glaciers suggest that peak water has already passed, and that the summer decline has begun. For basins fed by large, high-altitude glaciers, models suggest that the peak may not arrive for several decades. Because of these differences, a single global date for peak water is not meaningful.

The concept has important implications for planning. During the period of rising meltwater, communities may reasonably conclude from recent experience that water supplies are plentiful, or even increasing. Farmers may expand irrigated land, towns may grow, and new hydroelectric projects may be designed around current flows. If these decisions do not take account of the eventual decline, they risk creating a dependence on water that will not be available in the long term. The danger, several researchers have warned, is not simply that water will become scarcer, but that the temporary abundance will encourage people to become more reliant on it just before it diminishes.

Some commentators have argued that the impact of glacier loss on water supplies has been exaggerated. They point out that in many large river basins, glacier melt accounts for only a small share of the total annual flow, most of which comes from rain and seasonal snow. For the people living along these rivers, changes in rainfall patterns may matter far more than the fate of distant glaciers. Researchers generally accept this point, but argue that annual totals can be misleading. The contribution of glaciers is often concentrated in particular seasons and in years of drought, when other sources fail. A glacier that supplies a modest share of a river's water over a whole year may supply most of it in a dry late summer.

Glaciers also affect water supplies in less obvious ways. Meltwater keeps rivers cool, which matters for fish and for power stations that use river water for cooling. As glaciers retreat, lakes can form behind unstable piles of rock left by the ice, and these may burst without warning, sending floods into valleys below. Managing the consequences of glacier loss therefore involves not only planning for reduced summer water but also monitoring new hazards.

None of this implies that nothing can be done. Reservoirs can store water from wetter periods, irrigation can be made more efficient, and planners can use scenarios based on peak water rather than on the experience of recent decades. What the concept teaches, above all, is that present conditions can be a poor guide to the future when they are being sustained by a resource that is steadily being used up.

lesson.title: Counter-intuitive ideas
lesson.text: Some Hard passages explain an idea that goes against common sense. Here, for example, melting glaciers first increase the amount of water available and only later reduce it. Questions will test whether you have followed the argument precisely, and distractors will offer the "common-sense" version. When a passage signals surprise (paradoxically, counter-intuitively, at first sight, in fact), slow down and restate the idea in your own words before reading the options.
lesson.example: Passage: "Paradoxically, the new bypass increased traffic in the town centre, because it made the town easier to reach." Why did traffic increase? Correct: improved access attracted more visitors. Trap: the bypass sent traffic through the centre.

passages.topic: Architecture and history — how medieval cathedrals stayed standing
passages.title: Stone, Light and Balance

paragraphs.text: Visitors to the great cathedrals built in Europe between the twelfth and fifteenth centuries are often struck by two apparently contradictory impressions. The buildings are enormous and made almost entirely of stone, yet their interiors seem light, even weightless: walls are pierced by vast windows, columns are slender, and vaults rise to heights that would have seemed impossible to earlier builders. How such structures remained standing, without steel frames or modern calculations, has fascinated engineers for centuries.

The key lies in understanding how stone behaves. Stone is extremely strong when it is squeezed – in compression – but weak when it is pulled or bent. A stone building therefore stands only as long as the forces within it flow through the masonry as compression, following paths that remain inside the material. An arch achieves this by transforming the downward weight of what it carries into forces that travel along its curve to its supports. However, those forces do not arrive at the supports vertically. An arch also pushes outwards, and the outward push, or "thrust", becomes greater as the load increases and as the arch becomes flatter.

Earlier European churches dealt with this thrust in the simplest possible way: by making their walls very thick. A massive wall could absorb the outward push of a stone vault because the combined weight of the wall redirected the thrust downwards into the foundations. But thick walls allowed only small windows, since any large opening would weaken the wall at precisely the point where it needed to resist the vault. The resulting buildings were solid and often impressive, but relatively dark.

The builders of the later cathedrals combined several innovations that changed this situation. Pointed arches, rather than semicircular ones, directed more of the vault's weight downwards and produced less outward thrust for a given height. Ribbed vaults concentrated the loads of the ceiling onto a small number of points, rather than spreading them along the whole length of a wall. And, most visibly, flying buttresses – arches of stone springing from separate piers outside the building – reached over the side aisles to meet the walls at the points where the vault's thrust arrived, carrying that thrust away from the main structure and down to the ground.

The effect of these innovations taken together was that the walls between the points of support no longer had to resist the vault. They could be made thinner, and much of their area could be replaced by glass. The spectacular windows of the period were thus not a decoration added to a solid structure but a consequence of a structural system that had moved the work of support elsewhere.

It is sometimes assumed that the medieval builders understood these principles in the way a modern engineer would, or alternatively that they worked by pure luck. Neither view appears to be correct. The builders had no theory of forces in the modern sense and did not calculate stresses. They relied instead on geometrical rules of proportion, passed down within workshops, and on accumulated experience of what had stood and what had failed. Failures were not rare: parts of several cathedrals collapsed during or after construction, and in at least one well-known case the choir vault fell only a few years after completion and had to be rebuilt with additional supports. Each failure added to the knowledge of the building trade.

Modern analysis has shown that many of the surviving structures work with a considerable margin of safety, because the stresses in the stone are generally far below the level at which it would be crushed. What matters is not the strength of the material but the geometry of the structure: as long as the lines of thrust stay within the masonry, the building remains stable. This insight has shifted attention from the material to the shape, and it helps explain why buildings that seem daringly thin have survived for eight hundred years. It also explains why these buildings can be vulnerable to changes that alter their geometry, such as the movement of foundations, which may push the lines of force outside the stone.

lesson.title: Technical explanations without technical knowledge
lesson.text:
Hard passages sometimes explain an engineering or scientific principle. You are not expected to know the subject; everything you need is in the text. Distractors in such passages often: sound technically plausible but are not stated, which is an outside-knowledge trap; confuse two related forces or components;

reverse the direction of a relationship (taller walls → more outward push, not less). Paraphrase each technical sentence into plain language as you read, for example: "the roof pushes the walls outward".
lesson.example: Passage: "The heavier the load on an arch, the more strongly it pushes sideways against its supports." Which is true? Correct: increasing the load increases sideways force. Trap: heavier arches need no side support.

between the heavy material used and the light appearance of the interiors
between the height of the vaults and the width of the columns
between medieval and modern methods of construction

the arch is made steeper.
the arch carries more weight or is flatter.
the stone is placed in compression.

Large openings would have weakened walls needed to resist thrust.
Builders preferred dark interiors for religious reasons.
Their vaults were too low to allow tall windows.

questions.evidence: any large opening would weaken the wall at precisely the point where it needed to resist the vault

flying buttresses
pointed arches
thick walls
