questions.explanation: Ribbed vaults concentrate loads (A) and flying buttresses carry thrust away (B). Neither is said to reduce thrust. The distractors confuse related components.

questions.text: What does the writer imply about the large windows of the later cathedrals?

options.text: They were added after the buildings were completed.
They made the buildings structurally weaker.
They were made possible by the way support was redistributed.
They were mainly intended to reduce the weight of the walls.

Their success was largely due to chance.
They learned from experience, including structural failures.
They calculated the stresses in each part of a building.

questions.explanation: The writer explicitly rejects both "modern theory" (A, D) and "pure luck" (B) with "Neither view appears to be correct".

questions.text: According to paragraph G, why might an old cathedral become unstable?

options.text: because the stone gradually loses its strength
because changes in shape can move the lines of force outside the stone
because its margin of safety was always very small
because modern visitors add too much weight

questions.evidence: changes that alter their geometry, such as the movement of foundations, which may push the lines of force outside the stone
questions.explanation: A is contradicted by "what matters is not the strength of the material". C is contradicted by "considerable margin of safety". D is not mentioned.

passages.topic: Psychology and technology — navigation apps and spatial memory
passages.title: Lost Without the Map?

paragraphs.text: For most of history, finding one's way through an unfamiliar city required attention and effort. Travellers studied maps, noted landmarks and gradually built a mental picture of how streets connected. Today many people rely instead on satellite navigation applications that announce every turn in advance. The convenience is undeniable, but it has prompted a question that psychologists and neuroscientists have begun to investigate seriously: if we no longer need to form mental maps, will we gradually lose the ability to do so?

Interest in this question owes much to research on a group of people famous for their navigational skill: licensed taxi drivers in London. To qualify, drivers must learn the layout of tens of thousands of streets and be able to plan routes between any two points without consulting a map, a process that typically takes several years. Brain scans comparing qualified drivers with people who were not taxi drivers found that a region of the brain known to be involved in spatial memory, the hippocampus, was larger in its rear part among the drivers. Moreover, the difference was greater among drivers who had been working for longer.

This finding was striking, but on its own it could not show that learning the streets had changed the drivers' brains. It was possible, for example, that people who already had a larger hippocampus were more likely to choose the job or to succeed in the training. A later study addressed this problem by following trainee drivers over time. Brain scans taken before training showed no difference between the trainees and a comparison group. After several years, the trainees who had qualified showed growth in the relevant region, whereas those who had failed or abandoned the training, and the members of the comparison group, did not. This design made it considerably more plausible that the training itself was responsible.

If intensive navigation can strengthen the relevant brain systems, could relying on navigation apps weaken them? Several studies have explored this possibility. In one, researchers found that people who reported using satellite navigation more often performed worse on tests of spatial memory, such as remembering the layout of a virtual environment. When a subset of participants was tested again several years later, those whose use of navigation apps had increased most showed the greatest decline in their spatial memory over that period.

The researchers were careful not to overstate their conclusions. People who find navigation difficult may be more likely to rely on apps in the first place, which would produce the same association in the opposite direction. The follow-up results made that explanation less likely, since participants did not report beginning to use apps because they felt they had a poor sense of direction. Even so, the study relied partly on participants' own reports of how often they used navigation apps, and it did not randomly assign people to use them or not. Such an experiment would be difficult to carry out over a period of years.

Laboratory experiments offer a clearer, if narrower, picture. When people follow turn-by-turn instructions through a route, they typically remember less about the environment than people who navigate using a map or their own judgement: they recall fewer landmarks and are less able to draw the route afterwards. Brain-imaging studies have found that activity in regions associated with planning routes is lower when people follow instructions than when they must choose their own way. These results concern short-term effects of a single journey, however, and cannot on their own show that the habit of using apps produces lasting changes.

It would be wrong, then, to conclude that navigation apps are harming the brains of an entire generation. What the evidence does suggest is that spatial memory, like many mental abilities, responds to use: it is strengthened by active practice and may weaken when the effort is consistently handed over to a device. Some researchers have proposed that apps could be designed to encourage rather than replace this effort – for example, by showing the overall route and nearby landmarks rather than announcing each turn in isolation. For individuals, the simplest suggestion is occasionally to switch the app off and find the way without it.

lesson.title: Correlation, causation and research design
lesson.text:
Many research passages distinguish between finding that two things occur together (correlation) and showing that one causes the other (causation). Hard questions test whether you notice the writer's caution. Distractors turn "is associated with" into "causes", or ignore a limitation the writer mentions.

Watch for signals of study design: compared, followed over time, randomly assigned, before and after. Watch also for the writer's caveats: this does not prove, cannot rule out, it is possible that.
lesson.example: Passage: "People who drink more coffee tend to live longer, but coffee drinkers may also differ in income and exercise." Correct conclusion: the link may be explained by other factors. Trap: coffee extends life.

whether dependence on apps may reduce our ability to form mental maps
why travellers find unfamiliar cities confusing

questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase. A, C and D are not raised as questions.

those who were tested in a virtual environment

options.text: It was carried out over too short a period.
It included only people with a poor sense of direction.
It depended partly on what participants said about their own behaviour.
It randomly assigned participants to groups.

questions.evidence: the study relied partly on participants' own reports of how often they used navigation apps
questions.explanation: "Participants' own reports" = "what participants said about their own behaviour". D reverses the other limitation: the study did not randomly assign participants.

questions.text: What does the writer say about the laboratory experiments in paragraph F?

options.text: They prove that apps cause permanent memory loss.
They were carried out only with taxi drivers.
They found no difference between map users and app users.
They show short-term effects but not long-term ones.

questions.evidence: These results concern short-term effects of a single journey ... cannot on their own show that the habit ... produces lasting changes
questions.explanation: A turns this into proof of a lasting effect, which the writer denies. C contradicts the reported differences.

questions.text: Which statement best reflects the writer's conclusion?

options.text: Navigation apps are damaging the brains of a whole generation.
Spatial memory depends on use, and apps might be designed to support it.
People should never use navigation apps.
The research on navigation is too weak to draw any conclusions.

questions.evidence: spatial memory ... responds to use ... apps could be designed to encourage rather than replace this effort
questions.explanation: A is explicitly rejected ("It would be wrong ... to conclude"). C is too extreme compared with "occasionally switch the app off". D contradicts "What the evidence does suggest".

passages.topic: Ecology — wolves, elk and a disputed chain of effects
passages.title: What the Wolves Changed

paragraphs.text: In 1995 and 1996, a small number of grey wolves were captured in Canada and released into Yellowstone National Park in the United States, where wolves had been deliberately eliminated by the early twentieth century. In the years that followed, a remarkable story spread through scientific papers, documentaries and popular articles. According to this account, the return of the wolves had set off a chain of effects through the entire ecosystem. By hunting elk – large deer that had become very numerous in the wolves' absence – the predators had allowed trees such as willow and aspen, which elk eat, to recover along rivers. The recovering trees in turn stabilised riverbanks, provided habitat for birds and supplied food and building material for beavers, whose dams created wetlands. The wolves, it was said, had even changed the shape of the rivers.

Ecologists call this kind of chain a "trophic cascade": a change at the top of a food web that spreads downwards through the animals and plants below. The idea was not new, and cascades had been clearly demonstrated in some simpler systems, such as coastal waters where sea otters, by eating sea urchins, protected kelp forests from being grazed away. Yellowstone seemed to offer a spectacular example on land, and the story became one of the most widely cited arguments for restoring large predators.

Two mechanisms were proposed to explain how wolves might affect trees. The first was simple: wolves kill elk, so fewer elk remain to eat young trees. The second was more subtle. Researchers suggested that elk, aware of the danger of wolves, avoided places where they would be especially vulnerable to attack – such as river valleys with limited visibility or escape routes – and that plants in these places recovered even if elk numbers had not fallen much. This idea, which became known as the "landscape of fear", was particularly appealing because it suggested that predators could reshape ecosystems through behaviour alone.

Later research has made the picture considerably more complicated. Studies that tracked elk with satellite collars found that elk did adjust their behaviour in response to wolves, but mainly at certain times of day, since wolves hunt mostly around dawn and dusk and at night. Elk could still use supposedly risky areas during daylight hours, and there was little evidence that they abandoned such places altogether. Other studies measuring tree growth found that recovery was patchy: willow and aspen had grown taller in some places but not in others, and in many areas young trees were still being heavily browsed.

Researchers also pointed out that wolves were not the only factor affecting elk numbers, which declined considerably after the reintroduction. Populations of bears and mountain lions, which also prey on elk, had increased. Human hunting of elk that wandered outside the park continued. A series of dry years may have reduced the quality of the elk's food. Distinguishing the contribution of wolves from these other influences is extremely difficult in a large, open ecosystem where no controlled experiment is possible.

A further complication concerns the rivers themselves. During the decades without wolves, heavy browsing and the loss of beavers had allowed many streams to cut deeper channels, lowering the water table beside them. Where this had happened, even a large reduction in elk browsing did not necessarily allow willows to return, because the ground beside the streams had become too dry. Some researchers have therefore argued that parts of the ecosystem may have shifted into a new state from which they cannot easily return simply by restoring the missing predator.

None of this means that the wolves had no effect. Most researchers accept that wolves have contributed to the decline in elk numbers and that this has benefited trees in at least some places. What has been questioned is the simplicity and scale of the original story. The Yellowstone case suggests that the effects of restoring a predator depend on many other features of an ecosystem, including what has changed during the predator's absence. Restoring a missing species may be a necessary step in repairing an ecosystem, but it is not always a sufficient one.

lesson.title: When a famous story is revised
lesson.example: Passage: "The statue was long believed to be Roman. Recent tests suggest parts are Roman but the head was added in the eighteenth century." Best summary: the statue combines ancient and later parts. Traps: it is entirely Roman and it is an eighteenth-century fake.

groups.title: Choose the correct letter
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: According to the popular account in paragraph A, the recovery of trees along rivers was

options.text: the direct result of wolves attacking trees.
a consequence of wolves reducing the pressure from elk.
caused by beavers building dams.
unrelated to the reintroduction of wolves.

questions.evidence: By hunting elk ... the predators had allowed trees such as willow and aspen, which elk eat, to recover
questions.explanation: The wolves helped trees indirectly, by reducing elk. C reverses the sequence, since beavers came after the trees recovered. A is not supported.

questions.text: Why does the writer mention sea otters and kelp forests?

options.text: to show that trophic cascades have been clearly demonstrated in some systems
to argue that the Yellowstone story was false
to compare the size of marine and land predators
to show that cascades occur only in the sea

questions.evidence: cascades had been clearly demonstrated in some simpler systems, such as coastal waters where sea otters ...
questions.explanation: The otters show an established example of a cascade. D is contradicted by "on land". B confuses this paragraph with the later revision of the story.

questions.text: What made the "landscape of fear" idea especially attractive?

options.text: It proved that elk numbers had fallen dramatically.
It implied that predators could affect plants without greatly reducing prey numbers.
It showed that wolves hunt mainly during the day.
It explained why beavers had disappeared.

questions.evidence: plants in these places recovered even if elk numbers had not fallen much ... predators could reshape ecosystems through behaviour alone
questions.explanation: The idea's appeal was that fear alone could have effects. A contradicts "not fallen much". C contradicts Paragraph D, which says wolves hunt mainly around dawn, dusk and night.

questions.text: What did studies using satellite collars reveal about elk behaviour?

options.text: Elk completely abandoned river valleys after wolves returned.
Elk showed no response to the presence of wolves.
Elk changed their behaviour, but mainly at particular times.
Elk moved permanently outside the national park.

questions.evidence: elk did adjust their behaviour ... but mainly at certain times of day
questions.explanation: This captures both parts of the finding. A is contradicted by "little evidence that they abandoned such places". B is contradicted by "did adjust".

questions.text: Why does the writer list bears, mountain lions, human hunting and dry years in paragraph E?

options.text: to show that these factors were more important than wolves
to explain why the role of wolves is hard to isolate
to suggest that wolves had no effect on elk numbers
to describe the results of a controlled experiment

questions.evidence: Distinguishing the contribution of wolves from these other influences is extremely difficult
questions.explanation: The list shows other possible causes, which makes the wolves' role hard to separate. A and C go further than the passage, since the writer never ranks or denies the wolves' effect (see Paragraph G). D contradicts "no controlled experiment is possible".

questions.text: According to paragraph F, why did willows sometimes fail to return even where browsing fell?

options.text: Beavers ate the young willows.
The land beside some streams had become too dry.
Wolves avoided the river valleys.
Elk numbers increased again.

questions.evidence: even a large reduction in elk browsing did not necessarily allow willows to return, because the ground beside the streams had become too dry
questions.explanation: This is stated directly. A, C and D are not mentioned.

questions.text: What is the writer's overall conclusion about the Yellowstone story?

options.text: The wolves were solely responsible for restoring the ecosystem.
The original story was entirely mistaken.
Wolves had real effects, but restoring them alone may not reverse all earlier changes.
Predators should not be reintroduced to national parks.

questions.evidence: None of this means that the wolves had no effect ... Restoring a missing species may be a necessary step ... but it is not always a sufficient one
questions.explanation: This is the qualified middle position. A and B are the two extremes the writer rejects. D is not stated and conflicts with "necessary step".

passages.topic: Wildlife — the migration of the Arctic tern
passages.title: The Longest Journey

paragraphs.text: The Arctic tern is a slender seabird, weighing little more than a hundred grams – roughly the weight of a small apple. Its grey and white feathers, black cap and bright red beak make it easy to recognise, but its appearance gives little hint of its most remarkable characteristic. Each year, the Arctic tern makes the longest migration known of any animal, travelling from its breeding grounds in the far north to the seas around Antarctica and back again.

Arctic terns breed during the northern summer in a wide area around the Arctic, including parts of northern Europe, Greenland, Canada and Alaska. They usually nest in colonies on the ground, often on small islands or coastal gravel, where they lay one to three eggs in a simple hollow. The adults defend their nests fiercely, diving at any intruder – including humans – and striking with their sharp beaks. Once the chicks can fly, the birds begin their journey south.

For many years, the full extent of this journey could only be estimated. Scientists knew that terns ringed in the north were later found in the south, but they had little information about the routes the birds took. This changed in the early twenty-first century, when researchers attached tiny tracking devices, weighing about as much as a paper clip, to terns nesting in Greenland and Iceland. The devices recorded the level of daylight, which allowed the birds' approximate position to be calculated each day.

The results were surprising. Rather than flying directly from north to south, the birds followed winding routes. Many flew south along the coast of western Europe and Africa, then some crossed the Atlantic to follow the coast of South America, while others continued along the African side. On their return journey, they travelled in a large S-shaped path across the Atlantic. These routes are much longer than the straight-line distance, but they allow the birds to take advantage of prevailing winds, which reduce the energy needed for flight. The tracked terns covered, on average, around 70,000 kilometres in a single year.

The journey is not made in a single effort. The terns stop for several weeks in areas of the North Atlantic where food is plentiful, feeding on small fish and other creatures near the surface of the sea. Here they build up the energy they need to continue. They also feed while travelling, catching fish by hovering briefly above the water and then diving in.

Because they spend the northern summer in the Arctic and then travel to Antarctic waters during the southern summer, Arctic terns experience two summers each year. As a result, they probably see more daylight than any other creature on Earth. Near the poles, the sun does not set at all for part of the summer, so for much of their lives the terns live in almost continuous light.

Arctic terns are also long-lived for a bird of their size. Individuals have been recorded reaching an age of more than thirty years. Over such a lifetime, a single tern may fly a total distance roughly equal to three return journeys from the Earth to the Moon.

Although the species is widespread, some populations have declined, and scientists are concerned about the effects of changes in the ocean on the fish the terns depend on. Because they breed in the north, feed in the Atlantic and spend part of the year in the far south, Arctic terns are affected by conditions across a large part of the planet – which also makes them useful indicators of the health of the world's oceans.

lesson.title: Numbers and dates
lesson.text: In easy sets, many statements contain a number, a date or a distance. Find that figure or a close equivalent in the passage (70,000 may appear as seventy thousand, and half as 50%). Then check what the number refers to. A statement can use the right number for the wrong thing (FALSE), or add a detail about the number that the passage never gives (NOT GIVEN).
lesson.example: Passage: "The tower is 90 metres tall." Statement: "The tower is 90 metres wide." → FALSE? No: the passage says nothing about width, so it is NOT GIVEN. It would be FALSE only if the passage gave a different width.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage? Write
TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this

questions.text: An Arctic tern weighs more than a kilogram.
questions.evidence: weighing little more than a hundred grams
questions.explanation: A hundred grams is far less than a kilogram, so the passage contradicts the statement.

questions.text: Arctic terns usually return to the same nesting site every year.
questions.evidence: Paragraph B describes where terns nest ("in colonies on the ground, often on small islands or coastal gravel").
questions.explanation: The passage never says whether individual birds return to the same site each year, so the statement cannot be confirmed or contradicted.

questions.text: Adult terns may attack people who come close to their nests.
questions.evidence: diving at any intruder – including humans – and striking with their sharp beaks
questions.explanation: "Striking ... intruders including humans" = "may attack people".

questions.text: Before the tracking study, scientists had no evidence that Arctic terns travelled south.
questions.evidence: Scientists knew that terns ringed in the north were later found in the south
questions.explanation: Scientists already had evidence from ringed birds before the tracking study. What they lacked was information about the routes.

questions.text: The terns' routes between north and south were longer than a direct flight would be.
questions.evidence: These routes are much longer than the straight-line distance
questions.explanation: "Straight-line distance" = "direct flight".

questions.text: Terns rest for several weeks in the North Atlantic where there is plenty of food.
questions.evidence: The terns stop for several weeks in areas of the North Atlantic where food is plentiful
questions.explanation: "Stop" = "rest", and "plentiful" = "plenty of food".

questions.text: Arctic terns sleep while flying over the ocean.
questions.evidence: Paragraph E describes feeding while travelling, but the passage never mentions sleep.
questions.explanation: Nothing confirms or contradicts the statement.

questions.text: Arctic tern populations have declined in every region where they breed.
questions.evidence: Although the species is widespread, some populations have declined
questions.explanation: "Some" contradicts "every region". This is a qualifier trap. Note that it is FALSE, not NOT GIVEN, because "some populations have declined" means the decline is not universal.

passages.topic: Food science and business — the invention of frozen food
passages.title: The Fisherman's Discovery

paragraphs.text: People have preserved food by cold for thousands of years, storing it in cellars, caves or pits packed with ice and snow. By the late nineteenth century, factories in several countries were producing ice artificially, and meat and fish were being frozen for transport over long distances. Yet frozen food had a poor reputation. When it was thawed, it was often soft, watery and lacking in flavour, and many shoppers regarded it as suitable only for people who could afford nothing better.

The man who did most to change this reputation was Clarence Birdseye, an American naturalist who, in the 1910s, spent several years working in Labrador, in the far north-east of Canada. There, he observed how local Inuit fishermen preserved their catch. In temperatures far below freezing, fish pulled from holes in the ice froze almost instantly in the open air. When they were cooked months later, Birdseye noticed, they tasted almost as fresh as newly caught fish.

Birdseye realised that the speed of freezing was the key. When food freezes slowly, large ice crystals form inside it, breaking the walls of the cells. When the food thaws, water escapes through the damaged cells, and the texture and flavour are lost. When food freezes very rapidly, the crystals remain small and the cells are largely undamaged. The problem with commercial frozen food was not freezing itself but the slow methods being used.

After returning to the United States, Birdseye set out to reproduce the conditions of the Arctic in a factory. His first business, established in the early 1920s, failed through lack of money. Undeterred, he developed a new machine in which food was packed into flat cartons and pressed between metal plates chilled to very low temperatures. Because the packages were thin and in close contact with the cold metal, they froze in a fraction of the time required by earlier methods. He also froze food in the carton in which it would be sold, which made it easier to store, transport and display.

The new process attracted the attention of large food companies, and in 1929 Birdseye sold his business and his patents for a considerable sum. The following year, frozen vegetables, fruit, meat and fish went on sale in a group of shops in the state of Massachusetts, under a brand name based on Birdseye's own.

Success did not come immediately. Few shops owned freezers to display the food, and few households owned freezers to store it at home. The manufacturers began renting display freezers to shops at low cost, and sales grew gradually through the 1930s. During the Second World War, when metal for food cans was in short supply in the United States, frozen foods packed in cardboard became more attractive, and their popularity increased considerably.

Birdseye himself continued to invent throughout his life, taking out many patents on subjects ranging from lighting to the removal of water from food. But it is for quick freezing that he is remembered. His achievement was not the discovery of freezing, which was already widely used, but the combination of scientific understanding with practical engineering and a new approach to packaging and selling – a combination that transformed the way many people buy and eat food.

lesson.title: "First", "only" and other strong words
lesson.text:
Statements often contain words that make a strong claim: first, only, never, always, all, the most. The passage may support the topic but not the strength of the claim.

If the passage says someone was among the first, a statement saying they were the first is usually NOT GIVEN. It would be FALSE only if the passage names someone earlier. If the passage says others had tried before, then a statement that X was the first to try is FALSE.
lesson.example: Passage: "Several companies had made electric cars before 1900." Statement: "The first electric car was made in 1920." → FALSE, because cars existed before 1900.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Before Birdseye's work, meat and fish were already being frozen for transport.
questions.evidence: meat and fish were being frozen for transport over long distances
questions.explanation: This happened by the late nineteenth century, before Birdseye's work in the 1910s.

questions.text: In the early twentieth century, frozen food was generally considered to be of high quality.
questions.evidence: frozen food had a poor reputation ... suitable only for people who could afford nothing better
questions.explanation: "Poor reputation" contradicts "high quality".

questions.text: Birdseye was the first person to freeze fish.
questions.evidence: "Inuit fishermen preserved their catch ... fish ... froze almost instantly" (Paragraph B), and meat and fish were already being frozen commercially (Paragraph A)
questions.explanation: The passage shows that fish were frozen before Birdseye, which makes "the first" impossible.

questions.text: Birdseye worked in Labrador for more than ten years.
questions.evidence: spent several years working in Labrador
questions.explanation: "Several years" does not tell us whether the period was more or less than ten years. The passage neither confirms nor contradicts the statement.

questions.text: Slow freezing creates large ice crystals that damage food.
questions.evidence: When food freezes slowly, large ice crystals form inside it, breaking the walls of the cells
questions.explanation: "Breaking cell walls" = "damage food".

questions.text: Birdseye's first company was successful.
questions.evidence: His first business ... failed through lack of money
questions.explanation: "Failed" contradicts "successful".

questions.text: Frozen food first went on sale in Massachusetts in 1930.
questions.evidence: in 1929 Birdseye sold his business ... The following year, frozen vegetables ... went on sale in a group of shops in the state of Massachusetts
questions.explanation: "The following year" after 1929 = 1930. The passage describes this as the moment the products went on sale.

questions.text: Birdseye later regretted selling his business.
questions.evidence: Paragraph E states that he sold the business "for a considerable sum". His feelings about the sale are never mentioned.
questions.explanation: Nothing confirms or contradicts any regret.

passages.topic: Society and culture — the changing public library
passages.title: More Than Books

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the public library had a clear and familiar purpose. It lent books, provided a quiet place to read and study, and offered reference works such as encyclopaedias and dictionaries that most families could not afford to buy. Librarians helped users find information, and silence was expected, if not always achieved.

The arrival of the internet at the end of the century led many commentators to predict that libraries would soon become unnecessary. If information could be found instantly online, and books could be bought cheaply or read on screens, why would anyone need a building full of printed material? In a number of countries, local authorities under financial pressure reduced library opening hours, and some branches were closed.

The predicted disappearance, however, has not taken place. In many places, libraries remain among the most heavily used public buildings, although the ways in which they are used have changed considerably. Book lending in many areas has fallen from its peak, but visits have fallen less sharply, and some libraries report that the number of people coming through their doors has grown.

One reason is that access to the internet is not as universal as it may seem. Many people do not have a computer or a reliable internet connection at home, and a growing number of essential services – from applying for jobs to claiming benefits and booking medical appointments – are now available mainly or only online. Libraries provide free computers and internet access, and staff often help people who have little experience of using them. In this sense, the library's traditional role of providing access to information continues, even though the form of that information has changed.

Libraries have also taken on new functions. Many now offer spaces where people can meet, work or study together, and noise is often allowed in some areas while quiet zones are kept for those who need them. Some have created "makerspaces" equipped with tools such as 3D printers, sewing machines and recording equipment that members of the public can use. Others lend items that people need only occasionally, such as tools, musical instruments or cooking equipment. Libraries run activities for young children, language classes, reading groups and advice sessions on subjects such as money and health.

These changes have not been welcomed by everyone. Some regular users regret the loss of silence and feel that libraries are becoming community centres in which books are no longer central. Supporters of the changes reply that libraries have always adapted to the needs of their communities, and that lending tools or hosting classes is consistent with the original idea of the public library: giving everyone access to resources they could not easily obtain on their own.

The buildings themselves have changed too. Several cities have built large new central libraries in recent decades, designed with open, flexible spaces, cafés and areas for events, and some of these have become popular public landmarks. At the same time, smaller neighbourhood branches in many areas continue to face uncertain futures, since their funding often depends on local budgets.

lesson.title: Cause-and-effect statements
lesson.text:
A statement may connect two facts with because, so, led to, as a result. Check carefully: The passage gives the same cause → TRUE.

The passage gives a different cause, or says the connection does not exist → FALSE. The passage mentions both facts but gives no link between them → NOT GIVEN.
lesson.example: Passage: "The café changed its menu in May. Its sales rose in June." Statement: "Sales rose because of the new menu." → NOT GIVEN. Both events are mentioned, but no cause is stated.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: In the twentieth century, libraries offered reference books that many families could not afford.
questions.evidence: reference works such as encyclopaedias and dictionaries that most families could not afford to buy
questions.explanation: The statement says "many" and the passage says "most". Since most includes many, the statement is TRUE.

questions.text: Some commentators expected the internet to make libraries unnecessary.
questions.evidence: led many commentators to predict that libraries would soon become unnecessary
questions.explanation: "Predict" = "expected".

questions.text: Libraries were closed because too few people used them.
questions.evidence: local authorities under financial pressure reduced library opening hours, and some branches were closed
questions.explanation: The passage mentions financial pressure but does not say the closures were caused by low use. The cause in the statement is neither confirmed nor contradicted.

questions.text: In many areas, book lending has decreased.
questions.evidence: Book lending in many areas has fallen from its peak
questions.explanation: "Fallen" = "decreased".

questions.text: All government services can now be accessed only online.
questions.evidence: a growing number of essential services ... are now available mainly or only online
questions.explanation: "Mainly or only" shows that not all services are online-only, which contradicts "all".

questions.text: Libraries in some places lend musical instruments.
questions.evidence: Others lend items ... such as tools, musical instruments or cooking equipment
questions.explanation: "Others" means some libraries, which matches "some places".

questions.text: All regular library users support the recent changes.
questions.evidence: These changes have not been welcomed by everyone. Some regular users regret the loss of silence
questions.explanation: This directly contradicts "all ... support".

questions.text: New central libraries have attracted more visitors than old ones.
questions.evidence: New central libraries "have become popular public landmarks"
questions.explanation: No comparison of visitor numbers with older libraries is made.

passages.topic: Transport history — the world's first underground railway
passages.title: Trains Beneath the Streets

paragraphs.text: By the middle of the nineteenth century, London was the largest city in the world, and its streets were among the most crowded. Horse-drawn buses, carts and carriages competed for space in narrow roads, and journeys across the city could take hours. The problem was made worse by the fact that the main railway lines, built by separate private companies, ended at stations on the edge of the central area. Passengers arriving from the rest of the country then had to continue their journeys by road.

Several people proposed a solution: a railway running beneath the streets, connecting the main-line stations with the business district of the City of London. The idea was widely ridiculed at first. Critics doubted that passengers would be willing to travel in tunnels filled with smoke from steam engines, and some worried that the digging would damage buildings above. Nevertheless, after years of argument and difficulty in raising money, construction of the first line began in 1860.

The method used was known as "cut and cover". Workers dug a deep trench along the line of a street, built a brick-lined tunnel inside it, and then covered the tunnel and rebuilt the road on top. The method was relatively cheap, but it caused enormous disruption: streets were closed for long periods, and the route had to follow existing roads wherever possible in order to avoid demolishing buildings.

The line, about six kilometres long, opened in January 1863 between Paddington and Farringdon. It was an immediate success, carrying tens of thousands of passengers on its first day. The trains were pulled by steam locomotives specially designed to reduce the amount of smoke released in the tunnels, though travellers still complained about the smoky and sulphurous air, especially in the deeper sections. Openings were left in some places to allow smoke to escape.

The success of the first line encouraged further construction, and the network grew steadily. A major change came in 1890, with the opening of the first deep-level line. Rather than being built just below the surface, it ran through circular tunnels dug far underground using a large cutting device called a tunnelling shield, which allowed digging to continue without disturbing the streets above. Because steam engines could not safely be used in such deep, narrow tunnels, the line was worked by electric trains – a new technology at the time.

Electric trains proved cleaner and more efficient, and in the early twentieth century the older sub-surface lines were also converted to electric power. The network continued to expand into the surrounding countryside, encouraging the growth of new suburbs whose residents travelled into the city each day. The tube-shaped tunnels of the deep lines gave the system its popular nickname, "the Tube".

Today, London's underground network carries several million passengers on an average weekday. Many other cities around the world followed London's example, building their own underground railways, and the basic methods pioneered in London – cut-and-cover construction for shallow lines and tunnelling shields for deep ones – remained in use, with many improvements, for more than a century.

lesson.title: Sequence and time words
lesson.text: Statements may test the order of events using before, after, later, until, at first, soon. Put the events from the passage on a simple timeline in the margin as you read. A statement that reverses the order is FALSE. A statement about timing that the passage does not settle, such as how long something lasted when only the start date is given, is NOT GIVEN.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The bridge opened in 1901; electric trams crossed it from 1910."
Statement: "Trams used the bridge from the day it opened." → FALSE, because the trams started nine years later.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: In the mid-nineteenth century, main-line railway stations were located in the centre of London.
questions.evidence: the main railway lines ... ended at stations on the edge of the central area
questions.explanation: "On the edge" contradicts "in the centre".

questions.text: The idea of an underground railway was initially popular with the public.
questions.evidence: The idea was widely ridiculed at first
questions.explanation: "Ridiculed" is the opposite of "popular".

questions.text: Construction of the first line started in 1860.
questions.evidence: construction of the first line began in 1860
questions.explanation: "Began" = "started".

questions.text: The first underground line was built by a government department.
questions.evidence: The passage says the main railway lines were "built by separate private companies" (Paragraph A), but it never says who built the underground line.
questions.explanation: Nothing confirms or contradicts the statement. Do not assume the underground line was built the same way as the main lines.

questions.text: The first line was about six kilometres long.
questions.evidence: The line, about six kilometres long
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: No passengers complained about smoke on the first line.
questions.evidence: travellers still complained about the smoky and sulphurous air
questions.explanation: This contradicts "no passengers complained".

questions.text: The first deep-level line used electric trains.
questions.evidence: the first deep-level line ... was worked by electric trains
questions.explanation: "Worked by" = "used".

questions.text: The older sub-surface lines were converted to electric power before 1890.
questions.evidence: The first deep line with electric trains opened in 1890 (Paragraph E), and "in the early twentieth century the older sub-surface lines were also converted" (Paragraph F)
questions.explanation: The conversion happened after 1900, not before 1890, so the statement reverses the sequence.

passages.topic: History of everyday objects — the pencil
passages.title: A Short History of the Pencil

paragraphs.text: The pencil is so ordinary that few people ever think about how it is made or where it came from. Yet its history involves a lucky discovery, a wartime shortage and a series of small improvements that together produced one of the world's most successful tools. Billions of pencils are manufactured every year, and the basic design has changed surprisingly little in more than two centuries.

Despite its common name, the "lead" in a pencil contains no lead at all. It is made from graphite, a soft, dark form of carbon. The confusion dates back to the sixteenth century, when an unusually pure deposit of graphite was found in the north-west of England. People at the time believed the shiny black substance was a type of lead, and called it "black lead" – a name that has survived in everyday language ever since.

The English graphite was so pure that it could be cut into thin sticks and used directly for writing and drawing. At first the sticks were simply wrapped in string or sheepskin to keep the user's hands clean. Later, craftsmen began inserting them into grooved pieces of wood. Because the deposit was rare and valuable, its output was strictly controlled for long periods, and the mine was guarded to prevent theft.

Other countries lacked such pure graphite and struggled to make pencils of the same quality. Some manufacturers ground impure graphite into powder and mixed it with substances such as sulphur or glue to hold it together, but the results were often brittle or scratchy. The breakthrough came in France at the end of the eighteenth century. Cut off by war from supplies of English graphite, the French government asked an engineer, Nicolas-Jacques Conté, to find an alternative. Conté mixed powdered graphite with clay, shaped the mixture into rods and baked them in a kiln.

Conté's method had a major advantage beyond simply replacing English graphite. By changing the proportion of clay to graphite, manufacturers could control how hard or soft the pencil was. More clay produced a harder pencil that made lighter, finer lines; more graphite produced a softer pencil that made darker lines. This is the basis of the grading system still used today, in which letters such as H (for hard) and B (for black) indicate the type of line a pencil will make. Conté's process, with some refinements, remains the standard method of manufacture.

Further improvements followed in the nineteenth century. Machines were developed to cut wooden casings in large numbers, making pencils cheaper to produce. Manufacturers began to make pencils with six sides rather than round ones, which helped to stop them rolling off desks. Towards the end of the century, erasers began to be attached to the ends of some pencils, although in several countries pencils are still commonly sold without them.

Today, pencils face competition from pens and digital devices, but they remain widely used. They are cheap, they work in very cold conditions and at unusual angles, and their marks can be erased. For artists, architects and schoolchildren, the combination of simplicity and control that Conté's invention made possible has proved difficult to improve upon.

lesson.title: Don't let common sense answer for you
lesson.text: Some statements sound obviously true because of what you already know or expect. In TFNG, "sounds true" is not evidence. If you find yourself thinking "that must be right" but you cannot point to a sentence, the answer is probably NOT GIVEN. This trap is especially common with everyday topics.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The first bicycles had no pedals; riders pushed along with their feet."
Statement: "Early bicycles were uncomfortable to ride." It sounds likely, but nothing about comfort is stated → NOT GIVEN.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The basic design of the pencil has changed greatly over the last two centuries.
questions.evidence: the basic design has changed surprisingly little in more than two centuries
questions.explanation: "Changed surprisingly little" contradicts "changed greatly".

questions.text: Pencil "lead" is made from graphite rather than lead.
questions.evidence: the 'lead' in a pencil contains no lead at all. It is made from graphite
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.text: The graphite found in England was mixed with clay before use.
questions.evidence: The English graphite was so pure that it could be cut into thin sticks and used directly
questions.explanation: "Used directly" contradicts the idea that it was mixed with clay. Mixing with clay was Conté's later method for replacing English graphite.

questions.text: The English graphite mine was protected against theft.
questions.evidence: the mine was guarded to prevent theft
questions.explanation: "Guarded" = "protected".

questions.text: Conté had worked as a pencil maker before the government asked for his help.
questions.evidence: Conté is described only as "an engineer"
questions.explanation: His earlier work is not described. Being an engineer does not rule out previous pencil-making, so the statement is neither confirmed nor contradicted.

questions.text: Adding more clay to the mixture makes a pencil harder.
questions.evidence: More clay produced a harder pencil
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: Six-sided pencils were introduced to make them easier to hold.
questions.evidence: six-sided pencils "helped to stop them rolling off desks"
questions.explanation: The passage gives a different reason. Because it states the purpose, and that purpose differs from the one in the statement, the answer is FALSE. If no reason had been given at all, it would be NOT GIVEN. Common sense may suggest easier holding, but only the passage counts.

questions.text: Pencils are used more often than pens in schools today.
questions.evidence: Pencils "remain widely used" and are used by schoolchildren
questions.explanation: No comparison with pens in schools is made.

passages.topic: Geography and environment — the shrinking Dead Sea
passages.title: The Sea That Is Disappearing

paragraphs.text: On the border between Jordan and the territories to its west lies one of the most unusual bodies of water on Earth. The Dead Sea is a salt lake whose surface lies more than four hundred metres below sea level, making its shores the lowest land surface on the planet. Its water is roughly ten times saltier than that of the ocean – so salty that fish cannot survive in it, which gives the lake its name, and so dense that swimmers float easily on the surface without effort.

The Dead Sea has no outlet. Water enters it mainly from the River Jordan and from smaller streams and springs, and leaves only by evaporation in the intense heat of the region. For thousands of years, the amount of water flowing in and the amount evaporating remained roughly in balance, and although the level varied naturally, the lake remained broadly stable.

Since the middle of the twentieth century, this balance has been lost. The main cause is that much of the water that once flowed into the lake is now used before it arrives. Countries in the region, which face serious water shortages, have built dams, pipelines and canals to divert water from the Jordan and its tributaries for drinking and agriculture. As a result, the flow reaching the Dead Sea is now only a small fraction of what it once was.

A second cause is industry. At the southern end of the lake, companies extract valuable minerals such as potash, which is used in fertilisers. To do so, they pump water into large shallow ponds, where it evaporates in the sun, leaving the minerals behind. This process speeds up the loss of water from the lake as a whole.

The consequences are clearly visible. The surface of the lake has been falling by more than a metre per year in recent decades, and its area has shrunk considerably. The northern and southern parts, once connected, are now largely separated, with the southern part kept filled mainly by water pumped in for mineral extraction. Hotels and beaches that were once at the water's edge now stand far from it, and visitors must walk or be driven a considerable distance to reach the shore.

A more dangerous consequence has been the appearance of sinkholes – sudden holes in the ground that can open without warning. As the lake retreats, fresh groundwater flows into areas where layers of salt lie beneath the surface. The fresh water dissolves the salt, creating underground cavities, and eventually the ground above collapses. Thousands of sinkholes have formed along the shores, damaging roads, farmland and buildings, and some areas have been closed to the public.

Various solutions have been proposed. The most ambitious involves carrying water from the Red Sea, far to the south, through a long pipeline or canal. The height difference between the two seas could be used to generate electricity, and part of the water could be converted into drinking water, with the remaining salty water flowing into the Dead Sea. Supporters argue that the project could slow the lake's decline and provide water for the region. Critics warn that mixing large amounts of seawater with the Dead Sea's unusual water could have unpredictable effects, such as changes in its colour or the growth of algae. The project has been discussed for many years, but its future remains uncertain.

lesson.title: Partial matches
lesson.text:
A statement may be half right: one part matches the passage and the other part does not. Check every part of the statement.

If any part is contradicted → FALSE.

If one part is confirmed and another part is not mentioned → NOT GIVEN.

The answer is TRUE only when every part is supported.
lesson.example: Passage: "The river flows south and is used for irrigation." Statement: "The river flows south and is used for drinking water." The first part matches, but drinking water is not mentioned → NOT GIVEN.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The water of the Dead Sea is about ten times saltier than seawater.
questions.evidence: Its water is roughly ten times saltier than that of the ocean
questions.explanation: "Roughly" = "about", and "the ocean" = "seawater".

questions.text: Water leaves the Dead Sea through a river flowing south.
questions.evidence: The Dead Sea has no outlet ... leaves only by evaporation
questions.explanation: This contradicts the idea of a river carrying water out.

questions.text: The Dead Sea's level remained completely unchanged for thousands of years.
questions.evidence: although the level varied naturally, the lake remained broadly stable
questions.explanation: "Varied" contradicts "completely unchanged". This is a qualifier trap.

questions.text: Water from the Jordan is diverted for agriculture and drinking.
questions.evidence: divert water from the Jordan and its tributaries for drinking and agriculture
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.text: Mineral extraction at the southern end of the lake began before dams were built on the Jordan.
questions.evidence: Paragraph C describes the dams and Paragraph D describes mineral extraction, but no dates are given for either.
questions.explanation: The order of the two developments cannot be determined from the passage.

questions.text: The Dead Sea's surface has fallen by more than a metre per year and tourist numbers have fallen as a result.
questions.evidence: "falling by more than a metre per year" (Paragraph E) confirms the first part. Hotels are now far from the water, but tourist numbers are never mentioned.
questions.explanation: This is a partial match: one part is confirmed and the other is absent, so the whole statement is NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Sinkholes form when fresh water dissolves underground salt.
questions.evidence: The fresh water dissolves the salt, creating underground cavities, and eventually the ground above collapses
questions.explanation: The process matches the statement.

questions.text: The Red Sea project has been approved and construction has begun.
questions.evidence: The project has been discussed for many years, but its future remains uncertain
questions.explanation: An "uncertain" future is incompatible with approval and construction having begun.

passages.topic: Psychology and the media — the "Mozart effect"
passages.title: The Music That Made Headlines

paragraphs.text: In 1993, a short article in a leading scientific journal reported an intriguing experiment. A group of university students listened for ten minutes to one of three things: a sonata by Mozart, a recording of relaxation instructions, or silence. Immediately afterwards, they completed tasks that involved imagining how shapes would look when folded or cut. Students who had listened to Mozart performed noticeably better on these spatial tasks than those in the other two conditions. The improvement, however, was temporary: it lasted only around ten to fifteen minutes.

The researchers made modest claims. They did not suggest that listening to Mozart made people more intelligent in general, only that it produced a short-lived improvement in one specific type of reasoning. Nevertheless, the finding quickly attracted attention far beyond the scientific community. Newspapers and magazines reported that "Mozart makes you smarter", and the term "the Mozart effect" became widely used.

As the story spread, it changed. Although the original study had involved only adults, many reports suggested that playing classical music to babies and young children would improve their intelligence. Businesses began selling recordings of classical music specifically marketed to parents. In one American state, the governor proposed that the parents of every newborn child should receive a free classical music recording, and the plan was put into practice. Some childcare centres were encouraged to play classical music every day.

Meanwhile, other scientists attempted to repeat the original experiment. Some found similar results, but many did not, and the effects that were found were generally small. In 1999, a review that combined the results of a large number of studies concluded that any benefit of listening to Mozart was very small and might not be real at all. The authors of the original study responded that some attempts to repeat it had used different tasks or procedures, and that the effect should only be expected under particular conditions.

A more convincing explanation emerged from research into mood and arousal – the degree to which a person feels alert and energised. Several studies found that improvements in spatial tasks occurred after listening to any music, or even a story, that people enjoyed and that made them feel more alert. In one study, students performed better after listening to a lively piece by Mozart than after a slow, sad piece by another composer; but when the researchers measured the students' mood and alertness, the difference between the two conditions disappeared. Another study found that children performed better on spatial tasks after listening to popular music they liked than after listening to Mozart.

These results suggest that the original finding may have been genuine but misunderstood. Music by Mozart may improve performance briefly, not because of any special property of Mozart's music, but because pleasant, energetic sounds make people more alert. The same effect could be produced by many other experiences, such as a cup of coffee or an interesting conversation.

None of this means that music has no educational value. There is a separate body of research on the effects of learning to play an instrument, which involves years of practice, concentration and discipline rather than simple listening. This research is more complex, and its conclusions are still debated, but it addresses a quite different question from the one asked in the famous 1993 experiment.

lesson.title: What was claimed vs what was found
lesson.text: Medium passages often separate what a study found, what others claimed it found, and what later research showed. A statement may describe a claim as if it were a finding. For example, "the study showed that music makes babies smarter" may be FALSE if the study tested only university students. Always ask: who says this, and on what evidence?
lesson.example: Passage: "The trial tested the drug on adults; newspapers reported it would help children." Statement: "The trial showed the drug helps children." → FALSE, because the trial involved only adults. (If the passage had not said who was tested, it would be NOT GIVEN.)

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: In the 1993 experiment, students listened to Mozart for ten minutes.
questions.evidence: A group of university students listened for ten minutes to one of three things: a sonata by Mozart ...
questions.explanation: The students in the Mozart condition listened for ten minutes.

questions.text: The improvement in spatial reasoning lasted for several hours.
questions.evidence: it lasted only around ten to fifteen minutes
questions.explanation: This contradicts "several hours".

questions.text: The original researchers claimed that Mozart's music increased general intelligence.
questions.evidence: They did not suggest that listening to Mozart made people more intelligent in general
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction. The claim of general intelligence came from the media, not from the researchers.

questions.text: The students in the 1993 study were all studying music at university.
questions.evidence: The participants are described only as "university students"
questions.explanation: Their subjects of study are never mentioned, so the statement cannot be confirmed or contradicted.

questions.text: A free classical music recording was given to parents of newborn babies in one American state.
questions.evidence: the governor proposed that the parents of every newborn child should receive a free classical music recording, and the plan was put into practice
questions.explanation: "Put into practice" confirms the recordings were actually given, not just proposed.

questions.text: Sales of classical music recordings rose sharply after the study was published.
questions.evidence: Businesses began selling recordings ... marketed to parents
questions.explanation: The passage mentions that recordings were marketed but gives no sales figures or trends. Do not infer a rise in sales from the fact that recordings were marketed.

questions.text: The 1999 review found strong evidence of a Mozart effect.
questions.evidence: any benefit ... was very small and might not be real at all
questions.explanation: This contradicts "strong evidence".

questions.text: In one study, the difference between lively and sad music disappeared when mood and alertness were taken into account.
questions.evidence: when the researchers measured the students' mood and alertness, the difference between the two conditions disappeared
questions.explanation: The statement closely paraphrases this sentence.

questions.text: Research on learning a musical instrument has reached clear and agreed conclusions.
questions.evidence: its conclusions are still debated
questions.explanation: "Still debated" contradicts "clear and agreed".

passages.topic: Urban development — turning streets over to pedestrians
passages.title: Streets for People

paragraphs.text: In many European cities today, the historic centre is dominated by pedestrian streets: shoppers stroll, children play and café tables spread across what were once busy roads. It is easy to assume that these streets have always been like this. In fact, most were full of cars and buses until the second half of the twentieth century, and turning them over to pedestrians was often highly controversial.

One of the earliest and most influential examples was in Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark. In 1962, the city closed its main shopping street, a route of just over a kilometre winding through the old centre, to motor traffic. The decision was fiercely opposed. Shopkeepers feared that customers who could not drive to their doors would go elsewhere, and newspapers predicted that the street would be empty. One frequently quoted objection held that such streets suited the warm climate and outdoor culture of southern Europe but would never work in a cold northern country – as critics put it, "We are Danes, not Italians."

The critics were proved wrong. Within a year, the number of pedestrians using the street had risen substantially, and many shops reported higher sales. The experiment was made permanent, and over the following decades further streets and squares in the centre were closed to cars. Many of the squares that had served as car parks were cleared and turned into public spaces.

Copenhagen's approach was notable for being gradual. Rather than removing cars from the centre all at once, the city reduced the number of parking spaces in the centre by a small percentage each year over a long period. This gave residents, workers and businesses time to adjust their habits, and it allowed the city to monitor the effects of each change. At the same time, the city invested heavily in cycling routes and public transport, so that people had practical alternatives to driving into the centre.

The changes were accompanied by careful observation. From the late 1960s, the Danish architect Jan Gehl and his colleagues carried out systematic studies of how people used the city's public spaces: how many people walked along particular streets at different times of day, where they chose to sit, and how long they stayed. These studies showed that when streets were made more comfortable for people on foot, people spent more time in them – not only walking through but sitting, talking and watching others. Gehl argued that the quality of public space, not the climate, determined whether people used it.

The Copenhagen model has been widely studied and imitated. Many cities have since created pedestrian streets and squares, often following similar principles: introducing changes gradually, providing alternatives to driving, and measuring how people actually use the new spaces. Results have varied. Pedestrian streets that connect busy destinations and are lined with shops and cafés tend to thrive, while those in quieter locations, or created without improving access by other means, have sometimes struggled to attract people.

The debate is not over. In some cities, shop owners continue to argue that restrictions on cars harm their businesses, while others point to studies suggesting that pedestrians and cyclists visit shops more often, even if they spend less on each visit. What the history of Copenhagen's shopping street shows, at least, is that confident predictions of failure are not always reliable – and that a city's culture can change along with its streets.

lesson.title: NOT GIVEN when the topic is mentioned
lesson.text:
At Medium level, NOT GIVEN statements usually deal with a topic that the passage does discuss. For example, the passage discusses shopkeepers' fears, and the statement makes a specific claim about those shopkeepers that the passage never settles. Don't choose TRUE or

FALSE just because the topic appears. Ask: Does the passage decide this specific claim?
lesson.example: Passage: "Residents objected to the new bus lane, and the council held a public meeting." Statement: "The council changed its plans after the meeting." The meeting is mentioned, but its outcome is not → NOT GIVEN.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Most pedestrian streets in European city centres have been car-free for centuries.
questions.evidence: most were full of cars and buses until the second half of the twentieth century
questions.explanation: This contradicts "car-free for centuries".

questions.text: Copenhagen's main shopping street was closed to cars in 1962.
questions.evidence: In 1962, the city closed its main shopping street ... to motor traffic
questions.explanation: "Motor traffic" = "cars".

questions.text: Some shopkeepers in Copenhagen later admitted they had been wrong to oppose the scheme.
questions.evidence: Shopkeepers' fears are described (Paragraph B), and "many shops reported higher sales" (Paragraph C)
questions.explanation: The shopkeepers are discussed, but the passage never says whether any of them admitted being wrong. This is NOT GIVEN on a topic the passage does mention.

questions.text: The number of pedestrians on the street increased within a year of the change.
questions.evidence: Within a year, the number of pedestrians using the street had risen substantially
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.text: Copenhagen removed all parking from its centre in a single year.
questions.evidence: Rather than removing cars from the centre all at once, the city reduced the number of parking spaces ... by a small percentage each year
questions.explanation: This contradicts "all ... in a single year".

questions.text: The city improved cycling and public transport at the same time as reducing parking.
questions.evidence: At the same time, the city invested heavily in cycling routes and public transport
questions.explanation: "Invested heavily" = "improved".

questions.text: Jan Gehl's studies began before the shopping street was pedestrianised.
questions.evidence: The street was closed "in 1962" (Paragraph B), and the studies ran "From the late 1960s" (Paragraph E)
questions.explanation: The studies began after pedestrianisation, not before. This requires comparing dates from two paragraphs.

questions.text: Gehl believed that climate was the main factor in whether people used public spaces.
questions.evidence: Gehl argued that the quality of public space, not the climate, determined whether people used it
questions.explanation: This directly contradicts the statement.

questions.text: Copenhagen's main shopping street is now the longest pedestrian street in Europe.
questions.evidence: The street is described as "a route of just over a kilometre"
questions.explanation: No comparison with other European pedestrian streets is made, so the length alone cannot confirm or contradict "the longest".

passages.topic: Business — how loyalty programmes work
passages.title: Points of Loyalty

paragraphs.text: A traveller who flies with a particular airline, a shopper who scans a card at the supermarket, a coffee drinker whose tenth cup is free – all are taking part in loyalty programmes, schemes that reward customers for repeated purchases. Such programmes are now so common that many households belong to a dozen or more. Yet their modern form is relatively recent, and the way they make money is less obvious than it first appears.

Rewarding regular customers is an old idea. In the nineteenth century, some shops in the United States gave customers copper tokens with their purchases, which could be exchanged for goods, and later "trading stamps" were collected in books and redeemed for household items. The modern era, however, began in 1981, when a major American airline launched a programme that gave travellers "miles" based on the distance they flew, which could later be exchanged for free flights. Other airlines copied the idea within weeks, and the programmes spread to hotels, car rental firms and, eventually, retailers of almost every kind.

The obvious purpose of these schemes is to encourage customers to return. A traveller who is close to earning a free flight has a reason to choose the same airline again, even if another company offers a slightly lower fare. Programmes that offer different levels of membership – with benefits such as priority boarding or access to airport lounges for the most frequent travellers – strengthen this effect, because customers want to reach or keep a higher status.

Many economists, however, doubt that loyalty programmes create much genuine loyalty. Research suggests that the customers who join are often those who would have used the company frequently anyway, and that many people belong to competing programmes at the same time, which reduces any single company's advantage. When every airline or supermarket offers a scheme, the schemes may simply become a cost of doing business rather than a way of standing out.

For many companies, the most valuable product of a loyalty programme is not loyalty but information. Every time a member scans a card or logs in, the company learns what that person bought, when, where and at what price. Over time, this builds a detailed picture of individual habits, which can be used to target offers, design stores and decide which products to stock. Some privacy campaigners have raised concerns about how this information is collected and shared, although companies generally argue that it allows them to offer customers more relevant rewards.

Airline programmes have developed into large businesses in their own right. Airlines sell miles in large quantities to banks, which give them to customers who use their credit cards, and to hotels and shops that offer them as rewards. In several cases, an airline's loyalty programme has been estimated to be worth more than the airline's flying operations. This is possible partly because the airline controls both the price at which it sells miles and the number of miles needed for a free flight, and can change the second at any time.

A further source of profit is known as "breakage": the proportion of points or miles that are never used. Points expire, customers lose interest, or balances are too small to exchange for anything useful. Every point that is never redeemed represents money the company has received, or a reward it has promised, without any cost. Estimates of breakage vary widely between programmes, but for some it is thought to be considerable.

None of this means that loyalty programmes are simply a trick. Many members receive real benefits, from free flights to discounted groceries, and frequent customers in particular can gain substantial value. But understanding how the programmes are designed helps explain why companies are so eager to sign customers up, and why the rewards are often less generous than they first seem.

lesson.title: Synonyms and antonyms
lesson.text: In Medium sets, statements rarely repeat the passage's words. You must recognise that rarely ≈ seldom, expanded ≈ grew, and that expanded is the opposite of shrank. A statement built on a synonym is a TRUE candidate. A statement built on an antonym is a FALSE candidate. Always confirm with the whole sentence, because negatives (not, never, few) can reverse the meaning.
lesson.example: Passage: "Few customers ever used the service." Statement: "The service was seldom used." → TRUE. Statement: "The service was popular." → FALSE.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Rewarding repeat customers was unknown before the twentieth century.
questions.evidence: In the nineteenth century, some shops in the United States gave customers copper tokens
questions.explanation: The practice existed before the twentieth century, so "unknown" is contradicted.

questions.text: Other airlines were slow to copy the programme launched in 1981.
questions.evidence: Other airlines copied the idea within weeks
questions.explanation: "Within weeks" is the opposite of "slow".

questions.text: Different membership levels give customers an extra reason to remain with a company.
questions.evidence: Programmes that offer different levels of membership ... strengthen this effect, because customers want to reach or keep a higher status
questions.explanation: "This effect" refers to encouraging customers to return, so the levels give an extra reason to stay.

questions.text: Research indicates that loyalty programmes attract many customers who were already frequent users.
questions.evidence: the customers who join are often those who would have used the company frequently anyway
questions.explanation: "Would have used ... frequently anyway" = "already frequent users".

questions.text: Customers who belong to several competing programmes spend more money overall.
questions.evidence: many people belong to competing programmes at the same time
questions.explanation: Multiple membership is mentioned, but nothing is said about how much these customers spend.

questions.text: Companies use data from loyalty programmes when deciding what products to sell.
questions.evidence: can be used to target offers, design stores and decide which products to stock
questions.explanation: "Stock" = "sell".
questions.editorialCorrection: Evidence quote did not match the passage word for word; replaced with the exact sentence from paragraph E.

questions.text: Most customers are unaware that their purchases are being recorded.
questions.evidence: Paragraph E mentions privacy campaigners' concerns about data collection.
questions.explanation: Customers' awareness is never discussed. The concerns do not tell us what most customers know.

questions.text: Airlines are unable to change the number of miles required for a free flight.
questions.evidence: the airline "controls ... the number of miles needed for a free flight, and can change the second at any time"
questions.explanation: "Can change ... at any time" contradicts "unable to change".

questions.text: Breakage rates are similar across all loyalty programmes.
questions.evidence: Estimates of breakage vary widely between programmes
questions.explanation: "Vary widely" contradicts "similar across all".

passages.topic: History of medicine — from mould to medicine
passages.title: The Long Road to Penicillin

paragraphs.text: The story of penicillin is often told as a tale of a single lucky accident. In September 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned to his laboratory in London after a holiday and noticed something unusual about a dish in which he had been growing bacteria. A mould had contaminated the dish, and around it the bacteria had been destroyed. Fleming identified the mould as a type of Penicillium and named the substance it produced "penicillin".

Fleming's observation was genuinely important, but the popular version of the story leaves out a great deal. Fleming published his findings in 1929 and showed that penicillin could kill several types of harmful bacteria without damaging human white blood cells. However, he found it extremely difficult to extract and purify the substance, which was unstable and was produced by the mould only in tiny quantities. He carried out some further experiments but did not test penicillin systematically as a treatment for infections in animals or people, and for about a decade his discovery attracted relatively little attention.

The work that turned penicillin into a medicine took place at the University of Oxford from the late 1930s. A team led by the Australian-born scientist Howard Florey, with the biochemist Ernst Chain, who had come to Britain from Germany, began a systematic investigation of natural substances that could kill bacteria. Chain came across Fleming's paper and recognised its potential.
