The team developed methods of extracting and purifying penicillin, a task in which another team member, Norman Heatley, played an essential part by designing ingenious equipment – including, at one stage, containers adapted from hospital bedpans – to grow the mould and collect the substance.

In 1940 the Oxford team carried out a crucial experiment. Eight mice were infected with a deadly bacterium; four were then given penicillin and four were not. The untreated mice died within a day, while those that received penicillin survived. The following year, the team treated its first human patient, a police officer suffering from a severe infection. He improved dramatically, but the supply of penicillin ran out before he could be cured, and he later died. The episode demonstrated both the drug's power and the urgent need to produce it in much larger quantities.

Wartime Britain lacked the industrial capacity to do this, so in 1941 Florey and Heatley travelled to the United States. Working with American government scientists and drug companies, they helped develop methods of growing the mould in large tanks. A new strain of Penicillium, found on a mouldy melon in an American market, turned out to produce far more penicillin than Fleming's original. Production increased enormously, and by the later years of the Second World War penicillin was available in large quantities to treat wounded soldiers.

In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize for their work on penicillin. Heatley, whose technical contribution had been vital, received no share of the prize, which can be awarded to no more than three people. His role was recognised much later, when the University of Oxford awarded him an honorary degree – the first ever given to a person who was not a medical doctor.

The history of penicillin illustrates how scientific discovery often depends not on a single moment of insight but on many people working over many years, and on technical and industrial skills as well as original ideas. Fleming himself was modest about his role and often emphasised the work of others. It was the combination of observation, investigation, engineering and large-scale production that transformed a contaminated laboratory dish into one of the most important medicines in history.

lesson.title: Who did what?
lesson.text:
When a passage involves several people, statements may attach an action to the wrong person. For example, the passage says Scientist A discovered X and Scientist B developed it, and the statement says B discovered X. That is FALSE, because the passage assigns the discovery to someone else.

Keep a quick note of person → action as you read. Also notice collective credit ("the team", "together", "shared"): a statement that one person did something alone may then be FALSE.
lesson.example:
Passage: "Lee designed the engine; Park built the first working model."
Statement: "Lee built the first working model." → FALSE.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Fleming noticed the effect of the mould after returning from a holiday.
questions.evidence: returned to his laboratory in London after a holiday and noticed something unusual
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.text: Fleming showed that penicillin harmed human white blood cells.
questions.evidence: penicillin could kill several types of harmful bacteria without damaging human white blood cells
questions.explanation: "Without damaging" contradicts "harmed".

questions.text: Fleming tested penicillin extensively on human patients.
questions.evidence: did not test penicillin systematically as a treatment for infections in animals or people
questions.explanation: This contradicts "tested extensively". The first human patient was treated by the Oxford team, not by Fleming.

questions.text: Chain found Fleming's article and saw that the discovery could be valuable.
questions.evidence: Chain came across Fleming's paper and recognised its potential
questions.explanation: "Came across" = "found", "paper" = "article", and "recognised its potential" = "saw that ... could be valuable".

questions.text: Heatley designed equipment used to produce penicillin at Oxford.
questions.evidence: Norman Heatley, played an essential part by designing ingenious equipment
questions.explanation: The action is correctly attributed to Heatley.

questions.text: Half of the mice given penicillin in the 1940 experiment died.
questions.evidence: four were then given penicillin ... those that received penicillin survived
questions.explanation: All the treated mice survived. The four that died were the untreated mice, so this statement confuses the two groups.

questions.text: The police officer was cured by penicillin.
questions.evidence: the supply of penicillin ran out before he could be cured, and he later died
questions.explanation: This contradicts "cured".

questions.text: The melon mould was discovered by Florey.
questions.evidence: A new strain ... found on a mouldy melon in an American market
questions.explanation: The passage does not say who found it. It cannot be assumed to be Florey just because he was in the United States.

questions.text: Heatley was disappointed not to receive the Nobel Prize.
questions.evidence: Heatley "received no share of the prize"
questions.explanation: His feelings about this are never mentioned.

passages.topic: Agriculture — bees for hire
passages.title: Pollinators on the Move

paragraphs.text: Every year, in the early weeks of spring, one of the largest managed movements of animals in the world takes place on the roads of the western United States. Trucks carrying tens of thousands of beehives travel, often at night, towards the almond orchards of California's Central Valley. By the time the almond trees flower, well over a million honeybee colonies – a large share of all the managed colonies in the country – will have been brought in to pollinate them.

Almonds, like many crops, depend on insects to carry pollen from one flower to another. Without pollination, the trees produce few nuts. In a natural landscape, wild bees and other insects might perform this service, but the almond orchards cover enormous areas planted with a single crop, and they offer little food or nesting space for wild insects at other times of the year. The local population of wild pollinators is therefore far too small to pollinate the trees during the short flowering period, which lasts only a few weeks.

The solution has been to rent bees. Beekeepers, many of whom travel from other states, bring their hives to the orchards, and farmers pay a fee for each colony. For many commercial beekeepers, these fees now make up a larger part of their income than the sale of honey. After the almond season, some hives are moved on to pollinate other crops, such as apples, cherries or blueberries, following the flowering seasons across the country.

The arrangement has become more important as the area planted with almonds has grown. Rising demand for almonds in many parts of the world has encouraged farmers to plant more trees, and the number of hives required has increased accordingly. At the same time, beekeepers have faced serious difficulties. Since the early 2000s, many have reported unusually high losses of colonies, particularly over the winter. The causes appear to be varied and are still being investigated, but they are thought to include parasites, diseases, exposure to certain pesticides and a lack of varied food.

Some researchers argue that the pollination system itself may add to the pressure on bees. Transporting hives over long distances is stressful for the colonies, and bringing bees from many different regions into the same orchards may help parasites and diseases spread between colonies. Moreover, during the weeks when the almonds are not in flower, the orchards provide almost no food for bees, since the ground between the trees is often kept bare.

In response, some farmers have begun to change their practices. A number now plant flowering plants between the rows of trees or along the edges of fields, providing food for bees before and after the almond flowers bloom and supporting wild insects as well. Others are experimenting with new varieties of almond tree that can partly pollinate themselves, which would reduce the number of hives needed for each area of orchard. These varieties may produce smaller harvests in some conditions, however, and it is not yet clear how widely they will be adopted.

The almond orchards illustrate a wider point. Pollination is often described as a free service provided by nature, but where natural systems have been greatly simplified, it becomes a service that must be organised, transported and paid for. Protecting a mixture of habitats around farmland may prove to be not only good for wildlife but also a sensible investment for farmers.

lesson.title: Proportions and approximate quantities
lesson.text:
Passages often express amounts with words rather than exact numbers: a majority, roughly a third, the bulk of, a handful, nearly all. Statements then use a different expression for the same, or a different, amount. Convert both into a rough figure:

a majority > 50%

roughly a third ≈ 33%

a handful = very few

If the figures are compatible → TRUE. If they are clearly incompatible (a handful vs most) → FALSE. If the passage gives no amount at all → NOT GIVEN.
lesson.example: Passage: "Nearly all the volunteers were students." Statement: "Most volunteers were students." → TRUE, because nearly all includes most.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Fewer than a million bee colonies are brought to the almond orchards each year.
questions.evidence: well over a million honeybee colonies
questions.explanation: "Well over a million" contradicts "fewer than a million".

questions.text: Almond trees flower for a period of several months.
questions.evidence: the short flowering period, which lasts only a few weeks
questions.explanation: "A few weeks" contradicts "several months".

questions.text: Wild insects alone cannot pollinate the almond orchards.
questions.evidence: The local population of wild pollinators is therefore far too small to pollinate the trees
questions.explanation: "Far too small" = "cannot ... alone".

questions.text: For many commercial beekeepers, pollination fees are a bigger source of income than honey.
questions.evidence: For many commercial beekeepers, these fees now make up a larger part of their income than the sale of honey
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.text: The fees paid for each hive have risen every year since the early 2000s.
questions.evidence: Farmers "pay a fee for each colony" (Paragraph C), and demand has increased (Paragraph D)
questions.explanation: No information is given about changes in the fee. Rising demand does not tell us fees rose every year.

questions.text: Scientists have identified a single cause for the high losses of bee colonies.
questions.evidence: The causes appear to be varied and are still being investigated
questions.explanation: "Varied" contradicts "a single cause".

questions.text: Moving hives long distances may cause stress to bee colonies.
questions.evidence: Transporting hives over long distances is stressful for the colonies
questions.explanation: This matches the statement. Note that the passage gives this as the view of "some researchers", which the hedge "may" in the statement fits.

questions.text: Most almond farmers now plant flowers between their trees.
questions.evidence: A number now plant flowering plants between the rows
questions.explanation: "A number" gives no proportion. It neither confirms nor contradicts "most", so this is a proportion trap.

questions.text: Self-pollinating almond varieties always produce larger harvests.
questions.evidence: These varieties may produce smaller harvests in some conditions
questions.explanation: This contradicts "always ... larger".

passages.topic: Architecture and engineering — wooden pagodas and earthquakes
passages.title: Towers That Bend

paragraphs.text: Japan experiences more earthquakes than almost any other country, and many of its historic buildings have been destroyed by them over the centuries. Yet one type of structure has a remarkable record of survival. Tall wooden pagodas – towers of five or sometimes three storeys built at Buddhist temples – have stood for hundreds of years, in some cases more than a thousand, through repeated earthquakes. Reliable records show that pagodas have been lost to fire, lightning and war, but very few, if any, appear to have been brought down by earthquakes.

This record is surprising because the pagodas are tall and slender, the kind of shape that might be expected to be especially vulnerable to shaking. Engineers and historians have long tried to explain it. Because the buildings were constructed by craftsmen working with traditional knowledge rather than written calculations, the reasons for their stability must be worked out from the structures themselves, and not all specialists agree on which features matter most.

One striking feature is the way each storey is constructed. Rather than being fixed rigidly to the storey below, each level rests on the one beneath it, connected by wooden joints without nails or metal fixings. During an earthquake, the storeys can move slightly independently of one another. Observers have described the motion as resembling that of a snake, with alternate floors swaying in opposite directions, so that the tower as a whole bends rather than breaks. This flexibility allows energy from the shaking to be absorbed as the wooden joints rub and shift against each other.

A second feature that has received much attention is the central pillar, a massive column of wood that runs up the middle of the pagoda. Surprisingly, in many pagodas this pillar is not connected rigidly to the surrounding structure and in some cases does not even rest on the ground, instead hanging from the top of the building. Some engineers have suggested that it acts rather like a pendulum or a stabiliser, limiting the movement of the storeys by knocking against them and preventing any single level from swinging too far. Others argue that its role in earthquakes has been exaggerated, and that the pillar may originally have had a religious rather than structural purpose.

The wide overhanging roofs of each storey also play a part. They are heavy, and their weight, spread outwards around the edges of each level, is thought to help the structure resist being pushed over. The roofs also protect the wooden framework from rain, which has helped the buildings avoid decay – an important factor in their long survival.

Researchers have tested some of these ideas by building scale models and placing them on "shaking tables" that reproduce the motion of earthquakes. Such tests have generally confirmed that the pagoda form is highly resistant to shaking, and that the flexible connections between storeys play an important role. The contribution of the central pillar, however, has been harder to measure, and the results of different experiments have not always agreed.

Whatever the precise explanation, the pagoda has inspired modern engineers. The designers of a very tall broadcasting tower completed in Tokyo in the early 2010s included a central concrete column, separated from the surrounding steel frame, as part of a system intended to reduce swaying during earthquakes, and they explicitly referred to the traditional pagoda as an influence. Modern buildings use calculations and materials unavailable to the original builders, but the principle that a structure may survive shaking by moving with it, rather than resisting it rigidly, reflects a lesson that the pagoda builders appear to have understood centuries ago.

lesson.title: Hedged statements and certain statements
lesson.text: Passages about research often express uncertainty: may, might, is thought to, one theory suggests, it remains unclear. A statement that presents such an idea as certain fact ("X causes Y", "engineers have proved") does not match. Usually it is FALSE if the passage explicitly says the matter is uncertain or disputed, and NOT GIVEN if the passage simply doesn't address it. Conversely, a statement that is itself hedged ("X may cause Y") can be TRUE when the passage reports X as a possible cause.
lesson.example: Passage: "It is still unclear why the birds left the island." Statement: "Scientists have established why the birds left." → FALSE.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Some wooden pagodas in Japan are more than a thousand years old.
questions.evidence: have stood for hundreds of years, in some cases more than a thousand
questions.explanation: "In some cases" = "some".

questions.text: Many pagodas have been destroyed by fire.
questions.evidence: pagodas have been lost to fire, lightning and war
questions.explanation: The passage confirms that pagodas have been lost to fire but gives no number. "Many" cannot be confirmed or contradicted. Compare the "some / many / most" traps in the earlier sets.

questions.text: The builders of the pagodas used detailed written calculations.
questions.evidence: craftsmen working with traditional knowledge rather than written calculations
questions.explanation: "Rather than written calculations" directly contradicts the statement.

questions.text: The storeys of a pagoda are firmly nailed together.
questions.evidence: connected by wooden joints without nails or metal fixings
questions.explanation: "Without nails" contradicts "firmly nailed".

questions.text: The flexible joints help the tower absorb the energy of earthquakes.
questions.evidence: This flexibility allows energy from the shaking to be absorbed as the wooden joints rub and shift
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.text: Engineers agree that the central pillar is the main reason pagodas survive earthquakes.
questions.evidence: Others argue that its role in earthquakes has been exaggerated ... results of different experiments have not always agreed
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly reports disagreement, which contradicts "engineers agree". This is the hedged-versus-certain pattern from the lesson.

questions.text: In some pagodas, the central pillar hangs without touching the ground.
questions.evidence: in some cases does not even rest on the ground, instead hanging from the top of the building
questions.explanation: This matches the statement.

questions.text: Shaking-table tests have been carried out on full-size pagodas.
questions.evidence: building scale models and placing them on 'shaking tables'
questions.explanation: The passage mentions tests on scale models only. It neither says that full-size pagodas were tested nor that they were not. A student who chooses FALSE is assuming that the only tests described are the only tests ever carried out.

questions.text: The designers of the Tokyo tower said they had been influenced by pagodas.
questions.evidence: they explicitly referred to the traditional pagoda as an influence
questions.explanation: "Explicitly referred to ... as an influence" = "said they had been influenced".

passages.topic: Energy — electricity from the tides
passages.title: Power from the Moon's Pull

paragraphs.text: Twice a day, in most coastal places, the sea rises and falls. These tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, with a smaller contribution from the Sun, and they are as predictable as a timetable: the height and timing of high and low water can be calculated years in advance. This predictability distinguishes tidal energy from wind and solar power, which vary with the weather. It has long encouraged engineers to try to turn the movement of the tides into electricity.

The simplest way of doing so is a tidal barrage – a dam built across the mouth of an estuary or bay where the difference between high and low tide is large. As the tide rises, water flows through gates in the barrage into the basin behind it. The gates are then closed, and when the sea outside has fallen, the trapped water is released through turbines, generating electricity. Some barrages also generate power as the tide flows in.

The world's first large tidal power station of this kind opened in 1966 on the estuary of the River Rance in north-western France, where the tidal range – the difference between high and low water – can exceed twelve metres. With a capacity of 240 megawatts, it remained the largest tidal power station in the world for about forty-five years. It still operates today, and its long working life has been cited as evidence that tidal barrages can be reliable over many decades.

In 2011, the Rance station was overtaken by a plant at Sihwa Lake in South Korea, with a slightly larger capacity. The Sihwa project had an unusual origin. A sea wall had been built in the 1990s to create a freshwater lake for farming and industry, but the enclosed water became badly polluted. Installing turbines allowed seawater to flow in and out again each day, improving the quality of the water as well as generating electricity. Unlike the Rance station, the Sihwa plant generates power only as the tide flows in.

Despite these successes, very few tidal barrages have been built. Their construction costs are enormous, and suitable sites – with a large tidal range and a shape that allows a barrage to be built – are rare. There are also environmental concerns. A barrage changes the flow of water in an estuary, which can alter the movement of sediment, affect the mud flats where many birds feed, and block the movement of fish. Several proposals for very large barrages, including some in Britain, have been studied in detail over many years but abandoned, partly because of these concerns and partly because of cost.

More recent efforts have focused on a different approach: tidal stream turbines. These work somewhat like underwater wind turbines, placed on the seabed in narrow channels where tidal currents flow quickly. Because they do not require a dam, they are expected to have a smaller effect on the surrounding environment, although this is still being studied. Several projects in Scotland, France and elsewhere have demonstrated that such turbines can supply electricity to the grid, but the harsh underwater conditions – powerful currents, salt water and difficulty of access for repairs – have made them expensive to build and maintain.

A further limitation is that tides, though predictable, are not constant. Power output falls to nearly zero around the moments of high and low water, when currents slow down, and it varies over a roughly two-week cycle according to the positions of the Moon and Sun. Tidal energy therefore cannot supply a steady flow of electricity on its own. Its supporters argue, however, that its predictability makes it easier to combine with other sources than weather-dependent forms of renewable energy.

lesson.title: Superlatives and rankings
lesson.text:
Words such as largest, first, oldest, most powerful make precise claims. The passage must support the exact ranking:

"One of the largest" ≠ "the largest", so a statement claiming "the largest" is usually NOT GIVEN.

If the passage names something bigger or earlier, the statement is FALSE.

Check what is being ranked (output vs physical size) and when ("was the largest until 2011" is not "is the largest").
lesson.example: Passage: "Opened in 1990, the dam was the country's biggest until a larger one was built in 2005." Statement: "The dam is still the country's biggest." → FALSE.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The timing of tides can be predicted years ahead.
questions.evidence: can be calculated years in advance
questions.explanation: "Calculated in advance" = "predicted ahead".

questions.text: Tidal barrages can only produce electricity when the tide is going out.
questions.evidence: Some barrages also generate power as the tide flows in
questions.explanation: This rules out "only ... going out".

questions.text: The tidal range at the Rance estuary can be more than twelve metres.
questions.evidence: the tidal range ... can exceed twelve metres
questions.explanation: "Exceed" = "more than".

questions.text: The Rance station is currently the largest tidal power station in the world.
questions.evidence: In 2011, the Rance station was overtaken by a plant at Sihwa Lake
questions.explanation: The Rance station was the largest for about forty-five years, but it no longer is. This is the "was / is" trap.

questions.text: The Rance station has required fewer repairs than other power stations of its age.
questions.evidence: The station "still operates today" and is cited as evidence of reliability
questions.explanation: No comparison of repairs with other power stations is made.

questions.text: The lake at Sihwa had water quality problems before the turbines were installed.
questions.evidence: "the enclosed water became badly polluted" (Paragraph D), before turbines improved it.
questions.explanation: "Badly polluted" = "water quality problems".

questions.text: The Sihwa plant generates electricity in both directions of the tide.
questions.evidence: the Sihwa plant generates power only as the tide flows in
questions.explanation: "Only" contradicts "both directions".

questions.text: Plans for large tidal barrages in Britain were rejected entirely for environmental reasons.
questions.evidence: abandoned "partly because of these concerns and partly because of cost"
questions.explanation: Cost was also a reason, so "entirely for environmental reasons" is contradicted.

questions.text: Tidal stream turbines have been shown to have no effect on the environment.
questions.evidence: they are expected to have a smaller effect ... although this is still being studied
questions.explanation: "A smaller effect" still means some effect, and the question is still being studied, so "shown to have no effect" is contradicted.

passages.topic: Social history — the invention of the weekend
passages.title: How the Weekend Was Made

paragraphs.text: For most people in industrialised countries, the two-day weekend seems a natural part of life. Yet the idea that ordinary workers should have two consecutive days free from paid work each week is barely a century old. For most of history, the typical working week for labourers and servants was six days long, with Sunday set aside for rest and religious observance in Christian countries.

The first steps towards a longer break came, somewhat unexpectedly, from workers' own habits. In parts of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Britain, many skilled craftsmen who were paid for the amount they produced rather than for their time took Monday off, a custom jokingly known as "Saint Monday". They made up for the lost day by working longer hours later in the week. Employers disliked the practice, which made production irregular, and the spread of factories, with machines that needed to run to a fixed schedule, made it increasingly difficult to maintain.

During the nineteenth century, a compromise gradually emerged in Britain. Campaigners, including religious groups who wanted workers to have time for church and education, argued for a shorter working day on Saturday. Laws limiting working hours in textile factories, which applied mainly to women and children, required them to finish earlier on Saturdays, and many employers extended the arrangement to other workers. By the later part of the century, a Saturday half-holiday had become common in many industries. It encouraged new forms of leisure: football matches, for example, were increasingly scheduled for Saturday afternoons, when large numbers of working men were free to attend.

The full two-day weekend arrived later, and its adoption was driven by several different forces. In the United States, some factories in the early twentieth century began giving Saturday as well as Sunday off, partly to accommodate Jewish workers, whose day of rest is Saturday. The most famous step, however, was taken by the car manufacturer Henry Ford, who in 1926 introduced a five-day, forty-hour week in his factories without reducing workers' weekly pay. Ford argued that workers with more free time would be more productive at work and would also have more opportunity to buy goods – including cars.

Economic crisis also played a role. During the Great Depression of the 1930s, when unemployment was extremely high, shorter working weeks were promoted in several countries as a way of sharing the available work among more people. In the United States, a law passed in 1938 set a standard working week, beyond which employers had to pay extra for additional hours; by 1940, the standard had been fixed at forty hours. In Britain and much of Europe, the two-day weekend became normal for many workers in the decades after the Second World War.

The weekend has never been universal. Many people – in hospitals, transport, shops and restaurants – have always worked on Saturdays and Sundays, and in recent decades the growth of services open seven days a week has increased their number. The day of rest also differs between cultures: in many countries with Muslim majorities, the weekend includes Friday, while some countries have changed the days of their weekend in recent years, in part to align more closely with international business partners.

Today, some companies and governments are experimenting with a four-day working week, arguing, much as Ford did, that shorter hours need not reduce productivity. Whether such experiments will spread remains to be seen. But the history of the weekend shows that the division of time between work and rest is not fixed by nature. It has been negotiated, contested and changed – and may well change again.

lesson.title: Generalisations and the groups they describe
lesson.text: A passage may describe what happened to one group (factory workers, one country, one company). The statement then generalises it to everyone, or applies it to a different group. The passage says it was true of one group only, or explicitly not of others → FALSE. The passage says nothing about the other group → NOT GIVEN.
lesson.example: Passage: "Miners in the region were given free housing." Statement: "All workers in the region received free housing." The passage says nothing about other workers → NOT GIVEN.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The two-day weekend for ordinary workers has existed for several centuries.
questions.evidence: barely a century old
questions.explanation: This contradicts "several centuries".

questions.text: "Saint Monday" was mainly practised by workers who were paid according to their output.
questions.evidence: craftsmen who were paid for the amount they produced rather than for their time took Monday off
questions.explanation: "Paid for the amount they produced" = "paid according to output".

questions.text: Employers encouraged the custom of taking Mondays off.
questions.evidence: Employers disliked the practice
questions.explanation: "Disliked" contradicts "encouraged".

questions.text: Nineteenth-century factory laws on Saturday hours applied equally to all adult workers.
questions.evidence: the laws "applied mainly to women and children"
questions.explanation: The passage names a specific group, which contradicts "equally to all adult workers". Other workers benefited only when employers chose to extend the arrangement.

questions.text: Football matches were scheduled on Saturday afternoons partly because many working men were free then.
questions.evidence: scheduled for Saturday afternoons, when large numbers of working men were free to attend
questions.explanation: The reason given matches the statement.

questions.text: Henry Ford reduced his workers' weekly pay when he introduced the five-day week.
questions.evidence: without reducing workers' weekly pay
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Ford's workers became more productive after the five-day week was introduced.
questions.evidence: Ford argued that workers with more free time would be more productive
questions.explanation: The passage reports Ford's argument, not the result. Whether productivity actually rose is not stated.

questions.text: The weekend was introduced at the same time in every European country.
questions.evidence: In Britain and much of Europe, the two-day weekend became normal for many workers in the decades after the Second World War
questions.explanation: The passage gives a broad period for "much of Europe". It does not say whether every country adopted the weekend at the same time or at different times.

questions.text: All countries with Muslim majorities have a Friday–Saturday weekend.
questions.evidence: in many countries with Muslim majorities, the weekend includes Friday
questions.explanation: The passage says "many", not "all", and it does not say which other day forms the weekend. The statement goes beyond the information given.

passages.topic: Linguistics — reviving endangered languages
passages.title: Bringing Languages Back

paragraphs.text: Linguists estimate that there are around seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, but that a large proportion of them are endangered. Many are spoken only by older people, and are no longer being learned by children as their first language. When the last fluent speakers of such a language die, it ceases to be used in everyday life. Estimates of how many languages may disappear during this century vary widely, but some suggest that it could be as many as half of those spoken today.

Languages decline for many reasons. Speakers of minority languages have often been encouraged, or forced, to adopt a more widely used language for education, employment and government. In some cases, children were punished for speaking their home language at school. Even without direct pressure, parents may choose to raise their children in a dominant language because they believe it will give them better opportunities. Once a generation of children grows up without speaking a language, its decline can be very rapid.

It has sometimes been assumed that this process cannot be reversed. The history of Hebrew suggests otherwise. For many centuries, Hebrew was used mainly for religious purposes, study and writing, and it had no community of native speakers using it in daily life. From the late nineteenth century, a movement in which the linguist Eliezer Ben-Yehuda played a prominent role promoted Hebrew as an everyday spoken language, creating new words for modern objects and ideas. Schools began to teach in Hebrew, and families began to use it at home. Today it is the first language of millions of people. Its revival is often described as unique, and linguists caution that it took place under unusual historical conditions that other communities are unlikely to share.

More modest revivals have nonetheless achieved significant results. In Wales, the proportion of people able to speak Welsh declined steeply during the twentieth century. From the 1960s onwards, campaigns led to the introduction of Welsh-medium schools, bilingual public signs, Welsh-language television and legal recognition of the language. The decline has slowed, and in some age groups the number of speakers has increased, largely because of education. Researchers note, however, that learning a language at school does not guarantee that it will be used outside the classroom, and the number of people who use Welsh in everyday life remains a central concern.

In Hawai'i, the number of children speaking the Hawaiian language had fallen to only a few dozen by the early 1980s. In 1984, a group of parents and teachers opened the first "language nest" preschool, in which young children were cared for entirely in Hawaiian by fluent speakers, many of them elderly. The model was based on a similar programme developed among the Māori of New Zealand. As the first children grew older, parents campaigned for schools that would continue their education in Hawaiian, and a system now extends from preschool to university level. The number of young speakers has grown to several thousand, although this remains small compared with the population of the islands.

Recent technology has added new tools. Recordings, online dictionaries and language-learning applications allow people to hear and practise languages that have few living speakers, and social media enable scattered communities to communicate in their own language. For some languages with no remaining fluent speakers, communities have used old recordings and written documents to begin reconstructing the language and teaching it again. Such efforts face obvious difficulties: written records may be incomplete, and recordings may preserve only certain types of speech.

Experience from many revival programmes suggests that success depends above all on whether a language is passed on to children and used in the home and community. Official status, schools and technology can support this process, but they cannot replace it. As one researcher has observed, a language survives not because it is recorded or taught, but because people choose to live their lives in it.

lesson.title: Hard TFNG — implications and precise scope
lesson.text:
At Hard level:

FALSE by implication. The contradiction may not be one sentence that says the opposite. It may follow clearly from two pieces of information. For example: the passage says a language had no native speakers for centuries, and the statement says it was always spoken at home. Tight NOT GIVEN. Statements stay very close to the passage's topic and vocabulary but add one unsupported element: a cause, a comparison, a motive or a result.

Scope words. Only, entirely, the main, never, all, completely are the words to check first. Before choosing, restate the statement's one precise claim in a few words, and test only that claim.
lesson.example: Passage: "The school opened with twelve pupils; within ten years it had over two hundred, though funding remained uncertain." Statement: "The school grew because its funding was secure." Growth is TRUE, but the stated cause contradicts "funding remained uncertain" → FALSE.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Experts agree that half of the world's languages will disappear this century.
questions.evidence: Estimates ... vary widely, but some suggest that it could be as many as half
questions.explanation: "Vary widely" and "some suggest" contradict "experts agree". A single estimate is presented as certain in the statement.

questions.text: In some places, children have been penalised for using their home language at school.
questions.evidence: children were punished for speaking their home language at school
questions.explanation: "Punished" = "penalised", and "in some cases" = "in some places".

questions.text: Hebrew continued to be spoken at home by a community of native speakers throughout its history.
questions.evidence: it had no community of native speakers using it in daily life
questions.explanation: This contradiction follows from the statement's claim about "throughout its history".

questions.text: Ben-Yehuda was solely responsible for the revival of Hebrew.
questions.evidence: a movement in which the linguist Eliezer Ben-Yehuda played a prominent role
questions.explanation: A "prominent role" in a "movement" implies others were involved, and the passage also mentions schools and families. This contradicts "solely", so it is FALSE by implication.

questions.text: Linguists believe the revival of Hebrew provides a model that most endangered languages could easily follow.
questions.evidence: linguists caution that it took place under unusual historical conditions that other communities are unlikely to share
questions.explanation: This contradicts the idea that most languages could easily follow the model.

questions.text: Education has been the main reason for the growth of Welsh speakers in certain age groups.
questions.evidence: in some age groups the number of speakers has increased, largely because of education
questions.explanation: "Largely because of" = "the main reason".

questions.text: The Hawaiian language nest programme was modelled on an earlier programme in New Zealand.
questions.evidence: The model was based on a similar programme developed among the Māori of New Zealand
questions.explanation: "Based on" = "modelled on". The Māori programme is implied to be earlier.

questions.text: Most of the fluent speakers in the first Hawaiian language nests had trained as teachers.
questions.evidence: cared for entirely in Hawaiian by fluent speakers, many of them elderly
questions.explanation: Their age is given, but their training is not. The topic appears, but the precise claim is not settled.

questions.text: Technology alone can ensure the survival of an endangered language.
questions.evidence: Official status, schools and technology can support this process, but they cannot replace it
questions.explanation: This directly contradicts "technology alone can ensure".

passages.topic: Medical research — placebos that patients know are placebos
passages.title: Honest Placebos

paragraphs.text: A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient – a sugar pill, for example, or an injection of salt water. For decades, placebos have been used in medical research as a point of comparison. When a new drug is tested, some patients receive the drug and others receive a placebo that looks identical, and usually neither the patients nor the doctors know who has received which. If the drug performs better than the placebo, it is considered effective.

A curious feature of such trials is that patients who receive the placebo often improve too. Some of this improvement has nothing to do with the placebo itself: many conditions get better naturally over time, and symptoms that are unusually severe when a patient joins a trial tend to become less extreme later, whatever treatment is given. But research suggests that part of the improvement is a genuine response to the experience of being treated – the expectation of relief, the ritual of taking a pill, and the attention and care of medical staff. These responses appear to be strongest for symptoms that patients experience and report themselves, such as pain, nausea and fatigue, and weakest or absent for measurable changes such as the size of a tumour.

Most doctors and researchers long assumed that for a placebo to work, patients had to believe they were receiving real medicine. This creates an obvious ethical difficulty: prescribing a placebo outside a research trial would appear to require deceiving the patient, which is contrary to modern standards of honesty and informed consent.

In 2010, a group of researchers in the United States tested this assumption directly. They recruited around eighty patients suffering from irritable bowel syndrome, a common digestive disorder whose symptoms include pain and discomfort. Half were given no treatment. The other half were given pills in a bottle clearly labelled "placebo pills", and were told honestly that the pills contained no medication. They were also told that placebo pills had been shown in research to produce improvement through mind–body processes. After three weeks, the group taking the open placebos reported significantly greater improvement in their symptoms than the group that received no treatment.

Since then, similar "open-label" placebo studies have been carried out for several other conditions, including chronic back pain, fatigue in cancer survivors and allergic reactions. Many have reported improvements in patients' self-reported symptoms. Researchers have proposed various explanations. Patients may still expect some benefit even when they know the pill is inactive, particularly if the explanation given to them is encouraging. The act of taking a pill regularly may also trigger learned associations between treatment and relief, built up over a lifetime of taking medicines.

Critics have raised several concerns. Most open-label studies have been small, and in many of them patients knew which group they were in, which makes it difficult to separate the effect of the pills from the effect of feeling that one is receiving care. Because the outcomes measured are usually patients' own reports, they may be influenced by patients' wish to please the researchers or to justify their participation. Some studies comparing open placebos with no treatment have found only small effects, and a few have found none.

Even supporters stress that open-label placebos are not a substitute for effective treatment of serious diseases. Their potential lies, if anywhere, in helping patients with long-lasting symptoms for which existing treatments are limited or have unpleasant side effects. The research has also prompted a broader reconsideration of the role that the context of treatment – the way a doctor explains a treatment, and the time and care given to a patient – may play in how patients feel, whatever medicine they receive.

lesson.title: Study details — who, how many, how long, compared with what
lesson.example: Passage: "Over three weeks, patients with back pain who did the exercises reported less pain than a group that did not." Statement: "The exercises cured back pain." → FALSE? No: the passage does not say the pain was cured, nor that it was not. The answer is NOT GIVEN, unless the passage adds something like "no patient was fully free of pain", which would make it FALSE.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: In typical drug trials, patients are told whether they are receiving a placebo.
questions.evidence: usually neither the patients nor the doctors know who has received which
questions.explanation: This contradicts "told".

questions.text: All of the improvement seen in placebo groups is caused by the placebo itself.
questions.evidence: Some of this improvement has nothing to do with the placebo itself
questions.explanation: "Some ... nothing to do with" contradicts "all".

questions.text: Placebo responses appear to be weaker for measurable physical changes than for symptoms patients report.
questions.evidence: strongest for symptoms that patients experience and report themselves ... weakest or absent for measurable changes
questions.explanation: This matches, including the hedge "appear".

questions.text: Many researchers once believed that placebos only work if patients are deceived.
questions.evidence: Most doctors and researchers long assumed that for a placebo to work, patients had to believe they were receiving real medicine
questions.explanation: Believing a placebo is real medicine = being deceived, and "most ... long assumed" includes "many ... once believed".

questions.text: The 2010 study involved several hundred patients.
questions.evidence: around eighty patients
questions.explanation: The passage gives the number, and it contradicts "several hundred".

questions.text: In the 2010 study, the comparison group received a different kind of pill.
questions.evidence: Half were given no treatment
questions.explanation: The comparison group received nothing, not a different pill.

questions.text: Patients in the open-placebo group were told the pills contained no medication.
questions.evidence: were told honestly that the pills contained no medication
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: Open-label placebos have been found to shrink tumours.
questions.evidence: Paragraph B says placebo responses are "weakest or absent" for measurable changes such as tumour size. Paragraph E lists the conditions studied with open-label placebos.
questions.explanation: No open-label study of tumours is reported. Paragraph B's general point does not settle what open-label placebos do, so the specific claim is neither confirmed nor contradicted. This is a Hard-level NOT GIVEN, because related information is present.

questions.text: Some studies of open placebos have found no effect.
questions.evidence: a few have found none
questions.explanation: "A few" = "some", and "none" = "no effect".

questions.text: Supporters recommend open-label placebos as a replacement for treatment of serious illnesses.
questions.evidence: Even supporters stress that open-label placebos are not a substitute for effective treatment of serious diseases
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

passages.topic: Economic history — the tulip mania reconsidered
passages.title: The Flower That Crashed

paragraphs.text: Few episodes in economic history are as widely cited as the "tulip mania" of the Dutch Republic in the 1630s. According to the familiar account, tulip bulbs became objects of such frantic speculation that single bulbs sold for the price of a house, people from every level of society sold their possessions to buy them, and when prices suddenly collapsed in February 1637, thousands were ruined and the Dutch economy was thrown into crisis. The story is regularly retold whenever prices of assets such as shares or property rise rapidly, as a warning of what can happen when enthusiasm replaces judgement.

Much of this familiar account comes not from the records of the time but from later writers, especially a popular book published in London in 1841, which described the mania in vivid detail. That book relied heavily on pamphlets written in the Netherlands during and shortly after the crash, many of which were moralising works designed to condemn greed. Since the 1990s, historians returning to the original archives – contracts, court records, letters and notarial documents – have argued that the popular story is greatly exaggerated.

Some elements of the traditional account are accurate. Tulips, introduced into Europe from the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century, had become fashionable luxury items among wealthy collectors in the Dutch Republic. The most prized varieties had petals with striking streaks and flames of colour, and they were extremely rare because – as scientists later discovered – the patterns were caused by a virus that also weakened the bulbs, so that they multiplied slowly. Prices for such rare bulbs did rise dramatically in the winter of 1636–37, and some of the highest recorded prices were genuinely enormous, comparable to the cost of a substantial house in a Dutch city.

Much of the trade in that final winter took place not in bulbs themselves but in contracts. Because bulbs remain in the ground for much of the year, buyers agreed to pay a certain price for bulbs that would be delivered after they were lifted in the summer. Many of these contracts were agreed in taverns, among groups of traders, and money often did not change hands at the time of the agreement. When prices fell sharply in February 1637, many buyers simply refused to honour their contracts. Disputes followed, and eventually the courts and local authorities encouraged settlements in which buyers paid only a small fraction of the agreed price, or nothing at all.

According to the historians who have studied these records, the number of people involved in the trade was relatively small, consisting largely of merchants and skilled craftsmen rather than the poor. Researchers found few, if any, documented cases of people who were bankrupted by tulip dealing, and no evidence that the collapse caused a wider economic crisis: the Dutch economy of the period continued to prosper. The losses that did occur were often losses on paper – promised payments that were never made – rather than money actually spent.

Why, then, did the episode become so famous? Part of the answer is cultural. The sudden collapse shocked a society in which trade and wealth were closely connected with religious and moral values, and the idea that people had been willing to exchange fortunes for flowers seemed to many observers a sign of dangerous foolishness. The pamphlets that described the episode were written to teach a moral lesson, and they were later read as factual history.

Not all economists accept the revised view entirely. Some argue that the rapid rise and fall of prices in the winter of 1636–37 still shows features of a speculative bubble, even if its economic effects were limited. The debate illustrates how difficult it can be to decide what counts as irrational behaviour in markets. What seems clear, however, is that the tulip mania was far smaller, and far less disastrous, than the version of the story that continues to be told.

lesson.title: Popular belief vs the passage's revised account
lesson.text:
Some Hard passages present a popular story and then a revised version based on newer research. Statements may describe the popular story as if it were what the passage accepts. Decide what the passage presents as fact, and treat the popular account as a belief that the passage reports.

A statement matching the popular story, when the passage says research contradicts it → FALSE.

A statement that "people believed X", when the passage says X was widely believed → TRUE, even if X itself is false.
lesson.example: Passage: "It was long claimed that the castle was built in a single year; records now show construction lasted a decade." Statement: "The castle was built in one year." → FALSE. Statement: "People once thought the castle was built in one year." → TRUE.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The popular account of tulip mania claims that the collapse damaged the Dutch economy.
questions.evidence: According to the familiar account ... the Dutch economy was thrown into crisis
questions.explanation: The statement is about what the popular account claims, not whether it is correct. It is therefore TRUE, even though Paragraph E rejects the claim itself.

questions.text: The 1841 book was based mainly on archival contracts and court records.
questions.evidence: That book relied heavily on pamphlets ... many of which were moralising works
questions.explanation: Returning to the archives is what later historians did, which contradicts the statement.

questions.text: The most valuable tulips were rare partly because of a disease affecting the bulbs.
questions.evidence: the patterns were caused by a virus that also weakened the bulbs, so that they multiplied slowly
questions.explanation: "Virus" = "disease", and multiplying slowly explains why the bulbs were rare.

questions.text: Some tulip bulbs were sold for prices similar to that of a house.
questions.evidence: some of the highest recorded prices were ... comparable to the cost of a substantial house
questions.explanation: This part of the traditional story is confirmed.

questions.text: Tavern owners charged traders a fee for contracts agreed on their premises.
questions.evidence: Many of these contracts were agreed in taverns, among groups of traders
questions.explanation: Taverns are mentioned as the place where contracts were agreed, but nothing is said about fees charged by their owners. The topic appears, but the precise claim is absent.

questions.text: Courts required buyers to pay the full agreed price for their contracts.
questions.evidence: buyers paid only a small fraction of the agreed price, or nothing at all
questions.explanation: This contradicts "the full agreed price".

questions.text: Historians have found evidence that large numbers of poor people were ruined by tulip trading.
questions.evidence: consisting largely of merchants and skilled craftsmen rather than the poor ... few, if any, documented cases of people who were bankrupted
questions.explanation: Both parts of the statement are contradicted.

questions.text: The authors of the moralising pamphlets had themselves lost money in the tulip trade.
questions.evidence: The pamphlets "were written to teach a moral lesson"
questions.explanation: Nothing is said about the authors' own trading or losses.

questions.text: All economists now agree that tulip mania was not a speculative bubble.
questions.evidence: Not all economists accept the revised view entirely. Some argue that ... still shows features of a speculative bubble
questions.explanation: This directly contradicts "all ... agree".

passages.topic: Atmospheric science — can we make it rain?
passages.title: Seeding the Clouds

paragraphs.text: In 1946, a scientist working at an American electrical company made a discovery that seemed to promise control over the weather. While experimenting with a freezer chamber filled with moist air, he dropped in some dry ice – frozen carbon dioxide – and saw a cloud of tiny ice crystals form instantly. Soon afterwards, a colleague found that particles of silver iodide, a chemical whose crystal structure resembles that of ice, could have a similar effect. Within months, aircraft were dropping dry ice into real clouds, and "cloud seeding" was born.

The principle behind cloud seeding is relatively simple. Many clouds contain water droplets that remain liquid even at temperatures well below freezing, because they lack particles around which ice crystals can form. If suitable particles are introduced, ice crystals begin to grow at the expense of the surrounding droplets. When the crystals become heavy enough, they fall, and may reach the ground as snow or, if they melt on the way down, as rain. Other techniques use particles of salt to encourage droplets to merge in warmer clouds.

Enthusiasm in the early years was enormous. Governments and private companies in many countries launched seeding programmes to increase rainfall for agriculture, to add snow to mountains that supply rivers, and to reduce damage from hail. Some commercial operators made confident claims of success. Yet it soon became clear that proving the technique worked was much harder than performing it.

The central difficulty is that clouds are naturally variable. Whether a particular cloud produces rain depends on many factors, and even without any intervention, rainfall varies greatly from one day, one storm and one year to the next. If rain falls after a cloud has been seeded, it is very difficult to know whether it would have fallen anyway. To measure the effect of seeding reliably, scientists must compare large numbers of seeded and unseeded clouds or storms, chosen at random, and look for a difference that is larger than natural variation would produce. Such experiments are expensive and take many years, and several early programmes that claimed success did not use them.

When randomised experiments were carried out from the 1960s onwards, their results were mixed. Some suggested increases in precipitation under particular conditions; others found no clear effect, or results that could not be reproduced when the experiment was repeated elsewhere. By the end of the twentieth century, many scientists regarded the evidence as inconclusive, and a major review in 2003 concluded that there was still no convincing scientific proof that deliberate weather modification had produced the intended effects.

More recent research has provided stronger evidence in some circumstances. In a project carried out in the mountains of the western United States in 2017, scientists used radar and instruments on aircraft to observe clouds that had been seeded with silver iodide. They were able to follow lines of ice crystals forming along the paths of the seeding aircraft and growing into snow that fell to the ground – direct observation of the process that had previously only been inferred. A separate long-term study of winter clouds over mountains in the same region estimated that seeding might increase snowfall by a modest percentage in suitable conditions, though the researchers stressed that suitable conditions occurred only on some days.

Several countries continue to operate large seeding programmes, and interest has grown in regions facing drought. Scientists generally agree that seeding cannot create rain from clear skies; at most, it may increase the precipitation from clouds that already have the right characteristics. Questions also remain about whether increasing rainfall in one area might reduce it elsewhere, although there is little evidence either way. The most accurate summary of the present state of knowledge may be that cloud seeding can work, sometimes and modestly – which is considerably less than its early promoters promised.

lesson.title: Evidence strength words
lesson.text:
Hard science passages grade evidence precisely: demonstrated, confirmed, suggested, consistent with, no clear evidence, inconclusive. Match the strength of the statement to the strength in the passage.

Statement stronger than the passage and the passage signals doubt ("remains uncertain") → FALSE.

Statement stronger than the passage but the passage does not address the doubt → NOT GIVEN.

Statement equal to or weaker than the passage → TRUE.
lesson.example: Passage: "Early results are consistent with a small benefit, but further trials are needed." Statement: "Trials have proved a large benefit." → FALSE. Statement: "Early results suggest some benefit." → TRUE.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The effect of dry ice on moist air was discovered during an experiment.
questions.evidence: While experimenting with a freezer chamber filled with moist air, he dropped in some dry ice ... and saw a cloud of tiny ice crystals form
questions.explanation: This matches the statement.

questions.text: Silver iodide was used in cloud seeding before dry ice.
questions.evidence: dry ice was used first, and "Soon afterwards, a colleague found that particles of silver iodide ... could have a similar effect"
questions.explanation: The statement reverses the sequence.

questions.text: Seeding works by providing particles on which ice crystals can form.
questions.evidence: they lack particles around which ice crystals can form. If suitable particles are introduced, ice crystals begin to grow
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.text: The scientist who discovered the effect of dry ice later directed government seeding programmes.
questions.evidence: Paragraph A describes the discovery, and Paragraph C says governments "launched seeding programmes".
questions.explanation: The scientist's later career is never mentioned. Do not connect the two paragraphs without evidence.

questions.text: Several early programmes that reported success did not use randomised comparisons.
questions.evidence: "several early programmes that claimed success did not use them" (Paragraph D), where "them" refers to randomised comparisons.
questions.explanation: You must resolve the pronoun "them" to confirm the match.

questions.text: The 2003 review found convincing proof that cloud seeding increases rainfall.
questions.evidence: there was still no convincing scientific proof
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: The 2017 project directly observed ice crystals forming along the paths of seeding aircraft.
questions.evidence: They were able to follow lines of ice crystals forming along the paths of the seeding aircraft
questions.explanation: The passage calls this "direct observation".

questions.text: The long-term study found that seeding increased snowfall on every day it was used.
questions.evidence: suitable conditions occurred only on some days
questions.explanation: The estimated increase applied "in suitable conditions", which occurred only on some days. This contradicts "every day".

questions.text: Seeding rain in one area has been shown to reduce rainfall in neighbouring areas.
questions.evidence: Questions also remain about whether increasing rainfall in one area might reduce it elsewhere, although there is little evidence either way
questions.explanation: The passage says the matter is unresolved, with "little evidence either way", so "has been shown" is contradicted. This is the evidence-strength rule from the lesson. If the passage had not mentioned the question at all, the answer would be NOT GIVEN.

passages.topic: Archaeology and technology — an ancient calculating machine
passages.title: The Machine from the Sea

paragraphs.text: In 1900, a group of sponge divers sheltering from a storm near the small Greek island of Antikythera discovered the wreck of an ancient ship on the seabed. Over the following months, divers recovered bronze and marble statues, pottery, glassware and coins from the wreck, which is thought to have sunk sometime in the first half of the first century BC. Among the finds was a shapeless lump of corroded bronze and wood, roughly the size of a shoebox, which attracted little attention at first.

Some months later, the lump broke apart, and a museum worker noticed that one fragment contained a toothed wheel – a gear. This was astonishing. Gearwheels of such precision were not otherwise known from the ancient world, and nothing of comparable complexity is known to have survived from the following thousand years. Some scholars at first suggested that the object must be much more recent, perhaps an astronomical instrument from a later ship that had sunk in the same place. Others insisted, correctly as it turned out, that it belonged to the ancient wreck.

For decades, understanding the mechanism was extremely difficult. The fragments were badly corroded, their gears were hidden inside layers of mineral deposits, and many parts were missing altogether. In the 1950s and 1970s, a British historian of science used early X-ray images to argue that the device was a kind of calculating machine that modelled the movements of the heavens. His interpretation was widely discussed but remained incomplete, since the images could not show the internal structure clearly.

A major advance came in 2005, when an international research team examined the fragments using advanced three-dimensional X-ray scanning and new techniques for photographing their surfaces. The scans revealed the positions of around thirty surviving gears, as well as thousands of tiny letters inscribed on the device, many of them previously unreadable. These inscriptions, which acted partly as a user's guide, helped the researchers to work out what the machine did.

The mechanism, the researchers concluded, was operated by turning a handle on its side. This moved a series of dials on the front and back. On the front, pointers showed the positions of the Sun and Moon against the background of the stars, and a small rotating ball, half light and half dark, displayed the phases of the Moon. On the back, spiral dials allowed the user to predict eclipses of the Sun and Moon, and another dial tracked the four-year cycle of the major athletic games held in different Greek cities, including the games at Olympia. Inscriptions refer to the planets, and many researchers believe that the device also displayed their positions, although the parts that would have done so are lost.

One of the most admired features was the way the mechanism reproduced the Moon's changing speed across the sky. The Moon appears to move faster at some times of the month than at others. The device imitated this variation using a pair of gears mounted slightly off-centre, with a pin on one gear sliding in a slot on the other – an arrangement that reflects a sophisticated understanding of both astronomy and mechanical design.

Many questions remain. The date at which the mechanism was made is disputed: estimates based on the style of its lettering and the astronomical cycles it models range across the second and early first centuries BC. Who designed it, and where, is also uncertain, although scholars have suggested links with several centres of Greek astronomy. It is not known whether the device was a unique creation or one of a tradition of similar instruments, all of which have otherwise been lost – though references in ancient writings to devices that modelled the heavens suggest that it may not have been the only one of its kind.

What is clear is that the Antikythera mechanism has changed modern understanding of ancient technology. It shows that, more than two thousand years ago, craftsmen could build compact machines of remarkable precision to represent scientific knowledge – a level of mechanical skill that would not be seen again in Europe until the astronomical clocks of the medieval period.

lesson.title: Dates, ranges and estimates
lesson.text: Hard passages often give approximate or disputed dates ("probably made between the second and first centuries BC", "estimates range from..."). A statement that fixes an exact date the passage leaves open is usually NOT GIVEN. It is FALSE only if the date falls clearly outside the passage's range. Also distinguish when an object was made, when it was lost, when it was found and when it was understood. Statements often swap these.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The ship sank sometime around 70 BC; the wreck was discovered in 1900." Statement: "The ship sank in 1900." → FALSE (the discovery date has been swapped in).
Statement: "The ship sank in 72 BC." → NOT GIVEN (possible within "around 70 BC", but not stated).

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The ship carrying the mechanism sank in 1900.
questions.evidence: the wreck "is thought to have sunk sometime in the first half of the first century BC"; 1900 is when it was discovered
questions.explanation: The statement swaps the discovery date for the sinking date.

questions.text: The mechanism was immediately recognised as important when it was brought up from the wreck.
questions.evidence: attracted little attention at first
questions.explanation: This contradicts "immediately recognised".

questions.text: All scholars initially agreed that the mechanism came from the ancient ship.
questions.evidence: Some scholars at first suggested that the object must be much more recent ... Others insisted ... that it belonged to the ancient wreck
questions.explanation: There was disagreement, which contradicts "all ... agreed".

questions.text: Early X-ray images allowed researchers to see the internal structure of the device clearly.
questions.evidence: the images could not show the internal structure clearly
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: The 2005 study revealed inscriptions that had not been read before.
questions.evidence: thousands of tiny letters ... many of them previously unreadable
questions.explanation: "Previously unreadable" = "had not been read before".

questions.text: The mechanism was powered by a system of weights.
questions.evidence: operated by turning a handle on its side
questions.explanation: The passage specifies a hand-turned mechanism, which is incompatible with power from weights.

questions.text: The surviving parts clearly show how the planets' positions were displayed.
questions.evidence: many researchers believe that the device also displayed their positions, although the parts that would have done so are lost
questions.explanation: Because those parts are lost, the surviving parts cannot "clearly show" this.

questions.text: The mechanism was made in 87 BC.
questions.evidence: estimates ... range across the second and early first centuries BC
questions.explanation: The year 87 BC falls within the range the passage gives, so it is not contradicted. But no exact year is stated, so it is not confirmed either. This is the approximate-date rule from the lesson.

questions.text: Ancient writings mention devices that represented the movements of the heavens.
questions.evidence: references in ancient writings to devices that modelled the heavens
questions.explanation: "Modelled the heavens" = "represented the movements of the heavens".

passages.topic: Psychology and law — how reliable is eyewitness memory?
passages.title: The Fallible Witness

paragraphs.text: For much of legal history, few forms of evidence have been as persuasive as the testimony of an eyewitness. A person who stands in court and declares, "That is the man I saw," can have a powerful effect on a jury, particularly if the witness appears confident. Yet decades of psychological research have shown that human memory does not work like a video recording. It is reconstructed each time we recall an event, and it can be altered, sometimes dramatically, by information received afterwards.

Some of the best-known demonstrations of this were carried out in the 1970s by the American psychologist Elizabeth Loftus and her colleagues. In one experiment, participants watched film clips of traffic accidents and were then asked questions about what they had seen. The key question was worded differently for different groups: some were asked how fast the cars were going when they "hit" each other, others when they "smashed into" each other. Participants who heard the word "smashed" gave higher estimates of speed. A week later, without seeing the film again, participants were asked whether they had seen any broken glass. There had been none in the film, yet those who had heard "smashed" were more than twice as likely to report having seen it.

Later research extended these findings considerably. Experiments showed that misleading information introduced after an event could lead people to report details that had not been present, to change their descriptions of people and objects, and, in some studies, to "remember" entire events that had never taken place. Such false memories could be held with great confidence and described in vivid detail, making them difficult to distinguish from genuine memories, both for the people who held them and for those listening.

The practical significance of this research became especially clear from the 1990s, when advances in DNA testing allowed the re-examination of evidence in old criminal cases. In the United States, a large number of people who had been convicted of serious crimes were later shown by DNA evidence to be innocent. Analyses of these cases found that mistaken identification by eyewitnesses had played a role in a clear majority of them. In many, the witnesses had been sincere and confident; they were not lying, but they were wrong.

Researchers have identified a number of factors that increase the risk of mistaken identification. Witnesses are generally less accurate when the event was brief or stressful, when a weapon was present – which tends to draw attention away from the face of the person holding it – and when the person they are identifying belongs to a different ethnic group from their own. The way identifications are carried out also matters. If the officer conducting an identification parade knows which person is the suspect, he or she may unintentionally signal this to the witness. Feedback given after an identification – such as "Good, you identified our suspect" – can make witnesses more confident without making them more accurate.

These findings have led to reforms in many places. Recommended procedures now include having identification parades conducted by officers who do not know which person is the suspect, telling witnesses that the offender may not be present, and recording the witness's level of confidence immediately, before any feedback is given. Some courts now allow expert witnesses to explain the limitations of memory to juries.

The relationship between confidence and accuracy has been reconsidered. It was long assumed by researchers that a witness's confidence was a poor guide to whether an identification was correct. More recent studies suggest a more complex picture: when an identification is carried out under good conditions and confidence is recorded immediately, high confidence can be a reasonably reliable indicator of accuracy. The problem is that confidence often grows over time, especially after feedback and repeated questioning, so that by the time a witness reaches court, his or her certainty may say little about the original memory.

lesson.title: Combining everything
lesson.text:
This final set combines the main TFNG skills: qualifiers, study details, causes, evidence strength and "was vs is". Work through each statement with a fixed checklist:

1. What is the one claim?

2. Where is it in the passage?

3. Does the passage settle this exact claim?

4. Yes, the same → TRUE.

5. Yes, the opposite or incompatible → FALSE.

6. No → NOT GIVEN.

Do not change an answer just because TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN "seems to have come up too often". Every set has its own balance.

groups.title: True / False / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the information given in the reading passage?
Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Memories are reconstructed rather than simply replayed.
questions.evidence: memory does not work like a video recording. It is reconstructed each time we recall an event
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: In Loftus's experiment, all participants were asked exactly the same questions.
questions.evidence: The key question was worded differently for different groups
questions.explanation: This contradicts "exactly the same questions".

questions.text: The film shown to participants included a scene with broken glass.
questions.evidence: There had been none in the film
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Participants who heard "smashed" were more likely to report seeing broken glass.
questions.evidence: those who had heard 'smashed' were more than twice as likely to report having seen it
questions.explanation: "More than twice as likely" includes "more likely".

questions.text: False memories are usually less detailed than genuine memories.
questions.evidence: Such false memories could be ... described in vivid detail, making them difficult to distinguish from genuine memories
questions.explanation: This contradicts the claim that false memories are less detailed.

questions.text: Most of the DNA exoneration cases involved witnesses who were deliberately lying.
questions.evidence: they were not lying, but they were wrong
questions.explanation: This directly contradicts "deliberately lying".

questions.text: The presence of a weapon tends to make witnesses more accurate in identifying faces.
