questions.evidence: witnesses are less accurate "when a weapon was present"
questions.explanation: This is the opposite of the statement.

questions.text: Positive feedback after an identification can increase a witness's confidence.
questions.evidence: Feedback given after an identification ... can make witnesses more confident without making them more accurate
questions.explanation: This matches the statement.

questions.text: The reforms described have been adopted in every country.
questions.evidence: These findings have led to reforms in many places
questions.explanation: "Many places" neither confirms nor rules out "every country". The passage does not tell us the full extent.

questions.text: Researchers have always believed that confidence recorded immediately is a good guide to accuracy.
questions.evidence: It was long assumed by researchers that a witness's confidence was a poor guide ... More recent studies suggest ...
questions.explanation: The earlier assumption was the opposite, which contradicts "always believed".

passages.topic: Urban environment — the case for street trees
passages.title: Why Our Streets Need Trees

paragraphs.text: When city budgets are tight, trees are often among the first things to be cut – sometimes literally. Planting schemes are postponed, and mature trees that cause inconvenience are removed rather than maintained. I believe this is a serious mistake. Street trees are not a decorative luxury but one of the most cost-effective investments a city can make in the health and comfort of its residents.

The most obvious benefit is shade. On a hot summer day, the temperature of a paved street beneath a row of large trees can be many degrees lower than that of an exposed street nearby. As heatwaves become more frequent, this is not merely a matter of comfort. Extreme heat is dangerous, particularly for elderly people and young children, and it seems to me irresponsible to leave the streets of our cities without the natural protection that trees provide.

Trees also help to manage rainwater. Their leaves intercept rain and their roots help water soak into the ground, reducing the amount that rushes into drains during storms. They absorb some pollutants from the air, although I would not want to exaggerate this effect: trees cannot solve the problem of air pollution on their own, and reducing traffic emissions remains far more important.

There is also growing evidence that trees affect how people feel. Streets with trees are generally perceived as more attractive, and people are more likely to walk along them. Some studies have linked greener neighbourhoods with lower levels of stress. I find these findings persuasive, even if the reasons for them are not fully understood.

Opponents of street trees raise several objections, and some of them deserve to be taken seriously. Roots can damage pavements and underground pipes, falling leaves must be cleared, and branches occasionally fall in storms. But these problems usually result from poor planning rather than from trees themselves. Choosing species suited to the space available, giving roots enough soil and maintaining trees properly can prevent most of them. Removing a healthy tree because its leaves are untidy is, in my view, rather like demolishing a house because its windows need cleaning.

Another common objection is cost. Trees must be bought, planted, watered and pruned, and in the early years many die if they are neglected. Yet when their benefits – lower cooling costs, reduced flooding, improved health – are taken into account, well-planned tree schemes pay for themselves many times over. The real waste of money is planting trees and then failing to look after them.

Cities should therefore treat trees as essential infrastructure, just like roads, pipes and street lighting. That means long-term budgets for maintenance, careful choice of species, and particular attention to poorer neighbourhoods, which often have far fewer trees than wealthier ones. A city that plants wisely today will be cooler, healthier and more pleasant for decades to come.

lesson.title: Spotting the writer's position early
lesson.text: In an argumentative passage, the writer's main position is usually clear in the first and last paragraphs. Middle paragraphs give reasons, deal with objections and offer qualifications. Write the writer's position in five words at the top of the passage, for example "cities need more trees; plan carefully". Many YES/NO answers follow directly from it, but check each qualification the writer adds.
lesson.example: Opening: "Cycling lanes are the best investment a city can make." Statement: "The writer believes cycling lanes are a poor use of money." → NO.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage? Write
YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.text: Street trees should be regarded as a decorative luxury.
questions.evidence: Street trees are not a decorative luxury but one of the most cost-effective investments
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly rejects this view.

questions.text: It is irresponsible to leave city streets without tree shade during heatwaves.
questions.evidence: it seems to me irresponsible to leave the streets of our cities without the natural protection that trees provide
questions.explanation: "It seems to me" marks the writer's own view, and it matches the statement.

questions.text: Trees are the most effective way of reducing air pollution.
questions.evidence: trees cannot solve the problem of air pollution on their own, and reducing traffic emissions remains far more important
questions.explanation: The writer considers reducing emissions more important, which contradicts "most effective".

questions.text: The link between trees and lower stress has been fully explained.
questions.evidence: even if the reasons for them are not fully understood
questions.explanation: The writer states the opposite.

questions.text: Some objections to street trees are worth considering.
questions.evidence: some of them deserve to be taken seriously
questions.explanation: "Deserve to be taken seriously" = "worth considering".

questions.text: Most problems caused by street trees are the result of poor planning.
questions.evidence: these problems usually result from poor planning rather than from trees themselves
questions.explanation: "Usually" = "most".

questions.text: Fruit trees are the most suitable species for city streets.
questions.evidence: The writer recommends "species suited to the space available" (Paragraph E) but never mentions fruit trees.
questions.explanation: No view on this claim is expressed.

questions.text: Poorer neighbourhoods should receive particular attention in tree planting.
questions.evidence: particular attention to poorer neighbourhoods, which often have far fewer trees
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

passages.topic: Education — homework for young children
passages.title: How Much Homework Is Too Much?

paragraphs.text: Few subjects provoke as much disagreement among parents as homework. Some complain that their children spend every evening on worksheets and have no time to play; others worry that their children's school sets too little and that they are falling behind. Teachers are caught in the middle, and school policies vary enormously, even between neighbouring schools. Having looked at the evidence, I have come to the view that for young children, in particular, much of the homework currently set does little good.

Research on homework in secondary schools generally finds a positive, if modest, relationship between the time students spend on homework and their achievement, at least up to a point. Beyond around two hours a night, additional homework appears to bring little further benefit. For primary school pupils, however, the picture is very different. Most studies have found little or no connection between the amount of homework young children do and how well they perform at school.

Supporters of homework for young children argue that it teaches good habits, such as working independently and managing time, which will be needed later. This is a reasonable hope, but I am not convinced that it is borne out in practice. Too often, homework for young children depends heavily on parents' help, and becomes a nightly struggle that teaches children to associate learning with conflict rather than curiosity.

Homework can also widen differences between children. Pupils whose parents have the time, confidence and education to help them are likely to complete it more successfully than those whose parents work long hours or are unfamiliar with the material. A task intended to help all children can therefore end up favouring those who are already advantaged. Schools rarely take this problem seriously enough.

This does not mean that young children should do nothing at home. Reading is the obvious exception. There is strong evidence that children who read regularly outside school, and who are read to by adults, develop better language skills, and I would encourage every family to make reading a daily habit. Short, practical activities – counting coins, measuring ingredients while cooking, talking about a book – can also support learning without turning the evening into a battle.

What young children need most after the school day, in my view, is time: time to play, to rest, to spend with their families and to pursue their own interests. These activities are not a waste of time that could be better spent on worksheets; they are an essential part of development. Schools that set large amounts of written homework for young pupils should ask themselves honestly whether it serves the children or simply reassures adults that learning is taking place.

lesson.title: Reported views vs the writer's view
lesson.text: Writers often present an opinion before responding to it: "Some parents argue that... This, however, overlooks...". The first sentence is not the writer's view. Always read on to the writer's reaction. Words such as however, yet, but, this overlooks, I disagree, there is some truth in this reveal whether the writer rejects, accepts or partly accepts the reported view.
lesson.example: Passage: "Some claim tests are useless. There is some truth in this for very young children, but for older students tests are valuable." Statement: "Tests are useless for all students." → NO.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Much of the homework given to young children is of little benefit.
questions.evidence: for young children, in particular, much of the homework currently set does little good
questions.explanation: "Does little good" = "of little benefit".

questions.text: More than two hours of homework a night brings large additional benefits for secondary students.
questions.evidence: Beyond around two hours a night, additional homework appears to bring little further benefit
questions.explanation: "Little further benefit" contradicts "large additional benefits". The writer presents this finding as part of the evidence that informs their view.

questions.text: Homework for young children clearly succeeds in teaching independent working habits.
questions.evidence: This is a reasonable hope, but I am not convinced that it is borne out in practice
questions.explanation: The supporters hold this view, but the writer doubts it, which contradicts "clearly succeeds".

questions.text: Homework may benefit children whose parents can help them more than other children.
questions.evidence: A task intended to help all children can therefore end up favouring those who are already advantaged
questions.explanation: This matches the statement.

questions.text: Schools generally give enough attention to the unequal effects of homework.
questions.evidence: Schools rarely take this problem seriously enough
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Reading at home is valuable for young children.
questions.evidence: Reading is the obvious exception ... I would encourage every family to make reading a daily habit
questions.explanation: This matches the statement.

questions.text: Children should be given homework during school holidays.
questions.evidence: School holidays are never mentioned.
questions.explanation: The writer expresses no view on this.

questions.text: Play is an important part of children's development.
questions.evidence: These activities are not a waste of time ... they are an essential part of development
questions.explanation: Play is among "these activities".

passages.topic: Education and technology — handwriting in a digital age
passages.title: The Case for the Pen

paragraphs.text: In many classrooms, the pen is losing ground to the keyboard. Students take notes on laptops, submit assignments online and, in some countries, schools have reduced the time spent teaching handwriting, particularly joined-up writing. This is understandable, but I believe it would be a mistake to abandon handwriting altogether.

Admittedly, typing has clear advantages. It is faster for most adults, produces text that is easy to read, and allows work to be edited, shared and stored without difficulty. For some students with physical difficulties that make writing by hand painful or slow, keyboards are an essential tool, and nobody should be forced to struggle with a pen when a better alternative exists.

Yet there is evidence that writing by hand offers benefits that typing does not. Several studies have found that young children who practise forming letters by hand learn to recognise them more quickly than those who learn by typing. The physical effort of shaping each letter seems to help fix its form in memory. I find this evidence convincing, and it suggests that handwriting should remain part of early education.

There is also research on note-taking. In some experiments, students who took notes by hand during lectures remembered the content better than those who typed, apparently because typing allowed them to copy the lecturer's words almost exactly, while writing by hand forced them to summarise and think about what they heard. These studies have not always been repeated with the same results, and I would not claim they settle the question. But they give teachers good reason to be cautious before replacing notebooks with laptops.

Some argue that handwriting is simply old-fashioned, and that spending time on it is a form of nostalgia. I disagree. The question is not whether handwriting is traditional but whether it is useful, and for learning to read and for thinking carefully about new material, there is reason to believe that it is. Moreover, there are still many situations – examinations in many countries, forms, quick notes – in which people need to write by hand legibly.

None of this means that schools should ignore digital skills. Children need to learn to type efficiently and to use technology well. The sensible approach is to teach both, and to choose the tool that best suits each task. Handwriting deserves its place in that choice, not because it is familiar, but because it works.

lesson.title: Concessions ("Admittedly...", "Of course...")
lesson.text: Writers make their arguments more convincing by admitting points that seem to support the other side: admittedly, of course, it is true that, I accept that, no doubt. A concession is the writer's view. The writer genuinely accepts it, even though it is not the main argument. So if the writer says "Admittedly, typing is faster", a statement "typing is faster than handwriting" is YES, even if the writer's overall position favours handwriting.
lesson.example: Passage: "Of course, electric cars are expensive. Even so, I believe they are worth buying." Statement: "Electric cars are costly." → YES.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Handwriting should be completely replaced by typing in schools.
questions.evidence: I believe it would be a mistake to abandon handwriting altogether
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: For most adults, typing is quicker than writing by hand.
questions.evidence: Admittedly, typing ... is faster for most adults
questions.explanation: This is a concession, and it is still the writer's view.

questions.text: Students who find writing painful should be required to use pens.
questions.evidence: nobody should be forced to struggle with a pen when a better alternative exists
questions.explanation: This contradicts "required to use pens".

questions.text: Learning to form letters by hand may help children remember them.
questions.evidence: The physical effort of shaping each letter seems to help fix its form in memory. I find this evidence convincing
questions.explanation: The hedge "may" in the statement fits "seems".

questions.text: The research on note-taking has conclusively settled the question.
questions.evidence: I would not claim they settle the question
questions.explanation: This contradicts "conclusively settled".

questions.text: Handwriting is mainly valued out of nostalgia.
questions.evidence: Some argue that handwriting is simply old-fashioned ... a form of nostalgia. I disagree
questions.explanation: This is the reported view that the writer rejects.

questions.text: Joined-up writing is easier to read than separate letters.
questions.evidence: Joined-up writing is mentioned only in Paragraph A, as something schools teach less.
questions.explanation: The writer gives no view on its readability.

questions.text: Schools should teach both handwriting and typing.
questions.evidence: The sensible approach is to teach both
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

passages.topic: Culture — should museums be free to enter?
passages.title: Open Doors

paragraphs.text: Should people pay to enter public museums? In some countries, national museums have long been free, while in others visitors expect to buy a ticket, sometimes an expensive one. The question is not only financial. It concerns what museums are for and whom they are meant to serve. My own view is that, for publicly funded museums, free entry to permanent collections is generally the better policy.

The strongest argument for free entry is that museums hold collections on behalf of the public. Many of their objects were acquired with public money, or given by donors who wanted them to be enjoyed by everyone. Charging for entry turns access to this shared inheritance into something that depends on the ability to pay. For families on low incomes, even a modest charge can be a real barrier, particularly if several family members want to visit.

There is evidence that charges affect who visits. When museums have removed charges, visitor numbers have often risen substantially. It must be said, however, that the increase has not always been as broad as supporters hoped. Much of the growth has sometimes come from people who were already regular museum-goers visiting more often, rather than from new audiences. Free entry, in other words, is necessary for wider access but not sufficient on its own.

Museums that want to reach people who rarely visit must do more than open their doors. They need to offer events, exhibitions and educational programmes that speak to a wide range of communities, and to work with schools and local organisations. I would argue that this outreach work is just as important as the question of charges, and it is too often underfunded.

Opponents of free entry point out that museums face serious financial pressures, and that visitors who can afford to pay – including many international tourists – should contribute to the cost of what they enjoy. This is a fair point. I see no objection to museums charging for special temporary exhibitions, which are expensive to organise, or inviting visitors to make voluntary donations. Some museums have found that clearly displayed donation boxes raise significant sums.

What I oppose is the idea that the main collections of public museums should be available only to those who can afford a ticket. A society that values its history, art and science should make them as accessible as possible. Free entry does not guarantee that everyone will come, but charging guarantees that some will not.

lesson.title: Strength of the writer's view
lesson.text: Writers don't only agree or disagree; they agree to a degree. A writer who says free entry is "generally the better policy" does not claim that "all museums must be free in all circumstances". Compare the strength words in the statement (always, all, must, never, completely) with the writer's own words (generally, usually, in most cases, can). If the statement is clearly stronger than the writer's view, the answer is usually NO.
lesson.example: Passage: "Charging for plastic bags is usually a good idea." Statement: "Charging for plastic bags is always right." → NO, because the writer allows exceptions.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Free entry is generally preferable for the permanent collections of publicly funded museums.
questions.evidence: for publicly funded museums, free entry to permanent collections is generally the better policy
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.text: A small entry fee cannot discourage low-income families from visiting.
questions.evidence: even a modest charge can be a real barrier
questions.explanation: This contradicts "cannot discourage".

questions.text: Removing charges has always attracted many new types of visitors.
questions.evidence: the increase has not always been as broad as supporters hoped. Much of the growth has sometimes come from people who were already regular museum-goers
questions.explanation: This contradicts "always ... new types of visitors".

questions.text: Free entry alone is enough to widen museum audiences.
questions.evidence: Free entry ... is necessary for wider access but not sufficient on its own
questions.explanation: "Not sufficient on its own" contradicts "alone is enough".

questions.text: Outreach programmes in museums often lack sufficient funding.
questions.evidence: it is too often underfunded
questions.explanation: "Too often underfunded" = "often lack sufficient funding".

questions.text: Museums should never charge for any exhibition.
questions.evidence: I see no objection to museums charging for special temporary exhibitions
questions.explanation: This contradicts "never ... any exhibition". The writer's view is less absolute than the statement.

questions.text: International tourists visit museums more often than local residents.
questions.evidence: International tourists are mentioned only as people who "can afford to pay"
questions.explanation: No comparison of how often they visit is made.

questions.text: Charging for entry will prevent some people from visiting museums.
questions.evidence: charging guarantees that some will not [come]
questions.explanation: This matches the statement.

passages.topic: Tourism — when too many visitors arrive
passages.title: Loving Places to Death

paragraphs.text: In recent years, a number of popular destinations have begun to complain of "overtourism". Residents of historic city centres find their streets blocked by crowds, their local shops replaced by souvenir stalls, and their rents pushed up as apartments are converted into short-term holiday rentals. Natural sites, from beaches to mountain paths, suffer from erosion and litter. In some places, residents have held protests against the very visitors on whom much of the local economy depends.

It would be easy to conclude that tourism itself is the problem. I think that conclusion is wrong. Tourism brings employment and income to millions of people, and travel can broaden understanding between cultures. The difficulty is not that people travel, but that visitors are concentrated in a small number of places, at the same times of year and even at the same times of day. The same number of tourists spread more evenly would cause far fewer problems.

Some destinations have responded with outright bans – closing sites completely or prohibiting certain types of tourism. Occasionally, when a site has been seriously damaged, a temporary closure may be justified to allow recovery. As a general policy, however, I find bans too blunt. They punish responsible visitors along with irresponsible ones and can devastate local businesses.

Better tools are available. Timed tickets, which require visitors to book a specific entry slot, can smooth the flow of people at popular attractions. Limits on the number of large cruise ships arriving on the same day can prevent sudden surges of thousands of passengers. Tourist taxes, if the revenue is used to benefit residents and maintain sites, can ensure that visitors contribute to the costs they create. None of these measures is perfect, but together they can make a real difference.

The growth of short-term holiday rentals deserves particular attention. In some city centres, they have reduced the housing available to local people and contributed to rising rents. Several cities have introduced rules limiting the number of days a year an apartment can be rented to tourists, or requiring owners to register. In my view, such regulation is necessary if historic centres are to remain places where people actually live, rather than becoming open-air museums.

Tourists themselves have a role to play. Visiting in the quieter seasons, exploring lesser-known towns and neighbourhoods, and staying longer rather than making brief day trips all reduce pressure on the most crowded places. Yet it would be unrealistic to rely on individual choices alone. Most visitors will continue to want to see the most famous sights, and it is up to authorities to manage those sights sensibly.

Tourism, well managed, can support rather than overwhelm the places people love to visit. The goal should not be fewer travellers in total, but travel that is spread more widely and planned more carefully.

lesson.title: "Rather than" and "not ... but"
lesson.text: Writers often reject one idea and propose another in the same sentence: "not X but Y", "Y rather than X", "instead of X, cities should Y". These structures give you two answers at once: a statement supporting X is NO, and a statement supporting Y is YES. Read such sentences slowly, because it is easy to reverse them.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The answer is not to close the park but to manage its paths better."
Statement: "The park should be closed." → NO. Statement: "Better path management is needed." → YES.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Tourism itself is the main cause of the problems described.
questions.evidence: It would be easy to conclude that tourism itself is the problem. I think that conclusion is wrong
questions.explanation: The writer rejects this directly.

questions.text: The concentration of visitors in particular places and times is the real difficulty.
questions.evidence: The difficulty is not that people travel, but that visitors are concentrated in a small number of places, at the same times
questions.explanation: This is the "not X but Y" pattern: Y is the writer's view.

questions.text: A temporary closure can sometimes be appropriate for a damaged site.
questions.evidence: Occasionally, when a site has been seriously damaged, a temporary closure may be justified
questions.explanation: This is a concession that the writer genuinely accepts.

questions.text: Bans are the most effective general response to overtourism.
questions.evidence: As a general policy, however, I find bans too blunt
questions.explanation: This contradicts "most effective".

questions.text: Tourist taxes are only acceptable if the money benefits residents and sites.
questions.evidence: Tourist taxes, if the revenue is used to benefit residents and maintain sites, can ensure that visitors contribute
questions.explanation: The writer says taxes can work under this condition, but does not say they are acceptable only under it. Whether they would be acceptable otherwise is not stated. This is a Medium-style trap placed here for practice.

questions.text: Cruise passengers spend less money locally than other tourists.
questions.evidence: Cruise ships are mentioned only in relation to sudden surges of passengers
questions.explanation: No view on spending is expressed.

questions.text: Regulating short-term rentals is necessary to keep historic centres lived in.
questions.evidence: In my view, such regulation is necessary if historic centres are to remain places where people actually live
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: Individual tourists' choices will be enough to solve overtourism.
questions.evidence: it would be unrealistic to rely on individual choices alone
questions.explanation: This contradicts "will be enough".

passages.topic: Transport policy — should public transport be free?
passages.title: The Price of a Free Ride

paragraphs.text: Several cities and even a few countries have made public transport free for everyone. The idea is attractive: free buses and trams should encourage people to leave their cars at home, reduce traffic and pollution, and help people on low incomes. It is not surprising that many campaigners now call for free public transport everywhere. I share their goals, but I am not persuaded that abolishing fares is the best way to achieve them.

The first problem is cost. Fares typically cover a substantial part of the running costs of public transport systems, and removing them means that the money must come from elsewhere – usually from taxes. That money could instead be spent on improving services: more frequent buses, new routes, longer operating hours and better stations. In my view, these improvements would do more to attract drivers than a lower price.

Surveys of drivers consistently suggest that what keeps them in their cars is not mainly the price of a ticket. It is the fact that public transport is often slow, infrequent, unreliable or simply does not go where they need to go. A free bus that comes once an hour and takes twice as long as driving will not persuade many people to change their habits. Evidence from cities that have introduced free travel tends to support this: passenger numbers usually rise, but a large share of the new passengers are people who previously walked or cycled, rather than drivers.

None of this means that fares should be high. For people on low incomes, the cost of travel can be a real burden, limiting their access to jobs, education and services. I strongly support reduced fares or free travel for those who need them most – such as students, older people, the unemployed and families with low incomes. Targeted support of this kind helps those who struggle to pay without spending public money on travellers who can easily afford their tickets.

Supporters of free transport point out that collecting fares is itself expensive, requiring ticket machines, inspectors and payment systems, and that removing fares can speed up journeys because passengers board more quickly. These are fair points, and in small towns with modest ticket income, free travel may well make sense. In large cities, however, where fares raise very large sums, the calculation is different.

The aim of public transport policy should be to make buses and trains a genuinely attractive alternative to the car. Price is part of that picture, but it is not the most important part. A fast, frequent and reliable service at a fair price will do more for our cities than a slow and crowded one that happens to be free.

lesson.title: Priorities and rankings in opinions
lesson.text: A writer may accept that something is good while arguing that something else is more important. For example: "Lower fares help, but reliability matters more." Statements may test the ranking. "Price is the most important factor" → NO. "Lower fares can help" → YES. Look for comparative language: more important, above all, the main, secondary, the first priority.
lesson.example: Passage: "Cheaper tickets are welcome, but the real priority is more frequent trains." Statement: "Frequency matters more than price." → YES.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The writer agrees with the aims of those who campaign for free public transport.
questions.evidence: I share their goals, but I am not persuaded that abolishing fares is the best way
questions.explanation: The writer agrees with the aims but not with the method.

questions.text: Improving services would attract more drivers than removing fares.
questions.evidence: In my view, these improvements would do more to attract drivers than a lower price
questions.explanation: This matches the writer's ranking.

questions.text: The main reason people drive is the price of public transport tickets.
questions.evidence: what keeps them in their cars is not mainly the price of a ticket
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Free travel mainly attracts people who previously walked or cycled.
questions.evidence: a large share of the new passengers are people who previously walked or cycled, rather than drivers
questions.explanation: The writer presents this evidence as supporting their view. "Mainly" is justified by the contrast "rather than drivers".

questions.text: Fares on public transport should be set at a high level.
questions.evidence: None of this means that fares should be high
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Free travel for older people should be funded by national government rather than cities.
questions.evidence: The writer supports free travel for older people (Paragraph D) but never discusses who should pay for it.
questions.explanation: No view is given on funding sources.

questions.text: Free public transport may be sensible in some small towns.
questions.evidence: in small towns with modest ticket income, free travel may well make sense
questions.explanation: This is a concession that the writer accepts.

questions.text: Electric buses should be introduced before fares are reduced.
questions.evidence: Electric buses are not mentioned.
questions.explanation: No view is expressed.

passages.topic: Science and society — admitting uncertainty
passages.title: The Courage to Say "We Don't Know"

paragraphs.text: When a new disease spreads, a new technology arrives or an environmental problem emerges, the public naturally turns to scientists for answers. Politicians want clear advice, journalists want simple headlines, and ordinary people want to know what to do. Faced with these demands, scientists are often tempted to speak with more certainty than the evidence allows. The temptation is understandable. It is also, I believe, one of the most damaging mistakes that science can make in public.

Science is, by its nature, a process of reducing uncertainty rather than eliminating it. Early in the study of any new problem, data are limited, and conclusions must be provisional. As more evidence accumulates, advice may change. To scientists, this is simply how knowledge advances. To members of the public who were told with apparent confidence that one thing was true, and are later told that something else is true, it can look like incompetence – or worse, deception.

Some communicators argue that admitting uncertainty will confuse people and weaken the impact of important messages. If experts say that they are not sure, the argument goes, people will ignore their advice altogether. This concern is not unreasonable, and there are certainly situations – such as an immediate threat to safety – in which clear instructions must be given quickly. But the research that exists on this question is more encouraging than the pessimists suggest. Several studies have found that when uncertainty is communicated clearly, in the form of a range of possible outcomes or an honest statement of what is not yet known, most people's trust in the source does not fall, and in some cases slightly increases.

What damages trust, the evidence suggests, is not uncertainty itself but the discovery that uncertainty was concealed. When confident predictions turn out to be wrong, people may reasonably conclude that they were misled, and they may become suspicious of future advice, even when it is well founded. A reputation for honesty, once lost, is very hard to regain.

Communicating uncertainty well is not easy. Vague expressions such as "possibly" or "there is some risk" mean very different things to different listeners. Numbers and ranges can be clearer, but they must be presented carefully, since many people find probabilities difficult to interpret. The most effective approach usually combines three elements: a statement of what is known with confidence, an honest account of what remains uncertain, and practical advice about what to do in the meantime.

There is also a responsibility on the other side. Journalists and politicians who demand simple certainties from scientists – and then criticise them when the advice changes – contribute to the problem they complain about. A more mature public conversation would treat changes in advice not as failures but as evidence that science is working as it should.

Scientists will never be able to offer the certainty that people understandably want. What they can offer is honesty about the limits of their knowledge. In the long run, that honesty is likely to prove a firmer foundation for public trust than any number of confident but fragile predictions.

lesson.title: Implied opinions
lesson.text:
At Medium level, writers often express views indirectly: through word choice ("so-called experts", "the understandable wish for certainty"), through irony, or by describing a consequence as harmful or beneficial. You must infer the writer's attitude from these signals. Ask: Does the language show approval, disapproval or doubt?

A view can be clear without the words "I think". But be careful not to over-read: tone alone does not create a view on a claim the writer never addresses.
lesson.example: Passage: "The council's latest plan – its third in two years – promises, once again, to solve the parking problem." Statement: "The writer doubts that the plan will succeed." → YES (shown through "third", "once again", "promises").

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: It is understandable that scientists feel pressure to sound certain.
questions.evidence: The temptation is understandable
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: Overstating certainty is a harmless way of making advice easier to follow.
questions.evidence: It is also, I believe, one of the most damaging mistakes
questions.explanation: "Most damaging" contradicts "harmless".

questions.text: Changes in scientific advice are a sign of poor scientific work.

questions.explanation: The public may see it as incompetence, but the writer does not.

questions.text: There are situations in which clear instructions must be given without delay.
questions.evidence: there are certainly situations ... in which clear instructions must be given quickly
questions.explanation: This is a concession accepted by the writer.

questions.text: Research shows that admitting uncertainty always increases public trust.
questions.evidence: most people's trust in the source does not fall, and in some cases slightly increases
questions.explanation: "In some cases slightly" contradicts "always increases".

questions.text: Concealing uncertainty is more damaging to trust than uncertainty itself.
questions.evidence: What damages trust ... is not uncertainty itself but the discovery that uncertainty was concealed
questions.explanation: This is a "not X but Y" structure.

questions.text: Numerical ranges are always easier for the public to understand than words.
questions.evidence: Numbers and ranges can be clearer, but they must be presented carefully, since many people find probabilities difficult
questions.explanation: "Can be" and "many people find ... difficult" contradict "always easier".

questions.text: Scientists should receive formal training in communicating with the media.
questions.evidence: Paragraph E discusses how to communicate, but formal training is never mentioned.
questions.explanation: This is NOT GIVEN on a topic the passage discusses.

questions.text: Journalists who demand simple answers share some responsibility for the problem.
questions.evidence: Journalists and politicians who demand simple certainties ... contribute to the problem they complain about
questions.explanation: "Contribute to" = "share some responsibility".

passages.topic: Environment and economics — carbon offsets
passages.title: Paying Someone Else to Cut

paragraphs.text: An airline invites passengers to "offset" the emissions from their flight by paying a small extra charge. A company announces that it has become "carbon neutral". Behind both claims usually lies a carbon offset: a payment to support a project elsewhere – planting trees, protecting a forest, supplying efficient cooking stoves – that is expected to reduce or remove an equivalent amount of greenhouse gas. The market for such offsets has grown rapidly, and so has the controversy surrounding it.

In principle, the idea is sound. A tonne of carbon dioxide has the same effect on the climate wherever it is emitted, so reducing emissions where it is cheapest to do so makes economic sense. Offsets can also direct money to projects in poorer countries that might not otherwise be funded. I have no objection to the principle. My concern is with how it has too often been applied.

The first difficulty is proving that a project achieves anything additional. If a forest was never under threat, paying to "protect" it does not reduce emissions at all. Investigations of some forest protection schemes have concluded that the reductions claimed were greatly exaggerated, because the projects assumed rates of deforestation far higher than those that would actually have occurred. The offsets were sold, but the climate gained little or nothing.

A second difficulty is permanence. Carbon stored in trees can be released again if the forest is later cut down or destroyed by fire, whereas carbon released by burning fossil fuels remains in the atmosphere for centuries. Treating the two as equivalent is, in my view, misleading unless projects include strong guarantees and plans for replacing any losses.

Supporters of offsets reply that the market is improving, with stricter standards, independent verification and better methods of measurement. This is true, and it is welcome. Some types of project – such as those that capture methane from landfill sites, where the reduction can be measured directly – have a stronger record than others. But standards remain uneven, and buyers often have little way of knowing which offsets are reliable.

Perhaps the most serious risk is that offsets allow companies and individuals to avoid reducing their own emissions. If a company can claim to be carbon neutral by buying cheap offsets, it has less incentive to change the way it operates. Offsets should come after serious efforts to cut emissions directly, not instead of them.

Used honestly and with high standards, offsets can play a supporting role in tackling climate change, particularly for emissions that are genuinely difficult to eliminate. But claims of "neutrality" based largely on offsets deserve scepticism. The most reliable way to reduce emissions is still the most obvious one: to produce fewer of them in the first place.

lesson.title: Conditional opinions
lesson.example:
Passage: "Online courses work well, but only for highly motivated learners."
Statement: "Online courses work well for all learners." → NO.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The basic principle behind carbon offsets is reasonable.
questions.evidence: In principle, the idea is sound ... I have no objection to the principle
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: Offsets can channel funding to projects in poorer countries.

passages.topic: Architecture and heritage — how should old buildings be restored?
passages.title: Restore or Preserve?

paragraphs.text: Every old building eventually faces the same question: when it begins to decay, what should be done? Stones crumble, timbers rot, windows break, and later owners add extensions or remove features. One answer is to repair the damage and return the building to its original appearance. Another is to protect it as it is, with all the marks of its history, making only the repairs necessary to keep it standing. The debate between these approaches has shaped the treatment of historic buildings for more than a century and a half.

In nineteenth-century France, the architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc became famous for bold restorations of medieval churches and castles. He believed that restoring a building meant returning it to a complete state – even, as he wrote, a state that may never have existed at any given time. Where parts were missing, he designed replacements based on his understanding of how a medieval builder would have completed the work. His restorations saved many buildings that might otherwise have collapsed, and they remain popular with visitors. But they also replaced genuine medieval work with nineteenth-century inventions, and it is now often difficult to tell which is which.

In England, the critic John Ruskin took the opposite view. For Ruskin, restoration was "the most total destruction which a building can suffer", because it replaced the original craftsmanship – the marks of the individual workers who had shaped each stone – with modern copies. The value of an old building, he argued, lay in its age and in the history visible on its surfaces. Buildings should be protected and maintained, not remade. Ruskin's ideas influenced the founding in 1877 of a society for the protection of ancient buildings, which campaigned against over-restoration.

Ruskin's insistence on honesty seems to me largely correct. A building that has been extensively "restored" to an imagined original state can mislead visitors about what the past actually looked like, and destroys evidence that later historians might have studied. Yet Ruskin's position, taken to its extreme, is difficult to apply. He was prepared, at least in theory, to let a building fall into ruin rather than restore it. Few people responsible for a historic building today would accept that outcome, and I do not think they should.

Modern conservation practice has largely settled on a middle path. International guidelines adopted in the twentieth century emphasise repairing rather than replacing, doing no more than is necessary, and making new work distinguishable from old – for example by using a slightly different material or leaving new stone plain rather than carved. Changes should, where possible, be reversible, so that future generations can make different decisions. I regard these principles as sensible, although applying them is often a matter of difficult judgement rather than simple rules.

Hard cases remain. When a building has been badly damaged by fire or war, should it be rebuilt exactly as before? Many cities have chosen to reconstruct destroyed landmarks, sometimes with great care and using original fragments. Strict followers of Ruskin would object that such reconstructions are copies, not originals. I have more sympathy with them than that objection suggests. A faithful reconstruction cannot replace what was lost, but it can restore a place's meaning for the community that lives there, provided that it is honestly presented as a reconstruction.

Ultimately, the treatment of old buildings reflects what we value in them. If we value them only as pictures of the past, restoration to a perfect state will seem attractive. If we value them as evidence and as survivors, we will be more cautious. The best practice, in my view, accepts both values but gives priority to the second.

lesson.title: Writers who evaluate historical figures' views
lesson.text: Some passages describe the positions of historical thinkers and then evaluate them. The statements usually concern the writer's evaluation, not what the historical figures believed. If a statement says "Ruskin's view was too extreme" and the writer says Ruskin "went too far", the answer is YES. If a statement simply repeats Ruskin's opinion ("restoration is a lie"), you must check whether the writer agrees with it.
lesson.example: Passage: "Smith insisted that all ornament was waste. His argument, though influential, ignored the pleasure people take in decoration." Statement: "All ornament is a waste." → NO (the writer criticises the view).

passages.topic: Education and psychology — praising effort
passages.title: The Trouble with "Growth Mindset"

paragraphs.text: Few ideas from psychology have spread through schools as quickly as the concept of the "growth mindset". The idea, developed by the American psychologist Carol Dweck and her colleagues, is that people hold different beliefs about ability. Those with a "fixed mindset" believe that intelligence is largely unchangeable; those with a "growth mindset" believe it can be developed through effort and learning. Students with a growth mindset, the research suggested, respond better to difficulty: they see mistakes as opportunities to learn rather than as proof of failure, and they persist longer with challenging tasks.

The idea has obvious appeal, and I think its central insight is valuable. Students who believe that they can improve are more likely to make the effort that improvement requires, and teachers who communicate that belief to their students are likely to create more encouraging classrooms. Dweck's early experiments, which found that children praised for their intelligence tended to avoid challenging tasks afterwards, while those praised for their effort sought out challenges, have deservedly been widely discussed.

Unfortunately, as the concept spread, it was often simplified. In some schools, "growth mindset" came to mean little more than posters on classroom walls with slogans about the power of effort, or the practice of praising children for trying hard regardless of what they had actually achieved. Dweck herself has criticised such practices, pointing out that praising effort that is not producing progress can be misleading, and that students also need new strategies and help from others, not simply encouragement to try harder.

There has also been debate about how large the benefits really are. Early studies were often small, and some reported impressive effects. More recent, much larger studies, including some involving many thousands of students, have found that brief growth-mindset programmes produce, on average, only small improvements in academic results. The effects tend to be larger for students who were previously struggling, and smaller or negligible for others. Some researchers have concluded from these findings that the concept has been oversold. I think that judgement is partly fair. The claims made for growth mindset by some enthusiasts – that it could transform the achievement of whole schools – were never supported by the evidence.

Yet a small average effect is not the same as no effect. An intervention that takes an hour or two and costs very little, and that produces even modest improvements for struggling students, may well be worthwhile. The mistake is to expect it to do more than it can. Beliefs about ability are only one of many factors that influence learning, alongside the quality of teaching, the support students receive at home and the resources available to schools.

What schools should take from this research, in my view, is not a set of slogans but a set of practices: giving students tasks that are genuinely challenging, providing feedback that helps them understand how to improve, and treating mistakes as a normal part of learning. These practices were valuable long before the term "growth mindset" was invented, and they will remain valuable whatever happens to the term's popularity.

lesson.title: Writers who partly agree
lesson.example: Passage: "Mindfulness can reduce stress for some people, but claims that it cures anxiety disorders go far beyond the evidence." Statements: "Mindfulness may help some people with stress" → YES. "Mindfulness cures anxiety disorders" → NO.

passages.topic: Technology and work — will machines take our jobs?
passages.title: Machines and Jobs

paragraphs.text: Every major wave of technological change has been accompanied by fears that machines will leave people without work. In the early nineteenth century, textile workers in England destroyed the new weaving machines that threatened their livelihoods. In the twentieth century, economists and politicians repeatedly warned that automation in factories would create mass unemployment. Today, similar fears surround artificial intelligence and robotics, which are able to perform tasks – driving, translating, diagnosing illness – that were until recently thought to require human judgement.

History offers some reassurance. Although particular jobs have repeatedly disappeared, the overall number of jobs has tended to grow over the long run. Machines have made many goods and services cheaper, allowing people to spend money on other things, and new industries have emerged that employ people in occupations that previous generations could not have imagined. The textile workers' fears were justified for them personally, but they were not justified for the economy as a whole.

It would be complacent, however, to assume that the past will simply repeat itself. The transition from one kind of work to another has often been extremely painful for those affected. Workers whose skills became obsolete did not automatically move into the new jobs; many experienced long periods of unemployment or were forced into lower-paid work, and some communities never recovered. The fact that an economy eventually adapts is little comfort to the individuals who bear the costs of adaptation.

Some economists argue that the current wave of technology is fundamentally different, because machines can now perform cognitive as well as physical tasks, and may eventually be able to do almost anything a human can do more cheaply. I do not think we can dismiss this possibility, but I am sceptical of the more dramatic predictions. Many jobs consist of a mixture of tasks, only some of which can be automated. In practice, technology has more often changed what workers do than replaced them entirely. It is too early to know whether this pattern will continue.

What seems clearer is that technology is likely to change the distribution of rewards. Workers whose skills complement new technology – who can use it, design it or do the things it cannot – have generally seen their wages rise. Those whose tasks can easily be performed by machines have often seen their wages stagnate. Without deliberate policies, the benefits of new technology may be shared very unequally.

Governments therefore have an important role to play. Education systems need to prepare young people not only for particular jobs but for a lifetime of learning, since many will need to change occupations more than once. Adults whose jobs disappear need realistic opportunities to retrain, and financial support while they do so. Some have proposed more radical measures, such as a basic income paid to every citizen regardless of employment. Such ideas deserve serious study, but they raise difficult questions about cost that their supporters sometimes pass over too quickly.

Technology is not a force of nature that simply happens to us. The ways in which it is developed and used reflect choices made by companies, governments and societies. The question is not only what machines will be able to do, but what we decide to do with them.

lesson.title: Predictions and certainty
lesson.text: When writers discuss the future, they vary in confidence: will certainly, is likely to, may, it is too early to say. A statement that turns the writer's "may" into "will" is usually NO if the writer stresses uncertainty. It is NOT GIVEN if the writer makes no prediction on that point at all.
lesson.example:
Passage: "It is possible that prices will fall next year, but nobody can be sure."
Statement: "Prices will definitely fall next year." → NO.

passages.topic: Health policy — taxing sugary drinks
passages.title: A Tax on Sweetness

paragraphs.text: Over the past decade, a growing number of countries have introduced taxes on sugar-sweetened drinks. The reasoning is straightforward. Such drinks contain large amounts of sugar but provide little nutritional value, and high consumption is associated with weight gain, tooth decay and a greater risk of diseases such as type 2 diabetes. By making these drinks more expensive, governments hope to reduce consumption and encourage manufacturers to use less sugar. Having followed the evidence on these taxes, I believe that, while they are no cure-all, they are a sensible part of public health policy.

One of the most encouraging findings concerns manufacturers rather than consumers. In countries where the tax rate depends on the amount of sugar a drink contains, many companies reformulated their products to fall below the threshold at which the tax applies. In some cases, the average sugar content of drinks sold fell substantially even before the tax came into force. This effect, which reduces sugar intake without requiring anyone to change their habits, may be the most valuable outcome of such taxes.

Critics raise several objections. The first is that these taxes fall most heavily on poorer households, which spend a larger share of their income on food and drink. There is something in this. However, poorer households also tend to suffer the highest rates of diet-related illness, and so stand to gain the most from reduced consumption. Moreover, if the revenue raised is spent on programmes that benefit those same communities, such as school sports or free drinking water, the overall effect can be progressive rather than unfair.

A second objection is that such taxes are an unwarranted intrusion by the state into personal choices. I find this argument unconvincing. Governments already tax alcohol and tobacco for similar reasons, and a tax does not prevent anyone from buying sugary drinks; it simply changes the price. People remain free to choose, but the cost to public health services of treating diet-related diseases is borne by everyone.

A third criticism has more force. Taxes on drinks affect only one source of sugar, and people may simply replace sugary drinks with other sweet foods. The evidence on this point is mixed, and it would be wrong to expect a drinks tax, on its own, to have a large effect on obesity. Diet is shaped by many factors – price, advertising, the availability of healthy food, working hours and education – and effective policy must address several of them together.

Finally, some point out that it is difficult to prove that sugar taxes have reduced rates of obesity or diabetes, since these conditions develop over many years and are influenced by many other factors. This is true, but it is not a strong argument against the policy. The same difficulty applies to most public health measures, and the evidence that the taxes reduce sugar consumption is already reasonably good.

Sugar taxes will not solve the problem of poor diet on their own. But as one element of a wider strategy, they are cheap to administer, raise revenue that can be put to good use, and encourage both manufacturers and consumers to reduce the amount of sugar they produce and consume. That seems to me a good bargain.

lesson.title: Responses to criticisms
lesson.example: Passage: "Critics say the tax hurts poorer families. There is something in this, but the health benefits for those families are also greatest." Statement: "The tax has some negative effect on poorer families." → YES (partly accepted).

passages.topic: Language and culture — English as a global language
passages.title: One Language for the World?

paragraphs.text: English is now used more widely than any language in history. It is the dominant language of international science, aviation, business and much of the internet, and it is studied by hundreds of millions of people who do not speak it as their first language. In many countries, the ability to speak English is associated with better job prospects and higher incomes. Whether this situation should be welcomed or feared has been debated for decades. My own view is that it brings real benefits, but that its costs are too easily overlooked by those of us who speak English as our first language.

The benefits are considerable. A shared language allows researchers from different countries to read one another's work and collaborate, businesses to trade across borders, and travellers to communicate almost anywhere. For individuals, learning English can open access to education, employment and information that might otherwise be unavailable. It would be patronising to suggest that people in other countries should be discouraged from learning it for their own protection.

Yet the spread of English also creates inequalities. Native speakers enjoy an advantage that they did nothing to earn: they can publish research, negotiate contracts and participate in international meetings in their first language, while others must work in a second or third language, often at considerable cost in time and money. Scientists whose first language is not English, for example, report spending significantly longer reading and writing papers, and their work may be rejected more often because of the language in which it is written rather than its quality.

Some commentators go further and claim that English is responsible for the disappearance of the world's smaller languages. This claim needs to be treated with care. Most endangered languages are under pressure not from English but from national or regional languages – the dominant languages of the countries in which their speakers live. Where English does threaten other languages, it tends to do so in particular domains, such as higher education or science, where local languages may stop developing the vocabulary needed to discuss new ideas.

This loss of domains is, I believe, a genuine concern. If a language is no longer used for science or university teaching, it may gradually come to be seen as suitable only for home and everyday life, and younger speakers may conclude that it is less valuable. Several countries have introduced policies to ensure that their languages continue to be used in higher education alongside English, and such policies seem to me entirely reasonable.

Native English speakers also have responsibilities. Too often, they assume that everyone else should adapt to them, and they make little effort to learn other languages or to speak clearly and simply when communicating with non-native speakers. Research on international communication has found, rather ironically, that native speakers are sometimes harder to understand in international settings than non-native speakers, because they use idioms, speak quickly and assume shared cultural knowledge.

English is likely to remain the world's main international language for the foreseeable future. The question is not whether people should learn it, but whether its dominance can coexist with a healthy diversity of other languages. That depends largely on choices made by governments, institutions and individual speakers – including those for whom English is their first language.

lesson.title: Balanced writers and "on the one hand ... on the other"
lesson.text: A balanced writer presents benefits and costs and may agree with both. A statement expressing a benefit can be YES, and a statement expressing a cost can also be YES. What produces NO is a statement that denies one side entirely ("English has brought no benefits") or pushes one side to an extreme.
lesson.example: Passage: "Tourism brings money to the island; on the other hand, it strains water supplies." Statements: "Tourism benefits the island's economy" → YES. "Tourism strains water supplies" → YES. "Tourism has no disadvantages" → NO.
