passages.topic: Science policy — why fund research with no obvious use?
passages.title: The Value of Useless Knowledge

paragraphs.text: Governments that fund scientific research face constant pressure to show that their money is well spent. Increasingly, researchers applying for grants are asked to explain the practical benefits their work will bring – new products, economic growth, improvements in health. In many countries, the share of public research funding directed towards projects with specific practical goals has grown, while funding for research driven purely by curiosity has come under pressure. I believe this trend, though understandable, is short-sighted.

The history of science contains many examples of discoveries whose practical importance was entirely unforeseen. Research into the behaviour of atoms in magnetic fields, pursued in the early twentieth century for purely theoretical reasons, eventually made possible the medical scanners now used in hospitals around the world. Studies of bacteria living in hot springs, which seemed of interest only to specialists, led to the discovery of an enzyme that became essential to modern genetic testing. Nobody applying for funding for these projects could have predicted such outcomes, because the knowledge needed to imagine them did not yet exist.

This is the central difficulty with requiring researchers to justify their work by its expected applications. The most important applications are often the least predictable. A funding system that rewards only research with obvious uses will tend to support work that develops existing knowledge in familiar directions, and may neglect exactly the kind of research that opens entirely new ones.

Supporters of goal-directed funding make a fair point: public money is limited, and taxpayers are entitled to expect that research will eventually benefit society. Some problems – developing vaccines, improving energy storage, understanding climate change – are urgent enough to justify targeted investment. I do not argue that all research should be curiosity-driven. The question is one of balance, and in my view the balance has shifted too far.

There is also a practical problem with asking researchers to predict the impact of their work. Because they know that funding depends on it, applicants are encouraged to exaggerate the likely benefits of their projects. Reviewers, who understand this, may discount such claims – making the whole exercise something of a ritual. The time spent writing and assessing speculative statements about impact might be better spent on the research itself.

A further argument concerns people rather than discoveries. Curiosity-driven research trains scientists who are able to think independently and to pursue new questions. Many of the researchers who later made practical breakthroughs gained their skills in fundamental research. Cutting support for such work therefore affects not only today's projects but the future supply of scientific talent.

None of this means that basic research should escape scrutiny. Research funding should still be allocated on the basis of the quality of the questions being asked and the ability of the researchers to answer them. But quality is not the same as immediate usefulness. A society that funds only the research whose value it can already see will, in the long run, discover less than one that is willing to support the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake.

lesson.title: Examples that support the writer's argument
lesson.text: Writers use historical examples to support their claims. A statement about an example can test whether you understand what the writer uses it to show. If the writer describes a discovery as "made by researchers with no practical aim in mind" in order to argue for curiosity-driven research, then the statement "the researchers were trying to solve a practical problem" → NO. Distinguish the example's facts from the argument the writer draws from them.
lesson.example: Passage: "Penicillin was found by accident, which shows that unplanned discoveries matter." Statement: "Unplanned discoveries can be important." → YES.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The trend towards goal-directed research funding is difficult to understand.
questions.evidence: I believe this trend, though understandable, is short-sighted
questions.explanation: "Understandable" contradicts "difficult to understand".

questions.text: The researchers who studied atoms in magnetic fields were aiming to develop medical scanners.
questions.evidence: pursued in the early twentieth century for purely theoretical reasons
questions.explanation: The writer uses this example to show that the application was unforeseen.

questions.text: The most valuable applications of research are often hard to foresee.
questions.evidence: The most important applications are often the least predictable
questions.explanation: This is a direct paraphrase.

questions.text: Taxpayers have a right to expect that research will eventually benefit society.
questions.evidence: taxpayers are entitled to expect that research will eventually benefit society
questions.explanation: The writer calls this "a fair point", a concession they accept.

questions.text: All scientific research should be driven by curiosity.
questions.evidence: I do not argue that all research should be curiosity-driven
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Researchers tend to overstate the likely benefits of their work in funding applications.
questions.evidence: applicants are encouraged to exaggerate the likely benefits
questions.explanation: "Exaggerate" = "overstate", and "are encouraged to" supports "tend to".

questions.text: Private companies fund more applied research than governments do.
questions.evidence: Private companies are not mentioned.
questions.explanation: No view is expressed.

questions.text: Basic research should be free from any form of assessment.
questions.evidence: None of this means that basic research should escape scrutiny
questions.explanation: This contradicts "free from any form of assessment".

questions.text: Curiosity-driven research is more enjoyable for scientists than applied research.
questions.evidence: The writer discusses the training value of curiosity-driven research (Paragraph F) but not scientists' enjoyment.
questions.explanation: No view is given.

passages.topic: History — individuals and forces in explaining the past
passages.title: Great Individuals or Great Forces?

paragraphs.text: For much of the nineteenth century, history was largely written as the story of remarkable individuals. Kings, generals, statesmen and inventors were presented as the principal agents of change, and the course of events was explained by their decisions, virtues and failings. The Scottish writer Thomas Carlyle gave this approach its most memorable expression when he declared that the history of the world was essentially the biography of great men. It is easy, from a modern perspective, to mock such claims. That mockery, I shall suggest, is not entirely deserved.

Against the "great man" view, later historians emphasised forces that no individual controls: changes in population, technology, climate, trade and the organisation of work. The philosopher Herbert Spencer argued, in direct response to Carlyle, that great individuals are themselves products of their societies, and that before a great man can remake his society, his society must make him. In the twentieth century, historians influenced by economics and the social sciences studied the lives of ordinary people over long periods, using records of prices, births, deaths and harvests. Their work transformed the discipline and revealed patterns that the study of rulers alone could never have shown.

The achievements of this approach are beyond dispute. Yet at its extreme, it produced a history in which people seemed to disappear altogether, carried along by vast impersonal processes like leaves on a river. Critics complained, not unreasonably, that such accounts made events appear inevitable in hindsight, when those living through them faced genuine choices whose outcomes were uncertain. A history without individuals has difficulty explaining why events took one course rather than another at moments when the balance was finely poised.

Consider the outbreak of a war, or the collapse of a government. Broad forces may explain why tensions existed, and why conflict or collapse became possible, or even likely. But whether it happened in a particular year, and in a particular way, may depend on the decisions of a small number of people, sometimes on accidents of timing, illness or personality. To insist that such factors are irrelevant seems to me a form of dogmatism no more defensible than Carlyle's.

It is sometimes suggested that the debate has been settled by a sensible compromise: individuals act, but within limits set by circumstances. This formula, often attributed in spirit to Karl Marx's observation that people make their own history but not under conditions of their own choosing, is hardly controversial, and it is correct as far as it goes. The difficulty is that it tells us little about how much weight to give to individuals and how much to circumstances in any particular case. That is a question that can only be answered by examining the evidence for each event, and the answer will differ from one case to another.

Recent work has approached the question more concretely. Some historians have studied cases in which leaders died suddenly or were removed by chance – for instance, through assassination attempts that narrowly succeeded or failed – and compared what followed. Such studies suggest that individual leaders can make a measurable difference to outcomes, particularly in political systems where power is concentrated in few hands, and less so where institutions constrain the individual. The findings are tentative, but they have the merit of turning a philosophical debate into a question that can, at least in part, be investigated.

Carlyle's view, then, was wrong in its sweep, but not in its instinct. Individuals matter, though neither always nor equally. The historian's task is not to choose between persons and forces but to discover, case by case, how they interacted.

lesson.title: Hard YNNG — double negatives, understatement and irony
lesson.text:
Hard passages express views through complex language:

Double negatives: "not without merit" = has some merit; "hardly unreasonable" = reasonable.

Understatement: "somewhat less than convincing" = unconvincing.

Irony: "a remarkably convenient conclusion" = a suspicious conclusion.

Attributed views dropped mid-sentence: "what its critics call X, and what might more fairly be called Y". The writer prefers Y.

Translate each such phrase into a plain statement of the writer's view before answering.
lesson.example:
Passage: "The theory is not without its attractions, but it has proved hard to test."
Statement: "The theory has some appeal." → YES.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Modern ridicule of Carlyle's position is completely justified.
questions.evidence: That mockery, I shall suggest, is not entirely deserved
questions.explanation: "Not entirely deserved" contradicts "completely justified". This relies on understatement.

questions.text: The study of ordinary people's lives revealed things that the study of rulers could not.
questions.evidence: "revealed patterns that the study of rulers alone could never have shown" (Paragraph B); "The achievements ... are beyond dispute" (Paragraph C)
questions.explanation: The writer endorses this.

questions.text: Critics were wrong to say that some social histories made events seem inevitable.
questions.evidence: Critics complained, not unreasonably, that such accounts made events appear inevitable
questions.explanation: "Not unreasonably" = reasonably, so the writer thinks the critics had a point. This relies on a double negative.

questions.text: Individual decisions can influence the timing and form of major events.
questions.evidence: whether it happened in a particular year, and in a particular way, may depend on the decisions of a small number of people
questions.explanation: This matches "timing and form".

questions.text: Denying the importance of individuals is as difficult to defend as Carlyle's position.
questions.evidence: a form of dogmatism no more defensible than Carlyle's
questions.explanation: "No more defensible than" = "as difficult to defend as".

questions.text: The idea that people act within limits set by circumstances is highly controversial.
questions.evidence: is hardly controversial
questions.explanation: "Hardly controversial" = uncontroversial, which contradicts "highly controversial".

questions.text: Spencer's work was more widely read than Carlyle's in the nineteenth century.
questions.evidence: Spencer's response is described (Paragraph B), but readership is not mentioned.
questions.explanation: No comparison is given.

questions.text: Studies of leaders removed by chance have provided definite proof of their influence.
questions.evidence: The findings are tentative
questions.explanation: "Tentative" contradicts "definite proof".

questions.text: Historians should decide in advance whether individuals or forces are more important.
questions.evidence: "That is a question that can only be answered by examining the evidence for each event" (Paragraph E); "discover, case by case" (Paragraph G)
questions.explanation: The writer opposes deciding in advance.

passages.topic: Economics and public policy — "nudging" people's choices
passages.title: The Gentle Push

paragraphs.text: In 2008, the economist Richard Thaler and the legal scholar Cass Sunstein published a book arguing that governments and organisations could improve people's decisions without restricting their freedom. Their key concept was the "nudge": a change in the way choices are presented that makes some options more likely to be chosen, while leaving all options available. Placing fruit at eye level in a canteen, rather than banning unhealthy snacks, is a nudge; so is sending a reminder letter that tells people most of their neighbours have already paid their taxes. The idea proved remarkably influential, and governments in several countries established special units to design and test such measures.

The appeal of nudging is understandable. It promises improvements at low cost, without the political difficulties of new taxes or prohibitions, and it is grounded in a substantial body of research showing that human decisions are influenced by factors that traditional economics ignored: habit, inertia, the way information is framed, and the behaviour of others. Some nudges have produced impressive results. One of the most frequently cited is automatic enrolment in workplace pension schemes. When employees must actively choose to join, many never do, not because they have decided against saving but because they never get round to it. When they are enrolled automatically, but remain free to leave, participation rises sharply. I regard this as a genuine and valuable policy success.

The enthusiasm that followed, however, has not always been matched by results. Many nudges that appeared promising in small experiments produced much smaller effects when applied at scale, and some produced none at all. A large analysis of trials run by government nudge units found that their average effects were real but considerably more modest than those reported in academic journals – a gap that probably reflects, at least in part, the tendency of journals to publish striking results. This does not show that nudging fails; it shows that its effects are usually incremental, and that each proposed nudge needs to be tested rather than assumed to work.

A more fundamental concern is that nudges may distract attention from policies that address the underlying causes of problems. It is cheaper and politically easier to send people reminders about healthy eating than to regulate food advertising or to tackle the poverty that limits many people's choices. If nudges come to be seen as a substitute for such policies rather than a complement to them, their net effect could be harmful. The founders of the approach have themselves warned against this, and I think their warning deserves more attention than it has received.

Critics also raise ethical objections. Nudges, they argue, work precisely by exploiting the ways in which people do not think carefully, and so manipulate people rather than persuading them. There is force in this where nudges are hidden or designed to serve the interests of whoever designs them rather than those of the people being nudged. But the objection loses much of its force when applied to transparent measures that people would endorse if they were asked. Moreover, there is no neutral way of presenting choices: every canteen must place its food somewhere, and every form must have some default option. The question is not whether choices will be influenced, but how, and for whose benefit.

Nudging, then, is neither the revolution its early champions sometimes suggested nor the sinister manipulation its fiercest critics describe. It is a useful set of tools, most valuable when carefully tested, openly applied and combined with more traditional policies. Its greatest contribution may prove to be less any individual intervention than the habit it has encouraged in governments of testing whether their policies actually work.

lesson.title: Distinguishing degrees of support

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The popularity of nudging is easy to explain.
questions.evidence: The appeal of nudging is understandable
questions.explanation: "Understandable" supports "easy to explain", and the writer goes on to give the reasons.

questions.text: Automatic enrolment in pension schemes has been a worthwhile policy.
questions.evidence: I regard this as a genuine and valuable policy success
questions.explanation: This is an explicit endorsement.

questions.text: Nudges usually produce effects as large as those reported in academic journals.
questions.evidence: considerably more modest than those reported in academic journals
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Evidence of small effects shows that nudging does not work.
questions.evidence: This does not show that nudging fails; it shows that its effects are usually incremental
questions.explanation: The writer rejects this conclusion.

questions.text: Nudges could be harmful if they replaced policies addressing underlying causes.
questions.evidence: If nudges come to be seen as a substitute for such policies ... their net effect could be harmful
questions.explanation: This matches the conditional view.

questions.text: Nudge units in some countries have been closed because of poor results.
questions.evidence: Nudge units and their trials are discussed (Paragraphs A and C), but closures are never mentioned.
questions.explanation: This is NOT GIVEN on a topic the passage discusses.

questions.text: All nudges are a form of manipulation.
questions.evidence: There is force in this where nudges are hidden ... But the objection loses much of its force when applied to transparent measures
questions.explanation: The writer accepts the objection only for some nudges, which contradicts "all".

questions.text: It is possible to present choices in a completely neutral way.
questions.evidence: there is no neutral way of presenting choices
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Nudging's main legacy may be encouraging governments to test their policies.
questions.evidence: Its greatest contribution may prove to be ... the habit it has encouraged in governments of testing whether their policies actually work
questions.explanation: "Greatest contribution" = "main legacy", and "may" is kept in the statement.

passages.topic: Science and ethics — bringing back extinct species
passages.title: Raising the Dead

paragraphs.text: For most of history, extinction has been final. When the last member of a species dies, its particular combination of genes disappears for ever. Advances in genetic technology have begun to challenge that assumption. Scientists can now read the genetic material preserved in some long-dead animals, and in principle could edit the genes of a closely related living species to recreate some of the extinct animal's characteristics. Projects have been proposed to produce animals resembling the woolly mammoth, the passenger pigeon and several other lost species. Supporters call this "de-extinction".

The idea has an obvious emotional appeal. Many extinctions were caused by human beings – through hunting, habitat destruction or introduced predators – and reversing them seems to offer a way of making amends. Supporters also argue that some extinct species played important roles in their ecosystems, and that restoring those roles could benefit other species. Mammoth-like animals, for example, might help to maintain the grasslands of the Arctic by trampling snow and knocking down trees. These arguments are not foolish, and I do not wish to dismiss them.

But what exactly would be brought back? The animals produced would not be mammoths but modified elephants carrying some mammoth genes. They would lack the behaviour that was learned by young mammoths from their mothers and passed down through generations, since there are no mammoth mothers left to teach them. Is an animal that looks like a mammoth, but has never lived as one, really a restored species? The question is not merely philosophical; it affects whether such animals could perform the ecological roles their supporters hope for.

A more practical concern is cost. Conservation budgets are small, and many species that still exist are close to extinction. Money spent on recreating lost animals is money not spent on protecting living ones, whose habitats are often disappearing now. Supporters reply that de-extinction research is largely funded by private donors who would not otherwise give to conventional conservation, and that the technology developed could help endangered species, for example by increasing their genetic diversity. The second point strikes me as the strongest argument in favour of the research. The first is harder to verify, and even if true, it does not answer the question of what will happen when the animals need long-term care and protected habitat.

There is also a subtler risk. If the public comes to believe that extinction can be reversed, the urgency of preventing it may diminish. Why protect a species at great expense, some might ask, if it can be restored later? I suspect that this fear is sometimes overstated, since the technology is slow, expensive and uncertain. But it would be naive to assume it has no basis, particularly when announcements about de-extinction projects are often reported in terms that exaggerate what has been achieved.

None of this means that the research should be abandoned. Studying the genes of extinct species can reveal much about how they lived and why they died out, and the techniques involved may prove valuable for species that still survive. What is needed is honesty about what de-extinction can and cannot do, and a clear principle that it must never be treated as a substitute for protecting the species and habitats that remain. The best way to deal with extinction is still to prevent it.

lesson.title: Rhetorical questions
lesson.text: Hard writers often use questions to express views: "But is this really conservation?", "Who, then, will care for these animals?". A rhetorical question usually implies a doubt or a negative answer. Translate it into a statement, for example: "This is not really conservation." Then compare. Be careful, though: a genuine open question that the writer leaves unanswered does not express a view, so statements about it may be NOT GIVEN.
lesson.example:
Passage: "Can a museum without visitors really be said to serve the public?"
Statement: "A museum without visitors does not truly serve the public." → YES.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: The arguments in favour of de-extinction should be dismissed as foolish.
questions.evidence: These arguments are not foolish, and I do not wish to dismiss them
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: An animal produced by de-extinction would not be identical to the original species.
questions.evidence: The animals produced would not be mammoths but modified elephants ... Is an animal that looks like a mammoth ... really a restored species?
questions.explanation: The rhetorical question implies "no", which supports the statement.

questions.text: Whether recreated animals are truly the original species is only a philosophical question.
questions.evidence: The question is not merely philosophical; it affects whether such animals could perform the ecological roles
questions.explanation: This contradicts "only".

questions.text: The potential benefit of the technology for living endangered species is the strongest argument for the research.
questions.evidence: The second point strikes me as the strongest argument in favour of the research
questions.explanation: "The second point" refers to helping endangered species, so you must resolve this reference to answer.

questions.text: The claim that de-extinction donors would not otherwise fund conservation is easy to confirm.
questions.evidence: "The first is harder to verify" (Paragraph D), where "the first" is the supporters' claim about private donors.
questions.explanation: "Harder to verify" contradicts "easy to confirm". To answer, you must identify which of the two points "the first" refers to.

questions.text: The mammoth project will be completed within the next decade.
questions.evidence: The writer says the technology is "slow, expensive and uncertain" (Paragraph E) but gives no timeline.
questions.explanation: No prediction is made.

questions.text: It is unrealistic to think that belief in de-extinction could weaken efforts to prevent extinction.
questions.evidence: it would be naive to assume it has no basis
questions.explanation: The writer thinks the fear has some basis, which contradicts "unrealistic to think".

questions.text: Media reports about de-extinction sometimes overstate what has been achieved.
questions.evidence: announcements about de-extinction projects are often reported in terms that exaggerate what has been achieved
questions.explanation: "Often" includes "sometimes", and "exaggerate" = "overstate".

questions.text: De-extinction research should be stopped.
questions.evidence: None of this means that the research should be abandoned
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

passages.topic: Urban technology — how smart is the "smart city"?
passages.title: Smart Cities and Wise Ones

paragraphs.text: Over the past two decades, the phrase "smart city" has become a fixture of urban planning. Technology companies promise that sensors, data and automated systems will make cities more efficient, sustainable and pleasant to live in: traffic lights that respond to real-time conditions, bins that report when they need emptying, energy networks that balance supply and demand automatically. Several entirely new cities have been planned around such technologies, and many existing cities have launched smart-city programmes. I have no quarrel with the use of data to improve urban services. My objection is to the way the smart city has often been conceived.

Much smart-city thinking begins with the technology and then looks for problems it might solve. This reverses the proper order. The most pressing problems of many cities – the cost of housing, inequality between neighbourhoods, inadequate public transport – are not primarily technical. They arise from decisions about land, money and political priorities. A sensor network cannot make housing affordable, and a traffic-management system cannot compensate for a transport network that does not reach the places where people need to go.

Where technology has helped, it has usually been in response to a clearly defined need. Cities that have used data to identify dangerous road junctions, to time bus services more accurately or to detect leaks in water pipes have achieved real improvements, often at modest cost. Such projects rarely attract the attention given to ambitious new "smart" districts, but their benefits are easier to demonstrate.

The new cities built from scratch as showcases of technology have, on the whole, had a disappointing record. Several have attracted far fewer residents than planned, and some remain largely empty years after construction. The reasons vary, but one common thread is that cities are not simply machines to be optimised. People choose where to live for reasons – work, family, culture, a sense of place – that no amount of technical efficiency can supply. A city designed around its infrastructure rather than its inhabitants risks being impressive to visit and unappealing to live in.

There are also questions of control. Smart-city systems generate enormous quantities of data about how residents move, consume and behave. Who owns that data, who can access it, and for what purposes? In several cases, arrangements between city authorities and private technology firms have been criticised for giving companies extensive access to public information with little public oversight. Residents are rarely asked whether they consent to being monitored, and it is not obvious that they would. These are not reasons to reject data collection outright, but they are reasons to insist that it be governed democratically and transparently.

Supporters of the smart city sometimes present their critics as opponents of progress. That is a misunderstanding. The question is not whether cities should use new technology, but who decides how it is used and for whose benefit. A wise city would begin by asking its residents what problems most affect their lives, and only then consider which tools, technological or otherwise, might help. Sometimes the answer will be a network of sensors. Often, it will be something far less glamorous: more buses, better maintenance, or simply listening to the people who live there.

lesson.title: Criticism of a framing, not the thing itself
lesson.text:
Some writers criticise how an idea is presented or pursued rather than the idea itself. A writer may support using data to improve cities while criticising the "smart city" slogan. Statements then test the difference:

"Data can help cities" → YES.

"Cities should avoid technology" → NO.

"The smart city label misrepresents priorities" → YES.

Ask: Is the writer against the thing, or against a particular way of thinking about it?

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.evidence: I have no quarrel with the use of data to improve urban services
questions.explanation: This is a double negative meaning "I accept it".

questions.text: Smart-city projects often start from technology rather than from existing problems.
questions.evidence: Much smart-city thinking begins with the technology and then looks for problems it might solve

questions.explanation: This matches "demonstrable benefits".

questions.text: Most new technology-based cities have met their population targets.
questions.evidence: "Several have attracted far fewer residents than planned" and "on the whole, had a disappointing record"
questions.explanation: The writer's judgement contradicts "most have met".

questions.text: Technology companies deliberately designed the new cities to fail.
questions.evidence: The writer attributes failure to cities being designed "around its infrastructure rather than its inhabitants" (Paragraph D) and never suggests any intention to fail.
questions.explanation: No view on deliberate intent is expressed. This is a trap for students who read criticism as an accusation.
questions.editorialCorrection: Quoted words inside the description corrected to match paragraph D exactly.

questions.evidence: These are not reasons to reject data collection outright
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.evidence: That is a misunderstanding
questions.explanation: The writer rejects this characterisation of critics.

questions.evidence: A wise city would begin by asking its residents ... and only then consider which tools
questions.explanation: This matches the order in the statement.

passages.topic: Medicine and society — when screening does harm
passages.title: The Hidden Costs of Looking

paragraphs.text: Few medical messages seem more obviously sensible than "early detection saves lives". If a disease is found before it causes symptoms, the reasoning goes, it can be treated more easily and with better results. Screening programmes – which test large numbers of apparently healthy people for signs of disease – have been built on this principle, and some have undoubtedly prevented many deaths. Yet the principle, stated so simply, is misleading. Screening can do harm as well as good, and the balance between the two is often closer than the public is led to believe.

The first source of harm is the false alarm. No test is perfectly accurate. When large numbers of healthy people are tested, even a small rate of false-positive results produces many people who are told that something may be wrong when nothing is. They may undergo further tests, some of them invasive, and experience weeks of anxiety before they are reassured. For an individual, this may seem a small price. Across a whole population, it is a substantial one.

A less obvious harm is overdiagnosis: the detection of genuine abnormalities that would never have caused any problem during the person's lifetime. Some early forms of disease grow so slowly, or not at all, that the patient would have died of something else long before they produced symptoms. Once detected, however, they are usually treated, because doctors cannot reliably tell which cases would have progressed. Patients receive surgery, radiation or medication that brings risks and side effects but no benefit. Crucially, these patients typically believe that screening saved their lives, and they become some of its most enthusiastic advocates. Overdiagnosis is thus not only a harm but one that tends to disguise itself as a success.

How common is overdiagnosis? Estimates vary widely depending on the disease, the test and the methods used to measure it, and researchers disagree about particular figures. What is not seriously disputed is that it occurs in several major screening programmes, and in some it is not rare.

None of this is an argument against screening as such. For some conditions, the evidence clearly shows that the benefits outweigh the harms for particular age groups, and I would encourage people in those groups to take part. The problem lies in presenting screening as though it offered benefits without costs, and in extending programmes to groups for whom the balance is less favourable, or to tests that have never been properly evaluated. Private clinics offering whole-body scans to healthy people are an example: they often uncover minor abnormalities of uncertain significance, which can lead to further investigations and treatment that do more harm than good.

The answer is better information. People invited to screening should be told, in plain terms, the likely benefits and harms: how many deaths might be prevented among those screened, how many false alarms will occur, and how many people might be treated unnecessarily. Some health services now provide such information, and research suggests that when people receive it, most still choose to be screened, though some decide not to. That seems to me exactly as it should be. The decision belongs to the individual, and it should be an informed one.

lesson.title: Counter-intuitive arguments
lesson.text: Some writers argue against a common assumption: "More testing is always better", "Early detection always saves lives". Statements may present the common assumption as if the writer held it. Before answering, write the common assumption and the writer's correction side by side. Also check for the writer's limits: arguing that screening can cause harm is not the same as arguing that screening should be abolished.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Some screening programmes have prevented many deaths.

questions.explanation: "Undoubtedly" shows that the writer accepts this.

questions.text: The claim that early detection saves lives is misleading when stated without qualification.

questions.text: False alarms are an insignificant problem when considered across a whole population.
questions.evidence: Across a whole population, it is a substantial one
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Doctors can usually identify which early abnormalities will progress to serious disease.
questions.evidence: doctors cannot reliably tell which cases would have progressed
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Patients who have been overdiagnosed usually realise that their treatment was unnecessary.
questions.evidence: these patients typically believe that screening saved their lives
questions.explanation: This is the opposite of realising the treatment was unnecessary.

questions.evidence: Estimates vary widely ... researchers disagree about particular figures
questions.explanation: This contradicts "agree on precise rates".

questions.text: Screening programmes in general should be abolished.
questions.evidence: None of this is an argument against screening as such ... I would encourage people in those groups to take part
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Private whole-body scans are more expensive than public screening programmes.
questions.evidence: Private scans are criticised for leading to unnecessary treatment (Paragraph E). Their price is never mentioned.
questions.explanation: No view on cost is expressed.

questions.explanation: This matches the writer's view.

passages.topic: Society and technology — living by online ratings
passages.title: Five Stars for Everything

paragraphs.text: It has become almost impossible to buy anything, eat anywhere or book any service without being invited to rate it. Restaurants, hotels, taxi drivers, doctors, plumbers and even university lecturers are awarded stars by the people who use them, and those ratings increasingly determine where others choose to go. The promise of this system is attractive: instead of relying on advertising or the opinions of a few critics, we can draw on the experiences of thousands of ordinary customers. In many respects, the promise has been fulfilled. But the culture of constant rating has costs that deserve more attention than they usually receive.

The first problem is that ratings tend to cluster at the top of the scale. On many platforms, the average rating is well above four out of five stars, and anything below that is treated as a sign of serious failure. For workers whose income depends on their scores, such as drivers on ride-hailing platforms, a small number of lower ratings can threaten their livelihood. A customer who gives three stars may think they are indicating "satisfactory" when they are, in effect, delivering a severe penalty. Is it reasonable that someone's job should depend on how strangers interpret a scale that was never clearly defined?

A second problem concerns what ratings actually measure. A patient's rating of a doctor may reflect how pleasant the consultation was, or whether the patient received the prescription they wanted, rather than the quality of the medical care. Studies of student evaluations of teaching have found that ratings are influenced by factors such as the expected grade and the teacher's personal manner, and do not always correspond closely to how much students learn. Ratings, in other words, measure satisfaction, which is not the same as quality – although it would be wrong to conclude that satisfaction is unimportant.

Third, rating systems can be manipulated. Businesses may encourage friends to post positive reviews, pay for fake ones, or pressure customers to change negative reviews. Platforms have introduced measures to detect such practices, with some success, but the problem has not disappeared. It would be unwise, therefore, to treat online ratings as neutral facts.

Defenders of rating systems point out that they have given consumers genuine power. Poor service that might once have gone unnoticed can now be exposed to thousands of potential customers, and businesses have strong incentives to respond to complaints. This is not a trivial achievement, and I have no wish to return to a world in which consumers had fewer ways to share their experiences.

What is needed is not the abolition of ratings but a more thoughtful use of them. Platforms could make their scales clearer, reduce the weight given to individual ratings in decisions about workers, and combine customer satisfaction with other measures of quality. Users, for their part, might read reviews rather than simply looking at the number of stars, and consider whether the qualities being rated are the ones that matter to them. A rating is a piece of information, not a verdict – and like any piece of information, its value depends on how it is interpreted.

lesson.title: Final review — the full YNNG method
lesson.text:
This final set combines the main YNNG skills: concessions, double negatives, rhetorical questions, conditional views, reported views and the difference between NO and NOT GIVEN. For each statement:

1. Find the section and decide whose voice it is.

2. Translate complex phrasing into a plain view.

3. Compare the statement's claim and strength with the writer's view.

4. If the writer never takes a position on that exact claim, the answer is NOT GIVEN.

groups.title: Yes / No / Not Given
groups.instruction:
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage?
Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

questions.text: Rating systems have in many ways delivered what they promised.
questions.evidence: In many respects, the promise has been fulfilled
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: A three-star rating is generally understood by customers as a serious criticism.
questions.evidence: A customer who gives three stars may think they are indicating 'satisfactory' when they are, in effect, delivering a severe penalty
questions.explanation: The writer says customers intend three stars as satisfactory, which contradicts "understood by customers as a serious criticism". The penalty is its effect, not the customers' understanding.

questions.text: It is fair for workers' jobs to depend on unclear rating scales.
questions.evidence: Is it reasonable that someone's job should depend on how strangers interpret a scale that was never clearly defined?
questions.explanation: The rhetorical question implies "no".

questions.text: Customer satisfaction is not a reliable measure of quality in every case.
questions.evidence: Ratings ... measure satisfaction, which is not the same as quality
questions.explanation: This matches the statement.

questions.text: Satisfaction is of no importance.
questions.evidence: it would be wrong to conclude that satisfaction is unimportant
questions.explanation: This is a direct contradiction.

questions.text: Measures to detect fake reviews have completely solved the problem.
questions.evidence: with some success, but the problem has not disappeared
questions.explanation: This contradicts "completely solved".

questions.text: Rating systems have given consumers real influence over businesses.
questions.evidence: they have given consumers genuine power ... This is not a trivial achievement
questions.explanation: The writer accepts the defenders' point.

questions.text: Ratings of hotels are more reliable than ratings of restaurants.
questions.evidence: Hotels and restaurants appear only in a list in Paragraph A.
questions.explanation: The writer never compares the reliability of ratings in different sectors.

questions.text: Younger consumers rely on online ratings more than older consumers.
questions.evidence: Age groups are not mentioned.
questions.explanation: No view is expressed.

passages.topic: History of technology — the development of the bicycle
passages.title: Two Wheels

paragraphs.text: The bicycle is so familiar today that it is easy to forget how long it took to develop. The first machine that could reasonably be called a bicycle appeared in Germany in 1817. Invented by Karl Drais, it had two wheels in line and a steerable front wheel, but no pedals: riders sat on a seat and pushed themselves along with their feet. Known as the "running machine", it enjoyed a brief period of fashion among wealthy young men, who raced them along city streets and public paths. Complaints from pedestrians led some cities to ban the machines from pavements.

The next major step came in the 1860s, when pedals were attached directly to the front wheel of a similar two-wheeled machine, probably first in France. The new "velocipede" could now be ridden without the rider's feet touching the ground. However, the machines were made largely of wood with iron tyres, and on the rough roads of the time they gave such an uncomfortable ride that they earned the nickname "boneshakers".

Because the pedals were fixed directly to the front wheel, each turn of the pedals moved the machine forward by exactly one turn of the wheel. To travel faster, designers made the front wheel larger. By the 1870s this had led to the "high-wheeler", often later called the "penny-farthing" after the difference in size between a large British coin and a small one. Some front wheels were as much as one and a half metres in diameter. The machines were fast and, on good roads, relatively comfortable, but they were also dangerous. Riders sat high above the ground, and if the front wheel struck an obstacle, they could be thrown forward over the handlebars.

The dangers of the high-wheeler meant that cycling remained largely the sport of athletic young men. The machine that changed this was the "safety bicycle", developed in England in the 1880s. One of the most successful early designs was produced in 1885 by John Kemp Starley. It had two wheels of similar size and a chain that connected the pedals to the rear wheel. Using gears of different sizes, the chain allowed a small wheel to turn quickly, so that the machine could be fast without being tall. Riders could now put their feet on the ground when they stopped.

Another important improvement came shortly afterwards. In 1888, a Scottish veterinary surgeon named John Boyd Dunlop developed an air-filled rubber tyre, reportedly to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable. Pneumatic tyres absorbed the shocks of uneven roads far better than solid ones, and they were quickly adopted by bicycle manufacturers. Within a few years, the basic design of the bicycle – two equal wheels, a chain drive and air-filled tyres – had taken the form it still has today.

The safety bicycle led to a cycling boom in the 1890s in Europe and North America. For the first time, large numbers of people could travel several kilometres quickly and cheaply without a horse. The bicycle was particularly significant for women, for whom it offered a new independence of movement. It also encouraged changes in women's clothing, as long, heavy skirts proved impractical for cycling. Some writers of the time argued that the bicycle had done more to promote women's freedom than almost anything else.

In the twentieth century, cars replaced bicycles as the main means of transport in many wealthy countries, although in others, and in some European cities, cycling remained common. In recent decades, concern about traffic, pollution and health has brought renewed interest. Many cities have built cycle lanes and introduced public bicycle-sharing schemes, while electric bicycles have made cycling practical for longer distances and hilly areas. More than two hundred years after the running machine, the bicycle is once again being promoted as a vehicle for the future.

lesson.title: Use names, dates and numbers first
lesson.text: In an easy Matching Information set, several questions contain or imply a specific detail: a date, an inventor, a number, or a distinctive object. Answer those first, because they are fastest to find. Then use the paragraphs you have not yet used to help locate the harder items. Remember that one paragraph can contain two answers.
lesson.example: Question: "the name of a person who improved the design". Scan for capital letters (names) and read the sentence around each one.

groups.title: Matching Information
groups.instruction:
The reading passage has seven paragraphs, A–G.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–G.
NB You may use any letter more than once.

questions.text: an explanation of why front wheels became larger
questions.evidence: each turn of the pedals moved the machine forward by exactly one turn of the wheel. To travel faster, designers made the front wheel larger.
questions.explanation: This is the explanation (cause → effect). Note that C is used twice in this set.

questions.text: a reference to restrictions on where early machines could be ridden
questions.evidence: Complaints from pedestrians led some cities to ban the machines from pavements.
questions.explanation: "Ban from pavements" = "restrictions on where machines could be ridden".

questions.text: the reason why one type of machine received an unflattering nickname
questions.evidence: they gave such an uncomfortable ride that they earned the nickname 'boneshakers'.
questions.explanation: The uncomfortable ride is the reason for the name. Paragraph C also mentions a nickname ("penny-farthing"), but it gives a different reason (coin sizes), and that name is not unflattering.

questions.text: a description of how a chain made it possible to build a lower, fast machine
questions.evidence: the chain allowed a small wheel to turn quickly, so that the machine could be fast without being tall.
questions.explanation: "Without being tall" = "lower".

questions.text: a mention of the effect of cycling on what people wore
questions.evidence: It also encouraged changes in women's clothing.
questions.explanation: "Clothing" = "what people wore".

questions.text: a claim about why a new type of tyre was first invented
questions.evidence: reportedly to make his young son's tricycle more comfortable.
questions.explanation: "Reportedly" matches "a claim".

questions.text: a reference to machines that use electrical power
questions.evidence: electric bicycles have made cycling practical for longer distances.
questions.explanation: "Electric" = "electrical power".

questions.text: a description of a risk faced by riders of one type of machine
questions.evidence: if the front wheel struck an obstacle, they could be thrown forward over the handlebars.
questions.explanation: This describes the risk of riding a high-wheeler.

passages.topic: Wildlife — how owls hunt in the dark
passages.title: Hunters of the Night

paragraphs.text: Owls are among the most effective night-time predators in the world. Of the roughly two hundred and fifty species, most hunt at dusk or during the night, catching mice, voles, insects, fish and even other birds. Their success depends on a remarkable set of adaptations that allow them to locate prey in near-darkness and approach it without being detected.

An owl's eyes are very large in relation to the size of its head, and in some species they take up a considerable proportion of the skull. They are also unusually shaped: rather than being round, they are elongated into a tube. This shape allows a large lens and a large area of light-sensitive tissue, which gather as much light as possible. The disadvantage is that the eyes cannot move within their sockets. To look in a different direction, an owl must turn its whole head.

Owls compensate for their fixed eyes with an extraordinarily flexible neck. Many species can rotate their heads by around 270 degrees – three-quarters of a full circle – in either direction. Special features of the bones and blood vessels in their necks allow them to do so without cutting off the supply of blood to the brain, something that would injure a human attempting the same movement.

Even more important than sight, for many species, is hearing. The flat, round face of many owls, known as the facial disc, is made of stiff feathers arranged to act rather like a satellite dish, collecting sound and directing it towards the ears. In several species, including the barn owl, the ear openings are positioned at different heights on each side of the head. A sound from below reaches one ear slightly before the other, allowing the owl to judge not only the direction but also the height of its source. Experiments have shown that barn owls can catch mice in complete darkness, guided by sound alone.

Locating prey is of little use if the prey hears the owl coming. Owls' flight is famously silent, thanks to the structure of their feathers. The leading edges of the main flight feathers have a comb-like fringe that breaks up the flow of air, reducing the noise it produces. The trailing edges have a soft fringe, and the surface of the feathers is covered in a velvety layer that absorbs sound. Engineers have studied these features in the hope of designing quieter aircraft and wind turbines.

Once an owl has caught its prey, it often swallows it whole or in large pieces. Its stomach cannot digest bones, fur and feathers, which are pressed together into a compact mass and brought back up through the mouth several hours later as a "pellet". These pellets, which collect beneath the places where owls roost, are valuable to scientists. By examining the bones inside them, researchers can identify exactly what an owl has eaten, and so learn about the populations of small mammals in an area without having to trap them.

Despite their skills, many owl species are declining. The loss of hunting grounds such as rough grassland, collisions with vehicles, and the use of poisons to control rodents have all taken a toll. In some areas, the provision of nest boxes and the protection of grassland at the edges of fields have helped owl numbers recover.

lesson.title: Work paragraph by paragraph
lesson.text: With a short, well-organised passage, an efficient method is to read one paragraph at a time and then look down the full list of questions to see which items that paragraph answers. This is often faster than taking each question and searching the whole passage. Mark each question as soon as you answer it, so that you don't read it again.
lesson.example: After reading a paragraph about an animal's eyes, check the question list for anything involving sight, vision, seeing, eyes, light.

groups.title: Matching Information
groups.instruction:
The reading passage has seven paragraphs, A–G.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–G.
NB You may use any letter more than once.

questions.text: an explanation of how owls avoid injury when turning their heads
questions.evidence: Special features of the bones and blood vessels ... allow them to do so without cutting off the supply of blood to the brain.
questions.explanation: This explains how injury is avoided.

questions.text: a reference to a practical use of owl research outside biology
questions.evidence: Engineers have studied these features in the hope of designing quieter aircraft and wind turbines.
questions.explanation: Aircraft design is a use outside biology.

questions.text: a description of how owls judge the vertical position of a sound
questions.evidence: ear openings are positioned at different heights ... allowing the owl to judge ... the height of its source.
questions.explanation: "Height" = "vertical position".

questions.text: the number of owl species
questions.evidence: Of the roughly two hundred and fifty species.
questions.explanation: This is the only number of species given in the passage.

questions.text: a reason why owls must turn their heads to look around
questions.evidence: the eyes cannot move within their sockets. To look in a different direction, an owl must turn its whole head.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C describes how the head turns, but the reason it must turn is in B. This is a similar-detail trap.

questions.text: a method of studying small animals without catching them
questions.evidence: researchers can ... learn about the populations of small mammals in an area without having to trap them.
questions.explanation: "Without having to trap" = "without catching".

questions.text: measures that have helped some owl populations
questions.evidence: the provision of nest boxes and the protection of grassland ... have helped owl numbers recover.
questions.explanation: This matches "measures that have helped".

questions.text: evidence that some owls can hunt without using their eyes
questions.evidence: barn owls can catch mice in complete darkness, guided by sound alone.
questions.explanation: "Guided by sound alone" means without sight. D is used twice.

passages.topic: Food history — from bitter drink to chocolate bar
passages.title: The Story of Chocolate

paragraphs.text: Chocolate is made from the seeds of the cacao tree, which grows naturally in the tropical rainforests of Central and South America. The seeds, usually called cocoa beans, grow inside large pods that sprout directly from the trunk and branches. Fresh beans are bitter and have little of the flavour we associate with chocolate. That flavour develops only after the beans have been fermented, dried and roasted – a process that people in Central America had mastered thousands of years ago.

Archaeologists have found traces of cacao in pottery vessels in Central America dating back more than three thousand years. For the Maya and later the Aztecs, cacao was consumed mainly as a drink, prepared from ground beans mixed with water and sometimes flavoured with chilli, vanilla or maize. The drink was usually poured from one vessel to another to create a foam, which was highly valued. Cacao was not only food: the beans were so valuable that they were used as a form of money, and records describe prices of goods, such as a turkey or a rabbit, in numbers of beans.

Spanish explorers encountered cacao in the early sixteenth century and brought it back to Europe. At first, Europeans found the bitter drink unappealing, but once it was sweetened with sugar and flavoured with spices such as cinnamon, it became fashionable among the wealthy. Over the following two centuries, chocolate houses opened in cities such as London, where customers gathered to drink chocolate and discuss business and politics. Because cacao had to be imported from distant plantations, it remained an expensive luxury.

The nineteenth century transformed chocolate from a drink into a food. In 1828, a Dutch chemist, Coenraad van Houten, patented a press that separated cocoa butter – the natural fat in the beans – from the solid part, producing a powder that mixed more easily with water. He also treated the powder with alkaline salts to reduce its bitterness. In 1847, a British company found that by mixing cocoa powder and sugar with melted cocoa butter, it could produce a paste that could be pressed into moulds and eaten as a solid bar.

Further improvements followed. In Switzerland in the 1870s, Daniel Peter succeeded in combining chocolate with milk – a difficult task because the water in milk tended to spoil the mixture. He used a form of condensed milk developed by his neighbour, Henri Nestlé, to create milk chocolate, which soon became the most popular form of chocolate in many countries. Shortly afterwards, another Swiss manufacturer, Rodolphe Lindt, invented a machine that stirred liquid chocolate for many hours, giving it a smoother texture that melted easily in the mouth.

As chocolate became cheaper and more popular, demand for cacao grew enormously, and production spread to other tropical regions. Today, the majority of the world's cacao is grown in West Africa, particularly in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, mainly on small family farms. Many of these farmers earn very low incomes, and the industry has faced criticism over poor working conditions. Certification schemes that aim to guarantee fair prices and better conditions have been introduced, although their effectiveness is debated.

Scientists are also concerned about the future of cacao itself. The trees grow only in a narrow band around the equator and are sensitive to temperature and rainfall, as well as to several serious diseases. Research is under way to develop more resistant varieties, and some farmers are growing cacao among other trees, which provide shade and may help protect the crop from changes in climate.

lesson.title: Dates as signposts
lesson.text: Historical passages usually move forward in time. If a question mentions or implies a period ("the earliest", "in the nineteenth century", "today"), use the dates in the passage to jump to the right paragraph. But be careful: a paragraph may mention a date only in passing, and the information asked for may be in a neighbouring paragraph.
lesson.example: Question: "a reference to a change in the eighteenth century". Scan for 17-- dates, then read the whole sentence to check that it describes a change.

groups.title: Matching Information
groups.instruction:
The reading passage has seven paragraphs, A–G.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–G.
NB You may use any letter more than once.

questions.text: a reference to cacao being used as currency
questions.evidence: the beans ... were used as a form of money.
questions.explanation: "Money" = "currency".

questions.text: an explanation of why chocolate remained costly in Europe for a long time
questions.evidence: Because cacao had to be imported from distant plantations, it remained an expensive luxury.
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives the reason with "because".

questions.text: the name of a person who helped another inventor by supplying an ingredient
questions.evidence: He used a form of condensed milk developed by his neighbour, Henri Nestlé.
questions.explanation: Nestlé supplied the ingredient that Peter needed.

questions.text: a description of where the pods grow on the tree
questions.evidence: pods that sprout directly from the trunk and branches.
questions.explanation: This describes where the pods grow.

questions.text: a process that made chocolate less bitter
questions.evidence: treated the powder with alkaline salts to reduce its bitterness.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C also mentions sweetening with sugar, but that improved the taste rather than removing bitterness through a process. D describes a specific process for reducing bitterness.

questions.text: a reference to places where people met to discuss business
questions.evidence: chocolate houses ... where customers gathered to drink chocolate and discuss business.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match. C is used twice in this set.

questions.text: doubts about schemes intended to help cacao farmers
questions.evidence: their effectiveness is debated.
questions.explanation: "Debated" = "doubts".

questions.text: a farming method that may help protect the crop
questions.evidence: growing cacao among other trees, which provide shade and may help protect the crop.
questions.explanation: This matches the statement, including "may".

passages.topic: Physical geography — why deserts form
passages.title: Lands Without Rain

paragraphs.text: Deserts cover roughly a third of the Earth's land surface. Many people picture them as endless seas of sand dunes under a burning sun, but this image fits only a minority of them. The feature that all deserts share is not heat or sand but a lack of water: they receive very little rainfall, and much of the rain that does fall evaporates quickly. Scientists often define a desert as a region that receives less than 250 millimetres of rain a year, although definitions vary.

The largest hot deserts, including the Sahara in Africa and the deserts of Arabia and Australia, lie roughly between 15 and 30 degrees north and south of the equator. Their location is no accident. Near the equator, intense heating causes warm, moist air to rise. As it rises, it cools and releases its moisture as heavy rain, which is why equatorial regions are so wet. The air, now dry, moves away from the equator at high altitude and eventually sinks back towards the surface in these subtropical latitudes. As it sinks, it becomes warmer and even drier, preventing clouds from forming.

Mountains can create deserts in a different way. When moist air blowing from the ocean meets a mountain range, it is forced upwards, cools and drops most of its moisture as rain or snow on the side facing the wind. By the time the air crosses the mountains and descends on the other side, it has lost most of its moisture. The land on this sheltered side lies in what is called a "rain shadow". Several deserts in western North America and in Central Asia owe their dryness partly to this effect.

Some of the driest places on Earth are found along coastlines. The Atacama Desert in South America, which runs along the Pacific coast, contains areas where no significant rainfall has been recorded for many years. Here, a cold ocean current flows along the coast, cooling the air above it. Cool air holds less moisture and does not rise easily, so clouds and fog may form over the sea but rarely produce rain over the land.

Distance from the sea is another cause. Air that has travelled thousands of kilometres across a continent has usually lost most of its moisture along the way. The Gobi Desert in Asia, located far from any ocean and also sheltered by mountains, is an example. Unlike the Sahara, the Gobi experiences very cold winters, when temperatures can fall far below freezing.

Indeed, not all deserts are hot. By the scientific definition, the largest desert in the world is Antarctica, which receives very little precipitation, most of it as snow. The Arctic is also classified as a desert in many places. In these regions, the cold air is extremely dry, and the small amount of snow that falls accumulates over long periods because it rarely melts.

Sand dunes, which dominate popular images of deserts, actually cover only around a fifth of the world's desert areas. Much larger areas consist of bare rock, gravel plains or dry lake beds. Where dunes do form, they are shaped by the wind, which can move them several metres a year and, in some places, bury roads and settlements. People living near such dunes have developed methods of slowing their movement, such as planting vegetation and building barriers.

lesson.title: Cause and effect in scientific passages
lesson.text: Many questions ask for "an explanation of" or "a cause of". In scientific passages, one paragraph may describe what happens and another may explain why. Look for cause words (because, as a result, this means, which causes, due to) and make sure the paragraph you choose contains the explanation, not just a description or example.
lesson.example: Question: "an explanation of why the coast is dry". A paragraph that simply says "the coast receives little rain" describes the fact but does not explain it. Look for the paragraph that gives the reason.

groups.title: Matching Information
groups.instruction:
The reading passage has seven paragraphs, A–G.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–G.
NB You may use any letter more than once.

questions.text: an explanation of why sinking air prevents clouds forming
questions.evidence: As it sinks, it becomes warmer and even drier, preventing clouds from forming.
questions.explanation: This is the explanation.

questions.text: a definition of a desert based on rainfall
questions.evidence: a region that receives less than 250 millimetres of rain a year.
questions.explanation: This is a definition based on rainfall.

questions.text: a reference to efforts to stop sand moving
questions.evidence: methods of slowing their movement, such as planting vegetation and building barriers.
questions.explanation: This matches "efforts to stop sand moving".

questions.text: an explanation of how a sea current contributes to dryness
questions.evidence: a cold ocean current ... cooling the air above it. Cool air holds less moisture and does not rise easily.
questions.explanation: This gives the cause-and-effect explanation.

questions.text: an example of a desert with very cold winters
questions.evidence: the Gobi experiences very cold winters.
questions.explanation: Antarctica (F) is cold all year round, but the question specifies cold winters, which matches the description of the Gobi.

questions.text: a description of what happens to air on the downwind side of mountains
questions.evidence: descends on the other side, it has lost most of its moisture.
questions.explanation: "Other side" = "downwind side".

questions.text: the proportion of deserts covered by sand dunes
questions.evidence: cover only around a fifth of the world's desert areas.
questions.explanation: "A fifth" is a proportion. Paragraph A mentions "a third", but that is the proportion of land covered by deserts, not the proportion of deserts covered by dunes.

questions.text: a reason why snow builds up in polar deserts
questions.evidence: accumulates over long periods because it rarely melts.
questions.explanation: This gives the reason.

passages.topic: Urban history — the invention of traffic lights
passages.title: Red, Amber, Green

paragraphs.text: Traffic lights are so ordinary that few people notice them, yet they control the movement of millions of vehicles every day and play a major role in preventing collisions. Their history reflects the growing problem of managing crowded streets, first with horses and carriages and later with motor vehicles.

The first traffic signal was installed in London in December 1868, outside the Houses of Parliament, where heavy traffic made crossing the road dangerous for members of Parliament and the public. Designed by a railway engineer, it was based on the signals used on railways, with movable arms that were raised or lowered by a police officer during the day. At night, a gas lamp showed red or green lights. Just a month after it was installed, however, the gas lamp exploded, injuring the police officer operating it. The signal was removed, and the idea was abandoned in Britain for several decades.

The arrival of the motor car in the early twentieth century made traffic control an urgent problem, particularly in the United States. Police officers directing traffic at busy junctions were exposed to danger and bad weather, and they could not always be seen clearly. In the 1910s, several American cities experimented with electric signals. One of the earliest, installed in 1914 in the city of Cleveland, used red and green lights and a buzzer to warn drivers that the lights were about to change.

These early signals had only two colours, which meant that drivers had no warning that the signal was about to turn red. In 1920, a police officer in Detroit, William Potts, introduced a system with a third light, amber, to indicate that the signal was changing. Potts, who had worked with railway signals, did not patent his design, and three-colour systems quickly spread to other cities.

Other inventors also contributed. In 1923, Garrett Morgan, an American businessman and inventor, patented a traffic signal with an additional position that stopped traffic in all directions for a short time, allowing vehicles already in the junction to clear it safely before traffic moving in the other direction was allowed to proceed. The idea of a brief period in which all traffic is stopped remains part of many modern signal systems.

For several decades, most traffic lights operated on fixed timers, changing at the same intervals regardless of how much traffic was waiting. This was inefficient: drivers could be kept waiting at a red light when no other vehicles were present. From the mid-twentieth century, sensors buried in the road surface began to detect waiting vehicles, allowing signals to respond to actual traffic. Today, many cities use networks of connected signals controlled by computers, which adjust timings across whole areas to reduce congestion.

Traffic lights have also been adapted to serve pedestrians and cyclists. Many crossings now include signals showing a walking figure, buttons that pedestrians press to request a crossing, and sounds or vibrating panels that help people with visual impairments know when it is safe to cross. Some cities have introduced countdown timers showing how many seconds remain before the lights change. More recently, some planners have argued that at certain junctions, removing traffic lights altogether and encouraging drivers to negotiate with one another carefully can make streets safer. The idea remains controversial.

lesson.title: "Firsts" and "problems"
lesson.text: Two very common question types in history passages are "the first..." and "a problem with...". For "first" questions, check that the passage really presents something as the first (earliest, first, the original, before any other). For "problem" questions, look for negative language (difficulty, danger, failed, exploded, was expensive). Both may appear in several paragraphs, so read each candidate sentence carefully.
lesson.example: Question: "a problem with an early design". Candidate sentence: "The first model worked well but was expensive to produce." The problem is cost, even though the design "worked well".

groups.title: Matching Information
groups.instruction:
The reading passage has seven paragraphs, A–G.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–G.
NB You may use any letter more than once.

questions.text: a reference to an accident involving an early signal
questions.evidence: the gas lamp exploded, injuring the police officer operating it.
questions.explanation: This describes the accident.

questions.text: a reason why police officers directing traffic were at a disadvantage
questions.evidence: Police officers directing traffic ... were exposed to danger and bad weather, and they could not always be seen clearly.
questions.explanation: This matches "at a disadvantage".

questions.text: a description of a signal that used sound to warn drivers
questions.evidence: a buzzer to warn drivers that the lights were about to change.
questions.explanation: "Buzzer" = "sound". C is used twice in this set.

questions.text: a mention of an inventor who chose not to protect his design legally
questions.evidence: Potts ... did not patent his design.
questions.explanation: Patenting protects a design legally. Morgan (E) did patent his design, which makes E a trap.

questions.text: a problem with signals that changed at regular intervals
