passages.topic: Health science — what happens while we sleep
passages.title: The Busy Night

paragraphs.text: Humans spend roughly a third of their lives asleep, yet for most of history sleep was regarded as a simple state of rest in which the brain more or less switched off. That view began to change in the 1950s, when researchers recording the electrical activity of sleeping people's brains discovered that sleep is not uniform. The brain passes through distinct stages during the night, some of which involve activity almost as intense as when a person is awake.

Sleep is usually divided into two main types. The first, non-rapid eye movement sleep, includes a light stage from which people are easily woken and a stage of deep sleep, during which brain waves become slow and large, breathing becomes regular, and it is much harder to wake the sleeper. The second type is rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, named after the quick movements of the eyes beneath closed eyelids. During REM sleep, the brain is highly active and most vivid dreams occur, but the muscles of the body are almost completely relaxed – which may prevent people from acting out their dreams.

The stages follow one another in cycles, each lasting roughly ninety minutes. A typical night includes four or five cycles. Their composition changes as the night goes on: deep sleep dominates the early cycles, while REM sleep becomes longer in the later ones. This is why a person woken shortly before their usual waking time is more likely to remember a dream.

Why do we sleep? Researchers now believe that sleep serves several purposes. One of the most studied is its role in memory. Experiments have shown that people who sleep after learning new information remember it better than those who stay awake for the same period. During sleep, the brain appears to replay and strengthen memories formed during the day, transferring some of them into longer-term storage. Different stages of sleep may contribute to different types of memory, although the details are still being investigated.

Sleep also seems to help the brain clean itself. Research in animals has suggested that during sleep, fluid flows more freely through the brain, washing away waste products that accumulate during waking hours. Some scientists believe that this process may be connected with long-term brain health, though much of the research so far has been carried out on mice, and its relevance to humans is not yet certain.

The timing of sleep changes over a lifetime. Newborn babies sleep for much of the day and night, in short periods. During adolescence, the body's internal clock tends to shift later, so that teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night and find it harder to wake early in the morning. Some researchers have argued that this should be taken into account when setting school starting times, and a number of schools that have started later have reported improvements in attendance and attention. Older adults, by contrast, often wake earlier and spend less time in deep sleep.

The consequences of too little sleep are well documented. Even one night of poor sleep can reduce attention and slow reaction times, and people who are sleep-deprived are often poor judges of how impaired they are. Long-term lack of sleep has been linked with a range of health problems. Yet in many modern societies, work schedules, long commutes and the use of electronic devices late at night mean that many people regularly sleep less than experts recommend.

lesson.title: Paragraphs that contain more than one answer
lesson.text: Some paragraphs are packed with information, and two or even three questions may point to the same one. Don't avoid a letter just because you have already used it, especially when the instructions say "You may use any letter more than once." On the other hand, some paragraphs may contain no answers at all. Your goal is to match each detail to the correct paragraph, not to use every letter.
lesson.example: If one paragraph mentions both "how long a cycle lasts" and "what happens to the muscles", both questions can have the same answer.

passages.topic: Economic history — what counts as money?
passages.title: From Shells to Screens

paragraphs.text: Money is so central to modern life that it is easy to assume it has always existed in roughly its present form. In fact, the objects and systems that societies have used as money have varied enormously, from shells and grain to metal, paper and, most recently, electronic records. What these objects have in common is not their physical form but their function: they are accepted as a means of exchange, a way of measuring value and a way of storing wealth for the future.

Economics textbooks have traditionally explained the origin of money with a simple story. In early societies, people traded goods directly – a farmer might exchange grain for a potter's bowls. But such barter was inconvenient, because each party had to want what the other offered. Money, the story goes, was invented to overcome this problem. Many anthropologists, however, have challenged this account. They point out that no society has been found in which barter was the main way of exchanging goods among neighbours. Instead, in many small communities, people kept track of debts and obligations: goods and help were given with the understanding that they would be returned later. On this view, systems of credit came before coins, not after them.

The earliest known coins were produced in the seventh century BC in Lydia, a kingdom in what is now western Turkey. They were made from electrum, a natural mixture of gold and silver, and were stamped with images that guaranteed their weight and purity. The idea spread quickly through the Greek world and beyond. Coins had clear advantages: they were durable, easy to count and could be carried from place to place, and the stamp of a ruler meant that their value did not have to be tested at every transaction.

Coins also created problems. Their value depended on the metal they contained, and rulers short of money were sometimes tempted to reduce the amount of precious metal while keeping the face value the same. When people realised this had happened, they often lost confidence in the coins, and prices rose. Large payments in coins were also heavy and difficult to transport safely over long distances.

Paper money emerged partly as a solution to this last problem. In China, merchants in the tenth and eleventh centuries began to use paper certificates, issued in exchange for deposits of coins, which could be carried more easily. The government later took over the issue of such notes, making China the first country to use government-issued paper money on a large scale. However, the authorities sometimes printed notes far faster than the economy grew, causing their value to fall sharply. Paper money did not become common in Europe until several centuries later.

For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the value of many currencies was linked to gold: in principle, holders of paper money could exchange it for a fixed quantity of the metal. This system limited how much money governments could create, which some saw as a guarantee of stability, while others argued that it made it harder to respond to economic crises. The link between major currencies and gold was finally broken in the early 1970s. Since then, most money has had value simply because governments declare it to be legal tender and people trust that others will accept it.

Today, only a small fraction of the money in developed economies exists as physical notes and coins. Most exists as numbers in bank accounts, transferred electronically. In some developing countries, mobile phones have become the main means of payment. In Kenya, for example, a service launched in 2007 allowed people without bank accounts to store and send money using simple text messages, and it was rapidly adopted by a large proportion of the population. Money's form has changed repeatedly; what has remained constant is its dependence on trust.

lesson.title: Similar details in several paragraphs
lesson.example: Coins appear in paragraphs C and E. Question: "a disadvantage of using metal coins". C describes their invention; E explains that coins were heavy to transport → E.

passages.topic: Psychology — why we put things off
passages.title: Tomorrow, Always Tomorrow

paragraphs.text: Almost everyone procrastinates occasionally, delaying tasks they intend to do even when they know that delay will make things worse. For some people, however, procrastination is a persistent habit that damages their work, finances and health. Surveys suggest that a substantial minority of adults regard themselves as chronic procrastinators, and among students the proportion appears to be considerably higher. Despite its familiarity, procrastination has only become a major subject of psychological research in recent decades.

A common assumption is that procrastinators are simply lazy or poor at managing their time. Researchers increasingly reject this explanation. Procrastinators are often busy – they may clean the house, answer emails or help friends while avoiding the one task they most need to do. The problem, many psychologists now argue, is not a lack of effort but a difficulty in managing emotions. Tasks that provoke unpleasant feelings, such as boredom, anxiety or self-doubt, are avoided because avoidance brings immediate relief. The relief is temporary, and the task remains, often accompanied by increasing guilt.

Another influential explanation concerns the way people think about the future. Studies using brain imaging have found that when people think about themselves in the distant future, patterns of brain activity resemble those that occur when they think about strangers. If the "future self" feels like another person, it becomes easier to leave difficult tasks for that person to deal with. People who feel more closely connected to their future selves tend to save more money and, some research suggests, to procrastinate less.

Procrastination also appears to be influenced by the nature of the task. People are more likely to delay tasks that are unclear, have distant deadlines or offer rewards only in the long term. A report due in three months provides little sense of urgency today, whereas the pleasures of other activities are immediate. Some researchers describe this as a conflict between two systems: one oriented towards immediate rewards and another capable of long-term planning, with the first often winning.

Several practical strategies have been tested. One of the most effective involves forming specific plans in advance, known as "implementation intentions": rather than deciding vaguely to "work on the essay", a person decides exactly when, where and how they will start – for example, "At nine o'clock tomorrow, at the library, I will write the first paragraph". Studies have found that such plans increase the likelihood of starting tasks. Breaking a large task into small steps, each with its own deadline, can also help, as can reducing distractions by, for instance, keeping phones in another room.

One of the more surprising findings concerns self-forgiveness. In a study of university students, those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before their first examinations procrastinated less when preparing for later ones. The researchers suggested that forgiving oneself reduced the negative feelings associated with the task, making it easier to approach next time. Harsh self-criticism, by contrast, may increase the unpleasant emotions that lead to avoidance in the first place.

Procrastination is not always harmful. Some writers have argued that a certain amount of delay allows ideas to develop and prevents people from committing too early to poor solutions. Researchers distinguish, however, between deliberate delay of this kind and the unwanted, self-defeating delay that characterises chronic procrastination. The first is a choice; the second feels like a failure to act on one's own intentions.

lesson.title: Research findings vs theories vs advice
lesson.example: Question: "a practical technique for reducing delay". A paragraph explaining why people delay is not the answer, even though it is on the same topic.

passages.topic: Architecture and engineering — how skyscrapers became possible
passages.title: Reaching for the Sky

paragraphs.text: Until the second half of the nineteenth century, the height of buildings was limited by two practical problems. The first was structural. Most large buildings were supported by their walls, and the taller a building became, the thicker its lower walls had to be to carry the weight above. A sixteen-storey office building completed in Chicago in 1891 using load-bearing brick walls needed walls nearly two metres thick at its base, taking up valuable space on the lower floors. The second problem was human: few people were willing to climb more than five or six flights of stairs every day, so upper floors were difficult to rent.

The solution to the second problem came first. Mechanical lifts, or elevators, had existed for some time, but they were feared because the ropes that raised them could break. In 1854, at an exhibition in New York, an American mechanic named Elisha Otis demonstrated a safety device. Standing on a raised platform, he ordered the rope holding it to be cut. Instead of falling, the platform stopped almost immediately, held by a mechanism that gripped the guide rails. The first passenger elevator using his device was installed in a New York shop in 1857. Over the following decades, elevators powered first by steam and later by electricity made upper floors as convenient as lower ones – and eventually more desirable, because they offered light, views and distance from street noise.

The structural problem was solved by the use of iron and later steel frames. Instead of relying on walls to carry the building's weight, engineers constructed a skeleton of vertical columns and horizontal beams that bore the loads, with the outer walls simply hung on the frame like a curtain. The Home Insurance Building in Chicago, completed in 1885, is often cited as the first skyscraper built on this principle, though historians debate whether it deserves the title. Steel frames allowed walls to be thin and windows to be large, and there was no longer a practical limit set by the thickness of walls at the base.

Chicago's leading role in these developments was no accident. A great fire in 1871 had destroyed much of the city centre, creating a demand for rapid rebuilding at a time when land values in the business district were rising sharply. Building upwards allowed developers to make the most of expensive plots. New York soon followed, and by the early twentieth century the two cities were competing to build ever taller towers.

As buildings grew taller, new concerns arose. Tall buildings blocked sunlight from reaching the streets below, turning some roads into dark canyons. In 1916, New York introduced regulations requiring buildings above a certain height to step back from the street as they rose, allowing light and air to reach street level. These rules gave many of the city's towers of the 1920s and 1930s their distinctive stepped, pyramid-like shapes.

At great heights, wind becomes a greater challenge than weight. Strong winds can make tall buildings sway, and although the movement may not be dangerous, it can make occupants feel unwell. Modern skyscrapers use a variety of techniques to reduce this, including shaping the building so that wind flows around it more smoothly and installing heavy weights near the top that move in the opposite direction to the building's sway, reducing the motion.

Elevators, which first made tall buildings practical, also limit them. Conventional elevators are raised by steel cables, and in very tall buildings the weight of the cable itself becomes a problem, so passengers must change lifts at intermediate floors. Engineers have developed lighter cable materials, and even elevators that move sideways as well as up and down, which could make still taller buildings more practical. Whether there is any real need for such heights, however, is a separate question, since the costs of building extremely tall towers are enormous, and many are built more for prestige than for practical necessity.

lesson.title: "A reference to" = a brief mention
lesson.text: When a question says "a reference to" or "a mention of", the information may be very small: a single phrase buried in a paragraph about something else. Don't expect the whole paragraph to be about it. By contrast, "a description of" or "an account of" usually needs a few sentences of detail. Adjust how carefully you scan according to the question's wording.
lesson.example: "A reference to an earthquake" might be satisfied by one clause such as "...which survived the 1906 earthquake..." in a paragraph mainly about building materials.

passages.topic: Marine science — the future of coral reefs
passages.title: Cities of the Sea

paragraphs.text: Coral reefs occupy less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are thought to support around a quarter of all marine species at some stage of their lives. Fish shelter and breed among their complex structures, and countless other creatures – crabs, sea urchins, sponges and worms – live in the crevices of the reef. Because of this richness, reefs are often compared to rainforests. They are also of great value to people: they protect coastlines from waves and storms, support fisheries on which millions depend, and attract tourists whose spending supports local economies.

Despite their rock-like appearance, reefs are built by living animals. Corals are colonies of tiny creatures called polyps, each only a few millimetres across, which build hard skeletons of calcium carbonate beneath themselves. Over thousands of years, the skeletons of successive generations accumulate to form massive structures. The largest reef system in the world, off the north-eastern coast of Australia, stretches for more than two thousand kilometres and can be seen from space.

The success of reef-building corals depends on a partnership. Inside the tissues of the polyps live microscopic algae, which use sunlight to produce food through photosynthesis. The algae provide the coral with most of its energy, and in return the coral gives them shelter and certain nutrients. It is these algae that give many corals their bright colours. The partnership is also why most reef-building corals are found in shallow, clear, sunlit water.

This relationship is sensitive to temperature. When the water becomes unusually warm for a prolonged period, the partnership breaks down and the corals expel the algae. Without them, the coral tissue becomes transparent, revealing the white skeleton beneath – a process known as "bleaching". Bleached corals are not immediately dead, and if temperatures return to normal quickly, the algae can return. But if the heat continues, the corals may starve. Mass bleaching events, affecting reefs across large areas at once, have become more frequent in recent decades as ocean temperatures have risen.

Other pressures add to the problem. Pollution from farmland can encourage the growth of seaweed that competes with corals for space, and sediment washed from the land can block sunlight. Overfishing removes species that help keep the reef healthy, such as fish that graze on seaweed. As the oceans absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, the water becomes slightly more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons.

Scientists and conservationists are trying a range of responses. Some are growing fragments of coral in underwater nurseries and transplanting them onto damaged reefs, rather like replanting a forest. Others are studying corals that have survived heatwaves, in the hope of identifying and breeding varieties that can tolerate higher temperatures. Such projects have had local successes, but they operate on a very small scale compared with the size of the world's reefs, and many researchers stress that they cannot replace efforts to limit rising temperatures.

There are some grounds for hope. Reefs that are protected from local pressures such as pollution and overfishing often recover more quickly after bleaching than those that are not, which suggests that good local management can increase their resilience. Some reefs in unusual locations, such as those exposed to naturally variable temperatures, appear to be more tolerant of heat. How much reefs can adapt, and how quickly, remains one of the most important questions in marine science.

passages.topic: Education history — how universities developed
passages.title: The Long Life of the University

paragraphs.text: Universities are among the oldest institutions in the world still performing something close to their original function. Several European universities founded in the Middle Ages continue to teach students today, and their traditions – from academic gowns to the titles of degrees – survive in universities around the world. Yet the idea of what a university is for has changed profoundly over the centuries.

The first institutions to be called universities emerged in Europe in the late eleventh and twelfth centuries, in cities such as Bologna, Paris and Oxford. They were not founded in a single act by a ruler; rather, they grew out of communities of teachers and students who organised themselves to protect their interests. The Latin word universitas originally meant a corporation or guild – any organised group of people with shared rights – and it was only later that it came to refer specifically to places of higher learning. At Bologna, the students themselves formed the guild, hired the teachers and could fine them for arriving late or failing to cover the syllabus.

Teaching in medieval universities was based largely on the reading and explanation of authoritative texts. Books were rare and expensive, since they had to be copied by hand, so a lecturer would read a text aloud and comment on it while students took notes. Students also took part in formal debates, in which they defended or attacked a proposition according to strict rules of argument. The main subjects were theology, law and medicine, preceded by a general course in the liberal arts, including grammar, logic and arithmetic.

For centuries, universities were concerned mainly with preserving and passing on existing knowledge rather than discovering new knowledge. Much of the important scientific work of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries was carried out outside universities, by independent scholars and members of scientific societies. This began to change in the early nineteenth century. The University of Berlin, founded in 1810, was organised around the principle that teaching and research should be combined, and that professors should be active scholars who advanced knowledge in their fields. This model proved extremely influential and was widely imitated, particularly in the United States, where it contributed to the development of graduate schools.

Universities also became more closely connected with practical needs. In the United States, a law passed in 1862 granted federal land to states to establish colleges teaching agriculture and engineering alongside traditional subjects. The aim was to make higher education useful to farmers and industrial workers, not only to those entering the professions. Many of these institutions later became major universities.

The greatest expansion of university education came after the Second World War. In many countries, governments invested heavily in higher education, believing that economic growth depended on a highly educated workforce. Student numbers, once limited to a small elite, grew enormously. In several countries, the proportion of young people entering university rose from a few per cent to a third or more within a few decades, and new universities were founded in large numbers.

This expansion has raised new questions. As universities have grown, so has debate about who should pay for them, how their quality should be measured, and whether all students benefit equally from a degree. Online teaching has added further uncertainty about the future of the traditional campus. Yet universities have repeatedly adapted to new circumstances over nine centuries, and many observers expect them to do so again.

lesson.title: Paraphrased time references
lesson.text: Questions rarely repeat exact dates. They may say "a development in the early nineteenth century" when the passage says "in 1810", or "the period after a major war" when the passage says "after 1945". Convert the question's time expression into a rough date range, then scan for dates or time phrases that fall within it.
lesson.example: Question: "a change in the medieval period". Look for dates roughly between 500 and 1500, or phrases such as "in the Middle Ages" or "twelfth century".

passages.topic: Business history — the rise of the supermarket
passages.title: The Self-Service Revolution

paragraphs.text: For most of history, buying food meant asking for it. In a typical grocery shop of the early twentieth century, customers stood at a counter and asked an assistant for each item they wanted. The assistant fetched the goods from shelves behind the counter, weighed or measured them, wrapped them and added up the bill. Shopping was slow, required many staff, and gave customers little opportunity to compare products or to discover new ones.

The first major challenge to this system came in 1916 in Memphis, in the United States, when a businessman named Clarence Saunders opened a shop in which customers served themselves. Shoppers entered through a turnstile, picked up a basket, walked along aisles lined with goods displayed on open shelves, and paid at a checkout on the way out. Every item was marked with its price. Saunders patented the idea and quickly opened many similar shops. Because fewer staff were needed, prices could be lower than those of traditional grocers.

The supermarket as we know it – a large store selling a wide range of food, including fresh meat and vegetables as well as packaged goods – developed in the 1930s. During the economic depression of that decade, stores offering low prices in large, simple buildings on the edge of town attracted customers who were anxious to save money. The spread of car ownership made such locations practical, since customers could drive there and carry home large quantities of goods. Many early supermarkets provided large car parks, which were rarely found at traditional shops.

After the Second World War, supermarkets expanded rapidly in North America and then in Europe. Their growth was closely connected with changes in the way people lived. Families moved to new suburbs, many households acquired refrigerators and freezers, allowing them to store food for longer, and more women entered paid employment, leaving less time for daily shopping. A weekly trip to the supermarket suited these new patterns of life.

The introduction of the barcode in the 1970s brought another major change. The first product scanned at a supermarket checkout, in Ohio in 1974, was a packet of chewing gum. Barcodes allowed checkout staff to process purchases much faster and with fewer errors. More importantly, they gave supermarkets detailed information about what was being sold, where and when. This allowed them to manage their stock precisely, order goods automatically as they sold out, and study the effects of prices and promotions.

Supermarkets have had significant effects on the places where they operate. They offer convenience, choice and, often, lower prices than smaller shops. But many small, independent grocers and specialist shops have been unable to compete, and in some towns the opening of a large supermarket on the outskirts has been followed by the decline of the traditional high street. Supermarkets' buying power has also given them considerable influence over farmers and suppliers, who sometimes complain that they are forced to accept low prices.

The supermarket is now changing again. Online ordering and home delivery have grown rapidly in many countries, while some chains have opened smaller stores in city centres to serve customers who shop more often, buying less each time. Self-service checkouts have extended Saunders' original idea, allowing customers not only to select their own goods but also to scan and pay for them. A century after the first self-service shop opened, the question is no longer whether customers will serve themselves, but how much of the shopping they will do without visiting a shop at all.

lesson.title: Innovations and their effects
lesson.text: Business and technology passages often describe an innovation in one paragraph and its effects in another. Questions may ask for "the introduction of..." (the innovation) or "a consequence of..." (the effect). Make sure your paragraph contains the specific part of the story that the question asks for.
lesson.example: Paragraph C: "In 1974, barcodes were first scanned at a checkout." Paragraph D: "Scanning allowed shops to track sales precisely." Question: "a benefit of the barcode" → D, not C.

passages.topic: Agriculture and development — the "Green Revolution"
passages.title: Feeding Billions

paragraphs.text: In the 1960s, many experts feared that parts of Asia were heading towards widespread famine. Populations were growing rapidly, and food production was struggling to keep pace. Some predicted that hundreds of millions of people would die of hunger within a few decades. That catastrophe did not occur on the scale predicted, and one of the main reasons was a set of agricultural changes that became known as the "Green Revolution".

At the heart of the Green Revolution were new varieties of cereal crops. Traditional varieties of wheat and rice were tall, and when farmers applied large amounts of fertiliser to increase yields, the plants grew so heavy with grain that their stems bent and collapsed, a problem known as "lodging". Plant breeders, working first in Mexico on wheat and later in the Philippines on rice, developed shorter, sturdier varieties that could support heavy heads of grain without falling over. These semi-dwarf varieties could therefore make full use of fertiliser, producing far higher yields.

The American scientist Norman Borlaug, who led much of the work on wheat in Mexico, became the best-known figure of the movement. In the mid-1960s, new wheat varieties were introduced on a large scale in India and Pakistan, during a period of severe drought and food shortage. Within a few years, wheat harvests in both countries had increased dramatically. A new rice variety, released in 1966, produced similar gains in parts of Asia. In 1970, Borlaug was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of his contribution to reducing hunger.

The new varieties did not work on their own. They required fertilisers, reliable supplies of water – usually from irrigation – and often chemical pesticides. Governments supported farmers with subsidies, loans and investment in irrigation systems and roads. Where these conditions were met, yields rose sharply. Where they were not, as in many parts of Africa with less irrigation and different crops, the Green Revolution had much less effect.

Critics soon identified problems. Because the new methods required money for seeds, fertilisers and equipment, wealthier farmers were often better able to adopt them than poorer ones, and in some areas inequality between farmers increased. Heavy use of irrigation lowered water tables in some regions, and the overuse of fertilisers and pesticides polluted soil and water. The spread of a small number of high-yielding varieties also replaced many traditional local varieties, reducing the genetic diversity of crops.

Supporters respond that these problems must be weighed against the scale of the achievement. Cereal production in developing countries more than doubled between the 1960s and the 1990s, and the prices of basic foods fell, benefiting poor consumers. Higher yields also meant that more food could be produced on existing farmland, reducing pressure to clear forests and other natural areas for agriculture.

Today, many agricultural scientists argue that a second, different kind of revolution is needed. Future increases in food production, they suggest, must be achieved with less water, fewer chemicals and greater resistance to changing climate conditions. Some emphasise improved crop varieties; others stress better management of soil and water, or greater support for small farmers. Most agree that the lessons of the first Green Revolution – both its successes and its costs – should inform what comes next.

lesson.title: Positive vs negative information
lesson.text: Balanced passages give both benefits and criticisms. Questions often specify the evaluative direction: "a criticism of", "an advantage of", "a concern about", "an achievement". When two paragraphs discuss the same subject, check whether each is positive or negative, and match the direction of the question.
lesson.example: Two paragraphs discuss fertiliser: one praises higher yields, the other describes water pollution. Question: "an environmental drawback of fertiliser use" → the negative paragraph.

passages.topic: Child development — how babies learn language
passages.title: Tuning In to Language

paragraphs.text: By their first birthday, most children have begun to understand some words, and many have produced their first. By the age of three, they are typically speaking in sentences. This rapid progress is all the more remarkable because nobody teaches young children the rules of their language directly. For a long time, it was debated whether children learn language mainly through general abilities to detect patterns, or whether they are born with specialised knowledge of language. Research on babies has provided some surprising insights into this question.

One of the first problems babies face is identifying individual words. In ordinary speech, words are not separated by pauses; they run together in a continuous stream of sound. How, then, does a baby know where one word ends and the next begins? In a well-known experiment published in 1996, researchers played eight-month-old babies a two-minute recording of an invented language consisting of nonsense syllables strung together without pauses. Within the stream, certain syllables always followed one another, forming "words", while other combinations occurred only by chance.

After listening, the babies were played short sequences, some of which were "words" from the invented language and some of which were combinations that had occurred less reliably. The babies listened for longer to the less familiar combinations, showing that they could tell the two apart. The researchers concluded that babies can track how often sounds occur together and use this information to identify likely words – a process known as statistical learning. The finding suggested that general pattern-detecting abilities play a larger role in early language learning than some theories had assumed.

Babies also become specialists in the sounds of their own language. Every language uses a particular set of sounds, and distinctions that are important in one language may be absent in another. Young babies can distinguish between sounds used in many different languages, including languages they have never heard. But by around ten to twelve months of age, this ability narrows: babies become better at distinguishing the sounds of their own language and worse at distinguishing sounds that are not used in it. In effect, they tune their perception to the language around them.

The way adults talk to babies seems to help. In many cultures, adults naturally speak to infants using a higher pitch, exaggerated intonation, slower speech and clearer pronunciation – a style sometimes called "parentese". Studies have found that babies prefer to listen to this style of speech, and that the amount of such speech they hear in the first year is associated with larger vocabularies later on. Some researchers suggest that the exaggerated sounds make it easier for babies to identify the features of their language.

Social interaction appears to be particularly important. In one study, American babies aged around nine months were exposed to Mandarin Chinese over a series of short sessions. One group interacted with a live Mandarin speaker who played and read with them; other groups heard the same amount of Mandarin through video or audio recordings. Only the babies who had interacted with a live speaker retained the ability to distinguish Mandarin sounds. The researchers proposed that social interaction increases babies' attention and motivation, helping them learn from what they hear.

These findings have practical implications. They suggest that talking with babies – not simply near them – and responding to their sounds and gestures supports language development, and that screens are a poor substitute for human interaction at this age. They also suggest that the first year of life, long before children say their first words, is a period of intense learning about language.

lesson.title: Experiments — design vs results vs interpretation
lesson.example: Paragraph C describes how babies listened to recordings. Paragraph D reports that they looked longer at new sounds and explains what this shows. Question: "a proposed explanation of the babies' behaviour" → D.

passages.topic: Earth science — how continental drift was finally accepted
passages.title: The Moving Continents

paragraphs.text: Looking at a map of the world, many people have noticed that the eastern coast of South America and the western coast of Africa seem to fit together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. The observation was made by several scholars from the sixteenth century onwards, but for a long time it was treated as a curiosity rather than as evidence. Most geologists assumed that continents and oceans had always occupied roughly their present positions, and that any major changes to the Earth's surface had involved land rising or sinking vertically.

In 1912, the German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed a far more radical idea. The continents, he argued, had once been joined together in a single great landmass, which had later broken apart, its fragments slowly drifting to their present positions. Wegener assembled an impressive range of evidence. Fossils of identical plants and animals, including land-dwelling reptiles that could not have crossed oceans, were found on continents now separated by thousands of kilometres. Distinctive layers of rock matched across the Atlantic. And traces of ancient glaciers were found in places that are now tropical, suggesting that those regions had once been much nearer the poles.

Wegener's theory was widely rejected, particularly by geologists in Britain and North America. The main objection was not to his evidence but to the absence of a convincing mechanism. Wegener suggested that the continents ploughed through the rock of the ocean floor, driven by forces related to the Earth's rotation. His critics calculated that such forces were far too weak, and that continents could not force their way through the solid rock beneath the oceans. Some also objected that Wegener was not a trained geologist – his background was in meteorology and astronomy – and that he had selected evidence to fit his theory. Alternative explanations for the fossil evidence were proposed, including now-vanished "land bridges" that had once connected the continents.

Wegener died in 1930 on an expedition to Greenland, his theory still widely dismissed. A few scientists continued to support it, and one of them proposed that slow currents in the hot rock deep within the Earth might carry the continents along. The idea attracted little attention at the time.

The decisive evidence came from the ocean floor itself, which was largely unexplored until the mid-twentieth century. Improved methods of measuring the depth of the sea, many developed for military purposes, revealed that the ocean floor was not the flat, featureless plain that had been assumed. Instead, a vast underwater mountain range ran down the middle of the Atlantic and continued around the globe. Maps produced in the 1950s showed a deep valley running along the crest of this ridge.

Studies of the magnetism of the ocean floor provided the crucial clue. As molten rock cools, iron-rich minerals within it align with the Earth's magnetic field, preserving a record of the field's direction at that time. The Earth's magnetic field has reversed its direction many times in the past. In the early 1960s, surveys revealed that the rocks on either side of the mid-ocean ridges formed parallel stripes of normal and reversed magnetism, and that the pattern on one side of a ridge was a mirror image of the pattern on the other. The most convincing explanation was that new ocean floor was continually being created at the ridges and spreading outwards on both sides, recording the reversals of the magnetic field as it formed.

Seafloor spreading supplied the missing mechanism. The continents did not plough through the ocean floor; rather, they were carried along as part of large, rigid plates of the Earth's outer layer, which moved as new material was added at the ridges and old material sank back into the Earth at deep ocean trenches. Within a few years, this theory of "plate tectonics" had been accepted by most geologists. It explained not only the fit of the continents and the distribution of fossils but also the locations of earthquakes and volcanoes, which are concentrated along the boundaries between plates.

The history of continental drift is often told as a story of a lone genius ignored by a narrow-minded establishment. The reality is more complicated. Wegener's critics were not simply prejudiced: they raised genuine scientific objections, and his proposed mechanism was indeed wrong. What finally changed minds was not a better argument but new kinds of evidence, obtained with technologies that did not exist in Wegener's lifetime. The episode illustrates both the importance of taking unconventional ideas seriously and the reasonable demand that a theory explain how, as well as that, something happens.

lesson.title: Hard Matching Information — abstract question wording
lesson.text:
At Hard level, questions describe the information in abstract, general terms. For example, "an explanation of why a theory was initially dismissed" rather than "why Wegener's ideas were rejected". There are more paragraphs (often eight or nine), several contain no answer, and the passage repeatedly revisits the same subject from different angles.

Strategy:

1. Translate each abstract question into what it would look like in this passage ("theory dismissed" → Wegener rejected → look for "critics", "no mechanism").

2. Identify the function of each paragraph as you read, for example "evidence", "objection", "new technology", "consequence". Hard questions often target paragraph functions.

3. Expect the correct sentence to use none of the question's words.

passages.topic: Psychology — the marshmallow test revisited
passages.title: The Temptation Experiment

paragraphs.text: In a series of experiments carried out at a university nursery school in California in the late 1960s and early 1970s, the psychologist Walter Mischel and his colleagues offered young children a simple choice. Each child, typically aged around four or five, was shown a treat – a marshmallow, a biscuit or another small snack. The researcher explained that he needed to leave the room. If the child could wait until he returned, they would receive two treats; if they could not wait, they could ring a bell, and the researcher would return at once, but they would receive only one. Some children ate the treat almost immediately; others waited the full fifteen or twenty minutes.

The original purpose of these studies was not to predict children's futures. Mischel was interested in the strategies children used to resist temptation. He found that children waited longer when the treat was hidden from view, or when they were encouraged to think about it in abstract terms – imagining the marshmallow as a fluffy cloud, for example – rather than focusing on its taste. Children who distracted themselves by singing, playing with their hands or covering their eyes also tended to wait longer.

The experiments became famous for a different reason. Years later, Mischel's team contacted the parents of some of the children who had taken part. The children who had waited longer at the age of four were, on average, described by their parents as more competent adolescents, and had achieved higher scores on university entrance tests. Later follow-ups reported associations with other outcomes in adulthood. These findings were widely publicised and gave rise to a popular belief that the ability to delay gratification in early childhood was a powerful predictor of later success, and that teaching self-control could transform children's lives.

The follow-up studies, however, had important limitations. The original participants were mostly the children of staff and students at a prestigious university, and so were far from representative of the population as a whole. And only a fraction of them could be traced for the follow-up studies, so the results were based on relatively small numbers.

In 2018, a team of researchers published a study designed to address these problems. They used data from a much larger and more diverse group of children, who had taken a similar waiting test at around the age of four and whose progress had been followed for more than a decade. They found that the association between waiting time and later academic achievement was considerably weaker than in the original follow-ups – about half as strong. More significantly, when they took account of factors such as the family's income and the child's early cognitive abilities, the association became much smaller still.

Another line of research suggested that a child's decision to wait may depend on more than self-control. In one experiment, before taking the marshmallow test, children were exposed to a researcher who either kept or broke a promise, such as a promise to bring better art materials. Children who had experienced the unreliable researcher waited, on average, far less time than those who had experienced the reliable one. The researchers argued that, for a child whose experience suggests that promises are often broken, eating the treat at once may be a rational decision rather than a failure of willpower.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the popular interpretation of the marshmallow test was too simple. Waiting time appears to reflect not only a child's capacity for self-control but also their circumstances: whether they have learned to trust adults, whether resources in their home are reliable, and other aspects of their environment. These same circumstances may also influence later success, which could account for part of the association observed in the original follow-ups.

None of this means that self-control is unimportant. Many studies using different methods have found that people with better self-regulation tend to experience better outcomes in various areas of life. But the marshmallow test offers a warning about how a single striking experiment can be turned into a simple lesson that its evidence cannot fully support – and about the danger of attributing to individual character what may partly be the result of circumstance.

lesson.title: Tracing how interpretations change
lesson.text: In passages that describe research over several decades, the same study may be interpreted differently at different times. Questions may ask for "the original interpretation", "a later challenge" or "an alternative explanation". Mark each paragraph with its stage in the story: original study → popular interpretation → challenge → new explanation → conclusion. Many hard questions become straightforward once you know the stage of each paragraph.

passages.topic: Urban history and public health — the sewers of Victorian London
passages.title: The Great Stink

paragraphs.text: In the middle of the nineteenth century, London was the largest and richest city in the world, yet much of its waste flowed, untreated, into the River Thames. For centuries, household waste had been collected in cesspits beneath or beside houses, which were emptied periodically by workers who sold the contents to farmers as fertiliser. As the city grew, this system broke down. Cesspits overflowed, and the introduction of the flushing toilet – which used large quantities of water – made the problem worse, since the extra water caused cesspits to overflow more quickly. Increasingly, waste was connected directly to the existing drains and sewers, which had been designed to carry rainwater, and these emptied straight into the river.

The Thames was also a major source of drinking water. Several private water companies drew water from the river, some of them from points close to where sewers discharged their contents. The city suffered repeated outbreaks of cholera, a disease that caused severe diarrhoea and killed tens of thousands of people in London during the middle decades of the century.

At the time, the dominant medical theory held that diseases such as cholera were caused by "miasma" – bad air, arising from rotting matter and filth. According to this theory, the smell of decay was not merely unpleasant but dangerous. In 1854, a doctor named John Snow challenged this view. Studying an outbreak in the Soho district of London, he mapped the homes of those who had died and found that they were clustered around a single public water pump. He persuaded local officials to remove the pump's handle, and argued that cholera was spread through contaminated water rather than bad air. His conclusions, however, were not widely accepted at first.

The crisis came in the unusually hot summer of 1858. The low level of the river and the high temperatures produced a smell so overwhelming that the period became known as the "Great Stink". The newly rebuilt Houses of Parliament stood beside the river, and members found it almost impossible to work. Curtains soaked in chemicals were hung at the windows in an attempt to block the smell. Within weeks, Parliament passed legislation providing funds for a new system of sewers – a remarkable speed for a project that had been discussed for years without action.

The scheme was designed and supervised by the engineer Joseph Bazalgette. His plan was to build large "intercepting" sewers running parallel to the river on both banks, which would collect waste from the existing sewers before it reached the Thames and carry it eastwards, downstream of the city, where it was released into the river on the outgoing tide. The project was enormous: it involved more than 130 kilometres of main sewers and a much larger network of smaller street sewers, as well as pumping stations to lift waste in low-lying areas. Bazalgette deliberately made many sewers larger than current needs required, reasoning that the population would continue to grow.

Part of the system was built within new embankments along the river, which reclaimed land from the Thames and provided space for roads, gardens and later an underground railway. The main system was largely completed by the mid-1870s. Its effect on public health was dramatic. When a cholera outbreak struck London in 1866, most of the deaths occurred in an area of the East End that had not yet been connected to the new system and whose water supply was contaminated. It was the last major cholera epidemic in the city.

The irony is that the sewers were built largely for the wrong reason. Most of those who supported the project did so because they believed the smell itself caused disease. The sewers succeeded in removing the smell, but they reduced cholera because they stopped waste from contaminating drinking water – exactly as Snow had argued. By the time the germ theory of disease became widely accepted later in the century, the infrastructure that protected Londoners was already in place.

Bazalgette's sewers remain in use today, still forming the core of London's drainage system. But the city's population is now far larger than he could have imagined, and heavy rainfall regularly causes the combined sewers, which carry both rainwater and waste, to overflow into the Thames. A new tunnel beneath the river has been built to capture much of this overflow – a twenty-first-century solution to a problem that the Victorians had largely, but not completely, solved.

lesson.title: Unintended consequences and ironies
lesson.text: Hard historical passages often highlight ironies: actions taken for one reason that had an unexpected result, or theories that were wrong but led to good outcomes. Questions may describe these indirectly: "a beneficial result of a mistaken belief", "an outcome that was not the main aim of a project". Look for contrast words such as although, ironically, even though, not because... but, unintended.

passages.topic: Anthropology and cognition — how different cultures count
passages.title: Numbers Without Words

paragraphs.text: For people who grow up using number words from early childhood, it is difficult to imagine thinking about quantities without them. Yet languages differ remarkably in how they express numbers. Some have words for numbers into the millions and beyond; others have only a handful. Studying these differences has allowed researchers to ask whether the ability to reason precisely about large quantities depends on having words for them.

Many number systems are based on ten, almost certainly because humans have ten fingers. But this is not universal. Some languages count in twenties, using fingers and toes. Traces of such systems survive even in European languages: French, for example, expresses eighty as "four twenties". Other systems use bases of five, twelve or even sixty – the last of which, inherited from ancient Mesopotamia, survives in the division of hours into minutes and minutes into seconds.

Some communities in Papua New Guinea use body-part counting systems. Instead of abstract number words, people count by touching or naming parts of the body in a fixed order, starting with the fingers of one hand and continuing up the arm, across the face and down the other side. In one such system, a count might reach over twenty body parts. The name of each body part serves as a number word within the sequence.

At the other extreme are languages with very few number words. Researchers have studied a small group living in the Amazon rainforest whose language appears to have no words for exact numbers at all – only terms that roughly mean "a small amount", "somewhat more" and "many". In experiments, members of this group were asked to match a line of objects – for example, placing the same number of batteries as there were spools of thread on a table. They performed accurately with two or three objects, but with larger numbers their responses became approximate: they placed roughly the right number, but often not exactly the right number.

These findings have been interpreted in different ways. Some researchers argue that they show that number words are a cognitive tool: without them, people can still judge quantities approximately, but cannot keep track of exact large numbers. Others caution against drawing strong conclusions. The group studied is very small, and in their way of life there is little need for exact counting; the results may reflect lack of practice or cultural expectations about the task rather than a fundamental limitation. It is also possible that the experimental tasks, designed by outsiders, were unfamiliar or seemed pointless to participants.

Research on young children supports the view that learning number words is a gradual process that changes how children think about quantity. Children in many societies can recite the counting sequence well before they understand what the words mean. A two-year-old who can say "one, two, three, four, five" may still be unable to give an adult exactly four objects when asked. Children typically learn the meaning of "one", then "two", then "three", over a period of many months, before suddenly grasping the principle that the last number in a count tells you how many objects there are.

Studies of adults who have never learned a formal number system from others offer further evidence. In some communities, people who are deaf and have not been taught a sign language develop their own systems of gestures, known as home signs, to communicate with their families. Researchers have found that such individuals can use gestures to indicate small numbers accurately, but that their gestures for larger numbers tend to be approximate, even though they handle money and other quantities in daily life.

Together, these studies suggest that the human mind has two basic systems for dealing with quantity: one for tracking small numbers exactly, up to about three or four, and another for estimating larger quantities approximately. Number words, according to this view, provide a way of linking these systems and extending exact reasoning to any number. If this is correct, then our ability to reason precisely about large numbers is not simply an innate gift but, in part, an invention of human culture – passed on, like writing, from one generation to the next.

passages.topic: Energy and technology — the long rise of solar power
passages.title: Power from Light

paragraphs.text: Solar panels are now a familiar sight on rooftops and in fields across the world, and in many places they produce electricity more cheaply than any other source. This is a recent development. For most of their history, solar cells were expensive curiosities, used only where no alternative was available. Understanding how they became mainstream requires looking at a history that spans nearly two centuries.

The scientific story begins in 1839, when a nineteen-year-old French physicist, Edmond Becquerel, observed that shining light on certain materials in a conducting solution produced a small electric current. This "photovoltaic effect" attracted some interest, and later in the century researchers built simple cells using the element selenium. These converted less than one per cent of the sunlight falling on them into electricity – far too little to be useful – and no one could fully explain how they worked. A satisfactory explanation of the interaction between light and matter had to wait for developments in physics in the early twentieth century.

The first practical solar cell was produced in 1954 by researchers at a telephone company laboratory in the United States. Working with silicon, the material that was also transforming electronics, they created a cell that converted around six per cent of sunlight into electricity. Newspapers greeted the invention with excitement, and one predicted that it might eventually provide almost limitless energy. The reality was more modest: the cells were extremely expensive, and the electricity they produced cost hundreds of times more than electricity from conventional power stations.

Space provided the first important market. Satellites needed a reliable source of power that could operate for years without refuelling, and cost was less important than weight and reliability. In 1958, a small American satellite became one of the first to carry solar cells, which continued to power its radio transmitter for several years – long after its conventional batteries had failed. Solar cells soon became the standard power source for satellites, and the demand from the space industry funded improvements in their efficiency.

On Earth, solar power remained a niche technology for decades. It was used in remote places far from electricity networks – lighthouses, telecommunications equipment in deserts, and later small devices such as calculators. Rising oil prices in the 1970s encouraged some governments to fund research into alternative energy, but when oil prices fell again in the 1980s, much of this support was withdrawn.

The transformation of solar power came from a combination of policy and manufacturing. In the early 2000s, several countries, notably Germany, introduced schemes guaranteeing households and businesses a fixed, above-market price for electricity generated from solar panels. The resulting demand encouraged manufacturers to build much larger factories. As production expanded, costs fell: each doubling of the total amount of solar capacity manufactured has been associated with a fall of roughly a fifth in the price of panels. Much of the later expansion of production took place in China, where large-scale manufacturing drove prices down further. Between 2010 and 2020, the cost of electricity from large solar installations fell by around ninety per cent.

Low cost has not solved every problem. Solar panels produce electricity only during daylight, and their output falls on cloudy days and in winter in regions far from the equator. As solar power supplies a larger share of electricity, networks must find ways of dealing with this variability – through batteries and other forms of storage, by connecting regions with different weather, and by adjusting demand. The cost of batteries has also fallen sharply, although storing large amounts of energy for long periods, such as from summer to winter, remains difficult and expensive.

The history of solar power offers a lesson about how technologies develop. For more than a century after the photovoltaic effect was discovered, solar cells were scientifically interesting but economically marginal. What made them important was not a single breakthrough in the laboratory but the steady reduction of costs through large-scale production, driven by markets that were deliberately created by government policy. Whether similar approaches can be used to accelerate other technologies is a question of considerable importance.

lesson.title: Distinguishing scientific discovery, technical development and economic change
lesson.text: Technology histories move through different kinds of events: a scientific discovery (a phenomenon is observed), a technical development (a practical device is made), and an economic or social change (cost falls, use spreads). Questions often specify one kind. For example, "the first practical application" is not the same as "the discovery of the effect". Label each paragraph accordingly.

passages.topic: Ecology — the cane toad and the problem of invasive species
passages.title: An Unwelcome Guest

paragraphs.text: In 1935, around a hundred cane toads were shipped from Hawaii to north-eastern Australia. The large, heavy-bodied amphibians, native to Central and South America, were intended to control beetles whose larvae were damaging the roots of sugar cane, a major crop in the region. The toads were bred in captivity, and within months thousands of young toads had been released into cane fields along the coast.

The plan failed. The beetles lived mainly in the upper parts of the cane plants, while the toads, which cannot climb well, hunted on the ground. There is little evidence that the toads had any significant effect on the pests they were introduced to control. They did, however, thrive in their new environment. Cane toads breed rapidly: a single female can lay tens of thousands of eggs at a time. In Australia, they had no natural predators adapted to them, and the warm, humid climate of the north suited them well.

The toads spread steadily across northern Australia, moving westwards at a rate that increased over the decades. Researchers who studied toads at the moving edge of the invasion found that these individuals had longer legs and more stamina than those in long-established populations, and that they tended to travel further each night. The toads at the front, it seems, were those most inclined to disperse, and when they bred with one another, their offspring inherited these traits, so that the invasion accelerated as it progressed.

The most serious consequences of the invasion arise from the toads' defences. Cane toads produce a powerful toxin in glands behind their heads. Many Australian predators, which have never evolved alongside such toxic prey, attack and eat the toads and are poisoned. Populations of some native lizards, snakes and a carnivorous marsupial called the northern quoll have fallen sharply in areas the toads have reached. Pet dogs are also sometimes poisoned.

There are signs that some native species are adapting. In areas where toads have been present for many decades, certain snake species appear to have developed a greater resistance to the toxin, or to have evolved smaller mouths that make it harder to swallow large toads. Some birds have learned to turn toads over and eat only the non-toxic parts. These changes suggest that the most severe effects may be concentrated in the years immediately after the toads arrive in a new area.

Efforts to control the toads have included community "toad-busting" events, in which volunteers collect and humanely kill toads; traps using sounds or chemical signals to attract them; and fences around important water sources during the dry season. None of these methods has halted the invasion across the continent, although some may reduce toad numbers locally. A more promising approach aims to protect predators rather than eliminate the toads. In "conditioned taste aversion" programmes, animals such as quolls are fed small pieces of toad meat treated with a chemical that causes nausea but is not fatal. Having learned to associate toads with sickness, the animals avoid eating them in the wild. Trials have shown that trained quolls survive longer after toads arrive than untrained ones.

The story of the cane toad is often told as a warning against introducing species to new environments, and it has influenced the much stricter rules that now govern such introductions in Australia and elsewhere. Biological control – using one species to control another – remains an important tool, and many carefully tested introductions have been successful. But the cane toad demonstrates how difficult it is to predict the behaviour of an organism in a new environment, and how hard it can be to reverse the consequences once a species has become established.

Some ecologists now argue that, in many cases, eradicating an established invasive species is unrealistic, and that conservation efforts should concentrate on helping native species survive alongside it. Others worry that such acceptance may reduce the urgency of preventing new invasions. Both groups agree, however, that prevention – stopping harmful species from arriving in the first place – is far cheaper and more effective than any response after the event.

passages.topic: History of everyday objects — the umbrella
passages.title: Under Cover

paragraphs.text: The umbrella is one of the oldest portable devices still in everyday use. Images of shades held over important people appear in the art of ancient Egypt, Assyria and China, dating back several thousand years. In these early societies, umbrellas were used mainly to provide protection from the sun rather than the rain, and they were often symbols of high rank. Only kings, nobles and religious leaders were entitled to have a servant hold a shade above them.

The Chinese are usually credited with developing umbrellas that could protect against rain. Early Chinese umbrellas were made of silk or paper, and some were treated with wax or oil so that they would repel water. There is evidence that folding umbrellas, which could be opened and closed with a mechanism of ribs and a sliding collar, were being used in China many centuries ago. From China, the umbrella spread to Korea, Japan and other parts of Asia.

In Europe, umbrellas were rarely seen for many centuries, and when they reappeared, they were associated mainly with women. Sunshades became fashionable accessories among wealthy women in France and Italy in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. A man carrying an umbrella, however, was widely regarded as weak or unmanly. It was assumed that a gentleman would travel by carriage, and that only someone too poor to afford one would need to protect himself from the rain.

This attitude began to change in the second half of the eighteenth century, largely thanks to one man. Jonas Hanway, a London merchant and traveller, carried an umbrella in public for around thirty years, despite being mocked in the streets. Carriage drivers, who feared that umbrellas would reduce demand for their services, were said to have shouted insults at him. Gradually, however, other men followed his example, and by the end of the century the umbrella had become an acceptable item for men in Britain. For some time, umbrellas were even nicknamed "Hanways".

Early European umbrellas were heavy and awkward. Their frames were made of wood or whalebone, and when wet, the covering of oiled cotton or silk became heavy and difficult to dry. A major improvement came in 1852, when an English manufacturer, Samuel Fox, designed an umbrella with a frame of steel ribs. Steel was lighter and stronger than earlier materials, and Fox's design became the basis for most umbrellas produced afterwards. In the twentieth century, compact folding umbrellas and waterproof synthetic fabrics made umbrellas smaller, cheaper and more convenient.

Today, around the world, hundreds of millions of umbrellas are sold every year, and in some cities it is possible to borrow one from a public sharing scheme on a rainy day. Yet the basic design has changed surprisingly little. Engineers have experimented with umbrellas that resist strong winds, umbrellas without central poles and even devices that blow a shield of air above the user's head, but none of these has replaced the traditional form. The umbrella remains a simple solution that works well enough to have survived for thousands of years.

lesson.title: Use the first sentence
lesson.text: In easy passages, the first sentence of each paragraph usually tells you the topic directly. Read it carefully, then skim the rest of the paragraph to confirm. If the rest of the paragraph develops the same idea, the first sentence is your main idea.

passages.topic: Urban planning — why cities need parks
passages.title: Green Spaces in the City

paragraphs.text: In the early nineteenth century, most large cities had very few public parks. Green spaces existed, but many were private gardens belonging to wealthy families or royal estates to which ordinary people had limited access. As industrial cities grew rapidly, their crowded, polluted streets offered working people few places to escape for fresh air or recreation. Reformers began to argue that public parks were a necessity rather than a luxury.

One of the most influential parks of this period was Central Park in New York, designed in 1858 by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux. Its designers created an artificial landscape of lakes, meadows, woods and winding paths, intended to give city dwellers the experience of the countryside. They also separated different types of traffic, building bridges and sunken roads so that carriages, horse riders and pedestrians rarely crossed paths. The park's success inspired similar projects in many other cities.

Today, research has confirmed many of the benefits that early park reformers believed in. People who live near parks tend to take more physical exercise, whether walking, running, cycling or playing sport. Spending time in green spaces has also been associated with lower levels of stress and improved mood, and some studies have found that patients recover more quickly from illness when they can see trees from their windows.

Parks also play an important role in city environments. Trees and other vegetation absorb rainwater, reducing the risk of flooding, and provide shade that lowers temperatures during hot weather. Parks give shelter to birds, insects and other wildlife, and can act as corridors that allow animals to move between different areas of a city.

In addition, parks bring people together. They are among the few places in a city where people of different ages, incomes and backgrounds can meet freely and without charge. Community events, markets and festivals are often held in parks, and simply sharing the same space can help neighbours get to know one another.

Maintaining parks, however, is expensive, and when public budgets are under pressure, parks are often among the first services to be cut. Without regular care, parks can become neglected, and people may begin to feel unsafe using them. Some cities have responded by involving local volunteers and charities in park management, or by allowing cafés and events that generate income. Many experts argue that parks should instead be treated as essential public services, funded as reliably as roads and schools.

lesson.title: Avoid headings that cover only one example
lesson.text: A paragraph often gives a general idea followed by several examples. A heading that names only one of those examples is too narrow. Choose the heading that covers the general idea behind them.
lesson.example: Paragraph: "Parks improve physical health. People walk, run and play sports there, and children have space to exercise." Heading "A place for children to play" is too narrow; "Benefits for physical health" is correct.

groups.title: Matching Headings
groups.instruction:

Write the correct number, i–ix.

questions.text: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: As industrial cities grew ... Reformers began to argue that public parks were a necessity.
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why industrial cities needed parks.

questions.text: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: One of the most influential parks ... The park's success inspired similar projects.
questions.explanation: Central Park was a landmark design that influenced others.

questions.text: Paragraph C

questions.explanation: The paragraph covers both physical and mental benefits.

questions.text: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: absorb rainwater ... provide shade ... give shelter to birds.
questions.explanation: Heading iv (wildlife) covers only one example, so it is too narrow. Heading viii covers flooding, temperature and wildlife.

questions.text: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: parks bring people together.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: Maintaining parks, however, is expensive ... parks are often among the first services to be cut.
questions.explanation: The main idea is the cost of maintenance. Heading ix is a detail: feeling unsafe is one consequence of neglect. Heading vii concerns building new parks, not maintaining existing ones.

passages.topic: Food and nature — honey
passages.title: Liquid Gold

paragraphs.text: Honey begins as nectar, a sugary liquid produced by flowers to attract insects. Worker bees collect nectar and carry it back to the hive in a special stomach. There, it is passed from bee to bee, and enzymes from the bees' bodies begin to break down the complex sugars into simpler ones. The bees then deposit the liquid into the cells of the honeycomb and fan it with their wings, evaporating much of its water. When the honey has become thick enough, they seal each cell with a cap of wax.

Humans have collected honey for thousands of years. A rock painting in a cave in eastern Spain, thought to be around eight thousand years old, shows a figure climbing towards a wild bees' nest and collecting honey. At first, honey was simply taken from wild colonies, often at great risk. Later, people began to keep bees in hollow logs, clay pots and woven baskets. In ancient Egypt, beekeepers moved their hives along the River Nile by boat, following the flowering seasons.

Honey has a remarkable ability to resist decay. Because it contains very little water and a great deal of sugar, and because it is slightly acidic, bacteria and other microorganisms cannot survive in it. Archaeologists have reported finding pots of honey in ancient tombs that were still recognisable as honey thousands of years later. If honey is kept sealed, it can last almost indefinitely, although it may gradually thicken and form crystals.

For much of history, honey was valued not only as food but also as medicine. Ancient doctors in several civilisations applied it to wounds and burns, and modern research has shown that certain types of honey can help prevent infection. Some hospitals today use specially prepared medical honey in wound dressings. Doctors warn, however, that honey should not be given to babies under one year old, as it may occasionally contain bacteria that can make them seriously ill.

Honey production faces several challenges. Bee colonies in many regions have suffered from diseases, parasites and the effects of pesticides, while the loss of wildflowers has reduced the food available to them. At the same time, the demand for honey has increased, and some honey sold in shops has been found to have been mixed with cheaper sugar syrups. Detecting such adulteration can be difficult, and scientists have developed new laboratory techniques to identify it.

lesson.title: Process paragraphs vs history paragraphs vs use paragraphs
lesson.text: In passages about products, paragraphs usually have different functions: how it is made, its history, its uses, its problems. Headings reflect these functions. Identify the function of each paragraph before choosing a heading, and watch for headings that mention the right subject but the wrong function (for example, "the history of beekeeping" for a paragraph about how bees make honey).

questions.explanation: This is a process paragraph about how nectar becomes honey.

questions.text: Paragraph B

questions.explanation: This is a history paragraph. Heading viii concerns modern practical advice, which the paragraph does not give.

questions.text: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Honey has a remarkable ability to resist decay ... can last almost indefinitely.
questions.explanation: Heading iv is a detail trap: tombs are only an example, and they are not specifically Egyptian in this paragraph.

questions.text: Paragraph D

questions.explanation: The paragraph covers both old and new medical uses.
