questions.explanation: Threats to colonies affect supply, and adulteration affects quality.

passages.topic: Physics in everyday life — how rainbows form
passages.title: Colours in the Sky

paragraphs.text: Rainbows have fascinated people throughout history, and many cultures have explained them through myths. In some traditions, the rainbow was a bridge between the human world and the world of the gods; in others, it was a great serpent or a sign of good fortune. Stories about treasure hidden at the end of the rainbow, which of course can never be reached, are found in several parts of the world.

A scientific explanation began to emerge in the seventeenth century. The French philosopher René Descartes studied how light passed through glass spheres filled with water, which acted as models of raindrops, and was able to calculate the angle at which rainbows appear. A few decades later, Isaac Newton showed, by passing sunlight through a glass prism, that white light is actually a mixture of all the colours of the spectrum. Together, these discoveries explained how rainbows are formed.

A rainbow is produced when sunlight enters raindrops. As the light passes from air into water, it bends, a process called refraction. Because each colour bends by a slightly different amount, the white light is separated into its colours. The light is then reflected off the back of the raindrop and bends again as it leaves. Each raindrop sends out light of all colours, but at slightly different angles, and an observer sees different colours coming from drops at different heights in the sky.

Seeing a rainbow requires particular conditions. The sun must be behind the observer and relatively low in the sky, while rain is falling in front of them. This is why rainbows are most often seen in the early morning or late afternoon, when showers are passing. Light from the rainbow reaches the eye at an angle of about forty-two degrees from the point directly opposite the sun. For this reason, when the sun is higher than about forty-two degrees above the horizon, no rainbow can be seen from the ground.

Sometimes a second, fainter rainbow appears outside the first. This double rainbow is caused by light reflecting twice inside the raindrops before leaving them. The second reflection reverses the order of the colours, so that in the outer rainbow red appears on the inside and violet on the outside. The sky between the two bows is noticeably darker than the surrounding sky.

Because a rainbow depends on the position of the observer, no two people see exactly the same rainbow. Each person sees light coming from a different set of raindrops. A rainbow is therefore not an object located in a particular place but an optical effect that moves as the observer moves – which is why it is impossible to reach its end.

lesson.title: Explanation paragraphs
lesson.text: In science passages, several paragraphs may explain the same phenomenon from different angles: why it happens, what conditions are needed, a special case, how it was first explained. Headings will differ in exactly these ways. Ask of each paragraph: Is it explaining the cause, the conditions, a variation, or the history of the explanation?

questions.text: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: many cultures have explained them through myths.
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about myths and stories.

questions.text: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: A scientific explanation began to emerge ... Together, these discoveries explained how rainbows are formed.
questions.explanation: This paragraph gives the history of the explanation. Heading ix is too narrow: it names Newton, but the paragraph covers Descartes too and concerns only the rainbow.

questions.text: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: As the light passes from air into water, it bends ... reflected off the back of the raindrop.
questions.explanation: This paragraph explains the cause.

questions.text: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Seeing a rainbow requires particular conditions.
questions.explanation: This paragraph describes the conditions.

questions.text: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: This double rainbow is caused by light reflecting twice ... reverses the order of the colours.
questions.explanation: The paragraph covers both the cause and the appearance of the second bow.

questions.text: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: no two people see exactly the same rainbow ... not an object located in a particular place.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

passages.topic: Work and society — working from home
passages.title: Home and Office

paragraphs.text: Working from home is often described as a new phenomenon, but for most of history it was normal. Before the industrial age, many people – farmers, weavers, shoemakers, shopkeepers – worked where they lived, and families often shared the work. It was the rise of factories and, later, large offices in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries that separated the place of work from the home and created the daily journey to work.

From the 1970s onwards, some commentators predicted that new communications technology would allow office workers to return to working at home. Telephones, fax machines and later computers and the internet made it possible, in principle, to do many office jobs from anywhere. However, for several decades the change happened far more slowly than expected. Most employers preferred staff to be present in the office, and many employees had neither the equipment nor the permission to work elsewhere.

This changed suddenly in 2020, when lockdowns imposed during the coronavirus pandemic forced millions of office workers to work from home almost overnight. Companies that had long resisted remote working discovered that much of their business could continue with staff working from kitchen tables and spare bedrooms. Video-calling software, previously used mainly for occasional meetings, became part of everyday life.

Many employees found that working from home had clear advantages. Without a daily commute, they saved time and money and had more flexibility to organise their day around family responsibilities. Some reported that they could concentrate better away from the noise and interruptions of a busy office.

There were also costs. Some workers struggled to separate work from home life, finding themselves checking emails late into the evening. Others, particularly those living alone, felt isolated. Young employees at the start of their careers often missed the chance to learn by observing experienced colleagues, and some managers worried that creativity and informal cooperation suffered when people rarely met in person.

The evidence on productivity is mixed. Some studies have found that people working from home get more done, while others have found the opposite, and the results appear to depend on the type of work, the home environment and how productivity is measured. What seems clear is that working from home suits some people and some tasks better than others.

As a result, many organisations have moved towards "hybrid" working, in which employees spend part of the week in the office and part at home. Some have reduced their office space accordingly. The arrangement aims to combine the flexibility of home working with the social and collaborative benefits of the office – although getting the balance right remains a challenge for many employers.

lesson.title: Paragraphs with "however" in the middle
lesson.text: Some paragraphs begin with one idea and then turn with however, but, yet or on the other hand. The main idea is often what comes after the turn, especially if the rest of the paragraph develops it. Don't choose a heading based on the first sentence alone if the paragraph changes direction.
lesson.example: "Many people expected the new road to reduce traffic. However, congestion soon returned, and journeys became as slow as before." → main idea: the failure of the road to reduce traffic.

groups.title: Matching Headings
groups.instruction:
The reading passage has seven paragraphs, A–G.
Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below.
Write the correct number, i–x.

questions.text: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: Before the industrial age, many people ... worked where they lived ... It was the rise of factories ... that separated the place of work from the home.
questions.explanation: Heading v ("a return to an older pattern") is tempting, but Paragraph A describes the older pattern itself, not a return to it. No paragraph presents modern home working as a return, so v is an unused distractor.

questions.text: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: some commentators predicted ... However, for several decades the change happened far more slowly than expected.
questions.explanation: The main idea follows "however".

questions.text: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: forced millions of office workers to work from home almost overnight.
questions.explanation: "Almost overnight" = "sudden", and "forced" = "unplanned".

questions.text: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Many employees found that working from home had clear advantages.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: There were also costs. Some workers struggled ... felt isolated.
questions.explanation: Heading ix is too narrow, since young workers are only one example. The paragraph also does not say they prefer offices.

questions.text: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: The evidence on productivity is mixed.
questions.explanation: "Mixed" = "unclear", and "productivity" = "output".

questions.text: Paragraph G
questions.evidence: 'hybrid' working ... aims to combine the flexibility of home working with the social and collaborative benefits of the office.
questions.explanation: This describes a compromise. Heading viii is a detail trap: office space is mentioned, but not its cost.

passages.topic: Geography — living with volcanoes
passages.title: In the Shadow of the Mountain

paragraphs.text: Around the world, hundreds of millions of people live within reach of an active volcano. At first glance, this seems surprising. Volcanic eruptions can destroy towns, and history records many disasters in which thousands of people died. Yet volcanic regions have attracted human settlement for thousands of years, and some are among the most densely populated places on Earth.

The main reason is the soil. Volcanic ash and rock, once they have been broken down by weather over many years, produce soils that are rich in minerals and extremely fertile. In regions such as the island of Java in Indonesia and the slopes of volcanoes in Central America and southern Italy, farmers can grow abundant crops of rice, coffee, fruit and vegetables. Where land is scarce, the fertility of volcanic soil can support large populations.

Volcanoes provide other resources too. The heat beneath volcanic regions can be used to produce geothermal energy: in some countries, such as Iceland, underground heat supplies much of the energy used for heating homes and generating electricity. Volcanic rocks are used for building, and some valuable minerals are formed by volcanic activity. Volcanoes also attract tourists, who come to see craters, hot springs and dramatic landscapes, bringing income to local communities.

The dangers, however, are real and varied. Lava flows can destroy buildings and roads, although they usually move slowly enough for people to escape. Far more deadly are fast-moving clouds of hot gas and rock that can race down the sides of a volcano, destroying everything in their path. Mudflows, formed when volcanic ash mixes with water from rain or melting ice, can travel great distances along river valleys. Ash falling from the sky can collapse roofs, damage crops and disrupt air travel over wide areas.

Scientists cannot yet predict precisely when a volcano will erupt, but they can often detect warning signs. Instruments measure small earthquakes beneath the volcano, changes in the shape of the ground as molten rock rises, and the gases released from its surface. When these signs increase, authorities may raise alert levels and prepare for evacuation.

Monitoring is only useful if people respond to warnings. In some cases, residents have been reluctant to leave their homes and farms, particularly after earlier warnings did not lead to eruptions. Successful evacuations depend on clear communication, well-planned escape routes and trust between scientists, officials and local communities. Education programmes, which teach residents about volcanic hazards and what to do in an emergency, have helped reduce deaths in several regions.

lesson.title: Advantages vs risks vs responses
lesson.text: Passages about hazards often contain paragraphs on why people live there (advantages), the dangers (risks) and how people reduce the dangers (responses). Headings will use words like attraction, benefit, threat, warning, preparation. Match the paragraph's overall direction: is it positive, negative or about solutions?

groups.title: Matching Headings
groups.instruction:
The reading passage has six paragraphs, A–F.
Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below.
Write the correct number, i–ix.

headings.text: The range of hazards an eruption can produce
A surprising pattern of settlement
Detecting signs of coming activity
Farming land of exceptional quality
Why lava flows are rarely fatal
Additional economic benefits of volcanic areas
The importance of public trust and preparation
The largest eruptions in history
Iceland's energy policy

questions.text: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: At first glance, this seems surprising ... Yet volcanic regions have attracted human settlement.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match. Heading viii is a keyword trap: disasters are mentioned only in passing.

questions.text: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: produce soils that are rich in minerals and extremely fertile.
questions.explanation: This paragraph describes an advantage.

questions.text: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Volcanoes provide other resources too ... geothermal energy ... building ... tourists.
questions.explanation: "Other" = "additional". Heading ix is too narrow, since Iceland is only one example.

questions.text: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: The dangers, however, are real and varied. Lava flows ... clouds of hot gas ... Mudflows ... Ash.
questions.explanation: This paragraph covers a range of risks. Heading v is a detail from one sentence.

questions.text: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: they can often detect warning signs.
questions.explanation: This paragraph is about monitoring as a response.

questions.text: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: Successful evacuations depend on clear communication ... and trust ... Education programmes.
questions.explanation: This covers trust and preparation, another response.

passages.topic: Evolution and animal behaviour — how wolves became dogs
passages.title: From Wolf to Dog

paragraphs.text: The dog was almost certainly the first animal to be domesticated, and the only one to be domesticated before the invention of farming. Genetic studies have shown beyond reasonable doubt that all dogs, from tiny terriers to enormous mastiffs, are descended from wolves – or, more precisely, from a population of wolves that is now extinct. Beyond this, however, almost every aspect of dog domestication remains the subject of debate.

One of the main questions is when it happened. The oldest widely accepted remains of domestic dogs, including a dog buried alongside two humans in Germany, date from around fifteen thousand years ago. Some researchers have identified older skulls, from Europe and Siberia, that they believe show dog-like features, suggesting that domestication began more than thirty thousand years ago. Others argue that these animals were simply unusual wolves. Genetic estimates of the time at which dogs and wolves separated have produced a similarly wide range of dates.

Where domestication took place is equally disputed. Different genetic studies have pointed to East Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. One proposal attempts to reconcile these findings by suggesting that dogs were domesticated twice, from separate wolf populations in the east and west of Eurasia, and that the two populations later mixed. This idea remains controversial, and some researchers believe that improved genetic evidence from ancient remains will eventually point to a single origin.

The traditional explanation of how domestication happened is that humans deliberately captured wolf pups and raised them, selecting the tamest animals to breed. Many researchers now consider this unlikely as a starting point. Adult wolves are dangerous, and raising wolves successfully requires considerable effort and experience; it is not obvious why hunter-gatherers would have attempted it.

An alternative view is that wolves largely domesticated themselves. According to this "self-domestication" hypothesis, some wolves began to scavenge around human camps, feeding on discarded bones and scraps. Wolves that were less fearful of humans, and less aggressive towards them, would have been able to exploit this food source more successfully. Over many generations, these wolves would have become increasingly tolerant of people, and people may gradually have begun to find them useful, for example as guards or hunting companions.

A famous experiment offers some support for this idea. Beginning in the 1950s, researchers in the Soviet Union bred silver foxes, selecting in each generation only those animals that were least fearful and aggressive towards humans. Within a few decades, the selected foxes had become remarkably friendly, seeking human attention, wagging their tails and whining. More surprisingly, they had also begun to show physical changes associated with domestic animals, such as floppy ears, curly tails and patches of white fur, even though they had been selected only for behaviour.

Whatever its origins, the relationship between dogs and humans has had profound effects on both. Dogs have been used for hunting, herding, guarding, pulling sledges and, more recently, guiding blind people and detecting drugs and diseases. Some research suggests that dogs have developed an unusual ability to interpret human gestures, such as pointing, which even chimpanzees find difficult. The long partnership has shaped the dog's mind as well as its body.

lesson.title: Headings that look alike
lesson.text: At Medium level, the list often contains pairs of headings on the same subject that differ in one key word: "disagreement about when" vs "disagreement about where", "a traditional explanation" vs "an alternative explanation". Underline the word that makes each heading different before reading. Then, for each paragraph, ask which of the pair fits its specific focus.

Write the correct number, i–x.

questions.evidence: One of the main questions is when it happened.
questions.explanation: Heading v is a detail trap: the German burial is only an example, and it is not claimed to be the oldest ever found.

questions.text: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Where domestication took place is equally disputed.
questions.explanation: The paired headings iv and i differ only in "timing" vs "location".

questions.text: Paragraph D

questions.explanation: "Traditional" = "long-established", and "consider this unlikely" = "doubts". Heading x is too narrow: danger is only one reason given.

questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

passages.topic: Environment and health — the problem of city noise
passages.title: The Unquiet City

paragraphs.text: Air pollution and water pollution are widely recognised as threats to health. Noise, by contrast, is often treated as a mere nuisance – annoying, perhaps, but not dangerous. A growing body of research suggests that this view is mistaken. The World Health Organization has identified environmental noise as one of the most significant environmental risks to health in Europe, second only to air pollution among the environmental factors it assessed.

The most obvious effect of noise is disturbed sleep. Even when people do not wake, noise during the night can cause brief changes in heart rate and blood pressure and shift the sleeper into lighter stages of sleep. Over years, chronic exposure to noise has been associated with an increased risk of high blood pressure and heart disease, probably because it keeps the body's stress response repeatedly activated. Studies of children living near busy airports have also found that aircraft noise can affect their reading and memory at school.

Road traffic is by far the largest source of noise in most cities, affecting many more people than aircraft or railways. The noise comes from two main sources: engines, which dominate at low speeds, and the contact between tyres and the road surface, which becomes the main source at speeds above about thirty to fifty kilometres per hour. This has an important implication. Electric vehicles, which are much quieter than petrol cars at low speeds, will reduce noise in slow-moving urban traffic but make little difference on faster roads.

A range of technical measures can reduce traffic noise. Special road surfaces, containing small spaces that absorb sound, can reduce tyre noise considerably, though they wear out faster than ordinary surfaces. Noise barriers along motorways and railways can protect nearby homes, and better insulated windows can reduce the noise that enters buildings. Lower speed limits can also help, both by reducing tyre noise and by encouraging smoother driving.

Planning decisions matter as much as engineering. Where new housing is built next to busy roads, bedrooms can be placed on the quiet side of the building, away from the traffic. Parks, courtyards and quiet streets provide relief from noise, and research suggests that access to a quiet space nearby can reduce the harmful effects of living in a noisy area. Some cities have produced detailed noise maps to identify the areas most affected and to guide their decisions.

Recently, some researchers and planners have argued that the goal should not simply be to reduce noise, but to improve "soundscapes" – the overall sound environment of a place. Not all sounds are unwelcome: many people enjoy the sounds of birdsong, flowing water or a lively market. Designing public spaces to include pleasant sounds, as well as to exclude unpleasant ones, may make cities more attractive places to live.

Despite the evidence, noise has received less attention from governments than other forms of pollution. It is invisible, leaves no trace once it has stopped, and its effects develop slowly over many years. Nevertheless, as more people live in cities, the problem is likely to grow, and many researchers argue that it deserves to be treated with the seriousness already given to cleaning the air.

lesson.title: Headings phrased as problems, causes and solutions
lesson.text: In problem-solution passages, headings are often abstract: "an underestimated threat", "the principal source", "technical remedies", "a change in approach". Decide which of these the paragraph mainly provides. A paragraph that mentions a cause briefly but spends most of its length on solutions is a solutions paragraph.

groups.title: Matching Headings
groups.instruction:
The reading passage has seven paragraphs, A–G.
Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below.
Write the correct number, i–x.

questions.text: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: often treated as a mere nuisance ... this view is mistaken.
questions.explanation: This is a problem paragraph that identifies an underestimated risk.

questions.text: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: disturbed sleep ... heart disease ... affect their reading and memory.
questions.explanation: The paragraph covers effects on both the body and the mind.

questions.text: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Road traffic is by far the largest source ... two main sources: engines ... and ... tyres.
questions.explanation: Heading ii contradicts the paragraph: electric cars will make "little difference on faster roads".

questions.text: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Special road surfaces ... though they wear out faster ... Noise barriers ... insulated windows.
questions.explanation: The paragraph presents solutions and one limitation. Heading x is a detail trap, because barriers are mentioned but their cost is not.

questions.text: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: Planning decisions matter ... bedrooms can be placed on the quiet side.
questions.explanation: This paragraph is about planning around people's needs.

questions.text: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: the goal should not simply be to reduce noise, but to improve 'soundscapes'.
questions.explanation: This describes a change in approach.

questions.text: Paragraph G
questions.evidence: noise has received less attention from governments ... It is invisible, leaves no trace.
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives the reasons for official neglect.

passages.topic: Geography and history — how maps have shaped our view of the world
passages.title: Drawing the World

paragraphs.text: Maps are among the oldest forms of human communication. Clay tablets from ancient Mesopotamia show plans of fields and towns, and a small tablet from the sixth century BC presents the known world as a flat disc surrounded by water, with Babylon near its centre. Such maps were not simply attempts to record geography accurately. They expressed ideas about the world and a society's place within it.

The scholars of ancient Greece took a more systematic approach. They argued that the Earth was a sphere, and one of them calculated its circumference with remarkable accuracy by comparing the angle of the sun's shadow at two places a known distance apart. In the second century AD, the geographer Ptolemy compiled a guide listing the positions of thousands of places using a grid of lines similar to modern latitude and longitude, and described methods for representing the curved Earth on a flat surface. His work was largely forgotten in Western Europe for centuries, but was preserved and developed by scholars in the Islamic world, and became highly influential when it was rediscovered in Europe in the fifteenth century.

Representing a sphere on a flat surface raises a problem that can never be fully solved: every flat map distorts something. The most famous example is the projection published in 1569 by the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator. His map was designed for sailors: a straight line drawn on it represented a route of constant compass direction, making navigation much simpler. But to achieve this, the map enlarges regions far from the equator. Greenland appears roughly the size of Africa, although Africa is in fact about fourteen times larger. Every map projection, in other words, involves choices about what to preserve and what to sacrifice.

For centuries, maps of large areas were compiled from travellers' reports and sailors' observations of varying reliability. Accurate mapping of whole countries became possible only with systematic surveys, which began in the eighteenth century. Surveyors measured a single baseline with great precision and then used a technique called triangulation, measuring the angles between distant points, to calculate positions across the country. National surveys took decades to complete but produced maps of unprecedented accuracy.

In the twentieth century, aerial photography and then satellite imagery transformed map-making. Areas that had never been surveyed on the ground could now be mapped from above, and changes such as the growth of cities or the retreat of forests could be observed over time. Satellite positioning systems, originally developed for military purposes, now allow anyone with a smartphone to know their location to within a few metres.

Yet maps are never simply neutral records of the world. Mapmakers decide what to include and what to leave out, which names to use and where to place boundaries. In the past, maps produced by colonial powers sometimes showed territories as empty that were in fact inhabited, or drew borders without regard for the people living there. Even today, the way disputed borders are drawn can differ depending on the country in which a map is published. Maps, then, reflect the interests and assumptions of those who make them as well as the land they depict.

Digital mapping has made maps more interactive and personal than ever before. Online maps can show traffic in real time, recommend routes and highlight businesses near the user. This convenience raises new questions, since the companies that produce such maps decide which places are shown prominently and which are not, and they may collect detailed information about users' movements. The long history of maps suggests that these questions of choice and influence are not new, even if the technology is.

lesson.title: The main idea may come last
lesson.text: In some paragraphs, the writer builds up examples and details and only states the main point in the final sentence, often introduced by thus, so, in other words, this shows that. If the first sentence seems too narrow to summarise the paragraph, read the last sentence carefully.

passages.topic: Business and environment — the cost of cheap clothes
passages.title: Fashion at Speed

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, clothing retailers typically introduced new collections a few times a year, following the seasons. From the 1990s onwards, a new business model changed this rhythm. Some retailers began to design, manufacture and deliver new styles to their shops in a matter of weeks, releasing small quantities of many designs and restocking those that sold well. Customers who visited a shop regularly would find new items each time. This approach, often called "fast fashion", allowed retailers to respond quickly to trends and encouraged shoppers to buy more often.

The model depends on low prices, which are made possible by large-scale production in countries where labour costs are low, efficient global supply chains and the use of inexpensive synthetic materials. As a result, the average price of clothing, relative to incomes, has fallen in many wealthy countries, and the number of garments bought per person has increased substantially. Some estimates suggest that the typical consumer now buys considerably more items of clothing each year than a generation ago, but keeps each item for a much shorter time.

The environmental costs begin long before the clothes reach the shops. Growing cotton requires large quantities of water and, in many regions, pesticides. Synthetic fibres such as polyester are made from oil, and their production consumes considerable energy. Dyeing and finishing fabrics can release chemicals into rivers where environmental regulation is weak. The textile industry as a whole is responsible for a significant share of global greenhouse gas emissions.

Further problems arise once clothes are discarded. Large quantities of used clothing end up in landfill or are burned. Much of the clothing donated to charity in wealthy countries cannot be sold locally and is exported to other countries, where a proportion is of such poor quality that it cannot be reused and ends up as waste. In addition, when synthetic garments are washed, they release tiny plastic fibres, some of which pass through water treatment plants into rivers and the sea.

Concerns have also been raised about working conditions. Many garment workers, most of them women, work long hours for low wages, and in some factories safety standards have been inadequate. A number of serious factory disasters have drawn international attention to these problems and led some brands to sign agreements committing them to improve safety inspections. Campaigners argue that progress has been uneven and that the pressure to produce quickly and cheaply makes lasting improvement difficult.

In response, alternative ways of buying and using clothes have become more popular. The market for second-hand clothing has grown rapidly, helped by websites and apps that make it easy to buy and sell used items. Some companies offer clothing rental, particularly for special occasions, and others offer repair services or take back old garments for recycling. However, recycling textiles into new fibres remains technically difficult, particularly for garments made from mixtures of materials.

Some governments are now considering or introducing regulations, such as requiring manufacturers to take responsibility for the collection and recycling of the clothes they sell, or restricting the destruction of unsold goods. Many analysts believe that such measures, combined with changes in consumer behaviour, will be necessary if the industry is to reduce its environmental impact significantly, since voluntary efforts by companies have so far had limited effect.

lesson.title: Two paragraphs on the same topic
lesson.text: Some passages have two neighbouring paragraphs that discuss the same subject from different angles, for example the environmental impact of production and the environmental impact of disposal. The headings will be similarly paired. Identify what distinguishes each paragraph's focus: stage, group affected, time period or type of response.

questions.explanation: This matches official action supplementing voluntary efforts.

passages.topic: Materials and technology — the story of glass
passages.title: A Transparent History

paragraphs.text: Glass occurs in nature. When lightning strikes sand, or when volcanic lava cools very quickly, the result can be a natural glass. One volcanic glass, obsidian, was prized by early humans because it could be chipped into blades sharper than any metal. Manufactured glass, however, appeared much later. The earliest known glass objects, small beads, were made in Mesopotamia more than four thousand years ago, and for many centuries glass remained a rare and valuable material, used mainly for jewellery and small decorative containers.

Early glass vessels were difficult to make. Craftsmen shaped molten glass around a core of clay and sand, then removed the core once the glass had cooled. The process was slow, and the resulting objects were small and usually opaque. The situation changed dramatically in the first century BC, probably in the eastern Mediterranean, with the discovery that molten glass could be inflated by blowing air into it through a hollow tube. Glassblowing allowed vessels of many shapes and sizes to be produced quickly and cheaply. Within a few decades, glass cups, bottles and jars had become common throughout the Roman Empire.

Making flat glass for windows was a greater challenge. For centuries, window glass was produced by blowing a large bubble and either spinning it into a disc or cutting it into a cylinder and flattening it. Both methods produced glass that was uneven, slightly distorted and limited in size. Large, perfectly flat sheets, such as those needed for mirrors or shop windows, required long and expensive grinding and polishing.

A solution emerged in the 1950s, when a British manufacturer developed the "float glass" process. Molten glass was poured onto the surface of a bath of molten tin. Because the glass floated on the perfectly flat surface of the metal, it formed a sheet of uniform thickness with smooth, flat surfaces on both sides, requiring no grinding or polishing. The process was cheaper and faster than earlier methods and is still used to make almost all of the world's flat glass. It made possible the vast glass facades of modern buildings.

Glass has also played a central role in science. Lenses made of glass allowed the development of spectacles, microscopes and telescopes, opening up the very small and the very distant to human observation. Glass laboratory equipment, which does not react with most chemicals and allows the contents to be seen, has been essential to chemistry. More recently, extremely pure glass has been drawn into fibres thinner than a human hair. Light sent through these optical fibres can carry vast quantities of information over long distances, and they now form the backbone of the internet.

Glass is, in principle, one of the most recyclable materials. It can be melted down and remade into new glass repeatedly without losing its quality, and using recycled glass reduces the energy needed in manufacturing. In practice, recycling rates vary widely between countries and between types of glass. Glass that has been mixed with other materials or treated with coatings is difficult to recycle, and in some places glass collected for recycling is contaminated or of mixed colours and ends up being used for lower-value purposes such as road construction.

lesson.title: Chronological passages with thematic headings
lesson.text: History passages move through time, but headings often describe the significance of each stage rather than its date: "a technique that made glass widely available", "a flat surface without grinding". Don't look for dates in the headings. Ask instead: "What changed at this stage, and why did it matter?"

passages.topic: Psychology — the secrets of memory champions
passages.title: The Palace of Memory

paragraphs.text: Every year, competitors at memory championships perform feats that seem almost impossible. Within a few minutes, some can memorise the order of a shuffled pack of playing cards, hundreds of random digits, or long lists of unrelated words. It is natural to assume that such people must be born with extraordinary brains. Research suggests, however, that the explanation lies mainly in technique.

Most memory champions rely on a method that has been known for more than two thousand years. According to a story told by Roman writers, a Greek poet named Simonides left a banquet hall shortly before its roof collapsed, killing everyone inside. He was able to identify the victims by recalling where each guest had been sitting. The experience, it was said, led him to realise that people remember places and images far more easily than abstract information. The technique he is said to have developed, known as the "method of loci" or "memory palace", involves imagining a familiar building or route and mentally placing vivid images representing the items to be remembered at particular locations along it. To recall the items, the person imagines walking through the building again.

The method was widely taught in the ancient world and in medieval and Renaissance Europe, when books were scarce and scholars and speakers needed to remember large amounts of material. With the spread of printing, and later of other ways of storing information, it gradually fell out of use in education, surviving mainly as a curiosity until its revival in modern memory competitions.

In a study published in 2003, researchers compared a group of leading memory competitors with people of similar age and education who had no special memory skills. Brain scans revealed no significant differences in the structure of the two groups' brains, and the competitors did not score higher on general tests of intelligence. What distinguished them was the way they used their brains while memorising: the champions showed greater activity in regions associated with spatial memory and navigation – exactly what would be expected if they were imagining themselves moving through familiar places.

If technique, rather than natural ability, is the key, then ordinary people should be able to improve dramatically with training. A later study tested this directly. Volunteers with no previous experience spent six weeks practising the method of loci for around half an hour a day. By the end of the training, many could remember more than twice as many words as before, and their improvement was still largely present when they were tested again several months later. Scans also showed that patterns of connections in their brains had become more similar to those of the champions.

The method has limits. It is extremely effective for memorising lists and sequences, but less useful for understanding complex ideas or developing skills. Memory competitors themselves often report that, in everyday life, they forget names, appointments and where they have left their keys, just like everyone else. The technique requires deliberate effort, and most people do not use it spontaneously.

Nevertheless, the success of memory athletes has encouraged some educators to consider whether the method might help students learn material that must be memorised, such as vocabulary or key facts. Such uses may be valuable in certain subjects, although most researchers emphasise that memorisation is only one part of learning, and that techniques for remembering information work best when combined with an understanding of what that information means.

lesson.title: Research paragraphs — question, method or conclusion?
lesson.text: In research-based passages, headings often describe the role of a paragraph within the investigation: "an ancient technique", "a comparison of brains", "training ordinary people", "limits of the method". Identify whether each paragraph introduces a question, describes a study, reports a result or evaluates it.

questions.explanation: This describes possible uses in schools, with caution.

passages.topic: World history — the Silk Roads
passages.title: Networks Across a Continent

paragraphs.text: The term "Silk Road" suggests a single highway along which caravans of camels carried silk from China to Rome. The reality was very different. The name was invented only in 1877, by a German geographer, and it describes not one road but a shifting network of overland and sea routes that connected East Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Europe over many centuries. Few merchants travelled the whole distance. Instead, goods passed from trader to trader, city to city, often changing hands many times before reaching their final destination.

Silk was certainly among the most valuable goods traded. Its production was a closely guarded secret in China for centuries, and it was highly prized in the Roman world, where some writers complained that fashionable citizens were spending enormous sums on it. But silk was only one of many commodities. Spices, precious stones, glassware, paper, porcelain, horses, textiles of many kinds, and metals all travelled along the routes, in both directions. For many periods, trade in horses from Central Asia to China was of greater importance to the Chinese state than the export of silk.

Ideas travelled as readily as goods. Buddhism spread from India into Central Asia and China largely along trade routes, carried by merchants and monks; cave temples with Buddhist paintings and sculptures still line parts of the routes today. Later, Islam spread along the same networks. Technologies moved as well: papermaking, for example, spread westwards from China into the Islamic world and eventually to Europe. Musical instruments, artistic styles, foods and farming techniques were also exchanged.

The routes carried dangers as well as benefits. Travellers faced deserts, mountain passes, extreme temperatures and bandits. Perhaps the most serious danger, however, was invisible. Diseases could travel with people and goods, and historians believe that the great plague known as the Black Death, which killed a large proportion of Europe's population in the fourteenth century, reached Europe partly by way of trade networks that linked it to Central Asia.

The prosperity of the routes depended heavily on political conditions. When large empires controlled long sections of the network and kept them relatively safe, trade flourished. The period in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries when much of Asia was ruled by the Mongols is often cited as an example: travellers could cross vast distances under a single authority. When empires collapsed or went to war, trade could be disrupted for decades, and caravan cities that depended on it declined.

From the fifteenth century onwards, the overland routes gradually lost importance. European sailors found sea routes around Africa to India and East Asia, and ships could carry far larger cargoes than camels, often at lower cost. The sea routes, which had existed for centuries alongside the overland ones, became dominant. Many once-great trading cities of Central Asia fell into decline.

In recent years, the idea of the Silk Road has been revived in a new form. Several governments have promoted large-scale investment in railways, ports, roads and pipelines to connect Asia with Europe and Africa, often explicitly referring to the historical routes. Historians have also used the concept to emphasise that exchange between civilisations was a normal feature of the past, rather than the exception – a reminder that the world was connected long before the modern age of globalisation.

lesson.title: Headings that are true of the passage but not of the paragraph
lesson.text: A tempting distractor may describe something that is true somewhere in the passage, but not in the paragraph you are working on. Before you choose a heading, check that the paragraph itself develops that idea. It is not enough for the passage as a whole to mention it.

passages.topic: Cultural history — how tea conquered the world
passages.title: A Leaf That Travelled

paragraphs.text: According to a Chinese legend, tea was discovered almost five thousand years ago when leaves from a wild tea plant blew into a pot of water being boiled for an emperor. Whatever the truth of the story, there is good evidence that tea was being drunk in China at least two thousand years ago, initially as a medicine and later as an everyday drink. By the time of the Tang dynasty, in the eighth century AD, tea drinking had spread throughout Chinese society, and a scholar named Lu Yu wrote a book describing in detail how tea should be grown, prepared and served.

From China, tea spread to neighbouring countries. Buddhist monks who had studied in China brought tea seeds to Japan, where tea became associated with meditation, since it helped monks remain alert. Over time, the preparation and serving of tea developed into a highly formal ceremony, in which every movement was carefully prescribed and which expressed values such as harmony, respect and tranquillity. The tea ceremony remains an important part of Japanese culture today.

Tea reached Europe in the early seventeenth century, carried by Dutch and Portuguese traders. At first it was an expensive novelty, sold in small quantities to the wealthy, sometimes as a medicine. In Britain, it became fashionable in the late seventeenth century among the upper classes, and over the following hundred years its price fell as imports increased. By the nineteenth century, tea had become the national drink, consumed by all social classes, and the custom of afternoon tea had become a social ritual.

Britain's growing demand for tea created a serious economic problem. China was for a long time the only major source of tea, and the Chinese authorities wanted payment largely in silver. As British purchases increased, large quantities of silver flowed out of the country. British traders sought goods that could be sold in China to balance this trade, with consequences that led to serious conflict between the two countries in the nineteenth century.

To reduce their dependence on China, the British began to grow tea in their colonies in South Asia. In the 1820s and 1830s, a variety of tea plant was found growing wild in Assam, in north-eastern India, and plantations were established there. Later, tea was planted in the hills of Darjeeling and on the island of Ceylon, now Sri Lanka. Within a few decades, these regions had become major producers, and the plantation system, which relied on large numbers of low-paid workers, transformed the landscape and economy of the areas concerned.

The way tea was sold also changed. In the early twentieth century, a New York merchant is said to have sent samples of tea to his customers in small silk bags, intending them to empty the tea into a pot. Some customers instead placed the bags directly into hot water. Whether or not this story is accurate, tea bags became increasingly popular during the twentieth century, particularly in Britain and North America, where they now account for the great majority of tea consumed.

Today, tea is the most widely consumed drink in the world after water. Its forms vary enormously: from the green teas of China and Japan to the sweet, spiced milk tea of India, the mint tea of North Africa and the iced tea popular in the United States. The history of tea shows how a single plant can become embedded in very different cultures, each of which has adapted it to its own tastes and traditions.

lesson.title: Separate "story" details from the main point
lesson.text: History passages often include anecdotes, legends or colourful stories. These are memorable, so headings often mention them as distractors. Ask whether the story is the paragraph's main idea, or only an illustration of a larger point, such as "tea becomes part of culture" or "production moves to new regions".

passages.topic: Psychology and philosophy — can evolution explain beauty?
passages.title: The Evolution of Taste

paragraphs.text: Why do human beings find certain things beautiful? Philosophers have debated the question for millennia, generally treating beauty as a matter of culture, reason or individual judgement. Over the past few decades, however, some researchers have proposed a different kind of answer. Human preferences, they suggest, may have been shaped by natural selection: we find certain things attractive because, in the environments in which our ancestors lived, being drawn to them helped people to survive and reproduce.

One frequently discussed example concerns landscapes. Studies in which people from many countries were shown photographs of different environments have found a widespread preference for scenes resembling open grassland with scattered trees, some water and distant views. Advocates of the evolutionary approach argue that this reflects the savanna environments of Africa in which early humans evolved – landscapes that offered food, water, shelter and the ability to see approaching danger. The popularity of parks designed in this style, they point out, is consistent with such an explanation.

A second line of research concerns human faces. Across many cultures, faces that are relatively symmetrical, and faces that are close to the average of a population, tend to be rated as more attractive. Some researchers have argued that symmetry and averageness may signal good health and genetic quality, since illness and developmental problems can produce asymmetries. On this account, preferring such faces would have helped our ancestors choose healthy partners.

These claims have attracted considerable criticism. The landscape studies, critics note, have often relied on participants who were already familiar with parks and pictures of such landscapes, and preferences in some populations differ from the predicted pattern; people who have grown up in forests or mountains sometimes prefer their own familiar surroundings. Moreover, the connection between facial symmetry and actual health has proved weaker in later research than early studies suggested. It is also difficult to test evolutionary explanations directly, since we cannot observe the environments and choices of our distant ancestors.

A further difficulty is the enormous variety of human aesthetic preferences. Standards of physical attractiveness have varied considerably between cultures and historical periods, and tastes in art, music and architecture differ even more. An evolutionary explanation that predicts universal preferences seems poorly suited to account for such diversity. Critics suggest that learning, fashion and social status often play a larger role than any biological predisposition.

Some researchers have sought a middle position. Evolution, they argue, may have provided human beings with general tendencies – an attraction to patterns, an interest in novelty, a sensitivity to signs of health – which culture then shapes in countless different ways. On this view, it is not surprising that some broad preferences appear widely while their specific forms vary. The question is not whether biology or culture explains beauty, but how the two interact.

Even this more modest position leaves much unexplained. Why should people value works of art that are deliberately difficult, unsettling or even ugly? Why do tastes change so quickly, sometimes within a single generation? Evolutionary approaches may illuminate some aspects of aesthetic experience, but it seems unlikely that they will ever provide a complete account of why human beings create and admire beautiful things.

lesson.title: Hard Matching Headings — implicit main ideas and argumentative structure
lesson.text:
In Hard passages:

the main idea is often implicit, spread across the paragraph rather than stated in one sentence;

headings are abstract and describe the paragraph's role in the argument, for example "a proposed explanation", "evidence that complicates it", "an objection", "a middle position"; distractors include headings that are true but too narrow, or that describe a different stage of the argument.

Strategy: for each paragraph, write two notes: its topic ("face symmetry") and its function ("evidence for the theory"). Choose the heading that fits both.

groups.instruction:

questions.explanation: This covers both the topic (landscape preference) and the function (a possible origin). Heading viii is a detail trap.

questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.explanation: These are problems of both method and evidence. Heading x contradicts the paragraph's function, which is criticism, not proof.

questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.explanation: Heading ix is too narrow, since fashion change is only one of the unanswered questions.

passages.topic: Psychology and education — measuring intelligence
passages.title: The Measure of a Mind

paragraphs.text: In 1904, the French government asked the psychologist Alfred Binet to find a way of identifying children who were struggling at school and might need extra help. Binet and his colleague Théodore Simon developed a series of tasks of increasing difficulty – naming objects, remembering sequences, solving simple problems – and compared each child's performance with that of typical children of different ages. Binet was careful to emphasise that the test was a practical tool for identifying children who needed support. He warned against treating its results as a measure of a fixed, inborn quantity.

His warnings were widely ignored. When intelligence tests were adapted and popularised in the United States in the following decades, they were often presented as measuring an innate ability that changed little over a lifetime. The "intelligence quotient", or IQ, was used to sort schoolchildren into different educational tracks, to select army recruits during the First World War, and, in some notorious cases, to support discriminatory policies. Critics have argued that the tests were used to lend a scientific appearance to existing prejudices.

Despite this troubling history, intelligence tests have proved to be among the most reliable measures in psychology. A person's score tends to be similar when the test is repeated, and scores on quite different kinds of mental tasks – vocabulary, arithmetic, spatial reasoning – tend to be correlated with one another. People who perform well on one kind of task tend, on average, to perform well on others. Test scores also predict, to a moderate degree, outcomes such as success at school and performance in many jobs.

One of the most puzzling findings concerns changes over time. In the 1980s, the researcher James Flynn showed that average scores on intelligence tests had been rising steadily in many countries throughout the twentieth century – by around three points per decade. Because tests are regularly adjusted so that the average score remains 100, the rise had gone largely unnoticed. A person with an average score in the 1930s would score well below average if tested against a modern population. Such rapid change cannot be explained by genetics, and has been attributed to factors including better nutrition, more years of schooling, smaller families and an environment that increasingly demands abstract thinking.

The size of the rise poses a difficult question. If average intelligence had really increased so much, our grandparents would, by modern standards, have been of well below average intelligence – which seems implausible. Flynn himself concluded that the tests measure not a single fixed ability but a set of skills, particularly skills in abstract classification and reasoning, that modern societies encourage and reward. Earlier generations were not less intelligent; their intelligence was directed towards different, more concrete tasks.

Some psychologists have argued that the traditional concept of intelligence is too narrow. The best-known alternative, proposed in the 1980s, suggested that human beings possess several relatively independent "intelligences" – including linguistic, mathematical, musical, spatial, physical, social and personal abilities. The idea proved very popular among teachers, who welcomed its recognition of children's diverse talents. Many researchers, however, have criticised it for lacking supporting evidence, and point out that most of these abilities are, in fact, correlated with one another.

The debate about intelligence testing is thus not simply about whether tests "work". They measure something real and useful, and they predict certain outcomes. But what they measure is shaped by culture and education, varies over time, and captures only part of the range of human abilities. Binet's original caution – that test results describe current performance rather than fixed destiny – appears, more than a century later, to have been well founded.

lesson.title: Paragraphs that contain a turn
lesson.text: A Hard paragraph may begin with one position and then qualify or overturn it. The heading must capture the whole movement of the paragraph, not just its first half. Look for headings that combine two ideas ("success, with limitations", "a finding and its puzzling implication"), and test whether both halves appear in the paragraph.

questions.explanation: The paragraph turns on "despite", which the heading reflects in "despite an uncomfortable past".

questions.explanation: Heading xi is too narrow, since teachers' views are only part of the paragraph.

questions.explanation: "Well founded" = "vindicated".

passages.topic: Economics and sociology — the value of trust
passages.title: The Invisible Asset

paragraphs.text: Economists have traditionally focused on tangible resources – land, machinery, money and the skills of workers – to explain why some countries and regions are wealthier than others. Increasingly, however, researchers have drawn attention to a less visible factor: trust. In societies where people generally trust one another, transactions are easier. Contracts can be simpler, fewer resources need to be spent on protection against dishonesty, and people are more willing to cooperate with strangers. Where trust is low, many exchanges that would benefit both sides never take place.

One influential study compared regions of Italy that had been given similar new powers of local government in the 1970s. Over the following decades, some regional governments proved far more effective than others. The researchers found that the more successful regions tended to have long traditions of civic participation – membership of clubs, choirs, sports associations and other voluntary organisations – which, they argued, had built networks of trust and cooperation over centuries. They called this resource "social capital".

Measuring trust is not straightforward. The most common method is to ask people in surveys whether they think that "most people can be trusted". Levels of agreement vary enormously between countries, from a large majority in some Nordic countries to only a small minority in others. Such surveys, however, measure what people say, not necessarily how they behave. Researchers have therefore also designed experiments that observe trust and honesty in action.

In one large experiment, researchers "lost" thousands of wallets in public buildings in dozens of countries, handing them in at the reception desks of banks, hotels, museums and offices, and recorded how many were returned to the owners, whose email addresses were written on a card inside. Some wallets contained no money; others contained a small or larger sum. Most people, including the researchers themselves, and a sample of economists who were asked to predict the results, expected that wallets with more money would be returned less often, since the temptation to keep them would be greater.

The results showed the opposite. In almost every country, wallets containing money were returned more often than wallets containing none, and wallets containing a larger sum were returned more often still. The researchers suggested that people's wish to see themselves as honest, and their concern for the owner's loss, outweighed the financial temptation: keeping a wallet full of money felt more like stealing than keeping an empty one. Return rates did vary considerably between countries, but the pattern held almost everywhere.

How is trust built or lost? Research suggests that it is influenced by the quality of institutions: people are more likely to trust one another when laws are enforced fairly, officials are honest and courts are reliable. Inequality also appears to matter, with more unequal societies tending to report lower levels of trust. Trust is easier to destroy than to create: a single scandal involving public officials can reduce it quickly, while rebuilding it may take many years of consistent behaviour.

None of this means that more trust is always better. Excessive trust can make people vulnerable to fraud, and healthy societies need institutions that check and verify, not only individuals who are willing to trust. The aim is not blind faith but well-founded confidence – trust that is justified by the trustworthiness of others. Nevertheless, the evidence suggests that this invisible asset may be as important for prosperity as many of the visible ones economists have traditionally measured.

lesson.title: Experiments with surprising results
lesson.text: Hard passages may describe an experiment whose results contradict expectations. The paragraph's main idea is then the surprise, not the method. Headings may express this as "a counter-intuitive finding" or "an outcome contrary to prediction". Separate paragraphs describing the method, the result and the interpretation carefully, because headings will target each.

questions.explanation: "Less visible" = "often overlooked".

questions.text: Paragraph B

questions.text: Paragraph C

questions.explanation: The main idea follows "however". Heading viii is not supported: the Nordic countries report high trust, but the paragraph says nothing about their honesty.

questions.text: Paragraph D

questions.explanation: This paragraph describes the method and predictions. Heading ix is a detail trap.

questions.text: Paragraph E

questions.explanation: This is the surprising result. Heading x misreads the paragraph, which is about the finding, not about economists.

questions.text: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: influenced by the quality of institutions ... Inequality also appears to matter ... easier to destroy than to create.
questions.explanation: This describes the conditions that strengthen or weaken trust.

questions.text: Paragraph G
questions.evidence: None of this means that more trust is always better. Excessive trust can make people vulnerable.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

passages.topic: Environment and resources — mining the deep sea
passages.title: Treasure on the Ocean Floor

paragraphs.text: Scattered across vast areas of the deep ocean floor, several kilometres below the surface, lie billions of potato-sized lumps of rock known as polymetallic nodules. They form extremely slowly – growing by a few millimetres over a million years – around a small fragment such as a shark's tooth or a piece of shell, as metals dissolved in seawater gradually accumulate. The nodules contain valuable metals, including nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese. Other deep-sea deposits, found around underwater volcanic vents and seamounts, contain further metals.

Interest in these resources has grown rapidly because of the transition to low-carbon energy. Electric vehicles, wind turbines and batteries for storing renewable energy require large quantities of metals such as nickel and cobalt. Supporters of deep-sea mining argue that the ocean floor could supply these metals without some of the problems associated with mining on land, such as the destruction of rainforests, the displacement of communities and, in some places, poor working conditions. The nodules lie loose on the sea floor, they point out, and could in principle be collected without digging deep mines.

Scientists have raised serious concerns. The deep sea is among the least explored environments on Earth, and each expedition to the areas where mining is proposed has discovered many species previously unknown to science. Many of these animals live attached to the nodules themselves, which provide one of the few hard surfaces on the soft ocean floor. Removing the nodules would remove their habitat, and because the nodules take millions of years to form, the habitat could not recover on any human timescale.

Beyond the areas directly mined, collecting machines would stir up clouds of sediment that could spread over large distances and settle on surrounding sea-floor communities, many of which feed by filtering particles from the water. Noise and light from mining operations could also disturb animals adapted to darkness and silence. Experimental disturbances of small areas of the sea floor carried out decades ago still show visible tracks and reduced numbers of animals today, suggesting that recovery, if it occurs at all, is extremely slow.

The underlying difficulty is the lack of knowledge. Scientists do not yet know how many species live in these environments, how they are distributed, or what role they play in wider ocean processes, such as the storage of carbon. Without this information, it is difficult to predict the consequences of mining or to judge which areas should be protected. Some researchers argue that decisions made now could cause irreversible damage before its extent is even understood.

Mining in international waters, beyond the control of individual countries, is overseen by an international body established under a United Nations agreement. It has granted exploration licences to a number of countries and companies but, at the time of writing, has not agreed on final rules for commercial extraction. Negotiations have proved difficult, with some countries pressing for mining to begin soon and others, together with a number of large companies, calling for a pause until the environmental effects are better understood.

Critics of deep-sea mining also question whether it is necessary. Improvements in battery technology may reduce the need for particular metals, and greater recycling of metals from used batteries and electronic devices could supply a significant proportion of future demand. Supporters respond that recycling alone cannot meet the rapid growth in demand expected over the coming decades. How this debate is resolved will determine whether one of the planet's last largely untouched environments remains so.

lesson.title: Debate passages — distinguishing sides and stages
lesson.text: Passages about controversial issues move between the case for, the case against, uncertainty and governance. Headings often use evaluative words ("the economic argument", "ecological unknowns", "a regulatory gap"). Several paragraphs may mention environmental issues; decide whether each is presenting a risk, a lack of knowledge, a counter-argument or a proposal.

questions.explanation: This is the case for deep-sea mining.

questions.explanation: This describes a risk to the immediate living surface. Heading ix is too narrow, and "fish" is inaccurate.

questions.explanation: This describes a risk beyond the site, the pair to heading ii.

questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.explanation: Heading xi is not supported, because the companies call for a pause but are not said to have left the sector.

questions.explanation: This questions the demand for new supplies.

passages.topic: Planetary science — where did the Moon come from?
passages.title: Origins of the Moon

paragraphs.text: For most of human history, the Moon's origin was a matter for myth. Scientific theories began to appear in the nineteenth century, and by the mid-twentieth century three main ideas were in circulation. According to the first, the young Earth had spun so rapidly that a portion of it broke away to form the Moon. According to the second, the Moon had formed elsewhere in the solar system and had later been captured by the Earth's gravity. The third held that the Earth and Moon had formed side by side from the same cloud of material. Each theory had supporters, but none could be decisively tested with the evidence then available.

The Apollo missions of 1969 to 1972 changed this situation. Astronauts brought back nearly four hundred kilograms of lunar rock and soil, allowing scientists to study the Moon's composition directly for the first time. The samples revealed that the Moon was depleted in iron and in substances that evaporate easily compared with the Earth, and that its surface had once been covered by an ocean of molten rock. These findings posed serious difficulties for all three existing theories. The first required the Earth to spin faster than seemed physically possible; the second could not explain why the Moon's composition was so similar to that of the Earth's outer layers; the third could not explain why the Moon had so little iron.

In the mid-1970s, a new explanation was proposed. Early in the history of the solar system, it suggested, a body roughly the size of Mars had collided with the young Earth at an angle. The impact would have melted and vaporised large parts of both bodies, throwing an enormous quantity of material into orbit around the Earth. From this debris, the Moon would have formed. The "giant impact" hypothesis could explain why the Moon has relatively little iron – since much of the impacting body's iron would have sunk into the Earth – and why it was once molten. Computer simulations in the following decades showed that such an impact was physically plausible, and by the late twentieth century it had become the leading theory.

The giant impact theory, however, soon faced a problem of its own. Simulations suggested that most of the material forming the Moon should have come from the impacting body rather than from the Earth. Since bodies formed in different parts of the solar system tend to have distinctive chemical "fingerprints" – particularly in the ratios of different forms, or isotopes, of elements such as oxygen – the Moon should differ noticeably from the Earth. Increasingly precise measurements, however, showed that the isotopic compositions of the Earth and Moon are almost identical.

Researchers have proposed several ways of resolving this puzzle. Perhaps the impacting body was itself chemically similar to the Earth, having formed in a nearby region of the solar system. Perhaps the collision was far more violent than originally assumed, thoroughly mixing material from both bodies. One recent proposal suggests that the impact produced a vast, rapidly spinning cloud of vaporised rock – larger than the Earth itself – from which both the Earth and the Moon condensed, sharing a common composition. Each of these ideas can explain the similarity, but each requires particular conditions whose likelihood is debated.

Some scientists have gone further, suggesting that the Moon may have formed not from one great impact but from a series of smaller ones, each producing a small moon that eventually merged with others. This idea, too, can account for the similarity in composition, since each impact would have taken most of its material from the Earth. It remains less widely accepted than versions of the giant impact theory, but it illustrates how open the question remains.

New evidence may help to decide between these possibilities. Samples from parts of the Moon not visited by the Apollo astronauts, including regions far from the landing sites, could reveal variations in composition that existing samples do not. Improved computer models and measurements of other elements may also narrow the range of possible scenarios. What seems clear is that the Moon was born in violence – but precisely how remains one of the most intriguing puzzles in planetary science.

lesson.title: Theories, tests and puzzles
lesson.text: Scientific-debate passages usually follow a pattern: early theories → a decisive source of evidence → a leading theory → a problem with it → proposed solutions → what remains unknown. Headings mirror these stages using abstract nouns ("a new source of data", "an unexpected similarity", "attempts at reconciliation"). Label each paragraph's stage before looking at the headings, then match.

questions.explanation: This describes what remains to be learned.

passages.topic: Archaeology and environmental history — Rapa Nui reconsidered
passages.title: Rethinking an Island's Story

paragraphs.text: Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island, is one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth, lying more than two thousand kilometres from the nearest populated land. It is famous for its nearly one thousand giant stone statues, known as moai, carved from volcanic rock by the island's Polynesian settlers and transported across the island to platforms along the coast. How a small population on an isolated island managed to carve and move such enormous figures has fascinated visitors since Europeans first arrived in 1722.

For several decades, the island's history was widely presented as a cautionary tale. According to this account, the islanders cleared their forests, partly to obtain logs for moving the statues. As the trees disappeared, the soil eroded, crops failed, and the islanders could no longer build canoes for fishing. Competition for scarce resources led to warfare and a collapse of population and society before Europeans arrived. The story was often cited as a warning of what might happen to the whole planet if humanity exhausted its resources.

More recent research has challenged much of this narrative. Few scholars dispute that the island's forests disappeared. But studies of seeds and pollen have suggested that rats, which arrived with the first Polynesian settlers, may have played a major role by eating the seeds of the island's palm trees and preventing new trees from growing. On this view, deforestation resulted from a combination of human activity and an introduced species, not simply from reckless cutting.

Evidence about the islanders' way of life has also been reinterpreted. Archaeologists have found that the islanders developed ingenious farming techniques suited to their windy, dry environment, such as covering fields with stones that protected crops from wind, retained moisture and released nutrients as they weathered. Studies of human remains have found relatively few injuries consistent with widespread warfare. Estimates of the population, meanwhile, suggest that it remained relatively stable until the arrival of Europeans, rather than collapsing beforehand.

According to many researchers, the most catastrophic changes came after European contact. Visiting ships introduced diseases to which the islanders had no immunity. In the 1860s, raiders seized a large proportion of the population and took them to work in Peru, where most died; a few survivors who were returned brought further disease. By the 1870s, only around a hundred islanders remained. The collapse of Rapa Nui society, in this interpretation, was caused less by its own environmental mistakes than by violence and disease brought from outside.

Even the question of how the statues were moved has been reconsidered. The older account assumed that large quantities of timber were needed to drag the statues on wooden sledges. Experiments by archaeologists have shown that replicas of the statues can be "walked" upright by small teams of people using ropes to rock them from side to side – a method consistent with local oral traditions describing the statues as walking to their platforms. If this was how they were moved, far less timber would have been required than was once supposed.

Not all researchers accept the revised account in full, and debate continues about the extent of environmental damage and conflict before European contact. Nevertheless, the island's story now appears considerably more complicated than the simple tale of self-destruction long told about it. Some scholars suggest that it offers a different lesson altogether: not of a society that destroyed itself, but of one that adapted resourcefully to a difficult environment, only to be devastated by forces beyond its control.
