passages.topic: Exploration history — the race to the ends of the Earth in Antarctica
passages.title: The Frozen Continent

paragraphs.text: Antarctica was the last continent to be discovered. For centuries, geographers had speculated that a great southern land must exist to balance the landmasses of the northern hemisphere, but no one had seen it. In 1820, an expedition led by the Russian naval officer Fabian von Bellingshausen became one of the first to sight the Antarctic ice shelf, although he himself did not describe it as a continent. Several other voyages in the same period reported land in the far south, and historians still debate who deserves credit for the first sighting.

The early twentieth century saw a series of attempts to reach the South Pole. The Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen had originally planned to travel to the North Pole but changed his plans secretly after learning that others had claimed to reach it. Drawing on experience gained from Arctic peoples, he relied on sledges pulled by dogs and on clothing made from animal furs. His team reached the South Pole in December 1911 and returned safely.

The British naval officer Robert Falcon Scott led a rival expedition. Scott used a combination of motor sledges, ponies and dogs, but the motor sledges broke down and the ponies suffered badly in the cold, so that for much of the journey his men pulled their own sledges. Scott's team of five reached the Pole in January 1912, about five weeks after Amundsen, only to find the Norwegian flag already there. All five died on the return journey, overcome by cold, hunger and exhaustion. Scott's diaries, found with the bodies months later, made him a national hero in Britain.

The Irish-born explorer Ernest Shackleton had earlier come within about 180 kilometres of the Pole, turning back to save his men's lives. In 1914, he set out to cross the entire continent. His ship, the Endurance, became trapped in sea ice and was eventually crushed. For many months the crew lived on the ice, then sailed in small boats to a remote island. Shackleton and a few companions then made an extraordinary voyage of more than 1,000 kilometres across stormy seas in an open boat to seek help. Remarkably, every member of the expedition survived.

The Australian geologist Douglas Mawson led an expedition that focused on scientific research rather than on reaching the Pole. His team mapped long stretches of coastline and collected valuable scientific data. During a journey across the ice in 1912, both of Mawson's companions died – one fell into a deep crack in the ice together with most of the food – and Mawson struggled back alone for weeks, arriving at his base just after the relief ship had departed. He was forced to spend another winter in Antarctica.

passages.topic: Energy — five renewable sources compared
passages.title: Power Without Fuel

paragraphs.text: Renewable energy sources are those that are naturally replenished and will not run out on any human timescale. Five sources currently make the largest contributions or show the greatest promise: solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal and tidal power. Each has distinctive strengths and weaknesses.

Solar power converts sunlight directly into electricity using photovoltaic panels. Its greatest advantage is flexibility: panels can be installed on the roofs of individual houses as well as in large fields, and they have no moving parts, so they require little maintenance. The cost of solar panels has fallen dramatically in recent years. Their obvious limitation is that they produce electricity only during daylight, and much less in cloudy weather.

Wind turbines use the movement of air to turn large blades connected to generators. Wind power is now one of the cheapest sources of new electricity in many countries. Turbines can be placed on land or at sea, where winds are stronger and more consistent. However, output varies with the wind, and some people object to turbines on land because of their visual impact on the landscape.

Hydroelectric power, generated by water flowing through turbines in dams, is the oldest and currently the largest source of renewable electricity worldwide. Unlike solar and wind power, its output can be controlled: operators can release more water when demand is high. Large dams, however, flood valleys, which may force communities to move and disrupt the movement of fish along rivers.

Geothermal power uses heat from within the Earth, usually by pumping hot water or steam from deep underground to drive turbines. It provides a constant supply of energy regardless of weather or time of day. Its use is limited mainly to regions with volcanic activity or hot rocks near the surface, such as Iceland, New Zealand and parts of the western United States, although new drilling techniques may extend it to other areas.

Tidal power harnesses the rise and fall of the tides. Its great advantage is predictability: the timing and strength of tides can be calculated years in advance. However, it can be generated economically only at a small number of coastal sites with a large difference between high and low tide, and the equipment must survive the harsh conditions of the sea. As a result, it currently supplies only a very small share of the world's electricity.

lesson.text: Features need not be people. Here they are types of energy. The statements describe characteristics such as advantages, disadvantages and requirements. Several energy types share some features (for example, several depend on the weather). Look for the detail that makes each statement fit only one source.

passages.topic: History of aviation — pioneers of flight
passages.title: The Road to the Sky

paragraphs.text: The dream of human flight is ancient, but practical progress began only in the late eighteenth century. In France in 1783, the brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier, who ran a paper-making business, launched a large balloon filled with hot air. Later that year, one of their balloons carried two men across Paris – the first recorded flight by human beings. The balloon, however, could not be steered; it simply drifted with the wind.

The English engineer George Cayley took a more scientific approach. In the early nineteenth century, he identified the separate forces that act on a flying machine – weight, lift, drag and thrust – and argued that an aircraft should have fixed wings rather than flapping ones. In 1853, when he was nearly eighty, one of his gliders carried a person, reportedly his coachman, across a small valley. Cayley's ideas laid the foundations of aircraft design.

In Germany, Otto Lilienthal made more than two thousand flights in gliders of his own design in the 1890s. He carefully recorded the results of his experiments and published them, and photographs of his flights were widely circulated, inspiring others around the world. In 1896, he crashed after his glider lost lift, and died the following day.

The American brothers Wilbur and Orville Wright, who ran a bicycle business, studied the work of earlier pioneers, including Lilienthal. They realised that the key problem was not lift or power but control, and developed a system for steering an aircraft by twisting its wings. On 17 December 1903, near Kitty Hawk in North Carolina, they achieved the first sustained, controlled flight in a powered aircraft. The first flight lasted only twelve seconds. Because few people witnessed their early flights, their achievement was not widely accepted for several years.

In Europe, the Brazilian aviator Alberto Santos-Dumont made a powered flight in Paris in 1906, before a large crowd and official observers. For a time, many Europeans regarded him, rather than the Wright brothers, as the true pioneer of powered flight. Santos-Dumont later designed a small, light aircraft and deliberately did not patent it, making the plans freely available so that others could build it.

Several pioneers may have "firsts", but each first is different (first balloon flight vs first powered flight). Match the exact achievement, not just the idea of being first.

passages.topic: Urban transport — four cities try new approaches
passages.title: Four Cities, Four Experiments
passages.passageNote: (The cities described below are fictional examples based on common transport policies.)

paragraphs.text: Cities around the world are experimenting with new ways to reduce traffic congestion and pollution. The experiences of four medium-sized cities – Ardmore, Belvale, Castleton and Dunmore – illustrate the variety of approaches being taken and the different results they have produced.

Ardmore chose to focus on buses. The city created a network of dedicated bus lanes on its main roads, so that buses were no longer delayed by other traffic, and introduced a simple flat fare for all journeys. Within three years, bus journeys had become significantly faster and more reliable, and passenger numbers had risen by about a third. Some shopkeepers initially complained that the loss of parking spaces on main roads would harm their businesses, but surveys later suggested that most had not lost trade.

Belvale took a different path, investing heavily in cycling. It built a network of cycle lanes physically separated from motor traffic, together with secure bicycle parking at stations and in the city centre. The number of people cycling to work more than doubled over five years. The city also introduced a public bicycle-sharing scheme, which proved particularly popular with students and tourists.

Castleton introduced a charge for driving into the city centre during working hours. The charge reduced traffic in the centre by around a fifth, and the revenue was used to improve public transport. The scheme was controversial at first, and a local newspaper campaigned against it, but public opinion became more favourable once residents experienced the reduction in traffic.

Dunmore concentrated on making its city centre more attractive for pedestrians. It closed several central streets to cars, widened pavements, planted trees and added seating. The pedestrian areas became popular places to meet and shop. However, because the city did not improve public transport at the same time, many people continued to drive to the edge of the centre, and traffic on the surrounding roads increased.

Comparing the four cities, analysts noted that the most successful schemes combined restrictions on cars with better alternatives. Castleton's charge worked partly because the money was invested in public transport, while Dunmore's experience showed that restricting traffic in one area without providing alternatives can simply move congestion elsewhere. Of the four cities, only Belvale recorded a significant improvement in the physical fitness of its residents, according to health surveys.

lesson.text: When a passage compares several places or organisations, each paragraph usually describes one. But the final paragraph often compares them directly ("only Lindholm...", "unlike the others..."). Include these comparison sentences in your search, because they can contain answers.

passages.topic: History of writing — five early scripts
passages.title: Marks That Speak

paragraphs.text: Writing was invented independently in several parts of the world, and it developed from very different beginnings. Five early writing systems show the variety of ways in which people found to record language.

The earliest known writing emerged in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, over five thousand years ago. It began as a system for recording goods and payments – quantities of grain, numbers of animals – using simple pictures pressed into clay tablets. Over time, the pictures became more abstract and were made with a reed stylus that produced wedge-shaped marks, giving the script its modern name, cuneiform, from the Latin word for "wedge". Because clay tablets survive well when baked, hundreds of thousands have been found.

In Egypt, a system of writing using pictorial signs, known as hieroglyphs, appeared at around the same time. Hieroglyphs were used for inscriptions on monuments and tombs and could represent both sounds and ideas. For everyday purposes, scribes used a faster, simplified form written with ink on papyrus. After the ancient Egyptian religion declined, knowledge of how to read hieroglyphs was lost for well over a thousand years. It was recovered in the 1820s by the French scholar Jean-François Champollion, who used a stone inscribed with the same text in three scripts, including Greek, as a key.

The oldest surviving examples of Chinese writing are inscriptions on animal bones and turtle shells dating from more than three thousand years ago. They record questions put to ancestors or spirits, for example about harvests, weather or military campaigns. Although the characters have changed in form over the centuries, the Chinese writing system is directly descended from this early script. It is therefore the oldest writing system in continuous use today.

In Central America, the Maya developed a sophisticated script that combined signs representing whole words with signs representing syllables. It was carved on stone monuments and painted in books made of bark. Most Maya books were destroyed by Spanish authorities in the sixteenth century, and for a long time the script could not be read. Major progress in understanding it was made only in the second half of the twentieth century, and scholars can now read most surviving inscriptions.

Around three thousand years ago, traders from the Phoenician cities along the eastern Mediterranean coast used a script of about twenty-two signs, each representing a single consonant sound. Vowels were not written. This simple system was far easier to learn than scripts with hundreds of signs. When the Greeks adopted it, they added signs for vowels, creating one of the first alphabets to represent both consonants and vowels – the ancestor of most European alphabets.

Look for that distinguishing detail: still in use today, only consonants, written on clay, deciphered recently.

passages.topic: Wildlife — surviving the winter
passages.title: Winter Survival

paragraphs.text: For animals living in cold climates, winter brings two serious problems: low temperatures and a shortage of food. Different species have evolved very different solutions. Five examples show the range of strategies found in nature.

The Arctic tern avoids winter altogether. Each year, it flies from its breeding grounds in the Arctic to the Antarctic and back, experiencing summer in both hemispheres. This journey, the longest migration of any animal, requires enormous energy, but it allows the tern to live in almost continuous daylight and to feed in rich waters for most of the year.

Black bears in North America spend the winter in dens, entering a deep, sleep-like state in which their heart rate and breathing slow dramatically. Unlike some smaller hibernating animals, their body temperature drops only a few degrees, which allows them to wake relatively quickly if disturbed. During this period, which can last several months, they do not eat, drink or pass waste, surviving instead on fat stored during the autumn. Remarkably, females give birth to cubs during the winter while still in the den.

The wood frog, found in North America as far north as the Arctic Circle, has an even more extreme strategy: it allows itself to freeze. During winter, up to two-thirds of the water in its body may turn to ice. Its heart stops beating and it stops breathing. High concentrations of sugar in its cells prevent them from being damaged by ice. When the weather warms in spring, the frog thaws and its heart starts beating again.

Many squirrels remain active throughout the winter. In autumn, they collect nuts and seeds and bury them in hundreds or thousands of separate locations. During winter, they find many of these stores again, using memory and smell. Not all the buried seeds are recovered, and those that are forgotten may grow into new trees, so that squirrels play an important role in spreading forests.

The snowshoe hare, which lives in the forests of northern North America, changes colour with the seasons. In summer, its fur is brown, but in autumn it grows a new white coat that makes it difficult for predators to see against the snow. Its large hind feet act like snowshoes, spreading its weight so that it can move across deep snow without sinking. Scientists have noticed, however, that as winters become shorter, some hares turn white before snow has fallen, making them more visible to predators.

lesson.text: When the features are animals or species, statements describe strategies, behaviours or physical characteristics. Several animals may share a general strategy (avoiding the cold), but each uses a specific method. Match the method, not the general goal.

passages.topic: Psychology — why do we dream?
passages.title: The Meaning of Dreams

paragraphs.text: Every night, most people spend around two hours dreaming, yet the purpose of dreams remains one of the great unsolved questions of psychology. Over the past century, researchers have proposed a number of very different theories, each emphasising a different aspect of dreaming.

The most famous early theory was developed by the Austrian physician Sigmund Freud at the beginning of the twentieth century. Freud argued that dreams express hidden wishes, often ones that the dreamer would find unacceptable if they were stated openly. To protect sleep, the mind disguises these wishes in symbolic form, so that a dream's surface content conceals a deeper meaning, which could be revealed through interpretation. Freud's ideas were enormously influential in the arts and in popular culture. However, later researchers criticised them for being impossible to test scientifically, since almost any dream could be interpreted as fulfilling some hidden wish.

In 1977, two American psychiatrists, J. Allan Hobson and Robert McCarley, proposed a radically different explanation, known as the activation-synthesis hypothesis. Based on studies of brain activity during sleep, they suggested that dreams begin with random signals from the brainstem during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. The higher parts of the brain then try to make sense of these signals, weaving them into a story. On this view, dreams have no hidden meaning; their strange and illogical features reflect the brain's attempts to interpret essentially meaningless activity. Critics argued that the theory could not explain why dreams so often contain coherent stories and themes connected to the dreamer's life.

The Finnish psychologist Antti Revonsuo proposed in 2000 that dreams evolved as a way of rehearsing responses to threats. According to this "threat simulation" theory, dreams allowed our ancestors to practise escaping predators or dealing with dangerous situations in a safe setting, improving their chances of survival. Revonsuo pointed out that threatening events – being chased, attacked or falling – are among the most common themes in dreams across cultures, and that people who have experienced real dangers tend to dream about threats more often.

Another group of researchers has focused on the role of sleep, and possibly of dreams, in memory. Experiments have shown that people who dream about a task they have just learned sometimes perform it better afterwards than those who do not. In one study, people who learned to find their way through a virtual maze and then took a nap were more successful on a later attempt if they reported dreaming about the maze. Supporters suggest that dreams may reflect the brain's process of reorganising and strengthening memories, although it is unclear whether dreaming itself helps memory or is simply a side effect of the process.

The American psychologist G. William Domhoff has emphasised the continuity between dreams and waking life. Analysing large collections of dream reports, he found that dreams mostly concern the people, activities and concerns that occupy the dreamer when awake, rather than random or symbolic content. Domhoff argues that dreaming is a form of thinking that occurs when the brain is disconnected from the outside world, and that dreams may not have any special function at all.

These theories are not necessarily incompatible. Dreams might have several functions, or none, and different theories may explain different kinds of dream. Advances in brain imaging are allowing researchers to study dreaming in new ways, but for now, the question of why we dream remains open.

passages.topic: Economic history — explaining the Industrial Revolution
passages.title: Why Britain? Why Then?

paragraphs.text: Between the mid-eighteenth and mid-nineteenth centuries, Britain experienced an economic transformation unlike anything seen before. Factories, steam engines and new machines dramatically increased production, and the economy began to grow at a sustained rate that eventually lifted living standards far above those of earlier centuries. Why this "Industrial Revolution" began in Britain, rather than elsewhere, has been debated by economic historians for generations. Several influential explanations have been proposed.

The economic historian Robert Allen has emphasised prices. In eighteenth-century Britain, he argues, wages were unusually high compared with those in most other countries, while energy, in the form of coal, was unusually cheap. This combination made it profitable for British businesses to invest in machines that replaced expensive labour with cheap energy. Many of the key inventions of the period – such as spinning machines and steam engines – were designed to do exactly this. In countries where labour was cheap and energy expensive, the same inventions would not have been worth adopting.

Joel Mokyr, by contrast, places greater weight on ideas and culture. He argues that Britain benefited from what he calls an "Industrial Enlightenment": a culture in which scientists, engineers and skilled craftsmen exchanged knowledge, and in which practical, useful knowledge was valued and widely shared through societies, publications and lectures. Mokyr does not deny that prices mattered, but he argues that economic incentives alone cannot explain why so many improvements were made, since inventors needed access to knowledge and a willingness to experiment.

Kenneth Pomeranz has approached the question by comparing Britain with the most advanced regions of China, particularly the lower Yangtze delta. He argues that, until around 1800, living standards and economic development in these regions were broadly similar to those of England. What allowed Britain to break away, in his view, were two largely fortunate circumstances: the location of large, easily accessible coal deposits close to centres of industry, and access to the land and resources of the Americas, which supplied cotton, food and timber that Britain could not have produced on its own limited land.

Deirdre McCloskey has argued that the most important change was in how people thought about commerce and innovation. In earlier societies, she contends, merchants and inventors were often regarded with suspicion or contempt. In the Netherlands and then Britain, attitudes changed, and people who made money through trade and new products came to be treated with new respect. This shift in social esteem, she argues, encouraged people to innovate, and was more important than material factors such as coal or capital.

Douglass North, together with other scholars, emphasised institutions – the rules that govern economic life. After political changes in the late seventeenth century, North argued, the British government became more constrained by Parliament and less able to seize property or cancel its debts at will. Secure property rights and a reliable legal system gave people confidence to invest and lend. Critics have questioned whether these changes were as significant or as sudden as North suggested, noting that property rights were already fairly secure in England before this period.

Most historians now accept that no single factor explains the Industrial Revolution. Prices, knowledge, resources, attitudes and institutions all probably played a role, and they may have reinforced one another. The debate continues, however, about their relative importance – and about whether Britain's experience could have happened elsewhere.

lesson.title: Arguments that overlap
lesson.text: Scholars often agree on some points and disagree on others. Two historians may both mention coal, but one argues that it was decisive while another treats it as secondary. Statements test these distinctions. For each feature, note: main cause proposed, key evidence, and what they reject.

passages.topic: Urban planning — five visions of the city
passages.title: Designing the Modern City

paragraphs.text: Few people have shaped modern cities as much as the planners and critics who, over the past century and a half, have tried to define what a good city should be. Their ideas have often conflicted, and many of the successes and failures of today's cities can be traced back to them.

At the end of the nineteenth century, the British reformer Ebenezer Howard was alarmed by the overcrowding and pollution of industrial cities. In 1898 he proposed the "garden city": a planned town of limited size, surrounded by a permanent belt of countryside, combining the economic opportunities of the city with the fresh air and green space of the countryside. Land would be owned collectively, so that rising land values would benefit the community rather than private landlords. The first garden city was begun in England in 1903, and Howard's ideas influenced the planning of suburbs and new towns in many countries.

The Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier offered a very different vision in the 1920s and 1930s. He proposed replacing crowded historic districts with tall apartment towers set far apart in open parkland, connected by wide highways. Different activities – living, working, leisure – would be separated into distinct zones. Le Corbusier believed that this rational order would provide light, air and efficiency for all. After the Second World War, many housing projects around the world were built on principles inspired by his ideas. Some became notorious: tower blocks isolated in empty open spaces often proved unpopular, and in several cities they were demolished only a few decades after being built.

In New York, Robert Moses held a series of powerful public positions from the 1920s to the 1960s. He was responsible for building an enormous number of parks, beaches, bridges and highways, transforming the city and its surrounding region. His highways, however, cut through established neighbourhoods, and his projects displaced large numbers of residents, many of them poor. Moses believed that such costs were a necessary price of modernisation.

The writer and activist Jane Jacobs became the most famous critic of these approaches. In her book published in 1961, she argued that planners had misunderstood how cities actually work. Successful neighbourhoods, she observed, were those with a mixture of homes, shops and workplaces, short blocks, old and new buildings side by side, and busy streets watched over by residents and shopkeepers – what she called "eyes on the street". Jacobs led a successful campaign against a highway Moses planned to build through Lower Manhattan, and her ideas encouraged a shift towards preserving and improving existing neighbourhoods rather than replacing them.

The Danish architect Jan Gehl, working from the 1960s onwards, focused on public spaces and the behaviour of people within them. Through careful observation – counting pedestrians, recording where people sat and how long they stayed – he showed that small changes in the design of streets and squares could greatly increase the time people spent in them. Gehl's methods have been used by many cities to redesign their public spaces for pedestrians and cyclists rather than cars.

Today, few planners follow any one of these visions entirely. Many new developments combine elements of several: green spaces inspired by Howard, the attention to street life championed by Jacobs, and Gehl's methods of observation. The failures of some mid-twentieth-century projects, however, remain a warning about the dangers of imposing a single theory on the complex life of a city.

lesson.text: For each person, a passage may describe their ideas, what happened when those ideas were applied, and how others reacted. passages.topic: Astronomy — telescopes that changed what we can see
passages.title: Windows on the Universe

paragraphs.text: For most of history, astronomers had only their eyes. The invention of the telescope transformed astronomy, and each major new type of telescope has revealed aspects of the universe that were previously invisible.

The first telescopes were made in the Netherlands in the early seventeenth century, using glass lenses to magnify distant objects. The Italian scientist Galileo Galilei built improved versions and, in 1609 and 1610, turned them towards the sky. He observed mountains and craters on the Moon, discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter, and saw that the Milky Way consisted of countless individual stars. His observations provided powerful evidence against the old belief that everything in the heavens revolved around the Earth. However, telescopes using lenses had a significant weakness: lenses bend different colours of light by different amounts, so images were surrounded by coloured fringes.

In 1668, the English scientist Isaac Newton built a different kind of telescope, which used a curved mirror instead of a lens to collect and focus light. Because mirrors reflect all colours in the same way, Newton's reflecting telescope avoided the problem of coloured fringes. Reflecting telescopes also have another advantage: large mirrors are easier to make and support than large lenses, which sag under their own weight. As a result, nearly all of the world's largest optical telescopes today use mirrors.

In the 1930s, an American radio engineer, Karl Jansky, was investigating sources of interference affecting radio communications. He detected a faint signal that repeated at intervals and eventually traced it to the centre of our own galaxy. His accidental discovery showed that objects in space emit radio waves as well as light. Radio telescopes, typically large dish-shaped antennas, can detect objects hidden behind clouds of dust that block visible light, and they operate day and night and in cloudy weather.

The Earth's atmosphere blurs and absorbs much of the light and other radiation coming from space. To avoid this, astronomers have placed telescopes in orbit. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, is the most famous example. Shortly after its launch, however, it was discovered that its main mirror had been ground to a slightly incorrect shape, producing blurred images. In 1993, astronauts installed corrective equipment during a repair mission, after which Hubble produced images of extraordinary clarity and made many important discoveries, including measurements that helped determine the age of the universe.

Some of the most remarkable recent achievements have come from combining many telescopes. In 2019, an international team published the first image of the shadow of a black hole, located in a distant galaxy. The image was produced by the Event Horizon Telescope, which is not a single instrument but a network of radio telescopes across several continents, whose observations were combined by computers. Working together, they acted like a single telescope almost the size of the Earth, achieving a level of detail no individual telescope could reach.

lesson.text: When features are instruments or technologies, statements often describe the problem each one solved or a limitation it had. Make a quick table for each feature: what it used, what it solved, what problem it had. Several technologies may share a general purpose, such as seeing further, but each solved a specific problem.

passages.topic: Education — methods of teaching foreign languages
passages.title: How Languages Are Taught

paragraphs.text: Methods of teaching foreign languages have changed considerably over the past two centuries, often in response to the perceived failures of earlier approaches. Five methods, in particular, illustrate the main shifts in thinking.

The grammar-translation method dominated language teaching in Europe during the nineteenth century and much of the twentieth. Originally used for teaching Latin and Ancient Greek, it focused on learning grammatical rules and vocabulary lists and on translating written texts between the learner's first language and the language being studied. Lessons were conducted largely in the learner's first language. Students could often analyse complex sentences accurately, but many were unable to hold even a simple conversation, because speaking and listening received little attention.

Towards the end of the nineteenth century, the direct method emerged as a reaction against grammar-translation. Its supporters argued that a second language should be learned in the way children learn their first: through direct contact with the spoken language. Teachers used only the language being taught, never translating, and explained meaning through pictures, objects and demonstrations. Grammar was learned by example rather than through explicit rules. The method required teachers who were fluent speakers, which made it difficult to adopt widely in state schools.

In the mid-twentieth century, the audiolingual method became influential, particularly in the United States. It was based on the psychological theory that learning consists of forming habits through repetition and reward. Students listened to and repeated model sentences many times, often in language laboratories equipped with tape recorders, and practised substituting words within fixed sentence patterns. Errors were corrected immediately to prevent bad habits from forming. Critics later pointed out that students could repeat patterns fluently but often struggled to use the language creatively in real situations.

From the 1970s onwards, communicative language teaching challenged the focus on form. Its advocates argued that the purpose of language is communication, and that learners should practise using language for real purposes – asking for information, expressing opinions, solving problems – rather than simply producing correct sentences. Classroom activities such as role-plays and pair work became common. Errors were often tolerated if they did not prevent communication. Some teachers and researchers, however, worried that grammatical accuracy suffered as a result.

Task-based learning, which developed from communicative ideas in the 1980s and 1990s, organises lessons around meaningful tasks, such as planning a trip or conducting a survey, that learners must complete using the target language. Language is studied mainly as it arises from the task, often in a later stage of the lesson where learners reflect on the language they used or needed. Supporters argue that this reflects how language is used outside the classroom; critics note that it can be difficult to ensure that learners meet all the grammar and vocabulary they need.

Many teachers today combine elements from several methods, choosing techniques according to the needs of their students. Research suggests that learners benefit from both meaningful communication and some explicit attention to grammar – a conclusion that would perhaps have surprised the strongest advocates of each earlier approach.

lesson.title: Features defined by contrast
lesson.text: When a passage describes methods that developed as reactions to one another, each method is often defined by what it rejected as well as by what it did. A statement such as "avoided the use of the learner's first language" could match a method whose paragraph says "unlike the previous method, teachers never translated". Read the contrast sentences carefully.

passages.topic: History of medicine — pioneers of vaccination
passages.title: Training the Body's Defences

paragraphs.text: Vaccines work by exposing the immune system to a harmless form or part of a disease-causing organism, so that the body learns to recognise and fight it. The history of vaccination spans more than two centuries and includes several major advances, each associated with particular scientists.

In the late eighteenth century, smallpox was one of the most feared diseases in the world. The English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease from cattle, seemed to be protected from smallpox. In 1796 he tested this by taking material from a cowpox sore and introducing it into a small cut on a boy's arm; when the boy was later exposed to smallpox, he did not become ill. Such an experiment would be considered unethical today. Jenner's method spread rapidly, and the word "vaccine" comes from the Latin word for cow. Nearly two centuries later, in 1980, smallpox became the first human disease to be declared eradicated worldwide.

Jenner's approach depended on a lucky natural relationship between two similar diseases. The French scientist Louis Pasteur, working in the 1870s and 1880s, showed that vaccines could be produced deliberately in the laboratory, by weakening the organisms that cause disease. He developed vaccines against diseases of farm animals and, in 1885, successfully treated a boy who had been bitten by a dog with rabies, using a series of injections of weakened material. Pasteur proposed that the term "vaccination" should be used for all such procedures, in honour of Jenner.

In the mid-twentieth century, polio paralysed or killed large numbers of children each year in many countries. Two American researchers developed vaccines using different approaches. Jonas Salk's vaccine, announced in 1955, used a virus that had been killed, and was given by injection. Albert Sabin developed a vaccine using a live but weakened virus, taken by mouth, which was cheaper and easier to give in large-scale campaigns and became the main vaccine used in many countries for decades. The two scientists were rivals and disagreed publicly about which approach was superior.

For many years, researchers explored the possibility of vaccines based on messenger RNA (mRNA) – molecules that carry instructions for making proteins in cells. The idea was to give the body instructions to make a harmless piece of a virus, which would then train the immune system. A major obstacle was that injected mRNA caused strong inflammation. In 2005, the Hungarian-born biochemist Katalin Karikó and the American immunologist Drew Weissman reported that modifying one of the building blocks of mRNA greatly reduced this inflammatory reaction. Their work received little attention at first, and Karikó had struggled for years to obtain funding for her research.

The value of their discovery became clear during the coronavirus pandemic, when mRNA vaccines were developed, tested and approved in less than a year – far faster than any previous vaccine. Karikó and Weissman were awarded the Nobel Prize in 2023. The speed of development depended not only on their work but on decades of earlier research by many scientists and on unprecedented investment by governments and companies.

lesson.text: When a paragraph mentions more than one person, check who did what. Collaborators may share credit for a discovery, and the passage may attribute a later development to one of them. Rivals may be described together while taking opposite approaches. If a feature in the list is a pair (for example, "Karikó and Weissman"), statements about either person's joint work match that pair.

passages.topic: Water resources — how five places cope with scarcity
passages.title: Every Drop Counts

paragraphs.text: As populations grow and climates change, many cities and countries face increasing pressure on their water supplies. Five places show the range of responses to water scarcity – and the difficulties involved.

Singapore, a small island state with limited land to collect and store rainwater, has long depended partly on water imported from neighbouring Malaysia under long-term agreements. To reduce this dependence, it has developed what it calls "four national taps": imported water, local rainwater collected in reservoirs, desalinated seawater, and highly treated recycled wastewater, marketed under the name NEWater. Most NEWater is supplied to industry, but a small amount is added to reservoirs and becomes part of the drinking water supply. Public education campaigns were used to overcome initial reluctance to drink recycled water.

Israel, much of which is desert, has become a world leader in water efficiency. Its farmers helped pioneer drip irrigation, which delivers small amounts of water directly to the roots of plants, greatly reducing waste. The country treats a very large proportion of its wastewater and reuses most of it for agriculture – a far higher share than in any other country. Since the early 2000s, it has also built large desalination plants along its Mediterranean coast, which now supply a substantial proportion of its drinking water.

Cape Town, in South Africa, came close to running out of water in 2018 after three years of severe drought. The city warned that it might reach "Day Zero", when most household taps would be turned off and residents would have to collect water from public distribution points. To avoid this, the authorities imposed strict limits on water use – at one stage, around fifty litres per person per day – and raised prices for high consumers. Residents responded by cutting consumption dramatically, and Day Zero was avoided, helped by the eventual return of rain.

Mexico City faces a different problem. Much of its water is pumped from an aquifer – a layer of water-bearing rock – beneath the city. Because water has been extracted faster than it is replaced, the ground has been sinking, in some areas by tens of centimetres per year. This has damaged buildings, roads and pipes, and leaks from damaged pipes waste a large proportion of the city's water. The city also imports water from distant sources, which must be pumped uphill at great cost in energy.

Los Angeles, in a dry region of the United States, has historically relied on water transported over long distances by aqueduct. In recent years, however, it has invested in capturing rainwater that would otherwise flow into the sea, for example by building parks and green spaces that allow water to soak into the ground and replenish local aquifers. The city also offered payments to residents who replaced water-intensive lawns with plants suited to dry conditions.

No single solution suits every place. Desalination requires large amounts of energy and is expensive, recycled water depends on public acceptance, and conservation campaigns work best when combined with fair pricing and reliable infrastructure. But the experience of these five places suggests that, with planning, even severe scarcity can be managed.

passages.topic: Earth history — explaining the extinction of the dinosaurs
passages.title: The End of an Era

paragraphs.text: Around sixty-six million years ago, about three-quarters of all plant and animal species on Earth disappeared, including all dinosaurs except the ancestors of modern birds. For much of the twentieth century, the cause of this mass extinction was a mystery. Several explanations have been proposed, and debate about their relative importance continues.

Before the 1980s, many scientists believed that the dinosaurs had declined gradually over millions of years, perhaps because of long-term changes in climate and sea level that altered their habitats and food supplies. Supporters of this "gradual decline" view pointed to evidence that the number of dinosaur species in some regions had fallen before the end of the period. Later studies, however, suggested that this apparent decline might partly reflect gaps in the fossil record rather than a real fall in diversity.

In 1980, a team led by the physicist Luis Alvarez and his son, the geologist Walter Alvarez, proposed that the extinction was caused by the impact of a large asteroid. Their evidence came from a thin layer of clay found in rocks of exactly the right age in several parts of the world. The clay contained unusually high concentrations of iridium, a metal that is rare in the Earth's crust but more common in asteroids. They calculated that the asteroid would have been about ten kilometres across, and that its impact would have thrown so much dust into the atmosphere that sunlight was blocked, plants died, and food chains collapsed.

A major difficulty for the impact hypothesis was the absence of a suitable crater. In the early 1990s, researchers identified a buried crater, around 180 kilometres across, near the village of Chicxulub on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Its age matched the extinction closely. Rocks around the Caribbean also contained evidence of enormous waves and of material thrown out by the impact. For many scientists, the discovery confirmed the Alvarez hypothesis.

Some researchers, however, have argued that massive volcanic eruptions in what is now India played a major role. Over hundreds of thousands of years, these eruptions produced vast floods of lava, known as the Deccan Traps, and released enormous quantities of gases that could have altered the climate and acidified the oceans. The geologist Gerta Keller has been among the most prominent advocates of this view, arguing that the eruptions were already causing environmental stress before the asteroid struck and that their role has been underestimated.

Recent research has attempted to establish the precise timing of the eruptions and the impact. Some studies suggest that the most intense phase of volcanic activity began shortly before the impact; others suggest that the impact may even have intensified the eruptions. Many scientists now favour a combined explanation, in which the asteroid was the main trigger of the extinction but volcanic activity contributed to environmental stress. Others maintain that the impact alone is sufficient to explain the timing and speed of the extinction.

Whatever its exact causes, the extinction opened new opportunities for the survivors. Mammals, which had mostly been small during the age of the dinosaurs, diversified rapidly over the following millions of years, eventually giving rise to many of the large animals of today – including, ultimately, humans.

lesson.title: Evidence attached to the right hypothesis
lesson.text: When a passage presents several hypotheses, each with its own evidence, statements often describe a piece of evidence rather than the hypothesis itself. Ask: "Which hypothesis is this evidence used to support or challenge?" Some evidence is used by two camps in different ways, so check the direction in the specific sentence.

passages.topic: Economics and psychology — does money buy happiness?
passages.title: Money and Well-Being

paragraphs.text: Does being richer make people happier? The question seems simple, but economists and psychologists have debated it for half a century, and their answers have become more nuanced as better data have become available.

In 1974, the economist Richard Easterlin published a study that became famous for an apparent paradox. Within a country at any given time, he found, richer people tended to report being happier than poorer people. Yet over time, as countries became richer, average reported happiness did not seem to increase. Easterlin suggested that people judge their income relative to others and to their own expectations: when everyone becomes richer, and expectations rise accordingly, people feel no better off. The "Easterlin paradox" became one of the most widely discussed findings in the study of well-being.

In 2008, the economists Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers challenged this conclusion. Using data from many more countries and a longer period, they reported that richer countries did, on average, have higher levels of life satisfaction, and that economic growth was associated with rising satisfaction over time. Crucially, they found that the relationship followed a consistent pattern when income was measured in proportional terms: a doubling of income was associated with a similar increase in satisfaction whether a person or country started rich or poor. Easterlin responded that their findings relied on short-term fluctuations and that the long-term relationship remained weak.

A different line of research distinguished between two aspects of well-being: people's overall evaluation of their lives, and their day-to-day emotional experience – how often they feel happy, stressed or sad. In a widely cited study published in 2010, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman and the economist Angus Deaton analysed survey data from hundreds of thousands of Americans. They found that life evaluation continued to rise with income, but that emotional well-being appeared to level off above an annual income of roughly seventy-five thousand dollars. Beyond that point, more money seemed to make people judge their lives more favourably without making their daily experience noticeably happier.

This finding was questioned by the psychologist Matthew Killingsworth, who collected data using a smartphone application that asked people at random moments how they were feeling. In a study published in 2021, he found no plateau: emotional well-being continued to rise with income well beyond the level identified in the earlier study. His method, he argued, measured feelings more directly than survey questions asking people to remember how they had felt the previous day.

Rather than continuing the dispute through separate publications, Kahneman and Killingsworth took the unusual step of working together, with the psychologist Barbara Mellers acting as a neutral mediator, to reanalyse Killingsworth's data. Their joint study, published in 2023, found that the two sets of results could be reconciled. For most people, happiness did continue to rise with income. But for the least happy group of people – those whose unhappiness was caused by problems such as illness or grief that money cannot solve – happiness stopped increasing above a certain income. Kahneman's earlier plateau, they concluded, had reflected this group.

Even researchers who find a strong link between income and happiness emphasise its limits. The association is, in general, modest, and many other factors – health, relationships, meaningful work and security – matter at least as much. Moreover, the effect of income appears to depend on how money is spent: some studies suggest that spending on experiences or on other people produces more lasting satisfaction than spending on possessions.

lesson.text:

some features may be unused.

For each feature, collect every mention before answering, and note the sequence (original claim → challenge → response).

passages.topic: Media history — how important was the printing press?
passages.title: The Revolution in Print

paragraphs.text: Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg began printing books in the German city of Mainz, using movable metal type. Within fifty years, printing presses were operating in more than two hundred European towns, and millions of books had been produced. Few historians doubt that printing had significant effects. How far-reaching those effects were, and how they came about, has been the subject of considerable debate.

The Canadian media theorist Marshall McLuhan, writing in the early 1960s, made some of the boldest claims. He argued that printing did not merely spread information more widely but changed the way people thought. A culture based on printed text, he suggested, encouraged linear, sequential and individual habits of thought, replacing a more communal and oral culture. McLuhan's arguments were widely read and highly influential, but many historians regarded them as speculative and supported by little systematic evidence.

In 1958, the French historians Lucien Febvre and Henri-Jean Martin had published a very different kind of study. Rather than making broad claims about the human mind, they examined the book as a commercial product: how printing businesses were financed, how paper was supplied, how books were distributed and sold. Their work showed that printers were business people who needed to make a profit and who chose what to print largely according to what would sell.

The most influential detailed argument for a "printing revolution" was made by the American historian Elizabeth Eisenstein in 1979. She argued that printing transformed European intellectual life through several features of the new technology. Printed texts could be reproduced in identical copies, allowing scholars in different places to refer to exactly the same text and to build on one another's work. Printing preserved texts more securely than hand copying, which was prone to errors and losses. Eisenstein connected these changes to major developments including the Protestant Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.

Eisenstein's emphasis on the reliability of print was challenged by the historian Adrian Johns in 1998. Johns argued that early printed books were far from fixed and trustworthy. Different copies of the same edition often contained variations, unauthorised editions and pirated copies were common, and readers had good reason to doubt whether a printed text was accurate. The reliability that later readers took for granted, Johns argued, was not a natural feature of printing but had to be established gradually through social practices, such as the development of trusted publishers and systems for regulating the book trade.

More recently, the historian Andrew Pettegree has drawn attention to the kinds of printed material that earlier accounts tended to overlook. Much of what early printers produced was not large scholarly books but short, cheap items: pamphlets, notices, calendars and news sheets. These were often the most profitable part of the business, and they may have had the greatest impact on ordinary people. Pettegree has also emphasised that many early printing businesses failed, and that the industry took decades to find a secure commercial footing.

These scholars disagree on many points, but their work together suggests that the effects of printing were real but complex. They depended not only on the technology itself but on the economic, social and political circumstances in which it was used – and they developed over generations rather than immediately.

lesson.text: Hard passages about academic debates may present scholars who build on, qualify or reject one another's work. The same topic, such as "the stability of printed texts", may be discussed by two scholars who take opposite positions. Statements will describe a position precisely. Read each scholar's section and note their distinctive claim, then check statements against that claim.

passages.topic: Archaeology — why did Classic Maya cities decline?
passages.title: The Abandoned Cities

paragraphs.text: Between roughly AD 250 and 900, the Maya of southern Mexico and Central America built great cities with stone temples, palaces, ball courts and inscribed monuments. Then, over a period of about a century and a half, many of the largest cities in the southern lowlands were abandoned. Construction of monuments stopped, royal inscriptions ceased, and populations fell dramatically. The Maya people did not disappear – millions of their descendants live in the region today, and some northern cities continued to flourish for centuries – but the political system of the southern lowlands collapsed. Explaining why has been a central question of Maya archaeology.

One explanation focuses on climate. Beginning in the 1990s, scientists analysed layers of sediment at the bottom of lakes in the region, as well as mineral deposits in caves, which preserve chemical signatures of past rainfall. These records indicate a series of severe droughts between about AD 800 and 1000, some of them lasting for years. The Maya depended on rain-fed farming and on reservoirs to store water through the dry season, and repeated droughts could have caused crop failures and water shortages. Critics point out, however, that the timing of abandonment varied from city to city and did not always coincide closely with the driest periods, and that some cities in drier areas survived longer than those in wetter ones.

A second explanation emphasises environmental damage caused by the Maya themselves. Large cities required vast amounts of timber for fuel and for producing lime plaster, which covered buildings and plazas. Pollen records suggest that forests were extensively cleared in some areas, which may have led to soil erosion and reduced agricultural productivity. Some researchers argue that deforestation may also have made droughts worse, since forests help to maintain local rainfall. Others caution that the Maya had sophisticated methods of managing land, such as terraces and raised fields, and that the extent of damage varied greatly between regions.

A third explanation stresses warfare. Inscriptions deciphered in recent decades reveal that Maya cities were frequently in conflict, often forming rival alliances led by powerful dynasties. In the eighth and ninth centuries, references to war appear to have increased, and some cities built defensive walls. Several researchers argue that endemic warfare disrupted trade and farming and drained resources, making cities more vulnerable to other pressures. Evidence of destruction at some sites supports this view, although warfare had been common throughout Maya history without causing collapse.

A fourth explanation focuses on political and economic change. Maya kings claimed authority partly on the basis of their relationship with the gods, which was believed to ensure rain and good harvests. If kings failed to deliver prosperity – for example, during drought – their authority may have been undermined, and people may have moved away from the royal centres. At the same time, trade routes appear to have shifted from inland rivers towards coastal sea routes, which may have benefited cities in the north at the expense of those in the south.

Most archaeologists now reject the search for a single cause. The collapse, they argue, resulted from several pressures interacting over time: population growth and environmental stress made cities vulnerable; drought intensified food shortages; competition and warfare increased; and the political system lost its legitimacy. Different cities may have declined for somewhat different combinations of reasons. This interpretation is less dramatic than a single catastrophe, but it fits the varied timing and pattern of abandonment better than any one factor alone.

passages.topic: Linguistics — does language shape thought?
passages.title: Words and Worlds

paragraphs.text: Does the language we speak shape the way we think? The question has fascinated linguists, psychologists and philosophers for more than a century. At one extreme lies the idea that language determines thought, so that speakers of different languages live in fundamentally different mental worlds. At the other lies the view that thought is largely independent of language, which simply provides labels for concepts that all humans share.

The idea is most closely associated with the American linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf, who wrote in the 1930s. Whorf argued that languages divide up experience in different ways, and that these divisions shape how speakers perceive reality. His most famous claim concerned the Hopi language of the south-western United States, which, he argued, had no words or grammatical forms referring to time as a quantity that could be divided and counted. He concluded that Hopi speakers must think about time very differently from speakers of European languages. Later researchers who studied Hopi in more detail found that it does, in fact, contain many expressions of time, and Whorf's specific claims about it have been widely rejected.

An important challenge to the idea that languages divide experience arbitrarily came from research on colour. In 1969, the anthropologist Brent Berlin and the linguist Paul Kay compared colour terms in about a hundred languages. Although the number of basic colour words varied greatly, they found strong regularities: languages with only two basic colour terms distinguished dark and light; those with three added red; and further terms were added in a largely predictable order. They argued that colour naming is constrained by universal features of human vision, not simply by culture. Their conclusions have since been refined, but their work was widely seen as evidence against strong forms of Whorf's view.

The psychologist Steven Pinker, writing in the 1990s, was among the most forceful critics of the idea that language shapes thought. He argued that people think in a kind of internal "mental language" that is independent of the particular language they speak, and pointed out that babies and animals are capable of complex thought without language. Pinker described the strong version of Whorf's hypothesis as "wrong, all wrong".

In recent decades, however, experimental research has revived interest in weaker versions of the idea. The cognitive scientist Lera Boroditsky and others have studied speakers of Kuuk Thaayorre, an Aboriginal language in northern Australia that uses compass directions – north, south, east and west – rather than words such as "left" and "right" to describe locations, even for small distances. Speakers of such languages, researchers found, are remarkably good at keeping track of which direction they are facing. When asked to arrange pictures showing a sequence of events, they tended to arrange them from east to west, whatever direction they were facing, whereas English speakers arranged them from left to right.

The linguist Guy Deutscher has proposed a moderate position. Languages, he argues, do not prevent their speakers from thinking particular thoughts. But they differ in what they oblige speakers to express. A language that requires speakers to mention the direction of every object, or the gender of every noun, trains them to pay habitual attention to certain aspects of experience. Over a lifetime, these habits may influence memory, perception and attention in subtle ways.

Most researchers today reject the strong claim that language determines thought, but many accept that it can influence thinking in particular areas, especially where languages differ in the distinctions they require speakers to make. The debate has shifted from whether language affects thought to how much, and in which areas.

lesson.title: Strong and weak versions of an idea
lesson.text: Debates often distinguish a strong version of a theory (language determines thought) from a weak version (language influences thought in some areas). Scholars may reject the strong version but accept the weak one. Statements may describe either. Check carefully which version each scholar supports, rejects or provides evidence for.

passages.topic: Economics and policy — how should we measure progress?
passages.title: Beyond the Numbers

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the performance of national economies was judged mainly by one number: gross domestic product, or GDP, which measures the total value of goods and services produced in a country over a year. GDP is useful for tracking economic activity, and its growth has often been treated as the primary goal of economic policy. Yet critics have long argued that it is a poor measure of how well people are actually living. Several alternative measures have been proposed.

The limitations of GDP were recognised even by one of its creators. In the 1930s, the economist Simon Kuznets, who developed early methods for measuring national income in the United States, warned that the welfare of a nation could scarcely be inferred from a measure of national income. GDP counts spending on activities that may reflect harm rather than benefit – the costs of repairing damage after a disaster, for example, or of treating pollution-related illness – and it ignores unpaid work such as caring for children or elderly relatives. It also says nothing about how income is distributed, or about whether current production is using up natural resources that future generations will need.

In 1990, the United Nations Development Programme introduced the Human Development Index (HDI), designed by the Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq with contributions from the Indian economist Amartya Sen. The HDI combines three dimensions: life expectancy, education and income. It was intended to shift attention from economic growth alone to the expansion of people's opportunities and capabilities. Countries with similar incomes can rank very differently on the HDI, revealing differences in health and education that GDP conceals. Critics have argued, however, that the choice of components and the way they are combined are somewhat arbitrary.

A different approach attempts to adjust economic measures directly. The Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) starts with consumer spending and then adds the value of beneficial activities that GDP ignores, such as household work and volunteering, while subtracting costs such as crime, pollution, the loss of natural resources and inequality. In several countries where it has been calculated, the GPI has grown much more slowly than GDP since the 1970s, or has even declined. Its critics point out that assigning money values to things such as environmental damage involves many uncertain assumptions.

The small Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan has pursued a more radical idea. Since the 1970s, its leaders have declared that "Gross National Happiness" is more important than gross national product. The country measures well-being through detailed surveys covering areas such as psychological well-being, health, education, culture, community life, good governance and the environment, and uses the results to guide policy. Bhutan's approach has attracted wide international interest, though some observers have noted that the country continues to face serious economic and social challenges.

In 2008, the French government asked a commission led by the economists Joseph Stiglitz, Amartya Sen and Jean-Paul Fitoussi to examine the limits of GDP. Its report, published in 2009, did not propose a single replacement. Instead, it recommended that governments use a range of indicators, including measures of household income and consumption rather than total production, the distribution of income, people's own assessments of their well-being, and the sustainability of current living standards for future generations. The report encouraged several countries and international organisations to develop broader "dashboards" of well-being indicators.

None of these alternatives has replaced GDP, which remains central to economic policy and debate. It is regularly updated, widely understood and comparable across countries. But the growing use of other measures reflects a recognition that a single number cannot capture everything that matters to a society.

passages.topic: Human evolution — why did our ancestors walk on two legs?
passages.title: Standing Up

paragraphs.text: Humans are unusual among mammals in walking habitually on two legs. Bipedalism was one of the earliest distinctive features of the human lineage, appearing millions of years before large brains or stone tools. Why it evolved has been debated since the nineteenth century, and many explanations have been proposed.

For much of the twentieth century, the most popular explanation was the "savanna hypothesis". According to this view, climate change in Africa caused forests to shrink and open grasslands to expand. Our ancestors, forced out of the trees, began walking upright to travel efficiently across open country and to see over tall grass to spot predators and food. The hypothesis was intuitively appealing and appeared in many textbooks.

Discoveries of fossils in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries created serious problems for the savanna hypothesis. The skeleton of Ardipithecus ramidus, a species that lived about 4.4 million years ago in what is now Ethiopia, was described in detail in 2009. It showed adaptations for walking upright on the ground combined with features suited to climbing trees, and plant and animal remains found with the fossils indicated that the environment was woodland rather than open grassland. Other early human relatives also appear to have lived in wooded environments. These findings suggested that bipedalism began before our ancestors moved into open savanna.

Another explanation focuses on energy. In 1980, the anthropologists Peter Rodman and Henry McHenry proposed that walking on two legs is more energy-efficient than the knuckle-walking of chimpanzees, which would have been an advantage as food sources became more widely scattered. In 2007, a study measured the energy used by chimpanzees and humans walking on treadmills and found that human walking used about three-quarters less energy than chimpanzee knuckle-walking. Interestingly, chimpanzees varied considerably: some individuals walked on two legs more efficiently than others, suggesting that natural selection could have acted on such variation.

The anthropologist Owen Lovejoy proposed in 1981 that bipedalism evolved because it freed the hands to carry food. In his model, males who could gather food and carry it back to females and young would have gained a reproductive advantage, and this behaviour would have been associated with the formation of pair bonds between males and females. The idea has been influential but controversial. Critics argue that it makes assumptions about social behaviour that are difficult to test from fossil evidence.

A further proposal concerns body temperature. The physiologist Peter Wheeler argued in the 1980s and 1990s that standing upright reduced the area of the body exposed to direct sunlight at midday and raised the body away from the hot ground into cooler, moving air. This would have helped our ancestors keep cool while searching for food in hot environments. However, since the evidence now suggests that early bipeds lived in partly wooded, shaded environments, the importance of this advantage for the origin of bipedalism has been questioned, although it may have become more significant later.

Most researchers now think that bipedalism probably evolved for a combination of reasons, and that it developed gradually, with early species combining upright walking with climbing. The evidence from Ardipithecus in particular has encouraged a view in which bipedalism originated among ancestors still closely tied to trees, rather than as a sudden adaptation to life on open plains.

passages.topic: History of food technology — the invention of canned food
passages.title: Food in a Can

paragraphs.text: For most of history, preserving food for long periods was difficult. People dried, salted, smoked or pickled food, but these methods changed its taste and texture and did not work for all foods. Armies and navies faced particular problems. Soldiers on long campaigns and sailors on long voyages often suffered from poor diets, and diseases caused by a lack of fresh food were common.

At the end of the eighteenth century, the French government, then at war with much of Europe, offered a large prize to anyone who could develop a better method of preserving food for its forces. The prize was eventually won by Nicolas Appert, a confectioner and chef from Paris. After years of experiments, Appert found that food sealed in glass bottles and then heated in boiling water would remain edible for months, or even years. In 1810, he published a book describing his method, and he was awarded the prize.

Appert did not know why his method worked. He believed that the key was to keep air away from the food. It was only about fifty years later that the French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that food spoils because of the growth of microorganisms, and that heating kills them. Appert's method succeeded because heating destroyed these microorganisms and sealing prevented new ones from entering.

Glass bottles had disadvantages: they were heavy and easily broken. In the same year that Appert published his book, a patent was granted in Britain for preserving food in containers made of tin-plated iron. Tin cans were stronger and lighter than glass, making them more suitable for transport. By the 1820s, British factories were producing canned food for the navy and for explorers travelling to remote regions.

Early cans were extremely heavy and difficult to open. Instructions sometimes advised users to open them with a chisel and hammer, and soldiers used knives or bayonets. Surprisingly, a dedicated can opener was not invented until around fifty years after cans came into use, when thinner metal made cans easier to open. Early openers were awkward to use, and the design familiar today, with a rotating wheel that cuts around the rim, appeared later still.

At first, canned food was expensive and used mainly by armies, navies and explorers. During the second half of the nineteenth century, machines were developed that could make cans much more quickly and cheaply, and canned food became available to ordinary households. It allowed people in cities to eat fruit, vegetables, meat and fish that had been produced far away and in different seasons, changing diets in many countries.

lesson.title: Predict before you look
lesson.text: In easy sets, each beginning points clearly to one sentence in the passage. Find that sentence and predict the ending in your own words, for example "...because the army needed food that would last". Then find the ending that expresses your prediction. This prevents you from being attracted by endings that simply repeat passage vocabulary.

passages.topic: Environment — why wetlands matter
passages.title: Nature's Sponges

paragraphs.text: Wetlands – areas where land is covered by water for all or part of the year – include marshes, swamps, bogs and the edges of lakes and rivers. For centuries they were widely regarded as useless or unhealthy land, associated with disease-carrying insects and difficult to farm or build on. As a result, many were drained. It is estimated that a large proportion of the world's wetlands have been lost since 1900, much of it converted to farmland or urban development.

Scientists now recognise that wetlands provide important services. One of the most valuable is flood control. During heavy rain, wetlands absorb and store large quantities of water, releasing it slowly afterwards. This reduces the peak flow of rivers and the risk of flooding downstream. When wetlands are drained, water runs off the land more quickly, and floods can become more frequent and severe.

Wetlands also improve water quality. As water moves slowly through wetland plants and soils, sediments settle out, and plants and microorganisms remove nutrients and some pollutants. For this reason, wetlands are sometimes described as the "kidneys" of the landscape. Some towns have created artificial wetlands to treat wastewater as a cheaper alternative to conventional treatment plants.

Wetlands support a remarkable variety of wildlife. Many birds depend on them for feeding and breeding, and migratory birds use them as resting places on long journeys. Wetlands also serve as nurseries for many species of fish, including some that are commercially important, whose young shelter among the plants before moving to open water.

Some types of wetland, particularly peatlands, store huge amounts of carbon. In waterlogged conditions, dead plant material decays very slowly and accumulates as peat over thousands of years. Although peatlands cover only a small proportion of the world's land surface, they are estimated to contain more carbon than all the world's forests combined. When peatlands are drained, the peat dries out and begins to decompose, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

In recent decades, many countries have begun to protect and restore wetlands. An international agreement signed in 1971 in the Iranian city of Ramsar encourages the conservation of wetlands of international importance. Restoration projects have blocked drainage channels, allowing water levels to rise again, and replanted native vegetation. Such projects can be slow to succeed, but many restored wetlands have attracted returning wildlife within a few years.

lesson.title: Cause, effect and purpose endings
lesson.text: Many beginnings contain because, so that, as a result, or verbs such as help, reduce or lead to. Decide whether the beginning needs a cause, an effect or a purpose, then look for endings of that type. An ending can be true but of the wrong type, for example a cause when the beginning needs a result.
