passages.topic: History of technology — lighthouses
passages.title: Lights Along the Coast

paragraphs.text: For as long as people have sailed at night, they have needed ways to avoid dangerous coastlines and find their way into harbours. The earliest aids to navigation were simply fires lit on hilltops or beaches. The most famous ancient lighthouse was built at Alexandria, in Egypt, in the third century BC. It was one of the tallest structures in the ancient world, and a fire burned at its top. It survived for many centuries before being badly damaged by earthquakes and eventually disappearing.

For centuries after the ancient period, lighthouses remained relatively simple. They burned wood, coal or candles, and later oil lamps. Much of the light they produced was wasted, because it shone in all directions, including upwards and towards the land, where it was of no use to sailors. Many lighthouses were visible only a few kilometres out to sea.

A major advance came in 1822, when the French physicist Augustin Fresnel designed a new kind of lens. Instead of a single thick piece of glass, which would have been extremely heavy, Fresnel's lens consisted of a series of rings of glass prisms arranged around a central lens. These prisms bent and reflected light so that almost all of it was directed into a strong, narrow beam aimed out to sea. Lighthouses fitted with Fresnel lenses could be seen from far greater distances – in some cases more than thirty kilometres. The design was quickly adopted around the world.

To help sailors identify particular lighthouses, each was given a distinctive pattern of light. Some flashed at regular intervals, others showed groups of flashes or lights of different colours. Sailors could look up these patterns in published lists and charts, allowing them to work out their position at night. Lighthouses also used sound signals, such as foghorns, when fog made the light impossible to see.

For most of their history, lighthouses were operated by keepers, who lived at or near the lighthouse, often with their families. Their work was demanding: they had to keep the lamps burning through the night, clean the lenses, wind the machinery that turned the light, and record weather conditions. Many lighthouses were located on isolated rocks or islands, where keepers could be cut off from the mainland for weeks during storms.

During the twentieth century, electric lamps replaced oil, and lighthouses were gradually automated. Automatic systems could switch the light on and off, detect failures and send alerts, removing the need for keepers to live on site. In many countries, the last keepers left their lighthouses in the 1980s and 1990s. Today, satellite navigation systems allow ships to determine their position precisely, and some lighthouses have been switched off. Many, however, continue to operate as a reliable backup, and others have been preserved as museums or holiday accommodation.

lesson.title: Beginnings with time words
lesson.text: Beginnings often include time references: "In ancient times,", "After the 1820s,", "Today,". These tell you exactly where to look in the passage. Endings from a different period may be true statements but describe the wrong time, which is a common trap.

passages.topic: Music history — the development of the piano
passages.title: From Harpsichord to Piano

paragraphs.text: Before the piano, the most important keyboard instrument in Europe was the harpsichord. When a harpsichord key is pressed, a small quill plucks a string. The mechanism produces a bright, clear sound, but it has one major limitation: the player cannot control how loudly each note sounds. Pressing a key harder or more gently makes almost no difference.

Around the year 1700, an Italian instrument maker named Bartolomeo Cristofori, working for a wealthy family in Florence, built an instrument that solved this problem. Instead of plucking the strings, it struck them with small hammers covered in leather. The harder the player pressed a key, the faster the hammer moved and the louder the note. Cristofori called his instrument a harpsichord "with soft and loud", in Italian gravicembalo col piano e forte – the origin of the words "pianoforte" and "piano".

At first, the new instrument attracted relatively little attention, and many musicians continued to prefer the harpsichord. Early pianos were quieter than later instruments and expensive to make. Over the course of the eighteenth century, however, instrument makers in Germany, Austria and England improved the design, and composers began to write music that took advantage of the piano's ability to vary volume and express emotion.

The nineteenth century brought major technical changes. Composers and performers demanded more powerful instruments that could fill large concert halls. Makers began to use cast-iron frames, which could withstand the enormous tension of thicker, tighter strings. This allowed pianos to produce a much louder and richer sound. At the same time, the range of the keyboard was extended, eventually reaching the eighty-eight keys found on most pianos today.

The piano also became a central feature of middle-class homes. Compact upright pianos, in which the strings run vertically rather than horizontally, took up less space than large grand pianos and were cheaper to produce. Before recorded music, playing the piano at home was one of the main ways in which families and friends enjoyed music together, and learning to play was considered an important accomplishment, particularly for young women.

In the twentieth century, the piano faced new competition. Radios and record players allowed people to hear music without playing it themselves, and sales of pianos declined in many countries. Electronic keyboards and digital pianos, which reproduce the sound of a piano using recorded samples, became popular because they are lighter, cheaper, do not need tuning and can be played quietly using headphones. Yet the traditional acoustic piano remains the standard instrument in concert halls and music schools around the world.

lesson.title: Name and invention beginnings
lesson.text: When a beginning names an inventor or product ("Cristofori's instrument..."), the ending often describes what was new about it or why it succeeded. Look for the sentence that explains the innovation's significance, not just its existence.

passages.topic: Environment — microplastics
passages.title: Tiny Pieces, Big Questions

paragraphs.text: Plastic has become one of the most widely used materials in the world, valued for being cheap, light and durable. Its durability, however, is also a problem: plastic does not biodegrade in the way that natural materials do. Instead, it gradually breaks into smaller and smaller pieces. Particles smaller than five millimetres across are known as microplastics.

Microplastics come from many sources. Some are produced when larger plastic items, such as bags and bottles, are broken down by sunlight, waves and friction. Others are released directly. Synthetic clothing made from materials such as polyester sheds tiny fibres every time it is washed, and many of these pass through wastewater treatment plants into rivers and the sea. Car tyres wear away gradually as vehicles are driven, releasing particles onto roads, from where they are washed into drains. Until recently, some cosmetic products also contained small plastic beads, although these have been banned in several countries.

Microplastics are now found almost everywhere scientists look. They have been detected in the deepest ocean trenches, in Arctic sea ice, in remote mountain lakes and in the air of cities. They have been found in the stomachs of fish, seabirds and whales, and in food and drinking water consumed by humans. Some research has also detected microplastics in human blood and tissues.

The effects of microplastics on living things are still being investigated. In laboratory experiments, some small animals exposed to high concentrations of microplastics have eaten less, grown more slowly or reproduced less successfully. Microplastics can also carry chemicals, either those added during manufacture or pollutants absorbed from the surrounding water. Researchers are uncertain, however, whether the concentrations found in the natural environment are high enough to cause significant harm, and the effects on human health remain largely unknown.

Because microplastics are so small and so widespread, removing them from the environment is practically impossible. Efforts therefore focus on reducing the amount released. Some washing machines are now fitted with filters that capture fibres before they enter the wastewater, and some countries are considering making such filters compulsory. Improved wastewater treatment can remove a large proportion of microplastics, although the captured particles then end up in sewage sludge, which is often spread on farmland.

Ultimately, many scientists argue, reducing microplastic pollution will require reducing the production and use of plastic, particularly single-use items, and improving recycling and waste management. International negotiations on a global agreement to address plastic pollution have begun, although countries disagree about how far such an agreement should go.

lesson.title: Scientific uncertainty in endings
lesson.text: Science passages often say that effects are not yet fully understood. An ending that states an effect as certain may not match a beginning about what scientists know. Match the level of certainty: if the beginning says "Researchers are still unsure...", the ending must express uncertainty or an unanswered question.

passages.topic: Society — community gardens
passages.title: Growing Together

paragraphs.text: Community gardens are areas of land cultivated collectively by groups of people, usually in towns and cities. Some are divided into individual plots, each tended by a different household; others are managed as a single shared garden. They may occupy vacant building sites, parts of parks, school grounds or land beside railways.

The idea is not new. During both world wars, governments in several countries encouraged citizens to grow vegetables in gardens, parks and public spaces to reduce pressure on food supplies. In Britain and the United States, these "victory gardens" produced a significant share of the fresh vegetables consumed at home. After the wars, many were abandoned as food became more plentiful and people returned to buying vegetables in shops.

Interest revived from the 1970s onwards. In some cities, residents began cultivating neglected vacant lots, partly to improve the appearance of their neighbourhoods and partly to grow fresh food in areas where it was difficult to buy. Today, community gardens are found in cities around the world, supported by local councils, charities and volunteer groups.

Supporters point to a range of benefits. Gardens provide fresh fruit and vegetables, which can be particularly valuable for families on low incomes. Gardening offers physical exercise and time outdoors, and several studies have found that people who take part report lower levels of stress. Gardens also bring people together: neighbours who might otherwise never meet work side by side, share tools and knowledge, and often organise events such as harvest festivals.

Many community gardens also have an educational role. Schools use them to teach children where food comes from and how plants grow, and some gardens run workshops on cooking, composting and saving seeds. For children who have grown up in cities, the experience of planting a seed and harvesting a vegetable can be a new and memorable one.

Community gardens face several challenges. One of the most serious is insecure access to land. Many gardens are established on land that is temporarily unused, and when the owner decides to build on it, the garden may have to close, even after years of work by volunteers. Gardens also depend on the continuing commitment of volunteers, and some decline when key organisers move away. In some areas, soil contaminated by previous industrial use must be tested and treated, or replaced with raised beds, before food can safely be grown.

passages.topic: Biology — the secrets of long-lived animals
passages.title: Masters of Longevity

paragraphs.text: Among animals, lifespans vary enormously. Some insects live only a few days, while certain species of tortoise, whale and fish can live for well over a century. Biologists have long observed that, in general, larger animals tend to live longer than smaller ones, and that animals with high metabolic rates – those that burn energy quickly – tend to have shorter lives. Yet some species break these patterns dramatically, and they have become the focus of research into the biology of ageing.

One of the most studied is the naked mole-rat, a small, almost hairless rodent that lives in underground colonies in East Africa. Most rodents of its size live only a few years, but naked mole-rats can live for more than thirty. Remarkably, they show few of the usual signs of ageing: their risk of dying does not appear to increase significantly as they grow older, and they rarely develop cancer. Researchers have identified several possible reasons, including cells that are unusually effective at repairing damage and proteins that remain stable for long periods.

Determining the age of wild animals is often difficult, and in some cases scientists have developed ingenious methods. The Greenland shark, which lives in the cold, deep waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic, grows extremely slowly – perhaps about a centimetre a year – and its age cannot be estimated from growth rings, as it can for many fish. In a study published in 2016, researchers analysed the lenses of the sharks' eyes, which contain proteins formed before birth that do not change afterwards. Using radiocarbon dating, they estimated that the oldest shark in their sample was at least 272 years old, and possibly much older, making the species the longest-lived vertebrate known.

The shark's great age appears to be connected with its extremely cold environment and slow lifestyle. Its metabolism is very slow, and it swims at remarkably low speeds. Females are thought not to reach maturity until they are well over a hundred years old. Such slow development has consequences for conservation: because populations take so long to replace individuals that are killed, for example when caught accidentally by fishing boats, they are highly vulnerable to decline.

The bowhead whale, which lives in Arctic waters, is the longest-lived mammal known. In the 1990s, harpoon points made of stone and ivory, of a type used by local hunters before the late nineteenth century, were found embedded in the bodies of whales killed by modern hunters. This prompted scientists to study the whales' ages using chemical changes in the eye, and some individuals were estimated to be around two hundred years old. Genetic studies have identified changes in genes involved in repairing DNA and controlling cell division, which may help the whales avoid cancer despite their enormous size and number of cells.

Researchers hope that understanding such species may eventually lead to treatments that help humans remain healthy for longer. However, they caution that the mechanisms involved are complex, that they have evolved in very different environments and bodies, and that findings in other species may not transfer directly to humans. The more immediate value of the research, many argue, lies in improving our basic understanding of why ageing happens at all.

lesson.title: Several endings on the same topic
lesson.text: At Medium level, three or four endings may all relate to the same animal or idea, differing in a key detail (method vs result, cause vs effect, one species vs another). Identify the specific relationship the beginning requires, then choose the ending that expresses that relationship for the correct subject.

passages.topic: Business — why ticket prices keep changing
passages.title: The Price Is Not Always Right

paragraphs.text: Two passengers sitting side by side on the same flight may have paid very different prices for their seats – one perhaps several times as much as the other. For many travellers this seems puzzling or even unfair. It is, however, the deliberate result of a pricing strategy known as "revenue management" or "dynamic pricing", which is now used not only by airlines but also by hotels, railways, concert venues and many online retailers.

The strategy was developed by airlines in the United States in the late 1970s and 1980s, after government controls on air fares were removed and competition increased. Airlines faced a particular problem: once a flight has departed, an empty seat can never be sold, so its potential revenue is lost for ever. At the same time, different customers are willing to pay very different amounts. Business travellers, whose employers pay and who often need to travel at short notice, are generally willing to pay more than holidaymakers, who can plan ahead and choose among alternatives.

Revenue management attempts to sell each seat to the customer willing to pay the most for it, while still filling the aircraft. Airlines divide the seats on a flight into many price categories, known as "fare classes", and use computer systems to decide how many seats to offer in each class at any given time. Cheaper tickets are typically available early and come with restrictions – such as no refunds or a requirement to stay over a weekend – which make them less attractive to business travellers. As a flight fills up and the departure date approaches, the cheaper classes are closed, and prices rise.

The systems rely on detailed forecasts of demand, based on historical booking data for similar flights, the time of year, special events and other factors. If bookings are slower than expected, cheaper seats may be released again; if demand is unusually strong, prices may rise earlier than usual. Modern systems update prices continuously and increasingly take account of competitors' prices.

Airlines argue that the approach benefits consumers as a whole. Because business travellers pay higher fares, airlines can offer cheap seats to price-sensitive travellers who might not otherwise fly, and operate routes that would not otherwise be profitable. Economists generally accept that such price discrimination can increase the number of people who are able to travel. Critics, however, argue that the complexity of the pricing makes it difficult for consumers to compare prices and to know whether they are getting a fair deal.

A widely held belief is that travel websites raise prices when a user repeatedly searches for the same flight, using stored information in the user's browser. Investigations have generally found little evidence that this is common practice. Prices often change between searches simply because seats in a cheaper fare class have been sold or because the airline's system has updated its prices in response to demand. The perception persists, however, and it reflects a wider unease about pricing that customers cannot see or understand.

lesson.title: Endings that reverse cause and effect
lesson.text: A strong Medium distractor uses the right ideas but in the wrong direction. For example, the passage says "prices rise as seats fill", and the ending says "seats fill because prices rise". Before choosing, check which idea is the cause and which is the effect in the passage, and make sure the complete sentence keeps that order.

passages.topic: Anthropology — is there a natural limit to our social circle?
passages.title: How Many Friends?

paragraphs.text: In the early 1990s, the British anthropologist Robin Dunbar proposed that there is a natural limit to the number of stable social relationships that a person can maintain. His reasoning began with primates. Monkeys and apes live in social groups whose size varies from species to species, and Dunbar noticed that group size was related to the size of the neocortex – the outer layer of the brain associated with complex thinking – relative to the rest of the brain. Species with a relatively larger neocortex tended to live in larger groups.

Dunbar argued that this relationship arises because keeping track of social relationships – who is allied with whom, who can be trusted, who owes favours – places heavy demands on the brain. By extending the relationship observed in primates to the size of the human neocortex, he predicted that humans should be able to maintain stable relationships with about 150 people. This figure became known as "Dunbar's number".

Dunbar supported his prediction by pointing to a range of human groups whose size clusters around 150: the average size of some traditional villages, of certain military units, and of groups of hunter-gatherers who gather together periodically. He also proposed that relationships are organised in layers, with around five very close relationships, fifteen close friends, fifty good friends and 150 meaningful contacts.

Dunbar also linked group size to how social bonds are maintained. Monkeys and apes spend a great deal of time grooming one another, which strengthens relationships but is time-consuming and can be done with only one individual at a time. Dunbar suggested that as human groups became too large for grooming to maintain, language evolved partly as a more efficient form of "vocal grooming", allowing people to bond with several others at once through conversation and gossip.

The idea has been widely popularised, and some companies have used it to limit the size of their offices or teams. Studies of social media have been used both to support and to question it. Although people may have hundreds or thousands of online "friends", research suggests that the number with whom they interact regularly and meaningfully is much smaller, and roughly consistent with Dunbar's estimates.

Critics, however, have challenged both the reasoning and the number. In a study published in 2021, a team of researchers reanalysed the primate data using updated information and more modern statistical methods. Their estimates of the predicted human group size varied enormously depending on the methods used, with a very wide range of possible values, from fewer than ten to more than five hundred. They concluded that the data could not support any precise figure. Others have pointed out that the size of human social networks varies considerably between individuals and cultures, and that the relationship between brain size and group size in primates may reflect factors other than social demands, such as diet.

Dunbar has defended his work, arguing that his critics misunderstood the approach and that the figure of 150 is supported by evidence from human groups themselves, not only by the primate data. The debate continues, but even critics generally accept that there are limits to the number of close relationships people can maintain, since relationships require time and attention, both of which are limited.

lesson.title: Claims, evidence and criticism in one passage
lesson.text: When a passage presents a theory, its supporting evidence and later criticism, beginnings may refer to any of these three. Check whether a beginning asks about what the theory claims, what evidence was used or what critics found. Endings from the wrong category are the main distractors.

passages.topic: Conservation — the return of the beaver
passages.title: Engineers of the River

paragraphs.text: The Eurasian beaver was once widespread across Britain, but it was hunted to extinction there by the sixteenth century, prized for its fur, its meat and a substance from its glands used in medicine and perfume. For more than four hundred years, Britain's rivers developed without the animal that had helped shape them for thousands of years.

Beavers are sometimes called "ecosystem engineers" because they change their environment dramatically. They fell trees and build dams across streams, creating ponds that provide safe places for their lodges. Over time, a series of dams can transform a narrow, fast-flowing stream into a network of ponds, channels and wetlands.

In the early twenty-first century, beavers began to return. An officially licensed trial reintroduction took place in Scotland in 2009, and around the same time beavers of uncertain origin – probably escaped from private collections or illegally released – were found living wild on rivers in both Scotland and England. Rather than removing a population discovered on a river in Devon, the authorities allowed a five-year monitored trial, which began in 2015.

Studies of these populations have documented several benefits. Beaver dams slow the flow of water, so that after heavy rain, water is held back and released gradually. In one study in south-west England, peak flows downstream of beaver dams during storms were found to be significantly lower than those upstream, which could reduce flooding in communities further down the river. The ponds also trap sediment and pollutants washed from surrounding farmland, improving water quality. Wetlands created by beavers support a greater variety of insects, amphibians and birds.

Beavers also create problems. Their dams can flood farmland, block drainage ditches and damage roads and paths. They sometimes fell trees that landowners value, including trees in orchards. Some farmers and anglers have also worried that dams could prevent fish such as salmon and trout from moving upstream, although research suggests that fish are often able to pass dams, particularly during high water, and that the ponds can provide valuable habitat for young fish.

To address these conflicts, a range of management techniques has been developed. Pipes can be installed through dams to limit the height of the water behind them. Valuable trees can be protected with wire mesh or special paint that beavers dislike. Where necessary, dams can be removed or, as a last resort, beavers can be relocated. Supporters argue that such techniques, together with compensation schemes for affected landowners, can allow beavers and people to coexist.

In recent years, beavers have been given legal protection in both Scotland and England, and licensed releases into the wild have begun in England. Their return is widely seen as a test of whether a society can accept a native species that changes the landscape in ways that are sometimes inconvenient. How successfully this is managed may influence debates about reintroducing other species.

lesson.title: Benefits and conflicts
lesson.text: Conservation passages often balance benefits (ecological, economic) against conflicts (with farmers or landowners). Beginnings may begin neutrally ("Beaver dams...") and require you to choose between a positive and a negative ending. Check the specific sentence the beginning refers to. Both kinds of ending may be true somewhere in the passage.

passages.topic: History — the evolution of the passport
passages.title: Papers, Please

paragraphs.text: Documents allowing people to travel have existed for centuries. In medieval Europe, rulers issued "letters of safe conduct" to travellers such as merchants and diplomats, requesting that they be allowed to pass freely and protected on their journey. These documents were issued to relatively few people, and they served more as a request for protection than as proof of identity or nationality.

For much of the nineteenth century, travel between many European countries was possible without a passport. The spread of railways made international travel faster and more common, and checking the documents of large numbers of passengers proved impractical. Several countries relaxed or abandoned passport requirements, and by the early twentieth century it was possible to travel through much of Europe without any formal travel document.

The First World War changed this situation dramatically. Governments, concerned about spies and anxious to control the movement of people who might avoid military service, introduced strict requirements for travellers to carry passports. At first, many people expected these measures to be temporary. They were not. After the war, most countries retained passport requirements, and controls at borders became a permanent feature of international travel.

Passports of this period varied greatly between countries in size, format and content. Some consisted of a single folded sheet, others of booklets. Some included a written description of the holder's appearance – height, eye colour, shape of face – while others included photographs. In 1920, an international conference organised by the League of Nations, the forerunner of the United Nations, agreed on common guidelines, recommending a standard booklet format with a photograph of the holder. Many travellers found the requirement to be photographed intrusive, but it gradually became accepted.

Later developments focused on efficiency and security. From the 1980s, passports began to include a "machine-readable zone" – lines of characters that could be read automatically by scanners at border controls, speeding up checks. After security concerns increased in the early twenty-first century, many countries introduced passports containing electronic chips that store the holder's personal details and a digital photograph, and in some cases fingerprints. These "biometric" passports are designed to make forgery more difficult and to allow automated gates to compare the traveller's face with the stored image.

Today, the value of a passport varies considerably depending on the country that issues it. Holders of some passports can visit many countries without applying for a visa in advance, while holders of others require visas for most destinations. Some commentators have noted that this means the freedom to travel depends heavily on a person's nationality, which is usually determined by where they happen to be born.

lesson.title: Beginnings that refer to consequences of events
lesson.text: History passages link events to their results: "The First World War led governments to...", "The 1920 conference resulted in...". Several endings may describe changes in the same area, such as passport design, from different periods. Match the specific event to its specific consequence, using the paragraph where the event appears.

passages.topic: Urban ecology — how wildlife adapts to cities
passages.title: Wild in the City

paragraphs.text: Cities are among the most rapidly changing environments on Earth. They are noisy, brightly lit at night, full of hard surfaces and often warmer than the surrounding countryside. For many species, these conditions are hostile. Yet a growing number of animals and plants not only survive in cities but appear to be adapting to them – in some cases through changes in behaviour, and in others through genetic evolution.

Some of the clearest examples involve changes in behaviour. Birds in noisy urban areas face a problem: their songs, which they use to attract mates and defend territories, can be drowned out by traffic. Studies in several European cities have found that blackbirds and great tits living in noisy areas sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in quieter areas, since higher notes are less masked by the low rumble of traffic. Some urban birds also sing earlier in the morning or at night, when traffic is lighter.

City animals also tend to be bolder than their rural relatives. Urban foxes, squirrels and birds often allow people to approach much more closely before fleeing. This makes sense in environments where humans are everywhere but rarely dangerous, and where fleeing at every approach would waste time and energy that could be spent feeding.

Some species find in cities features that resemble their natural habitats. The peregrine falcon, which traditionally nests on cliff ledges, has adopted tall buildings, cathedrals and bridges in many cities as substitute cliffs. Cities also provide an abundant supply of prey in the form of pigeons. In some regions, city populations of peregrines have become an important part of the species' recovery after steep declines in the twentieth century.

Beyond behaviour, there is growing evidence of genetic change. In a study published in 2018, researchers compared lizards living in cities in Puerto Rico with those in nearby forests. The urban lizards had longer limbs and larger toe pads with more of the small scales that help them grip, which appeared to help them move across smooth walls and painted surfaces. When the researchers raised lizards from both environments under identical conditions, the offspring of city lizards still showed these features, suggesting that the differences were inherited rather than simply the result of growing up in a city.

Another study found that moths collected from areas with heavy light pollution in Switzerland were significantly less attracted to artificial light than moths of the same species from dark rural areas. Because moths that fly towards lights are more likely to be killed by predators or exhausted, the researchers suggested that natural selection had favoured moths less drawn to light. This adaptation, however, may have a cost: moths that fly less may be less effective as pollinators.

Researchers caution that most species do not adapt successfully to cities, and that urban areas generally support fewer species than natural habitats. The species that thrive tend to be those that are flexible in their diet and behaviour. Nevertheless, cities are increasingly seen by scientists as natural laboratories in which evolution can be observed over relatively short periods of time.

lesson.title: Examples that illustrate a general point
lesson.text: Some beginnings name a specific example ("Blackbirds in cities..."), and the correct ending states what that example shows or how the animal has changed. Other endings may describe other animals' adaptations. Track which example belongs to which change, and don't be distracted by endings that are correct for a different species.

passages.topic: Work — testing the four-day week
passages.title: Four Days' Work, Five Days' Pay?

paragraphs.text: The idea of a shorter working week is not new. Over the past century and a half, working hours in industrialised countries have fallen substantially, and the five-day week has become standard in many of them. In recent years, interest has grown in going further: reducing the working week to four days without reducing pay. Supporters argue that many employees can achieve as much in four days as in five if unnecessary meetings and distractions are cut, and that the extra day off improves health and wellbeing.

Several large trials have tested the idea. One of the best known took place in the United Kingdom in 2022, involving around sixty companies and some three thousand employees. Organisations taking part agreed to reduce working time by about a fifth, typically to four days, while maintaining full pay. They were free to design their own arrangements: some gave all staff the same day off, others staggered days off so that the business remained open throughout the week.

The results were widely reported as encouraging. By the end of the six-month trial, the great majority of participating companies said that they would continue with the four-day week, and a number decided to make it permanent. Employees reported lower levels of stress and burnout, improved sleep, and better balance between work and family life. Among companies that provided financial data, revenue remained broadly stable over the trial period, and the number of employees leaving fell.

How did the companies maintain their output? Many reported cutting the length and number of meetings, reducing time spent on emails, and introducing periods of uninterrupted "focus time". Some employees said that the prospect of a longer weekend motivated them to work more efficiently. In some organisations, however, employees found that the pressure to complete the same work in less time increased stress on working days.

Critics have pointed to several limitations. The companies that took part volunteered to do so, and were likely to be those most enthusiastic about the idea and most confident that it would work in their business. Many were relatively small organisations in areas such as marketing, technology and professional services, where output is often difficult to measure precisely. It is less clear whether similar results would be achieved in sectors such as manufacturing, healthcare or retail, where work often depends on being physically present for fixed hours. In addition, a six-month trial may not reveal longer-term effects.

Supporters respond that the trials show a four-day week is at least possible in many types of organisation, and that further trials in a wider range of sectors are under way. Some governments have expressed interest, and a few public-sector organisations have begun experimenting. Whether the four-day week will eventually become as standard as the five-day week did in the twentieth century remains uncertain, but the idea has moved from the margins of debate into mainstream discussion.

lesson.title: Findings vs limitations
lesson.text: Research passages often report findings and then limitations ("however, the companies taking part were not typical..."). Beginnings may ask about either. Look for signal words that introduce limitations (however, critics note, one weakness, it is unclear whether). The ending must match the category the beginning requires.

passages.topic: Science and design — colour without pigment
passages.title: Colours from Structure

paragraphs.text: Most colours in nature are produced by pigments – chemicals that absorb some wavelengths of light and reflect others. The green of leaves, for example, comes from chlorophyll, which absorbs red and blue light and reflects green. But some of the most brilliant colours in the natural world have a quite different origin. They are produced not by chemicals but by the physical structure of surfaces, and they are known as "structural colours".

The brilliant blue wings of the morpho butterflies of Central and South America are a well-known example. Their wing scales contain no blue pigment. Instead, they are covered in microscopic ridges arranged in layers, spaced at intervals comparable to the wavelength of light. When light strikes these layers, reflections from different layers interfere with one another: blue light waves reinforce each other, producing an intense colour, while other wavelengths cancel out. If the scales are soaked in a liquid that fills the spaces between the ridges, the blue colour disappears, showing that it depends on the structure rather than any chemical.

The feathers of peacocks work in a similar way. The brown pigment melanin is present in the feathers, but the shimmering blues and greens are produced by tiny, regularly spaced structures within the feather. Because the colour depends on the angle from which light is reflected, structural colours often appear to change as the observer moves – an effect known as iridescence.

Structural colours have several remarkable properties. Because they do not depend on chemicals that can break down in sunlight, they can remain bright for very long periods. Specimens of beetles and butterflies collected more than a century ago often retain their original colours, whereas pigment-based colours in other specimens have faded. Some fossils of insects and feathers millions of years old still show traces of structural colour.

Scientists and engineers have begun to imitate structural colour for practical purposes. Because such colours do not require dyes, they could be used to produce coloured materials without potentially harmful chemicals. Researchers have developed paints and coatings based on structural colour that do not fade, and some companies have explored their use in cosmetics and textiles. Structural colours are also difficult to copy precisely, which makes them attractive for security features on banknotes and identity documents.

Imitating nature is not straightforward. The structures that produce colour in butterflies and birds are formed by complex biological processes, and reproducing them on a large scale at low cost remains a challenge. Some engineered structural colours also change appearance with viewing angle, which is desirable for security features but less so for paints, where a consistent colour is usually wanted. Researchers are exploring disordered structures, similar to those found in some bird feathers, which produce colours that look the same from all angles.

lesson.text: Science passages may explain a mechanism in several steps. Endings may describe the mechanism, its effect or a practical application. Some distractors misstate the mechanism in a way that sounds plausible, for example "pigments reflect blue light" when the passage says there is no blue pigment. Check the passage's exact explanation.

passages.topic: History of science and society — why good ideas spread slowly
passages.title: The Slow Road to Adoption

paragraphs.text: It is often assumed that a useful discovery will be adopted quickly once its benefits are demonstrated. History suggests otherwise. Many innovations whose value now seems obvious took decades, or even centuries, to be widely accepted. Understanding why can help explain the spread of new ideas today.

A striking example concerns scurvy, a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C, which killed large numbers of sailors on long voyages between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries. In 1601, an English captain, James Lancaster, reportedly gave lemon juice to sailors on one of his ships during a voyage to Asia, and the crew of that ship remained largely healthy while crews on other ships suffered badly. Yet the practice was not adopted systematically. In 1747, the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind carried out a small comparative trial, giving different treatments to groups of sailors with scurvy; those given citrus fruit recovered rapidly. Even so, it was not until 1795 that the British navy began to supply lemon juice regularly to its sailors.

Several factors explain the delay. The cause of scurvy was not understood, since vitamins would not be discovered until the twentieth century, and many rival remedies were promoted by respected physicians. Lind himself did not clearly conclude that citrus fruit was the single solution, and he later recommended methods of preserving juice by heating it, which destroyed much of its effectiveness. Without a clear explanation of why citrus worked, and with inconsistent results from preserved juices, it was difficult to persuade authorities to act.

The sociologist Everett Rogers, whose influential book on the "diffusion of innovations" was first published in 1962, identified several characteristics that affect how quickly new ideas spread. Innovations are adopted more readily, he argued, when their advantages over existing practices are clear; when they are compatible with people's existing values and habits; when they are simple to understand and use; when they can be tried on a small scale; and when their results are visible to others. An innovation that fails on several of these criteria may spread slowly, however beneficial it ultimately proves to be.

Rogers also emphasised the role of social networks. Innovations typically spread first among a small group of early adopters, who tend to be well connected and willing to take risks, and then more gradually among the majority. The opinions of respected individuals within a community can be more influential than scientific evidence. An innovation promoted by an outsider, or one that seems to challenge the status or expertise of established professionals, may meet resistance regardless of its merits.

These ideas help to explain more recent cases. Simple, inexpensive measures to improve health – such as the use of salt and sugar solutions to treat dehydration from diarrhoea – have sometimes spread slowly, not because they were ineffective, but because they required changes in behaviour, conflicted with local beliefs about illness, or were promoted without the involvement of trusted local figures. Where programmes worked through community health workers and local leaders, adoption was often much faster.

The lesson is not that evidence is unimportant, but that evidence alone is rarely sufficient. How an innovation is communicated, who promotes it, and how well it fits into existing practices can matter as much as how well it works.

passages.topic: Medicine and economics — why so few new antibiotics are developed
passages.title: The Missing Medicines

paragraphs.text: Antibiotics transformed medicine in the twentieth century. Infections that had once been frequently fatal became easily treatable, and antibiotics made possible many other medical advances, from major surgery to cancer chemotherapy, which leave patients vulnerable to infection. Yet bacteria evolve. Whenever antibiotics are used, bacteria that happen to be resistant survive and multiply, and over time, infections that were once easily treated have become resistant to many drugs. Health organisations regard antimicrobial resistance as one of the most serious threats to global health.

One might expect that such a threat would stimulate intense efforts to develop new antibiotics. Instead, the number of new antibiotics reaching the market has fallen considerably since the peak decades of discovery in the mid-twentieth century, and many large pharmaceutical companies have stopped research in the area altogether. Several small companies that succeeded in developing new antibiotics have gone bankrupt shortly afterwards.

The reason lies in the unusual economics of antibiotics. Developing any new medicine is expensive and risky, often costing hundreds of millions of dollars. Companies usually recover these costs by selling large quantities of a successful drug. But new antibiotics are, rightly, used as little as possible. To slow the development of resistance, doctors keep them in reserve for patients with infections that do not respond to older drugs. A new antibiotic may therefore be medically vital yet sold in very small quantities, generating far less revenue than a medicine for a long-term condition such as high blood pressure, which patients may take every day for many years.

Scientific difficulties add to the problem. The easiest antibiotics to discover – many of which were found in soil microorganisms – were identified decades ago. Finding new compounds that can penetrate bacterial cells, particularly those of certain types of bacteria with protective outer layers, and that are safe for patients, has proved extremely difficult. Many promising candidates fail in testing.

Governments and international organisations have therefore sought new ways of encouraging antibiotic development. Some offer "push" incentives, such as grants that fund early research and reduce the cost to companies. Economists have argued, however, that "pull" incentives, which reward companies for successfully bringing a useful antibiotic to market, are also needed, because the main problem is the lack of revenue after approval rather than only the cost of research.

One such approach was introduced in the United Kingdom, where the national health service agreed to pay companies a fixed annual fee for access to certain new antibiotics, regardless of how much of the drug is actually used. This model, sometimes compared to a subscription, separates a company's income from the quantity of antibiotics sold. It aims to reward companies for making valuable drugs available, while allowing doctors to use them sparingly.

Such schemes are still at an early stage, and their costs and effectiveness are being studied. Many experts argue that they will only succeed if adopted by several large countries together, since the global market for any single antibiotic is shared. Meanwhile, efforts to reduce unnecessary use of existing antibiotics – in human medicine and in farming, where they are sometimes used to promote the growth of animals – remain essential to slowing the spread of resistance.

passages.topic: Psychology — what makes an expert?
passages.title: The Making of Expertise

paragraphs.text: What separates world-class performers – concert musicians, chess champions, elite athletes – from everyone else? For much of history, the usual answer was talent: some people were simply born with exceptional abilities. In the late twentieth century, a very different answer became influential.

In a study published in 1993, the psychologist K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues examined violin students at a music academy in Berlin. Teachers were asked to identify students who were likely to become international soloists, those who were very good, and those likely to become music teachers. The researchers then asked the students to estimate how much time they had spent practising since childhood. By the age of eighteen, the best students had, on average, accumulated considerably more hours of practice – several thousand more – than those in the other groups.

Ericsson emphasised that not all practice is equally useful. What mattered, he argued, was "deliberate practice": focused, effortful activity designed specifically to improve performance, usually guided by a teacher, with clear goals and immediate feedback. Simply repeating familiar pieces or playing for enjoyment did not count. Deliberate practice, he suggested, is demanding and often not enjoyable, which is why relatively few people sustain it for long enough to reach the highest levels.

The research was popularised in a best-selling book published in 2008, which presented a figure of about ten thousand hours of practice as the requirement for mastery in any field. The "ten-thousand-hour rule" became widely known. Ericsson himself later criticised this interpretation, pointing out that ten thousand hours was simply an approximate average for one group of violinists at a particular age, that the number of hours needed varied greatly between fields and individuals, and that the popular version often ignored the distinction between deliberate practice and simply spending time on an activity.

Other researchers have questioned how much of the difference between performers practice can explain. In 2014, a team combined the results of dozens of studies across several domains. They found that deliberate practice was consistently associated with better performance, but that it accounted for only part of the differences between individuals – a substantial part in games such as chess, but much less in fields such as professions and education. Factors such as the age at which people started, working memory, and other characteristics, some of which may be partly inherited, also appeared to matter.

Ericsson and his supporters disputed some of these conclusions, arguing that many of the studies included did not measure deliberate practice accurately. The debate has not been fully resolved. Most researchers now accept a middle position: practice, particularly well-designed practice, is essential for developing expertise, and few people reach high levels without a great deal of it; but people differ in how quickly they improve and in the level they can ultimately reach.

This conclusion has practical implications. It suggests that teachers and coaches should focus on the quality of practice rather than simply its quantity, and that people should not be discouraged from pursuing an activity because they do not show early talent. At the same time, it suggests that claims that anyone can become world-class in any field through practice alone are likely to be exaggerated.

passages.topic: Science history — the long struggle to forecast the weather
passages.title: Predicting the Sky

paragraphs.text: For most of history, weather forecasting relied on local knowledge and folk sayings: observations of clouds, winds and animal behaviour, passed down through generations. Some of these contained genuine insight, but none could predict the weather reliably more than a few hours ahead.

Scientific forecasting became possible only when observations from distant places could be gathered quickly. The invention of the electric telegraph in the mid-nineteenth century made this feasible for the first time. In Britain, Robert FitzRoy, a naval officer who had captained the ship on which Charles Darwin sailed around the world, established a system for collecting weather reports by telegraph from coastal stations. From 1861, he issued storm warnings to ports and published daily forecasts in newspapers – a word he is credited with popularising. His forecasts were often inaccurate, and they attracted ridicule in the press and criticism from scientists who considered them unscientific. After FitzRoy's death in 1865, the published forecasts were temporarily stopped, although storm warnings to shipping, which fishermen and sailors had found valuable, were soon restored.

In the early twentieth century, scientists began to argue that the atmosphere obeyed physical laws that could, in principle, be expressed as mathematical equations. If the current state of the atmosphere were known precisely, it should be possible to calculate its future state. The British mathematician Lewis Fry Richardson attempted to do exactly this. Working by hand during breaks while serving as an ambulance driver in the First World War, he spent many weeks calculating a forecast for a single six-hour period over a small area of Europe. The result, published in 1922, was wildly wrong, predicting a pressure change far larger than any that had ever been observed.

Richardson's failure was later found to result partly from errors in the initial data and from features of his calculations that amplified small errors. His basic approach, however, was sound. He had also recognised the practical problem: calculating a forecast by hand took far longer than the weather itself. He imagined a vast hall in which thousands of people would perform calculations simultaneously, coordinated by a conductor, to keep pace with the weather.

The solution came with electronic computers. In 1950, a team in the United States used one of the first computers to produce a successful numerical forecast, based on simplified equations. Over the following decades, as computers became more powerful and observations from weather balloons, aircraft and eventually satellites improved, numerical forecasting became the basis of modern weather prediction.

In the 1960s, the meteorologist Edward Lorenz discovered a fundamental limit. Running a simple weather model on a computer, he found that tiny differences in the starting values – so small that they could not be measured in practice – eventually produced completely different forecasts. The atmosphere, he concluded, is a "chaotic" system, in which small uncertainties grow over time. This means that detailed forecasts can never be made reliably beyond a certain period, perhaps around two weeks.

Modern forecasting responds to this limit by running a model many times with slightly different starting conditions, producing an "ensemble" of possible outcomes. If most runs agree, forecasters can be confident; if they differ widely, the forecast is uncertain, and this uncertainty can be expressed as a probability. Thanks to better observations, models and computers, forecasts today are far more accurate than those of a few decades ago: a forecast for five days ahead is now roughly as reliable as a one-day forecast was in the 1980s.

passages.topic: Economics and environment — managing shared resources
passages.title: The Commons Revisited

paragraphs.text: In 1968, the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay entitled "The Tragedy of the Commons", which became one of the most widely cited articles in the social sciences. Hardin asked readers to imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding an extra animal to the pasture but bears only a small share of the cost of overgrazing, which is spread among all users. Acting rationally in their own interests, each herder will therefore keep adding animals, until the pasture is destroyed. Hardin concluded that shared resources are doomed to overuse unless they are either controlled by government or divided into private property.

Hardin's argument was influential in shaping policy. Governments in various countries took control of forests, fisheries and grazing lands that had previously been managed by local communities, or divided them into privately owned plots. The results were not always as intended. In some cases, government control was weak and resources were exploited more heavily than before, since traditional community rules had been removed but nothing effective had replaced them.

The political scientist Elinor Ostrom challenged Hardin's conclusion on the basis of extensive fieldwork. Studying communities around the world – alpine pastures in Switzerland, forests in Japan, irrigation systems in Spain and Nepal, fisheries in Turkey – she found many examples of shared resources that had been managed sustainably, in some cases for centuries, without either government control or private ownership. The users themselves had developed rules governing who could use the resource, how much each could take, and how rules were enforced.

Ostrom identified a number of features that successful arrangements tended to share. The boundaries of the resource and the group of people entitled to use it were clearly defined. The rules were adapted to local conditions and were made, at least in part, by the users themselves. Users monitored one another's behaviour, and those who broke the rules faced penalties that increased with repeated offences. There were accessible, low-cost ways of resolving disputes, and external authorities recognised the community's right to organise itself.

Ostrom did not argue that communities always succeed. Many shared resources had indeed been overused, and her principles described the conditions under which cooperation was more likely, not a guarantee. Her key point was that Hardin's model rested on an assumption that did not always hold: that users could not communicate or make agreements with one another. In real communities, people talk, build trust and create institutions. In 2009, Ostrom became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in economics, largely for this work.

Her findings raise difficult questions for global resources such as the atmosphere or the high seas. These involve enormous numbers of users – entire nations – who do not share a community, cannot easily monitor one another, and have very different interests. Many of the conditions that Ostrom found in successful local cases are therefore absent. Nevertheless, some researchers have argued that her insights still apply: that global problems may be better tackled through many overlapping agreements at different levels, rather than waiting for a single global solution.

passages.topic: Economic geography — why cities stay where they are
passages.title: The Weight of History

paragraphs.text: Why are cities located where they are? Many of the world's great cities grew up at sites that offered clear advantages at the time of their founding: a natural harbour, a river crossing, fertile surrounding land, or a defensible hill. Over centuries, however, many of these original advantages have become irrelevant. Harbours have silted up, rivers are no longer major transport routes, and defence against attack no longer depends on hills. Yet the cities remain. Economists have become increasingly interested in why.

One influential study examined towns in the south-eastern United States that had grown up at "portage" sites – places where boats travelling along rivers had to be unloaded and their cargo carried overland past waterfalls or rapids. In the era of river transport, these sites were natural locations for trade, storage and processing, and towns developed around them. With the arrival of railways in the nineteenth century, river transport declined, and the original reason for the towns' existence disappeared. Yet the study found that these towns remained significantly larger than would otherwise be expected, and they continue to be important economic centres today.

Economists describe this phenomenon as "path dependence": the idea that where things are today depends heavily on where they were in the past, even when the original reasons no longer apply. Once a city has grown, it develops advantages of its own. Businesses locate there because other businesses and workers are already present; workers move there because jobs are available; and roads, pipes, buildings and other infrastructure represent enormous investments that would be costly to abandon. These self-reinforcing advantages can keep a city growing long after the circumstances of its founding have changed.

Other research has found evidence of path dependence over much longer periods. A study of the former Roman Empire found that areas with a dense network of Roman roads tended, many centuries later, to have greater economic activity – but only in some regions. In parts of the former empire where the use of wheeled vehicles declined sharply after Roman rule ended, and where roads fell into disuse for centuries, the connection between Roman roads and modern prosperity was much weaker. This suggests that historical advantages persist only if they continue to be used.

Path dependence also has implications for recovery from disaster. Studies of cities that were heavily bombed during the Second World War found that most recovered their previous size relative to other cities within a few decades, despite enormous destruction. This suggests that the advantages of a city's location and its economic networks can survive even the destruction of much of its physical fabric.

Not all cities endure, however. Towns that depended on a single industry, such as mining, have sometimes declined sharply or been abandoned when that industry ended, especially where they lacked other advantages. And the persistence of cities in their existing locations is not always beneficial. Some cities are located in places that are increasingly vulnerable to flooding, rising sea levels or water shortages, and the same forces that keep them in place may make adaptation to such risks more difficult and costly.

For planners and policymakers, path dependence suggests both caution and opportunity. Efforts to create entirely new cities in locations without existing advantages often struggle to attract people and businesses. On the other hand, investments that strengthen existing centres may produce benefits that reinforce themselves over long periods, shaping economic geography for generations.

lesson.title: Final review — the complete method
lesson.text:
This final set combines the main skills: abstract endings, several true-but-unrelated endings, reversed cause and effect, and beginnings that require you to combine information. For each beginning:

1. Locate the passage section.

2. Predict the ending in plain words.

3. Match your prediction to the abstract ending.

4. Confirm meaning, scope and grammar.

passages.topic: Food production — making maple syrup
passages.title: From Tree to Table

paragraphs.text: Maple syrup is produced almost entirely in north-eastern North America, where the sugar maple tree grows in large numbers. The Canadian province of Quebec alone produces around seventy per cent of the world's supply. Long before European settlers arrived, Indigenous peoples of the region collected the sweet liquid, or sap, from maple trees and boiled it to produce sugar, and they taught early settlers the technique.

Sap is collected in late winter and early spring. At this time of year, the trees respond to a particular pattern of weather: nights when temperatures fall below freezing, followed by days when they rise above it. During the cold nights, the tree draws water up from its roots; during the warmer days, pressure inside the tree increases and pushes the sap out through any opening in the bark. Without these alternating conditions, the sap does not flow well. The collecting season typically lasts only four to six weeks.

To collect sap, producers drill a small hole in the trunk of each tree and insert a spout, known as a tap. Traditionally, a metal bucket was hung below the tap to catch the dripping sap. Today, many large producers instead connect thousands of trees with networks of plastic tubing, which carry the sap directly to a central building called a sugar house. Some systems use pumps to create a vacuum in the tubes, which increases the amount of sap collected. A healthy tree can be tapped every year for many decades without being harmed, provided that the holes are not too large or too numerous.

Fresh sap is clear and watery and contains only about two to three per cent sugar. To turn it into syrup, most of the water must be removed. This is done by boiling the sap in a large, shallow pan called an evaporator, heated by wood, oil or gas. As the water evaporates, the sap becomes thicker and sweeter, and it develops its characteristic colour and flavour. On average, about forty litres of sap are needed to make just one litre of syrup, which explains why maple syrup is relatively expensive.

Many modern producers first pass the sap through a machine that uses reverse osmosis – forcing the liquid through a fine membrane – to remove a large proportion of the water before boiling. This greatly reduces the amount of fuel and time required. The final stage of boiling, however, is still necessary to develop the syrup's flavour.

Maple syrup is graded according to its colour and taste. Syrup produced early in the season tends to be lighter in colour and more delicate in flavour, while syrup produced later is darker and has a stronger taste. Scientists are concerned that warmer winters may affect the industry in future, since the freezing nights on which sap flow depends are becoming less reliable in some areas.

lesson.title: Predict the word type
lesson.text: Before looking at the passage, decide what kind of word fills each gap. "is collected in early..." needs a time word such as a season or month. "takes about ... litres of sap" needs a number. Knowing the word type helps you ignore nearby words of the wrong kind.

passages.topic: Sport history — the marathon
passages.title: The Long Run

paragraphs.text: The marathon, a running race of just over forty-two kilometres, is one of the most famous events in modern sport. Its name comes from a story set in ancient Greece. According to legend, after the Greeks defeated a Persian army at the Battle of Marathon in 490 BC, a messenger named Pheidippides ran from Marathon to Athens to announce the victory, then collapsed and died. Historians doubt whether the story is accurate; the earliest accounts of the battle do not mention such a run, and the legend appears in writings produced several centuries later.

When the modern Olympic Games were first held in Athens in 1896, the organisers included a long-distance race from Marathon to Athens, inspired by the legend. The distance was about forty kilometres. The race was won by Spyridon Louis, a Greek water carrier, whose victory made him a national hero. Following the success of the Olympic event, marathons were organised in other cities; the Boston Marathon, first held in 1897, is the oldest annual marathon still running.

For the first few Olympic Games, the length of the marathon varied. The current distance of 42.195 kilometres – or 26.2 miles – dates from the London Olympics of 1908. According to the most widely repeated account, the course was designed to start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box in the Olympic stadium, and this produced the unusual distance. It was officially adopted as the standard marathon distance in 1921.

For much of the twentieth century, women were excluded from marathon running, partly because of mistaken beliefs that long-distance running was dangerous for them. In 1967, a woman ran the Boston Marathon after registering using only her initials; officials tried to remove her from the race. Pressure for change grew, and the Boston Marathon officially allowed women to enter in 1972. A women's marathon was first included in the Olympic Games in 1984, in Los Angeles.

Since the 1970s, marathon running has grown from a specialist sport into a mass participation event. Major city marathons in London, New York, Berlin and elsewhere now attract tens of thousands of runners, most of whom are amateurs aiming simply to finish or to beat their own previous times. Many raise money for charity, and some large races have become among the biggest single-day fundraising events in the world.

At the elite level, times have fallen steadily. Improvements in training, nutrition and, more recently, shoe technology have all contributed. In 2019, the Kenyan runner Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run the marathon distance in under two hours, although the time was not recognised as an official record because the event used conditions not permitted in normal races, such as a rotating team of pacemakers.

lesson.title: Numbers close together
lesson.text: Sports and history passages contain many dates, distances and figures near each other. The question sentence usually paraphrases the context of the correct number: "the distance was fixed", "women were first allowed". Find the number whose context matches, not just the first number you see in that paragraph.

passages.topic: Wildlife — the emperor penguin's winter
passages.title: Winter Fathers

paragraphs.text: The emperor penguin is the largest of all penguins, standing more than a metre tall and weighing up to around forty kilograms. It is also the only animal that breeds during the Antarctic winter, when temperatures on the sea ice can fall below minus forty degrees Celsius and winds can exceed one hundred and fifty kilometres per hour.

In autumn, emperor penguins leave the sea and walk, sometimes for many kilometres, to traditional breeding sites on stable sea ice. There, after a period of courtship, each female lays a single egg. She then passes the egg carefully to her partner, who balances it on his feet and covers it with a fold of feathered skin called a brood pouch. If the egg touches the ice for more than a few moments, the developing chick will freeze and die.

Having laid the egg, the female returns to the sea to feed, since she has used up much of her energy producing it. The male stays behind and incubates the egg through the darkest and coldest part of the winter, for about two months. During this time he does not eat at all, surviving on the fat stored in his body. By the time the chick hatches, a male may have lost up to around forty per cent of his body weight.

To survive the cold, the males gather in large, tightly packed groups called huddles, in which thousands of birds may stand close together. The temperature inside a huddle can be much higher than the air outside. The huddle constantly moves: birds on the cold outer edge gradually work their way towards the warm centre, while those in the centre move outwards, so that each bird spends only a limited time exposed to the wind.

When the chick hatches, the male can feed it with a milky substance produced in his throat, which provides nourishment for a few days until the female returns. The female, now well fed, takes over the care of the chick and feeds it with food brought up from her stomach. The male, weak and thin, then walks to the sea to feed for the first time in about four months.

For the rest of the winter and spring, the parents take turns to travel to the sea and bring back food for the chick. As the chick grows, it joins other chicks in groups known as crèches, which provide warmth and some protection while both parents are away. By early summer, when the sea ice begins to break up, the young penguins have grown waterproof feathers and are ready to enter the sea.

Because emperor penguins depend on stable sea ice for breeding, scientists are concerned about the effects of rising temperatures. In recent years, some colonies have failed to raise any chicks when the ice broke up earlier than usual, before the young had developed their waterproof feathers.

lesson.title: ONE WORD ONLY
lesson.text: When the instruction says ONE WORD ONLY, you must find the single key word. Look especially for nouns. Articles (a, the) and adjectives must be left out unless the single word itself is the adjective the sentence needs.

passages.topic: Architecture and materials — building with bamboo
passages.title: The Green Steel

paragraphs.text: Bamboo is a type of grass, not a tree, but some species grow as tall as many trees and have woody stems strong enough to be used in construction. In parts of Asia, Latin America and Africa, it has been used for thousands of years to build houses, bridges and scaffolding. Because of its combination of strength and lightness, it is sometimes called "green steel".

One of bamboo's most remarkable features is the speed of its growth. Some species can grow by several centimetres per hour during their fastest growing period, and certain large species have been recorded growing almost a metre in a single day. Most timber trees take decades to reach a size suitable for building, whereas many bamboo species can be harvested for construction after only three to five years. When bamboo stems are cut, the plant is not killed; new shoots grow from the underground root system.

Bamboo stems are hollow tubes divided at intervals by solid sections called nodes, which strengthen them and prevent them from bending too easily. The fibres in the walls of the stem run lengthwise and are extremely strong when pulled, giving bamboo a tensile strength comparable in some tests to that of certain types of steel, relative to its weight. Its flexibility also allows bamboo structures to bend without breaking in high winds, and some have survived earthquakes that destroyed more rigid buildings.

Bamboo does, however, have disadvantages. Untreated bamboo is attractive to insects, particularly beetles, which feed on the starch it contains, and it can rot if exposed to moisture for long periods. As a result, untreated structures may last only a few years. Traditional methods of protection include soaking the stems in water for several weeks to remove starch, or smoking them over a fire. Modern treatments use solutions of salts that penetrate the stem and make it resistant to insects and fungi. Properly treated and protected from direct rain, bamboo buildings can last for many decades.

Bamboo is also difficult to use with standard building methods. Unlike sawn timber, each stem is slightly different in diameter and wall thickness, and its round, hollow shape makes joints difficult to construct. Many countries lack building codes that specify how bamboo should be used, which makes it harder for architects and engineers to gain approval for bamboo buildings.

In recent decades, some architects have demonstrated bamboo's potential in ambitious designs. The Colombian architect Simón Vélez has built large bamboo structures, including pavilions and bridges, developing a technique in which the hollow sections near joints are filled with concrete to strengthen them. In Indonesia and other countries, architects have constructed schools and houses from bamboo, and manufacturers have developed engineered bamboo products – strips of bamboo glued and pressed together to form boards and beams of uniform size.

Supporters argue that bamboo could play an important role in reducing the environmental impact of construction, since it absorbs carbon dioxide as it grows, regenerates quickly and requires much less energy to process than steel or concrete. Its widespread adoption will depend, however, on developing standards, training builders and changing the perception, common in some countries, that bamboo is a material for poor people.

lesson.title: Adjective + noun answers
lesson.text: Sometimes the gap needs a two-word phrase such as an adjective with a noun ("natural resistance", "steel reinforcement"). Check whether the sentence already contains the adjective. If it does, you need only the noun; if not, you may need both words. Reading the complete sentence aloud in your head helps you avoid duplication.
