passages.topic: Plant science — why leaves change colour in autumn
passages.title: Autumn Colours

paragraphs.text: In many temperate regions, the leaves of deciduous trees – those that lose their leaves each year – turn brilliant shades of yellow, orange and red in autumn before falling. The spectacle attracts large numbers of tourists to places such as New England in the United States, Canada and parts of East Asia. The science behind these colours involves several different chemical substances in the leaves.

During spring and summer, leaves are green because they contain large amounts of chlorophyll, the pigment that allows plants to capture energy from sunlight through photosynthesis. Chlorophyll is constantly being broken down and replaced during the growing season. In autumn, as days become shorter and temperatures fall, trees prepare to shed their leaves. They stop producing new chlorophyll and begin to recover useful nutrients from the leaves, such as nitrogen, which can be stored in the branches and roots over winter.

As the green chlorophyll disappears, other colours become visible. Yellow and orange colours come from pigments called carotenoids – the same substances that give carrots their colour. These pigments are present in the leaves throughout the summer, helping to capture light and protect the leaf from damage, but they are hidden by the much larger quantities of chlorophyll. When the chlorophyll breaks down, the carotenoids are revealed.

Red and purple colours have a different origin. They are produced by pigments called anthocyanins, which, unlike carotenoids, are not present in most leaves during the summer. Instead, many trees actively produce them in autumn. Scientists are still debating why trees would spend energy making new pigments in leaves that are about to fall. One widely discussed explanation is that anthocyanins act as a kind of sunscreen, protecting the leaf while the tree recovers nutrients from it. Another suggests that red leaves may discourage insects from laying eggs on the tree.

Weather strongly influences the brightness of autumn colours. The most vivid displays usually follow a period of sunny days and cool, but not freezing, nights. Sunny days allow the leaves to produce sugars, while cool nights prevent these sugars from moving out of the leaves; the high concentration of sugar encourages the production of anthocyanins. A severe early frost, by contrast, can kill the leaves before the colours develop fully, and drought can cause leaves to turn brown and fall early.

Eventually, a layer of cells forms at the base of each leaf stalk, gradually cutting off the flow of water to the leaf and weakening its connection to the branch. The leaf then falls, often helped by wind or rain. Once on the ground, the leaves are broken down by fungi, bacteria and small animals, returning nutrients to the soil.

lesson.title: Plural and singular
lesson.text: Check whether the sentence needs a singular or plural noun: "a ... called" needs a singular; "substances known as ..." needs a plural. Copy the word in the same form that appears in the passage, and make sure it fits the grammar of the sentence.

passages.topic: Transport history — the hovercraft
passages.title: Riding on Air

paragraphs.text: A hovercraft is a vehicle that travels on a cushion of air, allowing it to move over water, mud, ice, sand and flat ground. Because it does not touch the surface beneath it, it experiences very little friction, and it can pass from water onto land without stopping. These unusual abilities have made hovercraft useful for purposes as varied as passenger ferries, rescue operations and military landings.

The idea of reducing friction by using air had been explored by several engineers since the nineteenth century, but the first practical hovercraft was developed in Britain in the 1950s by the engineer Christopher Cockerell. Cockerell, who had previously worked on radio equipment and later ran a boat-building business, carried out experiments using a vacuum cleaner, a pair of tin cans and a set of kitchen scales, which he used to measure the lifting force. He found that blowing air into a space between two cans, one inside the other, produced a much stronger lifting force than simply blowing air downwards.

Cockerell patented his design in 1955. At first, he struggled to interest manufacturers or the government, partly because it was unclear whether the new vehicle was a ship or an aircraft. The military, however, became interested, and for a time the invention was treated as secret. In 1959, a full-sized experimental craft, the SR.N1, crossed the English Channel between England and France, attracting widespread public attention.

Early hovercraft had a significant limitation: the cushion of air leaked away at the edges, so they could hover only a short distance above the surface and had difficulty crossing waves or obstacles. The solution was the addition of a flexible rubber "skirt" around the base of the craft, which held the air in place and allowed the hovercraft to travel over much rougher water and higher obstacles.

In 1968, a regular hovercraft passenger service began across the English Channel. The largest craft could carry several hundred passengers and dozens of cars, and could cross in around thirty minutes – much faster than conventional ferries. The service operated for more than thirty years. It ended in 2000, as competition from the Channel Tunnel, which opened in 1994, and from larger, more economical ferries made it unprofitable. Hovercraft were also expensive to run, since they used large amounts of fuel, and they were noisy.

Although large passenger hovercraft are now rare, smaller hovercraft remain in use. They are particularly valuable for rescue services working in areas of mud, shallow water or ice, where boats and land vehicles cannot operate. Some armed forces use hovercraft to carry troops and equipment from ships directly onto beaches. A small number of passenger services continue, including one linking the south coast of England with the Isle of Wight.

lesson.title: Paraphrased verbs
lesson.text: The question sentence often uses a different verb from the passage: "was first tested" for "made its first crossing", "was used for" for "was employed in". Identify the verb in the sentence, think of synonyms, and scan for the matching idea. The answer word itself will come directly from the passage.

passages.topic: Climate science — reading history in ice
passages.title: Frozen Archives

paragraphs.text: The great ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland were formed from snow that fell over hundreds of thousands of years and was gradually compressed into ice. Because each year's snowfall is buried by the next, the ice forms layers, with the oldest at the bottom. By drilling deep into the ice and extracting long cylinders known as ice cores, scientists can study a record of past conditions stretching back far beyond the beginning of human written history.

The longest continuous ice-core records come from Antarctica, where snowfall is low and the ice is very thick. One core, drilled by a European team at a site called Dome C, reached ice around 800,000 years old, covering eight cycles of ice ages and warmer periods. Researchers are now attempting to find ice more than a million years old, which could help explain a change in the rhythm of ice ages that took place around that time.

Ice cores contain several kinds of evidence. Perhaps the most valuable are tiny bubbles of air. As snow is compressed into ice, pockets of air between the snow grains become sealed, preserving samples of the atmosphere at the time. By analysing these bubbles, scientists can measure how much carbon dioxide and methane the atmosphere contained in the past. The records show that concentrations of these gases rose and fell in close step with temperature through the cycles of ice ages, and that current concentrations of carbon dioxide are far higher than at any time in the period covered by the cores.

Past temperatures are estimated from the ice itself. Water molecules contain different forms, or isotopes, of hydrogen and oxygen, some heavier than others. The proportion of heavier isotopes in snow depends on the temperature at the time it fell: colder conditions produce snow with fewer heavy isotopes. By measuring these proportions layer by layer, scientists can reconstruct changes in temperature over long periods.

Ice cores also preserve evidence of specific events. Large volcanic eruptions release sulphur and fine ash, which fall onto the ice and form identifiable layers; these can be used to date the ice precisely and to study the effects of eruptions on climate. Dust carried by the wind from distant deserts is more abundant in ice from glacial periods, indicating that the climate was then drier and windier. Traces of lead pollution in Greenland ice even record the rise and fall of metal production in the ancient world.

Dating the ice presents challenges. In the upper parts of a core, annual layers can often be counted directly, much like tree rings. Deeper down, however, the enormous weight of the ice above squeezes the layers until they become too thin to distinguish, and the ice may also be disturbed by its flow over the rock beneath. Scientists therefore combine several methods, using volcanic layers and models of ice flow to estimate ages where layers cannot be counted.

Ice cores have become one of the most important sources of evidence about the relationship between greenhouse gases and climate. Because the ice sheets are themselves affected by warming, some scientists have also begun efforts to collect and store cores from mountain glaciers that are melting rapidly, preserving their records before the ice disappears.

lesson.title: When the sentence rephrases a whole idea
lesson.text: At Medium level, the question sentence often restates a whole idea in different words, so you cannot find it by matching keywords. Instead, ask: "Which part of the passage is this sentence about?" Use the order of questions and the topic of each paragraph. Once you have found the right sentence, identify the one or two words that fill the gap exactly.

passages.topic: History of medicine — the conquest of surgical pain
passages.title: The End of Agony

paragraphs.text: Before the middle of the nineteenth century, surgery was a terrifying experience. Patients were fully conscious during operations, held down by assistants while surgeons worked as quickly as possible. Speed was the surgeon's most valued skill: some could amputate a leg in under a minute. Alcohol and opium were sometimes given to dull pain, but they were of limited use, and many patients died from shock. Surgery was generally a last resort.

Substances that could relieve pain had been known for some time. In 1799, the young English chemist Humphry Davy experimented with nitrous oxide, a gas that made people feel euphoric and laugh uncontrollably, and which became known as "laughing gas". Davy noticed that it relieved the pain of an inflamed gum and suggested in a published work that it might be used during surgical operations. The suggestion was ignored. For decades, laughing gas was used mainly for entertainment at public shows and parties.

It was an American dentist, Horace Wells, who first tried to use nitrous oxide for dental surgery in the 1840s, after watching a man at a public show injure his leg without apparently feeling pain. Wells had one of his own teeth removed while breathing the gas and felt nothing. In 1845, however, a public demonstration at a hospital in Boston went badly: the patient cried out during the procedure, and the audience concluded that the method did not work.

The following year, in October 1846, a Boston dentist, William Morton, successfully demonstrated the use of a different substance, ether, at the same hospital. A patient had a tumour removed from his neck while unconscious and later reported feeling no pain. The operation was widely reported, and news of the discovery spread rapidly across the Atlantic. Within months, surgeons in Britain and Europe were using ether.

Ether had drawbacks: it irritated the lungs, caused vomiting and was highly flammable – a serious danger in operating rooms lit by candles and gas lamps. In 1847, the Scottish doctor James Young Simpson, searching for an alternative, discovered that chloroform could produce unconsciousness more quickly and pleasantly. He and his colleagues tested it by inhaling it themselves at a dinner party, and woke up to find themselves on the floor. Chloroform soon became widely used, particularly in Britain.

Some people initially opposed the use of anaesthetics in childbirth, arguing that pain was natural or even morally necessary. Opposition weakened considerably after 1853, when the physician John Snow administered chloroform to Queen Victoria during the birth of her eighth child. The Queen described the effect as "soothing, quieting and delightful", and her example made pain relief in childbirth socially acceptable.

The arrival of anaesthesia changed surgery profoundly. Surgeons no longer needed to work at great speed and could attempt longer and more complex operations. However, the number of deaths after surgery did not immediately fall, because infections remained common; it was only after the introduction of antiseptic methods later in the century that surgery became much safer.

lesson.title: People and substances in close sequence
lesson.text: When a passage introduces several people and substances in quick succession, a sentence may describe one person's achievement with another's substance nearby. Before writing an answer, confirm that the person, date and substance in the sentence all match the same passage sentence.

passages.topic: Animal behaviour — the dance language of honeybees
passages.title: Directions by Dance

paragraphs.text: When a honeybee worker discovers a rich source of food, such as a field of flowers, she returns to the hive and communicates its location to her nestmates. The way she does this was explained in the mid-twentieth century by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who spent decades studying bees and was awarded a Nobel Prize in 1973 for his work. Von Frisch showed that bees perform "dances" on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, and that the form of the dance conveys information about the direction and distance of the food.

If the food is close to the hive – within roughly fifty metres – the bee performs a simple "round dance", moving in small circles, first in one direction and then the other. This tells other bees that food is nearby, but not in which direction. The other bees leave the hive and search the surrounding area, guided partly by the scent of the flowers carried on the dancer's body.

For food further away, the bee performs the more complex "waggle dance". She runs in a straight line while rapidly shaking her abdomen from side to side, then circles back to her starting point, alternately to the left and right, and repeats the straight run. The straight "waggle run" contains the key information.

The direction of the waggle run indicates the direction of the food in relation to the sun. Because the dance takes place in the dark hive on a vertical surface, the bees use gravity as a reference: straight up on the comb represents the direction of the sun. If the waggle run points straight upwards, the food lies directly towards the sun; if it points at an angle of forty degrees to the right of vertical, the food lies forty degrees to the right of the sun's direction.

The duration of the waggle run indicates distance: the longer the run lasts, the further away the food. Bees appear to judge distance by the amount of visual movement they experience while flying – the "optical flow" of the landscape passing beneath them – rather than by the energy they use. Experiments in which bees were trained to fly through narrow tunnels lined with patterns, which exaggerate optical flow, led them to signal distances much greater than they had actually travelled.

Von Frisch's interpretation was at first controversial. Some researchers argued that bees found food by smell alone and that the dance was not necessary. The debate was largely settled by later experiments, including one in which researchers used a small robotic bee to perform dances; real bees followed the robot's directions to locations where no food had been placed. More recently, researchers have used radar to track individual bees after they have watched a dance, confirming that they fly in the indicated direction.

Scientists have also found that the dance is not perfectly precise, since the directions indicated in successive waggle runs vary slightly. Some researchers suggest this imprecision may be useful, spreading recruits over a patch of flowers rather than sending them all to exactly the same point.

lesson.title: THREE WORDS limits
lesson.text: With a three-word limit, answers may be short noun phrases ("the waggle run", "angle to the sun"). Take only the words needed to complete the meaning: articles are optional where the sentence already has one. Check that your phrase does not repeat any word already in the sentence.

Complete the sentences below.
Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage for each answer.

questions.text: Von Frisch showed that bees dance on the ______ of the honeycomb.

questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: The round dance is used when food is found within about ______ of the hive.
questions.evidence: within roughly fifty metres.
questions.explanation: "Roughly" = "about", which is already in the sentence.

questions.text: In the waggle dance, the essential information is contained in the ______ .
questions.evidence: The straight 'waggle run' contains the key information.
questions.explanation: This is two or three words. "Key" = "essential".

questions.text: On the honeycomb, the direction of the sun is represented by ______ .

questions.explanation: "Represents" is already in the sentence as "represented by".

questions.text: Bees seem to measure distance using the ______ they see while flying.
questions.evidence: the 'optical flow' of the landscape passing beneath them.
questions.explanation: The alternative, "energy they use", is explicitly rejected in the passage.

questions.text: Bees trained in patterned tunnels signalled distances that were much ______ than the true distance.
questions.evidence: signal distances much greater than they had actually travelled.

passages.topic: Engineering and trade — the Suez Canal
passages.title: The Shortcut Between Seas

paragraphs.text: The Suez Canal, running through Egypt from the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea, is one of the most important waterways in the world. By allowing ships to travel between Europe and Asia without sailing around the southern tip of Africa, it shortens the journey between, for example, northern Europe and India by several thousand kilometres. A significant share of world trade passes through it each year.

The idea of connecting the two seas is ancient. Canals linking the Nile to the Red Sea were built and rebuilt in antiquity, but these fell into disuse. The modern canal was the work of a company led by the French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, who obtained permission from the ruler of Egypt in the 1850s. Construction began in 1859 and took ten years, employing tens of thousands of labourers. In its early years, much of the digging was done by hand by workers who were forced to take part; later, steam-powered machinery was introduced.

The canal opened in November 1869, with grand ceremonies attended by European royalty. Unlike the later Panama Canal, it has no locks: because the Mediterranean and Red Sea are at roughly the same level, water flows freely along its length. The canal was originally about 164 kilometres long and only eight metres deep, but it has been widened, deepened and lengthened several times, and it now extends for approximately 193 kilometres.

The canal quickly became of great strategic and economic importance, particularly to Britain, whose trade with India depended on it. In 1875, facing financial difficulties, the Egyptian ruler sold his shares in the canal company, and they were bought by the British government. Control of the canal became a source of international tension for many decades, culminating in a crisis in 1956 after Egypt nationalised the canal company.

Because large parts of the canal are too narrow for ships to pass one another, vessels travel in convoys, moving in one direction at a time and passing each other in designated wider sections or in lakes along the route. In 2015, a new parallel channel was opened along part of the canal, allowing ships to travel in both directions simultaneously over that section and reducing waiting times.

The canal's importance was vividly demonstrated in March 2021, when a giant container ship, the Ever Given, became stuck diagonally across the canal after being blown off course by strong winds. For six days, no ships could pass. Hundreds of vessels waited at either end, and some shipping companies decided to send their ships around Africa instead. The blockage delayed deliveries of goods around the world and caused significant financial losses. The ship was eventually freed by a combination of dredging and tugboats, helped by a high tide.

The incident prompted discussion about the vulnerability of global supply chains, which depend on a small number of narrow passages such as the Suez Canal. It also raised questions about the ever-increasing size of container ships, which can carry more goods at lower cost per container, but which are harder to manoeuvre in confined waterways.

lesson.title: ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER
lesson.text: With the instruction ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER, possible answers are a single word (locks), a single number (1869), or a number with one word (193 kilometres). A phrase of two words without a number is not allowed. When a measurement is needed, include the unit only if the sentence does not already contain it.

questions.evidence: it now extends for approximately 193 kilometres.

passages.topic: Architecture and physics — the acoustics of concert halls
passages.title: The Sound of a Room

paragraphs.text: Why do some concert halls sound wonderful and others disappointing? For most of history, the design of halls for music relied on tradition and trial and error. Some older buildings happened to sound excellent, while others, despite impressive architecture, were criticised by musicians and audiences. Only at the end of the nineteenth century did the science of room acoustics begin to develop.

The founder of modern architectural acoustics is generally considered to be Wallace Clement Sabine, a young physics lecturer at Harvard University. In 1895, he was asked to improve the sound in a new university lecture hall, where speech was almost impossible to understand. Working at night, when the building was quiet, Sabine measured how long it took for a sound to fade away after its source had stopped – a quantity now known as reverberation time. He moved cushions from a nearby theatre in and out of the hall to observe how absorbent materials affected the result. He discovered a simple mathematical relationship between the volume of a room, the amount of absorbent material within it, and its reverberation time.

Sabine's work showed that different purposes require different reverberation times. For speech, a short reverberation time is best, since echoes from each word blur into the next. For orchestral music, a longer reverberation time – typically around two seconds – gives the sound a sense of warmth and fullness. Sabine applied his findings to the design of Boston's Symphony Hall, which opened in 1900 and is still regarded as one of the best-sounding concert halls in the world.

Boston Symphony Hall followed a traditional rectangular design sometimes called the "shoebox" shape, also found in other highly regarded halls such as the Musikverein in Vienna, completed in 1870. Researchers have found that the narrow width of such halls is important: sound reflected from the side walls reaches listeners from the side shortly after the direct sound, producing a sense of being surrounded by the music, which listeners tend to prefer.

In the twentieth century, architects experimented with new shapes. One influential example is the Berlin Philharmonie, opened in 1963, which introduced a design in which the orchestra is placed near the centre of the hall and the audience sits around it in groups of terraced seating – a layout often called the "vineyard" style, because the terraces resemble the slopes of a vineyard. This arrangement brings listeners closer to the performers and gives the hall a more intimate atmosphere. Because it lacks nearby side walls for many seats, the terraces themselves are designed to reflect sound towards listeners.

Not all modern halls have been successful. Several large halls built in the mid-twentieth century were criticised for poor acoustics and had to be expensively renovated. Today, acousticians use computer simulations and scale models, sometimes built at one-tenth of the full size, to test how sound will behave before a hall is built. Even so, the final result can only be judged when the hall is complete and filled with an audience, whose bodies and clothing absorb sound.

lesson.title: Technical terms introduced in the passage
lesson.text: Science passages often introduce a special term and define it ("known as reverberation time", "so-called vineyard style"). Questions may describe the concept in plain words and ask for the term, or use the term and ask for part of its definition. Notice both halves of each definition as you read.

passages.topic: Industry and environment — aluminium from ore to recycling
passages.title: The Metal That Returns

paragraphs.text: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, yet for most of history it was almost unknown in its pure form. It never occurs naturally as a metal but only combined with other elements, from which it is extremely difficult to separate. In the mid-nineteenth century, small quantities could be produced by expensive chemical methods, and aluminium was considered a precious metal. According to a frequently told story, the French emperor Napoleon III served his most honoured guests with aluminium cutlery, while less important guests had to make do with gold.

This changed in 1886, when two young scientists – Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Héroult in France – independently discovered a practical method of producing aluminium using electricity. The process, still used today, involves dissolving aluminium oxide in a bath of molten material and passing a powerful electric current through it, causing pure aluminium to collect at the bottom. The oxide itself is obtained from bauxite, a reddish rock mined mainly in tropical regions such as Australia, Guinea and Brazil.

The electrical process made aluminium far cheaper, but it requires enormous amounts of energy. Aluminium smelters are among the largest consumers of electricity in the world, and they are often located near sources of cheap power, such as large hydroelectric stations. As a result, the environmental impact of producing aluminium depends heavily on how the electricity is generated.

Aluminium's properties have made it one of the most widely used metals. It is light, about one-third the weight of steel for the same volume, resists corrosion because a thin protective layer of oxide forms on its surface, and conducts electricity and heat well. It is used in aircraft, cars, window frames, electrical cables, cooking foil and, most familiarly, drinks cans.

One of aluminium's greatest advantages is that it can be recycled repeatedly without any loss of quality. Recycling aluminium requires only around five per cent of the energy needed to produce new aluminium from bauxite – a saving of approximately ninety-five per cent. It is estimated that a large proportion of all the aluminium ever produced is still in use today. In some countries, a used drinks can may be collected, melted down, made into a new can, filled and returned to shop shelves in as little as sixty days.

Recycling rates, however, vary widely between products and countries. Drinks cans are recycled at high rates in many places, especially where deposit schemes pay consumers to return them. Aluminium in other products, such as foil or items combining aluminium with plastic, is recycled less often because it is harder to separate. As demand for aluminium continues to grow – particularly for lightweight vehicles and electrical equipment – increasing recycling is seen as essential to reducing the industry's energy use and emissions.

lesson.title: Comparisons and percentages
lesson.text: Sentences may test comparisons: "Recycling uses about ... less energy than...". Make sure your answer expresses the same comparison as the passage, and that the figure refers to the correct things being compared. A percentage in the passage may describe savings in one sentence and share of production in the next.

passages.topic: Biology — lichens, partnerships of survival
passages.title: Living Together

paragraphs.text: Lichens are found almost everywhere on land: on rocks, tree bark, walls, roofs and gravestones, and in environments ranging from deserts to the Arctic. Although they are often mistaken for plants or mosses, lichens are not single organisms at all. Each lichen is a partnership between a fungus and one or more organisms that can make their own food through photosynthesis – usually green algae or a type of bacterium called cyanobacteria.

In this partnership, the fungus provides the structure and shelter. It forms the body of the lichen, anchors it to its surface, and protects the partner organisms from drying out and from strong sunlight. In return, the algae or cyanobacteria produce sugars through photosynthesis, which feed the fungus. Neither partner could survive alone in many of the harsh places where lichens grow. The relationship is often cited as a classic example of symbiosis – a close, long-term relationship between different species.

Lichens are remarkably tough. Many can survive being completely dried out for long periods, becoming active again within minutes when moisture returns. Some species survive extreme cold, and experiments have shown that certain lichens can remain alive after exposure to conditions resembling those of outer space. This resilience allows lichens to colonise bare rock where no other organisms can live, and by slowly breaking down the rock surface, they contribute to the formation of soil.

Most lichens grow very slowly, some by only a fraction of a millimetre each year. Because the growth rates of certain species are known, scientists can estimate how long a rock surface has been exposed – for example, after a glacier has retreated – by measuring the size of the largest lichens growing on it. This technique, known as lichenometry, is useful for dating surfaces that are too recent for other methods, although its accuracy depends on local conditions.

Lichens are also valuable indicators of air quality. Because they absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain, rather than through roots, they are highly sensitive to air pollution, particularly sulphur dioxide. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, many lichen species disappeared from industrial cities in Europe. As air quality improved in the late twentieth century following reductions in coal burning, lichens gradually returned. Scientists now use surveys of lichen species to monitor pollution, since different species tolerate different levels.

Humans have used lichens in many ways. Some species were traditionally used to produce dyes for wool and cloth; in some regions, lichens have been eaten, especially in times of famine; and reindeer in Arctic regions depend on lichens as a major source of winter food. Chemicals extracted from lichens have also been studied for possible medical uses.

Recent research has complicated the traditional picture of lichens as a partnership between just two organisms. In 2016, scientists reported that many lichens also contain a previously unrecognised type of yeast living within the fungal structure, suggesting that the relationship may be more complex than had been believed for over a century.

lesson.title: Distractors in lists
lesson.text: When the passage lists several items ("rocks, tree bark, walls and gravestones"), the sentence usually points to one of them through extra detail, for example "surfaces that humans have made". Read the question sentence closely for the clue that selects one item from the list.

passages.topic: Technology history — why keyboards are arranged as they are
passages.title: The Keyboard Puzzle

paragraphs.text: Almost every computer keyboard used for English – and many used for other languages – arranges its letters in the same pattern, known as QWERTY after the first six letters of the top row. The layout seems strange: common letters are scattered, and many frequent combinations require awkward finger movements. Why, then, has it survived for so long?

The layout originated in the 1870s with the typewriter developed by the American inventor Christopher Latham Sholes and his partners. Early typewriters had a mechanical problem: each key was connected to a metal arm, and if two arms next to each other were struck in quick succession, they could collide and jam. A popular explanation holds that Sholes deliberately arranged the letters to slow typists down and so reduce jamming.

Historians who have studied Sholes's patents and correspondence have questioned this account. They suggest that the aim was not to slow typists down but to separate letter pairs that frequently occur together, so that their arms would not be next to each other in the machine. Some researchers have also argued that the layout was influenced by the needs of telegraph operators, who were among the earliest users of typewriters and who transcribed messages sent in Morse code.

Whatever its origin, QWERTY became established when a major manufacturer adopted it in 1873, and typing schools began to train students on it. As more typists learned the layout, manufacturers had strong reasons to keep it, and new typists had strong reasons to learn it. Economists often cite QWERTY as an example of "path dependence" or "lock-in": once a standard becomes widely adopted, it can persist even if better alternatives appear, because switching would be costly for everyone involved.

The best-known alternative was designed in the 1930s by the American educational psychologist August Dvorak. His layout placed the most common letters in the middle row, where the fingers naturally rest, and arranged letters so that typing alternated between the hands as much as possible. Dvorak claimed that typists using his keyboard could type much faster and with less fatigue, and he conducted studies that appeared to support this.

Later researchers have been more sceptical. Some of Dvorak's studies were designed and conducted by Dvorak himself, who had a financial interest in his invention, and some later comparisons found only small differences in speed, which were difficult to separate from differences in training. A few economists have argued that the QWERTY story has been exaggerated as an example of lock-in, since the evidence that alternative layouts are substantially better is weaker than often claimed.

Today, as computers and phones no longer have mechanical arms that can jam, keyboards could in principle use any layout. Many devices even allow users to change the layout with a few clicks. Yet QWERTY remains dominant – a reminder that the persistence of a technology may depend as much on people's habits and skills as on its technical merits.

lesson.title: Claims vs evidence in completion tasks
lesson.text: Sentences may report either a popular claim or the evidence that tests it. Read the sentence's framing ("according to a popular explanation...", "later research found that...") and find the matching part of the passage. The same topic may yield different answers depending on whose view the sentence reports.

passages.topic: Animal communication — elephants and infrasound
passages.title: Voices Below Hearing

paragraphs.text: Elephants are highly social animals that live in family groups led by older females and maintain relationships with other groups over large areas. For a long time, researchers were puzzled by how scattered groups seemed to coordinate their movements, sometimes changing direction simultaneously while kilometres apart and out of sight of one another. Part of the answer emerged in the 1980s, when researchers discovered that elephants communicate extensively using sounds too low for humans to hear.

Sounds are described by their frequency, measured in hertz – the number of sound waves per second. Human hearing typically ranges from around twenty hertz to twenty thousand hertz. Sounds below this range are known as infrasound. In 1984, the American researcher Katy Payne, who had previously studied the songs of humpback whales, was observing elephants at a zoo in the United States when she noticed a faint throbbing sensation in the air, rather like the vibration felt near a large organ pipe. Suspecting that the elephants were producing sounds below the range of human hearing, she and her colleagues returned with recording equipment capable of detecting such sounds and confirmed her suspicion.

Elephants produce these low-frequency calls, often called "rumbles", using their large vocal folds, and some rumbles contain components well below twenty hertz. Low-frequency sounds lose less energy than high-frequency sounds as they travel, and are less easily blocked by vegetation. As a result, elephant rumbles can be detected by other elephants over distances of several kilometres – further in the cool, still air of evening and night, when atmospheric conditions allow sound to travel more effectively.

Field studies in Africa showed that rumbles serve many purposes. Females signal when they are ready to mate, and males respond from considerable distances. Family members separated while feeding use rumbles to keep in contact, and specific calls are associated with warnings of danger and with coordinating departures. Individual elephants appear to recognise the calls of family members and close associates, responding differently to them than to the calls of unfamiliar elephants.

Researchers later found that elephants may also detect vibrations travelling through the ground. Low-frequency calls and the stamping of feet produce seismic waves that can travel through the earth. Elephants have sensitive receptors in their feet and trunks, and in experiments, they responded to recorded seismic signals played through the ground, sometimes freezing and leaning forward on their front feet, a posture that may improve their ability to detect such vibrations. Seismic signals may travel even further than airborne sounds under some conditions, although how much elephants rely on them in the wild is still being investigated.

Understanding elephant communication has practical applications. Acoustic monitoring – placing recording devices in forests – allows researchers to estimate the number of elephants in areas where dense vegetation makes counting them by sight nearly impossible. Recorders can also detect gunshots, helping to identify illegal hunting. Some researchers have explored whether recordings of warning calls could be used to discourage elephants from entering farmland, reducing conflict between elephants and farmers.

passages.topic: Natural hazards — warning of tsunamis
passages.title: Racing the Wave

paragraphs.text: A tsunami is a series of ocean waves caused by a sudden movement of large volumes of water, most often as a result of an undersea earthquake that lifts or drops a section of the sea floor. In the deep ocean, a tsunami may be less than a metre high and pass unnoticed beneath ships, yet it can travel at speeds comparable to those of a jet aircraft. As it approaches shallow coastal waters, it slows down and its height increases dramatically, sometimes reaching tens of metres.

Because tsunamis can cross entire oceans, a coastline may be struck many hours after the earthquake that caused it. This creates both a danger and an opportunity: if a tsunami can be detected and its arrival predicted, people can be warned to move to higher ground. For coasts close to the earthquake, however, the first waves may arrive within minutes, leaving very little time for official warnings. In such places, residents are taught to treat strong or long-lasting earthquake shaking as a natural warning and to move inland immediately without waiting for an alert.

The first organised warning system was established in the Pacific Ocean in 1949, after a tsunami generated by an earthquake near Alaska caused many deaths in Hawaii. For decades, the system relied mainly on seismic data: when a large undersea earthquake was detected, warnings were issued based on its size and location. This approach had an important weakness. Not every large undersea earthquake produces a significant tsunami, and warnings based on seismic data alone led to many false alarms. After repeated evacuations for waves that proved harmless, some people began to ignore warnings.

To address this problem, scientists developed ways of detecting tsunamis directly in the open ocean. The most important is a network of deep-ocean sensors that sit on the sea floor and measure changes in water pressure. When a tsunami passes overhead, the increased height of the water column produces a small but measurable rise in pressure. The sensor transmits the data by sound to a buoy at the surface, which relays it via satellite to warning centres. This allows forecasters to confirm whether a tsunami has been generated and to estimate its size.

The devastating tsunami in the Indian Ocean on 26 December 2004 exposed the lack of a warning system in that region. The earthquake off the coast of Sumatra was one of the most powerful ever recorded, and the resulting waves struck coastlines in more than a dozen countries, some several hours later. Scientists in the Pacific detected the earthquake, but there was no system in place to communicate warnings to the affected countries, and around 230,000 people died. Following the disaster, an Indian Ocean warning system was established, and systems in other regions were strengthened.

Technology alone cannot guarantee safety. Warnings must reach people quickly and in a form they understand, which requires effective communication systems, such as sirens and mobile phone alerts, and public education. Evacuation routes must be clearly marked, and in low-lying areas without natural high ground, some communities have built vertical evacuation structures – strong, tall buildings designed for people to climb. Researchers emphasise that the "last mile" – delivering warnings to individuals and ensuring they respond appropriately – is often the weakest part of the warning chain.

lesson.title: Sentences that combine information from different places
lesson.text: A Hard sentence may combine a fact from one paragraph with a condition from another. Locate the sentence using its most distinctive element first, then check that the answer is consistent with the whole sentence. The question order still follows the passage, but one question may need you to glance back at an earlier paragraph.

passages.topic: Science methods — how radiocarbon dating works
passages.title: Clocks in Carbon

paragraphs.text: Radiocarbon dating, developed by the American chemist Willard Libby in the late 1940s, transformed archaeology by allowing the age of organic materials – wood, bone, charcoal, shells, cloth and seeds – to be measured directly. Libby received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960 for the method, which is now used in fields ranging from geology to art history.

The method depends on a rare, unstable form of carbon known as carbon-14. It is produced continuously in the upper atmosphere when cosmic rays from space strike nitrogen atoms. Carbon-14 combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide, which mixes through the atmosphere and is taken up by plants during photosynthesis. Animals then absorb it by eating plants or other animals. As a result, all living things contain carbon-14 in roughly the same proportion to ordinary carbon as the atmosphere does.

When an organism dies, it stops taking in new carbon. The carbon-14 already in its tissues gradually decays, changing back into nitrogen at a steady rate. Half of the carbon-14 in a sample decays in about 5,730 years – a period known as its half-life. After another 5,730 years, half of the remainder decays, and so on. By measuring how much carbon-14 remains in a sample relative to ordinary carbon, scientists can calculate how long ago the organism died. After about 50,000 years, too little carbon-14 remains to be measured reliably, which sets an upper limit on the method.

Libby's original method assumed that the proportion of carbon-14 in the atmosphere had always been constant. Later research showed that this was not the case: the amount has varied over time, owing to changes in the Earth's magnetic field and in solar activity, which affect the number of cosmic rays reaching the atmosphere. Radiocarbon ages therefore need to be corrected, or "calibrated". Calibration uses samples of known age – most importantly tree rings, which can be dated to the exact year by counting, as well as layered lake sediments and cave formations – to produce a curve that converts radiocarbon measurements into calendar dates.

Early radiocarbon laboratories needed relatively large samples, since they measured carbon-14 by detecting the particles given off as it decayed, a slow process. From the late 1970s, a new technique called accelerator mass spectrometry allowed scientists to count carbon-14 atoms directly. This required samples a thousand times smaller, making it possible to date precious objects, such as fragments of ancient manuscripts or single seeds, with minimal damage.

Human activity has also affected carbon-14 levels. The burning of fossil fuels, which contain no carbon-14 because they are millions of years old, has diluted the proportion in the atmosphere. By contrast, nuclear weapons tests in the 1950s and early 1960s nearly doubled the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere for a time. This "bomb pulse" has declined since testing largely stopped, but it has found an unexpected use: because atmospheric levels changed rapidly and are well recorded, scientists can use it to date materials formed since the 1950s with great precision – for example, to estimate the age of human cells or to detect forged artworks that claim to be older.

lesson.title: Process explanations with conditions
lesson.text: Technical passages explain processes with conditions ("only while an organism is alive", "after death, no new ... is taken in"). Sentences may test the condition rather than the main process. Read carefully for words like only, after, until, once, as long as, since the answer often sits next to them.

Complete the sentences below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.

questions.text: Carbon-14 is formed when ______ hit nitrogen atoms in the upper atmosphere.
questions.evidence: when cosmic rays from space strike nitrogen atoms.
questions.explanation: "Strike" = "hit".

questions.text: Living things obtain carbon-14 only as long as they continue to take in new ______ .
questions.evidence: When an organism dies, it stops taking in new carbon.
questions.explanation: This is the condition. "New" is already in the sentence.

questions.text: The time taken for half of the carbon-14 in a sample to decay is called its ______ .

questions.text: Levels of carbon-14 have varied partly because of changes in the Earth's ______ and in solar activity.
questions.evidence: changes in the Earth's magnetic field and in solar activity.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: The most important material used for calibration is ______, which can be dated exactly.
questions.evidence: most importantly tree rings, which can be dated to the exact year.
questions.explanation: "Most importantly" identifies the answer among the three materials listed.

questions.text: Because they are very old, fossil fuels contain no ______ .
questions.evidence: fossil fuels, which contain no carbon-14 because they are millions of years old.
questions.explanation: This is a hyphenated term plus a number, within the limit.

passages.topic: Safety science — understanding dangerous crowds
passages.title: The Physics of Crowds

paragraphs.text: Disasters in which people are crushed or trampled in crowds have occurred at religious gatherings, sports stadiums, concerts and festivals around the world. Such events are often described as "stampedes", a word that suggests panicking people running wildly and trampling others. Researchers who study crowd safety argue that this description is usually misleading. In most crowd disasters, the fundamental problem is not panic but density: too many people in too small a space.

Studies of crowds have found that people can move comfortably when there is plenty of space around them. As density increases, movement slows. At around four to five people per square metre, individuals can no longer move freely and begin to be pushed involuntarily by those around them. At still higher densities – above about six people per square metre – a dangerous phenomenon can occur, known as "crowd turbulence". Forces are transmitted through the tightly packed crowd in waves, so that people are pushed several metres in one direction and then another, unable to control their own movement.

In such conditions, the combined pressure from many bodies can become enormous. Most deaths in crowd disasters are caused not by trampling but by compressive asphyxia: people are squeezed so tightly that they cannot expand their chests to breathe. This can happen while victims are still standing. If someone falls, others may be pushed over them, and those on the ground cannot get up because of the pressure of people around them.

Investigations frequently find that disasters were preceded by warning signs that were not recognised or acted upon, such as increasing density, slowing movement or people climbing barriers to escape. Problems often arise at bottlenecks – narrow points such as entrances, stairways or bridges – where the flow of people exceeds the space available, or where two flows meet in opposite directions. Poor communication can make matters worse, since people at the back of a crowd, unaware of the danger ahead, continue to push forward.

A well-known example of improvement through redesign is the site of a ritual at the annual pilgrimage to Mecca, where large numbers of pilgrims perform the symbolic stoning of pillars. After several serious incidents, including one in 2006 in which hundreds of people died, the structure was rebuilt as a multi-level building with many entrances and exits, allowing the crowd to be spread across several floors. Pilgrims' movements were also organised into scheduled time periods, and the flow was monitored using cameras. These changes have been credited with greatly reducing the number of incidents.

Today, crowd safety experts use computer simulations to model how people move through venues and to identify potential bottlenecks before events take place. Video analysis can measure crowd density in real time, allowing organisers to stop people entering an area before it becomes dangerously full. Experts emphasise, however, that the most important measures are often simple: controlling the number of people admitted, providing enough space and exits, keeping flows in one direction, and training staff to recognise the early signs of danger.

lesson.title: Final review — precision under pressure
lesson.text:
This set combines the main Sentence Completion skills: heavy paraphrase, word-limit extraction, same-type distractors, and conditions. For each question:

1. Locate the section by meaning.

2. Predict the word type.

3. Extract the minimum words that complete the meaning.

4. Check the limit, spelling and grammar.

passages.topic: Climate history — the year without a summer
passages.title: A Summer That Never Came

paragraphs.text: In April 1815, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, erupted in the largest volcanic explosion in recorded history. The eruption, heard more than a thousand kilometres away, destroyed much of the mountain and killed tens of thousands of people on the island and nearby, many from the direct effects of the eruption and many more from the starvation and disease that followed as crops and water supplies were ruined.

The eruption's effects reached far beyond Indonesia. Besides ash, which fell over a wide area, Tambora ejected enormous quantities of sulphur gases high into the stratosphere, the layer of the atmosphere above the level at which weather occurs. There, the gases formed tiny droplets of sulphuric acid, known as sulphate aerosols, which spread around the globe. Because they were above the weather, they were not washed out by rain and remained in the stratosphere for many months. The aerosols reflected part of the incoming sunlight back into space, cooling the Earth's surface.

The consequences were felt most severely in 1816, which became known in parts of Europe and North America as "the year without a summer". In New England, in the north-eastern United States, snow fell in June, and frosts in July and August killed crops across the region. In Western Europe, the summer was cold and exceptionally wet. Harvests of wheat and potatoes failed across large areas, food prices rose sharply, and famine and disease spread. In some regions, desperate people rioted or left their homes in search of food; many farmers in New England moved west to settle new land.

At the time, few people connected these events with a volcano on the other side of the world. The link was established only much later, as scientists studied records of past climate and recognised the effects of large eruptions on global temperatures. Evidence from ice cores, which contain layers of sulphate deposited after major eruptions, has helped confirm the scale of Tambora's impact.

The unusual weather also left cultural traces. In June 1816, a group of young English writers spent the summer near Lake Geneva in Switzerland. Confined indoors for days by storms and heavy rain, they held a competition to write ghost stories. One of the group, Mary Shelley, then eighteen years old, began the story that would become her novel Frankenstein. Some art historians have also suggested that the vivid orange and red sunsets painted by artists in the following years, including the English painter J. M. W. Turner, may reflect the effect of volcanic particles scattering sunlight, although this interpretation is debated.

The events of 1816 are now studied as a warning of how vulnerable food supplies can be to sudden changes in climate. They are also relevant to discussions of proposals to cool the planet deliberately by injecting particles into the stratosphere to reflect sunlight. The Tambora example shows that such particles can indeed lower temperatures, but also that the resulting changes in weather patterns can be severe and unevenly distributed.

lesson.title: Cause chains across time
lesson.text: Some passages describe a chain of events that unfolds over months or years: eruption → particles in the atmosphere → cooling → crop failures → social effects. Sentences may target any link. Keep a mental timeline and check that your answer belongs to the correct link in the chain, not the one before or after it.

passages.topic: Agriculture and conservation — the Arctic seed vault
passages.title: A Safe Place for Seeds

paragraphs.text: On a remote island in the Norwegian Arctic, a tunnel leads more than a hundred metres into a mountain. At its end are three chambers containing more than a million samples of seeds from crops grown around the world. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, opened in 2008, is designed to protect the genetic diversity of the world's food crops against loss from natural disasters, war, disease or simple mismanagement.

The vault is not the first seed bank. Around the world, there are more than a thousand such facilities, which store seeds of crop varieties and their wild relatives so that plant breeders and researchers can use them to develop new varieties – for example, varieties resistant to new diseases or better suited to changing climates. Many of these banks, however, are vulnerable. Some have been damaged by floods, fire or equipment failures, and some have been destroyed or abandoned during wars.

Svalbard serves as a backup for these collections. Seed banks send duplicate samples to the vault, where they are stored in sealed packages. The depositing institutions retain ownership of their seeds, and only they may withdraw them. The vault is sometimes described as an insurance policy: if the original collection is lost, the duplicate can be used to restore it.

The location was chosen for several reasons. The island is remote and geologically stable, and the vault is built well above sea level, so that it would remain dry even if polar ice melted. The seeds are kept at about minus eighteen degrees Celsius, a temperature at which many seeds can remain viable for decades or even centuries. The surrounding permafrost – ground that remains permanently frozen – was expected to keep the seeds cold naturally even if the vault's cooling equipment failed.

The vault's value was demonstrated in 2015, when the first withdrawal was made. An international agricultural research centre, which had been based near Aleppo in Syria, had been forced to relocate because of the conflict in that country. Using the duplicates it had deposited at Svalbard, it was able to rebuild its collection at new sites in Lebanon and Morocco. The centre later returned a new set of duplicate seeds to the vault.

The vault has faced challenges of its own. In 2016, unusually warm temperatures caused permafrost around the entrance tunnel to thaw, and meltwater entered the tunnel, although it did not reach the seed chambers. The incident prompted improvements, including waterproofing the tunnel and building drainage channels, and raised questions about whether the site's natural protection would remain reliable as the Arctic warms.

Supporters emphasise that the vault is only one part of efforts to conserve crop diversity. Seeds in storage are frozen at one moment in time and cannot adapt to changing conditions, whereas crops grown by farmers continue to evolve in response to local environments. Maintaining diversity in farmers' fields, as well as in seed banks, is therefore considered essential.

passages.topic: Animal history — how cats became domestic
passages.title: The Cat That Walked In

paragraphs.text: Unlike dogs, which were domesticated from wolves by hunter-gatherers, cats appear to have joined human communities much later and largely on their own terms. All domestic cats are descended from a wild species, the African wildcat, which still lives across North Africa and the Middle East. Genetic studies of modern cats and of ancient remains have helped scientists trace how and when this wild animal became a household companion.

The process probably began around ten thousand years ago in the region of the Middle East where farming first developed. When people began to grow and store grain, their stores attracted mice and rats. These, in turn, attracted wildcats, which found a reliable supply of prey around human settlements. People probably tolerated or welcomed the cats because they helped protect food supplies. Over many generations, the cats that were least fearful of humans would have had the greatest success in these new surroundings.

The earliest evidence of a close relationship between people and cats comes from the island of Cyprus, where archaeologists discovered a grave around 9,500 years old containing a human skeleton buried alongside a cat. Because wildcats are not native to Cyprus, the cat, or its ancestors, must have been brought to the island by boat, suggesting that people valued cats enough to transport them.

Cats achieved their greatest status in ancient Egypt. Egyptians kept cats as pets, associated them with a goddess, and in some periods mummified enormous numbers of them. Killing a cat could be severely punished. Egyptian paintings show cats sitting under chairs, wearing collars and accompanying people on hunting trips.

A large genetic study published in 2017 suggested that cats spread in two main waves. The first occurred with the spread of farming from the Middle East into Europe. The second, several thousand years later, involved cats from Egypt, which spread widely across Europe, Africa and Asia, probably carried on trading ships, where they would have been useful for controlling rats. The same study found that cats changed relatively little in appearance during most of their history with humans; the tabby pattern, for example, became common only in the Middle Ages.

In fact, domestic cats remain surprisingly similar to their wild ancestors. Many can survive independently if necessary, and domestic and wild cats can still breed together. Some researchers describe cats as only "semi-domesticated". Unlike dogs, which were bred intensively for particular tasks, cats were rarely bred selectively until the nineteenth century, when cat shows became popular and people began to develop distinct breeds.

passages.topic: Earth science — why the sea is salty
passages.title: Salt of the Earth

paragraphs.text: Seawater contains, on average, about 3.5 per cent dissolved salts – roughly thirty-five grams in every litre. The most abundant is sodium chloride, ordinary table salt, but seawater also contains magnesium, sulphate, calcium, potassium and many other substances in smaller amounts. Rivers and lakes, by contrast, generally contain very little salt. Why should the oceans be so different?

The main source of the salt is the land itself. Rain is slightly acidic, because it absorbs a small amount of carbon dioxide from the air. When it falls on rocks, it slowly breaks them down, a process known as weathering, releasing minerals that dissolve in the water. Rivers carry these dissolved minerals to the sea. The amounts in river water are too small to taste, but over millions of years, the quantities delivered to the oceans have been enormous.

A second source lies beneath the ocean floor. Along mid-ocean ridges, where the plates of the Earth's crust are moving apart, seawater seeps into cracks in the rock, is heated by molten rock below, and rises again through openings called hydrothermal vents. As it passes through the hot rock, the water dissolves minerals and carries them into the ocean. Underwater volcanic eruptions also release substances such as chlorine into the sea.

Salt accumulates in the oceans because water leaves the sea mainly by evaporation, and evaporation removes only pure water, leaving the salts behind. The water returns to the land as rain and eventually flows back to the sea, carrying more dissolved minerals with it. Over time, this cycle has concentrated salts in the oceans.

One might expect the sea to grow steadily saltier, but scientists believe its average saltiness has remained fairly stable for hundreds of millions of years. This is because salts are also removed from seawater. Some minerals are taken up by marine organisms to build shells and skeletons, which settle on the sea floor when the organisms die. Others form new minerals in sediments on the ocean floor. In shallow, enclosed seas in hot climates, evaporation can be so intense that salt crystallises out of the water, forming thick deposits that may later be buried and preserved as rock salt.

Saltiness is not the same everywhere. Where large rivers flow into the sea, or where heavy rainfall occurs, seawater is less salty. Where evaporation is high and there is little rainfall, as in the Red Sea, it is saltier. Differences in saltiness and temperature affect the density of seawater and help drive the large-scale circulation of the world's oceans.

passages.topic: Engineering and art — the science of folding
passages.title: The Engineering of Folds

paragraphs.text: Origami, the art of folding paper into shapes and figures, has a long history, particularly in Japan, where it has been practised for centuries. Traditional origami creates birds, flowers and animals from a single square of paper, usually without cutting or gluing. In recent decades, however, the principles of folding have attracted the attention of mathematicians and engineers, who have found that origami techniques can solve surprisingly practical problems.

A central challenge in many areas of engineering is how to pack a large, flat structure into a small space and then unfold it reliably when needed. One solution was developed in the 1970s by the Japanese astrophysicist Koryo Miura. His folding pattern, now known as the Miura fold, allows a large sheet to be collapsed into a compact block and then opened in a single movement by pulling on opposite corners. In 1995, the pattern was used to fold the solar panels of a Japanese satellite, allowing large panels to be launched in a compact form and unfolded once the spacecraft was in orbit.

Folding techniques have also been applied in medicine. Engineers have designed tiny tubes called stents, used to hold open narrowed blood vessels, that can be folded into a very small shape, inserted into the body through a thin tube, and then expanded inside the blood vessel. Researchers are also developing small folded devices that could be swallowed and then unfold inside the body to carry out tasks such as removing objects that have been accidentally swallowed.

In car safety, the way an airbag is folded affects how quickly and evenly it inflates in a collision. Engineers have used mathematical methods inspired by origami to design folding patterns that allow airbags to inflate rapidly and in the correct shape. Folding principles have also been used in packaging, furniture, emergency shelters that can be transported flat and assembled quickly, and even in designing materials whose strength or shape can be changed by folding.

Mathematicians have contributed by studying the rules that determine what shapes can be folded from a flat sheet. Computer programs can now calculate the pattern of folds needed to produce almost any desired three-dimensional shape. These advances have transformed origami as an art form, allowing artists to create extremely complex figures, while also providing engineers with new tools.

lesson.text: Word-bank options usually do not match the passage wording exactly. For example, the passage says "launched into orbit" and the option says "space"; the passage says "inflate rapidly" and the option says "quickly". Match the meaning. passages.topic: Games and history — the long journey of chess
passages.title: Kings, Queens and Computers

paragraphs.text: Chess is one of the oldest board games still widely played, and its history spans many cultures. Most historians believe that its earliest known ancestor was a game called chaturanga, played in India around the sixth century AD. The name referred to the four divisions of an ancient Indian army – infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots – which were represented by the pieces that later became pawns, knights, bishops and rooks.

From India, the game spread to Persia, where it became known as shatranj. When Arab forces conquered Persia in the seventh century, the game was adopted throughout the Islamic world, and Arab and Persian players wrote the first detailed studies of chess strategy and collections of chess problems. From there, chess reached Europe, probably through Spain and Italy, by around the tenth century, carried along trade routes and through contact between cultures.

In early versions of the game, some pieces were much weaker than today. The piece that became the queen could move only one square diagonally, and the bishop could move only two squares diagonally. As a result, games were slow and could last a very long time. In Europe towards the end of the fifteenth century, the rules changed dramatically: the queen became the most powerful piece on the board, able to move any distance in any direction, and the bishop gained its modern long-range move. The faster, more aggressive game that resulted spread rapidly and forms the basis of modern chess.

Over the following centuries, chess became closely associated with intellectual ability. Chess clubs and cafés became meeting places for players, and from the nineteenth century, international tournaments and an official world championship were established. Chess clocks were introduced to limit the time players could spend on their moves.

In the twentieth century, chess became a major challenge for researchers in computer science. Early computer programs played poorly, but they improved steadily as computers became more powerful. In 1997, a computer developed by the company IBM, called Deep Blue, defeated the reigning world champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match – an event widely seen as a milestone in artificial intelligence. Today, chess programs running on ordinary computers are far stronger than any human player, and professionals use them extensively to prepare and analyse games. Rather than reducing interest in the game, computers and online platforms have helped chess attract more players than ever before.

passages.topic: Biology and materials — spider silk
passages.title: Threads of Steel

paragraphs.text: Spider silk is one of the most remarkable materials in nature. Weight for weight, some types of spider silk are stronger than steel, yet they are also highly elastic, stretching considerably before breaking. This combination of strength and flexibility allows a spider's web to absorb the impact of a flying insect without breaking.

Spiders produce silk in special glands in their abdomen. Inside the glands, the silk exists as a liquid containing proteins. As the spider draws the liquid out through small openings called spinnerets, the proteins line up and bond together, and the liquid hardens into a solid thread. The process takes place at normal temperatures and uses only water as a solvent, unlike the manufacture of many artificial fibres, which requires high temperatures and harsh chemicals.

Many spiders can produce several different kinds of silk, each from a different gland and each suited to a particular purpose. Some silk is very strong and is used for the frame of the web and for the "safety line" that a spider trails behind it when it moves. Other silk is stretchy and sticky, used for capturing prey. Still other kinds are used to wrap prey or to build protective cases for eggs.

Because of its extraordinary properties, scientists have long wished to produce spider silk in large quantities. Farming spiders, however, is impractical: many species are territorial and will eat one another if kept together, and each spider produces only small amounts of silk. Researchers have therefore tried to produce silk proteins using other organisms. Genes responsible for silk proteins have been inserted into bacteria, yeast and even goats, whose milk then contains the proteins.

Turning these proteins into fibres that match natural silk has proved difficult. The proteins must be spun in a way that reproduces the precise structure created by the spider, and early artificial fibres were considerably weaker than natural silk. Progress has been made in recent years, and some companies now produce artificial silk fibres for use in clothing and other products. Potential future uses include strong, lightweight materials, surgical threads and materials for repairing damaged tissues in the body.

passages.topic: Technology history — the moving staircase
passages.title: Stairs That Move

paragraphs.text: Escalators are now so common in shopping centres, airports and railway stations that it is easy to forget that they were once a novelty. Several inventors in the nineteenth century patented designs for moving staircases, but most were never built. The first working escalators appeared in the 1890s.

In 1896, the American inventor Jesse Reno installed a device he called an "inclined elevator" at Coney Island, an amusement area in New York. It was essentially a sloping conveyor belt with ridges rather than steps, and it carried passengers upwards at an angle of about twenty-five degrees. Visitors rode it for fun rather than for practical purposes. Reno later installed similar devices in railway stations and department stores.

Around the same time, another American inventor, Charles Seeberger, developed a design with flat, moving steps. He sold his patents to the Otis Elevator Company, which built an escalator for the Paris Exposition of 1900, where it won a prize. The word "escalator", which Seeberger created by combining the Latin word for steps with the word "elevator", was originally a trademark belonging to the Otis company. It later became a general term, and the company lost its exclusive right to the name in the 1950s.

In 1898, the London department store Harrods installed a moving staircase to carry customers between floors. Because many customers were nervous about using the new machine, according to a frequently repeated story, staff were stationed at the top to offer them brandy or smelling salts to calm them.

Early escalators posed safety problems. Clothing and shoes could be caught where the moving steps met the landing, and some early designs required passengers to step off sideways. A key improvement was the "comb plate" at each end: a plate with teeth that fit into grooves on the surface of the steps, guiding feet and objects safely off the moving surface.

Escalators transformed the design of buildings and transport systems. Unlike lifts, which carry a limited number of passengers at a time and require them to wait, escalators move people continuously and can carry thousands of passengers per hour. This made them particularly valuable in underground railway stations and in department stores, where they encouraged customers to visit upper floors. Today, a busy escalator in a large station may carry more than ten thousand people in an hour.

lesson.title: Summaries that skip parts of the passage
lesson.text: A summary may leave out whole sentences or even a paragraph of the passage. If you cannot find the next answer in the paragraph you are reading, move forward. Don't force an answer from the wrong paragraph.

passages.topic: Evolution — why zebras have stripes
passages.title: The Riddle of the Stripes

paragraphs.text: Why do zebras have black and white stripes? The question has puzzled biologists since at least the nineteenth century, when both Charles Darwin and his contemporary Alfred Russel Wallace discussed it without reaching a firm conclusion. Over the years, scientists have proposed a variety of explanations, and the debate has only recently begun to move towards a consensus.

One of the oldest ideas is that stripes provide camouflage. In tall grass, or when seen from a distance, the stripes might break up the outline of the animal, making it harder for predators to spot. Studies of how lions and hyenas see, however, have cast doubt on this idea. These predators, which hunt mainly at dawn, dusk and night, have poorer vision than humans for fine detail; at the distances at which they would normally detect prey, zebra stripes would probably appear as a uniform grey and would provide no special advantage.

A related suggestion is that when zebras run together in a herd, their stripes create a confusing visual effect that makes it hard for a predator to single out an individual. Although this idea is appealing, there is little direct evidence that lions have more difficulty catching zebras than other prey of similar size. In fact, zebras are among the lions' most frequently caught prey.

Another hypothesis is that stripes help zebras stay cool. Black stripes absorb more heat than white ones, and it has been suggested that the difference might create small air currents over the skin. Experiments using barrels covered with striped and plain hides have produced mixed results, and most researchers now consider the cooling effect, if it exists at all, to be too small to explain the stripes.

The explanation that currently has the strongest support concerns biting flies. In Africa, flies such as horseflies and tsetse flies spread serious diseases, and zebras, whose coats are relatively short, may be especially vulnerable to their bites. A comparison of different species and subspecies across Africa found that stripes were most pronounced in areas where biting flies were most active. In a study published in 2019, researchers filmed flies approaching horses on a farm in Britain, some wearing striped coats and others plain ones. The flies approached striped coats just as often but were far less successful at landing on them: they failed to slow down properly and often flew past or bumped into the coat.

Why stripes should confuse flies is not fully understood. One possibility is that the pattern disrupts the flies' ability to judge their speed and direction as they approach. Researchers stress that stripes might serve more than one purpose, but the evidence that they protect against biting insects is now considerably stronger than for any of the other explanations.

lesson.text: When a passage discusses several hypotheses, the summary may report them in a condensed form, including which ones were supported and which were rejected.
