passages.topic: Archaeology and linguistics — cracking Linear B
passages.title: The Script No One Could Read

paragraphs.text: In 1900, the British archaeologist Arthur Evans began excavating the ruins of a great palace at Knossos, on the island of Crete. Among the finds were thousands of clay tablets inscribed with an unknown script. Evans identified two related forms of writing, which he named Linear A and Linear B. Linear B, found in large quantities, was later also discovered at sites on the Greek mainland.

Evans believed that the tablets were written in the language of the Minoans, the Bronze Age people of Crete, and that this language was unrelated to Greek. Because of his great authority, this view was widely accepted, and for decades few scholars seriously considered that Linear B might represent an early form of Greek. Evans also delayed publishing many of the tablets, which made it difficult for others to study them.

Important groundwork was laid by the American classical scholar Alice Kober in the 1940s. Working without knowing what language the script represented, she analysed the tablets systematically, recording how often each sign appeared and in which positions. She showed that some words appeared in several related forms, differing only in their endings, which suggested that the language used grammatical endings to indicate, for example, gender or case. Her methods allowed scholars to group signs that probably shared a consonant or vowel. Kober died in 1950, before the script was deciphered.

The decipherment was achieved in 1952 by Michael Ventris, a British architect who had become fascinated by the script as a schoolboy after hearing Evans lecture. Ventris was not a professional scholar of ancient languages, but he had a remarkable talent for languages and patterns. Building on Kober's work, he constructed a grid arranging the signs according to their probable shared sounds. He then noticed that certain words that appeared only on tablets from Crete might be the names of places on the island, such as Knossos itself. When he tested sound values based on these names, recognisable Greek words began to appear.

Ventris had himself expected the language to be something other than Greek, and he was surprised by his result. He collaborated with the scholar John Chadwick, a specialist in the history of the Greek language, to test and develop the decipherment. Their conclusions were confirmed when a tablet discovered in 1953 contained drawings of vessels accompanied by words that, when read using Ventris's system, correctly described the vessels shown – such as the number of handles on each pot.

The decipherment showed that Greek had been written several centuries earlier than previously thought, and that Greek-speaking people had controlled Knossos in its later period. The tablets themselves turned out to be mainly administrative records: lists of goods, livestock, workers and offerings. They contain no literature, but they provide a detailed picture of the economy and organisation of Bronze Age palaces. Linear A, the older script, remains undeciphered.

lesson.title: People's roles in a summary
lesson.text: When a summary narrates who did what, gaps may ask for a profession, a method or a result. Before answering, identify which person the summary sentence refers to, and find the part of the passage describing that person's contribution. Words describing a different person nearby are the main distractors.

passages.topic: Technology — how satellite navigation works
passages.title: Finding Your Place from Space

paragraphs.text: Satellite navigation systems allow devices ranging from smartphones to aircraft to determine their position almost anywhere on Earth. The best known is the Global Positioning System (GPS), developed by the United States military and made fully operational in the 1990s. Other countries and regions have developed similar systems, and many modern devices can use signals from several of them.

GPS relies on a group of around thirty satellites orbiting the Earth at an altitude of about twenty thousand kilometres. They are arranged so that, at any time, at least four are visible from almost any point on the planet's surface. Each satellite continuously broadcasts a signal containing its position and the precise time at which the signal was sent.

A receiver on the ground calculates its distance from each satellite by measuring how long the signal took to arrive. Because radio signals travel at the speed of light, even a tiny error in timing produces a large error in distance: an error of one millionth of a second would place the receiver about three hundred metres from its true position. For this reason, each satellite carries extremely accurate atomic clocks.

Knowing its distance from one satellite tells the receiver only that it lies somewhere on a large sphere centred on that satellite. Distances from three satellites narrow the possible positions to a single point. In practice, a fourth satellite is needed because the receiver's own clock, unlike the satellites' atomic clocks, is not accurate enough; the extra measurement allows the receiver to correct its own clock error. This method of calculating a position from distances is known as trilateration.

Remarkably, GPS must also take account of the effects described by Albert Einstein's theories of relativity. Because the satellites move at high speed, their clocks run slightly slower than clocks on the ground; because they are further from the Earth's gravity, they also run slightly faster. The combined effect is that the satellite clocks gain about thirty-eight millionths of a second each day. Though tiny, this would cause position errors of several kilometres per day if it were not corrected, so the satellite clocks are adjusted before launch to compensate.

Other sources of error remain. As signals pass through the upper atmosphere, they are slowed slightly by charged particles, and in cities they may bounce off buildings before reaching the receiver, which makes the distance appear longer. Various techniques, including the use of signals on two different frequencies and ground stations that broadcast corrections, can reduce these errors. As a result, ordinary receivers can typically determine their position to within a few metres, and specialised equipment can achieve accuracy of a few centimetres.

lesson.text: In technical summaries, word-bank options are often abstract nouns (accuracy, delay, distance, correction). Read the summary sentence and identify exactly which quantity or idea it is talking about, then match it to the passage. Several options may sound technical and plausible; only one describes the right part of the process.

passages.topic: Social history — coffee and the coffeehouse
passages.title: From Bean to Coffeehouse

paragraphs.text: Coffee is now one of the most widely consumed drinks in the world, but its early history is surrounded by legend. A popular story tells of an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi who noticed that his goats became unusually lively after eating the red berries of a certain shrub. The story first appears in writing many centuries after the events it describes, and historians regard it as a legend. What is more certain is that coffee plants grew wild in the highlands of Ethiopia, and that the use of coffee as a drink developed across the Red Sea in Yemen.

The earliest reliable evidence of coffee drinking comes from Yemen in the fifteenth century, where members of Sufi religious communities drank it to help them stay awake during night-time prayers and devotions. From Yemen, coffee spread to Mecca, Cairo and other cities of the Middle East, and by the sixteenth century it had become popular in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire.

As coffee spread, a new kind of public space emerged: the coffeehouse. Coffeehouses became places where men gathered to talk, play games, listen to music and discuss news. Because they encouraged conversation, including criticism of those in power, coffeehouses sometimes worried authorities, and there were several attempts to ban them in different cities. None of these bans lasted long.

Coffee reached Europe in the seventeenth century through trade with the Ottoman Empire, arriving first in Venice. Coffeehouses soon opened in London, Paris, Amsterdam and Vienna. In London, they became known as "penny universities", since for the price of a cup of coffee, customers could join discussions with merchants, writers and scientists. Some coffeehouses became associated with particular professions: one, frequented by ship owners and merchants, developed into a famous insurance market, and others became centres of trading in shares.

For a long time, Yemen controlled much of the world's coffee supply, and the export of fertile coffee seeds was restricted. In the late seventeenth century, however, the Dutch obtained coffee plants and began cultivating them in their colonies, particularly on the island of Java. Coffee was later introduced to the Caribbean and to South America. By the nineteenth century, Brazil had become the world's largest producer – a position it still holds – with coffee grown on large plantations that relied for much of the century on the labour of enslaved people.

Today, coffee is grown in more than fifty countries, mainly by small farmers in tropical regions, and millions of people depend on it for their living. The prices farmers receive can vary sharply from year to year, depending on harvests and world markets, which makes their incomes uncertain. Climate change is also expected to reduce the area suitable for growing coffee in some regions.

lesson.text: A single summary sentence may compress a whole paragraph into one line. Identify the main point of that paragraph, then find the precise word or phrase the gap requires. Several details from the paragraph may seem possible; choose the one that completes the summary's specific idea.

passages.topic: Postal history — the first postage stamp
passages.title: Paying for the Post

paragraphs.text: Before the 1840s, sending a letter in Britain was expensive and complicated. Charges were calculated according to the distance a letter travelled and the number of sheets of paper it contained. They were normally paid by the person who received the letter, not by the sender. A letter from London to Edinburgh could cost more than a labourer earned in a day. Many recipients refused letters they could not afford, and in those cases the Post Office had carried them for nothing.

People found ingenious ways to avoid paying. Because a letter could be refused, some senders marked the outside with small symbols or patterns of dots that passed on a short message. The recipient read the cover, understood the message and handed the letter back unopened. Members of Parliament were entitled to send letters free of charge. This privilege was widely abused by friends and relatives, who asked them to sign envelopes.

In 1837, a schoolteacher and reformer named Rowland Hill published a pamphlet arguing that the system should be completely reformed. Hill had studied the Post Office's costs. He concluded that the expense of actually transporting a letter was tiny compared with the cost of calculating charges and collecting money on delivery. He proposed a single low rate of one penny for any letter within Britain below a certain weight, regardless of distance, paid in advance by the sender. Proof of payment would be a small printed label stuck to the letter.

Post Office officials opposed the plan, predicting that the lower charge would cause heavy financial losses. Merchants and many members of the public supported it, however, and Parliament approved it. On 6 May 1840, the first adhesive postage stamp, the Penny Black, became valid for use. It carried a portrait of the young Queen Victoria but no country name. Britain still follows this tradition: it is the only country that does not print its name on its stamps.

The Penny Black was in use for less than a year. It was printed in black ink. The red ink used to cancel stamps, so that they could not be reused, was difficult to see on it and could be removed. In 1841, it was replaced by a red stamp, the Penny Red, which was cancelled with black ink.

In terms of use, the reform was a great success. The number of letters sent in Britain roughly doubled in the first year and continued to grow rapidly, encouraging personal correspondence, business and the spread of news. Revenue, however, took much longer to recover. It was several decades before the Post Office's profits returned to their earlier level. Other countries soon adopted prepaid stamps: Switzerland and Brazil in 1843, and the United States in 1847.

lesson.title: Options that appear in the passage in a different context
lesson.text: At Medium level, the word bank often contains a word that the passage does use, but for a different idea. For example, the passage may say that old postal charges depended on distance and that the new charge depended on weight. Both words appear, but only one fits a given gap. When an option matches a passage word exactly, check which sentence that word came from.

passages.topic: Marine biology — how whales hold their breath
passages.title: Built for the Deep

paragraphs.text: Some marine mammals can dive to extraordinary depths and remain underwater for remarkably long periods. The sperm whale regularly hunts squid more than a thousand metres below the surface. The record for a single dive by any mammal belongs to Cuvier's beaked whale: one was recorded staying underwater for more than three hours. Human free-divers, by contrast, can rarely hold their breath for more than a few minutes. How do these animals manage without breathing for so long?

One surprising answer is that deep-diving mammals do not take a large breath before diving. Many actually breathe out before they descend. Under the enormous pressure of the deep sea, air in the lungs becomes compressed, and some of its nitrogen can dissolve into the blood. If the animal rises too quickly, this gas can form bubbles, causing the painful and dangerous condition known to human divers as "the bends". These animals reduce the risk by diving with little air in their lungs, and their ribcages allow the lungs to collapse safely.

Instead of the lungs, the main store of oxygen is in the blood and muscles. Deep divers have a much larger volume of blood relative to their body size than land mammals, and their blood contains a high concentration of haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen. Their muscles are packed with myoglobin, a related protein that stores oxygen within the muscle itself. So much myoglobin is present that the muscles of some whales and seals appear almost black. In 2013, researchers discovered that the myoglobin of diving mammals carries a positive electrical charge, which causes the molecules to repel one another. This allows very high concentrations to be stored without the proteins sticking together.

Divers also use their oxygen sparingly. As soon as a dive begins, the heart rate slows dramatically, sometimes to only a few beats per minute. Blood vessels to the skin, gut and other organs narrow, so that the oxygen-rich blood is directed mainly to the brain and heart. This set of changes, known as the "dive response", also occurs in humans when the face is placed in cold water, but in a much weaker form.

Even so, oxygen eventually runs short on the longest dives. Muscles then switch to producing energy without oxygen, a process that generates lactic acid. The animal must later spend time at the surface recovering, breathing repeatedly to clear this waste product before diving again. Beaked whales appear to make most of their dives well within their aerobic limit – the time they can remain underwater using oxygen alone – and only occasionally exceed it.

Understanding these adaptations has practical value. Some researchers are studying how myoglobin is stored at high concentrations, which could inform the development of artificial blood substitutes. Others have investigated whether loud underwater noise from military sonar causes beaked whales to surface too quickly. This may explain why some have been found stranded with injuries resembling the bends.

lesson.title: Numbers, units and ideas that go against expectation

Summaries also often test ideas that go against expectation. If the passage says that divers breathe out before diving, a gap after "Rather than filling their lungs, many divers ..." needs that surprising action.

passages.topic: Transport science — traffic jams without a cause
passages.title: Jams from Nowhere

paragraphs.text: Most drivers have experienced it. Traffic on a motorway slows to a crawl, then speeds up again, and there is no sign of any accident, roadworks or junction to explain the delay. Such "phantom" traffic jams seem to appear from nowhere. Research over the past few decades has shown that they arise from the behaviour of drivers themselves.

The process begins with a small disturbance. When traffic is dense, a single driver may brake slightly, perhaps because of a moment's distraction or a vehicle changing lanes. The driver behind reacts a fraction of a second late and has to brake a little harder, and the next driver harder still. Each reaction amplifies the one before, so that a gentle slowing near the front becomes a complete stop further back. The jam then moves backwards along the road, against the direction of traffic, even as individual vehicles leave its front and drive on.

In 2008, Japanese researchers demonstrated this effect in a simple experiment. They asked twenty-two drivers to travel around a circular track at a steady speed of thirty kilometres per hour, keeping a constant distance from the car in front. At first, the cars moved smoothly. Within minutes, however, small variations in speed had grown until a cluster of stopped cars formed and travelled backwards around the circle, without any obstacle at all.

Mathematicians have described such jams using equations similar to those that describe waves in fluids. The models show that above a certain density of vehicles, smooth traffic flow becomes unstable, and any small disturbance is likely to grow. Below that density, disturbances fade away. This explains why phantom jams are common only when roads are busy.

Several measures can reduce the problem. Variable speed limits, displayed on overhead signs, can lower speeds when traffic becomes dense. Although this seems counter-intuitive, slower but steadier traffic may carry more vehicles over a period than fast traffic that repeatedly stops. Drivers can help by leaving larger gaps, which give them time to slow down gradually. Some researchers have suggested that drivers should try to keep an equal distance from the vehicles in front of and behind them, rather than simply following the car ahead.

Automated vehicles may offer a longer-term solution. In a 2017 experiment, researchers placed a single self-driving car among about twenty human-driven cars on a circular track. The car was programmed to smooth out variations in speed, and its presence was enough to dampen the waves of stopping and starting, reducing fuel use across all the vehicles. Researchers caution, however, that such results would need to be confirmed on real motorways with much larger numbers of vehicles.

lesson.title: Near-synonyms that differ in strength

passages.topic: History of medicine — the invention of the stethoscope
passages.title: Listening to the Chest

paragraphs.text: For most of history, doctors examining a patient's chest had limited ways of learning what was happening inside. They could observe breathing, feel the pulse, or tap the chest and listen to the sound it produced, a technique called percussion. Some pressed an ear directly against the patient's chest to hear the heart and lungs. This method was often ineffective, particularly with overweight patients, and many doctors considered it undignified.

In 1816, the French physician René Laennec was asked to examine a young woman with symptoms of heart disease. Because of her age and sex, he felt that placing his ear on her chest would be improper. According to his own account, he then remembered seeing children playing with a long piece of wood: one scratched one end with a pin while another listened at the other end and heard the sound clearly. Laennec rolled several sheets of paper into a tight tube and placed one end on the patient's chest and the other at his ear. He was surprised to hear the heartbeat more clearly than ever before.

Laennec soon replaced the paper roll with a hollow wooden cylinder about twenty-five centimetres long, which could be taken apart for carrying. He named the instrument the stethoscope, from Greek words meaning "chest" and "to look at". More importantly, he spent the next three years listening to the chests of patients at a Paris hospital. When patients died, he compared what he had heard with what was found in their bodies after death. In this way, he linked particular sounds with specific diseases of the lungs and heart.

In 1819, Laennec published a detailed book describing his findings. It introduced many terms that doctors still use today to describe chest sounds. The book was translated into other languages, and the stethoscope spread rapidly among doctors in Europe and North America, although some older physicians at first dismissed it as a passing fashion. Laennec himself died in 1826, at the age of forty-five, of tuberculosis, one of the lung diseases he had helped to diagnose.

The instrument changed considerably over the following decades. In the 1850s, a version was developed with two earpieces connected by flexible rubber tubes, allowing doctors to listen with both ears. Later improvements included a chest piece with two sides: a flat diaphragm for hearing high-pitched sounds and a small bell-shaped cup for low-pitched ones.

Today, the stethoscope remains a symbol of the medical profession, although its role is changing. Ultrasound scanners, some small enough to carry in a pocket, can show images of the heart and lungs, and electronic stethoscopes can amplify and record sounds. Some doctors argue that these technologies will make the traditional stethoscope unnecessary. Others maintain that it remains a quick, cheap and useful tool, particularly where modern equipment is not available.

lesson.title: Finding where the summary starts
lesson.text: A summary rarely covers the whole passage. Here, the summary begins with the story of the invention, so the first answer is not in Paragraph A. Words in an earlier paragraph can look correct but belong to a different part of the story. Read the summary's first sentence, find its matching paragraph, and start searching there.
lesson.example: If a summary begins "After moving to Paris, she ...", skip the paragraphs about her childhood and start where Paris is first mentioned.

passages.topic: Social psychology — the bystander effect reconsidered
passages.title: The Crowd That Did Nothing?

paragraphs.text: In March 1964, a young woman named Kitty Genovese was murdered outside her apartment building in New York. Two weeks later, a newspaper published a report claiming that thirty-eight respectable citizens had watched the attack over more than half an hour and that none had called the police. The story caused national shock and was widely taken as evidence that city dwellers were indifferent to one another.

The case inspired two psychologists, John Darley and Bibb Latané, to investigate why people fail to help in emergencies. In a series of experiments in the late 1960s, they found that individuals were less likely to help, and slower to do so, when they believed others were also present. In one study, participants who thought they alone could hear someone having a seizure over an intercom almost always went for help. Those who believed that four other people were also listening often did not. Darley and Latané proposed that responsibility is spread across everyone present, so that each individual feels less obliged to act. They called this process "diffusion of responsibility", and the finding became known as the bystander effect.

Later investigations revealed that the original newspaper account was seriously inaccurate. Most of the neighbours could not see the attack, and many heard only brief noises that they did not recognise as an assault. At least one neighbour did call the police, and another went down to help the victim, who died in her arms. The figure of thirty-eight witnesses appears to have been exaggerated. The story that launched the research, in other words, was largely a myth.

The laboratory findings themselves have proved more durable, but they have also been refined. A large review in 2011, which combined the results of more than a hundred studies, confirmed that the presence of others generally reduces helping. However, it found that the effect was weaker in situations that were clearly dangerous. This may be because such emergencies are recognised more quickly, and because other people can provide physical support when someone intervenes.

More recently, researchers have studied real incidents rather than staged ones. A study published in 2019 analysed security-camera recordings of public conflicts in three countries: the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and South Africa. In around nine out of ten incidents, at least one bystander intervened, and typically several did. Moreover, the chance that someone would help increased as the number of bystanders rose. The authors argued that, although any single individual in a large group might be less likely to act, the larger pool of people made it more likely that somebody would.

These findings do not simply overturn the bystander effect; they change how it should be understood. Groups can inhibit individuals, but they can also be a source of help. The original image of the passive, uncaring crowd, shaped more by a misleading news story than by evidence, now appears to have been considerably overstated.

lesson.title: Hard word banks and revised findings
lesson.text: At Hard level, the word-bank options are abstract nouns and adjectives, and the summary often compresses a story in three stages: the original claim, the research it inspired, and a later revision. Options that fit the original claim become traps when the gap describes the revision. For each gap, decide which stage the sentence describes before choosing.
lesson.example: Passage: "The bridge was once thought unsafe; tests later showed it was sound." Summary: "Later tests showed that the bridge was ______" Options: A dangerous B safe. Answer: B. A matches the earlier belief, not the later finding.

passages.topic: Entomology — how locusts change form
passages.title: Two Forms of One Insect

paragraphs.text: Desert locusts are grasshoppers that live across the dry regions of North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia. For long periods they are harmless, living alone and scattered across the landscape. Occasionally, however, their populations explode and they form swarms that can contain billions of insects. A swarm can travel more than a hundred kilometres in a day and consume as much food in a day as millions of people. The worst outbreaks have threatened the food supply of entire regions.

Remarkably, solitary and swarming locusts belong to the same species. For a long time they were thought to be different species, because they look and behave so differently. Solitary locusts are green or pale brown, avoid one another and tend to fly at night. Swarming, or "gregarious", locusts are brightly coloured in yellow and black, are strongly attracted to each other, and fly by day. Only in 1921 did the Russian-born scientist Boris Uvarov show that the two forms were stages of the same insect, which can switch from one to the other.

The trigger for the change is crowding. After heavy rains, vegetation grows in the desert and locusts breed rapidly. As the vegetation dries out again, the insects become concentrated in the few remaining green patches, where they repeatedly bump into one another. Experiments showed that the key stimulus is touch: repeatedly stroking the hind legs of a solitary locust for a few hours was enough to make it behave gregariously. In 2009, researchers found that this contact causes a rise in the chemical serotonin in the locust's nervous system. Blocking serotonin prevented the change, while giving it to solitary locusts triggered gregarious behaviour.

The change in behaviour happens within hours, but the change in colour and body shape takes longer, developing over several generations. Gregarious females also pass the tendency on to their offspring, so that the young of crowded parents are already inclined to join groups. Once swarms have formed, bands of young locusts that cannot yet fly march across the ground together, while adults form flying swarms that travel with the wind.

Why should crowded locusts become attracted to one another rather than spreading out? One explanation involves cannibalism. In crowded bands, locusts will eat those in front of them, and research suggests that marching is partly driven by individuals moving forward to escape being eaten by those behind while chasing those ahead. The bright colours of gregarious locusts, meanwhile, may warn predators that they are unpleasant to eat, since swarming locusts often feed on toxic plants.

Control efforts today concentrate on early warning. Satellite data on rainfall and vegetation allow scientists to identify areas where locusts are likely to breed, and teams on the ground survey these areas so that insecticides can be applied before swarms form. When monitoring fails, for example in regions affected by conflict, outbreaks can spread widely, as happened in East Africa in 2019 and 2020.

lesson.title: Summaries that contrast two states
lesson.text: When a passage describes one thing in two states (solitary and swarming, before and after), it gives parallel details for each state, and every detail is a potential answer. Before writing, check which state the summary sentence refers to. A detail from the other state will be the same type of word and will look correct.
lesson.example: Passage: "In winter the fox's coat is white; in summer it is brown." Summary: "During the warmer months, its coat turns ______" Answer: brown. "White" is the same type of word but describes the other state.

passages.topic: Neuroscience — how learning to read changes the brain
passages.title: The Reading Brain

paragraphs.text: Writing was invented only around five thousand years ago, and for most of that time only a small minority of people could read. In evolutionary terms, this is far too short a period for the human brain to have developed a special region for reading. Yet brain imaging shows that in literate people, one small area on the left side of the brain, towards the back, responds strongly and consistently to written words, in whatever script a person has learned. How can the brain have a reading area if it did not evolve to read?

The French neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene has proposed an answer that he calls "neuronal recycling". Cultural inventions such as reading, he argues, take over brain circuits that evolved for other purposes and that happen to be well suited to the new task. The area activated by written words, sometimes called the "visual word form area", lies within a region involved in recognising objects and faces. According to this view, its original function was the fine visual discrimination of shapes, and learning to read partly redirects it towards letters.

Support for this idea comes from studies comparing adults who learned to read in childhood, adults who learned only as adults, and adults who never learned. In a study published in 2010, Dehaene and colleagues scanned the brains of such groups in Portugal and Brazil. In readers, the response of the word-form area to written words was strongly related to reading skill. The same study found that as responses to words increased, responses to faces in the same area declined slightly, and in literate people face processing shifted more towards the right side of the brain. Reading, it seems, competes with face recognition for space.

Neuronal recycling may also explain a common difficulty. Young children learning to read often confuse mirror-image letters such as b and d, and may write letters or whole words backwards. Dehaene points out that the visual system evolved to treat mirror images as the same object: a tiger facing left is the same animal as a tiger facing right. This useful ability must be partly unlearned for reading. Studies have found that people who cannot read find it much harder than readers to tell mirror-image shapes apart.

The theory is not universally accepted. Some researchers argue that the word-form area is better understood as a region that links visual input with language areas, rather than as a recycled shape-recognition area, and that its location reflects these connections. Others note that the reported decline in face responses is small, and that illiterate adults often differ from literate ones in many ways besides reading, such as schooling and occupation, which makes comparisons difficult.

Whatever its exact explanation, the research has a clear message about the brain's flexibility. Even in adulthood, learning to read changes how the brain is organised, a finding with encouraging implications for adult literacy programmes.

lesson.title: Options that fit several gaps
lesson.text: In Hard word banks, the distractors are chosen so that many options fit the grammar of several gaps. For example, weaker / stronger, identical / different and invention / evolution are all grammatically possible in more than one place. Grammar will not narrow the choice much. You must decide each gap by meaning, and it helps to write your own prediction before looking at the options.
lesson.example: Summary: "After training, the athletes' reaction times became ______" Options: A shorter B longer C faster. A and C both fit the grammar; the passage phrase "reaction times fell" decides it: A.

passages.topic: Plant domestication — how a wild grass became maize
passages.title: From Grass to Grain

paragraphs.text: Maize, also known as corn, is one of the world's most important crops, grown on every continent except Antarctica. Yet its wild ancestor looks so different that, for much of the twentieth century, botanists argued about where maize came from. The plant now generally accepted as its ancestor is teosinte, a wild grass that grows in Mexico and Central America. Teosinte has many thin stalks and produces small ears with only five to twelve kernels, each enclosed in a case so hard that it can pass through an animal's digestive system undamaged.

The American geneticist George Beadle argued as early as the 1930s that teosinte was maize's ancestor. Many scientists found it hard to believe that a plant with so few, inedible seeds could have given rise to maize, whose ears carry hundreds of exposed kernels, and some proposed that maize descended from a now-extinct wild maize instead. In the 1970s, after retiring, Beadle crossed maize and teosinte and grew tens of thousands of the resulting plants. He found that the two could interbreed easily and that the differences between them depended on a surprisingly small number of genes.

Genetic evidence later settled the question. A study published in 2002 compared the DNA of maize with that of teosinte populations across Mexico. It found that maize was most closely related to a type of teosinte from the valley of the Balsas River in south-western Mexico, and suggested that maize had been domesticated only once, around nine thousand years ago. Archaeologists have since found microscopic traces of maize on stone tools from the same region, dating from about that time.

One of the key changes involved a single gene, known as tga1, which controls the hard case around each kernel. A small change in this gene left the kernels exposed, making them easy to eat. Another gene, tb1, affects the branching of the plant: in maize, a more active version of this gene suppresses the many side branches of teosinte, producing a single tall stalk with a few large ears. Early farmers, by repeatedly planting seeds from the plants they preferred, gradually increased the frequency of these useful versions of genes.

Domestication was a long process. The earliest maize cobs found by archaeologists, dating from about six thousand years ago, come from a cave in Oaxaca, Mexico, and are only a few centimetres long, smaller than a modern person's thumb. Over thousands of years, as maize spread north and south across the Americas, farmers selected plants adapted to many different climates, from the cool highlands of the Andes to the short growing seasons of what is now Canada.

Today, maize depends entirely on human beings. Its kernels are firmly attached to the cob and enclosed in leaves, so it cannot scatter its own seeds. If a cob falls to the ground, the many seedlings that emerge compete with one another and usually die. Without farmers to separate and plant its seeds, maize would disappear within a few generations.

lesson.title: Extracting answers from long noun phrases
lesson.text: Hard passages pack information into long noun phrases, such as "a type of teosinte from the valley of the Balsas River in south-western Mexico". The summary gap usually needs only one part of that phrase, and the summary itself often supplies the rest ("teosinte from the valley of the ______"). Read the words on both sides of the gap, then take only the words that are missing.
lesson.example: Passage: "a small wooden box with a brass lock". Summary: "the letters were kept in a small wooden ______" Answer: box (not "wooden box").

passages.topic: Materials science — why Roman concrete has lasted
passages.title: Stone That Heals Itself

paragraphs.text: Many structures built by the ancient Romans are still standing after two thousand years. They include harbour walls exposed to the sea and the great dome of the Pantheon in Rome, which remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Modern concrete, by comparison, often begins to crack and crumble within decades. Why Roman concrete has lasted so well has long interested engineers.

Roman builders mixed lime, water and a volcanic ash called pozzolana, named after the town of Pozzuoli near Naples, where it was found in large quantities. The ash reacted with the lime to produce a strong binding material. For marine structures, the Romans packed this mixture into wooden frames lowered into the sea, and the concrete hardened underwater.

In 2017, a team of researchers examining samples of Roman harbour concrete reported a surprising finding. Over centuries, seawater seeping through the concrete had dissolved some of the volcanic material and caused new minerals to grow within the pores and cracks, including a rare crystal called aluminous tobermorite. Rather than weakening the structure, as seawater does to modern concrete, this process appears to have strengthened it over time.

Another puzzle concerned small white lumps of lime, known as lime clasts, found throughout Roman concrete. They had generally been regarded as evidence of careless mixing or poor-quality materials. A study published in 2023 proposed a different explanation. The researchers argued that the Romans used quicklime, a highly reactive form of lime, and mixed it hot, a method that left these lumps behind. When cracks later formed and water entered them, the lime in the clasts dissolved and then formed calcium carbonate, filling the cracks. In laboratory tests, samples made using this hot-mixing method sealed their cracks within about two weeks, whereas comparable samples made without lime clasts did not.

Not all experts are convinced that the Romans deliberately designed their concrete to heal itself; the clasts may have been an accidental result of their methods. It is also important to note that Roman concrete was generally weaker than modern concrete when first set, and the Romans did not use steel reinforcement. Modern reinforced concrete often fails because the steel inside rusts and expands, cracking the surrounding material, a problem the Romans avoided simply by not using metal.

Nevertheless, the research has practical interest. Cement production is responsible for a significant share of global carbon dioxide emissions, and concrete that lasts longer, or that repairs its own cracks, would need to be replaced less often. Some companies are already experimenting with materials inspired by Roman techniques, although adapting them to modern building methods and safety standards will take time.

lesson.title: Summaries that correct an earlier belief
lesson.text: When a passage replaces an old interpretation with a new one, the word bank often contains words for both. A gap may ask what something "had usually been interpreted as" (the old view) or what a new study "suggested" (the new view). Check the verb tense and the reporting words around each gap to decide which view it describes.
lesson.example: Passage: "The marks were thought to be damage; they are now known to be decoration." Summary: "The marks had long been regarded as ______" Options: A damage B decoration. Answer: A.

passages.topic: Exploration history — the lost Franklin expedition
passages.title: The Lost Expedition

paragraphs.text: In May 1845, two British naval ships, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror, sailed from England under the command of Sir John Franklin. Their aim was to complete the discovery of the Northwest Passage, a sea route through the Arctic linking the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. The ships carried 129 men and supplies intended to last three years, including large quantities of tinned food, which was still a relatively new technology. After being seen by whalers in Baffin Bay in the summer of 1845, the expedition was never seen by Europeans again.

Dozens of search expeditions were sent over the following years. In 1854, the explorer John Rae learned from Inuit people that a group of starving white men had been seen dragging a boat southward some years before, and that bodies had later been found. In 1859, a search party discovered a note left in a stone cairn on King William Island. It recorded that the ships had been trapped in ice since September 1846, that Franklin had died in June 1847, and that the survivors had abandoned the ships in April 1848 and set out on foot for the mainland. None survived.

For more than a century, the causes of the disaster were debated. In the 1980s, researchers exhumed the bodies of three crew members who had died early in the expedition and been buried on Beechey Island, where the permafrost had preserved them remarkably well. Tests of their hair and tissue revealed high levels of lead. The researchers proposed that the men had been poisoned by lead from the solder used to seal the tins of food, and suggested that lead poisoning, which can cause weakness and confusion, might have affected the crew's judgement.

This explanation became widely known, but later studies have questioned it. Analysis of bones from other crew members showed that high lead levels were not unusual among British people of the period, who were exposed to lead from many everyday sources. A study published in 2018, which examined the distribution of lead in bones and teeth, concluded that the men's exposure was not markedly greater than that of their contemporaries and was unlikely to have been the main cause of the disaster. Other factors, including scurvy, tuberculosis, starvation, extreme cold and two winters trapped in the ice, are now thought to have played at least as large a role.

The wrecks themselves were eventually located with the help of Inuit oral history, which had long preserved accounts of a ship seen in the ice and of the places where it sank. Guided partly by these accounts, a Canadian search team found Erebus in 2014, and Terror was found in 2016, in a bay considerably further south than many searchers had expected. Both are remarkably well preserved in the cold water, and divers have since recovered objects including plates, instruments and personal belongings.

The story of the Franklin expedition has been retold many times, often as a heroic tragedy. Historians now emphasise how much the searchers might have learned, and how many lives might have been saved, had they listened more closely to Inuit knowledge of the region. That knowledge, more than a century and a half later, helped to solve one of the most famous mysteries of Arctic exploration.

lesson.title: Final review — the complete Summary Completion method
lesson.text: This final set combines the main skills: finding the section the summary covers, predicting the word type, recognising paraphrase, rejecting nearby dates of the same type, and extracting the minimum words within the limit. For each gap: (1) locate the matching sentence; (2) predict what is missing; (3) copy the exact words; (4) check the word limit, the spelling and the grammar of the completed sentence.

passages.topic: Food history — the pineapple in Europe
passages.title: The Royal Fruit

paragraphs.text: The pineapple is native to South America, where it was probably first cultivated in the region of present-day Brazil and Paraguay. By the time Europeans arrived in the Americas, it was grown widely across the Caribbean. Christopher Columbus and his crew encountered the fruit on the island of Guadeloupe in 1493 and were struck by its sweetness, which was rare in a world where sugar was still expensive.

Carrying pineapples back to Europe proved difficult. The voyage across the Atlantic took several weeks, and most fruits rotted long before they arrived. Only a few survived in good condition, and those that did were extremely valuable. As a result, the pineapple quickly became a symbol of wealth and luxury. Kings and nobles were painted holding pineapples, and the fruit appeared as a decoration on buildings, gateposts and furniture.

Because importing pineapples was so unreliable, wealthy Europeans tried to grow them at home. This was a considerable challenge in a cold climate. The first success in Europe is usually credited to growers in the Netherlands in the late seventeenth century. Gardeners built special heated greenhouses, known as "pineries", and placed the plants in pits filled with rotting tree bark, which produced heat as it decayed. A single fruit could take up to four years to grow, and a gardener had to keep the temperature steady throughout the winter.

The cost of producing a pineapple in this way was enormous. In eighteenth-century Britain, a single home-grown fruit could cost as much as a new carriage. Some people did not eat their pineapples at all. Instead, they displayed them at dinner parties as a centrepiece, and the same fruit might be passed from one party to another until it began to rot. Businesses even rented out pineapples by the evening to people who wanted to impress their guests but could not afford to buy one.

In the nineteenth century, the situation changed. Faster steamships made it possible to transport fresh fruit across the ocean, and large plantations were established in places such as the Azores and, later, Hawaii. The invention of canning allowed pineapples to be preserved and sold far from where they were grown. By the early twentieth century, canned pineapple had become an ordinary food in many countries.

Today, pineapples are grown in many tropical countries, with Costa Rica among the largest producers. Once a fruit for kings, the pineapple is now one of the most widely eaten tropical fruits in the world, although it remains a popular decorative symbol of welcome and hospitality.

lesson.text: In an easy set, each group of notes usually comes from one paragraph. Before you look for any answer, read the headings and write the matching paragraph letter next to each one ("Origins" → A, "A luxury item" → B). Then search only that paragraph for the gaps under the heading.
lesson.example: Heading: "Growing pineapples in Europe". Look for the paragraph that describes greenhouses and gardeners, not the one about ships or prices.

passages.topic: Wildlife — how sea otters keep warm
passages.title: Warm in Cold Water

paragraphs.text: Sea otters live along the coasts of the northern Pacific Ocean, from Japan and Russia to Alaska and California. They are the heaviest members of the weasel family, with adult males weighing up to about forty-five kilograms, yet they are among the smallest marine mammals. Unlike most animals that live in cold seas, they spend almost their entire lives in the water, often floating on their backs.

Most marine mammals, such as seals and whales, stay warm thanks to a thick layer of fat, called blubber, under their skin. Sea otters have almost no blubber. Instead, they rely on their fur, which is the densest of any animal: a single square centimetre can contain more than a hundred thousand hairs. The fur traps a layer of air next to the skin, keeping it dry and warm.

To keep this insulation working, the fur must be kept clean. Sea otters spend several hours every day grooming, rubbing and combing their fur with their paws and blowing air into it. If the fur becomes dirty or covered in oil, it loses its ability to hold air, and the otter can quickly become dangerously cold. For this reason, oil spills are a serious threat to them.

Staying warm also requires a great deal of energy. A sea otter's body produces heat at a rate two to three times higher than that of a land mammal of the same size. To fuel this, an adult must eat about a quarter of its body weight every day. Its diet includes sea urchins, crabs, clams and other shellfish, which it gathers from the sea floor.

Sea otters are one of the few animals that use tools. Floating on its back, an otter places a flat stone on its chest and strikes a hard shell against it until the shell breaks. Some otters keep a favourite stone in a loose pocket of skin under the arm and use it again and again.

Sea otters were hunted almost to extinction for their valuable fur in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. After an international agreement banned the hunting in 1911, their numbers slowly recovered in many areas. Their return has benefited coastal ecosystems: by eating sea urchins, which feed on kelp, otters help underwater kelp forests to grow.

passages.topic: History of technology — the zip fastener
passages.title: A Fastener That Took Decades

paragraphs.text: Today the zip is found on clothes, bags, tents and countless other items, but it took more than sixty years to develop a version that worked reliably. The story begins in 1851, when the American inventor Elias Howe, best known for his work on the sewing machine, patented an "automatic continuous clothing closure". Howe never produced or marketed it, and the idea was largely forgotten.

In 1893, another American, Whitcomb Judson, exhibited a device he called a "clasp locker" at the World's Fair in Chicago. It was designed mainly to fasten shoes and consisted of a series of hooks and eyes that were joined by pulling a slider. Judson founded a company to manufacture it, but the device was expensive and clumsy and tended to spring open unexpectedly, and it sold poorly.

The breakthrough came from Gideon Sundback, a Swedish-born engineer who worked for Judson's company. In 1913 he designed a new fastener in which small metal teeth, rather than hooks, fitted neatly into one another as the slider moved. He also designed a machine that could produce the fastener in large quantities. His design, patented in 1917, is essentially the one still used today.

Even then, the fastener was not immediately used on clothing. Its first major customers included the United States Army, which used it on uniforms and equipment during the First World War, and makers of boots and tobacco pouches. The name "zipper" was introduced in 1923 by the rubber company B.F. Goodrich, which used the fasteners on its rubber boots; the name referred to the sound the fastener made.

Clothing manufacturers were slow to adopt it. Many people were worried that the metal teeth would rust or catch on the skin. In the 1930s, however, the fastener began to appear on children's clothing, since it allowed young children to dress themselves more easily. Fashion designers soon followed, and a campaign in men's magazines praised trousers with zips rather than buttons.

Today, billions of zips are made every year, and a large share are produced by a single Japanese company, YKK. Modern zips are made from metal or plastic, and some are waterproof, for use in diving suits and outdoor clothing.

lesson.title: Dates in a timeline
lesson.text: History notes are often organised as a timeline, with dates at the start of each bullet. A passage may give two dates for the same invention: when it was designed and when it was patented. Before you write a date, read the note carefully to see which event it refers to.
lesson.example: Passage: "He built the engine in 1885 and patented it in 1886." Note: "patent granted: (1) ______" Answer: 1886.

passages.topic: Plant biology — the baobab tree
passages.title: The Upside-Down Tree

paragraphs.text: Baobab trees grow in the dry savannas of mainland Africa, Madagascar and Australia. There are eight species, six of which are found only in Madagascar. With their enormously thick trunks and short, root-like branches, baobabs look as if they have been planted upside down, and many African legends explain their strange shape.

The most remarkable feature of the baobab is its ability to store water. Its trunk is made of soft, spongy wood that can hold large quantities of water absorbed during the rainy season. A large tree can store more than a hundred thousand litres. During the dry season, when the tree loses its leaves, it draws on this supply. The trunk visibly swells after the rains and shrinks during the dry months.

Baobabs can live for a very long time. Because their wood does not form clear annual rings, their age is difficult to measure, but radiocarbon dating has shown that some trees are more than two thousand years old. Old trees often become hollow inside, and hollow baobabs have been used as shelters, water stores and even, in one well-known case in South Africa, as a bar.

Almost every part of the tree is useful to people. The leaves are eaten as a vegetable, and the fruit – a large, hard-shelled pod – contains a dry, powdery pulp that is rich in vitamin C. The pulp can be mixed with water to make a drink. The bark contains strong fibres that are made into rope, baskets and cloth, and the seeds can be pressed to produce oil.
Baobab flowers are large and white and open at night. They have a strong smell and are pollinated mainly by fruit bats, which feed on their nectar. In some regions, bush babies and insects also help.

In the early twenty-first century, scientists noticed that several of the oldest and largest baobabs in southern Africa had died or lost their largest trunks within a few years. The reasons are not fully understood, but researchers have suggested that changes in climate, including higher temperatures and drought, may be responsible.

lesson.title: What counts as one word
lesson.text: With the instruction ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER, a single letter (such as the C in "vitamin C") counts as one word, and a number counts as a number, not a word. Units that are already printed in the notes should not be copied again. If a note says "over 100,000 (3) ______", only the unit is missing.
lesson.example: Passage: "It is rich in vitamin A." Note: "rich in vitamin (1) ______" Answer: A.

passages.topic: Marine biology — how dolphins sleep
passages.title: Half Asleep

paragraphs.text: All mammals need sleep, but for animals that live in water and breathe air, sleep poses a problem. A dolphin cannot breathe automatically as humans do; it must consciously rise to the surface and open its blowhole each time it takes a breath. If it fell completely asleep, it could drown. How, then, do dolphins rest?

The answer, discovered in the 1970s by Russian scientists who recorded the brain activity of bottlenose dolphins, is that dolphins sleep with only one half of the brain at a time. While one half rests, the other remains awake, controlling breathing and watching for danger. This is known as unihemispheric sleep. After a period of time, the two halves swap roles.

During this kind of sleep, the eye connected to the sleeping half of the brain is closed, while the other eye stays open. In groups, dolphins resting side by side often keep their open eye turned towards the other members of the group, which may help them stay together and avoid predators such as sharks.

Dolphins sleep in this way for a total of around eight hours a day, often in several shorter periods. While sleeping, they may swim slowly near the surface, rest motionless at the surface in a position known as "logging" because they resemble a floating log, or rest near the sea floor in shallow water, rising occasionally to breathe.

Newborn dolphins and their mothers appear to behave very differently. Some studies found that during the first weeks after birth, neither the calf nor its mother showed normal signs of sleep, remaining constantly active. Scientists believe that this may help protect the calf, which cannot hold its breath for long and is vulnerable to predators, although later research has questioned whether they truly go without sleep.

Some birds also use unihemispheric sleep. Ducks at the edge of a sleeping group, for instance, keep one eye open towards the outside of the group. Frigatebirds, which make long flights over the ocean, have been recorded sleeping with one half of the brain while flying.

lesson.title: Symbols in notes
lesson.text: Notes often use symbols instead of words. The most common are: → (leads to / results in), = (means / is), ≈ (approximately), + (and), ↑ and ↓ (increase and decrease), and e.g. (for example). Translate each symbol into words before you search the passage. For example, "logging = resting still at the (6) ______" means "logging is resting still at the ______".
lesson.example: Note: "total ≈ (1) ______ per day". Passage: "about six hours a day". Answer: six hours.

passages.topic: Physical geography — icebergs
passages.title: Floating Mountains

paragraphs.text: Icebergs are large pieces of freshwater ice that have broken off glaciers or ice shelves and float in the sea. The process by which they break away is called calving. Most icebergs in the North Atlantic come from glaciers on the west coast of Greenland, while the largest icebergs in the world break off the great ice shelves surrounding Antarctica.

Because ice is less dense than seawater, icebergs float, but only a small part of each one is visible. Roughly nine-tenths of an iceberg's volume lies beneath the surface. This is the origin of the expression "the tip of the iceberg", used to describe a small visible part of a much larger problem. The hidden underwater part may extend far out to the sides, making icebergs dangerous for ships even at a distance.

Icebergs vary enormously in size and shape. Small pieces less than a metre high are known as "growlers", and slightly larger ones as "bergy bits". Some Antarctic icebergs are flat-topped and cover thousands of square kilometres; one that broke away in 2000 had an area larger than the island of Jamaica.

The danger icebergs pose to shipping became clear in April 1912, when the passenger liner Titanic struck one in the North Atlantic and sank, with the loss of more than 1,500 lives. After the disaster, several countries established the International Ice Patrol in 1914, which monitors icebergs in the North Atlantic and warns ships of their positions. Today it uses aircraft, satellites and radar.

As they drift into warmer waters, icebergs gradually melt. Most North Atlantic icebergs melt within two or three years. As they melt, they release fresh water and minerals such as iron into the ocean, which can encourage the growth of tiny plants called phytoplankton, providing food for other marine life.

Icebergs have sometimes been proposed as a source of drinking water for dry countries. Plans to tow them over long distances have been studied, but none has yet been carried out, mainly because of the cost and the difficulty of preventing the ice from melting on the way.

passages.topic: Economic history — the trade in natural ice
passages.title: The Frozen Water Trade

paragraphs.text: In the early nineteenth century, ice was a luxury in hot climates. It could be made artificially only in tiny quantities, and there was no way of keeping food cold except with natural ice. In 1806, a young Boston businessman named Frederic Tudor had an idea that most people considered absurd: to cut ice from the frozen lakes of New England in winter and ship it to the Caribbean.

His first cargo, sent to the island of Martinique, was largely a failure. Much of the ice melted, and the local population had no idea what to do with the rest; there were no ice houses to store it, and few people wanted to buy it. Tudor lost a great deal of money and was imprisoned for debt more than once in the following years. He persisted, however, building insulated ice houses in the ports he supplied and giving away cold drinks to create demand.

Two technical improvements made the trade profitable. Tudor experimented with insulating materials and found that sawdust, a waste product from timber mills that was available cheaply, was highly effective at slowing melting when packed around blocks of ice in ships' holds. Then, in the 1820s, his supplier Nathaniel Wyeth invented a horse-drawn ice cutter that sliced frozen lakes into a grid of uniform blocks. Regular blocks could be stacked closely together, which reduced melting and made storage much more efficient.

By the 1830s, Tudor was shipping ice as far as India. The voyage to Calcutta lasted four months and crossed the equator twice, yet a large share of the cargo survived. The trade grew rapidly, and by the mid-nineteenth century, ice from New England was exported to many parts of the world. At home, ice became a household necessity: "iceboxes", wooden cabinets cooled by blocks of ice delivered regularly to people's homes, allowed families to keep food fresh for longer.

The natural ice trade had serious weaknesses. Mild winters could produce thin ice and poor harvests, causing shortages and sharp price rises. As cities grew, many lakes and rivers became polluted, raising concerns about the cleanliness of ice cut from them. Meanwhile, inventors were developing machines that could make ice artificially.

By the early twentieth century, mechanical refrigeration had become reliable and affordable, and ice factories could produce clean ice all year round. The natural ice trade declined rapidly, and within a few decades electric refrigerators in homes had replaced the icebox. Yet the trade had left a lasting mark: it had created the expectation that cold food and drink should be available everywhere.

lesson.title: Notes grouped by topic, not by paragraph
lesson.text: At Medium level, notes are often organised by topic ("Key innovations", "Problems") rather than following the passage paragraph by paragraph. One heading may therefore collect details from different parts of the passage, and the last gap may come from a paragraph earlier than the one before it. Use the heading to decide what kind of information you need, then look for it wherever it appears.
lesson.example: Heading: "Problems". The passage mentions one problem in Paragraph B and another in Paragraph E. Both belong under the same heading, even though other information comes between them.

passages.topic: Animal behaviour — the intelligence of octopuses
passages.title: Minds in Eight Arms

paragraphs.text: Octopuses are molluscs, related to snails and clams, yet they display abilities usually associated with animals that have much larger and more complex brains. They can solve problems, recognise individual humans and, in some experiments, appear to learn by watching others. Their intelligence is especially intriguing because their evolutionary line separated from our own more than five hundred million years ago, meaning that complex minds evolved independently in octopuses and in vertebrates.

The nervous system of an octopus is organised very differently from ours. An octopus has around five hundred million neurons, a number comparable to that of a dog, but about two-thirds of them are located not in the brain but in the arms. Each arm can taste and touch, and appears able to carry out some actions with a degree of independence, such as reaching for food, even when separated from the central brain.

Laboratory studies have documented impressive problem-solving. Octopuses have learned to unscrew the lids of jars to reach food inside, and some have escaped from their tanks, travelled across laboratories and returned. In one well-known study published in 1992, octopuses that watched another octopus choose an object of a particular colour were more likely to choose that colour themselves, suggesting learning by observation, although later attempts to repeat the experiment produced mixed results.

Octopuses also appear to play. In experiments in which floating objects were placed in their tanks, some octopuses repeatedly pushed the objects into a current of water and caught them again, behaviour that researchers compared to a child bouncing a ball. In the wild, the veined octopus has been filmed carrying coconut shells, which it later assembles into a shelter, one of the few examples of tool use among invertebrates.

Their skin provides another remarkable ability. Special cells containing coloured pigment allow octopuses to change colour and pattern within a fraction of a second, for camouflage or signalling. Surprisingly, octopuses are thought to be colour-blind, and researchers are still investigating how they manage to match the colours of their surroundings; one suggestion is that the skin itself may detect light.

Researchers emphasise that octopus intelligence should not be judged simply by comparison with human intelligence. Octopuses live short lives – most species only one or two years – and they are largely solitary, so their abilities probably evolved to deal with the challenges of finding food and avoiding predators rather than living in social groups. The growing recognition of their capacities has led some countries to extend animal-welfare laws to cover them.

lesson.example: Passage: "The drug reduced pain, but the trial was small." Notes: "• result: less pain – limitation: (1) ______ trial". Answer: small.

passages.topic: History of science — the discovery of the first synthetic dye
passages.title: The Accidental Colour

paragraphs.text: Before the mid-nineteenth century, all dyes used to colour cloth came from natural sources: plants, insects and shellfish. Some colours were very expensive. Purple was especially costly, because the most famous purple dye, used since ancient times, was extracted from thousands of sea snails to produce a tiny quantity. Purple clothing had long been associated with royalty and power.

In 1856, William Henry Perkin, an eighteen-year-old chemistry student in London, was working during the Easter holidays in a small laboratory at his home. His teacher, August Hofmann, was interested in making quinine, a medicine used to treat malaria, which was obtained from the bark of a South American tree and was expensive. Perkin attempted to produce quinine artificially from chemicals found in coal tar, a waste product of the gas used for lighting.

The experiment failed to produce quinine. Instead, it left a dark, sticky residue. When Perkin tried to clean his flask with alcohol, he noticed that the residue dissolved to give a brilliant purple solution. Testing it on silk, he found that it dyed the fabric a strong colour that did not fade quickly in sunlight or wash out.

Recognising the commercial potential, Perkin left his studies, obtained a patent and, with financial support from his father, built a factory to produce the dye. The colour, later called mauve, became extremely fashionable, helped by the fact that Queen Victoria wore a mauve dress to a royal wedding in 1858. The colour was so popular in the following years that the period has sometimes been called the "mauve decade".

Perkin's discovery launched the synthetic dye industry. Chemists in Britain, France and especially Germany developed many new dyes from coal tar, producing reds, blues and greens that were cheaper and more consistent than natural dyes. German companies, which invested heavily in research laboratories and trained chemists, soon dominated the industry.

The consequences extended far beyond fashion. The chemical knowledge and companies built on synthetic dyes later contributed to the development of medicines, photography and other products. The German scientist Paul Ehrlich, observing that certain dyes stained particular cells and bacteria, developed the idea of chemicals that could target disease-causing organisms, an idea that helped establish modern drug treatment.

lesson.title: Aim versus result
lesson.text: Stories of discovery often describe what someone was trying to do and what actually happened. Notes separate these with labels such as "aim" and "result". The two are easily confused because both appear close together in the passage. Before you write, check which label is printed before the gap.
lesson.example: Passage: "He set out to find a new route to India but reached the Caribbean." Notes: "aim: route to (1) ______" Answer: India.

passages.topic: Resources and environment — the global shortage of sand
passages.title: Running Out of Sand

paragraphs.text: Sand seems to be one of the most abundant materials on Earth, yet in many parts of the world it is becoming scarce. After water, sand and gravel are the resources most used by humans. Estimates suggest that around fifty billion tonnes are extracted each year, mainly for construction. Concrete, which is roughly three-quarters sand and gravel by weight, is the largest single use; sand is also used to make glass, to build roads and to create new land.

Not all sand is suitable. Desert sand, although plentiful, is generally useless for concrete. Shaped by the wind, its grains are rounded and smooth, so they do not bind together well. Construction requires the angular grains found in rivers, lakes and coastal areas, where water has shaped them more gently. As a result, demand falls heavily on a limited number of places, and even desert countries such as the United Arab Emirates have imported sand for building projects.

Extraction on this scale causes considerable damage. Removing sand from riverbeds can deepen channels, lower water tables and undermine bridges and riverbanks. In coastal areas, it can accelerate erosion and damage the habitats of fish and birds. In the Mekong Delta in Vietnam, sand mining, combined with dams upstream, has contributed to the loss of land to the sea, threatening farming communities.

In some countries, the high value of sand has encouraged illegal extraction. Sand is often mined at night by unlicensed operators, and in India, where construction has grown rapidly, criminal groups known as "sand mafias" have been linked to violence against journalists and officials who try to stop them.

Several alternatives are being explored. Crushed rock can be manufactured into sand of the right shape, although producing it requires energy. Recycled concrete from demolished buildings can replace a proportion of new material. Researchers are also testing whether desert sand can be made usable by processing it, and some are developing building materials that require less sand altogether.

Despite its importance, sand extraction is poorly monitored in most countries, and there is little reliable information on how much is taken or where. A report published by the United Nations Environment Programme in 2019 called for better data, stronger regulation and treating sand as a strategic resource rather than an unlimited one.

You may copy it in words or figures, but the unit already printed in the note must not be repeated. Also check what the number measures: amount extracted, share of a mixture, or year.

passages.topic: Engineering and environment — how the Netherlands holds back the sea
passages.title: Holding Back the Sea

paragraphs.text: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, and much of the rest would be flooded regularly by rivers or the sea without protection. For centuries, the Dutch have built dykes – earth banks – to defend their land and have drained lakes and marshes to create farmland, known as polders. Windmills, and later steam and electric pumps, were used to remove the water.

On the night of 31 January 1953, a severe storm combined with a high spring tide drove the North Sea against the coast of the south-western Netherlands. Many dykes, weakened and in poor condition, were breached, and seawater flooded large areas of land. More than 1,800 people died, tens of thousands of animals were drowned, and around a hundred thousand people had to leave their homes.

In response, the government launched the Delta Works, one of the largest flood-protection projects ever undertaken. Its central idea was to shorten the coastline by closing off the estuaries – the wide mouths of rivers – in the south-west of the country with dams and barriers, so that far fewer kilometres of dyke had to be defended. The programme took several decades to complete.

The original plan was to close the largest estuary, the Eastern Scheldt, completely with a dam. By the 1970s, however, environmental groups, fishermen and oyster farmers objected strongly. A complete dam would have turned the salt water behind it into fresh water, destroying a rich tidal environment and the shellfish industry that depended on it. After intense debate, the government chose a more expensive solution: a storm surge barrier with sixty-two large gates that remain open in normal conditions, allowing the tide to flow in and out, and close only during dangerous storms. The barrier was completed in 1986.

The last major structure, the Maeslantkering, was completed in 1997 to protect the port of Rotterdam. It consists of two enormous movable arms, each about as long as the Eiffel Tower is high, which normally rest in dry docks at the sides of the channel. When a severe storm is forecast, they float into position and sink to close the waterway, while at other times ships can pass freely.

Rising sea levels and heavier river flows caused by climate change have led the Netherlands to rethink its approach. Under a programme called "Room for the River", completed in the 2010s, some dykes were moved further inland and certain low-lying areas were designated to flood safely during high water. The aim is to work with natural processes rather than simply building ever higher defences.

lesson.title: Arrows that show cause and effect
lesson.text: An arrow (→) in notes links a cause to its effect or an action to its result. If the gap comes before the arrow, you need the cause; if it comes after, you need the result. Read the passage sentence that links the two and decide which side of the relationship the gap asks for.
lesson.example: Passage: "Heavy rain caused the river to overflow." Note: "(1) ______ → river overflowed". Answer: heavy rain (the cause).

passages.topic: Biology and health — the body clock and jet lag
passages.title: The Body's Clock

paragraphs.text: Almost every living thing, from bacteria to humans, has internal rhythms that follow a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours. These circadian rhythms – from Latin words meaning "about a day" – regulate when we feel sleepy or alert, and affect body temperature, hormone levels and digestion. In humans, the master clock is located in a small group of cells in the hypothalamus, a region at the base of the brain.

The internal clock does not run exactly to time. In experiments in which volunteers lived in caves or special rooms without daylight or clocks, their daily cycles drifted, typically becoming slightly longer than twenty-four hours. In normal life, the clock is kept in step with the day by external cues, of which the most important is light. Light detected by special cells in the eye signals to the master clock, adjusting its timing.

One of the clock's main outputs is the hormone melatonin, produced by the pineal gland in the evening as darkness falls. Melatonin helps prepare the body for sleep. Bright light, especially light at the blue end of the spectrum, suppresses its production, which is why exposure to screens late at night may delay sleep.

Jet lag occurs when travellers cross several time zones quickly, so that their internal clock is out of step with local time. They may feel tired during the day, wake during the night, and suffer from poor concentration and digestive problems. The body clock can usually adjust by only about one hour per day, so recovery from a large time difference can take several days. Most people find travelling eastwards more difficult than travelling westwards, since it requires the clock to be moved earlier, whereas the natural tendency of the clock is to run slightly late.

Several strategies can reduce jet lag. Exposure to daylight at the right time of day at the destination helps to reset the clock, as does avoiding light at the wrong time. Some travellers take melatonin, which, when taken at the correct time, can help shift the clock, although its use is regulated differently in different countries.

Similar problems affect shift workers, whose working hours regularly conflict with their internal clocks. Long-term shift work has been associated with a higher risk of several health problems, and researchers are studying how work schedules and lighting could be designed to reduce the disruption.

lesson.title: Technical terms in notes

lesson.example: Passage: "Chlorophyll, the green pigment in leaves, absorbs light." Note: "light absorbed by (1) ______" Answer: chlorophyll.
