passages.topic: Archaeology — the Terracotta Army
passages.title: The Silent Army

paragraphs.text: In March 1974, farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an in northern China struck fragments of pottery. They had discovered part of one of the most remarkable archaeological sites in the world: a vast underground army of life-sized clay soldiers, buried more than two thousand years ago to accompany the first emperor of a unified China, Qin Shi Huang, in the afterlife.

Qin Shi Huang came to power as king of the state of Qin in 246 BC, when he was only thirteen years old, and by 221 BC he had conquered the rival states to create a single empire. He introduced standard systems of writing, weights, measures and money, and began linking existing defensive walls into an early version of the Great Wall. Work on his tomb began soon after he became king and is said to have involved hundreds of thousands of labourers.

Three large pits containing figures have been excavated. The largest holds soldiers arranged in battle formation, with archers at the front, followed by infantry and war chariots drawn by horses. Archaeologists estimate that the pits contain around eight thousand soldiers, although only a portion have been fully excavated. No two faces are exactly alike: the bodies were made from a limited number of moulds, but the heads, hair and facial features were shaped individually by hand.

Today the figures are the colour of clay, but they were originally brightly painted. When they are exposed to air after more than two thousand years underground, the paint dries, curls and flakes off within minutes. This is one reason why excavation has proceeded slowly: archaeologists have been reluctant to uncover more figures until better methods of preserving the paint are available.

The soldiers once carried real weapons, including bronze swords, spears and crossbows. Some bronze weapons found in the pits remained remarkably sharp and showed little corrosion. Early studies suggested that they had been deliberately coated with chromium to protect them, but more recent research concluded that the good condition of the metal was probably due mainly to the properties of the surrounding soil.

The emperor's own burial mound, which lies nearby, has never been opened. An ancient historian wrote that it contained a model of the empire with rivers of mercury, and scientific tests of the soil have found unusually high levels of mercury. Chinese authorities have decided not to excavate the tomb until methods exist that can protect its contents.

passages.topic: Public health — using bacteria to fight mosquito-borne disease
passages.title: Fighting Disease with Bacteria

paragraphs.text: Mosquitoes of the species Aedes aegypti spread several serious viral diseases, including dengue, Zika and chikungunya. Dengue alone infects many millions of people each year in tropical and subtropical regions. Traditional control methods – spraying insecticides and removing the standing water in which mosquitoes breed – are expensive and often only partly effective, and mosquitoes can develop resistance to insecticides.

A different approach uses Wolbachia, a type of bacterium found naturally in around half of all insect species, including many butterflies and flies, but not normally in Aedes aegypti. In the 2000s, researchers in Australia succeeded in introducing Wolbachia into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in the laboratory. They found that the bacterium made it much harder for viruses such as dengue to multiply inside the mosquito, reducing its ability to transmit them to people.

Crucially, Wolbachia can spread through a mosquito population on its own. Female mosquitoes carrying the bacterium pass it on to all their offspring through their eggs. If a female without Wolbachia mates with a male that carries it, her eggs do not hatch. As a result, females carrying Wolbachia have a reproductive advantage, and after mosquitoes with the bacterium have been released for a few months, it can become established in most of the local population without further releases.

The method was first tested in two small towns in northern Australia in 2011. Later, larger programmes were carried out in several countries. In a trial in the Indonesian city of Yogyakarta, the results of which were published in 2021, neighbourhoods were randomly chosen either to receive Wolbachia mosquitoes or not. Cases of dengue requiring hospital treatment fell by around three-quarters in the treated areas compared with the untreated ones.

A separate strategy uses Wolbachia differently. Only male mosquitoes carrying the bacterium are released, in large numbers. Because their matings with wild females produce eggs that do not hatch, this approach aims to reduce the size of the mosquito population rather than to change it. Since male mosquitoes do not bite, releasing them does not increase the risk to people.

Supporters argue that Wolbachia methods are more sustainable than repeated insecticide spraying and are safe for humans and the environment. Researchers continue to monitor whether viruses might eventually evolve to overcome the bacterium's effects, and whether the method works as well in large cities with dense and varied populations.

lesson.title: Notes that break a process into steps
lesson.text: When a passage explains a process (how something spreads, how a method works), the notes may turn each step into a short line. The passage often explains the steps in a different order from the notes, or combines two steps in one sentence. lesson.example: Passage: "Seeds are carried by birds, which drop them far from the parent plant." Notes: "• seeds carried by (1) ______ • dropped far from (2) ______" Answers: birds; parent plant.

passages.topic: History of science — mapping the ocean floor
passages.title: Drawing the Invisible

paragraphs.text: In the middle of the twentieth century, the floor of the deep ocean was one of the least known places on Earth. Early measurements had been made by lowering weighted ropes to the sea bed, a slow method that produced only scattered depths. After the First World War, echo sounders – devices that measure depth by timing how long a sound pulse takes to return from the sea floor – made it possible to record continuous profiles as ships moved, but most of the data remained unanalysed.

In 1948, Marie Tharp, who had studied geology and mathematics, joined a research laboratory at Columbia University in New York. At that time, women were not permitted to work aboard the laboratory's research vessels, so Tharp worked on land, turning thousands of depth readings collected by male colleagues, particularly the geologist Bruce Heezen, into maps.

Working on profiles across the North Atlantic, Tharp noticed something unexpected. A deep valley appeared to run along the centre of a great undersea mountain range, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, in profile after profile. She suggested that it was a rift, where the sea floor was being pulled apart – evidence consistent with the then-controversial idea that the continents moved. According to Tharp's later account, Heezen at first dismissed the suggestion. He was persuaded only when the locations of earthquakes, plotted by another member of the laboratory, were found to follow the line of the valley.

Instead of the conventional method of showing depth with contour lines, Tharp and Heezen presented the ocean floor as a physiographic diagram: a drawing that showed the landscape as it might appear if the water were removed. This choice was partly practical. The United States Navy, concerned about submarine warfare, classified detailed depth data as secret, and a picture that gave an impression of the terrain without precise numbers could be published.

Their maps, culminating in a map of the entire world ocean floor published in 1977 and painted by the Austrian artist Heinrich Berann, revealed a global system of ridges tens of thousands of kilometres long. The images helped persuade scientists and the public that the ocean floor was geologically active, and they supported the developing theory of plate tectonics.

For much of her career, Tharp received little recognition; her name often appeared after Heezen's, and her contribution was overlooked. In later years, however, her role was increasingly acknowledged, and in 1997 the Library of Congress named her one of the most important cartographers of the twentieth century.

lesson.title: Hard Note Completion — abstract headings and heavy paraphrase
lesson.text: At Hard level, headings are abstract ("Working conditions", "Method of presentation") and the notes rarely share words with the passage. With ONE WORD ONLY, you must also find the single word that carries the meaning. Strategy: turn each note into a question ("What was she excluded from?"), find the sentence that answers it, and choose the one word that fits both the meaning and the grammar of the note.
lesson.example: Note: "excluded from (1) ______ on grounds of sex". Passage: "women were not allowed on the expeditions". Answer: expeditions.

passages.topic: History of science — solving the problem of longitude
passages.title: The Clock That Found the Sea

paragraphs.text: For centuries, sailors could determine their latitude – their position north or south – fairly easily, by measuring the height of the sun or certain stars above the horizon. Longitude, their position east or west, was far harder to establish. Because the Earth rotates through fifteen degrees every hour, a navigator who knew the time at a reference point, such as the home port, and compared it with local time on the ship could calculate how far east or west the ship had travelled. The difficulty was carrying accurate time across the ocean: the pendulum clocks of the period were useless on a rolling ship.

Errors in longitude caused many shipwrecks. In 1707, a British naval fleet ran onto rocks off the Isles of Scilly, with the loss of around 1,500 sailors, partly because of a navigational error. In 1714, the British Parliament passed the Longitude Act, offering a prize of up to twenty thousand pounds for a practical method of finding longitude at sea to within half a degree. A committee known as the Board of Longitude was established to judge proposals.

Many leading scientists believed that the answer lay in astronomy, particularly in measuring the position of the Moon against the stars, the "lunar distance" method. John Harrison, a carpenter from the north of England with no formal scientific education, pursued a different solution: a clock accurate enough to keep time at sea.

Harrison spent more than three decades on the problem. His first three sea clocks were large and heavy, designed to resist the motion of the ship. His fourth timekeeper, known as H4 and completed in 1759, was very different: it resembled a large pocket watch, only about thirteen centimetres across. On a voyage to Jamaica in 1761–62, it lost only about five seconds, well within the accuracy required for the prize.

The Board of Longitude, however, was reluctant to award the full prize. Some members favoured the astronomical method, and they questioned whether Harrison's success could be repeated. They demanded further trials and required him to hand over his designs and have copies made by other craftsmen. Harrison received partial payments, and in 1773, when he was eighty years old, he was awarded a further sum by Parliament after appealing directly to King George III, although he never officially received the prize itself.

Marine chronometers based on Harrison's principles became standard equipment on ships, but they remained expensive for many years. The navigator James Cook used a copy of H4, made by the watchmaker Larcum Kendall, on his second voyage to the Pacific and praised its accuracy. By the nineteenth century, chronometers were widely produced, and they remained essential for navigation until the arrival of radio time signals and, later, satellite systems.

lesson.title: Many numbers, names and competing methods
lesson.text: Hard history passages contain many figures (dates, sums of money, measurements) and several named people. Distractors are usually real passage details of the same type attached to a different event: the year of a disaster instead of the year of a law, a watchmaker's name instead of a navigator's. For each gap, find the exact event the note describes before choosing a figure or a name.
lesson.example: Passage: "A shipwreck in 1707 led Parliament to pass a law in 1714." Note: "law passed: (1) ______". Answer: 1714.

passages.topic: Medical science — allergies and the "old friends" hypothesis
passages.title: Too Clean?

paragraphs.text: During the twentieth century, allergic diseases such as hay fever, asthma and eczema became dramatically more common in wealthy countries. The rise was too rapid to be explained by genetic change, and researchers began looking for environmental causes. In 1989, the British epidemiologist David Strachan published a study of more than seventeen thousand British children, which found that those with more older brothers and sisters were less likely to develop hay fever.

Strachan suggested that infections in early childhood, spread by contact with older siblings, might protect against allergies. With smaller families, higher standards of cleanliness and fewer infections, children's immune systems might develop in a way that made them more likely to react to harmless substances such as pollen. This idea became known as the "hygiene hypothesis", and it was widely reported as meaning that modern homes were simply too clean.

Later research complicated the picture. Many common childhood infections, such as measles, do not appear to protect against allergies, and some viral infections actually increase the risk of asthma. At the same time, studies found strong protective effects from other kinds of exposure. Children who grew up on traditional farms, in close contact with animals, were considerably less likely to develop asthma and allergies than other children living in the same regions. A study published in 2016 compared two farming communities in the United States with similar genetic origins: the Amish, who use traditional farming methods and live close to their animals, and the Hutterites, who use industrial farming methods. Asthma was four to six times less common among Amish children, and dust from Amish homes contained far more microbial material.

These findings led the microbiologist Graham Rook to propose a revised explanation, sometimes called the "old friends" hypothesis. According to this view, what matters is not infections in general but exposure to the microorganisms with which humans evolved over millions of years – those found in soil, animals, untreated water and the human gut. These "old friends" are thought to help train the immune system to tolerate harmless substances. Modern life has reduced contact with them through urban living, antibiotics, processed diets and changes in childbirth and feeding.

Researchers emphasise that this does not mean that hygiene should be abandoned. Handwashing and clean water prevent serious infections and save many lives. The loss of beneficial microbial exposure is linked less to cleaning homes than to broader changes in how people live, including less time outdoors and less contact with nature. Some scientists have therefore suggested replacing the term "hygiene hypothesis", which they regard as misleading.

Studies are now investigating whether exposure to beneficial microbes can be deliberately increased, for example through probiotics or changes to the design of urban green spaces. Early results are mixed, and researchers caution that it is not yet clear which microbes matter most, or at what age exposure is most important.

lesson.title: A hypothesis and its revision in the same notes
lesson.text: When notes cover a scientific idea that was later revised, headings such as "Original hypothesis", "Problems with it" and "Revised view" divide the notes by stage. The passage uses similar vocabulary for all three stages (infection, exposure, microbes, hygiene). Before writing, confirm that your answer comes from the stage named in the heading above the gap.
lesson.example: Headings: "Original view: caused by (1) ______" and "Revised view: caused by (2) ______". The passage gives both causes in consecutive paragraphs; each answer must come from the matching stage.

passages.topic: Atmospheric science — the discovery of the ozone hole
passages.title: A Hole in the Sky

paragraphs.text: High in the atmosphere, between about fifteen and thirty-five kilometres above the Earth's surface, lies a layer relatively rich in ozone, a form of oxygen. This ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, which can cause skin cancer and cataracts in humans and damage plants and marine life.

In 1974, the chemists Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland published a paper warning that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) – synthetic chemicals widely used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays – could damage the ozone layer. CFCs were valued because they were stable and non-toxic, but this stability meant that they survived long enough to drift up into the stratosphere. There, ultraviolet radiation would break them apart, releasing chlorine atoms, each of which could destroy many thousands of ozone molecules. The chemical industry strongly disputed the warning.

The first dramatic evidence came from an unexpected source. Scientists of the British Antarctic Survey had been measuring ozone above their research station at Halley Bay since the 1950s, using ground-based instruments. In 1985, Joseph Farman and his colleagues reported that ozone levels over Antarctica in spring had fallen by around a third since the 1960s. Satellite instruments operated by NASA had also recorded low values, but the data-processing software had been programmed to reject extremely low readings as probable errors, so the decline had not been noticed.

The Antarctic losses were far greater than models had predicted. Further research showed why. In the extremely cold Antarctic winter, clouds form in the stratosphere, and chemical reactions on the surfaces of their ice particles convert chlorine into forms that are released rapidly when sunlight returns in spring, causing sudden, severe destruction. This seasonal thinning became known as the "ozone hole".

The discovery prompted unusually rapid international action. The Montreal Protocol, agreed in 1987, committed countries to reducing the production of CFCs; later amendments phased them out almost completely. It became the first United Nations treaty to be ratified by every member state. In 1995, Molina and Rowland, together with the Dutch scientist Paul Crutzen, were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work on ozone.

Because CFCs remain in the atmosphere for many decades, recovery is slow. Recent assessments suggest that the Antarctic ozone hole is gradually shrinking and may return to its 1980 levels by around the 2060s. The treaty has also brought an additional benefit: since many CFCs are powerful greenhouse gases, phasing them out has also reduced warming.

lesson.title: Chains of cause and effect across paragraphs
lesson.text: Hard science passages explain a chain: a chemical is released → it rises → it is broken apart → it destroys something. Notes may present each link as a separate line, and a single link may be explained in one paragraph while its consequence is described in another. Follow the chain in order, and make sure the word you choose belongs to the link the note describes.
lesson.example: Passage: "Sunlight breaks the molecule apart, releasing chlorine, which destroys ozone." Note: "released by sunlight: (1) ______" Answer: chlorine (not "ozone", which is destroyed).

passages.topic: Space science — the growing problem of space debris
passages.title: Crowded Orbits

paragraphs.text: Since the first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched in 1957, humans have placed thousands of objects in orbit around the Earth. Many are no longer working. Together with spent rocket stages and fragments from explosions and collisions, these form a growing cloud of space debris. Space agencies track more than thirty thousand objects larger than about ten centimetres, and estimate that there are around a million pieces between one and ten centimetres across, too small to track but still dangerous.

Debris is dangerous because of its speed. In low Earth orbit, objects travel at around seven to eight kilometres per second. At such speeds, even a fleck of paint can damage a spacecraft window, and a piece of debris a centimetre across can strike with the energy of an exploding hand grenade. The International Space Station has to change its orbit several times a year to avoid pieces of debris, and its most vulnerable parts are protected by layered shields.

In 1978, the NASA scientist Donald Kessler proposed that the problem could become self-sustaining. If the density of objects in a particular orbit became high enough, collisions would create fragments, which would cause further collisions, producing still more fragments in a chain reaction. Eventually, some orbits could become so crowded with debris that they would be unusable for generations. This scenario is now known as the Kessler syndrome.

Two events in the 2000s greatly increased the amount of debris. In 2007, China tested an anti-satellite missile by destroying one of its own old weather satellites, creating thousands of trackable fragments. In 2009, an active American communications satellite and an inactive Russian satellite collided accidentally over Siberia – the first accidental collision between two intact satellites – producing another large cloud of debris.

International guidelines now recommend that satellites in low orbits be removed within twenty-five years of the end of their missions, either by lowering them so that they burn up in the atmosphere or by moving them to less crowded "graveyard" orbits. Compliance, however, has been incomplete. The situation has become more urgent as companies launch large constellations of thousands of small satellites to provide internet services, greatly increasing the number of objects in low orbit.

Various methods of active removal are being developed, including nets, harpoons and robotic arms to capture defunct satellites and drag them out of orbit. In 2018, a British-led experimental mission successfully tested a net and a harpoon on targets it had released itself. Removing debris is expensive, however, and raises difficult questions about who should pay, since the fragments belong to many different countries and companies.

lesson.title: Very compressed notes
lesson.text: Some notes are compressed into almost pure symbols and abbreviations: "est. 1m pieces 1–10 cm: too small to (2) ______". Expand each note into a full sentence before searching ("An estimated one million pieces between one and ten centimetres are too small to ..."). The expanded sentence will be much easier to match to the passage, and it shows you the grammar the gap needs.
lesson.example: Note: "pop. ↑ 3× since 1950". Expanded: "The population has tripled since 1950."

passages.topic: Archaeology and dating methods — the age of cave art
passages.title: Dating the First Artists

paragraphs.text: Cave paintings are among the most striking evidence of early human creativity, but determining their age has always been difficult. Radiocarbon dating, the standard method for organic materials, can be used only when paintings contain carbon, such as charcoal. Many paintings, however, were made with mineral pigments such as red ochre, a form of iron oxide, which contain no carbon. Moreover, taking samples of pigment damages the artwork.

Over the past two decades, researchers have increasingly used a different technique, uranium-series dating. In many limestone caves, water trickling over the walls deposits thin layers of calcium carbonate, the mineral that forms stalactites. Where such a crust has formed over a painting, it can be dated. The water contains tiny amounts of uranium but almost no thorium; once the crust forms, the uranium gradually decays into thorium at a known rate. Measuring the ratio of thorium to uranium reveals how long ago the crust formed. Because the crust lies on top of the painting, its age gives a minimum age for the art beneath: the painting must be older.

In 2012, a team led by the archaeologist Alistair Pike applied the method to paintings in eleven caves in northern Spain. One red disc in the cave of El Castillo was found to be at least forty thousand years old, making it among the oldest known cave art in Europe. In 2018, another team reported that red markings in three Spanish caves, including a ladder-like shape and hand stencils, were more than sixty-four thousand years old – about twenty thousand years before modern humans are thought to have arrived in Europe. If this was correct, the art must have been made by Neanderthals.

The Neanderthal claim proved controversial. Some researchers argued that the method can overestimate ages: if water dissolves and removes some of the uranium from the crust after it forms – a process called leaching – the thorium-to-uranium ratio will be higher, and the crust will appear older than it really is. They also questioned whether some of the red markings were deliberate art at all, suggesting that they might be natural stains.

The dating team responded by taking several samples through each crust, from the surface inwards. If the method is working properly, the layers should become progressively older towards the painting; this pattern, they argued, was present in their samples. They also pointed out that other evidence, such as pierced shells coloured with pigment found in a Spanish cave, suggests that Neanderthals were capable of symbolic behaviour.

The debate continues, and the technique has since been applied elsewhere. In 2019, dating on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi indicated that a painted hunting scene was at least forty-four thousand years old. Together, such results suggest that art-making may be older and more widespread than was once thought, although many specialists stress that each date must be judged carefully.

lesson.title: Final review — the complete Note Completion method
lesson.text: This final set combines all the main skills: matching abstract headings to the passage, expanding compressed notes, following a process in order, separating a claim from its criticism and its defence, and copying the minimum words within the limit. For each gap: (1) identify the heading's section; (2) expand the note into a sentence; (3) find the matching idea; (4) copy the exact words and check the limit and grammar.

passages.topic: History of writing — early writing surfaces
passages.title: Surfaces for Writing

paragraphs.text: Before printing, and long before screens, the material on which people wrote shaped how texts were produced, stored and shared. Over thousands of years, several writing surfaces were developed, each suited to the resources and needs of the societies that used them.

Papyrus was first made in Egypt around 3000 BC from the papyrus plant, a tall reed that grew along the River Nile. The stems were cut into thin strips, laid in two layers at right angles and pressed together; the plant's own sap helped bind them. The sheets were joined end to end to form long rolls. Papyrus was light and relatively cheap to produce in Egypt, and it was exported across the Mediterranean. However, it became brittle and cracked when folded, and it decayed quickly in damp climates, which is why most surviving examples come from the dry sands of Egypt.

Parchment was made from animal skin, usually that of sheep, goats or calves. The skin was soaked, scraped clean and stretched on a frame to dry. According to an ancient story, it was developed in the city of Pergamon, in what is now Turkey, when supplies of papyrus were cut off; the word "parchment" comes from the city's name, although animal skins had been used for writing earlier. Parchment was very durable and could be written on both sides, and it could be folded into pages, which encouraged the use of the book, or codex, in place of the roll. Its main disadvantage was cost: a single large book could require the skins of hundreds of animals.

Wax tablets were used widely in ancient Greece and Rome for everyday writing. A wooden board was hollowed out and filled with a layer of beeswax, and the writer scratched letters into the wax with a pointed tool called a stylus. The flat end of the stylus could be used to smooth the wax, so that the tablet could be used again and again. Tablets were ideal for school exercises, notes and accounts, but they were unsuitable for permanent records, because the writing could easily be erased or melted.

Paper was invented in China. Official records credit its development to Cai Lun, a court official, in AD 105, although simpler forms existed earlier. It was made by breaking down plant fibres, such as tree bark, hemp and old rags, in water, spreading the mixture on a screen and letting it dry into a thin sheet. The technique spread slowly westwards, reaching the Islamic world in the eighth century and Europe several centuries later. Paper was much cheaper than parchment and could be produced in large quantities, which made it essential to the spread of printing in the fifteenth century.

Each of these materials survives in some form today. Parchment is still used for a few legal and ceremonial documents, papyrus is produced for tourists in Egypt, and paper, despite predictions of a "paperless office", remains one of the most widely used materials in the world.

lesson.title: Work row by row
lesson.text: In an easy table, each row usually comes from one paragraph. Find the paragraph that describes the item in the row heading, then look for the details asked for by each column. Finish one row before you move to the next, and the answers will follow the order of the passage.
lesson.example: Row "Parchment", column "Made from". Go to the paragraph about parchment and look for the material: animal skin.

passages.topic: Engineering — the main types of bridge
passages.title: Spanning the Gap

paragraphs.text: Engineers have developed several basic types of bridge, each suited to particular distances and conditions. Although modern bridges use advanced materials, the principles behind the main types have been understood for centuries.

The beam bridge is the simplest. It consists of a horizontal beam supported at each end, like a plank laid across a stream. When a load crosses, the top of the beam is squeezed and the bottom is stretched. Because the beam bends more as its length increases, simple beam bridges are suitable only for short spans, usually less than about eighty metres, although longer crossings can be made by placing many beams in a row on supporting piers. They are cheap and quick to build, which makes them common on motorways.

The arch bridge carries its load outwards along a curve into supports at each end, called abutments. Because the arch is squeezed rather than bent, it can be made from materials that are strong in compression, such as stone. The Romans built many stone arch bridges, some of which are still in use after two thousand years. Arch bridges need solid ground at both ends to resist the outward push of the arch.

The suspension bridge hangs its deck from vertical cables attached to two main cables, which pass over tall towers and are anchored firmly in the ground at each end. Because the main cables are pulled rather than pushed, they can be made of steel wire, which is extremely strong in tension. Suspension bridges can cross the longest distances of any bridge type – the main span of the Çanakkale Bridge in Turkey, opened in 2022, is more than two kilometres long – but they are expensive and can be affected by strong winds, which may cause the deck to move.

The cable-stayed bridge also uses cables, but they run directly from one or more towers to the deck, often in a fan or harp-like pattern. No massive anchorages are needed, so these bridges are usually cheaper than suspension bridges for medium-length spans, typically between about two hundred and one thousand metres. Their clean appearance has made them popular in modern cities, and the number built has increased sharply since the 1970s.

Choosing a bridge type depends on the length of the gap, the ground conditions, the traffic the bridge must carry, the available budget and, increasingly, the desired appearance. In many projects, engineers combine types, for example using beam spans for the approaches and a cable-stayed section over the main channel.

passages.topic: Zoology — camels and their relatives
passages.title: Camels and Their Relatives

paragraphs.text: Camels and their relatives, known as camelids, first evolved in North America around forty-five million years ago. Some migrated to Asia across a land bridge, eventually giving rise to the camels of Africa and Asia, while others moved into South America, where their descendants include the llama and the alpaca. Camelids later died out in North America itself.

The dromedary, or Arabian camel, has a single hump and is found mainly in North Africa, the Middle East and India, where almost all are domesticated. Its hump stores fat, not water, which can be broken down for energy when food is scarce. A dromedary can survive for more than two weeks without drinking and can then drink over a hundred litres in about ten minutes. It has long been used to carry goods across deserts and to provide milk and meat.

The Bactrian camel has two humps and lives in the cold, dry deserts and steppes of Central Asia, including Mongolia and China. It grows a thick, shaggy coat in winter to survive temperatures that can fall below minus thirty degrees Celsius, and sheds it in large patches in spring. Most Bactrian camels are domesticated, but a separate species, the wild Bactrian camel, survives in small numbers in the Gobi Desert and is critically endangered. Remarkably, it is able to drink salty water that other mammals cannot.

The llama was domesticated in the Andes mountains of South America several thousand years ago. It is the largest of the South American camelids and was used by the Incas and earlier peoples mainly as a pack animal, capable of carrying loads over difficult mountain terrain. Llamas are sometimes used today to guard flocks of sheep, since they will chase away dogs and foxes.

The alpaca, smaller than the llama, was bred mainly for its fine wool, which is soft and warm and does not contain the natural oil found in sheep's wool. It comes in more than twenty natural colours. Alpacas are kept in large herds on high grasslands in Peru, Bolivia and Chile, and in recent decades they have also become popular on farms in other parts of the world.

All camelids share certain features, including padded feet rather than hard hoofs, which help them walk on sand or rocky ground, and a digestive system with three stomach compartments. They are also known for spitting when annoyed, although they usually direct it at other animals rather than at people.

passages.topic: Geology — the three main groups of rock
passages.title: The Rock Cycle

paragraphs.text: Geologists divide rocks into three main groups according to how they form: igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic. Over millions of years, rocks can change from one type into another through processes such as melting, erosion and burial, in a never-ending sequence known as the rock cycle.

Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and becomes solid. When it cools deep underground, it does so slowly, allowing large crystals to grow; granite, used widely in buildings and kitchen worktops, is a common example. When molten rock erupts from a volcano as lava and cools quickly at the surface, the crystals are very small or absent, producing rocks such as basalt, which forms much of the ocean floor. Some volcanic rocks, such as pumice, contain so many gas bubbles that they can float on water.

Sedimentary rocks form from fragments of other rocks, or from the remains of living things, that are deposited in layers, usually in water. Over time, the layers are buried, compressed and cemented together. Sandstone forms from grains of sand, while limestone is made largely from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms. Sedimentary rocks cover about three-quarters of the Earth's land surface, and they are the only type in which fossils are commonly found, since the heat involved in forming the other types usually destroys them.

Metamorphic rocks are formed when existing rocks are changed by intense heat and pressure, usually deep within the Earth, without melting. The minerals in the rock recrystallise, and the rock often develops bands or layers. Limestone, for example, becomes marble, which has been prized by sculptors for thousands of years, while mudstone and shale become slate, which splits easily into thin sheets and has long been used for roofs.

Each rock type is valuable to people in different ways. Igneous rocks are generally hard and resistant to wear, making them useful for building and road surfaces. Sedimentary rocks contain most of the world's coal, oil and gas. Metamorphic rocks provide some of the most attractive decorative stones.

The rock cycle never stops, but it operates extremely slowly. A granite formed deep underground may take tens of millions of years to be exposed at the surface by erosion and uplift, broken down into sand, and eventually turned into sandstone.

passages.topic: History of technology — calculating devices
passages.title: Counting Machines

paragraphs.text: For most of history, calculations were done in the head, on the fingers or with pebbles. The word "calculate" itself comes from the Latin calculus, meaning a small stone used for counting. As trade and science became more complex, people developed devices to make arithmetic faster and more reliable.

The abacus is one of the oldest calculating tools. Early versions consisted of lines drawn in sand or on a board, on which counters were moved. The familiar frame with beads sliding on rods developed later; the Chinese version, the suanpan, was in use by the fourteenth century at the latest. Skilled users can add and subtract on an abacus remarkably quickly, and it is still used in parts of Asia to teach children mental arithmetic.

In 1642, the French mathematician Blaise Pascal, then only nineteen years old, built a mechanical calculator to help his father, a tax official, with his work. Pascal's machine used a series of interlocking gear wheels and could add and subtract directly. About fifty were made, but they were expensive and difficult to repair, and the machine was never a commercial success.

The slide rule, invented in England in the 1620s, worked in a completely different way. It consisted of two rulers marked with logarithmic scales that slid against each other, allowing users to multiply and divide by adding and subtracting lengths. Slide rules were cheap, portable and fast, though they gave results to only about three significant figures. For more than three centuries they were the standard tool of engineers and scientists; the engineers who designed the first aircraft and space rockets relied on them.

Mechanical calculators became practical office machines in the nineteenth century. The arithmometer, produced in France from the 1850s, was the first to be manufactured and sold in large numbers, and it was used by banks and insurance companies. Later machines were operated by keys and cranks, and in the twentieth century many were driven by electric motors, but they remained heavy and noisy.

The electronic calculator made all these devices obsolete almost overnight. The first desktop electronic calculators appeared in the early 1960s, and in the early 1970s pocket calculators became available. Their prices fell dramatically within a few years, and by the end of the decade slide rules had largely disappeared from shops and classrooms.

passages.topic: Primatology — the great apes compared
passages.title: Our Closest Relatives

paragraphs.text: The great apes – orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos – are humans' closest living relatives. All are intelligent, long-lived and slow to reproduce, and all are threatened by habitat loss, hunting and disease. Yet they differ considerably in where they live, what they eat and how they organise their societies.

Orangutans live only in the rainforests of the islands of Borneo and Sumatra in South-East Asia. They are the most tree-dwelling of the great apes, spending almost all their time in the forest canopy. Their diet consists mainly of fruit, supplemented by leaves, bark and insects. Unlike the other great apes, orangutans are largely solitary: adult males live alone, and females are accompanied only by their young. A mother gives birth only about once every seven to eight years, the longest interval of any mammal.

Gorillas are the largest of the apes; adult males can weigh more than twice as much as females. They live in the forests of central Africa. Their diet is mainly leaves, stems and shoots, and because this food is plentiful, they need to travel relatively short distances each day. Gorillas live in stable groups, usually led by a single mature male called a silverback, after the grey hair on his back, who protects the group and decides where it will travel.

Chimpanzees live across a wide belt of Africa, in forests, woodland and savanna. They eat mainly fruit but also leaves, insects and sometimes meat, and they are known to hunt monkeys in cooperative groups. They live in large communities of up to around a hundred and fifty individuals that split into smaller parties, and males defend the community's territory, sometimes violently. Chimpanzees make and use a wide variety of tools, such as sticks for fishing termites out of their mounds.

Bonobos, which closely resemble chimpanzees, live only in the forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River. Their societies differ strikingly from those of chimpanzees: females hold high status and form strong alliances, and conflicts are frequently resolved through social contact rather than aggression. Bonobos were recognised as a separate species only in 1929.

Protecting the great apes is increasingly urgent. All species are classified as endangered, and three orangutan species and some gorilla populations are critically endangered. Conservation measures include protected areas, efforts to reduce hunting and the illegal trade in young apes, and programmes to reduce the spread of human diseases, to which apes are highly vulnerable.

passages.topic: History of technology — sources of artificial light
passages.title: Lighting the Night

paragraphs.text: For most of human history, artificial light was dim, expensive and dangerous. The economist William Nordhaus once calculated that the amount of work needed to pay for an hour of reading light has fallen by a factor of many thousands since ancient times, making light one of the most dramatic examples of technological progress.

Candles were used from ancient times. Early candles in Europe were usually made from tallow, a form of animal fat, which was cheap but smoky and smelt unpleasant as it burned. Candles made from beeswax burned cleanly and brightly but were so expensive that they were used mainly in churches and wealthy homes. In the nineteenth century, candles made from paraffin wax, a by-product of the oil industry, became common and cheap.

Oil lamps have an equally long history. In the ancient Mediterranean world, small clay lamps burned olive oil. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, whale oil was widely used in Europe and North America, and the demand for it drove a huge whaling industry. In 1780, the Swiss inventor Aimé Argand designed a lamp with a hollow, circular wick and a glass chimney, which supplied more air to the flame and produced a light many times brighter than earlier lamps. From the 1860s, kerosene, refined from petroleum, replaced whale oil as the main lamp fuel.

Gas lighting was introduced in the early nineteenth century. Gas was produced by heating coal and was piped to street lamps and buildings. London's first gas-lit street appeared in 1807, and by the middle of the century gas lighting was common in large cities, making streets safer and allowing shops and factories to operate after dark. However, gas lamps produced heat and soot, consumed oxygen, and occasionally caused explosions.

The electric light bulb was developed by several inventors in the 1870s, including Joseph Swan in Britain and Thomas Edison in the United States. Edison's contribution lay not only in improving the bulb, which used a thin carbon filament that glowed when an electric current passed through it, but also in developing a complete system of generation and distribution: he opened the first central power station in New York in 1882. Early bulbs were inefficient, releasing most of the energy they used as heat rather than light.

The latest revolution is the light-emitting diode, or LED. Although LEDs were first developed in the 1960s, they could produce only red and green light until the invention of efficient blue LEDs in the 1990s made white LED lighting possible; the Japanese scientists responsible received the Nobel Prize in 2014. LEDs use a fraction of the energy of traditional bulbs and can last for tens of thousands of hours.

passages.topic: Water resources — methods of desalination
passages.title: Fresh Water from the Sea

paragraphs.text: About ninety-seven per cent of the Earth's water is salty, and much of the remaining fresh water is locked in ice. As populations grow and droughts become more frequent, many countries are turning to desalination – the removal of salt from seawater or salty groundwater – to supply drinking water. There are now more than fifteen thousand desalination plants worldwide, and they are especially important in the Middle East and North Africa.

The oldest large-scale method is thermal distillation. Seawater is heated until it evaporates, leaving the salt behind, and the steam is then cooled to produce fresh water. Modern plants use a process called multi-stage flash distillation, in which heated seawater passes through a series of chambers at progressively lower pressures, so that it boils at lower temperatures. Thermal plants are reliable and can treat very salty or dirty water, but they consume large amounts of energy, and they are often built next to power stations so that they can use waste heat.

Most new plants use reverse osmosis. In this process, seawater is forced at high pressure through a semi-permeable membrane with pores so small that water molecules can pass through but salt cannot. Reverse osmosis often uses less than half the energy of distillation, and its costs have fallen sharply since the 1990s, largely thanks to more efficient membranes and devices that recover energy from the high-pressure waste stream. Its main weakness is that the membranes can become blocked by particles, algae and bacteria, so the seawater must be carefully treated first.

For small communities in sunny, remote areas, solar stills offer a simple alternative. A solar still is essentially a shallow basin covered by a sloping sheet of glass or plastic. Sunlight evaporates water in the basin, and droplets condense on the cover and run down into a collecting channel. Solar stills require no fuel and little maintenance, but they produce only small quantities – typically a few litres per square metre per day – so they cannot meet the needs of large populations.

All desalination methods produce brine, a very salty waste liquid, which is usually returned to the sea. For each litre of fresh water, roughly one and a half litres of brine are produced. If it is not discharged carefully, the brine can sink to the sea floor and harm marine life, and it may also contain chemicals used to clean equipment.

Researchers are working on ways to make desalination cheaper and cleaner, including powering plants with solar and wind energy and extracting valuable minerals such as lithium and magnesium from brine. Supporters argue that desalination will be essential for water security; critics respond that reducing leaks, reusing wastewater and conserving water are often cheaper first steps.

passages.topic: History and astronomy — calendar systems
passages.title: Measuring the Year

paragraphs.text: Every calendar attempts to fit human timekeeping to the movements of the Earth, Moon and Sun. The difficulty is that these cycles do not divide into each other neatly. The solar year – the time the Earth takes to orbit the Sun – is about 365.24 days, while a lunar month, from one new moon to the next, is about 29.5 days. Different societies have solved the problem in different ways.

The ancient Egyptian civil calendar was one of the first to be based on the solar year. It had twelve months of thirty days each, followed by five extra days, making 365 days in total. Because it ignored the extra quarter of a day, it gradually drifted out of line with the seasons, by one full day every four years. The Egyptians, however, also tracked the rising of the star Sirius, which coincided roughly with the annual flooding of the Nile, a crucial event for farming.

The Islamic calendar is purely lunar. It consists of twelve months that follow the phases of the Moon, giving a year of about 354 days. It makes no attempt to stay aligned with the seasons, so religious festivals such as Ramadan move through the seasons, returning to the same time of year roughly every thirty-three years.

The Julian calendar, introduced in Rome by Julius Caesar in 46 BC, set the year at 365 days with an extra day added every fourth year, giving an average year of 365.25 days. This was far more accurate than earlier Roman calendars, but it was still about eleven minutes longer than the true solar year. Over the centuries the error accumulated, so that by the sixteenth century the calendar was around ten days out of step with the seasons, which caused problems for calculating the date of Easter.

In 1582, Pope Gregory XIII introduced a reformed calendar. Ten days were removed – in Catholic countries, 4 October was followed directly by 15 October – and the rule for leap years was changed: years divisible by 100 would no longer be leap years unless they were also divisible by 400. The Gregorian calendar was adopted quickly in Catholic countries but more slowly elsewhere; Britain did not change until 1752, and Russia not until 1918.

The Maya of Central America used several interlocking calendars, including a 365-day solar calendar and a 260-day ritual calendar. The two combined in a cycle of fifty-two years, known as the Calendar Round. For longer periods, the Maya used a system called the Long Count, which recorded the number of days since a starting point in the distant past.

lesson.text: A passage comparing systems may contain a dozen numbers that look alike (365, 354, 365.25, 260). Before you choose a number, say in words what it measures ("the length of the Islamic year").
lesson.example: Passage: "Planet A orbits in 88 days; Planet B in 225 days." Row: "Planet B | orbit (days): (1) ______". Answer: 225.

passages.topic: Technology — types of rechargeable battery
passages.title: Storing Electricity

paragraphs.text: Batteries store energy in chemical form and release it as electricity. Since the first battery was built by the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta in 1800, many types have been developed, each with a different balance of cost, weight, lifespan and safety. Four rechargeable types have been especially important.

The lithium-ion battery is now the most widely used rechargeable battery, powering phones, laptops and electric vehicles. It stores much more energy for its weight than older types, which is why it made portable electronics and practical electric cars possible. It was commercialised in 1991, and three of the scientists who developed it received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019. However, lithium-ion batteries can overheat and catch fire if damaged or poorly made, and they depend on materials such as lithium and cobalt, whose mining raises environmental and social concerns.

The oldest rechargeable type is the lead-acid battery, invented by the French physicist Gaston Planté in 1859. It is heavy and stores relatively little energy for its weight, but it is cheap and can deliver the large bursts of current needed to start car engines, a use for which it is still standard. Lead-acid batteries are also among the most recycled products in the world: in many countries, almost all of them are collected and reprocessed.

Nickel-cadmium batteries, developed at the end of the nineteenth century, became common in portable devices such as power tools and cordless telephones in the late twentieth century. They are robust and perform well in cold conditions, but they suffer from a "memory effect": if they are repeatedly recharged before being fully used, they gradually hold less charge. Cadmium is also highly toxic, and the European Union has restricted their use in most products.

Sodium-ion batteries are a newer technology attracting considerable interest. They work in a similar way to lithium-ion batteries but use sodium, which can be obtained cheaply from salt and is far more abundant than lithium. They currently store less energy for their weight, which makes them less suitable for devices where weight matters, but they may be useful for storing electricity from wind and solar power in large installations. The first mass-produced cars using them appeared in China in 2023.

Researchers are also developing solid-state batteries, in which the liquid inside conventional batteries is replaced by a solid material. They promise greater safety and energy storage, but manufacturing them at low cost has proved difficult.

passages.topic: Animal behaviour — four great migrations
passages.title: Journeys of Survival

paragraphs.text: Every year, billions of animals make long journeys between breeding and feeding grounds. Migration allows them to take advantage of seasonal food supplies and suitable conditions for raising young, but it is costly and dangerous. Four species illustrate the remarkable variety of migratory journeys.

Monarch butterflies of eastern North America travel up to about four thousand kilometres each autumn from Canada and the northern United States to a small area of mountain forest in central Mexico, where millions cluster on fir trees for the winter. No individual completes the whole round trip: the journey north in spring is made over several generations, and the butterflies that return south in autumn have never made the trip before. They navigate using the position of the sun, combined with an internal clock located in their antennae.

In East Africa, around one and a half million wildebeest, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles, move in a great circuit through the Serengeti in Tanzania and the Maasai Mara in Kenya, following the rains that produce fresh grass. The most dangerous stage is the crossing of the Mara River, where many animals drown or are caught by crocodiles.

Grey whales make one of the longest migrations of any mammal, travelling between their feeding grounds in the Arctic waters off Alaska and warm, shallow lagoons on the coast of Mexico, where females give birth. The round trip can exceed sixteen thousand kilometres. During the migration, the whales eat very little, relying on fat stored during the summer.

European eels have one of the most mysterious migrations. Adult eels leave rivers across Europe and swim thousands of kilometres to the Sargasso Sea in the western Atlantic Ocean, where they are believed to spawn and die. Their tiny larvae drift back towards Europe on ocean currents, a journey that may take more than a year, before changing into young eels that swim up rivers. Although scientists are confident that the Sargasso Sea is the spawning area, no one has ever observed eels spawning there.

Many migrations are under threat. Roads, fences and dams block routes; habitat loss affects wintering and breeding sites; and climate change may alter the timing of food supplies. The number of young European eels arriving in rivers has fallen by more than ninety per cent since the 1980s, and the species is now considered critically endangered.

passages.topic: Materials — four textile fibres
passages.title: From Plant, Animal and Factory

paragraphs.text: Textile fibres fall into two broad groups: natural fibres, which come from plants and animals, and synthetic fibres, which are manufactured from chemicals, usually derived from oil. Each fibre has characteristic properties that make it suitable for particular uses.

Cotton, the most widely used natural fibre, grows as a soft, fluffy mass around the seeds of the cotton plant. It has been spun and woven for at least seven thousand years, with early evidence from both South Asia and the Americas. Cotton is comfortable to wear because it absorbs moisture and allows air to pass through, making it ideal for hot climates. However, growing it requires large quantities of water and, in many areas, pesticides, and cotton fabric creases easily.

Wool comes mainly from sheep. Its fibres are naturally crimped, or wavy, which traps air and makes wool an excellent insulator. Wool can absorb a considerable amount of moisture while still feeling dry, and it resists fire better than most other fibres, igniting with difficulty and often extinguishing itself. On the other hand, wool can shrink badly if washed in hot water, and some people find it scratchy against the skin.

Silk is produced by the larvae of the silk moth, which spin cocoons from a single continuous thread that can be more than a kilometre long. The Chinese produced silk for thousands of years and kept the method secret for many centuries. Silk is smooth, strong for its weight and has a natural shine, but it is expensive, and it is weakened by prolonged exposure to sunlight and perspiration.

Nylon, the first fully synthetic fibre, was developed by the chemist Wallace Carothers at the American company DuPont and introduced in 1938. It was first used for toothbrush bristles and then, famously, for women's stockings, which sold in enormous numbers when they went on sale in 1940. During the Second World War, nylon was used for parachutes and ropes. Nylon is very strong and elastic and dries quickly, but it does not absorb moisture well, which can make it uncomfortable in hot weather.

Synthetic fibres now account for more than half of all fibre production. Their low cost has helped make clothing cheaper, but they shed tiny plastic fibres when washed and do not biodegrade, raising environmental concerns. Researchers are developing new fibres from sources such as wood pulp and agricultural waste.

passages.topic: Engineering — earthquake-resistant buildings
passages.title: Buildings That Survive

paragraphs.text: Earthquakes rarely kill people directly; most deaths are caused by collapsing buildings. Engineers have therefore developed a range of techniques to help structures withstand the violent shaking of the ground. The aim is not to make buildings rigid enough to resist all movement, which is usually impossible, but to control how they move and to prevent collapse.

One of the most effective techniques is base isolation. The building is separated from its foundations by flexible bearings, often made of layers of rubber and steel. When the ground shakes, the bearings deform, allowing the ground to move beneath the building while the building itself moves much less. Base isolation has been used in hospitals and other buildings that must remain operational after an earthquake, but it is expensive and works best for low and medium-rise buildings on firm ground.

Dampers absorb the energy of shaking, in a similar way to the shock absorbers of a car. Some are fitted within the frame of the building; others take the form of a tuned mass damper, a heavy weight near the top of a tall building that moves in the opposite direction to the building's sway. The Taipei 101 tower in Taiwan contains a steel sphere weighing more than six hundred tonnes for this purpose, which has become a tourist attraction.

Many buildings rely on shear walls and bracing. Shear walls are stiff, reinforced walls, usually of concrete, that run through several floors and resist sideways forces, while diagonal steel braces, often arranged in an X-shape, strengthen the frame. These methods are relatively inexpensive and are widely used in new buildings, but they must be designed carefully, since a building that is too stiff can attract larger forces.

Traditional building methods often contain their own solutions. Wooden structures in Japan, such as temple pagodas, have survived many earthquakes because their flexible joints allow movement. In parts of Peru and Iran, builders have long reinforced earth walls with materials such as cane or timber. In Kashmir, a traditional style called taq combines timber beams with masonry, allowing walls to shift without collapsing; such buildings performed well in an earthquake in 2005, when many modern concrete buildings failed.

Techniques alone are not enough. Building codes must require safe design, and they must be enforced. Many deaths in recent earthquakes occurred in buildings that did not meet existing standards. Strengthening older buildings, known as retrofitting, is also important, but it is costly, and in many countries large numbers of vulnerable buildings remain.

passages.topic: Urban planning — public transport systems
passages.title: Moving People in Cities

paragraphs.text: As cities grow, they need ways to move large numbers of people quickly without filling streets with private cars. Four main types of public transport system are used around the world, each with a different combination of cost, capacity and impact on the city.

Metro systems – underground or elevated railways separated completely from road traffic – have the greatest capacity, carrying tens of thousands of passengers per hour in each direction. The first, in London, opened in 1863. Because trains never encounter traffic, metros are fast and reliable. However, they are extremely expensive to build, particularly when tunnels are required, and construction can take many years.

Trams, or light rail, run on tracks laid in the street, sometimes sharing space with cars and sometimes on reserved lanes. Many cities removed their tram networks in the mid-twentieth century, but since the 1980s trams have returned to cities across Europe and elsewhere. They cost far less than metros, and their permanent tracks are thought to encourage investment along their routes, since businesses and residents can see that the service will remain.

Bus rapid transit, or BRT, uses buses running on dedicated lanes, with stations where passengers pay before boarding, so that buses can load quickly. The system was pioneered in the Brazilian city of Curitiba in the 1970s and later adopted in cities such as Bogotá, whose TransMilenio network carries more than two million passengers a day. BRT can offer capacity approaching that of a metro at a small fraction of the cost, but it requires taking road space from cars, which can be politically difficult.

Cable cars, long associated with ski resorts, have become a form of urban transport in cities with steep hills. In Medellín, Colombia, a cable car system opened in 2004 connects poor hillside neighbourhoods to the metro, cutting journeys that once took over an hour to a few minutes. Cable cars are relatively cheap and quick to build, since they need only towers and stations, but their capacity is limited, typically a few thousand passengers per hour.

Transport planners increasingly combine these systems into integrated networks with shared tickets and connections. The best choice for any city depends on its size, shape and budget and the number of passengers expected.

passages.topic: Linguistics — theories of how language began
passages.title: The First Words

paragraphs.text: How and why human language began is one of the most difficult questions in science. Spoken words leave no fossils, and the earliest writing is only about five thousand years old, long after language itself emerged. In 1866, the Linguistic Society of Paris even banned discussion of the subject, considering it too speculative. In recent decades, however, researchers from linguistics, archaeology, genetics and animal behaviour have returned to the question, proposing several competing explanations.

One influential theory holds that language began with gestures. Chimpanzees and other apes use a large repertoire of hand and body gestures flexibly and intentionally, whereas their vocal calls appear to be largely fixed and tied to particular emotions. Supporters argue that our ancestors therefore first communicated with their hands, and that speech later took over, perhaps because it freed the hands for carrying tools and could be used in the dark. Critics point out that it remains unclear why a fully developed gestural system would have been abandoned for speech.

Another proposal, advanced in different forms by Charles Darwin and, more recently, by several researchers, suggests that language grew out of a musical "protolanguage" resembling song. Early humans, according to this view, first used sequences of sounds to express emotion and attract partners, and only later attached specific meanings to them. The idea draws support from the observation that infants respond to melody and rhythm in speech long before they understand words. Its weakness is that it does not explain how meaning became attached to sounds.

The anthropologist Robin Dunbar has argued that language evolved as a form of social bonding, replacing the grooming that monkeys and apes use to maintain relationships. As human groups grew larger, there was not enough time to groom every companion, and talking, especially gossip about other people, allowed individuals to maintain many relationships at once. Dunbar points to the fact that much everyday conversation still concerns social matters. Critics respond that gossip requires a language that is already complex, so the theory explains why language was useful rather than how it began.

A fourth line of research links language to tool-making. Brain-imaging studies have found that making complex stone tools activates brain areas that overlap with those involved in processing language, particularly areas concerned with organising actions into sequences. Some archaeologists suggest that teaching others to make such tools created pressure for more precise communication. However, overlapping brain activity does not prove that one ability caused the other.

Most researchers now suspect that language emerged gradually from several of these sources rather than from any single one. Genetic evidence, including studies of a gene called FOXP2, which is involved in controlling the movements of speech, suggests that some of the biological foundations were already present in the ancestors that humans share with Neanderthals. Exactly when fully modern language appeared, however, remains a matter of debate.

passages.topic: Psychology — three models of memory
passages.title: Models of Memory

paragraphs.text: Psychologists have long tried to describe the structure of human memory. Because memory cannot be observed directly, they have built models – simplified descriptions of how information might be stored and retrieved – and tested their predictions in experiments. Three models have been particularly influential.

The multi-store model, proposed by Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin in 1968, divides memory into three separate stores. Information first enters sensory memory, which holds a brief impression of what we see and hear for no more than a second or two. If we pay attention to it, it passes into short-term memory, which can hold only around seven items for about twenty to thirty seconds unless they are repeated, a process known as rehearsal. Information that is rehearsed enough is transferred to long-term memory, which is thought to have almost unlimited capacity. The model was supported by studies of patients with brain damage, some of whom could form no new long-term memories despite a normal short-term memory. Critics argued, however, that it was too simple, particularly in treating short-term memory as a single store.

In 1974, Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed the working memory model, which replaced the idea of a single short-term store with a system of several components. A "central executive" directs attention and coordinates two subsystems: the phonological loop, which holds sounds and words, and the visuospatial sketchpad, which holds images and spatial information. In 2000, Baddeley added a fourth component, the episodic buffer, which links working memory with long-term memory. Evidence came from dual-task experiments: people can perform a visual and a verbal task at the same time with little difficulty, but two verbal tasks interfere with each other, suggesting separate systems.

A different approach, the levels of processing framework, was put forward by Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart in 1972. Rather than dividing memory into stores, it proposed that how well information is remembered depends on how deeply it is processed. Shallow processing, such as noticing whether a word is printed in capital letters, produces weak memories; deep processing, which involves thinking about meaning, produces stronger ones. Experiments confirmed that people remember words better when they have been asked questions that make them think about the words. The main criticism is that "depth" is difficult to define and to measure independently of how well something is remembered.

Modern research using brain imaging has refined these models rather than replacing them. It has confirmed, for example, that different brain regions are involved in holding verbal and visual information, consistent with the working memory model. Many psychologists regard the three approaches as complementary descriptions of different aspects of memory rather than as rivals.

lesson.title: Years and technical terms spread across rows
lesson.text: In Hard passages about research, several dates and technical terms appear close together, and some belong to later additions to a model ("In 2000, Baddeley added a fourth component"). When a cell asks for a year, decide whether it means the original proposal or a later change. When it asks for a term, check which component or process the row and column describe.
lesson.example: Passage: "The theory was proposed in 1950 and revised in 1972." Cell: "Proposed (year): (1) ______". Answer: 1950.

passages.topic: Climate science — methods of removing carbon dioxide
passages.title: Taking Carbon Back

paragraphs.text: Most climate scientists agree that limiting global warming will require not only cutting emissions of carbon dioxide but also removing some of the gas already in the atmosphere. Several methods of carbon dioxide removal have been proposed. They differ greatly in cost, in how long they store carbon, and in the risks they carry.

The most familiar method is planting forests. Growing trees absorb carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and store carbon in their wood and in the soil. Reforestation is relatively cheap and brings additional benefits for wildlife and water supplies. However, it requires large areas of land, which may compete with food production, and the carbon it stores is vulnerable: forests can be destroyed by fire, disease or logging, releasing the carbon again.

Direct air capture uses machines that draw in air and pass it over chemicals that bind carbon dioxide. The captured gas can then be pumped deep underground into rock formations, where it can remain for thousands of years. The first commercial plant of this kind opened in Switzerland in 2017. The method needs little land, and the amount of carbon stored can be measured precisely. Its main drawbacks are cost and energy use: removing a tonne of carbon dioxide currently costs several hundred dollars, and the process requires large amounts of energy, which must itself come from low-carbon sources.

Enhanced weathering aims to accelerate a natural process. When certain rocks, such as basalt, are exposed to rain, they react slowly with carbon dioxide, which is eventually carried to the ocean and stored as carbonate for very long periods. Crushing these rocks into fine powder and spreading them on farmland greatly increases the surface area available for reaction. Trials suggest that the rock dust may also improve soil quality and crop yields. Uncertainties remain, however, about how much carbon is actually removed, since it is difficult to measure in open fields.

Ocean fertilisation involves adding iron to areas of the ocean where its scarcity limits the growth of phytoplankton, tiny plants that absorb carbon dioxide. When the plankton die, some of their carbon sinks to the deep ocean. Experiments in the 1990s and 2000s showed that iron could trigger large blooms of plankton, but little of the carbon appeared to sink deep enough to be stored for long, and scientists raised concerns about possible harm to marine ecosystems. International agreements now restrict such experiments to legitimate scientific research.

Experts emphasise that no removal method can replace cutting emissions. The quantities of carbon dioxide released each year are so large that removal can deal with only a small fraction of them, mainly emissions from activities that are especially difficult to eliminate, such as aviation and certain industrial processes.

lesson.title: The same word in different rows
lesson.text: In Hard comparison passages, the same word may appear in the description of several items. passages.topic: History of medicine — four major epidemics
passages.title: Waves of Disease

paragraphs.text: Epidemics have shaped human history as powerfully as wars and revolutions. Four great outbreaks illustrate how disease has interacted with trade, cities and science.

The Plague of Justinian struck the Byzantine Empire in 541, during the reign of the emperor Justinian, and recurred in waves for about two centuries. Contemporary writers described enormous death tolls in Constantinople. For a long time, historians debated what disease it was, but in the 2010s DNA recovered from the teeth of victims buried in Germany confirmed that it was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which also causes bubonic plague. Some historians argue that it weakened the empire and hindered its attempts to reconquer lost western territories, although the scale of its impact is disputed.

The Black Death, caused by the same bacterium, reached Europe in 1347, probably carried by ships from the Black Sea, and killed perhaps a third to a half of the population within a few years. The disease was spread mainly by fleas carried by rats, although some researchers believe that human fleas and lice also played a major role. Its consequences were profound: with so many workers dead, surviving labourers could demand higher wages, and in some regions the old feudal system of obligations began to break down.

Cholera, a bacterial infection that causes severe diarrhoea, spread from the Ganges delta in India in a series of pandemics from 1817 onwards, carried along trade routes and by troops. Cholera is transmitted through water contaminated with human waste. In 1854, the London physician John Snow traced an outbreak to a single water pump, and the disease became a major force behind investment in sewers and clean water supplies in the growing industrial cities of the nineteenth century.

The influenza pandemic of 1918–1920, often misleadingly called the "Spanish flu" because wartime censorship meant that it was first widely reported in neutral Spain, infected around a third of the world's population and killed tens of millions of people. Unusually, it killed many young, healthy adults. The movement of troops at the end of the First World War helped it spread around the world. The pandemic encouraged the development of public health systems and international cooperation in tracking disease.

Historians caution against simple conclusions about the effects of epidemics. The same disease could have very different consequences in different places, depending on existing economic and social conditions. What epidemics reveal most clearly, perhaps, is how closely human health is tied to the ways in which people live, trade and move.

lesson.title: The same detail for more than one row
lesson.text: Sometimes a detail appears in the passage for two different items. Here both cholera and influenza were carried by troops, and two epidemics were caused by the same bacterium. A detail that belongs to one row may be the trap for another. For each gap, return to the paragraph about the item in that row and check that the answer is stated for that item.
lesson.example: Passage: "Both the dog and the fox hunt at night, but only the fox stores food." Row "Dog | habit: (1) ______". Answer: hunts at night; "stores food" belongs only to the fox.
