passages.topic: Economics — theories of international trade
passages.title: Why Nations Trade

paragraphs.text: Why do countries trade with one another, and who benefits? Over more than two centuries, economists have proposed a series of theories, each building on or challenging its predecessors.

In The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, Adam Smith argued against the prevailing view, known as mercantilism, that a country became rich by exporting as much as possible and importing as little as possible, accumulating gold and silver. Smith proposed instead the principle of absolute advantage: if one country can produce a good more efficiently than another, and the second country can produce a different good more efficiently, both gain by specialising and trading. The theory, however, seemed to leave no role in trade for a country that was less efficient at producing everything.

David Ricardo addressed this problem in 1817 with the theory of comparative advantage. Using the example of England and Portugal producing cloth and wine, he showed that even if one country is more efficient at producing both goods, both countries can still gain from trade if each specialises in the good in which its relative disadvantage is smallest – or, put differently, in which its opportunity cost is lowest. Comparative advantage remains one of the most important ideas in economics, although it assumes that workers and resources can move easily between industries, which is often not the case.

In the early twentieth century, the Swedish economists Eli Heckscher and Bertil Ohlin explained comparative advantage in terms of countries' resources. Countries, they argued, export goods that make intensive use of the factors of production they have in abundance – land, labour or capital – and import goods that require factors that are scarce at home. A country with plentiful labour, for example, would export labour-intensive goods such as clothing. When the economist Wassily Leontief tested the theory with data from the United States in 1953, however, he found that American exports were, surprisingly, more labour-intensive than its imports, a result known as the Leontief paradox.

By the 1970s, economists had noticed that much world trade took place between similar, wealthy countries exchanging similar products – German and French cars, for example – which traditional theories struggled to explain. The "new trade theory", associated especially with Paul Krugman, who received the Nobel Prize in 2008, emphasised economies of scale: producing on a large scale lowers costs, so firms concentrate production in a few locations and sell worldwide, while consumers benefit from greater variety.

None of these theories claims that trade benefits everyone equally. Even when a country gains overall, particular industries and workers may lose, and many economists now argue that the benefits of trade depend on policies that help those affected to adjust.

lesson.title: Challenges that come from other people
lesson.text: In a table of theories, the "Limitation or challenge" column may contain a finding by a different researcher (Leontief's test of the Heckscher–Ohlin theory), or a problem that the next theory was designed to solve (the weakness in Smith's theory that Ricardo addressed). The answer for one row may therefore appear in the paragraph about the next person. Read each theory's paragraph and the paragraph that follows it.
lesson.example: Passage: "Theory X could not explain Y. Theory Z was later proposed to solve this." Row "Theory X | weakness: could not explain (1) ______". Answer: Y.

passages.topic: Palaeontology — why the megafauna disappeared
passages.title: The Vanished Giants

paragraphs.text: Around fifty thousand years ago, the world was home to many enormous animals: mammoths and woolly rhinoceroses in Eurasia, giant ground sloths in the Americas, and in Australia a wombat-like marsupial called Diprotodon, which was the size of a car. Over the following tens of thousands of years, most of these megafauna – usually defined as animals weighing more than forty-five kilograms – disappeared. On some continents, more than half of all large mammal genera became extinct. Scientists have debated the causes for more than a century.

The "overkill" hypothesis, developed by the American geoscientist Paul Martin in the 1960s, holds that human hunters were responsible. Martin pointed out that extinctions often followed soon after humans arrived in a region: in Australia around fifty thousand years ago, in the Americas around thirteen thousand years ago, and on islands such as New Zealand, where giant flightless birds called moas disappeared within about two centuries of human settlement around 1300. Large animals, which reproduce slowly, would have been especially vulnerable to even modest levels of hunting. Critics note, however, that relatively few sites preserve clear evidence of humans killing extinct megafauna.

The climate hypothesis attributes the extinctions to environmental change at the end of the last ice age. As the climate warmed, open grasslands that supported large grazing animals were replaced in many areas by forests, and the steppe on which mammoths depended shrank dramatically. Supporters point out that some extinctions coincide with rapid climate changes. Yet the megafauna had survived many earlier cycles of warming and cooling without comparable losses, which is difficult to explain if climate alone was responsible.

Many researchers now favour a combination of causes. According to this view, climate change placed populations under stress, reducing and fragmenting them, while human hunting delivered a final blow. Studies of ancient DNA from woolly mammoths show that their populations declined over thousands of years. The last mainland populations disappeared around ten thousand years ago, but a small group survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean until about four thousand years ago, long after the pyramids of Egypt had been built.

Other explanations have been proposed but have received less support. One suggested that a comet struck North America around 12,900 years ago, causing sudden climate change; another proposed that diseases carried by humans or their dogs devastated animals with no immunity. Neither has found strong evidence.

The debate has practical relevance. The loss of large plant-eating animals changed ecosystems profoundly: without animals to eat and trample vegetation, forests and shrubs spread, fires became more frequent, and the seeds of some plants were no longer dispersed. Some conservationists now argue that reintroducing large herbivores, such as bison or wild horses, could help restore some of these lost ecological functions.

lesson.title: Final review — the complete Table Completion method
lesson.text: This final set combines all the main skills: identifying each row's paragraph, placing details in the claim, evidence and weakness columns, choosing between several similar numbers and dates, and copying the minimum words. For each gap: (1) name the row and column; (2) predict the type of answer from the column and the neighbouring cells; (3) find the detail in the paragraph about that row; (4) check the word limit and the grammar of the cell.

passages.topic: Industry and environment — how paper is recycled
passages.title: Second Life for Paper

paragraphs.text: Paper is one of the most widely recycled materials in the world. In many European countries, more than seventy per cent of used paper is collected for recycling. Recycling reduces the number of trees that must be cut down and uses considerably less energy and water than making paper from new wood fibres.

The process begins with collection. Used paper is gathered from homes, offices and businesses, either mixed with other recyclable materials or kept separate. At a sorting facility, it is separated into grades, such as newspaper, cardboard and office paper, because each grade contains fibres of a different quality and is suited to different products.

The sorted paper is then taken to a paper mill, where it is placed in a large vat called a pulper. There it is mixed with water and stirred vigorously until the fibres separate and form a thick, porridge-like mixture known as pulp. Screens remove unwanted items such as staples, plastic and glue.

Next, the ink must be removed. In a process called de-inking, air is blown into the pulp together with soap-like chemicals. The ink particles stick to the air bubbles, rise to the surface and form a foam, which is skimmed off. For some products, such as brown cardboard, de-inking is unnecessary. If white paper is required, the pulp may also be bleached.

The cleaned pulp is then sprayed onto a moving mesh screen. As water drains away, the fibres bond together into a continuous sheet. The sheet passes between heavy rollers that squeeze out more water, and then over heated cylinders that dry it. Finally, the paper is wound into enormous rolls, which are cut to size for use.

Paper cannot be recycled indefinitely. Each time it is processed, its fibres become shorter and weaker, and after about five to seven cycles they are too short to bond together. New fibres from wood must therefore be added to maintain quality. Paper that has been contaminated with food or grease, such as used pizza boxes, is often unsuitable for recycling.

lesson.title: Follow the sequence words
lesson.text: In an easy flow-chart, the passage describes the process step by step, using sequence words such as begins, then, next and finally. Each box normally matches one or two sentences, in the same order. Find the sequence word that starts each stage, and look for the answer within that stage before moving on.
lesson.example: Passage: "Next, the ink must be removed." Box: "de-inking: ink ... removed". This box matches the stage introduced by "Next".

passages.topic: Food production — making cheddar cheese
passages.title: From Milk to Cheddar

paragraphs.text: Cheddar, named after a village in south-west England, is one of the most popular cheeses in the world. Although it is now made in many countries and in huge factories, the basic stages of production have changed little since the nineteenth century.

Production begins with fresh milk, which is usually heated briefly to kill harmful bacteria, a process called pasteurisation. The milk is then cooled slightly and placed in large vats, where a starter culture of bacteria is added. These bacteria convert the natural sugar in milk, lactose, into lactic acid, which gives the cheese part of its flavour.

Next, a substance called rennet is added. Traditionally obtained from the stomachs of young calves, rennet is now often produced by microorganisms. It causes the milk to set into a soft, jelly-like mass within about forty minutes. This is cut into small pieces, called curds, which release a watery liquid known as whey. The curds and whey are heated and stirred, and the whey is then drained away.

The stage that gives cheddar its name is known as "cheddaring". The curds are allowed to join together into large slabs, which are cut, stacked on top of each other and turned repeatedly. The weight of the slabs presses out more whey and gives the cheese its dense, firm texture. The slabs are then cut into small pieces, a process called milling, and salt is mixed in, which helps to preserve the cheese and control the activity of bacteria.

The salted curds are packed into moulds and pressed, often overnight, to form solid blocks. The blocks are then wrapped, traditionally in cloth covered with fat and today often in plastic, and placed in a cool store to mature. During this ripening period, enzymes break down proteins and fats, developing flavour. Mild cheddar may be matured for about three months, while mature or "vintage" cheddar may be kept for more than two years.

Although industrial production dominates, a small number of farms still make traditional cloth-wrapped cheddar by hand, and in 2007 the name "West Country Farmhouse Cheddar" was given legal protection in Europe.

passages.topic: Wildlife — the life cycle of the Atlantic salmon
passages.title: The Salmon's Journey

paragraphs.text: Atlantic salmon spend part of their lives in fresh water and part in the sea. Their life cycle is one of the most remarkable in the animal kingdom, involving journeys of thousands of kilometres and a return, in most cases, to the very river in which they hatched.

Life begins in autumn or winter, when an adult female digs a shallow nest, called a redd, in the gravel of a fast-flowing stream and lays several thousand eggs, which are fertilised by a male. The eggs remain buried in the gravel throughout the winter. In spring they hatch into tiny fish called alevins, which stay hidden in the gravel, feeding on a yolk sac attached to their bodies.

When the yolk sac has been used up, the young fish emerge from the gravel and begin to feed on insects. At this stage they are known as fry, and later, as they grow and develop dark markings along their sides, as parr. Parr remain in the river for between one and four years, depending on how quickly they grow, which is affected by water temperature and food supply.

Eventually, the parr undergo a transformation that prepares them for life in salt water. Their bodies become silver, and their internal organs change so that they can cope with sea water. The young fish, now called smolts, swim downstream to the sea, usually in spring.

Atlantic salmon travel long distances to feeding grounds in the North Atlantic, some as far as the waters off Greenland, where they feed on smaller fish and shrimp-like creatures and grow rapidly. After one or more years at sea, they return to fresh water to breed. Scientists believe that they use the Earth's magnetic field to navigate across the ocean, and then their sense of smell to identify their home river.

Swimming upstream, adults leap waterfalls and other obstacles and stop feeding altogether. After spawning, many die, exhausted, but unlike Pacific salmon, which always die after breeding, some Atlantic salmon survive, return to the sea and breed again. Numbers of wild Atlantic salmon have fallen sharply in recent decades because of factors including dams, pollution, overfishing and warming seas.

lesson.title: Flow-charts with a list of options
lesson.text: When you choose answers from a list, the options are usually paraphrases rather than exact passage words, and there are more options than gaps. First decide the type of word each box needs (a place, a food, a colour, an action), then find the stage in the passage, and finally choose the option with the same meaning. Cross out each option as you use it.
lesson.example: Box: "young birds leave the (1) ______". Passage: "the chicks fly from the nest". Options: A tree B nest C ground. Answer: B.

passages.topic: Food production — making olive oil
passages.title: Pressing the Olive

paragraphs.text: Olive oil has been produced around the Mediterranean for at least six thousand years. Today Spain is by far the largest producer, followed by Italy and Greece. Although modern mills use machines rather than stone presses, the basic steps have remained similar.

The quality of the oil depends first on the harvest. Olives are picked in autumn and winter, either by hand, by combing the branches, or by machines that shake the trees so that the fruit falls onto nets spread on the ground. Olives picked early, while still green, produce less oil but with a stronger, more peppery flavour; riper, darker olives give more oil with a milder taste.

Speed is essential, because olives begin to ferment and lose quality soon after they are picked. Ideally they are processed within twenty-four hours. At the mill, the olives are first cleaned: leaves and twigs are blown away and the fruit is washed in water.

The whole olives, including their stones, are then crushed into a paste. Traditionally this was done with large stone wheels; most modern mills use metal crushers. The paste is next mixed slowly for twenty to forty minutes, a stage called malaxation, which allows tiny droplets of oil to join together into larger drops that are easier to separate. The temperature must be kept low, usually below twenty-seven degrees Celsius, to protect the oil's flavour; oil produced in this way may be labelled "cold extracted".

The oil is then separated from the solid material and water. In traditional mills, the paste was spread on mats and pressed. Today most mills use a centrifuge, a machine that spins the paste at high speed so that the heavier solids and water are thrown outwards and the lighter oil separates. The oil may be passed through a second centrifuge to remove any remaining water.

Finally, the oil is left to settle or is filtered, and it is stored in stainless steel tanks away from light and air, which cause it to deteriorate. The best oils, called extra virgin, must meet strict chemical standards and pass a tasting test by trained experts.

lesson.title: Times and temperatures in a process
lesson.text: Process passages often give several times and temperatures ("within twenty-four hours", "twenty to forty minutes", "below twenty-seven degrees"). The box tells you which one you need: a limit on time before processing, the length of a stage, or a maximum temperature. Check the words around the number in the passage, and do not copy the unit if it is already in the box.
lesson.example: Box: "baked at (1) ______ degrees". Passage: "The loaves are baked at 220 degrees for 30 minutes." Answer: 220.

passages.topic: Public health — treating drinking water
passages.title: From River to Tap

paragraphs.text: In many cities, drinking water comes from rivers, lakes or reservoirs. Before it reaches people's homes, this water must be treated to remove dirt, harmful microorganisms and unpleasant tastes. Although methods vary, most large treatment plants follow a similar sequence of steps.

Water is first drawn from the source through an intake, where screens stop large objects such as leaves, branches and fish from entering the plant. It may then be stored for a period in a reservoir, where some of the heavier particles sink to the bottom naturally.

The next stage is coagulation. Chemicals, often aluminium or iron salts, are added to the water. They cause tiny particles of dirt, which are too small to settle on their own, to stick together. The water is then stirred gently, a process called flocculation, so that the particles form larger clumps known as floc.

The water then flows slowly into large tanks, where the heavy floc sinks to the bottom in a process known as sedimentation. The sludge that collects on the bottom is removed, and the clearer water at the top passes on to the next stage.

Filtration removes the remaining particles. The water passes through layers of sand and gravel, and sometimes charcoal, which also helps to remove unpleasant tastes and smells. The filters must be cleaned regularly by pumping water backwards through them.

Finally, the water is disinfected to kill any remaining bacteria and viruses. Chlorine is the most common disinfectant, and a small amount is usually left in the water to protect it as it travels through the pipes. Some plants use ultraviolet light or ozone instead. In many countries, fluoride is also added to help prevent tooth decay. The treated water is stored in covered tanks before being pumped to homes.

lesson.title: Named stages
lesson.text: Many process passages give each stage a technical name (coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation). The flow-chart may print the name and ask for a detail, or print the detail and ask for the name. Mark each named stage in the passage as you read; the answers are usually in the sentence that introduces or explains the name.
lesson.example: Passage: "In the final stage, called glazing, the pot is coated with liquid glass." Box: "(1) ______: pot coated with liquid glass". Answer: glazing.

passages.topic: Construction — making fired clay bricks
passages.title: Building Blocks

paragraphs.text: Fired clay bricks are among the oldest manufactured building materials. The earliest known examples were made in Mesopotamia more than five thousand years ago, and today billions are produced every year. Whether they are made by hand in a small village or by machine in a large factory, bricks pass through the same basic stages.

The process starts with the raw material. Clay is dug from pits, often close to the brickworks. It is left outside for a period, sometimes through a winter, a process known as weathering, during which rain and frost break it down and make it easier to work.

The clay is then ground and mixed with water to make it soft and workable. Sand may be added to reduce shrinking, and other materials can be added to change the colour of the finished brick. Stones and other lumps are removed.

Next, the bricks are shaped. In hand-making, a lump of clay is thrown into a wooden mould dusted with sand so that the clay does not stick. In most factories, however, the clay is forced through a shaped opening to form a long continuous column, rather like toothpaste from a tube, which is then cut into individual bricks by wires. This method is called extrusion.

The shaped bricks contain a great deal of water and must be dried slowly before firing, otherwise they may crack. Traditionally they were stacked outside to dry in the air for several weeks; modern factories use heated drying chambers, which take a few days.

Finally, the bricks are fired in a kiln at temperatures of around 1,000 degrees Celsius. The heat causes changes in the clay that make the bricks hard and durable. Many modern factories use tunnel kilns, in which bricks move slowly on carts through different heating and cooling zones. After cooling, the bricks are sorted and packed.

lesson.title: Word banks with similar options
lesson.text: A word bank may contain two options that are similar in meaning, such as "kiln" and "oven", or "frost" and "wind". Only one matches what the passage actually says. When two options both seem possible, go back to the passage sentence and choose the one that is supported, not the one that sounds most likely.
lesson.example: Passage: "The pots are dried in the sun." Options: A sun B fire. Answer: A, even though pots are also later fired.

passages.topic: Astronomy — the life cycle of stars
passages.title: Lives of the Stars

paragraphs.text: Stars may appear unchanging, but each one has a life story, beginning with its birth and ending, sometimes spectacularly, with its death. Because these changes take millions or billions of years, astronomers cannot watch a single star through its whole life. Instead, they have pieced the story together by observing many stars at different stages, much as a visitor from another planet might work out the human life cycle by photographing a crowd of people of all ages.

Every star begins in a nebula, a vast cloud of gas, mostly hydrogen, and dust. If part of the cloud becomes dense enough, perhaps after being disturbed by the shock wave from a nearby exploding star, it begins to collapse under gravity. As the material falls inwards, it spins faster and heats up, and a hot, dense ball, known as a protostar, forms at the centre. A protostar shines, but not yet by the process that powers true stars.

That process begins when the temperature in the core reaches about ten million degrees Celsius. At this point, nuclear fusion begins: hydrogen nuclei join together to form helium, releasing enormous amounts of energy. The outward pressure produced by this energy balances the inward pull of gravity, and the star becomes stable. It is now a main-sequence star, and it will spend around ninety per cent of its life in this phase. The Sun, which is about 4.6 billion years old, is roughly halfway through its main-sequence life.

What happens next depends on the star's mass. When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the core contracts and heats up, while the outer layers expand enormously and cool, and the star becomes a red giant. For a star similar in mass to the Sun, the outer layers then drift gently away into space, forming a glowing shell of gas called a planetary nebula, despite having nothing to do with planets. The small, extremely hot core that remains is known as a white dwarf. It no longer produces energy by fusion and slowly cools over billions of years.

Stars more than about eight times as massive as the Sun end their lives far more violently. They swell into red supergiants, and fusion in their cores continues to produce heavier and heavier elements, up to iron. Because fusing iron does not release energy, the core suddenly collapses, and the outer layers are blasted into space in a gigantic explosion called a supernova, which can briefly outshine an entire galaxy. The collapsed core becomes an incredibly dense neutron star or, if the original star was very massive, a black hole, from which not even light can escape.

The material thrown out by supernovae is not wasted. It enriches the gas clouds of the galaxy with heavy elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron, and eventually new stars and planets form from it. The iron in human blood and the calcium in human bones were made inside stars that died long before the Sun was born.

lesson.title: Follow the right branch
lesson.text: When a flow-chart divides, each branch begins with a condition, such as "star similar to the Sun" or "star over eight times the Sun's mass". The passage usually describes one branch completely and then the other, often with words such as "by contrast", "however" or "for larger stars". Before you answer a gap in a branch, find the sentence in the passage that matches the condition at the top of that branch.
lesson.example: Branch: "small dogs: live about (1) ______ years". Passage: "Large breeds live around eight years, whereas small breeds often reach fifteen." Answer: fifteen, not eight.

passages.topic: Science and society — how research is peer reviewed
passages.title: Checking the Science

paragraphs.text: When a scientific discovery is reported in the news, it has usually appeared first in an academic journal. Most respected journals publish research only after it has passed a process known as peer review, in which other experts in the field examine it for errors and weaknesses. Although the system is often called the foundation of modern science, it is surprisingly young in its current form: many famous journals did not use outside reviewers routinely until the 1960s and 1970s.

The process begins when researchers write up their work in a manuscript, which includes their methods, results and conclusions, and submit it to the journal of their choice. It is first read by an editor, usually a senior scientist, who decides whether it falls within the journal's subject area and whether it seems original and important enough to be worth reviewing. A large proportion of submissions do not get past this stage. Such papers receive what is known as a desk rejection, and the authors are free to submit them elsewhere. At the most selective journals, the majority of manuscripts are rejected in this way, often within a few days.

If the editor is interested, the manuscript is sent to two or three independent specialists. These reviewers are usually unpaid and, in most journals, remain anonymous so that they can criticise the work freely. Only after they have agreed to take part do they receive the full paper. They assess whether the methods are suitable, evaluate the reasoning behind the conclusions, and check whether the conclusions are actually supported by the data. Reviewers cannot usually repeat the experiments themselves; instead, they rely on the information that the authors have provided.

Reviewers frequently identify gaps and may ask the authors to carry out additional experiments before the work can be accepted. They then write reports and recommend a decision. The editor, who does not have to follow the reviewers' advice, considers the reports and makes the final decision: to accept the manuscript as it is, which is rare, to reject it, or to ask the authors for revisions.

In the last case, the authors change the paper and return it with a detailed response to each point raised by the reviewers, explaining what they have changed or, if they disagree, why they have not. The revised version may be sent back to the same reviewers, and this cycle can be repeated several times. As a result, the whole process from first submission to publication often takes many months.

Peer review has its critics. It is slow, it relies on the unpaid work of busy researchers, and it does not reliably detect deliberate fraud. Some journals have experimented with open review, in which the reviewers' names and reports are published alongside the paper, in the hope of making the process more transparent.

lesson.title: When the passage is not in chronological order
lesson.text: In medium and hard passages, the writer may not describe the process strictly in order. A paragraph may mention a later stage before an earlier one, or add background between stages. Use the flow-chart, not the passage, to decide the order of events, and look for time words such as "before", "once", "only after" and "at the final stage" to place each detail.
lesson.example: Passage: "Before the concert, the orchestra rehearses for weeks. The players are chosen by audition." Flow-chart order: audition → rehearsal → concert.

passages.topic: History — mummification in ancient Egypt
passages.title: Preparing for Eternity

paragraphs.text: The ancient Egyptians believed that a person's body had to be preserved so that the soul could recognise it and use it in the afterlife. Although the earliest Egyptians were buried in the hot, dry sand of the desert, which preserved them naturally, by around 2600 BCE they had developed deliberate methods of preservation. The most elaborate of these, used for kings and wealthy nobles, has been described by the Greek historian Herodotus and confirmed by modern scientific studies of mummies.

After death, the body was taken to a tent known as the place of purification, usually on the west bank of the Nile, the side associated with the setting sun and the dead. There it was washed in water from the river. The embalmers then began their work by removing the brain. A long hook was pushed in through the nose, and the brain, which the Egyptians believed was of little importance, was pulled out in pieces and thrown away.

Next, a cut was made in the left side of the body, and the stomach, liver, lungs and intestines were removed. These organs were dried and stored in four containers known as canopic jars, each protected by a particular god. The heart, however, was left in the body, because it was thought to be the centre of a person's intelligence and would be weighed in the afterlife to judge the dead person's life.

The body was then covered and packed with natron, a type of salt collected from dry lake beds, which absorbed moisture and prevented decay. This drying stage lasted about 40 days. Afterwards, the body, now dark and shrunken, was washed again and rubbed with oils so that the skin would remain flexible. To give it a more lifelike shape, the empty body was stuffed with linen, sawdust and sometimes leaves.

Finally, the body was wrapped in hundreds of metres of linen bandages. As they worked, the embalmers placed small protective charms, called amulets, between the layers, and priests recited spells. A painted mask was placed over the face of the most important individuals. The entire process, from death to burial, took about 70 days, after which the mummy was placed in its coffin and taken to the tomb.

Mummification was expensive, and poorer Egyptians could afford only simpler methods. In one of these, oil was injected into the body instead of the organs being removed. Nevertheless, even the simplest methods were intended to achieve the same purpose: to give the dead a body to live in forever.

lesson.title: Choosing between similar numbers
lesson.text: Process passages often contain several numbers for different stages, such as the time for one step and the time for the whole process. Before writing a number, read the words around it in the passage and check that they describe the same stage as the box. Words such as "in total", "the whole process" and "this stage alone" are important signals.
lesson.example: Passage: "Drying takes ten days; the whole process lasts a month." Box: "leaves dried for (1) ______ days". Answer: 10.

passages.topic: Environment — how garden compost is made
passages.title: Black Gold

paragraphs.text: Composting is the controlled decay of plant and food waste into a dark, crumbly material that gardeners value so highly that it is sometimes called "black gold". Around a third of household rubbish in many countries consists of food and garden waste. When this is buried in landfill sites, it decays without oxygen and produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. When it is composted, it becomes a valuable resource instead.

A good compost heap needs a balance of two kinds of material. Gardeners call nitrogen-rich materials, such as grass cuttings, vegetable peelings and coffee grounds, "greens", while carbon-rich materials, such as dry leaves, straw and cardboard, are known as "browns". Too many greens produce a wet, smelly heap; too many browns make the process extremely slow. Experts recommend roughly two to three parts of browns for every part of greens by volume, although the exact proportion is not critical.

Once the materials are mixed, bacteria and other microorganisms begin to break them down. As they feed and multiply, they produce heat, and the temperature inside a well-made heap rises quickly, sometimes reaching 60 to 70 degrees Celsius within a few days. This hot phase is useful, because temperatures this high kill most weed seeds and disease-causing organisms that might otherwise be spread around the garden.

The microorganisms need oxygen to work efficiently, and the centre of the heap soon runs short of it. For this reason, the heap should be turned every week or two with a garden fork, which mixes the material and lets air into the middle. If the heap is too dry, water can be added; the ideal material is as damp as a squeezed-out sponge.

As the most easily digested material is used up, the heap gradually cools down. In this cooler phase, fungi and larger creatures such as worms and woodlice move in. The fungi are particularly important, because they can break down tough materials such as woody stems, which bacteria find difficult to digest. After between three months and a year, depending on the materials and the care taken, the compost is ready.

Finished compost smells pleasantly of earth. Added to soil, it provides nutrients for plants, encourages useful organisms, and improves the soil's structure. It also increases water retention, so that sandy soils dry out less quickly, while it helps heavy clay soils to drain more freely.

lesson.title: Word banks that test paraphrase and word form
lesson.text: At medium level, the options in a word bank are rarely the same words as the passage. "Rises" may appear as "builds", and "destroyed" as "killed". Some options are also distractors because they are the wrong word form: an adjective cannot fill a gap that needs a verb. Check the grammar of each box before you look at the list.
lesson.example: Box: "the mixture (1) ______ overnight". Options: A thickens B thick. Only A, a verb, fits.

passages.topic: Health — what happens to donated blood
passages.title: The Gift of Blood

paragraphs.text: Every few seconds, somewhere in the world, someone needs blood. It is used in surgery, after accidents, during childbirth and in the treatment of diseases such as cancer. Blood cannot be manufactured, so hospitals depend entirely on donors. What most donors do not realise, however, is that the blood they give is usually not given to a patient in the form in which it leaves their body.

Before donating, each volunteer answers questions about their health and travel, and a drop of blood is taken from a finger. This test measures the level of haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen, to make sure that the donor is not at risk of becoming anaemic. The donation itself takes only about ten minutes, during which around 470 millilitres of blood, a little under a pint, is collected into a sterile bag containing a chemical that stops it from clotting. Healthy adults replace the lost fluid within a day or two, although the red cells take several weeks to recover.

At the same time, small samples are taken and sent to a laboratory, where they are tested to identify the blood group and screened for infections such as hepatitis and HIV. Any donation that fails these tests is destroyed. Meanwhile, the bag of blood is taken to a processing centre, where it is spun at high speed in a centrifuge. Because the components of blood have different densities, they separate into layers: heavy red cells at the bottom, a thin layer of platelets and white cells in the middle, and yellowish plasma at the top. White cells are removed by filtering, since they can cause reactions in patients.

Each component is then stored differently. Red cells, which are used for patients who have lost blood, are kept in a refrigerator and must be used within about 35 days. Plasma, which contains proteins that help blood to clot, is frozen and can be stored for up to three years. Platelets, which are given to patients with cancer and certain blood disorders, are the most difficult to keep: they must be stored at room temperature and constantly shaken, and they last only seven days.

When a hospital needs blood, the components are matched to the patient's blood group and given by transfusion, through a tube into a vein. In this way, a single donation can help as many as three different patients. Because platelets expire so quickly, blood services must collect them continuously, and they regularly appeal for new donors, particularly among young people, fewer of whom give blood than in the past.

lesson.title: Three branches, one gap each
lesson.text: Some flow-charts split into three or more branches, one for each product or outcome, and then join again. The passage usually describes the branches in a single paragraph, often in a list. Match each branch to its own sentence, and be careful with numbers and storage conditions, because the three branches will contain similar information.
lesson.example: Passage: "Apples keep for months in a cold store; strawberries last only two days." Branch: "strawberries: last (1) ______". Answer: two days.

passages.topic: Arts and crafts — how a violin is made
passages.title: The Luthier's Art

paragraphs.text: The design of the violin has changed remarkably little since the instruments made in northern Italy in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, above all by Antonio Stradivari. Although factories now produce violins in their thousands, the finest instruments are still made by hand by specialist craftspeople known as luthiers, and a single violin may take two or three months to complete.

Everything begins with the choice of wood. The top, or belly, of the violin is usually made from spruce, a light, strong softwood that vibrates freely, while the back, sides and neck are made from maple, a harder wood often chosen for its attractive, flame-like pattern. Before it can be used, the wood must be seasoned, which means that it is stored for years, sometimes decades, so that it dries slowly and becomes stable; fresh wood would shrink and crack as it dried.

Many luthiers start by building the sides, which are called ribs. These are thin strips of maple, only about one millimetre thick, that are bent into shape with a hot iron and glued around a mould, a wooden form with the outline of the instrument. Small blocks of wood at the corners and ends strengthen the frame.

The top and back are carved from thick pieces of wood, first on the outside to create the gentle arch of the violin, and then on the inside. This hollowing out is the most skilful part of the process. The luthier repeatedly taps the plate and listens to its tone, removing wood little by little until it sounds right. Two f-shaped holes are cut in the top to allow the sound to escape.

Before the top is attached, a long, thin strip of spruce called the bass bar is glued inside it, under the lowest string. It strengthens the top and helps it to carry low notes. Then the top and back are glued to the ribs. To protect the edges from cracking, a narrow channel is cut around them and filled with a decorative inlay of three thin strips of wood, known as the purfling.

The neck and scroll, carved from a single piece of maple, are then fitted, and the violin is coated with many thin layers of varnish, each of which must dry, sometimes in sunlight, before the next is applied. Some makers believe that the recipe for Stradivari's varnish was the secret of his instruments' sound, although scientific studies have found little evidence for this. Finally, the strings, bridge and other fittings are added and adjusted.

lesson.title: Technical vocabulary
lesson.text: Craft and technology passages often introduce special terms, explained in the same sentence ("a thin strip called the purfling"). When the flow-chart gives the description, the answer is the technical term; when the flow-chart gives the term, the answer is part of the description. Read both halves of the explanation in the passage.
lesson.example: Passage: "The potter uses a wheel-head, the flat disc that spins." Box: "clay placed on the (1) ______". Answer: wheel-head.

passages.topic: Geography — how limestone caves form
passages.title: Underground Cathedrals

paragraphs.text: Some of the most spectacular landscapes on Earth are hidden underground. Limestone caves, with their long passages, vast chambers and strange rock formations, are found on every continent except Antarctica. The largest known cave passage, Son Doong in Vietnam, is big enough to contain a forty-storey building. Yet these caves are created by nothing more powerful than rainwater, working very slowly over hundreds of thousands of years.

Limestone is a rock made mainly of calcium carbonate, often formed from the shells of ancient sea creatures. Pure water has little effect on it. However, as rain falls through the air, it absorbs a small amount of carbon dioxide, and it absorbs much more as it passes through the soil, where decaying plants and animals release the gas. The result is a weak acid, called carbonic acid, which slowly dissolves limestone.

Limestone is not a uniform block. It is divided by vertical cracks, called joints, and by horizontal divisions between the layers of rock, known as bedding planes. The slightly acidic water seeps down through these weaknesses, and as it does so, it gradually widens them. Over thousands of years, narrow cracks become wide channels.

The most rapid dissolving takes place at or just below the water table, the level below which the rock is completely filled with water. Here, water moves slowly through the rock and is in contact with it for a long time, so channels grow into tube-shaped passages. Later, a nearby river may cut its valley deeper, and as a result, the water table falls. The passages above it drain and fill with air, and a new level of passages begins to form lower down. For this reason, many cave systems consist of several levels, each marking a former position of the water table.

Once a cave is filled with air, a different process begins. Water dripping from the roof contains dissolved calcium carbonate, and when it meets the cave air, it loses some of its carbon dioxide. The water can then no longer hold all of the dissolved rock, so a tiny amount of calcite, a form of calcium carbonate, is left behind. Drop by drop, icicle-shaped stalactites grow downwards from the roof, while the water falling to the floor builds stalagmites upwards. Where the two eventually meet, they form a single column. Growth is extremely slow, often less than a centimetre in a hundred years.
Caves are fragile environments. The touch of a human hand can leave oils that stop formations from growing, and many show caves now control the number of visitors and the lighting to protect them.

lesson.title: Cause-and-effect chains
lesson.text: Natural processes are often explained as a chain of causes and effects: A causes B, which causes C. Words such as "as a result", "this means that", "so" and "when" connect the stages. In the flow-chart, each arrow represents one of these links. If you are unsure of an answer, ask: what caused this stage, and what did it cause next?
lesson.example: Passage: "Heavy rain raised the river, so the fields flooded." Flow-chart: heavy rain → river rises → fields (1) ______ Answer: flooded.

passages.topic: Technology — refining crude oil
passages.title: Separating the Black Stuff

paragraphs.text: Crude oil, as it comes out of the ground, is of little direct use. It is a thick mixture of thousands of different hydrocarbons, compounds of hydrogen and carbon whose molecules range from very small to very large. The job of a refinery is to separate this mixture into useful products and to change some of them into others that are in greater demand. A large modern refinery can process several hundred thousand barrels of crude oil every day.

The first and most important stage is fractional distillation. The crude oil is pumped into a furnace and heated to about 400°C, at which temperature most of it turns into vapour. This hot mixture of vapour and liquid is then fed into the bottom of a tall steel tower called a fractionating column, which may be as tall as sixty metres. The column is hottest at the bottom and becomes progressively cooler towards the top.

As the vapours rise through the column, they cool. Each hydrocarbon condenses back into a liquid when it reaches the level where the temperature has fallen below its boiling point, and it is collected on trays at that height. Hydrocarbons with small molecules have low boiling points, so they rise furthest before condensing; those with large molecules have high boiling points and condense near the bottom. In this way, the crude oil is separated into groups called fractions, according to their boiling points.

The lightest fractions, collected at the top of the column, include refinery gases such as propane, which is used for heating and cooking, and petrol, which is used in cars. Further down are kerosene, used as jet fuel, and diesel. The heaviest fractions do not evaporate at all but remain as liquid at the bottom of the column. They include fuel oil for ships, lubricating oil and bitumen, the black, sticky substance used for surfacing roads.

Unfortunately, crude oil naturally contains more heavy fractions than the market needs, and not enough light ones such as petrol. Refineries therefore use a process called cracking, in which large molecules are broken down into smaller, more valuable ones. This is done using high temperatures and a catalyst, a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.

Finally, the products are treated to remove impurities. The most important of these is sulphur, which, if left in fuels, produces sulphur dioxide when burned, a gas that causes acid rain. Modern regulations in many countries now limit the amount of sulphur that fuels can contain to a tiny fraction of the levels allowed in the past.

lesson.title: Longer word limits
lesson.text: With NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER, you can write short phrases, but you should still write the shortest phrase that fully answers the gap. Numbers must include the unit if the unit is not in the box. Extra words from the passage do not earn marks, and exceeding the limit loses the mark even if the key word is correct.
lesson.example: Box: "water heated to (1) ______". Passage: "heated to 90 degrees Celsius". Answer: 90 degrees Celsius / 90°C.

passages.topic: Biology — how the immune system fights infection
passages.title: The Body's Defenders

paragraphs.text: Every day, the human body is exposed to enormous numbers of bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, yet most people remain healthy most of the time. This is thanks to the immune system, a network of cells, tissues and chemicals that is often compared to an army, although, unlike an army, it has no central command. Instead, its many parts communicate through chemical signals, and its response to an invader develops in stages, from general defences that act within minutes to highly targeted ones that take days to organise.

The first line of defence is not a response at all but a set of barriers. The skin, when unbroken, is almost impossible for microbes to penetrate. The airways are lined with sticky mucus that traps particles, which tiny hairs then sweep upwards to be swallowed, and anything swallowed meets the powerful acid of the stomach. Tears and saliva contain enzymes that break down the walls of bacteria. Most potential invaders get no further.

Those that do, perhaps through a cut, set off the second line of defence, known as the innate immune response. Damaged cells release chemicals that cause inflammation: blood vessels widen and become leaky, which is why an infected area becomes red, swollen, warm and painful. The extra blood flow brings white blood cells called phagocytes, which swallow and digest microbes. The innate response is rapid, but it treats every invader in much the same way and cannot remember those it has met before.

The third line of defence, the adaptive response, is slower but precise. Its key link with the innate system is a group of cells called dendritic cells. These collect fragments of invading microbes and travel with them to the lymph nodes, the small glands that swell in the neck during a sore throat. There they present the fragments to two types of white blood cells, T cells and B cells. Each of the body's billions of T and B cells can recognise only one particular shape, so only a tiny number will match a given invader. When a match is found, those particular cells are activated and multiply rapidly, producing thousands of identical copies within a few days. This is why an adaptive response takes time.

The activated cells then attack in two different ways. B cells release antibodies, Y-shaped proteins that lock onto the invader. Antibodies can prevent viruses from entering cells, and they also mark microbes so that phagocytes recognise and destroy them more easily. Antibodies, however, cannot reach viruses once they are inside the body's cells. This is the task of killer T cells, which identify and destroy infected cells, together with the viruses hidden inside them.

Once the infection has been defeated, most of the activated cells die. A small number, however, survive as memory cells, which can persist for decades. If the same invader returns, these cells recognise it immediately, and the response is so fast and strong that the person usually does not notice any illness at all. This is the principle behind vaccination, which exposes the immune system to a harmless version or part of a pathogen, so that memory cells are created without the risk of disease.

lesson.title: Paraphrased boxes
lesson.text: In hard flow-charts, the boxes rarely use the passage's words. "Trigger" may stand for "set off", "carry fragments to" for "transport pieces of ... to", and "long-lived" for "persist for decades". Look for the meaning of each box, not its words. Once you find the matching sentence, the answer itself must still be copied exactly from the passage.
lesson.example: Box: "the plan was (1) ______ because of cost". Passage: "the scheme was eventually abandoned as too expensive". Answer: abandoned.

passages.topic: Medicine — how a new drug is developed
passages.title: From Laboratory to Pharmacy

paragraphs.text: Developing a new medicine is one of the most expensive and uncertain activities in modern industry. Estimates of the average cost of bringing one drug to market vary widely, from under one billion to more than two billion US dollars, depending on how the cost of failed projects is counted. The process commonly takes ten to fifteen years, and of every ten medicines that enter testing in humans, only about one is eventually approved. Understanding why requires following a drug through each of its stages.

Modern drug development usually begins not with a drug but with a disease. Researchers first try to identify a target, usually a protein in the body that plays a key role in the disease; if the protein's activity could be blocked or increased, the disease might be slowed or cured. Once a target has been chosen, the search for a molecule that affects it begins. In a process known as high-throughput screening, robots test hundreds of thousands of chemical compounds against the target in a matter of weeks. Most have no effect, but a few "hits" are selected, and chemists then modify their structures to make them more effective and less toxic.

The most promising compound then enters preclinical testing, in which it is studied in cells grown in the laboratory and in animals. These tests examine how the body absorbs, distributes and removes the compound, and whether it causes damage to organs. Although the use of animals is controversial, regulators in most countries still require such evidence before a drug can be given to humans.

Clinical trials in humans take place in three phases. In Phase I, the drug is given to a small group of healthy volunteers, typically between twenty and eighty people. The main aim is not to find out whether the drug works but to check that it is safe and to establish the correct dosage. Phase II involves several hundred patients who have the disease, and it is here that researchers obtain the first real evidence of whether the drug is effective. This is also the stage with the most failures: many compounds that looked promising in animals simply do not work in humans.

Phase III is the largest and most expensive stage, involving thousands of patients in many hospitals, often in several countries. The new drug is compared either with a placebo, an inactive substance that looks identical to the real treatment, or with the best existing treatment. To prevent bias, most trials are "double-blind": neither the patients nor the doctors know who is receiving which treatment.

If the results are positive, the company submits all its data to regulatory agencies, such as the US Food and Drug Administration or the European Medicines Agency, which decide whether the benefits of the drug outweigh its risks. Even after approval, the process is not over. Some side effects are so rare that they appear only when a drug has been taken by hundreds of thousands of people, so doctors and patients continue to report problems, and a drug may occasionally be withdrawn years after it was first sold.

Critics argue that the system is too slow, and during emergencies, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, some stages have been run at the same time rather than one after another. Others point out that the high rate of failure is itself evidence that careful testing is necessary.

lesson.title: Long processes with background information
lesson.text: Hard passages mix the stages of a process with statistics, history and opinion. Only some of the sentences describe the stages. Skim the passage first and mark where each stage begins; then ignore sentences that give background, such as costs and criticisms, unless a box asks for them.
lesson.example: Passage: "Critics say the test is too expensive. In the test, samples are frozen." Box: "samples (1) ______". Answer: frozen. The first sentence is background.

passages.topic: Evolution — how new species arise on islands
passages.title: Laboratories of Evolution

paragraphs.text: When Charles Darwin visited the Galápagos Islands in 1835, he collected specimens of small brown birds without paying them much attention. Only after he returned to England did an expert tell him that they belonged to more than a dozen different species, many of them found on only one or two islands. The observation helped Darwin to develop his theory of evolution, and islands have remained natural laboratories for studying how new species form, a process known as speciation.

Speciation normally requires that a single population be divided into groups that can no longer breed with each other. On continents, this may happen when a river changes course or a mountain range rises. Islands provide the separation in a different way: a few individuals, perhaps birds blown off course by a storm or lizards carried on floating vegetation, reach an island far from their original population. From that moment, the two groups evolve independently.

Change begins with mutations, random alterations in genetic material that occur in every generation. Most have little effect, and many are harmful, but a few turn out to be useful. Because mutations are random, different ones appear in each separated group. In small populations, which are typical of newly colonised islands, chance plays an unusually large role: some genetic variants may disappear, or become common, purely by luck rather than because they are useful. This process, known as genetic drift, can make a small island population very different from its parent population in relatively few generations.

More important in the long term is natural selection. Each island has its own conditions: its own climate and vegetation, its own food supply, and its own competitors and predators. Individuals whose characteristics suit these conditions survive and reproduce more successfully, so, over many generations, useful characteristics become more common. On the Galápagos, the beaks of finches became adapted to the foods available on each island, from the thick, powerful beaks of species that crack hard seeds to the thin, pointed beaks of those that pick insects from leaves.

If isolation continues for long enough, the differences between the groups accumulate until, even if the barrier disappears and they meet again, they can no longer interbreed successfully. At this point, they have become separate species. The time this takes varies enormously: in some island birds it seems to have taken only a few thousand years, while in other groups it has taken millions. If, on the other hand, the groups are reunited before this point and their populations merge, the differences may disappear.

The same features that make islands so productive of new species also make those species vulnerable. Many island animals evolved without large predators and therefore lost their defensive behaviour; some island birds, such as the dodo of Mauritius, even lost the ability to fly. When humans arrived, bringing rats, cats, pigs and other predators, many such species were quickly driven to extinction. Islands make up only a small fraction of the world's land area, yet they have seen a large proportion of the bird extinctions recorded since 1500.

lesson.title: Word banks with near-synonyms and opposites
lesson.text: In hard word banks, several options may be possible in general, and some are the opposite of what the passage says. "Conditions" and "climates" may both seem to fit, but only one matches the passage's meaning if the passage lists more than climate. "Merged" may appear where the passage describes groups being "divided". Always confirm the option against a specific sentence.
lesson.example: Passage: "The two companies split in 2010." Options: A joined B separated. Answer: B; A is the opposite.

passages.topic: Science history — the Haber–Bosch process and its consequences
passages.title: Bread from Air

paragraphs.text: In 1898, the British scientist William Crookes warned that the world was heading for famine. The population was growing, and crops need nitrogen, yet almost all of the nitrogen on Earth exists as a gas in the air, in a form that plants cannot use. Farmers relied on natural fertilisers, above all guano, the accumulated droppings of seabirds, from islands off Peru, and on Chilean nitrate, mined in the Atacama Desert. Both supplies were limited, and Crookes predicted that they would run out within a few decades.

The solution was found in Germany. In 1909, the chemist Fritz Haber showed in his laboratory that nitrogen from the air could be combined with hydrogen to make ammonia, a compound from which fertilisers can be produced. The problem was scale: Haber's apparatus produced about eighty grams of ammonia an hour. The engineer Carl Bosch, working for the chemical company BASF, spent four years developing equipment that could operate safely under the extreme conditions required, and in 1913 the first industrial plant opened at Oppau. Both men were later awarded Nobel Prizes.

The process itself has changed little since then. Nitrogen is obtained from the air, while hydrogen is today produced mainly from natural gas, although coal is still widely used in China. The two gases are compressed to about 200 times atmospheric pressure, heated to around 450 degrees Celsius, and passed over a catalyst based on iron. Even under these conditions, only around fifteen per cent of the gases react each time they pass through the reactor. The ammonia is therefore removed by cooling, which turns it into a liquid, and the unreacted gases are recycled through the reactor again and again.

The consequences have been enormous. Synthetic fertiliser made it possible to grow far more food on the same land, and scientists estimate that roughly half of the world's population today is fed by crops grown with nitrogen from the Haber–Bosch process. Without it, the world could support perhaps only four billion people. For this reason, it has been described as the most important invention of the twentieth century.

The benefits, however, have come at a cost. The process consumes around one to two per cent of the world's energy supply, most of it from fossil fuels, and is responsible for a significant share of global carbon dioxide emissions. Moreover, much of the fertiliser applied to fields is not taken up by crops. It is washed into rivers and eventually reaches the sea, where it feeds huge growths of algae. When these algae die and decay, they use up the oxygen in the water, creating dead zones in which fish and other animals cannot survive. More than four hundred such zones have been identified in coastal waters worldwide.

The process also had a darker history. During the First World War, the same ammonia was used to make explosives, allowing Germany to continue fighting after its supplies of Chilean nitrate were cut off. Today, researchers are trying to produce the hydrogen using renewable electricity and to develop crops that need less fertiliser, in the hope of keeping the benefits of Haber and Bosch's invention while reducing its costs.

lesson.title: Flow-charts that combine history and process
lesson.text: Some flow-charts show a sequence of events over time, from a problem to a solution and its effects, instead of a technical process. They may include dates and quantities. Look for time expressions (by 1900, in 1909, four years later) and cause-and-effect words (as a result, consequently), and check that each date or figure belongs to the right event.
lesson.example: Passage: "The idea was proposed in 1901 but not tested until 1905." Box: "first test: (1) ______". Answer: 1905.

passages.topic: Economics — how interest rates affect inflation
passages.title: The Price of Money

paragraphs.text: In most developed economies, the job of keeping inflation, the rate at which prices rise, low and stable belongs to the central bank, such as the Bank of England or the US Federal Reserve. Many central banks aim for inflation of around two per cent a year. Their main tool is surprisingly simple: they set a single interest rate, known as the policy rate, at which commercial banks can borrow from or deposit money with the central bank. When inflation is too high, the central bank raises this rate. How such a small change can affect an entire economy is explained by what economists call the transmission mechanism.

The effect begins even before the rate itself changes. Central banks now publish their views on the likely future path of interest rates, a practice known as forward guidance. If a central bank signals that rates will rise, lenders and borrowers begin to adjust their behaviour in advance, and the eventual rise has a stronger effect as a result.

Once the policy rate rises, the change spreads through two main channels. In the first, commercial banks, whose own borrowing costs have increased, raise the interest rates they charge on loans and mortgages, and usually also raise the rates they pay to savers. In the second, higher interest rates make the country a more attractive place for foreign investors to hold their money. As they buy the currency, its value rises, and as a result imported goods become cheaper, which directly reduces inflation.

The first channel then changes the behaviour of households and businesses. Higher repayments leave borrowers with less money to spend, while higher returns encourage people to save rather than spend. Households tend to cut back most on large purchases, such as cars, furniture and holidays, that are often paid for with borrowed money. Businesses, facing higher borrowing costs, postpone plans to build factories or buy new equipment.

The result is lower demand for goods and services throughout the economy. With fewer customers, companies find it harder to raise prices and have less need to hire additional workers, so wage growth also slows. Gradually, the rate at which prices rise falls back towards the central bank's target. Confidence matters too: if people believe that the central bank will keep inflation under control, they are less likely to demand large pay rises, which makes the bank's job easier.

The process, however, is slow and uncertain. Most central banks estimate that a change in interest rates has its full effect on inflation only after between one and two years, which means that they must base their decisions on forecasts of the future rather than on today's figures. There is also a risk of going too far. If rates are raised more than necessary, demand may fall so sharply that businesses close and unemployment rises, pushing the economy into a recession. Central bankers often compare their task to steering a large ship: the effect of turning the wheel is felt only long after the decision has been made.

lesson.title: Abstract processes
lesson.text: Economic and social processes have no physical steps; the stages are changes in behaviour, prices or expectations. The passage may use many abstract nouns (demand, confidence, expectations) that look alike. Decide which quantity each box is describing, and check the direction of change: rise or fall, more or less.
lesson.example: Passage: "Higher taxes reduce spending, which lowers prices." Box: "less (1) ______ → prices fall". Answer: spending.

passages.topic: Forensic science — DNA profiling in criminal investigations
passages.title: The Evidence Within

paragraphs.text: Since it was first used in a criminal case in England in 1986, DNA profiling has transformed the investigation of crime. It has identified the perpetrators of crimes committed decades earlier, and in the United States alone it has helped to free several hundred people who had been wrongly convicted. Yet the technique is often misunderstood. Contrary to what television dramas suggest, a DNA profile does not examine a person's entire genetic code, and a "match" is a statement about probability rather than certainty.

The process begins at the crime scene. Investigators wearing protective clothing collect samples that may contain human cells, such as blood, saliva, hair roots or skin cells left on objects that someone has touched. Each item is sealed, labelled and recorded in what is known as the chain of custody, a written record of everyone who has handled the evidence. Without this record, lawyers may argue in court that a sample was contaminated or even replaced, and the evidence may be rejected.

In the laboratory, DNA is extracted from the cells and purified. Crime-scene samples often contain very small amounts, sometimes the DNA from only a few cells, so the next step is to copy selected sections millions of times using a technique called the polymerase chain reaction, or PCR. Without this technique, which was developed in the 1980s, most crime-scene samples would be far too small to analyse.

More than 99 per cent of human DNA is identical in all people, so profiling focuses on regions where individuals differ. These are short sequences that are repeated a different number of times in different people, known as short tandem repeats. Early systems used as few as four regions; the US system used thirteen for many years, and today many countries analyse around twenty. The copied fragments are then separated according to their size by a method called capillary electrophoresis, and the result, a list of numbers for each region, forms the profile.

The profile can then be compared with that of a suspect or, if there is no suspect, searched against a national database containing the profiles of convicted offenders and, in some countries, people who have been arrested. If the profiles are different, the suspect is excluded; indeed, one of the most valuable uses of DNA evidence is to prove innocence. If they match, scientists calculate the probability that an unrelated person chosen at random would have the same profile. With twenty regions, this figure is usually less than one in a billion. Relatives, however, share much of their DNA and are much more likely to match.

Even a genuine match does not prove guilt. The most sensitive modern techniques can detect DNA from just a handful of cells, and DNA can move between people and objects through indirect contact, a phenomenon called secondary transfer. A person's DNA may be found on a weapon, for example, because the real attacker shook hands with them earlier. For this reason, experts increasingly warn that courts should consider how and when DNA arrived at a scene, not simply whose DNA it is.

lesson.title: Final review — putting every skill together
lesson.text: This final set combines the main challenges of Flow-chart Completion: paraphrased boxes, a branch, several numbers, technical terms, background information and a word limit of TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER. Work systematically: read the whole flow-chart, locate the start of the process in the passage, predict each answer type, check the branch conditions, confirm each number's stage, and finally reread every completed box for grammar and word limit.
lesson.example: Branch: "if no match → suspect (1) ______". Passage: "If the profiles differ, the suspect is ruled out." Answer: ruled out.

passages.topic: Everyday technology — how a bicycle pump works
passages.title: Under Pressure

paragraphs.text: The bicycle pump is one of the simplest machines in everyday use, yet it demonstrates a basic principle of physics: when a gas is squeezed into a smaller space, its pressure rises. A good pump allows a cyclist to inflate a tyre to several times the pressure of the surrounding air in less than a minute.

The main body of the pump is a long tube called the barrel, usually made of aluminium or strong plastic. At the top, the cyclist holds a handle, which is fixed to a metal rod running down the centre of the barrel. At the lower end of the rod is the piston, a disc that fits closely inside the barrel.

The piston is surrounded by a flexible washer made of rubber or leather. When the handle is pushed down, the washer presses firmly against the wall of the barrel, forming a seal, so that the air below the piston is squeezed. When the handle is pulled up, the washer bends slightly, allowing air to flow past it into the lower part of the barrel, ready for the next stroke.

At the bottom of the barrel is a one-way valve, which allows air to leave the pump but prevents it from flowing back in. From here, a flexible hose carries the air to the tyre. At the end of the hose, a nozzle is pressed onto the valve of the tyre and held in place with a small lever.

Larger pumps, designed to stand on the floor, often have a gauge, a small dial mounted near the base, which shows the pressure inside the tyre. This allows the cyclist to inflate the tyre to exactly the pressure recommended by the manufacturer, which is usually printed on the side of the tyre.

lesson.title: Use the given labels to find your place
lesson.text: In an easy diagram, the passage describes the object part by part, and several labels are already given. These completed labels are anchors: find them in the passage first, and the missing parts will usually be described in the same or the next sentence. Position words, such as "at the top", "around" and "at the end of", tell you where each part belongs.

passages.topic: Engineering — the layers of a modern road
passages.title: More Than Meets the Eye

paragraphs.text: Most people think of a road as a strip of black material on the ground, but a modern main road is a carefully designed structure, often more than half a metre deep. Each layer has a particular job, and together they spread the weight of heavy vehicles so that the ground below is not damaged.

The foundation of every road is the subgrade, which is the natural soil on which the road is built. Before construction begins, it is levelled and compacted with heavy rollers. If the soil is weak, engineers may strengthen it with lime or cement.

On top of the subgrade is the sub-base, a thick layer of crushed stone. Besides spreading the load, it allows water that gets into the road to drain away, which is important because water that remains in a road can freeze and expand in winter, causing cracks and potholes.

Above this is the base, the main structural layer of the road. It is made of coarse asphalt or, in some roads, concrete, and its job is to spread the load of traffic over a wide area of the layers below.

The top two layers are both made of asphalt, a mixture of stone chips and bitumen. The lower of these is called the binder course, and it bonds the surface to the base. The very top layer, the one that drivers see, is the surface course. Usually only about 40 millimetres thick, it is designed to be smooth, waterproof and resistant to skidding. Because it wears out fastest, it can be removed and replaced without disturbing the layers beneath.

lesson.title: Cross-sections with layers
lesson.text: A layered diagram shows a structure as a series of bands, from top to bottom. The passage usually describes the layers in order, either from the surface downwards or from the ground upwards. Decide which direction the passage takes, then match each layer to its paragraph. Labels may ask for the layer's name, material, thickness or purpose.
lesson.example: Passage: "Beneath the carpet lies a layer of foam, and below that, the wooden floor." Layers: carpet → (1) ______ → wooden floor. Answer: foam.

passages.topic: Agriculture — inside a modern beehive
passages.title: A House for Bees

paragraphs.text: For thousands of years, people collected honey by destroying the nests of wild bees. The modern beehive, developed in the nineteenth century, changed this. It consists of a series of wooden boxes, placed one on top of another, which beekeepers can open and inspect without harming the colony.

The hive stands on a raised stand, which keeps it off the damp ground. The base of the hive is a floor, often made of wire mesh, through which small parasites called mites fall out of the hive. At the front of the floor is the entrance, a narrow gap through which the bees come and go. In winter, beekeepers often make the entrance narrower still to keep out mice.

Directly above the floor is the brood box, the largest box in the hive. This is where the queen lays her eggs and where the young bees develop. Like all the boxes, it contains a row of removable wooden frames, each holding a thin sheet of wax, on which the bees build their honeycomb.

Above the brood box is a flat grid called the queen excluder. Its gaps are large enough for the worker bees to pass through, but too small for the queen, who is larger. This ensures that no eggs are laid in the boxes above, which are called supers. The supers are the boxes where the bees store honey, and it is these that the beekeeper removes at harvest time.

At the top of the hive is a sloping or flat roof, usually covered with metal to keep out the rain. Small gaps under the roof provide ventilation, which is essential because a busy hive produces a great deal of heat and moisture.

lesson.title: Labels that describe a function
lesson.text: Many labels do not ask for the name of a part but for what it does or contains, such as "where bees store (1) ______". With a word bank, find the part in the passage, read what it is used for, and choose the option that matches that use. Options that name other parts of the object are common distractors.
lesson.example: Label: "drawer: used for storing (1) ______". Passage: "The top drawer holds cutlery." Options: A plates B cutlery. Answer: B.

passages.topic: Human biology — the structure of the eye
passages.title: Windows on the World

paragraphs.text: The human eye is often compared to a camera, and the comparison is a useful one. Both have a system for letting in light, a way of focusing it, and a surface on which an image is formed. The eye, however, is far more adaptable than any camera and can work in bright sunlight and in near darkness.

Light first passes through the cornea, the clear, curved surface at the front of the eye, which does most of the work of bending light rays. Behind the cornea is the iris, the coloured ring that gives a person's eyes their colour. In the centre of the iris is an opening called the pupil. In bright light, the iris makes the pupil smaller to protect the eye; in dim light, it makes the pupil larger to let in more light.

The light then passes through the lens, a transparent structure that fine-tunes the focus. The lens is attached to a ring of ciliary muscles, which change its shape: they make it thicker to focus on nearby objects and thinner to focus on distant ones. With age, the lens becomes less flexible, which is why many older people need glasses for reading.

Most of the eye is filled with a clear, jelly-like substance called the vitreous humour, which helps the eye keep its round shape. Light travels through it to the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. The retina contains millions of cells that turn light into electrical signals. These signals are carried to the brain by the optic nerve, and it is the brain that turns them into the images that we see.

lesson.text: When a diagram shows a cross-section, some parts are at the front or outside and others are deep inside. The passage usually follows the path of something through the object: here, the path of light. Follow that path in the passage and on the diagram at the same time.
lesson.example: Passage: "Water enters through the tap, passes through a filter and leaves through the spout." Label at the middle: "(1) ______". Answer: filter.
