passages.topic: History of technology — the traditional tower windmill
passages.title: Harnessing the Wind

paragraphs.text: Windmills were once a common sight across much of Europe. By the middle of the nineteenth century, England alone had around ten thousand of them, most used for grinding grain into flour. The most advanced type was the tower mill, many of which still stand today, although few are in working order.

A tower mill consists of a fixed tower, usually built of brick or stone, which tapers towards the top. Most towers were between four and seven storeys high, and the tallest in England reached ten storeys. On top of the tower sits the cap, which can rotate, so that the sails can always face into the wind.

The sails, usually four in number, were originally wooden frames covered with cloth, which the miller spread or rolled up depending on the strength of the wind. They are attached to a thick shaft, called the windshaft, which passes through the cap. As the sails turn, the windshaft turns a system of gears, which passes the movement down to the lower floors.

In early tower mills, the miller had to turn the cap by hand. From the 1740s, however, many mills were fitted with a fantail, a small wind wheel mounted at the back of the cap, at right angles to the sails. Whenever the wind changes direction, the fantail begins to turn and slowly rotates the cap until the sails face the wind again.

The grain was raised to the top floor by a sack hoist, powered by the sails themselves. It then passed down through the building by gravity. On a floor near the middle of the mill, a pair of millstones ground the grain into flour, which was collected in sacks on the floor below.

lesson.text: Some labels need a number, such as a height, a count or a date. When the word limit allows a number, check that the number refers to the same part as the label. A passage about a building may include heights, numbers of floors and dates of construction all in one paragraph.
lesson.example: Passage: "The tower, built in 1820, has six floors and is 25 metres tall." Label: "tower: (1) ______ floors". Answer: six / 6.

passages.topic: Earth science — a soil profile
passages.title: Beneath Our Feet

paragraphs.text: If you dig a deep hole in undisturbed ground, you will see that soil is not the same all the way down. It is arranged in layers, called horizons, which together make up a soil profile. Soil scientists label the horizons with letters, and by studying them they can learn how the soil formed and what it can be used for.

At the surface is the O horizon, a thin layer of fallen leaves, twigs and other organic matter that has not yet fully decayed. Beneath it lies the A horizon, better known as topsoil. This layer is full of plant roots, worms and microorganisms, and its dark colour comes from humus, the rich material formed when plant and animal remains break down. Topsoil is the most fertile part of the profile.

In many soils, particularly in forests, there is a pale layer below the topsoil known as the E horizon. As rainwater soaks down through it, minerals and fine particles are washed out and carried to lower levels, leaving mainly sand behind. This process is called leaching.

The minerals do not disappear. They are deposited in the next layer, the B horizon or subsoil, where clay and iron collect. The subsoil is usually more compact than the topsoil and is often reddish or brown in colour.

Below the subsoil is the C horizon, which consists of weathered parent material, the partly broken pieces of the rock from which the soil above developed. At the very bottom is the R horizon, the solid bedrock. Because soil forms extremely slowly, a profile of one metre may take thousands of years to develop.

lesson.title: Opposites in the word bank
lesson.text: A word bank often contains an option with the opposite meaning of the correct answer, such as "washed out" and "deposited", or "added" and "removed". These traps work because both options belong to the same topic. When a label describes a process, decide carefully whether something is being gained or lost at that level.
lesson.example: Passage: "Rain removes salt from the upper layer." Label: "upper layer: salt (1) ______". Options: A added B removed. Answer: B.

passages.topic: Earth science — the structure of a volcano
passages.title: Mountains of Fire

paragraphs.text: There are around 1,350 potentially active volcanoes on land around the world, and at any given time a few dozen of them are erupting. The most familiar kind, the steep, cone-shaped volcano seen in photographs of Mount Fuji in Japan, is known as a stratovolcano. Its name comes from its internal structure: it is built up, eruption after eruption, from alternating layers of ash and hardened lava.

Deep below a volcano, usually between one and ten kilometres beneath the surface, lies a magma chamber, a large reservoir of molten rock. Magma is lighter than the solid rock that surrounds it, so it tends to rise. It travels upwards through a narrow pipe called the conduit, and when the pressure of gases dissolved in the magma becomes great enough, it forces its way to the surface.

Most of the magma escapes through the main vent at the top of the volcano. Around it, explosions and collapses create a crater, a bowl-shaped hollow at the summit. Some magma, however, finds other routes to the surface, breaking out through a side vent on the slope of the mountain, where it may build a smaller cone of its own.

Once magma reaches the surface, it is called lava. In a stratovolcano, the lava is thick and sticky and does not travel far; lava flows move slowly down the slopes, burning everything in their path, but rarely threatening human lives directly. Far more dangerous is what happens above the volcano. During an explosive eruption, a vast eruption column of gas, ash and rock fragments can rise more than twenty kilometres into the sky.

When such a column collapses, it can produce the most deadly feature of all: a pyroclastic flow, an avalanche of hot gas and rock that races down the mountain at over one hundred kilometres an hour. In AD 79, pyroclastic flows from Vesuvius destroyed the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum, killing thousands of people who had been unable to escape.

lesson.title: Similar technical terms
lesson.text: Passages about natural features often contain pairs of terms that are easy to confuse, such as "magma" (molten rock underground) and "lava" (molten rock at the surface), or "main vent" and "side vent". The diagram tests whether you have noticed the difference. When a passage defines a term, underline the definition and compare it closely with the position of the label.
lesson.example: Passage: "Groundwater lies below the surface; runoff flows over it." Label on the surface: "(1) ______". Answer: runoff.

passages.topic: Human biology — the layers of the skin
passages.title: The Body's Largest Organ

paragraphs.text: The skin is the largest organ of the human body. In an adult, it covers an area of about two square metres and makes up around one seventh of total body weight. It protects the body from injury, infection and harmful sunlight, keeps it at a steady temperature, and allows us to feel touch, heat and pain. It consists of three main layers.

The outermost layer is the epidermis. Although it is thin, only about 0.1 millimetres on most of the body, it is remarkably tough. The cells at its surface are dead and filled with a hard protein called keratin, which makes them waterproof and resistant to damage. These cells are constantly being rubbed off and replaced; in fact, the entire surface of the skin is renewed roughly every four weeks. New cells are produced at the bottom of the epidermis, where there are also cells called melanocytes, which produce melanin, the pigment that gives skin its colour and absorbs harmful ultraviolet light.

Beneath the epidermis is the dermis, which is much thicker. It contains collagen, a strong protein that gives skin its strength and flexibility, as well as blood vessels and nerve endings, which are responsible for the sense of touch. The dermis also contains sweat glands, which help to cool the body, and hair follicles, the small tubes from which hairs grow. As people age, the body produces less collagen, and the skin becomes thinner and forms wrinkles.

The deepest layer is the hypodermis, sometimes called the subcutaneous layer. It is made up mainly of fat, and its thickness varies greatly from one part of the body to another and from one person to another. The fat insulates the body against cold, acts as a cushion that protects the muscles and bones beneath from knocks, and stores energy that the body can use when food is scarce.

lesson.title: Several labels in one layer
lesson.text: In a layered diagram, one layer may have two or more labels: its name, what it contains, and what it does. The passage will usually describe the whole layer in one paragraph, so read that paragraph carefully and match each label to a different detail. Do not give the layer's name when the label asks for its contents.
lesson.example: Passage: "The crust, the thinnest layer, is made of granite and basalt." Labels: "(1) ______: thinnest layer" and "made of granite and (2) ______". Answers: crust, basalt.

passages.topic: Plant biology — inside a leaf
passages.title: A Factory in Every Leaf

paragraphs.text: A leaf may look simple, but under a microscope its cross-section reveals a structure as carefully organised as any factory. Its purpose is photosynthesis: using the energy of sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, releasing oxygen as a by-product. Each layer of the leaf plays its own part in this process.

The upper surface of the leaf is covered by a waxy cuticle, which reduces water loss by evaporation, giving many leaves their shiny appearance. Beneath it is the upper epidermis, a single layer of cells that is thin and transparent, so that light can pass straight through it to the cells below.

The next layer, the palisade layer, is where most photosynthesis takes place. Its cells are tall and narrow, arranged side by side like the posts of a fence, and they are packed with chloroplasts, the tiny green structures that contain the pigment chlorophyll and capture light energy. Because they are near the top of the leaf, these cells receive the most light.

Below the palisade layer is the spongy layer. Its cells are rounded and loosely arranged, with many air spaces between them. These spaces allow gases to move easily through the leaf: carbon dioxide reaches the cells that need it, and oxygen and water vapour move out. Running through the spongy layer are the veins, which contain two kinds of tube. Xylem carries water and minerals from the roots, while phloem carries the sugar produced by photosynthesis to the rest of the plant.

The lower surface of the leaf is formed by the lower epidermis. It contains thousands of tiny pores called stomata, through which gases enter and leave the leaf. Each pore is surrounded by two guard cells, which open the stomata during the day to let in carbon dioxide and close them at night or during dry weather to prevent water loss. Most plants have far more stomata on the lower surface of their leaves than on the upper surface, where the heat of the sun would cause them to lose more water.

lesson.title: Adjectives and nouns

With TWO WORDS, you may need an adjective and a noun together, such as "air spaces". Make sure your answer fits the grammar of the label as well as its meaning.

passages.topic: Energy — a hydroelectric power station
passages.title: Power from Falling Water

paragraphs.text: Hydroelectric power stations generate around one sixth of the world's electricity, more than any other renewable source. The largest, the Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River in China, can produce more electricity than twenty large coal-fired power stations. All of them work on the same basic principle: the energy of falling water is turned into electrical energy.

The dam itself is a massive wall, usually of concrete, built across a river valley. Behind it, water collects to form a reservoir, an artificial lake that may stretch back for many kilometres. The higher the water level in the reservoir is above the power station, the more energy each litre of water can provide.

Water leaves the reservoir through an intake near the base of the dam. The intake is protected by a metal grille, which prevents branches, rubbish and fish from being drawn in. From here, the water rushes down a steep pipe called a penstock. As it falls, it gains speed, and at the bottom of the penstock it strikes the curved blades of a turbine, making it spin rapidly.

The turbine is connected by a shaft to a generator directly above it. Inside the generator, large magnets rotate within coils of copper wire, and this movement converts the turning motion into electricity. The electricity then passes to a transformer, which increases its voltage so that it can be carried long distances along power lines with less energy being lost.

Having passed through the turbine, the water flows out through a channel known as the tailrace and returns to the river below the dam. Because the amount of water flowing through the turbines can be adjusted within minutes, hydroelectric stations are particularly useful for meeting sudden increases in demand.

During floods, the reservoir may receive more water than the turbines can use. To prevent water from pouring over the top of the dam, which could damage it, the excess is released through a spillway, a wide channel built into or beside the dam.

lesson.title: Following the flow through a structure
lesson.text: Diagrams of power stations, water systems and engines often show something flowing through them: water, air or fuel. The passage usually follows the same path from start to finish. Trace the flow with your finger on the diagram as you read, and stop at each gap to find the part the passage is describing at that point.

passages.topic: Technology — how a refrigerator keeps food cold
passages.title: Moving Heat

paragraphs.text: A refrigerator does not create cold. Instead, it moves heat from the inside of the cabinet, where it is not wanted, to the outside, where it does not matter. It does this by pumping a special fluid, called a refrigerant, around a closed loop of pipes, making it change repeatedly between a liquid and a gas.

The key to the process is a simple physical fact: when a liquid evaporates and turns into a gas, it takes in heat from its surroundings. This is why a person feels cold after swimming, as the water evaporates from their skin. Inside the refrigerator, usually at the back of the freezer compartment, is a set of pipes called the evaporator. Here, the refrigerant, which boils at a very low temperature, evaporates and absorbs heat from the food and air inside the cabinet.

The refrigerant, now a gas, flows to the compressor, a pump driven by an electric motor, usually found in a box at the bottom of the refrigerator at the back. The compressor squeezes the gas, greatly raising its pressure and, as a result, its temperature.

The hot gas then passes through the condenser coils, the black metal grid often visible on the back of a refrigerator. As the gas cools, it condenses into a liquid, and the heat it took from the food is released into the kitchen. This is why the back of a refrigerator feels warm to the touch.

Finally, the liquid refrigerant passes through the expansion valve, a narrow opening that separates the high-pressure and low-pressure parts of the system. As the liquid passes through it, its pressure drops suddenly, and it becomes very cold, ready to enter the evaporator and absorb heat once again.

The compressor does not run all the time. A thermostat measures the temperature inside the cabinet and switches the compressor on when the temperature rises and off when it has fallen to the chosen level. This is the source of the quiet humming sound that starts and stops throughout the day.

lesson.title: Word banks for processes inside a machine
lesson.text: When a diagram shows a machine at work, many labels describe changes: something rises or drops, is absorbed or released, becomes a liquid or a gas. The word bank will contain both directions. For each label, find the part in the passage and ask: what changes here, and in which direction?
lesson.example: Passage: "In the boiler, water turns to steam." Label: "boiler: water becomes (1) ______". Options: A ice B steam C liquid. Answer: B.

passages.topic: History — the defences of a medieval castle
passages.title: Built for War

paragraphs.text: In the eleventh and twelfth centuries, castles spread across Europe as kings and lords sought to control the lands they had conquered. The earliest were simple wooden towers on mounds of earth, but by the thirteenth century castle design had developed into a sophisticated science, in which each feature was intended to make an attack as difficult and costly as possible.

An attacker's first obstacle was often the moat, a wide, deep ditch that surrounded the castle and was usually filled with water. It prevented enemies from digging tunnels under the walls and from bringing siege towers close to them. The only way across was a drawbridge, a wooden bridge that could be raised by chains when the castle was threatened.

The entrance itself was protected by a strong gatehouse. Behind the doors hung a portcullis, a heavy iron grille that could be dropped quickly to block the passage. In the roof of the passage were holes, known as murder holes, through which defenders could drop stones or pour boiling water onto attackers trapped between the gates.

The castle was enclosed by a thick outer wall called the curtain wall, strengthened at intervals by towers. Along the top of the walls ran the battlements, a walkway protected by a low wall with regular gaps through which defenders could shoot while remaining partly hidden. Narrow arrow slits in the walls allowed archers to fire out, while being very difficult targets to hit from outside.

Inside the curtain wall was an open courtyard called the bailey, which contained stables, workshops, a kitchen and a well; a reliable water supply was essential if the castle was to survive a long siege. The strongest building of all was the keep, a massive tower that was usually the lord's home and served as the last refuge if the outer defences fell.

The arrival of powerful gunpowder cannons in the fifteenth century made high stone walls vulnerable, and castles gradually lost their military importance. Many became comfortable country houses, while others were abandoned and left to fall into ruin.

lesson.title: Words from other languages and unusual spellings
lesson.text: Passages about history often use specialist words, some of them borrowed from other languages, such as "portcullis" or "bailey". These are easy to misspell under time pressure. When you find an answer of this kind, copy it one letter at a time. A misspelled answer is marked wrong, even if you have found the correct part.
lesson.example: Passage: "The knights wore a hauberk, a shirt of chain mail." Label: "(1) ______: shirt of chain mail". Answer: hauberk, not "hawberk".

passages.topic: Geography — the features of a valley glacier
passages.title: Rivers of Ice

paragraphs.text: About ten per cent of the Earth's land surface is covered by glacial ice today, and during the last ice age, which ended around 11,700 years ago, the figure was about three times higher. Much of the scenery of northern Europe and North America, from the lakes of Finland to the deep valleys of the Rockies, was shaped by glaciers. Valley glaciers, which flow down mountain valleys like slow-moving rivers, show most of the features of glaciers in a small area.

A valley glacier usually begins in a cirque, also known as a corrie, a deep, armchair-shaped hollow high on a mountainside. The upper part of the glacier is its accumulation zone, where more snow falls each year than melts. Over many years, the snow is buried and compressed, gradually turning into dense glacial ice.

Ice may seem rigid, but under its own great weight it flows slowly downhill, typically at a speed of a few centimetres to a metre a day. Where the glacier passes over a steep slope or bends, the brittle surface cannot stretch fast enough and breaks, forming crevasses, deep cracks in the ice that can be dangerous to climbers because they are often hidden by snow.

As the glacier moves, it tears pieces of rock from the valley floor and walls and carries them along. Rock that has fallen from the valley sides collects along the edges of the glacier, forming a ridge known as a lateral moraine. Where two glaciers join, their lateral moraines combine to form a single line of rock down the middle of the ice, called a medial moraine.

Lower down the valley, in the ablation zone, the glacier loses more ice than it gains, mainly by melting, but also by evaporation. The front edge of the glacier, where the ice ends, is known as the snout. Meltwater streams flow out from beneath it, carrying fine rock particles that give them a milky colour.

When a glacier melts back, it leaves behind the rock it has been carrying. A long ridge of rock, called a terminal moraine, often marks the furthest advance of the ice. Because many glaciers are now shrinking rapidly, their terminal moraines lie hundreds of metres or even several kilometres in front of their present snouts.

lesson.title: Alternative names in the passage
lesson.text: A passage may give two names for the same feature: "a cirque, also known as a corrie". Either name can usually be accepted if it fits the word limit, but the label may already contain one of them. Also watch for adjectives that separate similar features, such as "lateral" (at the side) and "terminal" (at the end).
lesson.example: Passage: "the estuary, or river mouth". Label: "(1) ______: where the river meets the sea". Answer: estuary / river mouth.

passages.topic: Botany — the cross-section of a tree trunk
passages.title: Reading the Rings

paragraphs.text: A tree trunk is not a solid block of wood. When a trunk is cut across, it reveals a series of rings, each with its own structure and function. Together they allow the tree to support its enormous weight, transport water and food, and grow a little wider every year, sometimes for thousands of years.

The outside of the trunk is covered by the outer bark, a layer of dead cells that protects the living tissue inside from insects, disease, extreme temperatures and, in some species, fire. Just inside the outer bark is the inner bark, also known as the phloem. This is a living layer that carries sugars, produced in the leaves by photosynthesis, down to the rest of the tree. Because the phloem lies so close to the surface, a tree can be killed if a strip of bark is removed right around its trunk.

Beneath the phloem lies the cambium, a layer so thin that it can barely be seen. It is, however, where growth takes place: its cells divide to produce new phloem on the outside and new wood on the inside. In this way, the trunk becomes thicker every year.

The new wood produced by the cambium forms the sapwood. This pale, living layer carries water and minerals upwards from the roots to the leaves, sometimes to a height of more than a hundred metres. As the tree grows, the older, inner sapwood gradually dies and becomes heartwood. The heartwood is usually darker in colour, and although it no longer carries water, it is very hard and gives the tree its support. At the very centre of the trunk is the pith, a small area of soft tissue left over from the tree's first year of growth.

In regions with distinct seasons, the cambium grows quickly in spring, producing large, pale cells, and more slowly in late summer, producing small, dark cells. The result is a visible growth ring for each year of the tree's life. By counting these rings, scientists can find out a tree's age, and by measuring their width, they can learn about the climate of the past: wide rings indicate good growing years, and narrow rings indicate years of drought or cold.

lesson.title: Circular diagrams: from outside to centre
lesson.text: A circular cross-section, such as a tree trunk, the Earth or a cable, is arranged in rings from the outside to the centre. The passage usually describes them in the same order, using words such as "just inside", "beneath this" and "at the very centre". Match each ring in turn, and be careful with rings that have similar functions but carry different substances.
lesson.example: Passage: "A cable has a plastic coating; beneath it is a copper wire." Outer ring: "plastic (1) ______". Answer: coating.

passages.topic: Human biology — the structure of the heart
passages.title: The Tireless Pump

paragraphs.text: The human heart is a muscular organ roughly the size of a closed fist, and it beats around 100,000 times a day, pumping about 7,000 litres of blood around the body. It is, in effect, two pumps side by side. The right side collects blood that has travelled around the body and sends it to the lungs to collect oxygen, while the left side receives this oxygen-rich blood and pumps it out to every other part of the body. Because diagrams of the heart are drawn as though the viewer were facing the patient, the right side of the heart appears on the left of the diagram.

Each side of the heart has two chambers. The upper chambers, called atria, receive blood, and the lower chambers, called ventricles, pump it out. Oxygen-poor blood returning from the body enters the right atrium through two large veins and passes down into the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve, whose three flaps close to prevent blood flowing backwards. The right ventricle then pumps the blood into the pulmonary artery, which carries it to the lungs. This is the only artery in the adult body that carries oxygen-poor blood.

Blood from the lungs returns to the left atrium and passes down through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The left ventricle has the hardest job of all, since it must push blood around the whole body, and its muscular walls are about three times thicker than those of the right ventricle. It pumps blood into the aorta, the largest artery in the body, which is about the width of a garden hose and arches over the top of the heart before running down through the chest and abdomen.

The two sides of the heart are completely separated by a thick muscular wall called the septum. Before birth, there is an opening in this wall, since a baby in the womb receives oxygen from its mother rather than from its own lungs. The opening normally closes within days of birth; if it does not, the result is a so-called "hole in the heart", which may need to be repaired by surgery.

The heartbeat is controlled by electrical signals. Each beat begins in a small group of cells in the wall of the right atrium called the sinoatrial node, often described as the heart's natural pacemaker. The signal spreads across the atria, making them contract, and then, after a brief delay that allows the ventricles to fill, down to the ventricles. When this system fails, an artificial pacemaker, a small battery-powered device placed under the skin, can be fitted to take over the job.

lesson.title: When left and right are reversed
lesson.text: Anatomical diagrams are drawn as if you are facing the person, so the heart's right side appears on the left of the page, and its left side on the right. Hard passages expect you to notice this. Rely on the labels that are already complete (such as "right atrium") rather than on the side of the page, and check each answer against the passage's description of function, not position alone.
lesson.example: Diagram of a person facing you: label on the left of the page, "(1) ______ hand holding a pen". Passage: "She writes with her right hand." Answer: right.

passages.topic: Engineering — inside a jet engine
passages.title: How Jets Fly

paragraphs.text: Every large passenger aircraft today is powered by a type of jet engine called a turbofan. Although these engines are enormously complex, containing tens of thousands of parts, they rely on a simple principle described by Isaac Newton more than three centuries ago: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. By pushing a vast quantity of air backwards, the engine pushes the aircraft forwards.

The most visible part of a turbofan is the fan at the front, a ring of large, curved blades that can be more than three metres in diameter. The fan draws in huge amounts of air, but surprisingly little of this air passes through the centre of the engine. Most of it, known as bypass air, flows around the core of the engine and out of the back. In modern engines, this bypass air produces about 80 per cent of the thrust, and because it is not heated, it makes the engine both quieter and more efficient than older designs.

The remaining air enters the engine's core, where it first passes through the compressor. This consists of many rows of small, fan-like blades, each row squeezing the air further, so that by the time it leaves the compressor it is at up to 40 times its original pressure. The compressed air then enters the combustion chamber, where it is mixed with fuel and burned. The temperature here can reach 1,500°C, hotter than the melting point of the metals from which the chamber is made, so the walls must be continually cooled by a layer of air.

The hot, expanding gases rush out of the combustion chamber and through the turbine, a series of blades that is driven round by the gases rather than driving them. The turbine is connected by a long central shaft to the compressor and the fan at the front, so the energy it takes from the gases is used to keep them turning. In this way, once the engine has been started, it keeps itself running as long as fuel is supplied.

Finally, the gases leave through the exhaust nozzle at the back of the engine, adding to the thrust produced by the bypass air. At take-off, the engines of a large passenger aircraft together produce a force equivalent to the weight of several hundred cars.

Engine manufacturers are constantly trying to improve efficiency. The main trend has been towards ever larger fans and a higher proportion of bypass air, since moving a large amount of air slowly is more efficient than moving a small amount quickly. The limit is the size of the aircraft itself: a larger fan requires more ground clearance beneath the wing.

lesson.title: Figures and parts in the same label
lesson.text: Hard labels may combine a part with a figure: "(2) ______ produces about (3) ______ of the thrust". Such labels contain two gaps from the same sentence, one a name and one a number. Read the whole sentence, identify which word in the passage matches each gap, and include units (per cent, times, metres) only if they are not already in the label.
lesson.example: Label: "(1) ______: about (2) ______ of the total". Passage: "Wheat accounts for about 40 per cent of the total." Answers: wheat; 40 per cent.

passages.questionTypeDetail: Diagram Label Completion (layers, with word bank)
passages.topic: Earth science — the layers of the atmosphere
passages.title: Layers of Air

paragraphs.text: The atmosphere is a thin envelope of gases, held around the Earth by gravity. Compared with the size of the planet, it is remarkably shallow: if the Earth were the size of an apple, most of the atmosphere would be thinner than the apple's skin. Yet it is far from uniform. Scientists divide it into five main layers, defined mainly by the way the temperature changes with height.

The lowest layer is the troposphere, which extends from the ground to a height of about 12 kilometres, although it is higher over the equator and lower over the poles. It contains around three quarters of the mass of the atmosphere, and almost all of its water vapour. As a result, it is where almost all weather happens, from clouds and rain to storms. In the troposphere, the temperature falls with height, by about 6.5°C for every kilometre, which is why mountain tops are cold even in summer.

Above the troposphere is the stratosphere, which reaches up to about 50 kilometres. Here, the pattern is reversed: the temperature rises with height. This is because the stratosphere contains the ozone layer, which absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation and is warmed by it. The air in the stratosphere is very calm and dry, so long-distance aircraft often fly in its lowest part to avoid turbulence.

The mesosphere, from about 50 to 85 kilometres, is the coldest layer, with temperatures falling as low as minus 90°C at its top. Although the air here is extremely thin, it is dense enough to slow down meteors, pieces of rock from space that enter the atmosphere at great speed. Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere, producing the streaks of light known as shooting stars.

Above the mesosphere is the thermosphere, which extends up to several hundred kilometres. The air here is so thin that it would feel cold to a human, yet the few particles that exist are heated by the Sun to temperatures of well over 1,000°C. The thermosphere is where auroras occur, when charged particles from the Sun collide with gases in the air, and it is also where the International Space Station orbits the Earth.

The outermost layer, the exosphere, has no clear upper boundary. The particles here are so widely spaced that they rarely collide, and some escape the pull of gravity altogether. The exosphere gradually merges with space, at a height that some scientists place at around 10,000 kilometres.

lesson.title: Word banks where both directions are used
lesson.text: In some hard sets, both an option and its opposite are correct answers, for different labels. "Rises" may be correct in one layer and "falls" in another. Do not cross out an opposite just because its partner has been used. Decide each gap independently from the passage.
lesson.example: Passage: "Prices rose in spring and fell in autumn." Labels: "spring: prices (1) ______", "autumn: prices (2) ______". Options: A rose B fell. Answers: A, B.

passages.topic: Environment — the structure of a modern landfill site
passages.title: Burying the Problem

paragraphs.text: For most of history, rubbish was simply dumped in holes in the ground or piled in heaps on the edges of towns. As it decayed, rainwater washing through it produced a toxic liquid known as leachate, which seeped into rivers and underground water supplies, while the rotting waste released methane, an explosive and powerful greenhouse gas. Modern landfill sites are designed to prevent both of these problems, and in many countries they are among the most tightly regulated structures that engineers build.

Construction begins with the base. After the site has been excavated, the natural ground is covered with a layer of compacted clay about one metre thick, which water passes through extremely slowly. On top of the clay is laid a plastic liner, a sheet of high-density polyethylene around two millimetres thick, whose joints are welded together and tested for leaks. Together, the clay and the plastic form a double barrier between the waste and the ground below.

Above the liner is a drainage layer of gravel, in which a network of perforated pipes is buried. These pipes collect the leachate that trickles down through the waste and carry it to a treatment plant. Beneath the site, groundwater is regularly tested through monitoring wells, so that any leak can be detected at an early stage.

The waste itself is placed in the landfill in sections called cells. Each day's rubbish is spread in thin layers and crushed by heavy compactor vehicles to reduce its volume, and at the end of the day it is covered with around fifteen centimetres of soil. This daily cover reduces smells and prevents rubbish from being blown away or attracting birds and rats.

As the waste decomposes, it produces landfill gas, around half of which is methane. The gas is removed through vertical wells that are drilled down into the waste and connected by pipes. In many sites, the gas is burned to generate electricity; where this is not possible, it is at least burned off in a flare, turning the methane into carbon dioxide, which is a much less powerful greenhouse gas.

When a section of the landfill is full, it is sealed with a cap. The cap usually consists of another layer of clay, which keeps rainwater out, and so limits the amount of leachate produced. Finally, the cap is covered with topsoil and planted with grass, and the site may later become a park or a golf course. Even then, leachate and gas must be monitored for thirty years or more.

lesson.title: Long layered diagrams with mixed answer types
lesson.text: A detailed cross-section may have eight or more labels, and the answers may include materials, numbers with units, names of parts and substances. Hard passages also describe the layers in construction order (from the bottom up), while the diagram is labelled from the top down. Number the passage paragraphs against the diagram before you start answering.
lesson.example: Passage: "First a gravel base was laid, then paving stones on top." Diagram (top first): "paving stones", "(1) ______ base". Answer: gravel.

passages.topic: Human biology — how the ear works
passages.title: The Sense of Sound

paragraphs.text: Hearing is a remarkable feat of engineering. The human ear can detect sounds ranging from the faint rustle of leaves to the roar of a jet engine, a range in which the loudest sound carries more than a million million times as much energy as the quietest. It does this by converting vibrations in the air into electrical signals that the brain can interpret. The ear is usually described in three parts: the outer, middle and inner ear.

The outer ear consists of the pinna, the visible curved flap of skin and cartilage on the side of the head, and the ear canal. The pinna collects sound waves and directs them into the canal, and its shape also helps us to judge whether a sound is coming from in front or behind. The ear canal, about 2.5 centimetres long, is lined with small glands that produce wax, which traps dust and protects the ear from infection. At its inner end is the eardrum, a thin, tight membrane that vibrates when sound waves strike it.

The middle ear is an air-filled space containing three tiny bones, known collectively as the ossicles. They are named after their shapes: the hammer, which is attached to the eardrum, the anvil, and the stirrup, which at around three millimetres long is the smallest bone in the human body. Together, they pass the vibrations of the eardrum inwards, increasing their force about twenty times. The middle ear is connected to the back of the throat by the Eustachian tube, which equalises the air pressure on either side of the eardrum. This is why swallowing can relieve the discomfort people feel when an aircraft descends.

The inner ear contains the cochlea, a snail-shaped tube coiled two and a half times and filled with fluid. When the stirrup pushes against a small window into the cochlea, the fluid moves, bending thousands of tiny hair cells along its length. Hair cells at one end respond to high-pitched sounds, and those at the other to low-pitched sounds. The bending of the hairs produces electrical signals, which travel along the auditory nerve to the brain.

Next to the cochlea are three fluid-filled loops called the semicircular canals, which have nothing to do with hearing. They are arranged at right angles to one another and detect movements of the head, providing the brain with the information it needs to maintain the body's sense of balance. Infections of the inner ear can therefore cause dizziness as well as hearing loss.

Hair cells in the cochlea cannot be replaced once they are damaged, and exposure to loud noise, such as music played through headphones at high volume, is one of the most common causes of permanent hearing loss.

lesson.title: A group name or an individual name?
lesson.text: When a passage gives a group name and then the names of its members ("the ossicles: the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup"), check whether the label refers to the whole group or to one member. Numbers in the label ("three ______") point to the group; a description that fits only one item ("the smallest bone") points to the individual.
lesson.example: Passage: "The three primary colours are red, yellow and blue." Label: "three (1) ______". Answer: primary colours (not red).

passages.topic: Energy — the structure of a modern wind turbine
passages.title: Giants of the Wind

paragraphs.text: In 2000, the typical new wind turbine had blades around 35 metres long and could supply electricity for a few hundred homes. Today, the largest offshore turbines have blades longer than a football pitch, and a single machine can power many thousands of homes. Although they come in many sizes, almost all modern turbines share the same basic design: three blades mounted on a horizontal axis at the top of a tall tower.

The most visible parts are the blades, usually three in number, made of glass fibre or carbon fibre so that they are both light and extremely strong. On the largest offshore models, each blade is now more than 100 metres long, giving the rotor a diameter of over 200 metres. The blades are shaped like aircraft wings: as the wind passes over them, it creates lift, which makes the rotor turn.

The blades are attached to a central hub. Inside the hub is the pitch system, which turns each blade around its own length to change the angle at which it meets the wind. In this way, the speed of the rotor can be controlled, and in very strong winds, usually above around 25 metres per second, the blades can be turned edge-on to the wind so that the turbine stops altogether, preventing damage.

The hub is connected to the nacelle, a large housing on top of the tower that contains most of the machinery. The rotor turns relatively slowly, typically between 10 and 20 times a minute, which is far too slow for generating electricity efficiently. In most turbines, therefore, the main shaft drives a gearbox, which increases the speed of rotation around a hundred times before passing it to the generator. Some newer designs, known as direct-drive turbines, have no gearbox; instead, they use a very large generator that can work efficiently at low speeds.

On the roof of the nacelle are two instruments: an anemometer, which measures wind speed, and a wind vane, which measures its direction. When the wind changes direction, a computer instructs the yaw drive, a set of motors at the top of the tower, to rotate the whole nacelle so that the blades face into the wind again.

The nacelle sits on a tower of steel tubes, which is hollow and contains a ladder or lift so that engineers can reach the machinery. On land, towers are usually between 80 and 120 metres tall, while offshore they can reach up to 150 metres. The tower is fixed to a concrete foundation, which may contain several hundred cubic metres of concrete and must be strong enough to resist the enormous forces that the wind exerts on the turbine.

lesson.title: Final review — putting every skill together
lesson.text: This final set combines the main challenges of Diagram Label Completion: labels that give a name, a function or a measurement; passage paragraphs that do not follow the diagram's order; similar parts close together; alternative names; and numbers with units. Work systematically: study the diagram and the given labels, locate each part in the passage using position words, decide what kind of answer each gap needs, and check the word limit and spelling of every answer.
lesson.example: Label: "mast: up to (1) ______ high". Passage: "The masts are usually 30 metres tall, although some reach 45 metres." Answer: 45 metres (the maximum, as "up to" shows).

passages.topic: History of everyday objects — the zip fastener
passages.title: The Slow Success of the Zip

paragraphs.text: Few inventions are used as often, or noticed as rarely, as the zip. It fastens clothes, bags, tents and sleeping bags all over the world, and billions are produced every year. Yet it took more than forty years, and the work of several inventors, before this simple device became a success.

The first version was designed by Whitcomb Judson, an American engineer, who presented it at the Chicago World's Fair in 1893. Judson called his invention a "clasp locker" and designed it to fasten high boots, which at the time had to be laced up by hand, a slow and tiresome job. The clasp locker, however, was unreliable: it often came open unexpectedly or became stuck, and few people bought it.

The problem was solved by Gideon Sundback, an engineer born in Sweden, who worked for Judson's company, the Universal Fastener Company. In 1913, he developed what he called the "hookless fastener". Instead of hooks, it used rows of small metal teeth, which he increased from four per inch to ten per inch, making the fastener far more secure. Sundback also designed a machine that could produce his fastener cheaply and in large quantities.

At first, the new fastener was used mainly for money belts and tobacco pouches. Its real breakthrough came in 1923, when the B.F. Goodrich Company used it on a new range of rubber boots. The company named the boots "Zippers", after the sound the fastener made when it was opened and closed, and the name soon came to be used for the fastener itself.

It was still some time before zips appeared widely on clothing. In the 1930s, they were promoted for children's clothes, because they allowed young children to dress themselves. Fashion designers in Paris then began to use them in men's trousers, and by the end of the decade the zip had largely replaced buttons in many types of garment. Today, the largest manufacturer is the Japanese company YKK, which produces around half of all the zips in the world.

lesson.title: Scanning for names and numbers
lesson.text: In easy short-answer sets, most answers are names, places, dates and numbers, which are easy to spot because they begin with capital letters or are written as figures. Scan for these first, then read the surrounding sentence to check that it matches the question. Remember that there are usually several names and numbers in the passage, and only one fits each question.
lesson.example: Question: "In which city was the first store opened?" Passage: "Founded in Boston, the company opened its first store in Chicago." Answer: Chicago.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: At which event did Whitcomb Judson first show his invention?
questions.evidence: who presented it at the Chicago World's Fair in 1893.
questions.explanation: "Show" = "presented". The answer is three words, within the limit. The date 1893 is not an event.

questions.text: What type of footwear was the clasp locker designed for?
questions.evidence: designed it to fasten high boots.
questions.explanation: The rubber boots of 1923 were a later product by B.F. Goodrich, not the purpose of the clasp locker.

questions.text: In which country was Gideon Sundback born?
questions.evidence: Gideon Sundback, an engineer born in Sweden.
questions.explanation: He worked for an American company, but he was born in Sweden.

questions.text: How many teeth per inch did Sundback's improved fastener have?
questions.evidence: which he increased from four per inch to ten per inch.
questions.explanation: "Four" was the number before his improvement.

questions.text: What gave the zipper its name?
questions.evidence: named the boots 'Zippers', after the sound the fastener made when it was opened and closed.
questions.explanation: The name came from the sound, not from the company or the boots.

questions.text: Which company makes about half of the world's zips today?
questions.evidence: the Japanese company YKK, which produces around half of all the zips in the world.
questions.explanation: "About" = "around". B.F. Goodrich and the Universal Fastener Company are earlier companies.

passages.topic: Wildlife — the kiwi of New Zealand
passages.title: A Most Unusual Bird

paragraphs.text: The kiwi, a national symbol of New Zealand, is one of the strangest birds in the world. About the size of a chicken, it cannot fly, has tiny wings hidden beneath its feathers, and has no tail. Its feathers are so fine and loose that they look more like hair. Scientists recognise five species, all found only in New Zealand.

The kiwi is the only bird in the world with nostrils at the tip of its long beak. Because it is active mainly at night and has poor eyesight, it relies on its excellent sense of smell to find food, pushing its beak into the soil to sniff out worms, insects and fallen fruit.

Kiwi are also famous for the size of their eggs. Compared with the size of the mother, the kiwi lays one of the largest eggs of any bird: a single egg can weigh 20 per cent of the female's body weight, the equivalent of a human mother giving birth to a four-year-old child. In most species, it is the male that incubates the egg, sitting on it for up to twelve hours a day. The eggs take around 80 days to hatch, one of the longest periods for any bird, and the chicks leave the nest after about three weeks.

Before humans arrived, the kiwi had few enemies apart from birds of prey. However, the mammals introduced by European settlers, including cats, dogs, pigs and stoats, have had a disastrous effect. Stoats, which were brought to New Zealand in the 1880s in an attempt to control rabbits, kill more young kiwi than any other predator. Without protection, around 95 per cent of kiwi chicks die before they are old enough to breed.

Today there are thought to be around 70,000 kiwi left. To protect them, conservation groups collect eggs from the wild and hatch them in safety, a programme known as Operation Nest Egg. The young birds are returned to the wild once they weigh about one kilogram, when they are large enough to defend themselves against stoats.

lesson.title: Questions that paraphrase the passage
lesson.text: The question rarely repeats the passage word for word. "Sits on the eggs" may appear in the passage as "incubates"; "hatch" may appear as "the chicks emerge". Before you scan, think of other ways of saying the key words in the question, and look for their meaning, not just their form.
lesson.example: Question: "Who looks after the young?" Passage: "The chicks are cared for by both parents." Answer: both parents.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: Which sense does the kiwi mainly use to find food?
questions.evidence: it relies on its excellent sense of smell to find food.
questions.explanation: "Mainly uses" = "relies on". The kiwi has poor eyesight, so "sight" is wrong.

questions.text: What proportion of the female's body weight can a single egg weigh?
questions.evidence: a single egg can weigh 20 per cent of the female's body weight.
questions.explanation: "Proportion" is a paraphrase for a percentage. The number is followed by "per cent", which counts as part of the number.

questions.text: In most species, which parent sits on the egg?
questions.evidence: In most species, it is the male that incubates the egg.
questions.explanation: "Sits on" = "incubates".

questions.text: How long does it take kiwi eggs to hatch?
questions.evidence: The eggs take around 80 days to hatch.
questions.explanation: "Three weeks" is the time before the chicks leave the nest.

questions.text: Which introduced animal kills the most young kiwi?
questions.evidence: Stoats ... kill more young kiwi than any other predator.
questions.explanation: Cats, dogs and pigs were also introduced, but stoats kill the most.

questions.text: What is the name of the programme that hatches kiwi eggs in safety?
questions.evidence: conservation groups collect eggs from the wild and hatch them in safety, a programme known as Operation Nest Egg.
questions.explanation: The name is exactly three words, within the limit, and must be copied exactly.

passages.topic: History of flight — the first hot-air balloons
passages.title: Into the Sky

paragraphs.text: On a June day in 1783, a crowd in the small French town of Annonay watched in amazement as a huge cloth and paper bag rose into the sky and drifted for more than two kilometres before coming down in a field. It was the first public demonstration of a hot-air balloon, and it had been built by two brothers, Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier, whose family owned a successful paper business.

The brothers had noticed that paper bags held over a fire rose into the air. They believed, wrongly, that the smoke contained a special gas that made the balloon lift, and so they deliberately produced as much smoke as possible, burning a mixture of wool and straw. In fact, it is simply hot air, which is lighter than the cooler air around it, that makes a balloon rise.

News of the flight quickly reached Paris, and in September 1783 the brothers were invited to demonstrate their balloon at the royal palace of Versailles in front of King Louis XVI. Because no one knew whether living creatures could survive at a height, the balloon carried three animals: a sheep, a duck and a rooster. The flight lasted about eight minutes, and all three landed safely.

Two months later, on 21 November 1783, the first free flight carrying people took place in Paris. The passengers were a young scientist, Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier, and an army officer, the Marquis d'Arlandes. Their balloon rose to about 900 metres and flew for around 25 minutes, covering nine kilometres across the city. During the flight, they had to keep feeding the fire and put out several small fires in the balloon itself.

Only ten days later, the scientist Jacques Charles flew in a different type of balloon, filled with hydrogen, a gas lighter than air. For the next century, most balloons followed his design. Hot-air ballooning became popular again only in the 1960s, when modern balloons were developed with envelopes made of nylon and burners that use propane gas.

lesson.title: ONE WORD answers
lesson.text: When the limit is ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER, you must choose the single most important word. If the passage says "they burned straw and wool" and the question asks for one thing, read the question again: it may exclude one of them ("apart from wool"). Never write two words joined by "and".
lesson.example: Question: "Besides milk, what is added to the mixture?" Passage: "Milk and sugar are added." Answer: sugar.

Answer the questions below.
Choose ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: What did the Montgolfier family's business produce?
questions.evidence: whose family owned a successful paper business.
questions.explanation: The question asks what the business produced; the answer is the product.

questions.evidence: burning a mixture of wool and straw.
questions.explanation: "Apart from wool" excludes the first item.

questions.text: How many animals were carried in the balloon at Versailles?
questions.evidence: the balloon carried three animals: a sheep, a duck and a rooster.
questions.explanation: "Eight" is the number of minutes the flight lasted.

questions.evidence: flew for around 25 minutes.
questions.explanation: "Minutes" is in the question, so only the number is needed. "Eight minutes" was the flight with animals.

questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: What material are the envelopes of modern hot-air balloons made of?
