passages.topic: Environment — mangrove forests
passages.title: Forests Between Land and Sea

paragraphs.text: Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow along tropical and subtropical coastlines, in the zone between high and low tide. They are found in around 120 countries and cover about 150,000 square kilometres, an area roughly the size of Bangladesh. The largest single mangrove forest in the world is the Sundarbans, which stretches across the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers in Bangladesh and India, and is home to the Bengal tiger.

Few trees could survive in such conditions. The soil is waterlogged, contains very little oxygen, and is flooded twice a day by salt water. Mangroves have adapted in remarkable ways. Some species have prop roots, which arch out from the trunk and hold the tree steady in the soft mud. Others have breathing roots, known as pneumatophores, which stick up out of the mud like pencils and take in air at low tide. Mangroves also deal with salt in different ways: some filter it out at their roots, while others release it through their leaves.

Mangrove forests are extremely valuable. Their tangled roots provide shelter for young fish, crabs and shrimps, and many species that are caught in the open sea spend the early part of their lives there. The roots also trap mud and protect coasts from erosion, and studies after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami found that villages behind dense mangroves generally suffered less damage than those without them. In addition, mangroves store huge amounts of carbon in their soil, up to four times as much as the same area of tropical rainforest.

Despite these benefits, around a third of the world's mangroves have been lost over the past fifty years. The main cause has been the clearing of forests to make space for shrimp farms, although coastal development, rice fields and the collection of wood for fuel have also played a part. Many countries are now replanting mangroves, but success depends on choosing the right species and places, and on the involvement of local communities.

lesson.title: Questions about names and terms
lesson.text: Some questions ask for the name of something that the passage describes: "What are the roots that stick out of the mud called?" The passage will usually give the description and the name in the same sentence, linked by words such as "known as", "called" or a comma. The answer is the name, not the description.
lesson.example: Question: "What is the name of the bird's nest?" Passage: "The bird builds a mound of leaves, known as a scrape." Answer: (a) scrape.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: In roughly how many countries are mangroves found?
questions.evidence: They are found in around 120 countries.
questions.explanation: "Roughly" = "around". 150,000 is the area in square kilometres.

questions.text: Which large animal lives in the Sundarbans?
questions.evidence: the Sundarbans ... is home to the Bengal tiger.
questions.explanation: "Lives in" = "is home to".

questions.text: What is the scientific name for the roots that stick up out of the mud?
questions.evidence: breathing roots, known as pneumatophores, which stick up out of the mud like pencils.
questions.explanation: "Breathing roots" is the ordinary name; the question asks for the scientific name. Prop roots arch out from the trunk.

questions.text: Through which part do some mangroves get rid of salt?
questions.evidence: others release it through their leaves.
questions.explanation: "Get rid of" = "release". Some mangroves filter salt at the roots, but that is not getting rid of it through a part.

questions.text: How much more carbon can mangroves store than tropical rainforest?
questions.evidence: up to four times as much as the same area of tropical rainforest.
questions.explanation: The answer must include "times" to show the comparison.

questions.text: What has been the main reason for the loss of mangroves?
questions.evidence: The main cause has been the clearing of forests to make space for shrimp farms.
questions.explanation: "Main reason" = "main cause". Coastal development, rice fields and wood collection have "also played a part", so they are not the main reason.

passages.topic: Food science — why onions make us cry
passages.title: Tears in the Kitchen

paragraphs.text: Chopping an onion is one of the few everyday activities that reliably makes people cry. For centuries, cooks have offered advice on how to avoid it, from holding a piece of bread in the mouth to wearing swimming goggles. Only in recent decades, however, have scientists fully understood what is happening.

An onion stores chemicals known as sulphur compounds, which are kept separate from certain enzymes inside its cells. When a knife cuts through the onion, it damages the cells, and the two come into contact. A chemical reaction begins, and the sulphur compounds are converted into a new substance. In 2002, Japanese scientists discovered that a second enzyme then turns this substance into an irritating gas.

The gas rises from the chopping board and reaches the eyes, where it stimulates nerves that make the eyes produce tears to wash it away. The amount of gas released reaches its peak about 30 seconds after the onion has been cut, and then gradually decreases over the next few minutes.

For the onion, the reaction is a form of defence. In the wild, the unpleasant gas and the strong taste that develop when an onion is damaged discourage hungry animals from eating it. It is this same chemistry, ironically, that gives cooked onions much of their flavour.

Several simple methods can reduce the problem. Because the gas is released more slowly at low temperatures, keeping the onion in the fridge for half an hour before cutting it is often effective. A sharp knife helps too, since it crushes fewer cells than a blunt one. Cooks are also advised to cut the root end last, because it contains the highest concentration of the sulphur compounds.

Plant breeders have gone further. In 2015, a Japanese food company began selling onions that produce almost none of the irritating gas, and similar "tearless" varieties have since been developed in other countries. Some cooks, however, complain that these onions also have less flavour.

lesson.title: "Where", "how soon" and "which part"
lesson.text: Question words such as "where", "how soon" and "which part" ask for different kinds of information from "what". "Where" may need a place in a house, not a country; "how soon" needs a length of time; "which part" needs a part of an object. Match the answer type to the question word before you write anything.
lesson.example: Question: "Where should the medicine be stored?" Passage: "Keep the medicine in a cool cupboard for up to a year." Answer: (in) a cool cupboard.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: What does a knife damage when it cuts through an onion?
questions.evidence: When a knife cuts through the onion, it damages the cells.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: What type of chemicals does an onion store?
questions.evidence: An onion stores chemicals known as sulphur compounds.
questions.explanation: The enzymes are also inside the cells, but the question asks what the onion stores as chemicals.

questions.text: In which year was the second enzyme discovered?
questions.evidence: In 2002, Japanese scientists discovered that a second enzyme then turns this substance into an irritating gas.
questions.explanation: 2015 is the year tearless onions went on sale.

questions.text: How soon after cutting is the most gas released?
questions.evidence: The amount of gas released reaches its peak about 30 seconds after the onion has been cut.
questions.explanation: "The most gas" = "reaches its peak".

questions.text: What does the reaction discourage from eating onions?
questions.evidence: discourage hungry animals from eating it.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: Where should an onion be kept before it is cut?
questions.evidence: keeping the onion in the fridge for half an hour before cutting it is often effective.
questions.explanation: "Where" needs a place. "Half an hour" answers "how long", not "where".

questions.text: Which part of the onion should be cut last?
questions.evidence: Cooks are also advised to cut the root end last.
questions.explanation: "Which part" needs a part of the onion.

passages.topic: Animal intelligence — the octopus
passages.title: Clever Cephalopods

paragraphs.text: The octopus is one of the most intelligent animals without a backbone, and in some tests it performs as well as many mammals. Octopuses can open screw-top jars, find their way through mazes, and recognise individual human faces. What makes them so fascinating to scientists is that their intelligence evolved completely separately from ours: our last common ancestor was a simple worm-like creature that lived more than 500 million years ago.

An octopus has around 500 million neurons, or nerve cells, roughly as many as a dog. Remarkably, however, only about a third of them are in its brain. The remaining two-thirds are located in its eight arms, which can taste, touch and even make simple decisions without instructions from the brain. An arm that has been separated from the body can still react to food for some time.

The octopus differs from us in other ways, too. It has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, and the third pumps it around the rest of the body. Its blood is blue, because it uses a protein based on copper, rather than iron, to carry oxygen. Its skin contains thousands of cells called chromatophores, filled with coloured pigments, which allow it to change colour in a fraction of a second, either to hide from predators or to communicate.

Stories of octopus behaviour in captivity are legendary. Octopuses are known for escaping from their tanks, squeezing through tiny gaps, since they have no bones. At an aquarium in Germany in 2008, an octopus named Otto repeatedly caused the electricity supply to fail at night. Staff eventually discovered that he was climbing to the edge of his tank and squirting water at a bright lamp that he apparently disliked.

In the wild, octopuses have been observed using tools, a behaviour once thought to be limited to humans and a few other animals. In Indonesia, researchers filmed veined octopuses carrying coconut shells across the sea floor and later assembling them into a shelter. Despite their intelligence, most octopuses have short lives, living only one to two years, and females usually die soon after their eggs hatch.

lesson.title: Questions with "how many" and "what proportion"
lesson.text: "How many" needs a number; "what proportion" or "what fraction" needs a part of a whole, such as "two-thirds" or "40 per cent". When the passage contains several numbers close together, read each one with the noun that follows it ("500 million neurons", "three hearts") and choose the one that matches the noun in the question.
lesson.example: Question: "What fraction of the students passed?" Passage: "Of the 300 students, three-quarters passed." Answer: three-quarters.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: How many neurons does an octopus have?
questions.evidence: An octopus has around 500 million neurons.
questions.explanation: "500 million years" in Paragraph A refers to time, not neurons.

questions.text: What proportion of its neurons are in its arms?
questions.evidence: only about a third of them are in its brain. The remaining two-thirds are located in its eight arms.
questions.explanation: "A third" is the proportion in the brain.

questions.text: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.evidence: It has three hearts.
questions.explanation: "Eight" is the number of arms.

questions.text: Which metal does the protein in octopus blood contain?
questions.evidence: it uses a protein based on copper, rather than iron, to carry oxygen.
questions.explanation: "Rather than iron" means iron is not used.

questions.text: What are the colour-changing cells in octopus skin called?
questions.evidence: thousands of cells called chromatophores ... which allow it to change colour.
questions.explanation: The question asks for the name of the cells.

questions.text: What did Otto squirt at the lamp?
questions.evidence: squirting water at a bright lamp that he apparently disliked.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: What objects do veined octopuses use to make a shelter?
questions.evidence: veined octopuses carrying coconut shells across the sea floor and later assembling them into a shelter.
questions.explanation: "Make" = "assembling ... into".

passages.topic: Industry and environment — harvesting cork
passages.title: The Bark That Grows Back

paragraphs.text: Cork is one of the few products that can be taken from a tree without cutting it down. It comes from the thick outer bark of the cork oak, a tree that grows in the western Mediterranean. Portugal alone produces about half of the world's cork, and Spain most of the rest, with smaller amounts coming from Morocco, Algeria, Italy and France.

A cork oak cannot be stripped until it is around 25 years old. The first harvest produces what is known as virgin cork, which is rough and uneven and is used mainly for flooring and insulation rather than for high-quality products. After that, the bark is harvested every nine years, when it has grown back to a sufficient thickness. Only from the third harvest, when the tree is over forty years old, is the cork of good enough quality for the most valuable product: stoppers for wine bottles. Since a cork oak can live for more than 200 years, a single tree may be harvested around fifteen times.

The harvest takes place in early summer, when the tree is actively growing and the bark separates most easily from the trunk. It is done entirely by hand, by skilled workers using axes. They must cut deep enough to loosen the bark but not so deep that they damage the living layer underneath, which would prevent it from growing back. After stripping, each tree is painted with a number showing the year of the harvest, so that the next one can be planned.

Although wine stoppers make up only a small proportion of the cork produced by weight, they account for around two thirds of the industry's income. In the 1990s, this market came under threat. A chemical contamination known as cork taint was spoiling a significant number of bottles of wine, giving them a musty smell, and many producers switched to plastic stoppers and screw caps. The cork industry responded by investing heavily in new methods of detecting and removing the contamination, and it has since recovered much of its lost market.

Supporters argue that buying cork helps the environment. Because the trees are not cut down, cork forests remain standing for centuries, and they store large amounts of carbon. The forests of southern Portugal and Spain also support a rich variety of wildlife, including one of the world's most endangered cats, the Iberian lynx. If demand for cork fell, landowners might replace the forests with more profitable crops.

lesson.title: "First", "after that" and other limiting words
lesson.text: Medium questions often contain words that limit the answer to one stage or one case: "first", "after that", "the most", "mainly". The passage will usually give information for several stages or cases, and each is a possible distractor. Underline the limiting word in the question and find the sentence where the passage uses the same idea.
lesson.example: Question: "How often is the hedge cut after its first year?" Passage: "The hedge is cut hard in its first year and then trimmed every six months." Answer: every six months.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: Which country produces around half of the world's cork?
questions.evidence: Portugal alone produces about half of the world's cork.
questions.explanation: Spain produces "most of the rest", not half.

questions.text: At about what age is a cork oak stripped for the first time?
questions.evidence: A cork oak cannot be stripped until it is around 25 years old.
questions.explanation: "Forty years" is the age when stopper-quality cork is produced, not the first stripping.

questions.text: What name is given to the cork from the first harvest?
questions.evidence: The first harvest produces what is known as virgin cork.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: After the first harvest, how often is the bark removed?
questions.evidence: After that, the bark is harvested every nine years.
questions.explanation: "After the first harvest" matches "After that". Do not confuse this with the number of harvests in a tree's life (about fifteen).

questions.text: What tools are used to remove the bark?
questions.evidence: It is done entirely by hand, by skilled workers using axes.
questions.explanation: "By hand" describes the method; "axes" are the tools.

questions.text: What problem caused many wine producers to stop using cork?
questions.evidence: A chemical contamination known as cork taint was spoiling a significant number of bottles ... and many producers switched to plastic stoppers and screw caps.
questions.explanation: "Stop using cork" = "switched to plastic stoppers and screw caps".

questions.text: Which endangered animal lives in the cork forests?
questions.evidence: one of the world's most endangered cats, the Iberian lynx.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match; "cats" alone is too general.

passages.topic: Marine biology — living light in the ocean
passages.title: Lights in the Deep

paragraphs.text: Bioluminescence, the production of light by living things, is rare on land, where it is best known in fireflies and a few fungi. In the ocean, however, it is extremely common. A study of animals filmed off the coast of California found that 76 per cent of the species observed between the surface and a depth of four kilometres could produce their own light. In the deep sea, where sunlight never reaches, bioluminescence is the main source of light.

The light is produced by a chemical reaction. A light-emitting molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, with the help of an enzyme called luciferase, and energy is released in the form of light rather than heat. Some animals produce these chemicals themselves; others, such as many fish, rely on bacteria living inside special organs to produce the light for them.

Deep-sea animals use their light in many ways. The anglerfish has a long spine on its head that ends in a glowing lure, lit by bacteria, which attracts smaller fish close enough to be eaten. Some jellyfish use light as a "burglar alarm": when attacked, they flash brightly, attracting larger predators that may attack their attacker.

Perhaps the most ingenious use is camouflage. In the upper part of the ocean, where some light still penetrates from above, an animal swimming overhead appears as a dark shape to a predator below. Many fish, squid and shrimps have light-producing organs on their undersides, which they use to match the brightness of the light coming from the surface, so that their silhouettes disappear. This technique is known as counterillumination.

Most marine bioluminescence is blue, because blue light travels furthest in sea water, while red light is absorbed quickly. As a result, most deep-sea animals cannot see red light at all. One fish, the dragonfish, takes advantage of this: it produces red light, which it uses like a hidden torch to find prey that cannot see it.

On land, the purpose of bioluminescence is often different. Fireflies use their flashes mainly for courtship, each species having its own pattern that allows males and females to find each other. In the sea, the light is sometimes visible to people on shore, when waves breaking at night glow blue. This is caused by dinoflagellates, tiny single-celled organisms that light up when the water around them is disturbed.

lesson.title: Questions about purpose and cause
lesson.text: Questions such as "Why ...?", "For what purpose ...?" and "What causes ...?" ask for a reason. Short-answer reasons are usually a noun or a short phrase, such as "courtship" or "to attract prey". Look for words such as "to", "in order to", "because", "used for" and "the result of" in the passage.
lesson.example: Question: "For what purpose do the birds sing at dawn?" Passage: "Males sing at dawn to defend their territory." Answer: (to defend their) territory.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: What percentage of the species observed in the California study could produce light?
questions.evidence: 76 per cent of the species observed between the surface and a depth of four kilometres could produce their own light.
questions.explanation: "Four kilometres" is the depth, not a percentage.

questions.text: What is the name of the enzyme involved in producing the light?
questions.evidence: with the help of an enzyme called luciferase.
questions.explanation: Luciferin is the light-emitting molecule, not the enzyme; the two words look similar, so check carefully.

questions.text: What provides the light in the anglerfish's lure?
questions.evidence: a glowing lure, lit by bacteria.
questions.explanation: "Provides the light" = "lit by".

questions.text: What is the name of the technique used by animals to hide their silhouettes?
questions.evidence: they use to match the brightness of the light coming from the surface, so that their silhouettes disappear. This technique is known as counterillumination.
questions.explanation: "Hide" = "disappear". "Camouflage" is the general purpose; the question asks for the name of the technique.

questions.text: Which colour of light is quickly absorbed by sea water?
questions.evidence: blue light travels furthest in sea water, while red light is absorbed quickly.
questions.explanation: Blue is the colour that travels furthest, the opposite of the question.

questions.text: For what purpose do fireflies mainly use their flashes?
questions.evidence: Fireflies use their flashes mainly for courtship.
questions.explanation: "Purpose" is answered by "for courtship".

questions.text: What causes breaking waves to glow at night?
questions.evidence: waves breaking at night glow blue. This is caused by dinoflagellates.
questions.explanation: "Causes" = "is caused by".

passages.topic: Environmental history — the Dust Bowl
passages.title: When the Sky Turned Black

paragraphs.text: In the 1930s, a vast area of the southern Great Plains of the United States, covering parts of Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Colorado and New Mexico, suffered one of the worst environmental disasters in American history. For almost a decade, huge dust storms swept across the region, burying farms, killing livestock and forcing hundreds of thousands of people to leave their homes. The area became known as the Dust Bowl.

The disaster had its roots in the decades before. For thousands of years, the plains had been covered by deep-rooted prairie grasses, which held the soil in place through droughts and strong winds. From the late nineteenth century onwards, settlers ploughed up millions of hectares of this grassland. During the First World War, wheat prices rose sharply, and farmers, many using new petrol-powered tractors, ploughed even more land to grow wheat. When prices fell after the war, they ploughed still more in an attempt to maintain their incomes.

In 1931, a severe drought began. The crops failed, and without the grass to protect it, the dry topsoil was simply blown away. The storms reached their peak on 14 April 1935, a day that became known as Black Sunday, when a single storm carried an estimated 300,000 tonnes of dust across the plains, turning day into night. Dust from some storms travelled as far as Washington and New York, and ships in the Atlantic Ocean found it settling on their decks.

The human cost was enormous. Around 2.5 million people left the Plains states during the 1930s. Many travelled west to California, where they hoped to find work on farms, but often found only poorly paid seasonal labour. Their experiences were later described in John Steinbeck's novel The Grapes of Wrath, published in 1939.

The federal government responded with a series of measures. In 1935, it created the Soil Conservation Service, led by the scientist Hugh Bennett, which taught farmers methods such as contour ploughing, in which fields are ploughed along the natural curves of the land rather than in straight lines, and crop rotation. Farmers were paid to leave some land unploughed or to replant it with grass. The government also launched the Shelterbelt Project, planting around 220 million trees in long lines across the plains to break the force of the wind.

When the rains returned at the end of the decade, the storms ended. The lessons of the Dust Bowl, however, remain relevant, as scientists warn that climate change may bring similar droughts to many of the world's farming regions.

lesson.title: Names of events, organisations and places
lesson.text: History passages contain many proper nouns: names of events ("Black Sunday"), organisations ("the Soil Conservation Service") and places. Questions may describe these rather than name them ("the government agency set up in 1935"). Match the description in the question to the details in the passage, such as the date or purpose, and copy the name exactly, including capital letters.
lesson.example: Question: "What was the name of the treaty signed in 1648?" Passage: "The Peace of Westphalia, signed in 1648, ended the war." Answer: (the) Peace of Westphalia.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: What had held the soil of the plains in place before settlers arrived?
questions.evidence: the plains had been covered by deep-rooted prairie grasses, which held the soil in place.
questions.explanation: The hyphenated "deep-rooted" counts as one word, so the full phrase is within the limit.

questions.text: Which crop did farmers plant on more land during the First World War?
questions.evidence: During the First World War, wheat prices rose sharply, and farmers ... ploughed even more land to grow wheat.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: What name was given to the day of the worst dust storm?
questions.evidence: The storms reached their peak on 14 April 1935, a day that became known as Black Sunday.
questions.explanation: "Worst" = "reached their peak". The question asks for the name, not the date.

questions.text: About how many people left the Plains states during the 1930s?
questions.evidence: Around 2.5 million people left the Plains states during the 1930s.
questions.explanation: "300,000 tonnes" refers to dust.

questions.text: Which state did many of these people travel to?
questions.evidence: Many travelled west to California.
questions.explanation: Washington and New York are places the dust reached, not the people.

questions.text: Which organisation was set up in 1935 to teach farmers new methods?
questions.evidence: In 1935, it created the Soil Conservation Service ... which taught farmers methods such as contour ploughing.
questions.explanation: The Shelterbelt Project planted trees; it did not teach methods.

questions.text: Approximately how many trees were planted to reduce the effect of the wind?
questions.evidence: planting around 220 million trees in long lines across the plains to break the force of the wind.
questions.explanation: "Reduce the effect" = "break the force".

passages.topic: Water and technology — turning sea water into drinking water
passages.title: Drinking the Sea

paragraphs.text: Around 97 per cent of the water on Earth is salty, and much of the rest is locked in ice. As populations grow and droughts become more frequent, a growing number of countries are turning to the oceans for their drinking water. Today, around 300 million people around the world depend at least partly on desalination, the removal of salt from sea water, and there are more than 20,000 desalination plants in operation.

The oldest method is distillation, which imitates the natural water cycle: sea water is heated until it evaporates, and the vapour is then cooled and condensed as fresh water, leaving the salt behind. Because it requires large amounts of heat, thermal distillation is still common in the countries of the Persian Gulf, where energy from oil and gas has been cheap, but it has been replaced elsewhere by a more efficient technology.

This technology, now the most widely used in the world, is reverse osmosis. Sea water is pumped at very high pressure through membranes, thin sheets of plastic material with holes so small that water molecules can pass through but salt cannot. Improvements in these membranes, and in devices that recover energy from the high-pressure water, have reduced the energy required by more than half since the 1980s.

Desalination nevertheless has serious drawbacks. It remains more expensive than most other sources of fresh water, and it still uses large amounts of energy, most of which comes from fossil fuels. It also produces a by-product called brine, a highly concentrated salty liquid. For every litre of fresh water, around one and a half litres of brine are produced, and when it is returned to the sea, it can sink to the sea floor and harm marine life if it is not properly diluted.

Some countries have nevertheless become heavily dependent on the technology. In Israel, which has suffered repeated droughts, around 80 per cent of household water now comes from the sea. Its Sorek plant, when it opened in 2013, was the largest reverse osmosis plant in the world. Researchers are now working to reduce the environmental impact of desalination, for example by powering plants with solar power and by finding uses for the minerals in brine, such as magnesium and lithium.

lesson.title: Technical processes and their terms
lesson.text: When a passage explains a technology, it often names the method and then describes how it works. Questions may ask for the method, the equipment, the material or the by-product. Identify which of these the question wants: "which method", "what does it pass through", "what is the waste called".
lesson.example: Question: "What is the waste from the process called?" Passage: "The process leaves a thick residue, known as slag." Answer: slag.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: About how many people rely on desalination for at least some of their water?
questions.evidence: around 300 million people around the world depend at least partly on desalination.
questions.explanation: "Rely on" = "depend on". "20,000" is the number of plants.

questions.text: In which region is thermal distillation still common?
questions.evidence: thermal distillation is still common in the countries of the Persian Gulf.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: Which method is used most widely today?
questions.evidence: This technology, now the most widely used in the world, is reverse osmosis.
questions.explanation: Distillation is the oldest method, not the most widely used.

questions.text: Through what is the water pumped in this method?
questions.evidence: Sea water is pumped at very high pressure through membranes.
questions.explanation: "High pressure" describes how the water is pumped, not what it passes through.

questions.text: What is the salty by-product of desalination called?
questions.evidence: a by-product called brine, a highly concentrated salty liquid.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: What percentage of household water in Israel comes from the sea?
questions.evidence: In Israel ... around 80 per cent of household water now comes from the sea.
questions.explanation: "97 per cent" is the proportion of the Earth's water that is salty.

questions.text: Which renewable energy source is being used to power some plants?
questions.evidence: by powering plants with solar power.
questions.explanation: Oil and gas are fossil fuels, not renewable sources.

passages.topic: Technology history — the invention of the barcode
passages.title: Lines That Changed Shopping

paragraphs.text: Every day, billions of barcodes are scanned in shops, warehouses, hospitals and airports. Yet the idea took more than twenty-five years to become a practical reality, and it depended on technologies that did not exist when it was first imagined.

The story begins in 1948, when Bernard Silver, a graduate student at Drexel Institute of Technology in Philadelphia, overheard a supermarket executive asking one of the university's deans for a system that could automatically record product information at the checkout. Silver mentioned the problem to his friend Norman Joseph Woodland, and the two began to work on it.

Woodland found his inspiration while sitting on a beach in Miami. He had learned Morse code as a Boy Scout, and he began to think about how its dots and dashes might be turned into a visual code. Pushing his fingers into the sand, he drew them downwards into lines, some thick and some thin. To make the code readable from any direction, the two men later formed the lines into a circular design, like a target, and they received a patent for it in 1952.

Their invention, however, was far ahead of its time. Reading the code required a bright, precise light source and a computer to interpret the signal, and the equipment available was large, expensive and unreliable. The technology only became practical after the development of the laser, and of small, cheap computers, in the 1960s and early 1970s.

In 1973, the American grocery industry chose a standard code for all products, known as the Universal Product Code, or UPC. The design selected was a rectangular pattern of vertical lines created by George Laurer, an engineer at IBM, who had worked with Woodland. On 26 June 1974, at a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a shop assistant scanned the first product with a UPC barcode: a packet of chewing gum. The packet is now kept at a museum in Washington.

Barcodes have continued to develop. In 1994, a Japanese company, Denso Wave, invented the QR code, a square pattern that can store far more information than a traditional barcode. It was originally designed to track car parts during manufacturing, but it has since found countless other uses, from payments to restaurant menus.

lesson.title: "Who" questions with several people
lesson.text: When a passage mentions several people, each question describes a particular role: the person who had the idea, who designed a later version, who used it first. Read the whole question and match the role, not just the name that appears nearest to the key words. If the limit allows, write the full name as it appears.
lesson.example: Question: "Who built the first working model?" Passage: "Brown proposed the design, but it was his assistant, Clark, who built the first model." Answer: Clark.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: Who first heard about the need for an automatic checkout system?
questions.evidence: Bernard Silver ... overheard a supermarket executive asking one of the university's deans for a system that could automatically record product information at the checkout.
questions.explanation: "First heard" = "overheard". Woodland heard about it later from Silver.

questions.text: Which system of communication gave Woodland the idea for the barcode?
questions.evidence: He had learned Morse code as a Boy Scout, and he began to think about how its dots and dashes might be turned into a visual code.
questions.explanation: The beach is where he had the idea, not the system that inspired it.

questions.text: What shape did Silver and Woodland give their design to make it readable from any direction?
questions.evidence: To make the code readable from any direction, the two men later formed the lines into a circular design, like a target.
questions.explanation: The UPC pattern was rectangular, but that was Laurer's later design.

questions.text: Apart from small computers, what invention made the barcode practical?
questions.evidence: The technology only became practical after the development of the laser, and of small, cheap computers.
questions.explanation: "Apart from small computers" excludes the second item.

questions.text: Who designed the rectangular pattern used for the UPC?
questions.evidence: The design selected was a rectangular pattern of vertical lines created by George Laurer, an engineer at IBM.
questions.explanation: Woodland worked with Laurer, but Laurer created the UPC design.

questions.text: What was the first product to be scanned with a UPC barcode?
questions.evidence: a shop assistant scanned the first product with a UPC barcode: a packet of chewing gum.
questions.explanation: "A packet of chewing gum" is five words, so write only "chewing gum".

questions.text: What was the QR code originally designed to track?
questions.evidence: It was originally designed to track car parts during manufacturing.
questions.explanation: Payments and menus are later uses.

passages.topic: Wildlife — the migration of the monarch butterfly
passages.title: The Butterflies' Journey

paragraphs.text: Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies leave southern Canada and the northern United States and fly south, some travelling as far as 4,500 kilometres. Their destination is a small area of mountains in central Mexico, where they spend the winter packed together in their millions on the branches of oyamel fir trees. So many cluster on a single tree that the branches sometimes bend under their weight.

For a long time, the location of these winter sites was a mystery to scientists. The Canadian zoologist Fred Urquhart spent almost forty years tagging butterflies in an attempt to follow them, relying on thousands of volunteers across North America to report tagged insects. Finally, in 1975, two of his volunteers, working in Mexico, found the mountain forests where the monarchs gathered.

The most remarkable feature of the migration is that no single butterfly makes the whole round trip. In spring, the butterflies that spent the winter in Mexico fly north and lay their eggs, and then die. Over the summer, three or four more generations are born, each living only a few weeks, and each moving further north. The last generation of the summer, however, is different. Its members do not breed immediately, and they live for up to eight months, long enough to fly all the way to Mexico and back to the southern United States the following spring. Somehow, they find their way to forests that they have never seen.

Scientists have discovered that monarchs navigate using the sun. Because the sun's position changes during the day, they correct their direction using an internal clock located in their antennae. On cloudy days, they appear to use the Earth's magnetic field instead.

Monarch caterpillars feed on only one type of plant: milkweed. The plant contains toxic chemicals, which the caterpillars store in their bodies. They remain in the adult butterflies, making them poisonous to birds, and the monarch's bright orange colouring warns predators to leave them alone.

In recent decades, the number of monarchs spending the winter in Mexico has fallen sharply. The main reason is thought to be the loss of milkweed across the American Midwest, where it has been destroyed by herbicides used on farmland. Logging in Mexico and extreme weather have also contributed. Conservation groups now encourage people to plant milkweed in gardens along the migration route.

lesson.title: Answers that are spread over two sentences
lesson.text: Sometimes the key words of the question are in one sentence, and the answer is in the next, linked by a pronoun such as "it", "they" or "this". When you find the key words, read the sentence before and after them as well, and work out what the pronouns refer to.
lesson.example: Question: "What do the young birds eat?" Passage: "The young birds stay in the nest for a month. During this time, they feed only on insects." Answer: insects.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: Up to how far do some monarchs travel on their journey south?
questions.evidence: some travelling as far as 4,500 kilometres.
questions.explanation: "Up to" = "as far as". The unit must be included.

questions.text: On which type of tree do the butterflies spend the winter?
questions.evidence: on the branches of oyamel fir trees.
questions.explanation: "Trees" is in the question as "type of tree", so "oyamel fir" is enough.

questions.text: In which year were the winter sites discovered?

questions.explanation: "Its" refers to the last generation. The other generations live "only a few weeks".

questions.text: Where is the butterflies' internal clock located?

passages.topic: History of science — the colours of the past and the first synthetic dye
passages.title: The Colour That Built an Industry

paragraphs.text: For most of human history, bright colours were expensive. Dyes came from plants, insects and animals, and many were extremely difficult to produce. The most famous was Tyrian purple, made in the ancient Mediterranean from sea snails. The snails' glands produced tiny amounts of the dye, and more than 10,000 snails were needed to make a single gram. As a result, purple cloth became a symbol of power, and in the Roman Empire it was at times reserved for the emperor alone.

Other dyes also had a high value. Indigo, a deep blue dye obtained from plants grown in India, was traded across the world, and in the sixteenth century the Spanish brought back from Mexico a brilliant red dye made from cochineal, small insects that live on cactus plants. For a time, cochineal was one of the most valuable goods exported from the Americas, second only to silver.

This situation changed almost by accident. In 1856, an eighteen-year-old chemistry student in London, William Perkin, was attempting to make quinine, the only effective treatment for malaria at the time, which was then obtained from the bark of a South American tree. Working in a home laboratory during his Easter holiday, he experimented with chemicals obtained from coal tar, a waste product of the gas used to light cities. The experiment failed, but it left a black substance which, when dissolved in alcohol, produced a strong purple colour.

Perkin realised that he had found something valuable. He named his dye mauveine, patented it, and with the help of his father built a factory to produce it. Mauve became extremely fashionable, especially after Queen Victoria wore a mauve dress in 1862, and Perkin became wealthy while still a young man.

More importantly, his discovery showed that chemists could create entirely new substances from coal tar, and within a few decades hundreds of synthetic dyes had been developed. The industry was soon dominated by Germany, where companies invested heavily in research laboratories. The knowledge they gained led directly to other products, including photographic chemicals and some of the first synthetic medicines. The German scientist Paul Ehrlich, for example, used dyes to stain bacteria, work that eventually helped him develop one of the first drugs designed to kill a specific disease-causing organism.

lesson.title: Numbers written as words and as figures
lesson.text: Numbers may be written in the passage as figures (10,000) or as words (eighteen), and in the question in the other form. Both are correct in your answer if the meaning is the same. Watch for numbers that appear with "more than", "about" or "only": include them only if they are needed and fit within the word limit.
lesson.example: Question: "How old was the composer when he wrote his first symphony?" Passage: "He completed his first symphony at the age of eight." Answer: eight / 8.

passages.topic: Urban climate — why cities are hotter than the countryside
passages.title: Islands of Heat

paragraphs.text: On a calm summer night, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This effect, known as the urban heat island, was first recorded in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard, an amateur scientist best known for giving clouds the names we still use today. Comparing temperature readings from central London with those from the countryside, he found that the city was consistently warmer. On average, cities are one to three degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings over a year, but the difference is greatest at night, when it can reach twelve degrees.

Several factors combine to produce the effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and roofs absorb most of the sunlight that falls on them. The ability of a surface to reflect sunlight is called its albedo, and most urban materials have a low albedo, so they heat up during the day and release the stored heat slowly at night. Cities also have fewer trees and plants than the countryside. Plants cool the air around them by releasing water vapour through their leaves, a process called evapotranspiration, which works rather like sweating. In addition, cars, air conditioners and factories give off waste heat, and tall buildings trap warm air in narrow streets.

Urban heat islands are not merely uncomfortable. During heatwaves, they can be deadly, especially for elderly people and those living in poorly ventilated housing. The European heatwave of 2003 caused around 70,000 deaths, many of them in cities such as Paris, where temperatures remained high even at night, giving people no chance to recover. Higher temperatures also increase the demand for air conditioning, which uses more energy and releases more waste heat, making the problem worse.

Cities around the world are now trying to cool themselves. Some encourage "cool roofs", painted white or covered with reflective materials. Los Angeles has experimented with coating streets in a light grey material that reflects more sunlight than ordinary asphalt. Other cities are planting trees. In Medellín, Colombia, the city authorities created a network of green corridors along roads and waterways, and within a few years temperatures in these areas had fallen by around 2°C.

lesson.title: Questions that ask for a term
lesson.text: Some questions describe a scientific idea and ask for its name: "What term is used for ...?" The passage usually explains the idea in ordinary words and gives the term once, often in brackets, after "known as" or after a comma. Find the explanation that matches the question, then look nearby for the term.
lesson.example: Question: "What term describes the loss of soil by wind and water?" Passage: "Wind and water gradually remove the soil, a process known as erosion." Answer: erosion.

passages.topic: Health science — the gut microbiome
passages.title: The Hidden Organ

paragraphs.text: The human body is home to vast numbers of microorganisms, most of them living in the large intestine. For decades, textbooks stated that bacterial cells in the body outnumbered human cells by ten to one. In 2016, however, a group of researchers recalculated the figures and concluded that the true ratio was much closer to one to one: a typical adult contains around 38 trillion bacteria and around 30 trillion human cells. The bacteria in the gut, together with viruses and fungi, are known collectively as the gut microbiome, and some scientists now describe them as a "hidden organ" because of the many roles they play.

A healthy gut may contain several hundred species of bacteria, and although the most common groups are similar in most people, the exact mix of species varies greatly between individuals. It is shaped from the moment of birth. Babies born naturally acquire bacteria from their mothers during birth, while those born by caesarean section are first colonised by bacteria from the skin and from the hospital environment. Most studies suggest that these differences largely disappear during the first year of life, as diet and environment take over.

One of the microbiome's most important jobs is to digest dietary fibre, which the human body cannot break down by itself. Bacteria ferment the fibre and produce substances called short-chain fatty acids, which provide energy for the cells lining the gut and appear to reduce inflammation. Diets low in fibre, typical of many industrialised countries, may therefore reduce both the diversity of the microbiome and these benefits.

The microbiome can be seriously disrupted by antibiotics, which kill harmful and useful bacteria alike. In some patients, this allows a dangerous bacterium, Clostridioides difficile, to multiply, causing severe diarrhoea that is often resistant to further treatment. One remarkably effective remedy is a faecal transplant, in which gut bacteria from a healthy donor are transferred to the patient. In clinical trials, it has cured around 90 per cent of recurring infections, far more than antibiotics alone.

Research has also linked the microbiome with conditions ranging from obesity to depression, although most of this evidence comes from experiments on mice, and it is not yet clear whether changes in the microbiome cause these conditions or result from them. Studies of the Hadza, a hunter-gatherer people in Tanzania, have revealed a far more diverse microbiome than that of city dwellers, one that changes with the seasons as their diet shifts between meat and berries. Some researchers suggest that the modern microbiome has lost species that our ancestors carried for thousands of years.

lesson.title: Revised and outdated information
lesson.text: Hard passages about science often contrast an old belief with a new finding: "It was once thought that ...; however, recent research suggests ...". Questions may ask about either. Read the question carefully for words such as "earlier", "originally", "now" and "recent", and choose the information from the correct time.
lesson.example: Question: "How many planets were once thought to be in the solar system?" Passage: "Until 2006, Pluto was counted as the ninth planet; today there are officially eight." Answer: nine / 9.

passages.topic: Climate science — the thawing of permafrost
passages.title: The Ground Beneath the Arctic

paragraphs.text: Permafrost is ground that has remained frozen for at least two consecutive years, and in many places it has been frozen for tens of thousands of years. It underlies about a quarter of the land in the Northern Hemisphere, mainly in Siberia, northern Canada, Alaska and Greenland, and in places it extends to a depth of more than a kilometre. Above it lies the active layer, a shallow layer of soil that thaws each summer and refreezes in winter, and in which plants are able to grow.

The frozen ground contains enormous quantities of organic matter: the remains of plants and animals that died and were frozen before they could decompose. Scientists estimate that permafrost holds around 1,500 billion tonnes of carbon, roughly twice as much as is currently in the atmosphere. As the Arctic warms, nearly four times faster than the global average, the permafrost is beginning to thaw. When it does, microbes break down the organic matter and release carbon dioxide and methane, both greenhouse gases, which in turn cause further warming.

Thawing permafrost also changes the landscape itself. Where the ground contains large amounts of ice, it collapses as the ice melts, producing an uneven landscape of hollows, lakes and slumping hillsides known as thermokarst. One of the most dramatic examples is the Batagaika crater in Siberia, a huge depression more than a kilometre long that has been growing for decades, and which local people have called the "gateway to the underworld".

The consequences for people living in the Arctic are serious. Roads, pipelines and buildings constructed on permafrost can crack and collapse as the ground beneath them softens. In 2020, a fuel storage tank near the Russian city of Norilsk collapsed, releasing around 21,000 tonnes of diesel into rivers, in what was described as one of the worst environmental disasters in the Arctic's history; the company responsible blamed thawing permafrost for weakening the tank's supports.

There are also risks to health. In 2016, an outbreak of anthrax on the Yamal Peninsula in northern Russia killed a child and thousands of reindeer. Scientists believe that an unusually hot summer had thawed the frozen body of a reindeer that died of the disease decades earlier, releasing bacteria that were still able to infect other animals. Researchers have warned that other ancient microorganisms may also be released as the ground thaws, although the risk to humans is thought to be low.

lesson.title: Comparisons and quantities
lesson.text: Hard questions may ask for a comparison ("How much carbon does permafrost contain compared with the atmosphere?") rather than a simple number. The answer is often a phrase such as "twice as much" or "a quarter". Look for comparative language in the passage: "as much as", "times more", "compared with", "a fraction of".
lesson.example: Question: "How large is the lake compared with the old reservoir?" Passage: "The lake is three times the size of the old reservoir." Answer: three times (the size).

passages.topic: History of exploration — how Polynesians navigated the Pacific
passages.title: Wayfinders of the Pacific

paragraphs.text: Between about 3,000 and 700 years ago, the ancestors of today's Polynesians settled almost every habitable island in the Pacific Ocean, an area larger than all of the Earth's land combined. The last and most remote islands to be reached lie at the corners of what is called the Polynesian Triangle: Hawai'i in the north, New Zealand in the south-west, and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in the east. These voyages were made in double-hulled canoes, without compasses, charts or any other instruments.

How the navigators found their way was for a long time debated. In 1947, the Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl sailed a raft called the Kon-Tiki from Peru to Polynesia, in order to support his theory that the islands had been settled from South America by people drifting with the winds and currents. Most scholars rejected this view, and some argued the opposite extreme: that the Polynesians had discovered islands only by accident, when their canoes were blown off course.

Studies of traditional navigation have shown that both views underestimated the Polynesians. Navigators memorised the points on the horizon where particular stars rose and set, dividing the horizon into a mental map known as a star compass. By keeping the canoe pointed towards a rising star, and replacing it with another as it climbed too high, they could hold a course through the night. During the day, they used the sun and the direction of the ocean swells, which remain steady for long periods. Experienced navigators could feel the patterns of swells through the hull of the canoe, even at night, and some were said to lie down in the canoe to sense them more clearly.

As they approached land, navigators looked for other signs. Certain seabirds, such as terns, fly out to sea to fish in the morning and return to land in the evening, and rarely travel more than about 40 kilometres from shore. Clouds tend to gather over islands, and a green tint on the underside of a cloud could indicate a lagoon below it.

In 1976, a replica voyaging canoe named Hōkūle'a sailed from Hawai'i to Tahiti, a journey of over 4,000 kilometres, without instruments. It was guided by Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Micronesia, one of the few people who still practised the traditional methods. The voyage demonstrated that deliberate long-distance navigation had been possible, and it inspired a revival of traditional voyaging across the Pacific.

Heyerdahl was not entirely wrong, however. The sweet potato, a plant native to South America, was being grown in Polynesia long before Europeans arrived, and a genetic study published in 2020 found evidence that Polynesians and Native Americans had met around the year 1200. Most researchers believe that it was Polynesian voyagers who reached South America, rather than the other way round.

lesson.title: Heavily paraphrased questions
lesson.text: In hard sets, the question may share almost no words with the passage. "Mental tool for finding direction" may refer to a "star compass"; "the part of the canoe through which they felt the waves" may refer to the "hull". Focus on the meaning of each question, predict what kind of answer it needs, and read the relevant paragraph closely rather than scanning for single words.
lesson.example: Question: "What did sailors use to measure speed?" Passage: "A log tied to a knotted rope was thrown overboard, and the knots passing through the sailor's hands were counted." Answer: (a) knotted rope / (a) log.

passages.topic: Science and society — the replication crisis in psychology
passages.title: Can We Trust the Results?

paragraphs.text: In science, a single experiment is rarely enough to establish a fact. A finding is considered reliable only when other researchers, repeating the same study, obtain the same result, a process known as replication. In the early 2010s, however, a series of failed attempts to repeat famous experiments led many psychologists to fear that a large part of their field's published research might not be reliable. The situation became known as the replication crisis.

The most influential investigation was a project led by the psychologist Brian Nosek, which involved some 270 researchers around the world. They attempted to repeat 100 studies that had been published in three leading psychology journals in 2008. The results, published in 2015, were striking: while 97 per cent of the original studies had reported statistically significant results, only 36 per cent of the repeated studies did so. Many well-known effects, such as the idea that self-control is like a muscle that becomes tired with use, a theory called ego depletion, have since proved difficult to reproduce.

Researchers identified several causes. One is publication bias: journals have traditionally preferred to publish studies that find new and surprising effects, rather than those that find nothing. As a result, failed experiments were often never published at all. Another is the use of small samples, which make chance results more likely. A third concerns statistics. A result has traditionally been considered significant if its "p-value" is below 0.05, meaning, roughly, that such a result would be unlikely if there were no real effect. By analysing their data in many different ways and reporting only the analyses that crossed this threshold, a practice known as p-hacking, researchers could produce apparently significant results without any intention to deceive.

The crisis has led to important reforms. Increasingly, researchers publicly record their hypotheses and methods before collecting any data, a practice called pre-registration, which prevents them from changing their plans after seeing the results. Some journals now offer registered reports, in which they agree to publish a study on the basis of its design, before the results are known, so that the decision does not depend on whether the findings are exciting. Larger samples, often gathered through collaborations between many laboratories, and the sharing of data have also become more common.

Some scientists argue that the word "crisis" is too strong, and that the ability of the field to detect and correct its own errors shows that science is working as it should. Others note that similar problems have been found in medicine, economics and other disciplines, and that psychology deserves credit for confronting the issue first.

lesson.title: Abstract terms and practices
lesson.text: Passages about research methods and society use abstract terms for practices and problems, such as "publication bias" or "pre-registration". Questions describe these practices in other words. Read the definition in the passage, compare it carefully with the question, and give the term, which is usually two or three words.
lesson.example: Question: "What is the practice of checking a study before publication called?" Passage: "Before publication, articles are checked by other experts, a process called peer review." Answer: peer review.

passages.topic: Biology — the survival skills of tardigrades
passages.title: The Toughest Animals on Earth

paragraphs.text: Tardigrades are tiny animals, usually less than half a millimetre long, with plump bodies and eight stubby legs, each ending in claws. They were first described in 1773 by the German zoologist Johann Goeze, who called them "little water bears" because of the way they move. Around 1,300 species are now known, and they live almost everywhere, from mountain tops to the deep sea, but they are most easily found in the thin film of water on mosses and lichens.

Tardigrades are famous for their ability to survive conditions that would kill almost any other animal. When their surroundings dry out, they pull in their heads and legs and curl into a dry, barrel-shaped form known as a tun. In this state, called cryptobiosis, they lose around 97 per cent of the water in their bodies, and their metabolism almost stops. Many species produce special proteins that form a glass-like material inside their cells, protecting their internal structures from damage. They can remain in this state for years, and when water returns, they rehydrate and become active again within hours.

In the tun state, tardigrades have survived being frozen to temperatures just above absolute zero, heated to over 150°C for a short time, and exposed to pressures six times greater than those at the bottom of the deepest ocean. They can also survive doses of radiation hundreds of times higher than would kill a human. In 2016, Japanese researchers identified a protein, which they named Dsup, meaning "damage suppressor", that binds to the animal's DNA and shields it from radiation. When human cells grown in the laboratory were given the protein, they suffered around 40 per cent less damage from X-rays.

Tardigrades have even survived a trip into space. In 2007, dried tardigrades were carried into orbit on a European space mission and exposed to the vacuum of space for ten days. After returning to Earth, many of them rehydrated, and some went on to lay eggs that hatched normally. More controversially, in 2019 an Israeli spacecraft, Beresheet, crashed on the Moon while carrying thousands of dried tardigrades, leading to speculation that they might have survived the impact, although later experiments suggested this was unlikely.

Despite their toughness, tardigrades are not indestructible. In their active state, they are fairly fragile, and they depend on the tun state to survive difficult conditions. Scientists are studying their protective proteins in the hope of finding ways to store vaccines and other medicines without refrigeration.

lesson.title: Dense passages with many specific details
lesson.text: Some hard passages are packed with names, dates, numbers and technical terms, all of the same type. Before answering, quickly mark each date and number in the passage and note what it refers to. Then match each question to the right detail by checking every part of the question, not just the key word.
lesson.example: Question: "In which year was the second expedition?" Passage: "The first expedition sailed in 1910; the second, in 1912, reached the pole; a third was planned for 1915." Answer: 1912.

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: What name did Johann Goeze give to tardigrades?
questions.evidence: who called them 'little water bears' because of the way they move.
questions.explanation: The answer is exactly three words.

questions.text: What is the dried, curled-up form of a tardigrade called?
questions.evidence: curl into a dry, barrel-shaped form known as a tun.
questions.explanation: "Cryptobiosis" is the name of the state, not the form of the body. Read the question carefully: "form" points to "tun".

questions.text: What proportion of their body water do tardigrades lose in this state?
questions.evidence: they lose around 97 per cent of the water in their bodies.
questions.explanation: "Proportion" is answered with a percentage.

questions.text: What is the name of the protein that protects tardigrade DNA from radiation?
questions.evidence: a protein, which they named Dsup, meaning 'damage suppressor', that binds to the animal's DNA and shields it from radiation.
questions.explanation: "Damage suppressor" is the meaning of the name, not the name itself.

questions.text: By how much did this protein reduce the damage to human cells from X-rays?
questions.evidence: they suffered around 40 per cent less damage from X-rays.
questions.explanation: "Hundreds of times" refers to the doses of radiation tardigrades can survive.

questions.text: For how long were tardigrades exposed to the vacuum of space in 2007?
questions.evidence: exposed to the vacuum of space for ten days.
questions.explanation: 2007 is the year, which is already in the question.

questions.text: What was the name of the spacecraft that crashed on the Moon in 2019?
questions.evidence: an Israeli spacecraft, Beresheet, crashed on the Moon.
questions.explanation: Copy the spelling exactly.

passages.topic: Science and technology — atomic clocks and the measurement of time
passages.title: Counting the Seconds

paragraphs.text: For most of history, time was measured by the movement of the Earth. Until the middle of the twentieth century, the second was officially defined as 1/86,400 of the average length of a day. By the 1930s, however, the best mechanical clocks had revealed a problem: the Earth does not rotate at a perfectly steady rate. Its spin is gradually slowed by the pull of the Moon on the oceans, and it varies slightly from year to year because of movements in the Earth's core and atmosphere. A more reliable standard was needed.

It was found inside the atom. Atoms of a given element absorb and release energy at extremely precise frequencies, which never change. In 1955, the physicist Louis Essen built the first accurate atomic clock at the National Physical Laboratory in Britain, using atoms of the metal caesium. It was so successful that in 1967 the international scientific community redefined the second as the time taken for exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of radiation from a caesium atom. For the first time, time was measured by something other than the movement of the Earth.

Atomic clocks now underpin much of modern technology. Satellite navigation systems depend on them: each satellite carries atomic clocks and sends out signals showing the exact time, and receivers calculate their position from the tiny differences in the time these signals take to arrive. Because radio signals travel at the speed of light, an error of just one millionth of a second would place a receiver around 300 metres from its true position. Telecommunications networks, electricity grids and financial markets also rely on precise time.

The new definition created its own difficulty. Because the Earth's rotation is slowing, days measured by the Earth gradually drift out of step with time measured by atomic clocks. To keep them together, "leap seconds" have been added to the world's clocks since 1972, occasionally making the last minute of a day 61 seconds long. So far, 27 have been added. However, leap seconds cause problems for computer systems, and in 2022 the international body responsible for measurement decided to abolish them by 2035, allowing the difference between the two kinds of time to grow larger before any correction is made.

Meanwhile, scientists have built clocks far more precise than the caesium clock. The best of these, called optical clocks, use atoms of elements such as strontium, which oscillate much faster than caesium. The most accurate would lose less than one second in 15 billion years, longer than the age of the universe. Such clocks are so sensitive that they can detect the tiny effect of gravity on time predicted by Einstein: a clock raised by just one centimetre runs very slightly faster. Many scientists expect that the second will one day be redefined again, based on one of these new clocks.

lesson.title: Final review — putting every skill together
lesson.text: This final set combines all the main challenges of Short Answer questions: many numbers and dates of the same type, paraphrased questions, limiting words ("first", "so far"), names of people and organisations, and a strict word limit. Work systematically: identify the question word and the type of answer, scan for key words and their paraphrases, read the whole sentence, check every part of the question, and write the shortest correct answer.
lesson.example: Question: "How many medals has the team won so far?" Passage: "The team won three medals in its first season and has won eleven in total so far." Answer: eleven / 11 ("so far" matches the total, not the first season).

groups.title: Short Answer
groups.instruction:
Answer the questions below.
Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER from the passage for each answer.
groups.wordLimit: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

questions.text: Before atomic clocks, what fraction of an average day was the second defined as?
questions.evidence: the second was officially defined as 1/86,400 of the average length of a day.
questions.explanation: "Before atomic clocks" points to the old definition in Paragraph A, not the 1967 definition.

questions.text: Who built the first accurate atomic clock?
questions.evidence: In 1955, the physicist Louis Essen built the first accurate atomic clock.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.text: At which organisation was the first accurate atomic clock built?
questions.evidence: at the National Physical Laboratory in Britain.
questions.explanation: "Britain" is the country; the question asks for the organisation.

questions.text: In which year was the second redefined using caesium atoms?
questions.evidence: in 1967 the international scientific community redefined the second as the time taken for exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of radiation from a caesium atom.
questions.explanation: 1955 is when the first clock was built; 1972 is when leap seconds began.

questions.text: How far out of position would a receiver be because of an error of one millionth of a second?
questions.evidence: an error of just one millionth of a second would place a receiver around 300 metres from its true position.
questions.explanation: The unit must be included.

questions.text: How many leap seconds have been added so far?
questions.evidence: So far, 27 have been added.
questions.explanation: "61 seconds" is the length of a minute that includes a leap second.

questions.text: By which year are leap seconds due to be abolished?
questions.evidence: in 2022 the international body responsible for measurement decided to abolish them by 2035.
questions.explanation: 2022 is when the decision was made, not the deadline.

questions.text: Which element is used in some optical clocks?
questions.evidence: optical clocks, use atoms of elements such as strontium.
questions.explanation: Caesium is used in the older atomic clocks.

sections.heading: What it tests
sections.text: Multiple Choice checks whether you can find a specific part of the passage and understand it exactly. Some questions test a single detail. Others test the main idea of a paragraph, the writer's purpose, or something the writer implies without stating it directly.

sections.heading: The two formats you will meet
sections.text:
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D. One question, one answer.
Choose TWO letters, A–E. Two correct options. Each correct letter usually scores one mark.

sections.heading: How the correct answer works
sections.text: The correct option almost never repeats the passage word for word. It paraphrases the passage: the same meaning in different words. The wrong options (distractors) often do repeat passage words, because that makes them look attractive.

sections.heading: What evidence to look for
sections.text: You need one sentence, or a short group of sentences, that makes the option fully true. Partly true is not enough.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.text:
1. Word-match trap. An option copies words from the passage but changes the meaning.
2. True but irrelevant. The option is correct information, but it does not answer this question.
3. Half-right. The first half of the option matches the passage and the second half does not.
4. Extreme wording. Words such as always, only, all, never, completely are wrong unless the passage is equally strong.
5. Wrong paragraph. The option describes something from a different part of the passage.

Wrong paragraph. The option describes something from a different part of the passage.

sections.heading: Step-by-step strategy
sections.text:
1. Read the question stem only (not the options). Underline the key idea: a name, date, number or unusual term.
2. Questions follow the passage order, so use the previous answer's location to find the next one.
3. Scan for the key idea or a synonym of it. Read that sentence and the one before and after it.
4. Now read the options. Cross out any option that contradicts the passage or is not mentioned there.
5. Choose the option that matches the whole meaning of the evidence. Check the stem and the option together as one complete sentence.
6. For "main idea" or "purpose" questions, read the whole paragraph, then ask: Why did the writer include this?

sections.heading: Tiny example
sections.text:
Passage: "Although the bridge was completed in 1890, it was not opened to cars until 1924, after its deck was strengthened."
Why was there a delay before cars could use the bridge?
A The bridge was not finished until 1924.
B The structure needed to be made stronger.
C Cars had not yet been invented.
D The bridge was only designed for trains.
B is correct: deck was strengthened = made stronger. A copies the date 1924 but gives the wrong event (a word-match trap). C and D are not stated anywhere in the passage.

lessons.name: True / False / Not Given
lessons.title: How to attempt True / False / Not Given

sections.heading: What it tests
sections.text: This question type checks whether you can compare a statement with factual information in the passage, precisely and without adding your own knowledge. (For the writer's opinions, IELTS uses YES / NO / NOT GIVEN instead; that is Type 3.)

rows: The passage states the same information, usually in different words.
You can point to the sentence that confirms it.
The passage states the opposite or something incompatible with the statement.
You can point to the sentence that contradicts it.
The passage does not tell us whether the statement is true or false.
You cannot point to a sentence that confirms it or contradicts it.

sections.heading: FALSE vs NOT GIVEN: the key difference
sections.text:
Ask yourself: "Could the statement still be true without contradicting anything in the passage?" If yes, it is NOT GIVEN. If no, because the passage makes it impossible, it is FALSE.
Passage: "The museum opened in 1998." Statement: "The museum opened in 2005." → FALSE (both dates cannot be true).
Passage: "The museum opened in 1998." Statement: "The museum was popular when it opened." → NOT GIVEN (nothing is said about popularity).

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.text:
1. Qualifiers. All / some / most, always / often, only, first, the largest. Changing one of these words can turn TRUE into FALSE, or into NOT GIVEN.
2. Comparisons. The statement says X is bigger, earlier or cheaper than Y, but the passage gives information about X only. → usually NOT GIVEN.
3. Cause and effect. The passage says A and B happened. The statement says A caused B. If no cause is stated → NOT GIVEN.
4. Word-matching. A statement that repeats many passage words can still be FALSE or NOT GIVEN. Judge the meaning, not the vocabulary.
5. Outside knowledge. Never use what you know about the topic. Use only the passage.

sections.heading: Step-by-step strategy
sections.text:
1. Read the statement and underline the keywords (names, numbers, dates) and the qualifier or claim word (only, first, increased, because).
2. Scan the passage for the keywords or their synonyms. Statements follow passage order.
3. Read the relevant sentence carefully and compare the claim, not just the topic.
4. Decide: same meaning → TRUE; opposite or incompatible → FALSE; topic mentioned but claim not settled, or not mentioned at all → NOT GIVEN.
5. If you cannot find the information after a reasonable search, the answer is often NOT GIVEN. Check that the next statement's location comes after this point in the passage.
